excluded: Residue Rights (historic mill tailings for critical minerals): mineral prospecting and resource definition on mine waste (surface sampling and a NI 43-101 resource), which falls under the mineral exploration/prospecting exclusion
Dredgeline (legacy placer dredge tailings and bench gravels): placer gold/PGM prospecting through test pits and bulk sampling, so mineral prospecting
DumpCo (critical minerals in hardrock waste rock): ranks and samples abandoned mine dumps to define mineral resources, so mineral prospecting
Leachpad (residual metal in abandoned heap-leach pads and mill tailings): the candidate itself flags it as borderline mineral prospecting on mined surface piles, so excluded

scored.name: Orphan Patent Evidence-of-Use (bankrupt estates, FCC/teardown proof; incl. semiconductor, photonics, mature-node)
scored.one_line: Buy patents from Chapter 7/11 estates, ABC sales, dead startups (fabless, LiDAR, photonics, quantum, microLED) and lapse-bound owners for $2-50k; ML maps claims against FCC internal photos, teardowns, die shots, SEM cross-sections, datasheets, driver code and papers to build evidence-of-use charts; sell charted patents to NPEs, aggregators, defensive pools and funders.
scored.unproven_right: Issued patents with remaining term sold in bulk unread by trustees and lapse-bound owners.
scored.proving_step: ML claim-to-product mapping, attorney-verified EoU chart, occasional paid teardown or cross-section ($5-20k), PTAB-survival model.
scored.proven_buyer: RPX, AST, Unified Patents, LOT Network, Dominion Harbor, Acacia, Atlantic IP, IP Edge, Intellectual Ventures-style funds, Burford, Fortress IP, Parabellum, Western IDMs for cross-licence leverage.
scored.public_data: USPTO full text, assignments, maintenance events, PTAB; FCC EAS (fccid.io) internal photos; PACER 363 notices and schedules; die-shot archives; IEDM papers; Linux driver source; ITC 337 dockets; Ocean Tomo/IAM results.
scored.rough_step_up: ~100-1000x per charted hit; base charting hit rate ~1-5%, so ML could cut cost per hit 10-20x.
scored.frame: The rung is "own an unread orphan patent, then hand a buyer a charted, attorney-verified evidence-of-use package." Inside that rung, discovery (finding the infringing product and mapping the claims) is about 80-90% of the work, and the physical step (an occasional teardown or cross-section) is cheap. The catch is that the chart is not the proven asset. It is an opinion. The real value is only realised later through licensing or litigation, which takes years, costs millions per case and carries a ~65-70% PTAB invalidation risk on instituted claims. Buyers know this and discount heavily for it. Zoomed out to the whole monetisation chain, discovery is perhaps 10-20% of the work. So the 80%+ frame exists, but it is a pre-proof frame, not a proving frame like a drill hit.
scored.step_up: Unproven: patents from distressed estates, lapse-bound owners and bulk ABC sales typically clear at roughly $2k-$30k each (my estimate from memory of bankruptcy 363 sales and broker lots; not verified this run). Proven: brokered US patents have averaged about $100k-$250k asking per asset in Richardson Oliver Insights market reports across 2013-2022 (from memory), and only roughly 25-30% of listed packages sell. A strong EoU-charted asset reading on a large product might reach $250k-$1M. Realistic step-up is about 10-30x, with outliers at 100x. The "unproven" asset is not near zero; it already trades at four to five figures. That is far from Terranox's 10^4.
scored.hit_rate_capex: My estimates, not verified this run: perhaps 1-5% of random orphan patents read on a currently shipping product with enough remaining term and damages to be worth charting. A manual attorney chart costs about $3k-$15k, and a teardown or SEM cross-section adds $5k-$20k. Cost per hit today is therefore roughly $100k-$1M. ML triage could plausibly cut that 5-20x, which is a real lever, capped at 1/base rate (about 20-100x). Charting is already being automated by several AI patent-analytics startups, so the lever is not proprietary.
scored.data: The data is public and partly illegible: FCC internal photos, die shots, driver source, datasheets, PACER 363 schedules. The outcome (does it read on a product?) is NOT summarised in any legible field; USPTO only records legal status, assignments and maintenance fees. That part passes the rubric. It is weakened in two ways. Large-company products are already torn down and charted by TechInsights-style firms and aggregators. And the AI claim-charting tools (my recollection, unverified this run, includes Patlytics, IPRally and Amplified) make this extraction increasingly commodity.
scored.right_bought: Yes. The rights are bought, not claimed free first-come, from trustees, ABC assignees and lapse-bound owners who lack the expertise or budget to chart. Prices are low, but brokers (e.g. ICAP Ocean Tomo, Tangible IP) and aggregators already shop bankruptcy estates and surface the best lots. The discount is real only in the long tail. Remaining term and maintenance-fee deadlines also limit the window.
scored.buyer: The buyers are RPX and AST (defensive), Unified Patents, and NPEs and aggregators such as Dominion Harbor and Acacia, plus litigation funders like Burford and Fortress. This is a thin and cyclical market. Volumes are well below the 2011-2014 peak, there are few buyers per asset, and they pay for evidence of use but heavily discount for PTAB risk and time-to-cash. They are capitalised, but unlike a mine developer they cannot readily "develop" the asset at a known cost and payoff.
scored.ladder: The rungs above are: buy and chart, then sell to aggregators, then license directly, then run your own assertion campaigns (NPE), then fund your own and others' litigation, then become a large IP fund or defensive pool. The ceiling is the patent-monetisation market, about low-single-digit $B per year in licensing and settlements. Acacia, Intellectual Ventures and RPX are examples of peak outcomes, in the $1-5B range. There is no realistic trillion-dollar path, and the top rungs carry reputational and legal friction (anti-troll legislation, PTAB).
scored.fatal_flaw: The proving step does not actually prove anything. An evidence-of-use chart is a contestable opinion whose value is only realised after years of licensing or litigation (about $2-5M per case to trial, with roughly 65-70% of instituted PTAB final decisions invalidating all challenged claims). So buyers pay roughly 10-30x, not 10^3-10^4x, and the market is thin. The ladder tops out at a few-$B NPE or fund, not a trillion-dollar chain.
scored.one_line_reason: This is a real ML discovery edge on cheap, illegible orphan patents. But the hit only becomes an opinion, the step-up is about 10-30x into a thin NPE/aggregator market that discounts for PTAB risk, and the ladder caps at a few-billion-dollar patent fund.
sources: No web searches were run: the shared web search budget for this turn was already exhausted. All figures are from model memory or estimates and should be verified with a follow-up search.
Richardson Oliver Insights brokered patent market reports, 2013-2022 (from memory: average asking price per US patent about $100k-$250k, roughly 25-30% of packages sell)
USPTO PTAB trial statistics (from memory: roughly 65-70% of instituted final written decisions find all challenged claims unpatentable)
AIPLA Report of the Economic Survey (from memory: patent litigation to trial costs about $2-5M+ for mid-to-large cases)
Nortel 2011 bankruptcy patent auction: $4.5B for about 6,000 assets (an outlier at the top end of estate sales)

scored.name: Cryptic Clusters / Legacy Actinomycete Libraries: orphaned natural-product collections re-read for novel clusters
scored.one_line: Acquire mothballed pharma and academic actinomycete/fungal natural-product strain and extract libraries cheaply, sequence them, ML-rank silent biosynthetic gene clusters for novel high-value chemotypes (anti-Gram-negative, antifungal, ADC payloads), and ferment or express the top few to prove a compound.
scored.unproven_right: Ownership or exclusive commercial rights to physical strain/extract libraries, often for storage costs or low five figures.
scored.proving_step: Sequencing, ML novelty ranking, elicitation or heterologous expression, LC-MS and activity assay; ~$50-200k per cluster via CROs/biofoundries.
scored.proven_buyer: AMR pharma and funders (GSK, Roche, Basilea, Innoviva, BARDA, CARB-X, AMR Action Fund), oncology and ADC biotechs.
scored.public_data: NCBI/JGI genomes and metagenomes, MIBiG, antiSMASH-DB, NPAtlas, GNPS/MassIVE, scanned NP patents and fermentation literature, ATCC/DSMZ/NRRL catalogues.
scored.rough_step_up: Collection ~$10-100k to a novel validated scaffold worth $1-100M, ~100-1000x. Physical step is less trivial than drilling; antibiotic buyers are weak.
scored.frame: The candidate rung is "own a mothballed strain/extract library, prove one novel bioactive scaffold, sell/license the proven compound." Inside that rung discovery (sequencing + ML novelty ranking of BGCs) is at most ~25-35% of the work; the physical step is the opposite of trivial — elicitation or heterologous expression, fermentation scale-up, isolation, structure elucidation and activity/tox assays run ~$50-200k and 6-24 months per cluster, and across four large-scale heterologous-expression studies only 11-32% of clusters yielded any detectable natural product at all (J Ind Microbiol Biotechnol 2023 review, PMC10727000). So this is structurally the geothermal-in-coal-mine failure mode: finding the right cluster is easier than building the thing that proves it. The buyer side is also the weakest link in the rubric: there is no capitalised buyer standing ready the way a mine developer is. Comparable transaction: Basilea bought Spexis's entire preclinical Gram-negative antibiotic program for up to CHF 2M total including milestones (Jan 2024) — i.e. the "developer" in this analogy is in for hundreds of millions and will only pay single-digit millions for the proven asset. ADC payloads/antifungals are a better buyer pocket than antibiotics, which partially rescues C1 but not the physical-step problem.
scored.step_up: Unproven right: physical legacy libraries have changed hands for storage costs or effectively nothing — Sanofi transferred ~110,000 strains (~80,000 actinomycetes, 70 years of industrial effort) to Fraunhofer IME in 2020 as a shared-resource transfer, no sale price; Ginkgo bought Warp Drive Bio's genome-mining platform including >135,000 bacterial strains and >4M predicted BGCs in 2019 with terms undisclosed (plausibly low single-digit millions given it was a cast-off asset of Revolution Medicines). Deinove licensed access to 400 of Naicons' 45,000 strains, price undisclosed. So call the right $10k-low-7-figures (my estimate anchored on those three). Proven right: a single validated novel scaffold with in vivo activity transacts at roughly CHF 2M (Basilea/Spexis, whole program, up to, incl. milestones) to maybe $10-50M upfront for a strong antifungal/ADC payload (my estimate). That is ~10-100x on a per-asset basis, up to ~1000x only if you bought the library for storage costs AND got a best-case oncology payload — but the capex consumed to get there ($50-200k x many clusters, likely $5-20M to one validated scaffold) eats most of the multiple. Unlike the uranium case, the step-up is NOT immediate on a hit and NOT a market-observable repricing of the asset you own; the library does not reprice because one cluster worked.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Base hit rate is genuinely low, which is the candidate's best feature. Detection of any compound from a heterologously expressed cluster: 11-32% (four large-scale studies, 2023 review PMC10727000). Of 50 studies over Jan 2018-Jun 2023, only 63 new natural product families emerged. Probability a given silent cluster yields a novel compound with commercially relevant potency/selectivity/developability: my estimate <1-2%. Cost per proving attempt: $50-200k and months per cluster (candidate's own figure, consistent with CRO/biofoundry pricing; my estimate for a full isolate-to-structure-to-assay cycle is $80-250k). Theoretical ML lever = 1/base rate = 50-100x, so the ceiling is attractive. The problem is that ML can only improve the *selection* term, not the expression/fermentation failure term — and the 11-32% detection failure is overwhelmingly host/regulatory/pathway biology, not picking the wrong cluster. Realistic achievable capex reduction: 2-3x, not 10x. That caps C3 at 3.
scored.data: This is where it breaks against the rubric's hard C4 test. The signal is in NCBI/JGI genomes, MIBiG, antiSMASH-DB, NPAtlas, GNPS/MassIVE — public, yes, but LEGIBLE, not illegible. antiSMASH already annotates every cluster in those genomes automatically and publishes it; antiSMASH-DB, BiG-FAM/BiG-SLiCE and MIBiG already publish cluster-family assignments and novelty distance scores. In Terranox terms, the regulator has already written the answer into the status field: "novel cluster family, no known product" is a precomputed, queryable public annotation. Every genome-mining group on earth runs the same query. The genuinely illegible part — scanned fermentation notebooks, old NP patents, which physical strain in which freezer corresponds to which genome — is real but is metadata about *which* box to buy, not about whether the compound works, and the physical libraries are mostly unsequenced, so you pay sequencing capex before you can rank anything. Incumbents already do exactly this at scale: Ginkgo (Warp Drive platform, 135k strains, 4M BGCs), Fraunhofer IME + Sanofi's 110k-strain collection, Naicons (45-65k strains), Hexagon Bio, Lodo Therapeutics. The purchase discount is the one strong element: owners (pharma closing NP units, retiring academics, institutes paying freezer bills) really cannot read their own collections and really do part with them for storage costs.
scored.right_bought: What is bought is ownership or exclusive commercial rights to physical strain/extract collections plus their provenance records — acquirable for storage costs to low five/six figures, which is a genuine 10^2-10^4 discount to replacement cost (70 years of industrial collecting, per Fraunhofer). Critical encumbrance the rubric would want flagged: Nagoya Protocol / CBD access-and-benefit-sharing. Fraunhofer specifically advertises its collection as "all collected before 2014, Nagoya confirmed" — meaning provenance-clean pre-2014 material is the scarce, valuable kind and a library without documented country-of-origin consent may be commercially unusable. Any purchase diligence is ABS diligence. Second encumbrance: legacy pharma libraries often carry residual IP/royalty reach-through to the original owner, so "cheap" rights are frequently non-exclusive or burdened.
scored.buyer: Weak and thin. Antibiotics: AMR Action Fund, CARB-X, BARDA, Innoviva, Basilea, GSK, Roche — but the observable clearing price is CHF ~2M for a whole preclinical Gram-negative program (Basilea/Spexis, Jan 2024), and that market's broken economics are the whole reason the libraries were mothballed in the first place. The buyer is not capitalised in the sense the rubric requires: a mine developer pays $40k/ha because it collects $100k/ha; an AMR buyer does not pay proportionally because its own exit is subsidised and small. Antifungals and ADC payloads are materially better pockets (real oncology/ADC bidders with billions, willing to pay $10-100M+ for a differentiated payload) and are the only version of this thesis with a credible capitalised buyer. Pivoting the thesis entirely to ADC payloads/antifungals would raise C1 and C2 by about a point each; as written, with antibiotics as the headline, the buyer side is the second-biggest flaw.
scored.ladder: The ladder is real and long — library ownership, to validated scaffold, to lead optimization, to IND, to clinic, to approved drug and commercialization — and the top rung is a very large company. But it fails the Terranox property that makes a ladder climbable: each rung up is 10-100x more capital and a completely different capability set (med chem, tox, regulatory, clinical ops), with 10+ year cycle times and no self-sustaining cash from the bottom rung to fund the next. Terranox's rung throws off cash in months and the next rung is adjacent; here rung two alone is a $50-200M, 8-year commitment. Ladder exists, climb is not self-funding.
scored.fatal_flaw: The outcome is already summarised in a legible public field: antiSMASH / antiSMASH-DB / BiG-FAM / MIBiG already auto-annotate and novelty-score essentially every public BGC, so there is no illegible-data edge to exploit — and the proving step is the dominant cost and the dominant failure mode (11-32% of expressed clusters yield any detectable compound at all; $50-200k and 6-24 months each), which inverts Terranox's 95-5 ratio into roughly 30-70. ML can re-rank the cheap part and cannot fix the expensive part. This is the geothermal-in-coal-mines failure: building the plant is harder than finding the mine.
scored.one_line_reason: Cheap-to-buy rights and a genuinely low base hit rate, but the BGC novelty "answer" is already precomputed in public databases by antiSMASH and incumbents like Ginkgo/Fraunhofer/Naicons, the physical proving step dominates cost and time instead of being trivial, and the proven asset clears at low single-digit millions (Basilea/Spexis, CHF 2M) — so it scores 13/25 and fails C1 and C4, the two that matter.
sources: https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10727000 — heterologous expression of BGCs: natural-product detection 11-32% across four large-scale studies; 63 new NP families from 50 studies, Jan 2018-Jun 2023

scored.name: Hand Match / Marginalia: unrecognised historic letters and annotated books
scored.one_line: Buy bulk estate letters, unattributed autographs and early printed books with unidentified marginalia; handwriting-recognition ML matched against digitised archives identifies famous writers or readers; paleographer sign-off proves association copies.
scored.unproven_right: Title to estate ephemera lots or books catalogued with 'unidentified hand', $50-5k.
scored.proving_step: OCR and writer-ID embeddings, paper/ink checks and expert letter; physically only photography.
scored.proven_buyer: Christie's/Sotheby's book departments, Bonhams, RR Auction, Folger, Huntington, Beinecke, Morgan, British Library, Peter Harrington.
scored.public_data: Founders Online, Darwin/Newton/Jefferson papers, Library of Congress manuscripts, Transkribus corpora, EEBO, Folger digital, Annotated Books Online, eBay/ABE/ILAB listings.
scored.rough_step_up: ~10^2-10^4x; very low hit rate, thin market.
scored.frame: Rung = buy an "unidentified hand" lot or book, attribute the hand, then consign or sell it as an association copy or autograph. Inside that rung, discovery and attribution are about 95% of the work, and the physical step (photography, plus paper and ink checks) is trivial. That part passes. The problem is that a hit counts as proven only when a recognised paleographer or scholar endorses it and the provenance holds up. The ML match on its own does not prove anything. Example: Milton's First Folio (Free Library of Philadelphia, 2019) was attributed by Scott-Warren on purely paleographical grounds, and it is still described as "not exactly peer reviewed". A 2022 Raleigh-annotated book went to auction only "tentatively", with a reserve to match. Buyers exist (auction houses, the Folger, the Beinecke, dealers), but they are discretionary collectors and institutions with thin budgets, not a developer with a fixed economic use for the asset.
scored.step_up: Unproven: a $50-5k estate lot or book catalogued as "unidentified hand" (candidate figure, plausible). Proven comparables: an Edgar Allan Poe letter (a plea for $40) sold for $125,125 in 2020 (Inquirer). A Kerouac letter to Robert Lax sold for $11,000. Tolkien letters went for $2.7k-13k each in 2018 (Locus). A John Steinbeck letter sold for $32k at RR Auction. Taking a $50-500 lot to $10k-125k gives roughly 10^2-10^3x. A Milton- or Shakespeare-class association copy would be over 10^4x, but those are once a decade. Most real hits are minor figures at about 3-30x.
scored.hit_rate_capex: I found no published base rate. My estimate is well under 0.1% of "unidentified hand" lots belonging to anyone with market value, and under 0.01% for a famous writer. The cost per attempt is already low: buying a $50-500 lot plus photography. The lever is therefore not "10x cheaper drills". It is triage across inventory, and that is limited by how many lots exist and by expert sign-off time ($500-5k per opinion, my estimate), not by discovery capex. The lever exists, but the money it saves is small.
scored.data: Reference corpora are public and only partly machine-readable: Founders Online, the Darwin, Newton and Jefferson papers, LOC manuscripts, Transkribus, Annotated Books Online. Writer-ID ML is still a research topic: Siamese nets attributing letters to Potanin (2025), and a WACV 2024 paper noting that paleography has "no agreed-upon methodology". Is the outcome already written in a legible field? For letters, partly yes: famous letters are usually signed, so the signature is the field, and specialist dealers check anything signed. Unsigned marginalia is where the real illegibility edge lies. That edge is real but narrow, because heavily collected readers (Dee, Jonson, Harvey, Coleridge) are already tracked by specialists and by Annotated Books Online.
scored.right_bought: Yes. Title is bought outright and cheaply at estate sales, eBay, ABE and regional auctions, from sellers who cannot read the hands. Good on this criterion. Two risks. First, if a famous attribution is publicised, the consignor or the family estate may contest the sale or the copyright (the Cassady "Joan Anderson" letter sale was suspended in 2014 over ownership claims). Second, copyright in unpublished letters usually stays with the writer's estate, which limits publication value.
scored.buyer: Christie's and Sotheby's book departments, Bonhams, RR Auction, Peter Harrington, and research libraries (Folger, Huntington, Beinecke, Morgan, British Library). They are capitalised but discretionary. I found no published total for the rare book and manuscript auction market; my estimate is about $1-2B a year worldwide, and the rare book trade is described as "driven by the whims of a small number of rich individuals" (Cambridge, Economics of the Manuscript and Rare Book Trade).
scored.ladder: Weak. The rungs above are dealer, then auction house, then authentication service or archive or estate management. Even owning the whole chain puts you in a market of low single-digit billions a year. There is no path to a very large company, and supply of truly famous unrecognised hands cannot be scaled up.
scored.fatal_flaw: Value at the top comes from expert and scholarly consensus plus provenance, not from the ML match, and the supply of valuable unrecognised hands is tiny and fixed. The result is a boutique dealer with a few lucky finds a year in a market of about $1-2B a year (estimate), with no ladder to a large company.
scored.one_line_reason: Cheap bought rights and a real 10^2-10^3x step-up, but attempts already cost little, so the ML lever saves little money. Proving depends on paleographers, and the thin collector market has no ladder.

scored.name: Reuse-Rights Pipeline Easements: abandoned-in-place pipelines for CO2, H2 and fiber
scored.one_line: Take abandoned-in-place pipelines and easements from operators carrying decommissioning liabilities; ML over easement instruments proves broad 'any substance' assignable scope and continuity; sell to CO2/H2 trunkline and fiber developers.
scored.unproven_right: Assignment of abandoned pipeline easements plus idle pipe at negative or near-zero cost.
scored.proving_step: ML scope-clause reading across scanned grants, continuity check; buyer does in-line inspection.
scored.proven_buyer: CO2 trunkline developers (Summit/Tallgrass-type), hydrogen hubs, long-haul fiber.
scored.public_data: PHMSA NPMS and annual reports, FERC abandonment filings, state PUC dockets, county easement images.
scored.rough_step_up: ~>=1000x on a near-zero basis; broad-scope easements may be rare or contested.
scored.frame: The rung is "own an assembled, legally continuous, reuse-scoped corridor (easements plus idle pipe) and sell it to a trunkline or fiber developer." Reading easements (scope clause, assignability, whether it lapsed on abandonment, continuity) is maybe 30-50% of the work to get a sellable corridor (my estimate). The rest is physical and regulatory, and it is not trivial: in-line inspection, hydrotest, requalifying the pipe for a new service under 49 CFR 192.14/195 (CO2 runs dense-phase at about 1,200-2,200 psi, which many old gas lines are not rated for, and hydrogen needs pipe that resists embrittlement), adding compression, and getting through the new PHMSA CO2 rulemaking after the 2020 Satartia rupture. This is the same shape as the geothermal-in-coal-mines counter-example: the bespoke engineering is harder than finding the asset. Fiber is the exception, because pulling cable through empty pipe is cheap, but fiber does not need the pipe, only the right-of-way.
scored.step_up: On paper the ratio is huge because the basis is near zero or negative: the operator is carrying an abandonment liability, and abandoning in place costs about $10-50k/mile (my estimate). Proven value per mile, all my estimates and not sourced (searches unavailable): new CO2 pipeline build cost is about $2-4M/mile, with right-of-way about 10-20% of that, so a clean reusable corridor could be worth about $100k-1M/mile to a CO2 developer if the pipe also requalifies. For fiber, a right-of-way license is about $1-10k/mile per year, or a few $k-$50k/mile capitalised. The value is not realised when the scope is proven, though. It only appears after the buyer's inspection and requalification and only if a buyer exists. Navigator CO2 cancelled in 2023, Summit has stalled on permits and eminent-domain bans (South Dakota 2025), and that buyer pool is thin. Realistic step-up from a verified paper corridor to a sale is about 10-100x, not 10^4.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Proving is cheap, not expensive and mostly failing. Title and abstract review is about $300-2,000 per parcel (my estimate), and a corridor has hundreds to thousands of parcels. The base hit rate per parcel for broad, assignable language ("oil, gas and other substances", no reversion on non-use) might be 20-50% (my estimate). The rate that matters is whether every parcel in a 50-300 mile corridor passes. That is the per-parcel rate raised to the power N, close to zero for long runs, so the binding constraint is holdouts and gaps, not finding the right corridor. ML cuts the cost of reading parcels, but that cost was never the dominant capex. Curative work (buying new rights to fill gaps) and requalifying the pipe dominate, and ML does not cut those 10x.
scored.data: Good: county easement images are scanned, unstructured and scattered across thousands of recorders, and nobody summarises scope in a legible field. Bad: NPMS, PHMSA annual reports and FERC abandonment dockets already flag idle or abandoned status and diameter or MAOP in legible fields, so finding candidate pipes is easy. The ML edge only applies to the clause reading. Operators also have their own land departments and right-of-way records and can read their own grants.
scored.right_bought: Partially. Operators may hand over idle pipe for near zero to shed liability. But (a) under common law in many states, an easement is extinguished by abandonment, and some grants revert once use stops or once a FERC abandonment order issues, so the right may legally no longer exist when it becomes cheap. (b) Assignment of easements in gross can be contested by landowners, and expanding the use from gas to CO2 or hydrogen invites litigation. (c) Owners who see value reuse the line themselves, so the cheap ones are self-selected bad corridors. Examples I know of but did not verify this session: Tallgrass is converting its Trailblazer gas line to CO2, Williams pulled fiber through decommissioned gas pipe in the 1980s (WilTel), and Kinder Morgan and Denbury have done conversions.
scored.buyer: CO2 trunkline developers (Summit, Tallgrass, Denbury/ExxonMobil), hydrogen hub developers, and long-haul fiber companies (Zayo, Lumen). The CO2 and hydrogen buyers are capitalised but stalled by politics, permits and 45Q/45V uncertainty. The fiber buyers are capitalised, but they value the right-of-way at fiber-license rates, not pipeline rates.
scored.ladder: Strong in principle: assemble corridors, then run a conduit or right-of-way utility (fiber, power transmission, CO2), then become a carbon-transport or midstream operator, then integrate storage and sequestration. Corridor-utility companies can be very large (compare midstream MLPs and tower REITs).
scored.fatal_flaw: The proving step is not where the value or the difficulty is. Corridors that look cheap are often legally void (the easement lapsed on abandonment, or its scope has to be litigated per parcel), every parcel in the chain must pass (one gap kills the corridor), and turning a proven corridor into value still needs bespoke physical requalification and a CO2 or hydrogen buyer that is currently stalled. That is the geothermal-in-coal-mines failure mode, and owners who can read their own easements already do the good conversions themselves.
scored.one_line_reason: The reading is illegible and the ladder is real, but discovery is under half the rung, the required hit rate collapses across a whole corridor, the physical requalification is bespoke and hard, and the step-up waits for a thin, stalled buyer pool.

scored.name: Powered-Land Options: farmland options proven by utility load studies
scored.one_line: Option farmland next to substations ML predicts have load headroom; prove with a utility large-load study or will-serve letter; sell powered land to data-center developers. Rescore of powered brownfields with a real purchase discount.
scored.unproven_right: Options at $50-300/acre/yr or fee at $5-15k/acre from farmers.
scored.proving_step: Large-load service request and paid load-flow study ($50-250k, most fail on headroom).
scored.proven_buyer: Microsoft, Meta, Google, AWS, QTS, Vantage, Stack, Aligned, powered-land funds ($300k-2M/acre).
scored.public_data: FERC Form 715 (CEII), RTO expansion plans and retirements, EIA-860, IRPs, PUC large-load dockets, HIFLD substations, queue withdrawals, assessor rolls.
scored.rough_step_up: ~10^3-10^4x on option premium, 20-100x on land; many flippers and tightening utility rules.
scored.frame: Rung: option farmland near a substation, get a utility load study or will-serve letter, sell 'powered land'. Discovery (finding headroom) is maybe 30-40% of the work in this rung (my estimate). The rest is zoning and rezoning fights, water, fiber, utility negotiation, and above all posting ESA/contract collateral and paying for network upgrades, which is what turns a study result into delivered megawatts. The physical step (substation and transmission upgrades) is neither trivial nor abstracted, and buyers increasingly pay only for capacity that is contracted, not for a study letter. A capitalised buyer exists (hyperscalers, powered-land funds), but what it buys is energized or contracted capacity, not a study outcome.
scored.step_up: Unproven: Midwest/Southeast cropland is roughly $5-10k/acre (USDA 2025 national cropland average about $5.8k/acre, from memory), and options run about $50-300/acre/yr (candidate's figure, plausible). Proven: powered or entitled data-center land trades at roughly $300k-2M/acre in hot markets (Loudoun reported at $1-4M/acre; secondary markets $100-500k/acre, from memory of 2024-25 press). So land goes about 30-100x and the option premium goes 10^3x or more. But the jump needs a firm capacity commitment, not just a study. A study or a non-binding will-serve letter alone probably gets about 2-5x (estimate), because buyers have been burned by phantom capacity. All numbers here are recalled or estimated: the search budget was exhausted, so none were verified this run.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Study cost is $50-250k per site (candidate's figure; Texas SB6 of 2025 sets a roughly $100k large-load study fee, from memory). Base hit rate, meaning the study shows usable headroom on an acceptable timeline: I estimate 15-30% in constrained RTOs. AEP Ohio's large-load queue fell from about 30 GW to about 13 GW after its 2025 tariff required minimum-demand commitments, which shows most requests are speculative (from memory). The lever is capped at roughly 3-6x, not 10x. A proving attempt also costs only about $100k against a $10-100M exit, so capex is not the binding constraint.
scored.data: Public but semi-illegible: FERC 715 (CEII-gated, needs an NDA), RTO expansion plans, EIA-860, IRPs, PUC large-load dockets, HIFLD. But headroom is increasingly legible or contested. Utilities now publish large-load pipeline totals, and RTOs publish load forecasts. Incumbents (Tract, Cloverleaf Infrastructure, EdgeCore, Hunt, many land brokers, plus powerflow consultancies) already run load-flow screening on the same data. A prior hunt found ML adds only about +0.004 AUC over simple screening for powered sites. The headroom outcome is ultimately decided by the utility, not inferred from data, and it is allocated by queue position and collateral.
scored.right_bought: Yes, options can be bought from farmers, so the purchase discount is real, unlike brownfields. But the discount is eroding fast: data-center land prices are widely publicised, and farmers near substations now ask $30-100k+/acre or demand data-center contingent pricing (estimate from press patterns). More important, the land does not hold the value. Utility capacity attaches to the customer's service agreement and collateral, not to the parcel, and tightening tariffs (AEP Ohio, Georgia Power, Dominion GS-5, Texas SB6) penalise speculative flippers.
scored.buyer: Hyperscalers (Microsoft, Meta, Google, AWS), colo developers (QTS, Vantage, Stack, Aligned, CyrusOne), and powered-land funds. They are deep-pocketed and pay a lot for energized, contracted capacity with a near-term COD. They pay little for study-only sites.
scored.ladder: Strong ladder: land and options, then load study, then ESA/capacity commitment, then entitlements, then a powered shell, then an own-built substation or behind-the-meter generation, then a full data-center campus developer or operator (Tract and Cloverleaf show this path, and the top rungs are multi-$10B businesses). But each step up is capital- and execution-heavy, not discovery-heavy.
scored.fatal_flaw: Proving here is not a cheap discovery event that the landowner then owns. Utility capacity is allocated to whoever signs the ESA and posts collateral, not to whoever reads the data first. The study result is non-binding and decays as others queue. Rising tariffs specifically target speculative flippers. And well-funded incumbents (Tract, Cloverleaf, EdgeCore, brokers) already screen the same public grid data. So the 10^3x step-up needs heavy capital commitment and network upgrades, not an ML-found hit: discovery is a minority of the rung.
scored.one_line_reason: The farmland purchase discount is real and the ladder is big, but capacity belongs to whoever signs the ESA and posts collateral, not to whoever reads the grid data first. Incumbents already screen headroom, and the step-up needs capital and utility commitments rather than discovery. It fails the 80%-discovery frame much like the geothermal-in-coal-mines counter-example.

scored.name: Masterless: defunct-label masters via MMA
scored.one_line: Buy masters of defunct small labels from trustees, successors and heirs; ML proves chain of title and matches to streams; claim SoundExchange and Content ID; sell catalogues.
scored.unproven_right: Sound recording ownership held unknowingly, $1-5k.
scored.proving_step: Title reconstruction from trade press and records, fingerprinting, ISRC registration and claims.
scored.proven_buyer: Reservoir, Concord, BMG, UMG reissue arms, Kobalt/AWAL, sync libraries.
scored.public_data: SoundExchange unclaimed lists, Billboard/Cash Box scans, CCE, SoS dissolutions, PACER, Discogs, 45cat.
scored.frame: The rung is acquiring a master you can prove you own and that is matched to its revenue. Inside it, reconstructing chain of title and matching to streams is about 80-90% of the work. The physical step is trivial: ISRC registration, SoundExchange and Content ID claims, a DDEX delivery. Capitalised buyers exist (Reservoir, Concord, BMG, sync libraries), but they pay against trailing royalty income with clean title. They do not pay against the fact that you found it. So the frame is real, but the buyer prices off cash flow and not off discovery. That makes it more like buying a royalty stream than like Terranox's 10^4 jump.
scored.step_up: These figures are my estimates from memory; the search budget was used up and no live search ran. Master catalogues trade at about 8-15x net label share for clean, growing catalogues (about 15-20x at the 2021 peak) and about 5-10x for small or illiquid ones. A typical defunct small-label master earns perhaps $100-$2,000 a year (estimate). Bought at $1-5k, the expected sale value is about $1-15k, so most hits are 1-5x. A rare breakbeat or sampled master with heavy sync or streaming use could reach 100x. The step-up is fat-tailed, not a reliable 10^3, and the claimed 10^2-10^3x holds only for outliers.
scored.hit_rate_capex: These figures are estimates; no searches ran. A title-reconstruction attempt (archival research, contacting heirs and trustees, legal opinion on chain of title) costs perhaps $2-10k in labour and legal fees. The base hit rate for 'provably clean title plus meaningful revenue' is maybe 5-15%. That caps the ML lever at about 7-20x, which on paper matches the rubric's ~10x. In practice, the legal closing work (signatures from heirs, releases from bankruptcy trustees, termination-right exposure under 17 USC 203) is human and not ML-reducible. Realistically ML cuts the cost of a hit by about 2-4x.
scored.data: The illegible part is real: Billboard and Cash Box scans, the Catalog of Copyright Entries, state dissolution filings, PACER bankruptcy dockets, and Discogs/45cat label genealogies. Incumbents rarely link these. The outcome is partly legible already: SoundExchange publishes searchable lists of unregistered and unpaid rights owners, and Spotify and YouTube play counts are public. The most valuable orphans are therefore pre-flagged by revenue, and royalty heir-hunters and catalogue scouts already work them. Examples are Royalty Exchange marketplace sellers and the asset-recovery arms of distributors and administrators. The ML edge is in proving title, not in finding value.
scored.right_bought: Yes. The right is bought, not claimed first-come: you buy it from heirs, successors and bankruptcy trustees who do not know they hold it, likely for $1-5k (estimate). The risks are post-1978 masters being subject to artist termination after 35 years, disputed work-for-hire status, and successor entities (often majors that absorbed the distributor) asserting prior title. Each of these lowers the buyer's price or rules the asset out.
scored.buyer: Reservoir, Concord, BMG, Round Hill, Primary Wave, Hipgnosis/Recognition, Cooking Vinyl, and the reissue arms of the majors (Craft, UMe, Legacy). Sync libraries and royalty marketplaces (Royalty Exchange) also buy. They pay revenue multiples for portfolios with clean title and typically want deal sizes of $1M or more. That means aggregating hundreds of small masters into one bundle.
scored.ladder: The rungs above are: aggregating rescued masters into a catalogue, then a reissue and sync label, then distribution and rights administration, then a full independent label/publisher roll-up. The ladder exists, but the end state is a catalogue fund or mid-size label, worth billions at best (Reservoir is about $1-2B market cap). It does not lead to a trillion-dollar company. Recorded music is about a $30B global revenue industry.
scored.fatal_flaw: Unit economics on the typical hit are too small. Buyers price defunct small-label masters at 5-15x trailing royalties, and those royalties are usually hundreds of dollars a year. So the step-up is mostly 1-5x, not 10^3. The few high-value orphans are already revealed by public play counts and SoundExchange unpaid lists, so they are contested. The binding cost is legal chain-of-title closure, which ML cannot cut.
scored.one_line_reason: Clean frame and illegible data, but the step-up is a revenue multiple on tiny royalties (mostly 1-5x, rarely 100x). The valuable outcomes are already visible in public play counts and SoundExchange unpaid lists, and the ladder tops out at a catalogue fund. Figures are estimates because the search budget was exhausted.

scored.name: Continuation Forge: live patent families with pending continuations
scored.one_line: Buy patent families with a still-pending continuation from small inventors, robotics or materials startups and bankruptcy estates for $5-100k; ML finds written-description support in the spec for claims reading on products shipping today; prosecute to allowance with an EoU chart and sell.
scored.unproven_right: Pending US continuation plus priority chain and specification.
scored.proving_step: ML maps spec paragraphs and figures to teardowns, FCC photos, manuals, competitor filings, code; $3-60k prosecution; notice of allowance plus chart is the hit.
scored.proven_buyer: Burford, Fortress IP, Dominion Harbor, IP Edge, RPX, AST, IV, and OEMs buying defensively (CATL, LG, Panasonic, Tesla, Amazon Robotics, Figure, Agility).
scored.public_data: USPTO Patent Center file wrappers, bulk full text, assignments, PACER schedules, FCC EA photos, iFixit/TechInsights teardowns, SEC filings, GitHub.
scored.rough_step_up: ~50-1000x per hit; base hit rate under 5%.
scored.frame: The rung is: buy a family with a pending continuation, get a claim allowed that reads on a shipping product, and sell the asset with an EoU (evidence of use) chart. Inside that rung, finding the right spec support and the right target product is maybe 60-70% of the work (my estimate). The physical step, prosecution, is not trivial. It takes 1-3 years and $3-60k, and the examiner pushes back on written description (35 USC 112, Ariad/Novozymes). The bigger problem is that the asset's value is only realised later through assertion or litigation, at $2-5M+ per case under AIPLA survey ranges. Survival risk sits on top of that: PTAB IPR institution and Alice 101 invalidation. So the proven buyer is pricing litigation risk, not a drill core. The frame exists and buyers exist, but discovery is not 80%+ of the work.
scored.step_up: From memory, not verified this run (the search budget was used up): Richardson Oliver Insights brokered-market reports put average asking prices around $100-250k per US asset, and older reports were higher. Small-inventor, auction and bankruptcy patents often clear at $5-50k. A family with an allowed claim that a strong EoU chart shows reading on a high-volume product might sell for $250k-$2M to an NPE or a defensive aggregator such as RPX or AST. Outlier litigation outcomes can be 10^4x, but those take years and a contingency trial. Realistic immediate step-up: about 10-50x on a hit, not the claimed 50-1000x and nowhere near 10^3-10^4.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Allowance itself is easy. Continuations are allowed at high rates (my estimate: 70-90%, consistent with overall USPTO allowance rates). The real hit is an allowed claim that is both valid and infringed by a shipping product and that survives a buyer's diligence. Commonly cited figures say only about 1-5% of issued patents are ever licensed or asserted (my estimate, not sourced this run). Cost per attempt: $5-100k to buy plus $3-60k to prosecute, so roughly $20-150k. ML could plausibly raise the hit rate 3-5x. The ceiling is set by the 1/base-rate cap and by legal-validity risk that ML cannot reduce. Capex falls maybe 3-5x, not 10x.
scored.data: The data is public and largely already legible. USPTO bulk full text, PatentsView, Patent Center file wrappers and assignment data are all structured, and pendency status (pending continuation, PTA, expiration) is literally a legible status field. Specs are text, not scanned. The teardown side (FCC photos, iFixit, TechInsights) is less legible, but TechInsights already sells exactly this mapping to assertion firms. LLM claim-chart and EoU tools (Patlytics, Solve Intelligence, IPRally, ClaimMaster and others) are already doing the spec-to-product matching. The edge is thin.
scored.right_bought: Yes, the rights are bought. Sellers are small inventors, startups, and bankruptcy estates (via 363 sales). Some of them cannot read the option value of a live continuation, so a pricing gap exists. But brokers (Tangible IP, ICAP/Ocean Tomo auctions, Iceberg) and aggregators (IV, Dominion Harbor, IP Edge, Acacia) actively screen for live continuations as a premium feature. Bankruptcy trustees commonly use brokers too. The discount is real but not 10^4.
scored.buyer: Capitalised buyers do exist: litigation funders such as Burford and Fortress, NPEs and aggregators such as Dominion Harbor, IP Edge, Acacia and IV, and defensive buyers such as RPX and AST. OEMs buy defensively mainly through RPX and AST pools rather than one asset at a time. Their pricing discounts for IPR, Alice and litigation duration.
scored.ladder: There are rungs above. The next ones are acquire, prosecute, then assert or license directly, then fund your own litigation and run a portfolio licensing program. Above that you could become an Acacia/IV-scale aggregator. That top is bounded: the biggest examples are a few billion dollars (IV raised about $6B; Acacia's market cap is under $1B). The ladder ends in a litigation business with regulatory and reputational ceilings, not a trillion-dollar chain. It does not connect to making the products.
scored.fatal_flaw: This is already the standard NPE playbook. IP Edge, Dominion Harbor, IV and Acacia, plus brokers who screen for live continuations, already buy families with pending continuations and draft claims to read on shipping products. Pending status is a legible field, and LLM claim-charting tools are commoditising the matching. The proven value is not realised on allowance: it depends on years of litigation exposed to IPR and Alice. That caps the immediate step-up at about 10-50x rather than 10^3-10^4 and leaves no illegible-data moat.
scored.one_line_reason: Real frame and real buyers, but the step-up is only ~10-50x and depends on litigation. Continuation status is legible, incumbents already run this playbook, and the ladder ends in an NPE business worth billions at most.
sources: No new web searches completed: the shared 200-call WebSearch budget was used up before this run, so all figures are prior knowledge or estimates
Richardson Oliver Insights annual brokered patent market reports (prior knowledge; average asking price ~$100-250k per US asset)
AIPLA Report of the Economic Survey (prior knowledge; patent litigation costs $2-5M+ for >$25M at risk)
USPTO PTAB trial statistics (prior knowledge; high all-claims-unpatentable share among instituted IPRs)
Ariad v. Eli Lilly (Fed. Cir. 2010) and Novozymes v. Genencor (Fed. Cir. 2013) on written-description limits for later-drafted continuation claims

scored.name: Tracebird / Back-to-Birth: records-orphaned engines and LLPs
scored.one_line: Buy engines, gear and LLPs at scrap because traceability is broken; ML over registries, bankruptcy schedules, EETC/ABS filings and AD records rebuilds back-to-birth history; sell certified green time.
scored.unproven_right: Title to sound parts priced at zero life ($5-20k).
scored.proving_step: Cycle-history reconstruction, sworn statements, records-firm sign-off, borescope.
scored.proven_buyer: AerCap Engines, Willis Lease, FTAI, GA Telesis, AAR, StandardAero.
scored.public_data: FAA registry and deregistration, PACER airline schedules, EDGAR EETC/ABS filings, SDRs, NTSB, AD databases; most trace docs are private.
scored.frame: The rung is buying an untraceable LLP or engine and selling it as a certified serviceable part. Inside that rung, proving the history is about 85-90% of the work (my estimate). The part already exists, and a borescope plus shop inspection is cheap next to the paperwork. Capitalised buyers do exist: lessors (AerCap Engines, Willis Lease, FTAI) and USM dealers (AAR, GA Telesis). The problem is what proving means here. It means producing an unbroken cycle record that a regulator will accept (14 CFR 91.417 and the LLP traceability practice in FAA AC 20-62E). It does not mean finding something hidden. So the discovery share is real but legal and archival, not predictive.
scored.step_up: These figures are my estimates from prior knowledge, because the shared web-search budget ran out before any search returned. An LLP with broken back-to-birth trace sells at scrap or metal value, roughly $2-20k. A serviceable CFM56-7B or V2500 LLP with remaining life is worth roughly $100k-$1M; a new CFM56-7B full LLP stack lists around $4-5M. That puts the step-up at roughly 20-300x on a hit, in line with the candidate's claim. It is not 10^3-10^4.
scored.hit_rate_capex: These are estimates; none were found. Trace recovery by specialist records firms and MRO records teams probably costs $5-20k per part in labour, OEM or operator data requests and sworn statements. My guess is that most recoveries fail when a gap in the operator's records cannot be closed, with a base success rate perhaps 10-30%. That would cap the lever at about 3-10x. Even then, ML can only rank which parts are likely to be recoverable. It cannot make a recovery succeed, because the missing link is a private document that either exists or does not.
scored.data: The public sources (FAA registry and deregistrations, PACER bankruptcy schedules, EDGAR EETC/ABS filings, SDRs, NTSB, ADs) can show which airframe and tail an engine sat on and when. They do not contain cycle counts per serial-numbered LLP. The data that proves the part (operator tech logs, shop visit reports, OEM birth records) is private, as the candidate itself admits. Regulators and buyers do not accept inferred or ML-estimated cycles; LLP life must be documented. The outcome is not summarised in a public field, but the signal is not in public data either, so the ML edge is about lead generation, not proof. Buying the right is genuinely cheap: scrap dealers, teardown yards and bankruptcy estates sell this material.
scored.right_bought: Title to the physical part, bought at scrap or teardown prices ($5-20k, my estimate) from bankruptcy estates, part-out yards, insurers and brokers. The right is bought, not claimed for free.
scored.buyer: Engine lessors and USM dealers (AerCap Engines, Willis Lease, FTAI Aviation, GA Telesis, AAR, StandardAero) and MROs. They are capitalised but conservative. Many refuse LLPs with reconstructed trace whatever the paperwork, because of bogus-part liability.
scored.ladder: The rungs run part trace recovery, then whole-engine teardown and green-time trading (the FTAI module model), then engine leasing, then MRO and shop visits, then aircraft part-out and leasing. It is a real ladder into a market worth tens of billions of dollars, but incumbents (FTAI, AerCap, AAR) already hold every rung.
scored.fatal_flaw: The proof sits in private records, not public ones. Back-to-birth cycle history is either documented in operator and OEM files or it cannot be rebuilt, and regulators and buyers will not accept ML-inferred cycles for safety-critical LLPs. The ML can find leads but cannot prove a part, so the 10x capex lever falls apart.
scored.one_line_reason: The rung is clean (cheap scrap title, capitalised buyers, 20-300x step-up), but the proving step relies on private documents and regulatory acceptance, not on reading public data, so ML gives only a lead-ranking edge, and records specialists and USM incumbents already work these parts.

scored.name: ShelfClear: rescuing compounds shelved for species-specific tox findings
scored.one_line: Buy shelved preclinical or Phase 1 compounds dropped over tox flags that probably do not apply to humans (rodent liver enzyme induction, PPAR-alpha, alpha-2u-globulin, dog-specific CV). ML predicts which flags are irrelevant; a cheap human-relevant in vitro package clears the flag and the asset is licensed.
scored.unproven_right: Assignment or exclusive licence of a shelved compound and data package from pharma, defunct biotech estates or TTOs, often nominal upfront plus royalties.
scored.proving_step: Targeted mechanistic tox assays at a CRO (human hepatocytes, iPSC-cardiomyocytes, organ-on-chip), ~$0.1-0.3M.
scored.proven_buyer: Mid-size biotechs and pharma BD in-licensing IND-ready assets ($5-50M upfront precedents).
scored.public_data: FDA pharm/tox reviews in Drugs@FDA (scanned), EMA EPARs, NTP, ToxCast/Tox21, patents with in vivo data, ChEMBL, pipeline-discontinuation disclosures.
scored.rough_step_up: ~$0.1M to $10-50M, 100-500x. The flag is legible but its human relevance is not.
scored.frame: The rung is: buy a shelved compound, clear its tox flag, then license it out. Discovery (picking which flags are irrelevant to humans) is maybe 40-50% of the work inside that rung, not 80%+ (my estimate). Clearing the flag is not the sellable output. A buyer in-licensing an IND-ready asset is paying for efficacy, differentiation against the competitive landscape, and freedom to operate (patent life left; shelved compounds have often used up 5-10 years of it). A clean tox package is necessary but nowhere near sufficient. The proving step is also not reliably trivial. FDA and ICH S1B human-relevance arguments usually need mechanistic in vivo work (knockout or humanized mouse studies, or extra carcinogenicity bridging) on top of in vitro assays. Realistically that costs $0.5-3M and takes 12-24 months, not $0.1-0.3M (estimate). The precedent here is the 2004 FDA requirement that PPAR-class compounds complete two-year rodent carcinogenicity studies before any trial longer than six months. That rule caused 18-24 month delays, and in vitro data did not waive it (Ligand 10-K).
scored.step_up: Unproven: shelved assets from TTOs or biotech estates can be had for nominal upfront ($0-1M) plus royalties. But big pharma rarely out-licenses at nominal prices, and it often holds rights back (estimate). Proven: in 2024 the median upfront to preclinical biotechs was $47M, down from $75M in 2022 (JP Morgan via BioStock). Upfronts were about 6% of headline deal value in 2024, and early-stage upfronts were 1.5-3.7% of deal value in 2024-2025 (Goodwin). Those medians come from selected, efficacy-differentiated assets, often in hot modalities. A small-molecule rescue with a historical tox flag and a shortened patent life would more realistically get $2-15M upfront (estimate). On a hit, that is about 10-100x on total invested capital ($0.5-1M acquisition plus proving), not 100-500x.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Base hit rate of the proving step: if the target compound is well chosen, a mechanistic package showing a rodent-specific effect probably works 30-50% of the time. Rodent PPAR-alpha and alpha-2u-globulin mechanisms are textbook and already accepted (estimate). The real failure rate comes after: the share of tox-cleared shelved compounds that actually get licensed for meaningful money is probably 5-15% (estimate). Shelving is often driven by strategy or efficacy and the tox flag is just the stated reason. Cost per attempt: $0.1-0.3M as pitched, realistically $0.5-3M with in vivo bridging, plus acquisition and diligence costs (estimate). With a 30-50% base hit rate on the tox step, ML can lift it at most about 2-3x (lever capped at 1/hit rate). The uncertainty that dominates, licensability, cannot be predicted from public tox data.
scored.data: Mostly the wrong data. Drugs@FDA pharm/tox reviews and EMA EPARs exist only for drugs that were approved or submitted, which by definition were not shelved. Shelved preclinical and Phase 1 compounds almost never have public tox reports. Their tox data sits in the owner's private data room. The owner (the pharma tox team) can read its own data fine and knows the human-relevance frameworks, which are standard ICH S1B and IPCS mode-of-action practice. So the information asymmetry favors the seller. Tox21/ToxCast and ChEMBL are already legible and already mined. The discontinuation reason is often already written in a legible field (pipeline updates, Citeline, Cortellis, AdisInsight list the reason for discontinuation), although that field is frequently a cover story. Competitors in asset rescue and repurposing include Roivant, BridgeBio, Healx, Ligand, Cerevel, Rhizen, Aiolos and many family-office "NewCos". Pharma out-licensing programs (for example NCATS and the MRC-AZ compound library) already make shelved compounds available. The right can be bought, but it is priced by a seller who knows more than the buyer.
scored.right_bought: Bought: an exclusive licence or assignment from pharma, a defunct-biotech estate (via bankruptcy auction) or a TTO, usually low upfront plus milestones and royalties. That part fits the model. The catch is that the seller holds the full data package and the buyer only sees it after an NDA, so there is no public-data edge at the moment of purchase.
scored.buyer: Mid-size biotech and pharma BD in-licensing teams. They are capitalised, but they buy on efficacy, differentiation and patent life, not on tox clearance alone.
scored.ladder: Strong ladder: rescue, then IND, then Phase 1, then Phase 2 proof of concept, then partnering or commercialisation. That is the Roivant/BridgeBio "hub of subsidiaries" path to a large company, with each rung adding value. This is the candidate's best feature, but those rungs are capital-intensive clinical development, not discovery-dominated.
scored.fatal_flaw: The signal is not in public, illegible data. A shelved compound's tox package is private and held by a seller who can read it, and clearing the tox flag is not what a buyer pays for: efficacy, competitive position and remaining patent life set the price. So there is no frame where discovery from public data is 80%+ of the work and the output is sellable on its own.
scored.one_line_reason: This is the stranded-drug-rescue idea that was already killed. The data asymmetry runs toward the seller, the proving step is costlier than pitched, and the step-up depends on efficacy and patent life, not on the tox flag.
sources: https://www.biostock.se/en/?p=16648 (JP Morgan: preclinical median upfront fell from $75M to $47M; upfronts about 6% of deal value, H1 2024)
https://www.goodwinlaw.com/en/insights/publications/2026/03/insights-lifesciences-2025-yir-life-sciences-licensing-collaboration-deals (early-stage upfronts 1.5% to 3.7% of deal value, 2024-2025)

scored.name: DeadPatent Hits: re-proving unlicensed university compound patents against new targets
scored.one_line: ML over unlicensed university chemistry/biology patents and assay tables finds compounds hitting targets that became valuable after filing (GLP-1R small molecules, KRAS, NLRP3, Lp(a), TL1A). Option from the TTO, resynthesise and assay at a CRO, then license to biotech.
scored.unproven_right: Exclusive options or licences on issued but unlicensed university patents, ~$10-50k.
scored.proving_step: Resynthesis plus potency, selectivity and ADME assays at a CRO, ~$50-150k and 6-10 weeks; binary and mostly failing.
scored.proven_buyer: Biotechs, venture studios and pharma BD buying composition-of-matter starting points ($1-20M upfront).
scored.public_data: USPTO/EPO full text and compound listings, SureChEMBL, PubChem BioAssay, ChEMBL, AUTM/TTO listings, NIH RePORTER.
scored.rough_step_up: ~100-500x. Remaining patent life on old filings is a weakness; target 3-8 year old filings.
scored.frame: The rung is a preclinical out-licence of a validated hit or early lead. Inside it, discovery (picking compound against target) is perhaps 50-60% of the work, my estimate. Resynthesis, potency, selectivity and ADME are real wet-lab work that a CRO can run, but they are not trivial. More importantly, buyers rarely pay for a bare re-validated hit. Pharma BD pays for optimised leads with in vivo data, and that is a further $1-5M and 12-24 months of medicinal chemistry (estimate). So the rung where discovery is 80%+ does not have a capitalised buyer, and the rung that does have one is dominated by optimisation, not discovery.
scored.step_up: Unproven: a TTO option or licence on an unlicensed patent at about $10-50k (candidate's figure; plausible, since around 60-70% of US university patents are never licensed out, IPWatchdog/LESI). Proven: Harvard-Merck paid $20M upfront for preclinical small-molecule inhibitors, but BioCentury called that atypical. UT-CSPC paid $4.5M upfront for two preclinical candidates, and those were mAbs. My estimate for a re-validated hit with no in vivo data is $0-1M upfront, and many get $0 beyond milestones. That puts the realistic step-up at about 3-30x, not 100-500x, and the value is back-loaded into milestones that only pay if someone else spends the clinical capital.
scored.hit_rate_capex: The candidate puts cost per proving attempt at $50-150k and 6-10 weeks for resynthesis plus an assay panel, which is reasonable for CRO pricing. Published virtual-screening hit rates against a target are typically about 5-30% at the micromolar level (estimate from the literature). Clearing potency plus selectivity plus ADME is lower, perhaps 2-10%. ML already supplies much of the current hit rate, because incumbents dock these same ChEMBL/SureChEMBL compounds. So there is limited room to lift it further. The lever over the existing computational baseline is perhaps 2-3x, not 10x (estimate).
scored.data: This fails the illegibility test. SureChEMBL and ChEMBL already extract patent compound structures and assay values into structured, machine-readable form, and PubChem BioAssay is fully structured. Big pharma and AI-discovery firms (Recursion, Insilico, Iambic, Isomorphic, academic docking groups) already mine exactly this chemical space at scale. The outcome, activity against the new target, is not in a status field, which is a point in favour. But the inputs are legible to everyone, so there is no data moat.
scored.right_bought: Yes, the right can be bought cheaply. TTOs readily grant options for about $10-50k on dormant patents, and around 60-70% of university patents are never licensed out. The weakness is that the right is not scarce or strongly protective. Make-on-demand libraries such as Enamine REAL (tens of billions of compounds at about $100 each) give novel, unencumbered chemotypes for the same target. The old composition-of-matter patent therefore rarely blocks anyone, and a new-use claim on a published compound is weak IP.
scored.buyer: Biotechs, venture studios and pharma BD. They are well capitalised, but for hits they mostly buy from DEL/AI providers on cheap milestone-heavy terms (HitGen and Nuevolution with Merck, upfronts undisclosed and small). They pay real upfronts only for optimised leads or candidates with in vivo data.
scored.ladder: The ladder is strong in principle: hit, then lead, then candidate, IND, clinic, then a full pharma company. That makes it a trillion-dollar-category path, but each rung above the first costs 10-100x more and is not discovery-dominated.
scored.fatal_flaw: Hit substitution. Validated hits are close to a commodity, available from Enamine REAL plus docking or from DEL providers for about $100 per compound with no IP encumbrance. So an old university composition-of-matter patent on a re-validated hit commands little premium, and the valuable step-up happens later, in medicinal-chemistry optimisation, which is not discovery-dominated.
scored.one_line_reason: Rights are cheap and the ladder is real. But the patent data is already legible through SureChEMBL/ChEMBL, hits are commoditised by make-on-demand libraries, and buyers pay little for a re-validated hit, so the step-up is about 3-30x and not 10^3.

scored.name: Freezer Estate / Liquidation Strains / Strain Salvage: bankrupt synbio and fermentation strain banks
scored.one_line: Buy the strain and plasmid freezers, cell banks and notebooks of bankrupt or wound-down industrial biotech, synbio and ag-bio companies at scrap value; ML over dockets, patents and sequence data identifies the few strains that make molecules or traits with a live market, then a bench titer, assay or greenhouse test proves them for sale or licence to ingredient and ag majors.
scored.unproven_right: Section 363 or liquidator lots of biological materials, freezers and records, bought for thousands to low hundreds of thousands because trustees cannot describe them.
scored.proving_step: Sequencing, ML annotation and linking to patent sequence listings and target molecules, revival plus shake-flask/1-10L titer or greenhouse test ($10-100k per strain) at CROs.
scored.proven_buyer: Novonesis, IFF, Givaudan, DSM-Firmenich, ADM, Cargill, Ajinomoto, Ginkgo, Corteva, Bayer, Syngenta Biologicals, CDMOs (Liberation Labs). Precedent: Givaudan paid $200M+ for Amyris cosmetic ingredient assets.
scored.public_data: PACER dockets and APAs, USPTO/WIPO ST.26 sequence listings with deposit numbers, NCBI/UniProt/MIBiG, GenBank/JGI genomes, EPA biopesticide files, ingredient price data.
scored.rough_step_up: Lot $50-500k (a strain at $1-50k) to a $1-100M licensed production strain, ~10^2-10^3x; lumpy deal flow and competing bidders.
scored.frame: The proposed rung is "bankrupt strain lot to a bench-proven strain". Inside that rung, sorting out which strain is worth anything is maybe 40-50% of the work (my estimate). The rest is physical and specific to each strain: reviving organisms from freezers that may not have been kept running, re-sequencing them, and optimising titer. That is lab work, not a trivial drill. More important, the rung is not discrete or sellable. Ingredient majors buy strains that are already scaled and cost-competitive, or commercial product lines. They do not buy shake-flask titers. Scale-up from 1-10L to 100m3 plus techno-economic de-risking (an engineering and cost study showing it can be made profitably) is the real proving step, and it is the expensive, bespoke part. That is the geothermal-in-coal-mines counter-example: finding the right strain is easier than making it work at plant scale.
scored.step_up: Unproven: lots from trustees, mostly my estimate of $10k to low $100ks. The candidate's own figure is not sourced. Zymergen's Chapter 11 (Del. 23-11661) sold assets to Ginkgo and Pivot Bio, but I found no public per-asset price. Proven precedent: Givaudan paid $200M upfront plus up to $150M in earnouts for Amyris cosmetic ingredients (Amyris 8-K, 2023). That was a commercial portfolio with about $30M of 2022 sales plus a manufacturing deal, not a freezer of strains, so it is not a valid comparable for a bench-proven strain. A shake-flask titer probably moves the value of one strain from about $10k to about $50-300k at most (3-30x, my estimate). The 100-1000x only shows up after scale-up and commercial offtake (a buyer contracted to take the output), which takes years and $10-100M+.
scored.hit_rate_capex: No published base rate for revival plus a commercially relevant titer from shelved industrial strains. My estimate: maybe 5-20% of annotated strains revive and reproduce their recorded titers, and under 1-2% are commercially relevant at today's ingredient prices. Bench proving costs $10-100k per strain at CROs (the candidate's figure; plausible). The ML lever is weak. The debtor's own notebooks and LIMS (lab database) already record which strains hit which titers. Once the lot is bought, triage is a matter of reading the records, not prediction, and before the purchase the data isn't public. Realistic capex cut: about 2-3x, not 10x.
scored.data: Public sources are PACER APAs (asset purchase agreements), USPTO and WIPO ST.26 sequence listings, and GenBank. These say which molecules a company targeted, but not titer, robustness or freezer state. The outcome-relevant data (titers, scale-up runs) is private and sits inside the lot. So the public data is legible about targets and silent about outcomes. Before a bid, ML has little edge over a domain expert reading the debtor's 10-Ks and patents.
scored.right_bought: Yes, bought through 363 or Chapter 7 sales. But the bidders are sophisticated. Ginkgo and Pivot Bio bought Zymergen assets. Finch's 2026 strain-library-plus-patent auction was run by Rock Creek Advisors. In 2024 363 biotech auctions, Intergalactic's winning bid came in 250% above the stalking horse (opening) bid, and ContraFect's auction ran multiple rounds. Banks with real IP draw informed competitive bids, and the scrap-value lots are scrap for a reason. Freezer chain of custody, MTAs (material transfer agreements) and licensed-in IP add encumbrances.
scored.buyer: Novonesis, IFF, DSM-Firmenich, Givaudan, ADM, Cargill and Ginkgo are capitalised, but they mostly develop strains in-house. Their demand to license in bench-stage strains is thin and lumpy: a handful of deals a year at modest prices. Ag-bio buyers (Corteva, Bayer, Syngenta Biologicals) need regulatory data packages first.
scored.ladder: The ladder is real: strain triage, then licensing, then scale-up and process development, then CDMO (contract manufacturing) capacity such as distressed Liberation Labs-type plants, then owned ingredient brands and offtake. A credible path to a large company, but each rung above the first is capital-heavy and failure-prone. Amyris and Zymergen died on those rungs.
scored.fatal_flaw: A bench-proven strain is not the valuable asset. The value appears only after scale-up and techno-economic de-risking, which is the expensive, bespoke and mostly failing part, so discovery is never 80% of any sellable rung. Industrial synbio's graveyard (Amyris, Zymergen) consists of companies with good strains that failed at scale and cost.
scored.one_line_reason: Rights can be bought and the ladder is real. But the proving step is not the step-up event: buyers pay for scaled, cost-competitive production, not titers, and the outcome data is private inside the lot, so the public-data ML edge is small.
