scored.name: Extremo Rights / Nagoya Enzymes: exclusive ABS site rights mined from public metagenomes
scored.one_line: Sign cheap exclusive Nagoya access-and-benefit-sharing agreements for specific extreme sites (hot springs, soda lakes, vents, outfalls) whose public metagenome reads already contain ML-predicted commercial enzymes (PFAS/polyester hydrolases, thermo-alkaline proteases, CRISPR effectors); synthesise and assay, then sell the enzyme with legal provenance to an enzyme major.
scored.unproven_right: Exclusive ABS/PIC commercial-use agreement with a landowner or national authority for a named site, low five figures plus royalty, signed blind today.
scored.proving_step: Assemble public reads, ML-rank ORFs, synthesise 50-500 genes, express and run activity assays; weeks and tens of thousands of dollars, no field work.
scored.proven_buyer: Novonesis, IFF, dsm-firmenich, BASF Enzymes, Codexis; Veolia, Allonnia, Carbios-type licensees for plastic/PFAS degraders. In-licensing runs $1-50M upfront.
scored.public_data: NCBI SRA raw metagenomes, JGI IMG/M and GOLD, EBI MGnify, Earth Microbiome Project, ABS Clearing-House permits, BRENDA/UniProt.
scored.rough_step_up: $10-100k right to $1-50M enzyme deal, 10^2-10^3x. Weakness: reads are public so the edge erodes; the moat is the ABS permit plus first-to-patent.
scored.frame: The proposed rung is "exclusive ABS/PIC commercial-use agreement for a named extreme site" sold on to an enzyme major. Inside the narrow frame of "go from public raw reads to a ranked, expressed, assay-positive enzyme candidate," discovery really is ~80-90% of the work: the physical step (order 50-500 synthetic genes, express in E. coli/Pichia, run plate assays) is fully commoditised, no field work, weeks not years. But that is not the frame a capitalised buyer buys at. Novonesis / IFF / dsm-firmenich / BASF / Codexis in-license enzymes that have performance data at industrial conditions (thermostability over cycles, pH, inhibitor tolerance, titre in a production host, cost per kg of product). Getting from "active ORF in a microplate" to that is directed evolution plus strain and fermentation development — 1-3 years and the dominant share of the work. So the full-chain discovery share is more like 10-20%, and the sub-rung where it is 90% has no buyer who writes a cheque for it. This is structurally the geothermal-in-coal-mines failure: the bespoke build (engineering and scaling the enzyme) is much harder than finding the right site/sequence. Worse, the thing being "owned" is not an excludable asset: an ABS permit grants access to physical biomass from a jurisdiction, not exclusivity over a sequence that is already in SRA for anyone to download.
scored.step_up: Claimed $10-100k ABS agreement to $1-50M enzyme deal (10^2-10^3x). My read: the step-up is real in headline terms but is not attached to the purchased right. Industry in-licensing of a *validated* enzyme/platform runs roughly $0.5-5M upfront plus mid-single-digit royalties for early-stage assets, with $20-50M+ upfronts reserved for clinical-grade or platform-wide deals (my estimate from comparable biocatalysis/synbio licensing structures; not verified with a source this session — my web searches were blocked by a safety classifier before returning results, so every number here is flagged as estimate). An unvalidated assay-positive hit with no engineering package transacts far lower, commonly $0-250k upfront plus milestones, i.e. ~1-10x on a $50k right, not 10^3x. And the resale value of the ABS permit itself, absent the sequence IP, is approximately zero — there is no secondary market for site access agreements, unlike a staked mineral claim which has a liquid buyer at a published per-hectare price. Nothing re-rates "immediately on a hit": the value appears only after a buyer's own 6-18 month technical due diligence and scale-up gate.
scored.hit_rate_capex: This is the candidate's strongest leg. Classical function-based metagenomic screening hit rates are famously terrible — on the order of 1 active clone per 10^3-10^5 clones screened for a given activity (long-standing figure in the functional-metagenomics literature; my recollection, not verified this session). Sequence-and-ML-first candidate selection plausibly lifts per-construct success to ~1-20% expressed-and-active, which is a 10^2-10^3x apparent lever — far above the ~10x the rubric asks for, and above the 1/base-hit-rate cap only because the base rate is so low. But the lever is worth little in dollars because the proving step is already cheap: synthetic gene cost is roughly $0.07-0.15/bp, so a 1 kb ORF is ~$100-200 and 500 ORFs plus expression and primary assays is ~$75-200k all-in (my estimate from current gene-synthesis list pricing). Compare Terranox: an exploratory hole is $50-500k and you need many of them, so capex *is* the binding constraint and a 10x cut buys 10 more shots at a 10^4 jump. Here discovery capex is already a rounding error against the $5-50M of protein engineering, strain development and process validation that stands between a hit and a sale. Cutting the cheap step 100x does not move the economics of the expensive step. The hit-rate lever is pointed at the wrong bottleneck.
scored.data: Data leg is genuinely good and scores 4-5 on its own. NCBI SRA holds tens of petabases of raw metagenomic reads, most never assembled or annotated by anyone; JGI IMG/M, MGnify and the Earth Microbiome Project add large unassembled or thinly-annotated collections. The outcome is emphatically NOT summarised in a legible field — there is no regulator-written status column saying "this site contains a commercial PFAS hydrolase." That is the opposite of the failure mode that killed interconnection queues and powered brownfields, and is the one way this candidate beats most of the previously-killed list. The right leg is where it collapses. (a) The signal is public, so the edge is non-exclusive by construction — Basecamp Research, Ginkgo, Novonesis, BASF, Codexis, Arzeda and the protein-LM groups all mine public plus proprietary sequence today, and the majors run their own sampling programmes with decades of strain collections. (b) An ABS/PIC permit is not an exclusive property right in most national frameworks; authorities grant non-exclusive access to physical samples and generally cannot and will not sell you a monopoly on a site's genetic information. (c) Digital Sequence Information is being decoupled from site-level ABS entirely — the CBD's multilateral/Cali Fund approach taxes commercial users of DSI into a global pool rather than routing value to a bilateral site agreement, which directly deletes the premise that holding one site's permit confers any advantage over a competitor who downloads the same reads. (d) The landowner "who cannot read the data" owns nothing excludable to sell, so there is no purchase discount to arbitrage. The residual moat is first-to-patent, and publicly deposited reads are prior art that undercuts novelty on the natural sequence, pushing you to claim engineered variants — which is exactly the expensive rung you do not own yet.
scored.right_bought: A non-exclusive-in-practice access-and-benefit-sharing / prior-informed-consent commercial-use agreement with a landowner or national competent authority for one named extreme site, low five figures plus a royalty, signed before any assay. Nominally the "unproven right." In substance it is a compliance document and a contingent royalty liability, not a conveyance of an excludable asset — closer to buying a permit to walk on land than to buying the mineral title under it.
scored.buyer: Nominally Novonesis, IFF, dsm-firmenich, BASF Enzymes, Codexis, and remediation licensees (Veolia, Allonnia, Carbios-type). These are real, capitalised, and do in-license. But they buy performance packages, not permits or candidate lists, and they each already have internal discovery plus in-house sequence mining, so they are the incumbent competitor as much as the buyer. There is no buyer at all for the output of the one rung where discovery is 80%+ (a ranked, assay-positive ORF with legal provenance).
scored.ladder: Rungs above do exist and are legible: ranked candidate → engineered and expressed variant → production strain and fermentation process → formulated product → owning the application service (PFAS destruction contracts, textile/polyester recycling tolling). That is a credible climb to a very large company and is the honest strength alongside the data leg. Ceiling is high — enzyme majors are $10-20B+ revenue businesses. The problem is the bottom of the ladder, not the top: the smallest rung here is not independently sellable, so there is no self-funding first step from which to climb, which is the exact mechanism that makes Terranox work.
scored.fatal_flaw: The purchased right is not excludable. Because the sequence is already in public SRA, an ABS site permit blocks no competitor from finding and using the same enzyme, and DSI is being pulled out of bilateral site-level ABS into a multilateral fund, so the permit's scarcity value is trending to zero rather than appreciating on a hit. There is no mineral-title analogue: you cannot buy the thing that re-rates. Compounding it, the one rung where discovery is 80%+ of the work has no buyer, because the value-recognising step (engineering, expression, scale-up to industrial conditions) is the expensive bespoke build — the geothermal-in-coal-mines pattern the rubric explicitly rejects.
scored.one_line_reason: Best-in-class on illegible public data (petabases of unannotated SRA reads with no regulator-written answer field) and on hit-rate lever, but fails the core test: the ABS permit confers no exclusivity over an already-public sequence, so nothing re-rates on a hit, and the rung where discovery is 95% has no capitalised buyer because value only appears after years of protein engineering and scale-up. Total 12/25.
sources: No source URLs are cited because my web searches in this session were halted by a safety classifier before any results returned; every quantitative claim above is explicitly labelled as my own estimate or recollection and should be re-verified.

To verify, the checks that matter are: (1) CBD/Nagoya treatment of Digital Sequence Information and the Cali Fund mechanism at cbd.int/abs - does any national ABS framework grant EXCLUSIVE commercial rights to a named site's genetic resources? I expect no; (2) current synthetic-gene list pricing per bp (Twist, IDT, GenScript) to confirm the ~$100-200 per 1 kb ORF and ~$75-200k per 500-gene campaign estimate; (3) disclosed upfronts in enzyme in-licensing deals (Codexis, Novonesis, Carbios partner agreements) to test the $1-50M claim against unvalidated-hit-stage comparables, which I estimate at $0-250k upfront; (4) Basecamp Research's funding, database scale and partnership terms with Nvidia/Microsoft, as the closest direct competitor already executing sequence-first discovery with its own ABS-compliant sampling; (5) published functional-metagenomics hit rates (1 per 10^3-10^5 clones) to anchor the base rate C3 depends on.

scored.name: Unknown Sitter: face-matching early photographs to historical figures
scored.one_line: Buy unidentified daguerreotypes, tintypes and cartes de visite in bulk; face recognition against LoC and NARA portraits plus studio marks finds famous sitters; historian review proves them.
scored.unproven_right: Ownership of anonymous 19th-century photographs, $10-200.
scored.proving_step: Face embedding, studio directory check, expert attribution; flatbed scan.
scored.proven_buyer: Smithsonian NMAAHC, LoC, state historical societies, Swann, Heritage, Cowan's, Americana collectors.
scored.public_data: LoC Prints & Photographs catalog, NARA Brady collection, Civil War Photo Sleuth, eBay/Delcampe listings.
scored.rough_step_up: 1,000-10,000x for a famous sitter; small market.
scored.frame: The rung is "own an anonymous 19th-century photo and get it attributed to a named sitter." Inside that rung nearly all the work is discovery: the physical step is a flatbed scan and the purchase costs $10-200. The catch is that the proving step is not a drill core. Attribution is expert opinion and gets contested, so the "proof" is soft. Discovery is about 95% of the work, but the proof itself is weak.
scored.step_up: Unproven: a $2-$10 junk-shop or eBay tintype. Proven famous sitter: the authenticated Billy the Kid tintype sold for $2.3M ($2.6M with fees) in 2011, roughly 10^5-10^6x. But the newly face-matched cases have not turned into sales. The Croquet Kid ($2 in 2010) carried a $5M Kagin's appraisal, and I found no confirmed sale. The $10 Jesse James eBay tintype was described as possibly worth about $2M, which was a reported valuation and not a sale. For ordinary identified soldiers the premium is my estimate of about 2-5x, since I found no published price comparison. The headline 10^4 jump is real on paper but rarely realised.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Base hit rate for a famous, saleable sitter: my estimate is under 1 in 100,000 anonymous images (no source). Civil War Photo Sleuth: only 10-20% of surviving Civil War portraits are identified. In its first month users uploaded more than 2,000 photos, about half of them unidentified, and over 100 unknown photos were linked to specific soldiers. Experts judged over 85% of those proposed IDs probably or definitely correct (Mohanty et al., IJCAI 2020). Cost per attempt: $10-200 for the photo plus scan time. Expert attribution for a famous claim runs months to a year or more (Kagin's took over a year). ML cheaply cuts the screening cost, but the binding cost is expert authentication time and buyer acceptance, not screening. The lever on realised dollars is well under 10x.
scored.data: The signal is public and fairly illegible: images in eBay/Delcampe listings, the LoC P&P catalog, NARA Brady negatives. The outcome is NOT summarised in a legible field, which is good. But the core tool already exists free and public: Civil War Photo Sleuth (Virginia Tech, Kurt Luther) does face recognition against a reference set that started at over 15,000 identified Civil War soldier portraits. Dealers and collectors also hunt for famous faces as a matter of routine. So the edge is partly arbitraged.
scored.right_bought: Yes, and cheaply. The photo itself is the right, bought at $2-200 from sellers who cannot identify the sitter, with clean chattel title. This is the strongest part of the candidate.
scored.buyer: Auction houses (Heritage, Swann, Cowan's, Brian Lebel's Old West), wealthy collectors (e.g. William Koch) and institutions (LoC, NMAAHC, state historical societies). They are capitalised, but they pay only for provenance-grade attribution, and they heavily discount identifications that rest on face matching alone. Institutions often prefer donations to purchases.
scored.ladder: Weak. The rungs above (dealer, auction house, archive or licensing of image rights) together make a small market: on my estimate, a handful of $1M+ photo sales per decade and tens of $M a year in total 19th-century photography. There is no chain leading to a very large company.
scored.fatal_flaw: The proving step is not objective. A face-match attribution is an opinion that the capitalised buyer does not accept on its own: the Croquet Kid has a $5M appraisal, and I found no confirmed sale in the decade since. Hits are also too rare and the market too small for any ladder.
scored.one_line_reason: The rights are cheap and the step-up is huge on paper. But the "proof" is contested expert opinion that buyers discount, free tools like Civil War Photo Sleuth already exist, and the total market is tiny with no ladder above it.

scored.name: Gores: claiming title gaps from deed-description errors
scored.one_line: ML reconstructs every metes-and-bounds description in a county's scanned deeds and finds slivers no current deed covers; buy quitclaims from heirs or successors of the last owner of record and sell the strip to the blocked adjoiner, developer or title insurer.
scored.unproven_right: Residual record title in unconveyed slivers, effectively worth $0 to heirs or defunct entities.
scored.proving_step: OCR plus geometry reconstruction against parcel fabric, chain-of-title trace, one quitclaim and recording.
scored.proven_buyer: Commercial developers and adjoiners blocked at commitment, title insurers (First American, Fidelity), DOTs.
scored.public_data: County recorder deed images back to the 1800s, parcel GIS, state dissolution records, probate indexes.
scored.frame: The rung is "own record title to an unconveyed sliver (gore) and sell it to whoever is blocked by it." Inside that rung, finding the gore is most of the work, maybe 70-80% (my estimate): OCR the deeds, rebuild the metes-and-bounds geometry, trace the chain of title. The physical step is cheap: one quitclaim at roughly $100-1,000 to the heirs plus a recording fee. The weak part is the buyer. A blocked adjoiner or developer is not a buyer of an appreciating asset the way a mine developer is. They pay at most what the next-cheapest cure would cost them, and several cures exist: an uncontested quiet title action ($1.5k-10k, 2-6 months), a title insurer's gaps/strips/gores endorsement (CLTA 116.9 / ALTA 19.2), the strips-and-gores presumption, adverse possession or boundary by acquiescence where the adjoiner has occupied the strip, and marketable title acts that cut off claims more than 30-40 years old. So the frame and the cheap physical step exist, but the buyer's willingness to pay is capped.
scored.step_up: Unproven: a quitclaim from heirs or successors costs about $100-1,000 (the candidate's figure; I did not verify it; heirs often take a nominal amount). Proven: the realistic ceiling is the blocked party's cost to cure another way. That is about $1,500-5,000 for an uncontested quiet title (Alabama Extension) or $3k-10k (LegalClarity), plus the delay. A title-insurer endorsement can be cheaper still. Realistic step-up is about 3-30x, call it ~10x. The candidate's "$10k-500k hold-up" figure only applies in rare cases where a closing deadline is tight and none of the other cures is available. Even then courts and underwriters push back on someone who bought a strip just to hold up a sale. Nothing like 10^3-10^4.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Proving is not the expensive, mostly-failing step. A manual title search or abstract costs about $200-500 (my estimate), and a quitclaim plus recording a few hundred dollars. Once a real gore has been confirmed and its heirs located, getting the quitclaim is cheap and probably works more than half the time (my estimate). Where ML actually helps is the search: geometry reconstruction can find gaps humans never look for. But few of the gaps found will be worth money, because most gores are small, sit under fences that are presumed to settle ownership, or are already covered by insurer endorsements. That share is unknown; my estimate is about 1-5%. The cost that ML would cut 10x is low to begin with, so the lever is real but its dollar value is small.
scored.data: This is the strong criterion. County recorder deed images go back to the 1800s and are public but illegible: scanned, handwritten metes and bounds, scattered across indexes. Gaps between descriptions are not flagged in any legible field. Parcel GIS fabrics hide them by drawing parcels edge to edge. Title plants index by name and parcel; they do not reconstruct geometry. So the outcome is not summarised anywhere public, which beats prior hunts where regulators had already written the answer into a status field. The right can be bought cheaply from heirs or dissolved entities who don't know they hold anything, so it is bought, not claimed first-come. Incumbents (First American, Fidelity, Stewart title plants, and surveyors) find gores one transaction at a time and insure over them or cure them; they do not hunt for them.
scored.right_bought: Quitclaim deeds from the heirs or successors of the last owner of record, about $100-1,000 each (estimate). With unknown or many heirs you may need to buy fractional interests from several people, or bring your own quiet title action.
scored.buyer: Adjoiners or developers blocked at the title-commitment stage, and occasionally DOTs assembling right-of-way. Title insurers are less likely buyers than the candidate assumes: they usually insure over the gap with an endorsement or require a quiet title action rather than buying. The buyer's ceiling is their cheapest alternative cure, roughly $2k-10k.
scored.ladder: The ladder is weak. Possible rungs above: a title-curative services business (but that is selling a service, which the rubric excludes), land assembly for developers, or a title-plant or underwriting business built on a geometry-reconstructed chain of title. That last one is the only large prize, and it is a data business sold to title insurers rather than climbing to own a bigger asset. Owning gores does not lead naturally to developing the land they sit on.
scored.fatal_flaw: Hold-up value is capped by cheap alternative cures. A blocked party can quiet title uncontested for about $1.5k-10k in 2-6 months, buy an insurer's gaps/strips/gores endorsement, or rely on the strips-and-gores presumption, adverse possession or acquiescence, or a marketable title act. Courts also treat strategic gore-buyers as holdouts with little sympathy. The proven value is therefore about ~10x a cheap quitclaim, nowhere near 10^3-10^4, and each deal is a few thousand dollars.
scored.one_line_reason: The data edge here is real (illegible scanned metes and bounds, with gaps flagged in no field), but alternative cures cap the step-up near ~10x and a few thousand dollars per deal, and there is no ladder to a large owned-asset chain.

scored.name: Corridor Title / Orphan Easement / EasementGraph: dormant utility, pipeline and telegraph easement corridors
scored.one_line: Buy forgotten assignable easements in gross and corridor strips from successors of dissolved utilities, co-ops, interurbans, telegraph and pipeline companies; ML over scanned deed books stitches continuous corridors and proves scope (communications or any lawful purpose) and survival; sell insured corridors to HVDC and long-haul fiber developers.
scored.unproven_right: Recorded easements held by dissolved or merged grantees, bought by quitclaim or assignment for ~$10-5,000 each (roughly $0-500/mile).
scored.proving_step: OCR/NLP of grants, abandonment orders and merger chains; legal-description-to-geometry parsing; scope classification; title opinion and corridor title insurance. No construction.
scored.proven_buyer: Merchant HVDC and 345-765kV developers (Grain Belt class, Grid United, Invenergy, Pattern), utilities with contested routes, hyperscaler and long-haul fiber builders (Zayo, Lumen, Bandwidth IG, Conterra).
scored.public_data: County recorder deed books, state corporation dissolution/merger records, PSC/PUC franchise filings, RUS co-op records, STB/ICC interurban abandonments, PHMSA NPMS abandoned lines, BLM MLRS, historic topos.
scored.rough_step_up: Near zero to $20k-500k/mile as a continuous insured corridor, ~100-1000x.
scored.frame: Rung: own a recorded, assignable dormant easement corridor and prove its survival, scope and continuity, then sell it insured. The research itself (deed OCR, merger chains, geometry stitching) is maybe 50-60% of the work inside this rung. That is my estimate. The rest is legal and physical friction that discovery does not remove: getting quitclaims from many separate successors, curing every gap parcel, fighting fee-owner quiet-title and overburden suits, and getting a title insurer to write corridor cover on 100-year-old instruments. The physical step is not the problem. The legal step is the bespoke plant here, as in the coal-mine geothermal counter-example. Buyers exist (HVDC and fiber developers), but they buy continuous, scope-adequate corridors, not partial chains. So the rung that can actually be sold is close to doing the whole route assembly, not one easement.
scored.step_up: Unproven: about $10-5,000 per instrument by quitclaim (candidate's figure, not checked). Proven: what a developer avoids paying is its normal acquisition cost. My estimate for a 150-200 ft HVDC strip on Midwest farmland ($8-12k/acre, about 18-24 acres per mile, easement at 50-110% of fee value, plus per-structure payments) is roughly $100-300k per mile. Fiber easements run roughly $5-30k per mile (also my estimate). Fiber is the use where old telegraph and telephone scope can plausibly carry over. On paper that is 100-1000x per mile. Realistically, a typical old easement is 10-33 ft wide and limited to telegraph, telephone or pipeline use. It cannot carry an HVDC line, so for HVDC the proven value is close to zero. For fiber the realistic step-up is about 3-30x net of curing costs. All of these are estimates: my web search budget was used up and no figures were checked.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Base hit rate: there is no published figure. My estimate is that well under 5% of dormant grantee easements are all of: still alive (not extinguished by abandonment statutes, nonuse plus intent, or marketable record title acts), assignable (exclusive and apportionable in gross), wide enough and broad enough in scope, and joined with neighbours into a continuous run. For HVDC, effectively 0%. Cost per proving attempt: abstracting and title opinion run about $500-3,000 per parcel (estimate), and a corridor crosses about 5-15 parcels per mile. Every gap still has to be cured. ML can cut the abstracting cost, perhaps 3-5x. It cannot raise the legal survival or scope rate, which is set by the instruments and by state law, not by better reading. So the lever is real but well under 10x.
scored.data: Public and illegible: yes. County deed books are mostly scanned images going back before 1950, indexed by grantor and grantee name only, with no geometry. Corporate dissolution and merger chains are scattered across state Secretary of State records and old PUC dockets. The outcome is not summarised in any legible field. No registry records whether a 1928 telegraph easement still exists or what it covers. Survival and scope are mixed questions of law and fact, decided case by case, often by litigation. One example is the railroad and telegraph fiber class actions of the late 1990s and 2000s against AT&T, Sprint, Qwest and others, which ended in multi-state settlements after courts split on scope. That example is from memory, not checked. The data edge is genuine. Its weakness is that a legible answer may not exist until a court rules.
scored.right_bought: In part. Successors of merged utilities (AT&T/Lumen for Western Union and Bell lines, Kinder Morgan or Energy Transfer for old pipelines, co-op successors) are large companies. They tend to keep, rather than quitclaim, anything a lawyer flags as corridor-valuable, and they hold the same records. Truly dissolved grantees often have no successor who can sign, or their property passed to shareholders or escheated to the state, so the cheap quitclaim may not convey anything. The fee owners underneath have the stronger practical position, because they can quiet title on abandonment. The asset is cheap mainly because it is often legally worthless, not because the owners cannot read the data.
scored.buyer: Long-haul fiber builders (Zayo, Lumen, Bandwidth IG, Conterra, hyperscaler routes) are a real but modest buyer. They already route along highway rights-of-way, railroad licences and their own legacy telecom corridors at low per-foot rates, which caps what they will pay. Merchant HVDC developers (Grain Belt Express/Invenergy, Grid United, Pattern SunZia) need 150-200 ft rights-of-way with modern scope. They acquire through voluntary purchase above market value, backed by state utility status or eminent domain. That makes a patched-together legacy corridor at most a partial route de-risk, not a substitute.
scored.ladder: Corridor title, then corridor bank or landlord, then owning dark fiber or conduit on owned corridors, then co-developing transmission (a share of the HVDC developer's return), then a corridor REIT or utility-like infrastructure owner. The ladder is real and large: corridor owners like railroads and pipelines are long-lived monopoly assets. But rungs two and up depend on rung one producing continuous, scope-adequate corridors, and that is rare.
scored.fatal_flaw: Scope and width overburden plus continuity. A dormant telegraph, telephone or pipeline easement is usually 10-33 ft wide and limited to its original use. In most states it cannot legally be expanded to carry an HVDC line, so fee owners will win overburden and abandonment suits. A corridor is only worth anything when unbroken, and every gap must be cured by negotiation or eminent domain, which the developer would do anyway. The hard part is legal assembly and survival, not discovery, so ML does not move the 80%+ of the work that matters.
scored.one_line_reason: The data edge is real and nobody else is extracting it. But the proven value only appears for continuous, scope-adequate corridors, and those almost never survive. HVDC scope basically does not carry over. Fiber is the realistic use, and there the buyer pays modest per-mile rates. Legal assembly, not discovery, sets the hit rate.
sources: Web search budget for this run was exhausted (200-call limit shared by all agents); no live searches returned. All figures are my estimates or from memory and flagged as such.

From memory, not checked: railroad and telegraph right-of-way fiber-optic class action settlements (e.g., In re Telecommunications Right-of-Way litigation against AT&T, Sprint, Qwest and WilTel, 2000s) on scope and overburden of old easements
From memory: Restatement (Third) of Property: Servitudes ss. 4.10, 5.8-5.9 on easement scope and apportionment of easements in gross
From memory: Grain Belt Express landowner compensation offer (about 110% of market value for the easement plus per-structure payments), Invenergy and Missouri PSC filings
From memory: state marketable record title acts (e.g., Iowa, Minnesota, Michigan, Florida) extinguishing old unrecorded or unpreserved interests, with varying utility exemptions

scored.name: DuctFind / Dark Conduit Recovery: abandoned urban and long-haul conduit
scored.one_line: Buy abandoned or forgotten conduit (old telegraph/telephone ducts, defunct CLEC and 1998-2002 long-haul builds) from estates and successors at ~zero book value; ML over scanned franchises, as-builts, permits and bankruptcy schedules proves continuous routes and title; rod/mandrel tests confirm; sell or IRU to carriers and hyperscalers.
scored.unproven_right: Quitclaim/assignment of conduit and franchise/ROW rights from CLEC estates, utility successors, transit/telegraph successors and municipalities, often a few thousand dollars per system.
scored.proving_step: ML network reconstruction, then rodding/camera/mandrel tests ($2-5k per block) vs $1-3M/mile urban trenching or $60-150k/mile long-haul.
scored.proven_buyer: Zayo, Lumen, Crown Castle Fiber, Lightpath, hyperscaler network teams, AI-campus developers.
scored.public_data: Municipal franchises and council minutes, DOT street-opening permits, Sanborn and as-built maps, PACER schedules of 2001-03 telecom bankruptcies (Global Crossing, 360networks, Williams), PUC CPCN filings, county easements, FCC 477/BDC.
scored.rough_step_up: ~10^2-10^4x (e.g. $0.01/ft paid vs $100-300/ft urban; $20-80k/conduit-mile long-haul). Shares title-from-scans risk with killed telco-copper/rail ideas.
scored.frame: The rung is a proven, titled and continuous conduit route sold or leased (IRU) to a carrier or hyperscaler. My estimate is that only about 40-50% of the work in this rung is discovery (finding the route and reconstructing title from scans). The rest is physical and legal: getting manhole and vault access permits, rodding, clearing blockages, repairing collapsed sections, re-establishing franchise or ROW consent, and clearing landowner easement-scope challenges. Unlike a drill, which is a commodity service, the proving step here is site-specific remediation. That makes it closer to the geothermal-in-coal-mines counter-example than to Terranox. The buyer is well capitalised (Zayo, Lumen, Crown Castle Fiber, hyperscalers), but they buy only clean, continuous, documented routes with defensible rights. A partial route has close to zero value.
scored.step_up: These numbers are my estimates; no live search could be run. Proven value is capped by the buyer's alternative, which is new build: about $60-150k/mile for long-haul (candidate figure, consistent with industry ranges I know of) and $1-3M/mile in dense urban areas. Spare long-haul conduit traded in the 2000s for roughly $5-30k per conduit-mile, i.e. a fraction of build cost, because there was a glut. Urban duct can be worth $50-300/ft where it fills a real gap. If the right is bought for a few thousand dollars per system ($0.01-0.10/ft), the nominal multiple is 10^2-10^3. But the realistic acquisition cost includes legal title clearing and remediation, which is probably 10-30% of build cost. That puts the effective step-up nearer 10-100x than 10^4.
scored.hit_rate_capex: These figures are my estimates; no live search could be run. Rodding, camera or mandrel tests cost about $2-5k per block (candidate figure), plus permits and traffic control. Physical-continuity hit rates on old duct are probably moderate, around 30-60%: blockages and collapses are common, but most duct still exists. The low hit rate actually sits in title and rights continuity: whether an easement survived abandonment and whether a franchise is still valid, probably under 20%. ML can rank candidates, but its lever is capped at roughly 2-5x, not 10x. Each proving attempt is cheap relative to the asset, so discovery capex is not the binding cost. Legal clearance and remediation are.
scored.data: The signal is partly public and illegible: council minutes, franchise ordinances, Sanborn maps, scanned as-builts and street-opening permits. But the most valuable inventory is not lost. Bankruptcy outcomes for 2001-03 telecom estates are written into legible, docketed sale orders on PACER. Assets from 360networks, Global Crossing, Williams, Broadwing and others were sold as going concerns and later rolled up into Zayo, Level 3/Lumen and others. Incumbent LEC duct (old telephone and telegraph ducts) is actively mapped by Verizon and AT&T in their own GIS and 811/one-call records, and is regulated under pole and conduit attachment rules, so it is not orphaned. Truly ownerless conduit is mostly small urban CLEC builds and municipal or transit ducts. There, owners usually do know what they have, and the open question is the legal right, not the location. The rights can be bought from estates, but many estates are closed. Abandonment may also extinguish the easement entirely: the class-action settlements over fiber laid on railroad ROW show that landowners contest easement scope.
scored.right_bought: Quitclaim or assignment from surviving CLEC entities, closed-estate successors (which may need a reopened case or court approval), utility successors, transit or telegraph successor corporations, or municipalities. Municipal duct sales usually go through public procurement or RFPs, not cheap private quitclaims. Price per system could be a few thousand dollars where it exists. But a quitclaim conveys only whatever right exists, and the underlying franchise or ROW consent is often personal to the original grantee, non-assignable, or lapsed.
scored.buyer: Zayo, Lumen, Crown Castle Fiber (now Zayo), Lightpath, Uniti, hyperscaler network teams, and AI-campus and data-center developers needing diverse urban or metro entrances. These buyers are capitalised and do buy dark conduit and IRUs, but they demand clean continuity and title. Most of them also own the bulk of the surplus 2000-era conduit already.
scored.ladder: The ladder has real rungs. Proven conduit leads to pulling your own fiber and selling dark fiber or IRUs, then to a metro or long-haul fiber network operator, then to data-center interconnect, AI-campus connectivity and lit services. Zayo, built by rolling up conduit and fiber, shows a $10B+ outcome is possible. The upper rungs are crowded, capital-intensive and commoditised, so the path to a very large company exists but is not unique.
scored.fatal_flaw: The flaw is that the step-up depends on legal and physical remediation, not on discovery, and the high-value inventory is not actually lost. The 2001-03 long-haul conduit was resolved in legible bankruptcy sale orders and absorbed by Zayo, Lumen and others. ILEC duct is actively owned and mapped. For what remains, the binding constraint is whether the franchise or easement survived abandonment and is assignable, and whether a collapsed or blocked duct can be repaired cheaply. ML over scans does not resolve either question. This is the same title-from-scans failure mode as the killed telco-copper and rail-corridor ideas, plus a bespoke physical step.
scored.one_line_reason: The value multiple can be large and the buyers are real and capitalised. But discovery is under half the work in the sellable rung. Title survival and duct remediation dominate. The biggest inventory (2000-era long-haul) is already legibly resolved and owned by incumbents. So ML's lever is about 2-5x, not 10x.
sources: No live web searches ran: the shared search budget for this turn (200 calls) was used up before this scoring. Every number here is an estimate from prior knowledge or a figure from the candidate description.

Prior knowledge: 360networks, Global Crossing and Williams Communications bankruptcy asset sales (2001-2003) were docketed as legible sale orders, and the assets later consolidated into Level 3/Lumen and Zayo
Prior knowledge: class-action settlements over fiber-optic cable on railroad rights of way (late-1990s to 2000s), showing landowners contest the scope of easements
Prior knowledge: FCC pole and conduit attachment rules (47 USC 224) govern incumbent-utility duct access, so ILEC conduit is inventoried and actively owned
Candidate-provided figures: $60-150k/mile long-haul new build, $1-3M/mile urban trenching, $2-5k per block rod/mandrel test

scored.name: Orphan Game IP Title Clearing
scored.one_line: Buy rights to 1985-2010 games of defunct studios from estates and trustees; ML rebuilds chain of title; sell or license cleared IP to remaster publishers.
scored.unproven_right: Copyright/trademark/source claims, $1k-20k.
scored.proving_step: ML title search across Copyright Office, PACER schedules, TSDR, EDGAR, MobyGames; quitclaim/assignment; demand ranking.
scored.proven_buyer: Atari, Nightdive, Embracer spinouts, Limited Run, Netflix Games, GOG.
scored.public_data: Copyright Public Records and CCE, PACER/RECAP, TSDR, EDGAR, MobyGames, Internet Archive stats, SteamDB.
scored.frame: The rung is clearing title on an orphan game IP and selling or licensing it. Inside that rung, discovery (finding who holds what through bankruptcy schedules, assignments and estates) is maybe 50-60% of the work. The rest is legal negotiation with scattered heirs and trustees, quitclaims, and clearing third-party pieces (music, likeness, licensed engines, middleware). Those pieces are often the real blocker: No One Lives Forever stalled on overlapping WB, Activision and Fox claims, not on finding them. So it falls short of the 80%+ discovery bar. The physical step (the remaster itself) sits outside the rung, which is good. The buyer pool is real but thin and lightly capitalised: Atari, Nightdive (Atari-owned), Limited Run, Digital Eclipse, GOG, Piko.
scored.step_up: My estimate, no fresh source: the search budget was used up before any query ran. Unproven claims cost about $1k-20k, as the candidate states. A cleared mid-tier 1985-2010 IP likely licenses for a $10k-100k advance plus royalty, or sells for $50k-500k. A rare top title (System Shock-class) can reach $1M-10M+ in total value. Typical step-up is about 5-50x, and about 100x+ only for the rare top title. That is well below the 10^3-10^4 Terranox jump, and value comes from remaster sales over years, not immediately on clearing.
scored.hit_rate_capex: My estimate: perhaps 20-40% of title-clearing attempts end in a clean, sellable chain. A failed attempt costs about $5k-50k in lawyer time and outreach. ML can raise the share of attempts that succeed and cut the search cost. But failures come mainly from multi-party and third-party rights, and ML cannot negotiate those away. The lever is capped near 1/0.3, about 3x, not 10x.
scored.data: The data is public and scattered: Copyright Office records (pre-1978 Catalog of Copyright Entries scans; post-1978 recorded documents only partly online), PACER/RECAP bankruptcy asset schedules, TSDR trademark status and assignments, EDGAR asset sales, MobyGames credits. It is truly illegible across sources, and no single field states who owns an IP now. That is a real ML opening. The catch: the TSDR status field already flags dead trademarks, and the MobyGames publisher field narrows the search a lot. Demand signals (SteamDB, the Internet Archive, GOG wishlists) are legible and already watched by buyers.
scored.right_bought: Rights can be bought, not claimed for free: quitclaims or assignments from trustees, liquidators, estates and ex-founders, often for $1k-20k. Two caveats. First, the strongest IPs often still sit with large firms (Activision, WB, Embracer, Microsoft), which will not sell cheaply. Second, the incumbents doing exactly this, Piko Interactive, Nightdive and Atari's IP-buying arm, already outbid on anything with demand.
scored.buyer: Atari (an active IP buyer; it owns Nightdive and MobyGames), Limited Run, Digital Eclipse, GOG, Embracer spinouts, and some Netflix Games licensing. Total yearly spend on orphan retro IP is my estimate at tens of millions of dollars, not billions.
scored.ladder: clear title -> license -> publish re-releases on GOG/Steam/console (low capex) -> develop remasters -> run a retro catalog publisher. This is roughly what Atari already does. The ladder is real but tops out at Atari scale (market cap about $100-300M; my estimate), not a trillion-dollar path. The orphan-IP pool is finite and shrinking as it gets cleared.
scored.fatal_flaw: The pool of value is small and the step-up is low. Most orphan games are worth near zero after clearing. The few valuable ones carry multi-party and third-party rights that block clearing no matter how good the discovery is. And they are already chased by incumbent buyers (Piko, Nightdive/Atari, Limited Run) who also make up most of the buyer pool. The jump is about 10x, not 10^4, and the top of the ladder is a sub-$1B retro publisher.
scored.one_line_reason: Rights can be bought and the data is illegible, but discovery is not 80% of the rung, the jump is about 10x rather than 10^4, the hit-rate lever is capped near 3x by negotiation and third-party failures, and the ladder tops out at Atari scale.
sources: No web searches ran: the shared WebSearch budget for this turn (200 calls) was used up before this agent's first query. All numbers are model estimates from prior knowledge (Atari's acquisitions of Nightdive and MobyGames, Piko Interactive's orphan-IP buying, the public No One Lives Forever rights dispute) and should be checked in a follow-up run.

scored.name: LapseEdge: materials patents bought before maintenance-fee lapse
scored.one_line: Buy battery, magnet and catalyst composition patents for $2-10k from owners about to let them lapse; ML matches claim ranges to teardown literature; one ICP-MS/XRD teardown produces a claim chart; sell to funders, aggregators or the infringer.
scored.unproven_right: Lapse-bound composition/process patents from universities, dead startups and non-core owners.
scored.proving_step: ML claim-to-product ranking plus one $1-3k physical confirmation.
scored.proven_buyer: Burford, Fortress IP, RPX, AST, cell and magnet makers.
scored.public_data: USPTO maintenance-fee events, PatentsView, assignments, INPADOC, teardown reports, datasheets.
scored.frame: The candidate's rung is 'buy a lapse-bound patent, produce a claim chart backed by a teardown, sell it'. The claim chart itself is cheap: ML ranking plus one ICP-MS/XRD run at about $1-3k. But a claim chart is not the proven asset. Funders and aggregators pay against expected recovery, which also depends on validity surviving PTAB/IPR, enforceability, the size of the US damages base and the cost of litigating. Inside the rung as the candidate defines it, discovery is maybe 60-70% of the work (my estimate). Once you count what the buyer needs before paying a premium (a validity opinion at $10-50k+, damages analysis, and in the end litigation at $1-5M+), discovery falls to maybe 10-20% of the work that creates the value. Litigation plays the role that building the plant plays in the geothermal counter-example: it is the physical step, and it is bespoke and expensive. A brokered sale of a claim-charted asset does exist as a sellable rung, but it captures only a small part of the step-up.
scored.step_up: Unproven: patents about to lapse, which the owner values at roughly the maintenance fee they are refusing to pay (third-stage USPTO fee is about $7.7-8k for a large entity, about $3k small entity; my estimate of the asking price is the candidate's $2-10k). Proven and claim-charted: from my memory of Richardson Oliver Insights brokered-market reports, which I could not re-verify this turn, average prices run about $100-250k per asset and have been falling, with most listed packages never selling. That is about 10-50x, not 200-2000x. A 1000x outcome only comes from litigation verdicts or settlements in the $5-50M+ range, and those require the full litigation spend, so they are not an immediate step-up on a hit. On an expiring patent, the only damages available are up to 6 years of past damages under 35 USC 286, which caps upside further.
scored.hit_rate_capex: These are my estimates from prior knowledge; the shared web-search budget was used up and I could not verify them this turn. Base hit rate: probably under 5% of lapse-bound materials composition patents have detectable US infringement with damages large enough to fund. Composition is often trade-secret or not detectable by teardown, and most of the market is Asian cell and magnet makers whose US sales base is limited. Cost per attempt: about $2-10k to buy plus $1-3k for the teardown, so under $15k. Proving is already cheap, so ML has little room to cut capex 10x. The cost that dominates is downstream: AIPLA survey figures put cost through trial at about $2-4M+ for mid-stakes cases, and PTAB instituted petitions historically end with all challenged claims unpatentable in roughly 60-70% of final decisions (from memory). ML does not lower those costs or risks.
scored.data: USPTO maintenance-fee events, assignments, PatentsView and INPADOC are public and fully legible. Anyone can pull the list of lapse-bound patents, so the selection signal gives no edge. The illegible part is matching claim ranges (composition windows, process parameters) to teardown papers, datasheets and academic characterisation of commercial cells and magnets. That signal is real and incumbents largely do not extract it at scale for materials, which is a genuine plus. The outcome is not summarised in a legible field: infringement status is not public until a suit is filed. Rights can be bought cheaply from universities, dead startups and non-core owners who will not pay the fee. One weakness: being about to lapse is negative selection, because the owners who know the art best judged the patent not worth about $8k.
scored.right_bought: Yes. Patents are bought by assignment, recorded at USPTO, from owners who are signalling low value by declining the maintenance fee. The purchase is cheap and clean. The cheapness partly reflects real low value (short remaining term, weak claims, no known infringer), not only an information asymmetry.
scored.buyer: Litigation funders (Burford, Fortress IP, Parabellum), aggregators and defensive buyers (RPX, AST, Unified Patents, Intellectual Ventures, Acacia), and possibly the infringers themselves. They are capitalised, but they buy selectively. Funders typically want expected damages above about $10-20M, and AST and RPX buy defensively at low prices per asset. Battery, magnet and catalyst assertions against CATL, BYD, LG, Shin-Etsu and Chinese NdFeB makers face low US damages bases and hard discovery. Litigation-grade patent analytics firms (e.g. Ocean Tomo, ipCreate, Unified Patents' own screening) already do claim-to-product mapping, though less so for materials.
scored.ladder: The rungs above are: brokered sale, then running assertion and licensing yourself (the Acacia/IV model), then funding your own litigation, then possibly owning an IP portfolio that shapes freedom-to-operate in battery, magnet or catalyst supply chains. This is the NPE ladder. History caps it: Acacia is worth about $0.3-0.5B, and IV raised about $6B with mediocre returns. The ladder does not climb into making materials. Climbing ends in being a litigation company, not a vertically integrated industrial company, so there is no realistic trillion-dollar path.
scored.fatal_flaw: The value is realised through litigation (or the credible threat of it), not through a cheap proving step. A $2k claim chart does not turn a $5k patent into a $5M asset. Validity challenges at PTAB, $2-4M+ trial costs, short remaining term and mostly foreign infringers with small US damages bases mean the bespoke, expensive downstream step dominates, just as building the plant does in the geothermal counter-example. Brokered-market prices of roughly $100-250k per asset cap the immediate step-up at about 10-50x, not 10^3.
scored.one_line_reason: There is real illegible-data alpha in matching materials claims to teardowns, but the discovery-heavy rung does not sell at a 10^3 step-up. Realising the value requires PTAB-risky, multi-million-dollar litigation, so the frame breaks the way the coal-mine geothermal example does.
sources: No live web sources: the shared 200-search budget for this turn ran out before any of this agent's searches went through, so every figure here is from prior knowledge and is unverified
USPTO fee schedule (37 CFR 1.20): third-stage (11.5-year) maintenance fee about $7.7-8k large entity, about $3k small entity (from memory)
Richardson Oliver Insights brokered patent market annual reports: average price per asset about $100-250k, falling, low sell-through (from memory)
AIPLA Report of the Economic Survey: patent litigation cost through trial about $2-4M+ for $10-25M at risk (from memory)
USPTO PTAB trial statistics: about 60-70% of final written decisions find all challenged claims unpatentable (from memory)
35 USC 286: 6-year limit on past damages

scored.name: University and National-Lab Patent Evidence-of-Use (Shelfware, Bayh-Dole sweep, LabOption)
scored.one_line: Take cheap exclusive licences or options with enforcement rights on unlicensed university and DOE/NASA lab patents (incl. robotics, photonics, superconductors); ML finds the few already practised in large shipping products; prove with EoU charts and sell or sublicense.
scored.unproven_right: Exclusive option/licence from TTOs or lab tech-transfer, ~$0-25k.
scored.proving_step: ML claims-to-product matching (FCC photos, manuals, job posts, teardowns); EoU chart; exercise option.
scored.proven_buyer: Funders and PAEs (WARF v. Apple $234M, Caltech v. Apple/Broadcom $1.1B verdict precedents), aggregators, OEMs buying FTO.
scored.public_data: USPTO assignee and government-interest data, AUTM, TTO listings, iEdison, NIH RePORTER/NSF, OSTI, NASA T2 portal, FLC listings, FCC filings.
scored.rough_step_up: ~50-1000x+; hit rate ~0.5-5%; labs may refuse assertion-driven licensing.
scored.frame: The candidate rung is: hold an exclusive option, find evidence of use (EoU), then sell or sublicense. Inside that rung, finding the infringing product is perhaps 40-60% of the work (my estimate). It is not 80%+. An EoU chart is only a claim of infringement. Buyers pay for validity that survives an IPR challenge, enforceability and damages, and getting those takes litigation. AIPLA surveys put patent litigation through trial at roughly $2-5M for $10-25M at risk (from memory, not re-checked). That makes the physical step the expensive, bespoke part, the same shape as the coal-mine geothermal counter-example. The narrow rung of selling EoU-charted assets to aggregators does exist, but the price step-up there is modest.
scored.step_up: These are estimates; I could not verify them because the shared web-search budget was exhausted. Unproven: an exclusive option or licence on an unlicensed university or lab patent costs about $0-50k upfront plus royalty or revenue share. Proven on the brokered market: Richardson Oliver-style reports historically show average asking prices of about $100-300k per patent asset, with EoU-backed assets at the upper end. Proven means EoU-charted against a large shipping product but not litigated. So a typical hit is about 10-100x. Litigated jackpots are larger but rare and often reversed. WARF v. Apple ($234M in 2015) was reversed by the Federal Circuit in 2018. Caltech v. Apple/Broadcom ($1.1B in 2020) had its damages vacated in 2022 and settled in 2023 for an undisclosed amount. Those outcomes came after roughly $10M+ of litigation, not on a hit.
scored.hit_rate_capex: These are estimates, not verified this run. The candidate's own base hit rate is about 0.5-5% of unlicensed university patents being practised in a large product. Commonly cited estimates say most university patents (often quoted as over 50-70%) never generate licence income. Cost per EoU attempt with analysts is about $5-20k per patent, and ML could cut screening cost 10x+. However, discovery is not the binding capex. Litigation ($2-5M per case) and IPR invalidation risk dominate. A significant share of instituted PTAB claims are found unpatentable, often cited as a majority (my recollection). ML does not lower the cost of proof that buyers actually pay for, so the lever on total capex is small.
scored.data: Signal: patents and claims are public and legible (USPTO full text). Products are partly illegible: FCC internal photos, manuals, teardowns, job posts. The outcome is not summarised in a public field, because licence status sits in iEdison and TTO records that are largely non-public. Partial counter-point: TTO 'available technology' listings advertise unlicensed status. Incumbents already do claims-to-product matching with ML and analysts. Examples: patent-analytics firms such as Patlytics and Clarivate-type EoU services, Intellectual Ventures' former university programme, Dominion Harbor, IPNav-style PAEs, Allied Security Trust and RPX on the defensive side, and litigation funders such as Burford. The data edge is real but contested.
scored.right_bought: Yes, the right is bought, not free first-come. Options and licences are negotiated with TTOs at low upfront cost. Two frictions are large. First, AUTM's 'Nine Points to Consider' and many university policies discourage licensing to assertion entities. DOE and NASA labs face government-interest and march-in constraints and political sensitivity. Second, enforcement usually needs the university to join as a party, and the university can refuse. Many good-quality patents are also near expiry, since damages look back only 6 years. Sellers cannot easily read EoU evidence, so there is an information asymmetry, but the supply of willing sellers is narrowed by policy rather than by price.
scored.buyer: Capitalised buyers exist: PAEs, aggregators (RPX, AST), litigation funders, and OEMs buying patents for defence or freedom to operate. They pay for de-risked validity and enforceability more than for EoU alone. The brokered patent market is thin and has been soft relative to its 2011-2012 peak.
scored.ladder: The ladder is: option, then EoU, then sale to an aggregator, then running your own assertion or litigation, then a funded portfolio, possibly then product or FTO licensing. It is capped at a large IP-monetisation firm (Acacia/IV scale, single-digit $B). It is not a trillion-dollar path, because the top rung is litigation, not production, and policy and reputational limits restrict scale.
scored.fatal_flaw: The 'proving step' (an EoU chart) does not prove the asset. Value is realised only after multi-million-dollar litigation and survival at the PTAB, which is the bespoke physical step. University and AUTM policy against assertion licensing restricts supply. The headline precedents (WARF, Caltech) were reversed or vacated after years of litigation.
scored.one_line_reason: Discovery is cheap and ML helps, but the expensive, failure-prone step is litigation and validity, not discovery, so no 80%+ discovery rung exists with a clean 10^3x step-up.

scored.name: Open-Source Code Infringement Finder
scored.one_line: Buy software and networking patents cheaply and use ML over public source (Linux, AOSP, Chromium, GitHub) to prove code-level use in Big Tech products; sell to funders.
scored.unproven_right: Low-value software/method patents in bulk.
scored.proving_step: ML mapping claim steps to functions, traced to shipping binaries.
scored.proven_buyer: Funders, NPEs, defensive aggregators.
scored.public_data: GitHub/AOSP/Chromium/Linux repos and commits, USPTO full text, PTAB decisions.
scored.frame: The rung is "buy a cheap patent, then attach an evidence-of-use (EoU) claim chart and resell it as a chart-backed asset." Inside that rung, discovery (finding claim-to-code matches) is maybe 70-80% of the work. That rung is thin, though. Buyers such as funders, NPEs and aggregators (RPX, Unified Patents) pay a modest premium for a chart, but they discount it heavily because the real value only shows up in the next step: litigation or licensing, plus surviving Alice and IPR. That step is not trivial or abstracted. It costs millions and takes 2-4 years, and the claim may be invalidated. Inside the full monetisation frame, discovery is maybe 10-20% of the work (my estimate). This looks like the coal-mine geothermal counter-example: the bespoke litigation is much harder than finding the infringer.
scored.step_up: From memory, not verified (the search budget was used up, so no live searches ran). Distressed or bulk software patents (bankruptcy lots, near-lapse assets): roughly $5k-$30k each. Brokered-market average ask per US asset (Richardson Oliver brokered-market reports, around 2018-2022): roughly $150k-$300k, and actual sales come in lower. A chart-backed asset with clear EoU against a Big Tech product might sell for $250k-$1M+ (estimate). That is about 10-100x at the moment it is proven. Bigger multiples (verdicts of $10M-$500M+) only come after trial, not immediately. The candidate's 60-600x mixes the litigation outcome into the proving step.
scored.hit_rate_capex: My estimate: most bulk software patents have no clean EoU against a big target, with a base hit rate of maybe 1-5%. That caps the ML lever at about 20-100x. But one proving attempt (a manual claim chart from a search firm or analyst) already costs only about $3k-$20k (estimate). Discovery is not the expensive part. Litigation is: the AIPLA Economic Survey puts median cost through trial at roughly $2-4M+ for cases with $10M-$25M+ at risk (recalled, not verified). So cutting chart cost 10x saves little of the total capex. The real failure point is validity. From memory: when PTAB reaches a final decision, all challenged claims are found unpatentable in roughly 60-70% of cases, and Alice §101 motions knock out a large share of software claims.
scored.data: The data is public: GitHub, AOSP, Chromium, Linux, USPTO full text and PTAB decisions. Unlike Terranox's scanned assessment files, it is not illegible. Source code is highly structured and already searchable, and code-search plus LLM claim-charting tools already exist (Patlytics, IPRally, Amplified, Traindex-style EoU tools, and in-house analytics at RPX and Unified Patents). The outcome (does a product infringe?) is not summarised in any public field, which is good. One gap: open source does not prove what ships in a closed product binary. That gap is where the real proof work sits, and binary tracing is harder.
scored.right_bought: Yes. Patents are bought, not claimed first-come. They can be bought cheaply from bankrupt startups, from corporate portfolio pruning, and from inventors near the maintenance-fee deadline, and many sellers have not charted their assets against Big Tech. The catch for Linux and Android targets: Open Invention Network (OIN) and LOT Network cross-licenses cover many potential sellers' patents and many targets' Linux-system code. That shrinks both the pool of assertable patents and the set of reachable defendants.
scored.buyer: Litigation funders (Burford, Fortress IP, Parabellum), NPEs (Acacia, Dominion Harbor, IP Edge-style), and defensive aggregators (RPX, AST, Unified Patents). They are well capitalised, but they price on expected litigation value net of IPR and Alice risk, so they pay a small fraction of headline damages.
scored.ladder: Chart-backed resale, then running your own assertion with contingency counsel, then a litigation-finance fund, then a licensing platform (InterDigital or Acacia style). The ceiling is set by the cases themselves: the largest pure-play monetisation firms are worth single-digit billions. There is no path to a trillion-dollar company, because the chain ends in settlements, not production. Courts, policy (PTAB, Alice, venue rules) and reputation cap growth.
scored.fatal_flaw: The step-up does not happen on the proving step. A claim chart does not turn a patent into a proven asset the way a drill hit proves a deposit. Most of the value appears only after millions spent on litigation and surviving Alice and IPR invalidity challenges, where most software claims die. So discovery is not 80%+ of any sellable rung. The bespoke, expensive step (litigation) dominates, like the coal-mine geothermal case. On top of that, many potential sellers' patents and Linux targets fall under the OIN and LOT cross-licenses, and AI EoU charting is already crowded (Patlytics and others).
scored.one_line_reason: Rights are cheap and the outcome is not written into a public field, but proof only comes through costly litigation that often kills the patent, so the claim chart gives a 10-100x discounted bump rather than an immediate 10^3-10^4 step-up.

AIPLA Report of the Economic Survey (median patent litigation cost through trial, $2-4M+), recalled

scored.name: Foreign-Language Family Importer
scored.one_line: Buy Japanese, Korean, German and Chinese patents from shrinking domestic owners with open US paths or German/UPC enforceability; ML translates and maps to big products; sell to European funders under injunction threat.
scored.unproven_right: Foreign-language patents unread by Western markets, $5-30k.
scored.proving_step: Translation, product mapping, EoU chart.
scored.proven_buyer: European funders, Munich/Düsseldorf NPEs, IP Bridge-style funds.
scored.public_data: J-PlatPat, KIPRIS, CNIPA, DPMA, EPO register, UPC case data.
scored.frame: Rung: buy a foreign-language patent family, then produce a claim chart mapping it to a big product (evidence of use, EoU) and sell it as a litigation-ready asset. Inside that rung, discovery (translating, mapping claims to products, charting) is maybe 40-60% of the work (my estimate). The physical step is enforcement: German/UPC suits, validity fights at the BPatG/EPO, and US prosecution or continuation work. That step is neither trivial nor abstracted, and it is where buyers find the value. Buyers (funders, NPEs) exist and have capital, but they price in litigation risk, so the rung does not cleanly close at proof.
scored.step_up: Unproven: $5-30k per family (the candidate's figure; this matches my estimate that Japanese and Korean corporates prune or dump portfolios at near maintenance cost). Proven: from memory of Richardson Oliver Insights brokered-market data, average asking price is roughly $100-250k per US patent asset, and realised sale prices are lower. An EoU-charted family against a major product sold to an NPE or funder plausibly fetches $250k-2M (my estimate). That is about 10-100x typical and up to ~100-300x at the top end, not 10^3-10^4. Most value only arrives after 1-3 years of litigation or settlement.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Base hit rate: roughly 1-5% of patents in a pruned portfolio have a credible EoU read on a high-revenue product and survive validity scrutiny (my estimate; this is the industry rule of thumb that most patents are never licensable). Cost per proving attempt: manual EoU charting runs about $5-20k per patent via analyst firms (estimate). Triage on top of that adds about $0.5-2k per patent. ML could cut screening cost per family roughly 5-10x. The lever is capped near 20-100x by the base rate, but the binding cost is validity and enforcement, not screening.
scored.data: J-PlatPat, KIPRIS, CNIPA, DPMA and the EPO register are public and structured (full text, legal status, family data). Machine translation is already free and good: EPO Patent Translate, Google Patents and J-PlatPat's English interface. So the 'illegible because foreign-language' premise is weak, since Western analysts already read these routinely. The outcome (does it read on product X) is not written in any legal-status field, which is good. Product-side teardown data, however, is private or paid. Rights are bought, not free, which fits the rubric. But owners such as Panasonic, Sony, NEC, Fujitsu, Hitachi, Samsung and LG are sophisticated sellers. They work through brokers and government-backed funds and know which families map to products.
scored.right_bought: Assignment of patent families from shrinking or exiting Japanese, Korean, German and Chinese owners, through brokers or direct deals. Large Asian corporates have spun out families to NPEs before. Examples from memory: Panasonic families to Sovereign Peak Ventures, and NEC/Fujitsu-origin assets in IP Bridge and other vehicles.
scored.buyer: Litigation funders, Munich/Düsseldorf/UPC-focused NPEs, and patent aggregators such as IP Bridge (a Japanese government-backed fund doing exactly this), Intellectual Discovery (Korea), Sisvel, Acacia, Dominion Harbor and Atlantic IP. Several of these are direct competitors for the same supply, not just buyers.
scored.ladder: Buy families, chart them, sell; then assert in-house in Germany/UPC; then build a portfolio licensing program or pool; then become a full IP monetisation house (Acacia/IV scale). This is a real ladder, but the top of it is a litigation and licensing business worth low billions at most (Acacia, InterDigital-type valuations). It does not climb into the underlying industry, so there is no trillion-dollar path.
scored.fatal_flaw: The discovery edge is illusory, and the value sits in enforcement. Foreign-language patents are already legible: free machine translation exists, and IP Bridge, Intellectual Discovery, brokers and Asian corporates' own licensing arms already mine them. The step-up is only about 10-100x. It is realised mainly through years of costly German/UPC/US litigation and validity fights, not on proof. That is the geothermal-in-coal-mine pattern: the hard, bespoke step is enforcement, not finding.
scored.one_line_reason: Rights are bought, buyers have capital and the outcome is not in a status field. But translation is no longer a moat, incumbents such as IP Bridge already do this, the step-up is about 10-100x, and value comes from litigation rather than discovery. Scores below threshold (12/25). All numbers are my estimates from memory: the shared web-search budget was exhausted before any search ran.

scored.name: Replication-Proven Lab Materials Licences (ShelfLicense, Dormant Lab Option Book, Materials Claim Matcher)
scored.one_line: Take cheap exclusive or field-of-use options on unlicensed university and DOE/NASA/AFRL/NRL materials patents (catalysts, electrolytes, cathodes, alloys, magnets); ML over papers, SI data, citations and DFT screening (Materials Project/OQMD) picks claims that really work or contain untested winning compositions; a small contract-lab replication or synthesis run proves them; sublicense or sell to chemical and cell majors.
scored.unproven_right: Exclusive options/licences ($5-50k) from motivated TTOs and federal labs (37 CFR 404).
scored.proving_step: ML ranking, then $20-60k replication/synthesis of 10-50 compositions at a cloud or contract lab, plus FTO and claim mapping.
scored.proven_buyer: BASF, Johnson Matthey, Umicore, Clariant, Topsoe, 3M, LG, Panasonic; aggregators.
scored.public_data: AUTM/TTO pages, DOE Lab Partnering Service, NASA T2, Federal Register licence notices, OSTI and DTIC reports, PatentsView, Crossref and SI PDFs, Materials Project/OQMD/AFLOW.
scored.rough_step_up: ~10-500x; buyers discount anything not at cell scale.
scored.frame: The rung is: hold an option on a dormant lab materials patent and prove the claim at bench scale. Inside that rung, discovery (ML triage over papers, SI files and DFT databases) is maybe 50-60% of the work, not 80%+ (my estimate). The physical step is not trivial. Synthesis is the easy part. Making a result that a buyer will accept (cell-format or reactor-format testing, months of cycle-life or durability runs, scale-up, impurity tolerance) is bespoke wet-lab work that takes months. It is the same failure as the geothermal-in-coal-mines counter-example: finding the right patent is easier than proving it to the standard a buyer pays for. Capitalised buyers do exist (BASF, Umicore, Johnson Matthey, LG and others). But they buy de-risked, scaled data, not a 10-50 composition bench screen.
scored.step_up: All numbers are my estimates; no search could be run. Unproven: option or exclusive licence at $5-50k upfront plus patent cost reimbursement. That price is plausible for federal labs under 37 CFR 404 and for TTOs. Proven at bench: the realistic sublicence is $50-500k upfront plus a low single-digit royalty that only pays out years later, if the material reaches product. That is about 5-30x on cash outlay, and only sometimes. The candidate's own 10-500x figure assumes a buyer pays without cell-scale data, which buyers rarely do. Compare Terranox: about 10^4 on $/ha, realisable at once from a junior or major miner. There is no liquid spot market that reprices a bench-replicated materials patent overnight.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Base hit rate: from memory of AUTM survey patterns, most university patents are never licensed (roughly 1 in 3 to 1 in 5 inventions get licensed). Most licences earn little, and income sits in a handful of blockbusters. Commonly cited estimates put the share of published materials results that reproduce at 30-60%, and a much smaller share survive commercial-format testing (<5%, my estimate). Cost per proving attempt: the candidate's $20-60k covers bench synthesis plus FTO work. Proof a buyer accepts is more like $0.5-3M: pouch or 18650 cells, pilot reactor runs, 6-18 months (my estimate). ML can raise the bench hit rate. But the expensive, failing step is scale-up, and literature or DFT signals predict that poorly. The lever on the step that matters is perhaps 2-3x, not 10x.
scored.data: Public and illegible: yes. SI PDFs, OSTI and DTIC reports, patent claims, and Materials Project, OQMD and AFLOW data are scattered and unstructured. The outcome is not written into a legible field, which is a real plus over the regulator-status-field hunts. But much of the DFT signal is already structured and public. Many groups mine it (Citrine, Kebotix, Aionics, Mitra Chem, CuspAI, Orbital Materials, Periodic Labs, and big-pharma-style in-house teams at BASF and Umicore). So the edge is in linking papers to patents to whether the claim works, not in raw access. Incumbents do this partially, through scouting teams and open-innovation programmes.
scored.right_bought: Yes, the right is bought. Exclusive or field-of-use options from TTOs and federal labs are cheap ($5-50k, sometimes less for federal labs) and are negotiated, not free first-come. The sellers are motivated but can read the patents. They lack the means to validate them, not the ability to understand them. Problems: federal and university patents often have 8-14 years of term left by the time they are dormant, and option windows are short (12-24 months). Proving and selling must fit that window. Allied Minds is the cautionary precedent. It ran a near-identical model of licensing federal-lab and university IP to build companies, and destroyed most of its value from roughly 2015 to 2020.
scored.buyer: BASF, Johnson Matthey, Umicore, Clariant, Topsoe, 3M, LG Energy Solution, Panasonic, plus patent aggregators. These buyers are well capitalised. But they habitually take materials IP through low-upfront, royalty-heavy, milestone-gated deals. They often wait for patents to lapse, or design around composition claims, rather than paying a large upfront for bench data. Aggregators value materials patents mostly as litigation assets. Secondary-market patent prices typically run around $100-250k per asset and are heavy in electronics and software, not composition-of-matter materials (my recollection of broker-market data, not verified this session).
scored.ladder: The ladder is real. Option book, then bench proof, then scale-up and pilot, then a toll-manufactured materials business, then a vertically integrated materials or cathode or catalyst producer. Umicore and Johnson Matthey are multi-$10B outcomes. But each rung above the first is capital- and time-heavy (pilot lines at $10-100M). The bottom rung does not generate enough cash on its own to fund the climb.
scored.fatal_flaw: The proving step a buyer pays for is not the cheap bench replication. It is cell-scale or reactor-scale validation and scale-up, which costs $0.5-3M and takes months, and literature or DFT ML predicts it poorly. So discovery is not 80%+ of the rung, and there is no 10^3-10^4 immediate step-up. Buyers discount anything not proven at scale, and they pay mostly in deferred royalties.
scored.one_line_reason: The right is cheap and the data is illegible, but the physical proof a buyer will pay for is bespoke and costly (the geothermal-in-coal-mines failure). The step-up is about 10x, paid as deferred royalties, not an immediate 10^4. Allied Minds already ran this model and lost most of its value.
