scored.name: Orphan Lazarus: dormant orphan-designated assets with positive data
scored.one_line: Buy shelved compounds with orphan designation and positive signal from divestitures or dead biotechs; get FDA alignment on accelerated or single-trial path; sell, or approve for orphan exclusivity plus a rare pediatric PRV.
scored.unproven_right: Shelved compound with designation and IP, $0.1-3M.
scored.proving_step: ML linking designations to results and sponsor status; FDA Type C meeting (full proof is a trial).
scored.proven_buyer: BioMarin, Ultragenyx, Ipsen, Sobi, Chiesi, PRV buyers.
scored.public_data: FDA orphan database, EMA COMP register, ClinicalTrials.gov/AACT, PubMed, bankruptcy dockets, Google Patents.
scored.rough_step_up: ~30x at FDA alignment, more on approval; full proof is not 80% discovery.
scored.frame: The candidate rung is buying a shelved compound and getting FDA alignment. On my estimate, discovery (finding the shelved asset with a positive signal) is about 20-30% of the work. The rest is CMC and tech transfer, regulatory work, and a clinical trial that is still needed. A Type C meeting gives FDA's non-binding view, not proof. Buyers will not pay proven-asset prices on meeting minutes alone. The rung where value is actually proven ends at clinical data or approval, and there discovery is well under 20% of the work, because trials and manufacturing dominate. The physical step is neither trivial nor abstracted. This is the coal-mine-geothermal pattern: finding the asset is easier than developing it.
scored.step_up: These numbers are my estimates. The search budget was used up, so none of them were checked this run. Unproven: shelved orphan assets from dead biotechs or divestitures change hands for about $0.1-3M upfront (candidate's figure), usually plus milestones. After FDA alignment the asset might license for about $5-30M upfront: roughly 10-30x, often paid as contingent milestones rather than cash. After approval, an orphan asset with a rare pediatric PRV could be worth $150M+ (recent PRV sales were roughly $100-158M, from memory) plus commercial value: about 100-1000x. But that needs a $20-100M+ trial and years of work, so the multiple on total capital in is about 3-10x, not 10^4. Whether the rare pediatric PRV program has been reauthorized past its late-2024 sunset is unconfirmed; this is a key risk.
scored.hit_rate_capex: These are rough estimates from memory, not checked this run. About 20-25% of FDA orphan designations ever lead to an approved indication (roughly 1,000+ approvals against about 6,500+ designations). For rescued assets that already have positive Phase 2 signals, Phase 2 to approval in rare disease runs about 25-35%. One proving attempt is a pivotal or single-arm trial costing about $20-100M+ (rare disease trial cost, estimate). A Type C meeting is cheap (about $0.2-1M in consultants and preparation, estimate) but proves little. ML can improve which assets get picked, but it cannot cut trial cost 10x. The trial is a physical and clinical cost, not a discovery cost. The lever is capped near 1/0.3, about 3x, and only on selection.
scored.data: The sources are public: the FDA orphan designation database, EMA COMP register, ClinicalTrials.gov/AACT, PubMed, bankruptcy dockets and patents. But the outcome is largely already legible. ClinicalTrials.gov carries structured status fields (terminated or withdrawn, with a reason field) and many posted results. The FDA orphan database shows designation and approval status. Bankruptcy dockets list assets for sale through bankers. Sellers are sophisticated: pharma business development teams, liquidators, and investment banks running processes. They read the same data, so the purchase discount comes from their lack of capital, not from data they cannot read. Rights are bought rather than free, which is good. But the ML edge is thin: this is the same pattern as earlier hunts where regulators had already written the answer into status fields.
scored.right_bought: Exclusive license or asset purchase of IP, data packages, INDs and orphan designations from defunct biotechs (via bankruptcy 363 sales or liquidating trustees) or from pharma divestitures. Orphan designation is transferable with sponsor change notice to FDA. Price is about $0.1-3M upfront plus milestones and royalties (estimate).
scored.buyer: Rare-disease pharma (BioMarin, Ultragenyx, Ipsen, Sobi, Chiesi, Amryt/Chiesi, Jazz) for approved or late-stage assets. Large pharma buys PRVs (historically about $100-158M each; estimate from memory). These buyers are well capitalised, but they mostly pay for clinical data, not for FDA meeting minutes.
scored.ladder: Strong in principle: asset rescue, then trial execution, then approval and PRV sale, then commercial rare-disease franchise, then platform and manufacturing. Every rung above the first is a full biopharma build, but the path to a large company is real (BridgeBio and Roivant are precedents).
scored.fatal_flaw: The proving step is a clinical trial, not discovery. Turning a shelved orphan asset into a value-proven asset costs $20-100M+ and takes years, so discovery is far below 80% of the rung. FDA alignment alone is not a sellable step-up that a capitalised buyer pays proven prices for. The trial outcome and sponsor status are already legible in ClinicalTrials.gov and FDA status fields. Competition is crowded: Roivant, BridgeBio, Fortress, royalty and asset-rescue funds, and pharma business development teams.
scored.one_line_reason: This is a variant of the previously weak stranded-drug-rescue idea: finding the asset is easy and proving it (a trial) is the expensive physical work, so there is no rung where discovery is 80% or more.

scored.name: Orphan Sole-Source Defense Parts (SoleSource Shells, Orphan Tooling, stranded DLA NSN sources)
scored.one_line: Buy the drawings, tooling, TDPs and CAGE/approved-source standing of tiny closing or defunct machine shops and military electronics suppliers at scrap value; ML over DIBBS, FLIS/PUB LOG and scanned SAR/J&A records finds NSNs with recurring sole-source demand and dead approved sources; novate or SAR-qualify, deliver first awards via contract shops, and sell proven part families to aftermarket roll-ups.
scored.unproven_right: Asset purchase of tech data, tooling and approved-source status ($1k-200k) from estates, auctions and retiring owners.
scored.proving_step: ML ranking of NSN demand and source status; DCMA novation or SAR plus first-article test; first awards delivered.
scored.proven_buyer: TransDigm, Heico, Arcline/Kaman, AMETEK, defense PE roll-ups (15-25x EBITDA), DLA long-term contracts.
scored.public_data: DLA DIBBS solicitations and awards, FLIS/PUB LOG, SAM.gov CAGE status, FPDS, AMSC codes, GIDEP/DMSMS notices, PACER schedules, auction catalogues.
scored.rough_step_up: ~20-1000x; manufacturing and SAR are real steps; adjacent to killed FAA PMA.
scored.frame: The rung would be: buy a dead or closing approved source's TDP, tooling and standing, then win DLA awards on its NSNs. Discovery is not 80%+ of the work inside this rung. My estimate is that finding the right NSN or estate is about 30-45%. The rest is physical and bureaucratic. You need DCMA novation, or government consent where approved-source status is tied to a specific manufacturer and facility. Moving production to a contract shop usually means requalifying through a SAR or first-article test. Then you need repeated real manufacturing at mil-spec quality. Physical delivery is the main work, not a trivial or abstracted step. This is structurally the same failure as killed FAA PMA and as geothermal-in-coal-mines.
scored.step_up: My estimate, unverified. The unproven right is an asset purchase of tech data and tooling for about $1k-200k, the candidate's own range. A proven part family with about $0.3-2M a year of recurring DLA revenue at 25-40% EBITDA, sold at aftermarket multiples, is worth about $1-10M. TransDigm and Heico trade at roughly 20-30x EBITDA from memory; private tuck-ins clear nearer 10-15x. That is about 10-200x on a hit. It is not immediate: value appears only after novation or SAR approval plus delivered awards, about 1-3 years in. It does not come from the discovery itself.
scored.hit_rate_capex: My estimate, unverified. Proving costs about $20-150k per attempt: TDP purchase, legal novation work, SAR package prep, first-article test about $10-50k, and a tooling refurbishment or first lot. Engineering-review time runs 6-18 months. I would put the base success rate at about 20-40% for SAR approval plus winning the award, so the lever is capped at about 2.5-5x, not 10x. Most failures are on the government side (rejected or slow SARs, lost price competition) or on manufacturing, and ML ranking cannot fix those.
scored.data: Most of the outcome is already in legible fields. DIBBS solicitations list approved-source CAGE and part numbers plus AMSC/AMC codes, where AMSC C or similar means sole source for lack of data rights. SAM.gov shows CAGE status as active or expired. FLIS/PUB LOG gives demand and reference data, and FPDS gives award history. A lookup table of sole-source AMSC, an inactive CAGE and recurring demand probably captures most of the signal, as with killed interconnection queues. The genuinely illegible part is scanned J&A and SAR history and estate inventories, which is a thin edge. The right can be bought cheaply from estates and retiring owners, which is a real plus. But approved-source status often does not transfer with an asset sale, so what you buy is data, not standing.
scored.right_bought: Drawings, TDPs, tooling and possibly the corporate shell or CAGE of tiny closing or defunct defense machine shops and electronics suppliers. Asset purchases cost about $1k-200k (candidate range). Approved-source standing needs DCMA novation or government recognition and is not reliably conveyed.
scored.buyer: Real and well capitalised, but they buy proven EBITDA, not unproven rights: TransDigm, Heico (Wencor), Arcline/Kaman, AMETEK and defense aftermarket PE roll-ups. DLA buys parts, not rights. Competitors already doing this include many small DIBBS bid shops, reverse-engineering and SAR specialists, and PE platforms that buy orphan part lines.
scored.ladder: The rungs go: buy orphan TDPs, win DLA sole-source awards, run your own manufacturing, consolidate many part families into an aftermarket roll-up, then become an OEM-level supplier. That is the TransDigm playbook, about a $70-80B market cap from memory, so a big ladder exists. The trouble is the bottom rung, which is not discovery-dominated.
scored.fatal_flaw: The proving step is mostly manufacturing and government requalification, not discovery. Approved-source status is tied to the manufacturer, facility and process, so it rarely transfers cleanly with an asset purchase, and novation, SAR approval and first-article work take months and real capex. On top of that, the key outcome signals (sole-source AMSC codes, approved CAGE, inactive CAGE status, demand history) are already legible in DIBBS, SAM and FLIS. ML adds little over a lookup table, and the hit rate is set by DLA engineering review and production rather than by finding the asset. It is the same shape as killed FAA PMA.
scored.one_line_reason: It is adjacent to killed FAA PMA: cheap tech data can be bought, but proving it means requalification plus manufacturing, not discovery, and DIBBS, SAM and FLIS fields already expose most of the signal.

scored.name: Surplus Military and Government Aviation Lots to Serviceable (Scrap-to-Serviceable, Surplus Lift, Bone Yard Records)
scored.one_line: Buy DLA Disposition, GSA, GovPlanet and foreign-military surplus aircraft, engines, rotables and avionics priced as scrap; vision/NLP over listing photos, NSN text, scanned logbooks and FLIS finds civil-certifiable, high-life, traceable items; reconstruct records, get 8130-3 tags via Part 145 shops; sell to USM distributors, MROs and firefighting operators.
scored.unproven_right: Title to as-is surplus lots bought by weight or pallet.
scored.proving_step: Part and civil-equivalent identification, records/back-to-birth reconstruction, repair-station inspection and tag.
scored.proven_buyer: AAR, AerSale, VSE, Kellstrom, Coulson-type firefighters, engine MROs.
scored.public_data: DLA Disposition/GovPlanet/GSA Auctions listings and photos, FLIS/PUB LOG, AMARG inventory, FAA TCDS, registry and SDRs, ILS/PartsBase signals.
scored.rough_step_up: ~5-1000x per hit, ~10-50x per lot; demil/ITAR limits; adjacent to killed FAA PMA.
scored.frame: The rung would be "own an as-is surplus lot and turn it into tagged, eligible civil inventory." Discovery (spotting the civil-equivalent, high-life, traceable item in a lot) is maybe 30-50% of the work at most (my estimate). The rest is physical and regulatory: teardown and inspection at a repair station, overhaul (for engines and rotables, overhaul often costs 20-60% of the serviceable price), records reconstruction, and the FAA eligibility case under AC 20-62 / 14 CFR 21.9 for military-origin parts. Unlike drilling for Terranox, the proving step is not abstracted. It is the core cost and the core risk, which puts it closer to the geothermal-in-coal-mines counter-example than to Terranox. Capitalised buyers (AAR, AerSale, VSE, engine MROs, restricted-category firefighting operators) do exist and do buy tagged USM.
scored.step_up: No live numbers: the shared web-search budget was used up before this agent ran, so every figure below is an estimate from domain knowledge. Lots sold by weight or as scrap typically clear at about 1-10% of the serviceable USM price. A single high-value rotable or LRU bought for roughly $100-$1,000 might sell tagged for $5k-$100k, which is 10-100x gross per hit and occasionally ~1000x on an outlier. Net of overhaul, the shop's inspection-and-tag charge and records work, I'd put the per-lot multiple at ~3-20x. That is a C2 of 3, not 4-5.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Estimate, not sourced. A shot is cheap to take: buying a lot costs hundreds to low thousands of dollars. The expensive part is proving: repair-station inspection or test costs ~$1k-$10k per rotable and $100k+ for an engine teardown or overhaul. The base hit rate, meaning the share of surplus items that end up civil-eligible and saleable, is maybe 5-20%. Most military parts are military-unique, demil-coded, flight-safety-critical (FSCAP) items that must be mutilated, or have no paperwork trail an FAA repair station would accept. ML screening of listings could plausibly lift that 2-4x. It cannot cut proving capex 10x, because most of the capex comes after identification (overhaul and tagging), not in finding the item. The lever is real but capped well below 10x.
scored.data: The data is public: DLA Disposition, GovPlanet and GSA Auctions listings and photos, FLIS/PUB LOG cross-references from NSN to manufacturer part number, AMARG inventories, FAA TCDS and SDRs. It is only semi-legible, though. FLIS already maps NSNs to commercial part numbers in a structured field, and the auction listings carry demil codes and condition codes, so much of the answer is already written into legible fields. That repeats the 'regulator writes the answer into status fields' failure. Scanned logbooks are the truly illegible part, but they rarely ship with the lots.
scored.right_bought: The right is bought: title to as-is lots through competitive public auctions (GovPlanet/Liquidity Services and GSA). The seller is the government. It can't read the data, but it isn't negotiating either. Thousands of experienced surplus brokers and parts dealers bid on the same listings with the same FLIS lookups, so auction competition removes much of the 'priced as scrap' discount on anything recognisably valuable (my estimate). Supply is also policy-constrained. DoD demil and FSCAP rules require high-risk flight-critical parts to be mutilated instead of sold, and ITAR/EAR limits apply to many items.
scored.buyer: USM distributors and MROs (AAR, AerSale, VSE, Kellstrom, Werner), engine shops for military-derivative engines (T56/501-D, F108/CFM56, T700/CT7, PT6), and restricted-category operators flying ex-military types (Coulson and other firefighting C-130 and UH-60 operators). All are well capitalised and buy tagged inventory continuously.
scored.ladder: Rung 1: surplus lots to tagged USM. Rung 2: an in-house Part 145 repair station and engine/rotable overhaul. Rung 3: whole-airframe acquisition and restricted-category conversion (firefighting tankers, utility helicopters), plus lease pools. Rung 4: an aftermarket platform spanning parts, MRO and operations (AerSale/AAR-scale, several $B). A real ladder, but it tops out as a large aftermarket services firm, not a trillion-dollar path. Score 3.
scored.fatal_flaw: Discovery is not the bottleneck. The value is created by the physical and regulatory proving step: overhaul and inspection plus FAA eligibility of military-origin parts under AC 20-62 / 21.9, which ML cannot abstract. The supply that ML could find is either auction-competed by experienced surplus brokers using the same structured FLIS cross-reference, or barred from sale entirely by DoD FSCAP/demil mutilation rules. There is no frame where discovery is 80%+ and the right is cheap to buy.
scored.one_line_reason: This is a known, competitive surplus-broker business where the proving step (overhaul, records, FAA eligibility) is the main cost, FLIS already makes identification legible, and demil rules and auction competition remove the cheap-right advantage. It scores about 12/25: it fails C1 and C4, has a modest ~10-100x step-up per hit, and a hit-rate lever well under 10x.

scored.name: Billboard Permit Hunting / Grandfathered Wall: dormant legal-nonconforming sign rights
scored.one_line: Buy or lease parcels and building walls in capped jurisdictions (highways, NYC, LA, SF, Chicago, Houston) where an old sign right may still be legally valid; ML over scanned DOT permits, council minutes, NYC 1940/1980s tax photos and DOB/BSA records proves legal establishment and continuity; sell or lease to outdoor operators.
scored.unproven_right: Options or leases on parcels/walls whose owners think the right is dead, near zero to $10k.
scored.proving_step: Reconstruct sign existence, size and continuous use; DOT/city confirmation, DOB registration or BSA appeal. Continuity breaks kill many.
scored.proven_buyer: Lamar, Outfront, Clear Channel, Colossal-type wallscape operators, REITs.
scored.public_data: State DOT permit files, municipal sign inventories, NYC Municipal Archives tax photos, DOB BIS/NOW, BSA and OATH decisions, LADBS microfiche, historic street view, AADT.
scored.frame: The rung is: hold an option or lease on a wall or parcel, prove a valid legal-nonconforming sign right, then lease or sell it to an outdoor operator. Inside that rung, discovery and proof (archive research, the legal case, a DOB registration or BSA/DOT filing) is about 70-85% of the work by my estimate. The physical step is cheap: a static face or wallscape costs roughly $20k-$150k to build (estimate). The buyers (Lamar, Outfront, Clear Channel, wallscape operators) are well capitalised and already buy permits and ground leases. The frame is real but narrow, and the legal fight is not trivial: it is closer to litigation than to running an ML model.
scored.step_up: All estimates; I could not verify any of these online. Unproven: an option or lease on a wall whose owner thinks the sign right is dead, at about $0-10k. Proven: highway static billboard ground leases typically run about $2k-$30k a year, and a structure trades at about 8-15x cash flow, so roughly $50k-$500k per face. A good NYC or LA wallscape can rent for $100k-$1M+ a year, worth $1M-$5M+ capitalised. Against a $5k-$10k option that is about 10-500x, and above 1000x only at rare prime walls. Against the property's existing value the step-up is far smaller, because these walls and parcels are not near-zero assets. So the honest multiple is about 10-100x, with a fat tail.
scored.hit_rate_capex: All estimates; no search was possible. Base hit rate: probably under 10% of 'dormant' candidates survive. Most US sign codes count a right as abandoned after 12-24 months without use: NYC Zoning Resolution 52-61 extinguishes a non-conforming use after 2 years of discontinuance, and many state Highway Beautification Act programmes apply a 12-month abandonment rule. A sign that is truly dormant is therefore usually dead by law. Cost per proving attempt: a desk search is cheap (<$1k with ML). A real proof (expediter, zoning attorney, DOB filing, possible BSA appeal) costs about $25k-$150k and takes 1-3 years. ML only cuts the cheap desk-screening part. It does not cut the expensive legal step, so the realistic capex reduction is about 2-3x, not 10x.
scored.data: The signal is public and hard to read: NYC 1940 and 1980s tax photos, LADBS microfiche, DOT permit files, council minutes. That part is real. But much of the outcome is already written into legible fields. State DOT outdoor-advertising permit databases list each permit with an active, revoked or abandoned status. NYC has required Outdoor Advertising Company sign registration and inventories with DOB since Local Law 31 of 2001 (from memory, unverified), and operators had to register their sign inventory with supporting evidence. On top of that, outdoor operators' real-estate teams and NYC sign expediters already hunt pre-existing-use rights by hand using exactly these tax photos. Rights can be bought, because the wall owner can give an option or lease. But the right runs with the land, so the owner gains leverage once you show them it is valid, and operators already approach owners of prime walls.
scored.right_bought: Partly. An option or lease is bought from the owner, often cheaply. But the sign right is tied to the property, not a separate tradeable permit (except in some DOT regimes). Owners of prime walls in Manhattan, LA and SF are already approached by operators. And continuity rules mean a right that looks 'dormant' is usually extinguished as a matter of law, not just hidden from view.
scored.buyer: Lamar, Outfront Media, Clear Channel Outdoor, Colossal Media and other wallscape operators, plus REITs and landlords. They are capitalised and buy ground leases and permits routinely.
scored.ladder: Option or lease the wall, prove the right, then build and own the face yourself, convert it to digital where the code allows, and run an outdoor media operator. The ceiling is the US out-of-home market (about $9B a year in revenue; Lamar is worth about $12-15B, both figures from memory). It is a real ladder, but it is capped well below a trillion dollars, and caps on new permits in many jurisdictions limit how far it can grow.
scored.fatal_flaw: The continuity and abandonment rules. NYC ZR 52-61 ends a non-conforming use after 2 years of discontinuance, and most state DOT codes use 12-24 months, so most truly dormant sign rights are legally dead. The ones still alive are usually still in use, already registered in a legible DOT or DOB status field, and already known to operators. The proving step is a slow, expensive legal fight that ML does not make cheaper.
scored.one_line_reason: The economics are real but the multiple is middling (about 10-100x). Abandonment law means hidden dormant rights are mostly extinguished, the outcome sits in DOT and DOB status fields, operators already hunt these rights by hand, and ML only speeds up the cheap screening, not the costly legal proof.

Federal Highway Beautification Act 1965 (23 USC 131) and state DOT outdoor advertising permit and abandonment rules, from memory
Lamar Advertising and Outfront Media 10-K disclosures on ground leases and permit acquisitions, from memory

scored.name: Paw2Patient: proving shelved human compounds in companion animals
scored.one_line: Buy cheap veterinary rights to human-shelved compounds with targets conserved in dogs and cats, prove them in a small pilot in client-owned animals with natural disease, sell vet rights to animal health majors, then use canine data to restart the human program.
scored.unproven_right: Veterinary-field licence or full rights to shelved compounds, near zero to $250k.
scored.proving_step: Open-label pilot in 20-40 client-owned animals at vet oncology or academic clinics, ~$0.3-1M.
scored.proven_buyer: Zoetis, Elanco, Boehringer Ingelheim Animal Health, Merck Animal Health.
scored.public_data: Drugs@FDA reviews, abandoned-program disclosures, ChEMBL, Ensembl/Dog10K genomes, VetCompass, NCI Comparative Oncology records, FDA CVM Green Book.
scored.frame: Rung: buy veterinary rights to a shelved human compound, then run a 20-40 animal open-label pilot. Discovery (choosing the compound and indication) is maybe 40-50% of the work in this rung (my estimate). The physical step is not trivial. You need veterinary-grade drug supply and formulation, dosing and safety work in a new species, recruiting animals through vet oncology clinics, and patient owners. Anivive says its own trial-recruitment arm only brought in ~40% of the dogs for its pivotal study. The bigger problem is that the pilot is not the rung buyers pay for. Animal health majors mostly buy assets that are close to or already approved. Elanco only licensed Tanovea after its 2017 FDA conditional approval, and acquired it after full approval in 2021. The rung that is actually sellable sits after a ~6 year, ~$22.5M companion-animal approval, and inside that rung discovery is under 20% of the work.
scored.step_up: Unproven: the vet rights cost $0-250k (candidate's figure). Gilead's GS-9219 deal with VetDC and Karyopharm's verdinexor deal with Anivive were cheap, but their terms were not disclosed. Proven by a pilot only: animal health licences pay an undisclosed upfront plus milestones. For example, Oasmia/Abbott had up to $21.5M in milestones that were mostly back-loaded and tied to development and sales. My estimate for a pilot-proven asset is $1-5M of realisable value, so roughly 10-50x, not 100-1000x. Whole-company exits after approval, which is far beyond the pilot: Aratana sold for $234-245M and Kindred Bio for ~$440M, both after hundreds of millions spent over 7-10 years. That is weak compared with the money raised.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Base hit rate: no published success rate exists for veterinary pilots. My estimate is that 20-40% of open-label canine oncology pilots show a response signal worth pursuing, partly because these pilots are open-label and not randomised. At that base rate the ML lever is capped at about 2.5-5x, not 10x. Cost per attempt is ~$0.3-1M (candidate's figure; I consider it plausible), but approval adds ~$22.5M over 6+ years (Animal Health Institute via Veterinary Practice News). Some industry sources put it as high as $100M (Anivive). ML does nothing to cut that downstream cost, and that cost is most of the capital.
scored.data: The data that drives the choice is mostly legible and structured. ChEMBL, Ensembl/Dog10K, Drugs@FDA and the Green Book are curated databases that incumbents already mine. Anivive's AI picked verdinexor this way, and VetDC picked rabacfosadine. The pilot's outcome is not written into any public field, which works in the candidate's favour. But the edge comes from biology plus trial execution, not from extracting illegible files. The rights can be bought: pharma out-licenses vet fields, as Gilead did to VetDC, Karyopharm to Anivive, RaQualia to Aratana, and Lorus to Elanco. The owners are not unable to read their own data, though. They know their compound, and they negotiate royalties and milestones rather than selling at $1/ha-style discounts.
scored.right_bought: Veterinary-field licence to a shelved human compound. In practice it costs a low upfront fee plus royalties and milestones. Precedents: Gilead to VetDC (2011, GS-9219, North American vet rights), Karyopharm to Anivive (verdinexor), RaQualia to Aratana, Lorus to Elanco (option). Terms are undisclosed in most of these deals.
scored.buyer: Elanco, Zoetis, Boehringer Ingelheim Animal Health and Merck Animal Health. They are well capitalised but buy late. Elanco took Tanovea only after its FDA conditional approval, and bought Aratana and Kindred Bio as companies with approved or near-approved products.
scored.ladder: There is a real ladder: vet pilot, then vet approval and commercialisation, then restarting the human program with canine comparative-oncology data, then a full human pharma company. Each rung up costs more capital: ~$22.5M+ for vet approval and $100M+ for human Phase 2/3. Canine data has rarely been what rescued a human program; verdinexor/Karyopharm went the other way. The animal health market is ~$50B a year, but the exits so far are small: Aratana ~$245M, Kindred ~$440M.
scored.fatal_flaw: A 20-40 animal open-label pilot does not produce an asset that capitalised buyers pay a big step-up for. Majors buy after FDA CVM approval, which costs ~$22.5M and ~6 years. So the value jump sits behind development capex that ML does not reduce, unlike a drill hit that is sellable right away. The niche is also already occupied by AI-enabled incumbents doing exactly this: Anivive (verdinexor, full approval June 2026) and VetDC (rabacfosadine from Gilead).
scored.one_line_reason: The pilot step-up is probably only ~10-50x and not immediately sellable, because buyers wait for approval. Pilot hit rates are moderate, so the ML lever is under 5x. The data is legible and already mined, and Anivive and VetDC already run this model.

scored.name: SubsetRx: rescuing failed trials via responder subgroups
scored.one_line: Buy failed Phase 2/3 assets from wind-downs; ML over EMA Policy 0070 CSRs and FDA reviews finds a biomarker-defined responder subgroup, proven by retrospective assay of banked trial samples. Rescored stranded drug rescue.
scored.unproven_right: Asset assignment from bankruptcy or wind-down biotechs ($0.1-2M), including rights to trial samples.
scored.proving_step: Retrospective assay of banked samples plus re-analysis, ~$0.5-2M; buyers often still demand a prospective study.
scored.proven_buyer: Biotech acquirers, royalty funds, pharma in-licensing.
scored.public_data: EMA Clinical Data portal CSRs, Drugs@FDA reviews, ClinicalTrials.gov results, PACER dockets, Vivli/YODA (by application).
scored.rough_step_up: ~$1M to $10-50M, 10-50x; large buyer discount on retrospective subgroups.
scored.frame: The rung is: own a failed asset plus its banked samples, and turn it into a 'rescued' asset backed by a retrospective biomarker subgroup. Discovery (finding the subgroup) is maybe 20-30% of what it takes to get a price step-up. The rest is physical and slow, and none of it is abstracted: getting the samples back from wind-down CROs and biobanks, checking consent covers new uses, building and validating an assay (FDA asked for a validated assay and genomic status on 90% or more of subjects even in a case where the trial was positive), and then usually a prospective confirmatory trial, which costs $20-100M+ (my estimate) and is the real proving step for buyers. Unlike a drill core, a retrospective subgroup is not accepted proof, so the rung that is cheap to complete has no buyer who pays a real proven price.
scored.step_up: Unproven: failed or wind-down assets clear at about $0.1-4M (Humanigen's whole estate went on a $2M stalking-horse credit bid in 2024; Transdel sold to Cardium for $4M). Proven, if prospectively confirmed: licensing deals of $10-50M upfront are possible (my estimate). After a retrospective subgroup only, buyers pay a heavy discount; I'd estimate $2-10M, or 2-5x. Even the candidate's own optimistic case of 10-50x is 2-3 orders of magnitude below the 10^4 benchmark. Lantern Pharma, which has run exactly this 'rescue' thesis since 2019, has a small-cap valuation of roughly $50M (estimate, from memory), so the market has not re-rated rescued assets.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Base rate: post-hoc subgroups from failed trials rarely hold up when tested prospectively. Examples: the E5 sepsis subgroup failed its second Phase 3; Götte et al. 2017 show that subgroups selected for the most extreme effect overestimate it; Dyson 2021 found a BRCA1 subgroup with HR 0.59 against 0.97 overall but framed it as hypothesis-generating only. I'd estimate 5-15% of rescue subgroups confirm. Cost per attempt: $0.5-2M for the retrospective step, but $20-100M+ for the confirmatory trial that actually creates value (estimate). ML can cheaply generate many candidate subgroups, but it does nothing to cut the confirmatory trial cost, so the capex drop on the step that matters is far below 10x. ML also makes the multiplicity and false-positive problem worse.
scored.data: The data is real and illegible: EMA Policy 0070 CSRs are thousands of PDF pages with redactions, Drugs@FDA reviews are scanned PDFs, and ClinicalTrials.gov results sit in structured fields at the top level only. The outcome is partly summarised in legible fields: the primary endpoint failure is public, and EMA/FDA documents often report prespecified subgroup forest plots. The hidden signal you need, biomarker-by-response at patient level, is not in public CSRs. It sits in patient-level data (Vivli/YODA, access by application and often barred for commercial asset buyers) and in the physical samples. So public data can generate hypotheses but cannot show the edge. Owners can usually read their own data: sponsors ran the subgroup analyses before shelving the asset, and a wind-down sells exactly what failed.
scored.right_bought: Yes. Rights can be bought cheaply through 363 bankruptcy sales or wind-down assignments ($0.1-4M; Humanigen $2M credit bid, Transdel $4M). But sample rights are often not transferable. Informed consent may not cover new commercial assays, and samples are held by CROs or central labs that may already have destroyed them. The sellers (the sponsors) had the patient-level data and the subgroup analyses, so the information gap is small.
scored.buyer: Biotech acquirers, pharma in-licensing, royalty funds (Royalty Pharma, XOMA, Ligand). These are capitalised buyers, but they do not pay for retrospective-only subgroups; they want prospective confirmation or at least a Phase 2 run with patients selected by biomarker.
scored.ladder: The ladder is strong: rescued asset, then a confirmatory trial, then approval and commercialisation, giving a fully integrated biopharma (the Roivant/BridgeBio-style platform path). The catch is that each rung above the first costs $50M-1B and takes years, so the first rung does not pay for the climb.
scored.fatal_flaw: A retrospective subgroup found by searching many hypotheses in a failed trial is not accepted proof by regulators or acquirers. The value-creating proving step is a prospective confirmatory trial costing tens of millions, so discovery is a minority of the work in the only rung that has a buyer, and the step-up is about 10x, not 10^4x. Lantern Pharma has pursued this exact thesis since 2019 without a market re-rating.
scored.one_line_reason: Cheap distressed rights and a strong ladder, but the proving step that buyers accept is a prospective trial, not ML discovery, and the step-up is about 10x with a low confirmation rate. It fails C1 the same way geothermal in coal mines does.

scored.name: Isolate Rights / Strain Vault: dormant university and USDA microbial isolates for crop biologicals
scored.one_line: Take cheap exclusive licences on specific ARS NRRL and university culture-collection accessions whose public genomes carry clusters or insecticidal proteins ML-predicted to act on a named pest or pathogen (or other high-value uses), prove with one greenhouse or in vitro bioassay, file use patents and sell to crop-biologicals majors.
scored.unproven_right: Exclusive commercial licence on one accession from a TTO or ARS CRADA, ~$1-50k, because the collection cannot tell which tube matters.
scored.proving_step: Ferment and run a contract greenhouse or in vitro efficacy assay, tens of thousands of dollars, then a provisional use patent. EPA microbial AI fees (~$29-54k) fall later to the buyer.
scored.proven_buyer: Corteva, Syngenta Biologicals, Bayer, FMC, Novonesis, Pro Farm; deals in the $5-300M range.
scored.public_data: NCBI/JGI genomes of collection strains, antiSMASH/MIBiG, BPPRC Bt toxin database, EPA biopesticide dockets, scanned USDA screening reports and collection catalogues.
scored.rough_step_up: ~$5-50k to $1-50M, ~10^3x. Exclusivity over the strain is hard, so the moat is the use patent filed after the hit.
scored.frame: Rung: a strain plus a greenhouse or in vitro efficacy hit plus a provisional use patent, sold or licensed to a biologicals major. Inside that rung, discovery (picking which tube) is maybe 50-60% of the work. The other 40-50% is physical, bespoke and not abstracted: fermenting and formulating the strain, then greenhouse bioassays per pest and crop. The bigger problem is that buyers do not buy at this rung. They pay after multi-season field efficacy and some CMC/registration de-risking, and once you include that, discovery falls to roughly 10-20% of the frame. My estimate is that the buyable rung is "field-validated lead", not "greenhouse hit", and inside that rung the coal-mine-geothermal pattern shows up again: proving costs far more than finding.
scored.step_up: Unproven: an ARS NRRL Open Collection strain costs $0. The NRRL site says strains are free apart from postage, capped at 24 per lab per year. University TTO licences are an estimated $1-50k. Proven, the best public comparable is the Corteva-Lavie Bio exclusive biofungicide licence, a $5M advance in two instalments plus milestones and royalties (2023). That came after Lavie's AI discovery plus greenhouse and field work, not after a single greenhouse assay. The whole Lavie Bio platform (microbial bank, programmes, products, team) sold to ICL for $15.25M in 2025, plus $3.5M for the MicroBoost AI engine. Certis licensed the patented Szeged strain B. mojavensis R3B without disclosed terms. A greenhouse-only hit realistically goes from ~$30-50k all-in to an estimated $0.1-1M option value, about 3-20x. The 10^3x figure needs a field-validated asset, which costs $1-5M+ to get to (my estimate).
scored.hit_rate_capex: Base hit rate is low. In Ginkgo's own Bacillus biofungicide funnel, 4,171 strains gave 136 (about 3%) with significant disease control and 3 (about 0.07%, roughly 1 in 1,400) strong foliar or root-rot leads. Globachem tested more than 100 UHasselt strains and took 2 into a licence pending greenhouse trials (about 2%). Cost per greenhouse or in vitro attempt is an estimated $10-50k each, including fermentation. ML pre-filtering on genomes (antiSMASH, Bt toxin homology) could plausibly raise the first-pass hit rate from 3% to 15-30%, a 5-10x lever on greenhouse spend. But greenhouse-to-field attrition, which is roughly 70-90% of greenhouse hits failing in the field by industry consensus (my estimate), is mostly about colonisation, formulation and environment, not genome features, so ML barely touches the expensive step.
scored.data: The data is public and legible, and incumbents already mine it heavily. NCBI/JGI genomes are structured, and antiSMASH, MIBiG and BPPRC are curated, machine-readable databases built for exactly this genome-to-activity prediction. Ginkgo (which absorbed AgBiome's ~100k-strain platform), Lavie Bio/ICL (MicroBoost AI), Pivot Bio, Indigo, ProFarm and Novonesis all run in-silico-first screening on larger proprietary sequenced libraries. Ginkgo even markets ready-made "product headstarts". The scanned USDA screening reports are the only truly illegible layer, and they are small. The right itself is not scarce: NRRL Open Collection strains are free to anyone, so there is no cheap right to buy from an owner who cannot read the data. The only moat is a first-to-file use patent, which is the first-come regime the rubric rejects, and patents on naturally occurring strains face 35 USC 101 (Myriad/Funk Bros) limits. Claims have to rest on methods, formulations or combinations.
scored.right_bought: Not really bought. NRRL strains are free, a TTO licence is cheap but grants no exclusivity over the organism in nature or in other collections (the same species and often near-identical strains sit in DSMZ, ATCC and soil), and the defensible right is a self-filed use or formulation patent, which is first-come rather than bought at a discount from an uninformed owner.
scored.buyer: Real and capitalised: Corteva (paid $1.2B for Stoller, closed Symborg in 2023, $5M advance to Lavie Bio), Syngenta Biologicals, Bayer, FMC, Novonesis, ICL, Certis/Mitsui. They buy field-validated leads or companies, though, not greenhouse hits from unknown strains, and they already run in-house or partner ML discovery engines.
scored.ladder: There is a ladder: strain to greenhouse lead, then field lead, then EPA registration (applicant pays microbial AI fees), then fermentation and formulation manufacturing, then branded distribution and an integrated biologicals company. Stoller showed $400M+ revenue at 12x EBITDA. The ceiling is a multi-billion-dollar biologicals company, not a trillion-dollar one: the global ag-biologicals market is about $15-20B. The lowest rung is not one buyers pay for.
scored.fatal_flaw: The proving step that buyers pay for is multi-season field efficacy plus formulation and manufacturing, not a single greenhouse assay, and it is the hard bespoke part. Underneath that, the strains are free and the genomes are already legible, so there is no cheap illegible right to buy and no information edge over Ginkgo/AgBiome, Lavie Bio/ICL and Pivot Bio, who already do ML-first strain mining at scale. Lavie Bio, the closest analogue (an AI biologicals discovery company), sold its whole platform for $15.25M.
scored.one_line_reason: Fails like the geothermal-in-coal-mines example: picking the tube is easy with legible public genomes, while field proving, formulation and manufacturing are the expensive bespoke work. The strains are free rather than bought cheaply, and incumbents such as Ginkgo/AgBiome and Lavie/ICL already do the ML mining.

scored.name: Shelved Germplasm / Germplasm Trait Finder: licensing shelved public breeding lines
scored.one_line: Take cheap exclusive licences on registered-but-never-commercialised university and USDA-ARS germplasm and shelved breeding lines; ML over decades of scanned trial reports and genotype data matches them to traits now in demand (tar spot, Fusarium head blight, heat); one season of trials proves them for seed majors.
scored.unproven_right: Exclusive commercial licence or assignment of registered germplasm/lines from TTOs and public programmes, ~$5-25k each.
scored.proving_step: KASP marker panel plus a one-season 6-10 location trial or controlled phenotype screen, ~$10-80k per line. Base hit rate under 2%.
scored.proven_buyer: Bayer, Corteva, Syngenta, KWS, Limagrain, Beck's and regional breeders paying $0.5-10M for trait donors.
scored.public_data: Journal of Plant Registrations and Crop Science registration notes, GRIN-Global descriptors, state variety trial PDFs, PVP certificate exhibits, uniform regional nursery reports, T3/SoyBase/GrainGenes.
scored.rough_step_up: ~100-1000x; proof is seasonal and buyers are concentrated.
scored.frame: Rung: hold an exclusive right to a public line, prove it carries a trait now in demand, sell it to a seed major as a trait donor. My estimate is that discovery (matching a line to a trait from scanned reports) is about 50-60% of the work inside that rung. The proving step is not trivial: it takes a KASP marker panel plus a multi-location field or disease-nursery season, which means 1 season of waiting, weather risk and $10-80k per line. On top of that, the buyer needs 2-4 more seasons of backcrossing and introgression before the line is worth anything to them. This is closer to the geothermal-in-a-coal-mine counter-example than to a drill hit: finding the line is the easy part, and turning it into a usable trait is slow, bespoke biology.
scored.step_up: Unproven: public germplasm moves at nominal prices. UW-Madison charges a $100 transfer fee per released inbred and $500 per breeding population for private companies. Iowa State charges $500 per inbred for research and test-crossing, then $500 plus per-MVK royalties for commercialisation. NCSU charges about $200 per tomato line for a non-exclusive breeding licence. Proven: I found no disclosed price for a single trait-donor line. The disclosed deals are bundled programmes: DuPont Pioneer sold its alfalfa programme plus facilities to S&W for up to $49M, and Americot paid $6.8M for the NexGen brand plus DPL germplasm. Public FHB wheat cultivars (Maryland, Georgia going to AGS and UniSouth) are licensed for royalties, not lump sums in the millions. My estimate for a proven donor is $50k-500k upfront or a royalty stream, so roughly 10-100x on a $500-5k entry. The candidate's $0.5-10M figure is unsupported.
scored.hit_rate_capex: The candidate claims a base hit rate under 2%. That is unverified and is my estimate as well. Most lines registered for a trait already carry that trait, but finding a hidden, unscreened resistance to a new pathogen in old lines is rare, plausibly 1-5%. Cost per proving attempt is $10-80k (the candidate's figure; my estimate agrees for a multi-location trial or disease nursery plus KASP). A ~10x capex cut is possible in principle. But public programmes already screen at scale for free: USDA-ARS is screening germplasm and commercial varieties for tar spot, and Michigan State's NIFA Great Lakes Tar Spot Initiative is screening diverse maize germplasm. That removes much of the room for an ML lever.
scored.data: The data is public and partly illegible: scanned state variety trial PDFs, uniform regional nursery reports and old registration notes. The outcome is often already legible, though. Journal of Plant Registrations abstracts state the disease resistance in the first lines, GRIN-Global carries structured disease descriptors, and T3, SoyBase and GrainGenes hold structured genotype and phenotype data. Seed majors already mine these sources with large genomics teams. For new pathogens (tar spot), the old reports contain no phenotype at all, so ML over the text cannot find the trait; only new screening can.
scored.right_bought: This is the weakest link. Registering a line in Journal of Plant Registrations requires depositing seed with the USDA National Plant Germplasm System (NPGS), and GRIN then distributes that seed freely to anyone, so a registered line effectively cannot be held exclusively. USDA-ARS germplasm releases are typically public. University inbreds and populations go out non-exclusively at $100-500 (UW-Madison, Iowa State, NCSU). Exclusivity is only available on unreleased or shelved programme lines, which by definition have no public data trail. Even where a TTO grants exclusivity, the owners are breeders who can read their own data. They are not information-poor sellers.
scored.buyer: Bayer, Corteva, Syngenta, KWS, Limagrain and Beck's are capitalised but concentrated, with about 4-6 meaningful buyers. They have their own large germplasm banks and free access to NPGS. Disclosed deals are bundled programmes (S&W/Pioneer alfalfa up to $49M; Americot $6.8M), not single-line trait-donor purchases. The value of the trait is captured downstream through backcrossing, so buyers pay little for a raw donor line.
scored.ladder: The ladder is real: trait donor, then finished inbreds or varieties, then a regional seed brand, then a national seed company. Seed is a roughly $50B-plus global market, so the path to a very large company exists. Each rung is long, though (5-8 years per variety cycle), and the incumbents are entrenched, as Inari and Pairwise show.
scored.fatal_flaw: There is no exclusive, cheaply buyable right. Registered public germplasm must be deposited in NPGS and is freely distributed through GRIN to anyone, including the seed majors. They can therefore screen the same line themselves without paying for the step-up. Secondary flaws: the trait outcome is usually already written in the registration abstract or GRIN descriptors, and the proving step is a slow, bespoke biological season rather than a trivial physical step.
scored.one_line_reason: This fails on the right. Public germplasm is free to everyone through NPGS and GRIN or licensed non-exclusively for $100-500, the trait outcome is often already in legible registration and GRIN fields, and the step-up is roughly 10-100x at best, not 10^3.

scored.name: Orphan Cultivar: unreleased selections of retiring private breeders
scored.one_line: Buy unreleased seedling selections and trial archives from retiring private fruit, berry, hop and turf breeders and closing university programmes; ML reads scanned notebooks and regional trial reports to pick elite selections; multi-site trials prove them for club-variety licensing.
scored.unproven_right: Title to physical selections, budwood or rhizomes plus breeding rights and records, a few thousand dollars.
scored.proving_step: OCR/LLM ranking across years, then 2-3 seasons of contracted multi-site trials and a PVP/plant patent filing. Hit rate under 1%.
scored.proven_buyer: Club-variety managers and nursery consortia (IFORED, Driscoll's, Hop Breeding Company/Yakima Chief).
scored.public_data: USDA NIFA/CRIS reports, state experiment station bulletins, NC-140 apple trials, GRIN evaluations, PVP files, breeding archives.
scored.frame: Rung: own an unreleased selection and prove it as a licensable cultivar. Discovery (reading notebooks, ranking selections) is perhaps 10-20% of that rung (my estimate). The other 80%+ is physical, biological and slow: propagating budwood, planting multi-site trials, waiting for trees to bear fruit, storage and consumer testing, then PVP or plant patent filing. For tree fruit this takes 8-20 years. Agroscope says it takes 15-20 years to name a variety. The candidate's '2-3 seasons' only holds for strawberries or turf. This is the geothermal-in-coal-mines inversion: the bespoke physical step is harder than finding the asset.
scored.step_up: Unproven: a seedling or selection with records, roughly $0-5k (my estimate; I found no market comps for orphan selections). Proven tail: Cosmic Crisp (WA 38) earned WSU more than $8M in one fiscal year, inside $19.4M of total WSU royalties in FY25. Its terms were $1 per tree plus a 4.75% royalty per box. Honeycrisp was about $1 per tree. So a top hit is 10^3-10^4x on paper. But the value is not realised at proof. It comes years later, as trees are planted and fruit is sold, and it depends on a club manager's marketing spend (Cosmic Crisp had a $10.1M marketing budget). Most licensed cultivars earn little. I found no upfront fees for licensing an advanced selection.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Base rates: Agroscope reports 1 in about 30,000 seedlings becomes a variety. Zaiger trials about 700 selections a year and commercialises about 7 (about 1% at the advanced-selection stage). Cost per proving attempt: a multi-site trial of one selection over 3-10 years costs about $20-100k (my estimate), plus the propagation and land you must own. ML that ranks notebook text cannot replace genotype-by-environment field data. Public breeders already use genomic selection (RosBREED). Realistic lever: maybe 2-3x at the selection-to-trial stage, not 10x, because the outcome needs new phenotypes that no archive contains.
scored.data: The signal sits mostly in private, unpublished breeder notebooks, not public data. You only get it after buying, so it is not an edge for choosing what to buy. The public sources are already legible: NC-140 trial tables, station bulletins and GRIN evaluations publish ranked performance by selection. NC-140 is mainly a rootstock trial, so it is a weak source for scion selections. Rights can be bought cheaply from retiring breeders and their estates. The Bradford estate and Zaiger license through intermediaries. But adverse selection is severe: breeders already released or licensed their best, and what is left over is largely what they rejected.
scored.right_bought: Yes. Physical material, breeding rights and records can be bought from retiring private breeders, estates (for example the Glen Bradford estate licensing through BQ Genetics) or closing programmes, plausibly for low thousands. Caveats: much of the material may already be patented or licensed to nurseries, and university material goes through tech-transfer offices that know what it is worth.
scored.buyer: Capitalised buyers exist: Proprietary Variety Management (PVM, Cosmic Crisp), IFORED, Driscoll's, Hop Breeding Company / Yakima Chief, Dave Wilson and Zaiger licensees, and Excelsior in Chile. They buy proven cultivars, though, usually on royalty-only terms. They rarely pay a large lump sum for an unproven selection.
scored.ladder: Selection, then cultivar IP, then a nursery propagation monopoly, then club or brand management (PVM, IFORED), then growing, packing and global marketing (Driscoll's, about $6B in revenue). The ladder is real, but each rung needs years of biological lead time.
scored.fatal_flaw: Proving is not trivial or abstracted. It means 8-20 years of physical, multi-site field trials (Agroscope: 15-20 years, 1 in 30,000 seedlings). The step-up arrives slowly through royalties, not at the moment of a hit. Discovery is a small share of the rung, and leftover selections are adversely selected rejects.
scored.one_line_reason: The long-tail royalties and the ladder are real, but the proving step is slow, costly biological field trialling, the very inversion the coal-mine geothermal counter-example rules out. ML over notebooks cannot shortcut the phenotyping.

scored.name: Sleeper Hunter / Old Master Sleepers: misattributed Old Masters at regional auctions
scored.one_line: Buy 'circle of / follower of / unattributed' lots at regional auctions for $500-30k; ML over catalogues raisonnés, museum images, provenance indexes and scanned sale catalogues flags autograph works; IR reflectography, pigment, dendro and expert sign-off prove them for Sotheby's/Christie's.
scored.unproven_right: Full title to a physical lot bought at hammer from a provincial auctioneer or estate.
scored.proving_step: ML triage, then technical analysis ($5-20k) plus provenance chain and scholarly acceptance; the gate is expert opinion.
scored.proven_buyer: Christie's, Sotheby's, Phillips, Old Master dealers (Colnaghi, Agnews, Weiss), museums, art-finance lenders.
scored.public_data: RKD, Getty Provenance Index, Witt Library and Frick photoarchive, Heidelberg sale catalogues, museum open access (Met, Rijksmuseum, NGA), LiveAuctioneers/Invaluable/Drouot/the-saleroom feeds.
scored.rough_step_up: 10^2-10^4x on a hit (Salvator Mundi, Cimabue); base hit rate well under 1-5%.
scored.frame: The rung is buying a mis-catalogued lot and getting it re-attributed, so it can be resold at Sotheby's or Christie's or to a dealer. Inside that rung, discovery (spotting the lot) and proving (provenance plus scholarly acceptance) are maybe 70-85% of the work, and the physical step (buying at hammer, light conservation) is trivial. So far it looks like Terranox. The difference is the proving gate. It is not a cheap physical test like a drill core. It is the subjective sign-off of a handful of specialists and catalogue raisonné committees, who can take years and can refuse. You cannot abstract that step away the way drilling is abstracted. Capitalised buyers do exist: the auction houses, dealers such as Van Haeften, and museums.
scored.step_up: The headline cases are huge. Salvator Mundi was bought for about $1,175 in 2005 and sold for $450m in 2017 (about 10^5). A Rembrandt at Nye & Co (New Jersey, 2015) was estimated at $500-800. But the realised step-up from what an informed buyer actually pays is much smaller, because the hammer price already captures most of the value. The Nye Rembrandt hammered at $870k against that $500-800 estimate. An Adam's Dublin sleeper was estimated at EUR 800 and sold for EUR 120k. A Banbury 'Italian Old Master' (2025) made GBP 685k hammer after a bidding battle. Sotheby's 'Let the Little Children Come Unto Me' made $1.7m in 2014 as an anonymous Netherlandish work, then $10.59m in 2026 as Rembrandt (about 6x). So the step-up the buyer captures is about 3-20x. The 10^3-10^4 jump mostly goes to the uninformed seller. My score of 3 gives some credit for the rare true sleeper that nobody bids up.
scored.hit_rate_capex: This is my estimate; I found no published hit rate. Probably well under 1-2% of 'circle of' or unattributed lots are autograph works. Each proving attempt costs the purchase price ($500 to $30k+), plus $5-20k of technical analysis, plus 1-5 years of scholarly lobbying. ML triage could cut wasted purchases and technical analysis several-fold, so the capex lever is real but capped. The bigger constraint is that competitors see the same lots. Art Recognition's own figure is more than 500 authentications, and the 2024 Germann sale was the first work authenticated by AI alone. Even so, dealers such as Van Haeften say they 'would not under any circumstances' accept an AI attribution. ML does not lower the cost of the real gate.
scored.data: The signal sits in illegible, scattered public data: the RKD, the Getty Provenance Index, the Witt and Frick photoarchives, scanned Heidelberg catalogues and auction feeds. The outcome is not written into any legible field, which is a genuine plus. But this data is not hidden from competitors. Every lot is photographed and posted on the-saleroom, LiveAuctioneers and Invaluable for global online bidders. A professional cohort of sleeper hunters scans those feeds (London Old Master dealers, Philip Mould, Bendor Grosvenor-type scholars), and so do auction-house specialists.
scored.right_bought: You do buy full title, at the hammer price. But it is bought in an open ascending auction, not a private deal with an owner who cannot read the data. Once two informed bidders spot a lot, the price rises towards the proven value. That is what happened in the cases above: estimate $500-800 to hammer $870k, EUR 800 to EUR 120k, and GBP 685k at Banbury. You have to outbid the trade every time, so a buyer who reads the data no better than they do gets no discount. Buying privately from estates before they reach auction is possible but slow, depends on relationships and does not scale.
scored.buyer: Christie's, Sotheby's, Phillips, Old Master dealers (Van Haeften, Colnaghi, Weiss), museums and art-finance lenders. They are well capitalised, but the market is small. My estimate is that the Old Master auction segment is roughly $0.5-1bn a year, and Sotheby's whole July 2026 London Old Master week made $64.8m.
scored.ladder: The rungs above are thin: dealer, then your own auction house or art fund, then art-backed lending. There is no industrial chain to integrate up to, and nothing like a mine-to-reactor path. The ceiling is a very good dealer or boutique fund, not a very large company.
scored.fatal_flaw: The unproven right is sold in an open, globally broadcast auction where sleeper-hunting dealers and online bidders already bid hits up to near-proven value (the $500-800 Rembrandt hammered at $870k). The proving gate is subjective expert acceptance, and ML cannot make it cheaper or abstract it away. So the 10^4 step-up goes to the seller, not to the buyer, and the total market is too small for a ladder.
scored.one_line_reason: This looks like Terranox at a glance, but rights are bought in competitive open auctions, so the step-up gets competed away at the hammer. The proof is gated by subjective expert opinion rather than a cheap physical test, and the market and ladder are too small.

scored.name: Reverter Capital: possibility-of-reverter rights and orphan strips
scored.one_line: Buy reverter rights and rights of entry from heirs of grantors whose 'so long as used for school/church/railroad' conditions have failed, found by ML over scanned deed books; quiet title and sell fee or a release to the occupant.
scored.unproven_right: Contingent future interests held unknowingly by dispersed heirs, bought by quitclaim for $200-2,000.
scored.proving_step: Deed OCR to find conditional grants, cross-check against closures and current use, heir tracing, quiet-title action.
scored.proven_buyer: Occupants, developers and title insurers needing to clear the cloud; districts, dioceses and REITs selling closed sites.
scored.public_data: County scanned deed books, historic plats, NCES closed-school files, denominational closures, abandoned rail filings, FamilySearch probate; Marketable Title Act cutoffs as a filter.
scored.rough_step_up: 10^3x+ on a hit; very low hit rate and MTA limits.
scored.frame: The rung is: buy a contingent reverter or right of entry from heirs, then prove it and sell a release or the fee. Finding the conditional grant in deed books and matching it to a closure is discovery, which I estimate at roughly 30-50% of the work. The rest is not trivial: heir tracing (multi-generation, often dozens of fractional heirs), chain-of-assignment validity, and a contested quiet-title action. That action is the actual proving step, and outcomes turn on fine doctrine. Is it a fee simple determinable or a condition subsequent (Mahrenholz, Illinois, reversed on appeal)? Did the triggering event occur ('abandoned for school purposes' was not triggered by suspended classes in Griffis, Tennessee; the UK Supreme Court reversed the heirs' GBP 1.2m win in the Oxfordshire case)? Litigation, not drilling, is the hard part. This is close to the coal-mine-geothermal counter-example: finding the asset is easier than proving it.
scored.step_up: Unproven: quitclaim from heirs at an assumed $200-2,000 (candidate's figure, unverified; I found no published price data). Proven: no market price exists. The value is a negotiated release or a share of the sale proceeds, and the occupant (school district, church, trail) resists. Comparable: the UK Oxfordshire claim was worth GBP 1.2m but the heirs ultimately lost at the Supreme Court. Trails Act railroad-reversion takings paid about $49m in a single year across roughly 8,000 pending claims (2013 report), which my estimate puts at low thousands to tens of thousands of dollars per parcel owner. So the realistic step-up is my estimate of 10-100x on the rare clean hit (a $1k quitclaim turning into a $10k-100k release), not 10^3-10^4. Also, the 'proven' value is capped by the occupant's cost to litigate or insure over the cloud, so buyers pay nuisance value, not the land value.
scored.hit_rate_capex: I found no published base rate; these are my estimates. Of conditional grants found, most are already dead by statute. California Civ. Code 885.020/885.030 abolishes possibilities of reverter and expires powers of termination 30 years after recording unless a preservation notice is filed. Ohio 5301.49 and the Kentucky HB 256 draft use 40 years. Oklahoma uses 30. Minnesota's MTA barred the heirs' reverter claim in Wichelman v. Messner after they had bought quitclaims, which is exactly this business model failing in court. Florida (21 years, unverified) and Illinois (40-year Reverter Act) add more limits. The common-law rule in some states (e.g. Illinois) is that reverters are inheritable but not transferable inter vivos, so the right cannot even be bought. My estimate: under 5% of found grants are both live and assignable, and a fraction of those win. Cost per proving attempt (my estimate): heir tracing $2-10k, plus quiet title $10-50k+ if contested, plus 1-3 years. ML only reduces the search cost, which is the small part. Litigation cost per attempt does not fall, so the capex lever is well under 10x.
scored.data: Signal is genuinely illegible. Conditional habendum language sits in scanned pre-1950 county deed books, and no status field records 'reverter live/triggered'. Closures (NCES closed schools, diocesan closures, STB abandonments) are legible, but the deed condition is not, so the ML edge on extraction is real. The right can in principle be bought cheaply from unaware heirs. Two things undercut this. (a) Statutes extinguish most of the old interests, and in some states the interests are non-assignable. (b) The railroad sub-segment is already worked by Trails Act takings class-action counsel (Preseault, Haggart settlement, ~8,000 claims), so the outcome there is already being harvested.
scored.right_bought: Heir quitclaims are bought, not free, so this part fits the rubric. But the legal transferability of possibilities of reverter varies by state (not transferable inter vivos at common law in Illinois), and buying them invites champerty and bad-faith-cloud claims. Wichelman v. Messner shows heirs' quitclaims voided by the MTA.
scored.buyer: Occupants (school districts, dioceses, municipalities, trail operators), developers buying closed sites, and title insurers. None is a capitalised buyer eager to pay for a proven asset the way a mine developer is. They are adversaries who pay to make a cloud go away, and title insurers often just insure over stale reverters or rely on MTA cutoffs.
scored.ladder: Weak. The next rungs would be title clearing as a service (the rubric excludes selling a service), or redeveloping closed schools and churches (generic real-estate development where the reverter edge disappears). There is no natural chain to a very large company. The asset class is finite, shrinking every year as MTA and reverter-statute cutoffs run, and not renewable.
scored.fatal_flaw: The proving step is contested litigation on a shrinking, statute-extinguished asset class. Marketable Title Acts and reverter-duration statutes (California 30 years, Ohio, Kentucky draft and Illinois 40 years, Oklahoma 30, Minnesota MTA, which voided exactly this heir-quitclaim play in Wichelman v. Messner) kill most old reverters. Some states bar assigning them at all. The survivors require heir tracing plus a quiet-title fight with an unwilling occupant, so proving costs are dominated by legal work that ML does not cheapen.
scored.one_line_reason: The data really is illegible and the rights can be bought, but statutes extinguish most old reverters. Proving one is an adversarial quiet-title suit that ML does not make cheaper. A hit yields a nuisance-value release (roughly 10-100x) rather than 10^3x. There is no capitalised eager buyer and no real ladder.

scored.name: Orphan Railroad Fee Strips: defunct-railroad parcel quitclaims
scored.one_line: Buy bulk quitclaims from trustees and successor shells of defunct railroads (Penn Central, Milwaukee Road, Rock Island, Erie Lackawanna) that still hold record fee to forgotten parcels; ML finds valuable fee-owned strips; sell cleared title to adjoiners and developers.
scored.unproven_right: Bulk quitclaim of any remaining interest of a defunct railroad, at nominal price.
scored.proving_step: Georeference ICC valuation maps and railroad deed ledgers against parcel layers, flag parcels with no conveyance out, quiet title or insure.
scored.proven_buyer: Adjacent owners, title insurers, homebuilders and data-center developers blocked by a strip, municipalities.
scored.public_data: ICC Valuation Maps (NARA), railroad corporate records in state archives, county parcel GIS, railroad bankruptcy dockets.
scored.frame: The rung is buying a quitclaim, proving the railroad held fee and that no conveyance out was recorded, then selling title that has been cleared or insured. Discovery (georeferencing ICC val maps against deed ledgers and parcels) is perhaps 40-50% of the work, which is my estimate. The rest is legal: a quiet-title action per parcel, adjoiners fighting centerline-presumption and reversion claims, and title insurers who will not write over railroad gaps. So the physical step is not trivial. Litigation plays the part that the bespoke plant plays in the coal-mine geothermal example. Buyers exist (adjoiners, developers, title insurers), but each strip is a separate negotiation with one buyer. There is no capitalised market for the rung like mine developers buying proven claims.
scored.step_up: Unproven: a bulk quitclaim at a nominal price. My estimate is $1k-$100k per railroad estate. For comparison, a private buyer paid CSX $104,000 for a quitclaim on a 1.19-mile segment (sclawyersweekly). Proven: a fee strip is worth roughly the adjoining land per acre, about $5k-$500k/acre (estimate), or a holdout premium when it blocks a data-center or homebuilder site. Per parcel, the gain from a near-zero allocated cost can be 100-1000x on a rare blocking hit. Typical strips are narrow remnants, with value in the low thousands of dollars, so the realistic gain is 10-100x after legal cost. That same CSX quitclaim was worth $0: the court held the railroad owned only an easement, so fee title went to the adjoiners.
scored.hit_rate_capex: The base hit rate is low. Most railroad corridors were acquired as easements or as grants limited to railroad use ("so long as used for railroad purposes"). Those revert to adjoiners on abandonment, so the quitclaim conveys nothing (Kansas Supreme Court; SC CSX case; Washington Milwaukee Road split; the Indiana Firestone class settlement gave abandoned Penn Central land to adjoiners in 51 counties). Estimate: 1-5% of parcels are fee-owned and unconveyed with real value, which matches the candidate's own figure. Cost per proving attempt is dominated by quiet title, about $5k-$30k per parcel and 6-24 months contested (estimate). Desk research is only about $100-$500 per parcel. ML cuts desk-screening cost, but desk screening is not the binding cost. The lever on total capex is perhaps 2-3x, not 10x.
scored.data: The data is public and largely illegible. The NARA ICC valuation series holds about 125,000 right-of-way and tract maps (1915-1920 with later revisions), plus scanned deed ledgers and county parcel GIS. However, the val maps and their accompanying schedules often already record how each tract was acquired, which partly states the answer in a semi-legible form. Incumbents have also georeferenced their own maps: Union Pacific in 26 states with Esri, and CSX with Jones Edmunds. The defunct estates were mostly liquidated decades ago. American Premier Underwriters (Penn Central's successor) actively sold its abandoned land and was sued for it. The Rock Island and Milwaukee Road trustees closed out. Rails-to-trails takings litigation firms already map fee versus easement corridor by corridor.
scored.right_bought: Yes, the right is bought. A quitclaim of remaining interest from a successor shell or trustee can be bought cheaply, and some successors (APU, Conrail remnants) will sell. But a quitclaim warrants nothing, and many shells are dissolved, so there may be nobody left to sign. Adjoiners usually hold a competing claim through the centerline presumption and reversion, so the cheap right often turns out to be empty.
scored.buyer: Adjacent owners, title insurers (who would rather buy a release than litigate), homebuilders and data-center developers held up by a strip, and municipalities and trail agencies. Ability to pay is real only in the rare holdout case. Most adjoiners pay little, or simply sue, because state law often gives them the strip for free.
scored.ladder: The ladder is weak. Possible next rungs are assembling corridors for fiber, transmission or trails (contested under railbanking and takings law), or growing into a curative title and real estate assembly firm. The result looks like a niche title-curative business, not a path to a vertically integrated trillion-dollar chain. There is no physical production chain above the rung.
scored.fatal_flaw: Proving is litigation, not discovery. Most railroad strips were easements or grants limited to railroad use. Those revert to adjoiners by law, so the quitclaim the company buys is usually worthless, as in the SC CSX $104k quitclaim, the Kansas ruling and the Indiana Penn Central settlement. Even fee hits need contested quiet-title actions per parcel against neighbors who have the legal presumption, so ML does not drive the cost that binds.
scored.one_line_reason: The data is illegible, but the step-up only becomes real after per-parcel litigation against adjoiners who usually win by reversion. Discovery is not 80% of the rung, and the ML lever on total capex is about 2-3x.
