scored.name: SiteSeed: entitled build-to-suit tower sites
scored.one_line: Take cheap ground-lease options on parcels in coverage deserts; ML predicts which will clear zoning, FAA, NEPA/SHPO and RF need; entitle only those and flip permitted sites to tower companies.
scored.unproven_right: 2-3 year lease option on ~100x100 ft parcel, ~$500-2,000.
scored.proving_step: Entitlement filings (~$30-60k per site) concentrated on ML-predicted winners; zoning is the failure point.
scored.proven_buyer: SBA, American Tower, Vertical Bridge, Tillman, carrier BTS programs ($250k-1M+).
scored.public_data: County planning minutes and staff reports, FAA OE/AAA, FCC ASR and BDC maps, BEAD/5G Fund areas, Section 106 records.
scored.frame: The rung is "entitled, unbuilt tower site": an option plus permits, sold to a tower company. Inside it, discovery (picking the parcel and predicting permits) is maybe 50-60% of the work (my estimate). The rest is site acquisition and zoning hearings, RF and structural engineering, the NEPA/SHPO/tribal consultation package and FAA filings. That legwork is done by armies of site-acquisition contractors at roughly $30-60k per site; it is not abstracted the way drilling is for Terranox. The bigger problem is that the rung is not cleanly sellable on its own. Tower companies pay for a site that has an anchor tenant (a carrier lease, which creates cash flow), not for an empty permit. So the real proving event is a carrier signing up, and that depends on private carrier RF plans, not on public data.
scored.step_up: Unproven: a 2-3 yr ground-lease option at about $500-2,000 (candidate's figure, plausible). Entitled with no tenant: speculative sites trade thinly. My estimate is $10-50k, plus reimbursement of entitlement costs, because the buyer still has to put $150-300k (my estimate) into building the tower and needs a tenant. Entitled with an anchor carrier lease: tower companies value towers at about 15-25x tower cash flow. A single-tenant tower at about $20-30k/yr of rent is worth roughly $300k-600k (estimate, consistent with the candidate's $250k-1M+ range), but that value belongs to the tenant lease, not the permit. On total cost per proven site (about $40-60k), entitlement alone gives about 0.5-1x. With a tenant it is about 5-10x. The 10^3x figure on the option ignores the entitlement spend. Score 2.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Base hit rate for entitlement is high, not low. Telecommunications Act Section 332(c)(7) requires any denial to rest on substantial written evidence, and FCC shot-clock rules (150 days for a new tower) push localities to approve. My estimate is that 70-85% of properly sited tower applications are eventually approved, often with conditions or stealth designs. Cost per attempt is about $30-60k (candidate's figure; consistent with industry site-acquisition fees, my estimate). The lever is capped at 1/0.75, about 1.3x, nowhere near 10x. The low-hit-rate step is getting a carrier to commit, and public data cannot predict that well. I could not verify these figures because the web search budget for this turn was already used up, so all numbers are estimates from prior knowledge.
scored.data: The zoning, FAA and Section 106 records are public and partly illegible: county minutes and staff reports are scattered PDFs. But FCC ASR, FAA OE/AAA determinations and the BDC coverage maps are already structured, legible fields, and FAA no-hazard determinations come out almost automatically for short towers. The decisive signal, which carrier needs a site where, is private: carriers issue search rings to their own contractors. Incumbents (site-acquisition firms, Tillman, Vertical Bridge) already have the ring data and the local zoning knowledge. Score 2.
scored.right_bought: Yes. Ground-lease options can be bought cheaply from rural landowners who cannot read RF demand or the zoning record. But landowners are now aware of tower-lease value, and lease aggregators (e.g., Landmark Dividend, Radius) compete for the land side. The right is cheap to buy; the problem is that its value depends on someone else's private decision.
scored.buyer: Tower companies (American Tower, Crown Castle, SBA, Vertical Bridge, Tillman, DigitalBridge platforms) and carrier build-to-suit programs. They are well capitalised but buy towers with tenants, or commission build-to-suit sites inside their own search rings. A spec permit outside a ring has a thin market.
scored.ladder: The ladder is strong: entitled site, then build and own the tower, then lease-up and colocation, then a tower portfolio (AMT is worth about $90-100B), then small cells, fiber and edge sites. Score 4.
scored.fatal_flaw: The value step comes from an anchor carrier tenant, which is driven by private carrier RF plans and search rings, not from entitlement. Entitlement itself succeeds most of the time (about 70-85%, estimate) under federal shot-clock and substantial-evidence rules. So ML on public zoning data attacks a step that is neither the main failure point nor the source of value. That caps the lever at about 1.3x, and a permit-only flip lands near breakeven on total spend.
scored.one_line_reason: Good ladder and cheap options, but entitlement is mostly approved and the step-up depends on private carrier tenancy, not on discovery in public data, so this is not a Terranox frame.
sources: Web search budget for this turn was used up; no searches completed. All figures are estimates from prior knowledge and the candidate brief.
Telecommunications Act of 1996, 47 U.S.C. 332(c)(7) (substantial-evidence requirement for denials) - prior knowledge
FCC 2009 Shot Clock Ruling and 2018 Small Cell Order (150-day new-tower shot clock) - prior knowledge
Tower company valuation multiples, American Tower / SBA public filings (approx. 15-25x tower cash flow) - prior knowledge, estimate

scored.name: Hidden Lots: antiquated-subdivision legal-lot discovery
scored.one_line: ML reads chains of title to find single parcels in high-value markets that legally contain extra lots created by pre-1972 deeds, patents or plats; option the split or buy the parcel, win a Certificate of Compliance and sell the lot.
scored.unproven_right: Unrecognised separate legal lot inside a parcel, or an option on the split.
scored.proving_step: Chain of title back to patent/plat, show lawful creation and no merger, Certificate of Compliance (Gov Code 66499.35 or equivalent).
scored.proven_buyer: Luxury builders, HNW buyers, coastal land investors ($1-5M+ lots).
scored.public_data: County recorder deed images, BLM GLO patents, old plats, assessor maps, coastal commission records.
scored.rough_step_up: 10^3x+ on option; ~1.5-3x on whole-parcel purchase; merger doctrine kills many.
scored.frame: The rung is 'parcel with an unrecognised legal lot' becoming 'parcel with a recorded Certificate of Compliance (CoC)'. Inside that rung, discovery (title chain back to the patent, deed or plat, plus showing no merger) is maybe 60-70% of the work (my estimate). The rest is not trivial: a survey, county planning review, frequent conditional CoCs (which require the lot to meet current standards before issuance), and fights over merger under Gov Code 66451.10-.30. The bigger problem is that a CoC only confirms a legal lot. It does not make the lot buildable. In the high-value coastal markets the thesis targets, the value-creating step is entitlement: a Coastal Development Permit, CEQA review, water/sewer or septic, setbacks, slope and fire rules. That bespoke, slow, political step is the same shape as the geothermal-in-coal-mines counter-example. Builders and HNW buyers pay for buildable lots, not for CoCs, so the frame that has a capitalised buyer is 'entitled lot', and there discovery is well under 50%.
scored.step_up: The quoted 10^3x 'on option' is an artifact of a small option premium. It is not an asset step-up, and the owner has to sign the option, which tells them what you found. On a whole-parcel purchase at market, the realistic uplift is the value of the extra lot minus discounts for entitlement risk, carry and legal cost. If the extra lot is buildable and entitled, that is roughly 1.3-3x the parcel price. As a bare CoC without entitlement, it is likely 1.1-1.5x. These are my estimates. I could not verify any comps this turn because the shared web search budget was already used up (0 of 5 searches ran).
scored.hit_rate_capex: Cost per proving attempt (my estimates, not verified): title chain and abstract $1-5k; boundary/ALTA survey $5-20k; land-use attorney $10-50k; county CoC application fee about $2-10k. Total about $20-80k and 6-24 months per parcel. ML could raise the hit rate of the desk screen. But the expensive failures happen after discovery: merger findings, conditional CoC terms, and refused CDPs or permits. ML cannot predict those well from deeds. So the capex lever is maybe 2-3x, not 10x. Base hit rate is unknown. After Gardner v. County of Sonoma (2003, Cal. Supreme Court: pre-1893 antiquated maps do not by themselves create legal lots), a large share of the old-plat candidates simply fail (my recollection of case law, not re-verified this turn).
scored.data: Partially fits. Assessor parcels (APNs) are tax units, not legal lots, so the outcome is genuinely not written into a legible field. The signal sits in scanned recorder deed images, BLM GLO patents and old plats. That is truly illegible, and few people read it at scale. However, land-use attorneys, title officers, surveyors and lot-legalization consultants already do this work parcel by parcel for owners. Owners in $1-5M+ markets are sophisticated, and many already pull a title report before selling. Their brokers increasingly flag lot-split potential because SB 9 (2021) publicised splits.
scored.right_bought: The right cannot be bought separately from the owner. It is embedded in the fee parcel, so you must buy the whole parcel at market (paying full price for the existing house or land) or get an option, which requires disclosing the opportunity to the owner. This is not a $1/ha mineral right that can be staked or bought cheaply. Capital per shot is the full parcel price ($1-5M+). That inverts Terranox's economics: cheap shots become very expensive shots.
scored.buyer: Luxury builders and HNW buyers, but only for buildable, entitled lots. Legal-lot status alone sells at a heavy discount. In urban California, SB 9 lot splits now let many single-family parcels be split anyway, which erodes the scarcity of 'hidden lots' outside the coastal zone.
scored.ladder: The rungs run legal lot, entitled lot, built home, then a land development or homebuilding company. That is a real ladder, but it ends in fragmented, cyclical, local residential development. It is not a trillion-dollar chain, and the higher rungs are not where ML discovery gives an edge.
scored.fatal_flaw: A Certificate of Compliance proves a legal lot, not a buildable one. In the high-value coastal markets that drive the step-up, the real value step is bespoke entitlement (Coastal permits, CEQA, water and septic). That is harder than discovery, which is exactly the coal-mine geothermal failure mode. On top of that, the right can only be acquired by buying the whole parcel at full market price, which kills the cheap-shot economics.
scored.one_line_reason: The data is illegible and the outcome is unsummarised, which is real. But discovery is not 80% of the sellable rung: entitlement dominates. The step-up on a whole parcel is about 1.1-3x, not 10^3. And each shot costs a full $1-5M parcel.
sources: No web searches ran: this turn's shared search budget was already used up, so every figure is my estimate or recollection and is unverified.
Gardner v. County of Sonoma (2003) 29 Cal.4th 990, from recollection: antiquated subdivision maps do not by themselves create legal lots or entitle a CoC.
Cal. Gov Code 66499.35 (Certificate of Compliance, including conditional CoCs) and 66451.10-66451.30 (merger), from recollection.
Cal. SB 9 (2021), urban lot splits, from recollection.

scored.name: Floodway Flip / Floodway Lot Revival: LiDAR-driven FEMA map revisions
scored.one_line: Buy land and paper lots trading at deep discounts because stale 1970s-90s FEMA studies map them in a floodway or SFHA; ML over 3DEP LiDAR, scanned FIS backup models and satellite inundation history finds mis-mapped parcels; file LOMA/LOMR-F/LOMR; sell buildable lots.
scored.unproven_right: Fee or option on mapped floodway/SFHA land.
scored.proving_step: Survey, HEC-RAS re-model and elevation certificate; FEMA LOMA/LOMR-F/LOMR ($5-40k, pooled per reach).
scored.proven_buyer: Production homebuilders, lot banking funds, BTR funds, local builders.
scored.public_data: FEMA NFHL, FIS reports and hydraulic backup (Map Service Center), 3DEP point clouds, Global Flood Database, LOMC history, DOT bridge as-builts, tax-delinquent rolls.
scored.rough_step_up: ~20-200x for floodway-to-buildable lots; ~1.2-2x for SFHA-to-X; DEM-vs-BFE lookup may do most of the work.
scored.frame: Rung = own flood-mapped land, get a FEMA map change, sell it as remapped land. In the SFHA-to-Zone-X version (a LOMA/LOMR-F on natural high ground), discovery is most of the work, maybe 70-85% (my estimate). But that version only gives a 1.2-2x step-up. The 20-200x version (floodway land to buildable lots) does not happen on paper alone. It needs a hydraulic re-model with a no-rise showing, community sign-off, often a CLOMR first, plus entitlement and horizontal development (roads, utilities, pads, typically tens of thousands of dollars per lot, my estimate). Inside that frame discovery is probably 20-40%, the same failure as the geothermal-in-coal-mines counter-example. Capitalised buyers (production builders, lot-banking and BTR funds) exist, but they mostly buy finished or entitled lots, not land with a fresh LOMR.
scored.step_up: No sourced numbers: the shared web search budget ran out before any query ran. Estimates from prior knowledge: SFHA-to-X removal adds about 10-50% to land value, so roughly 1.2-2x. The SFHA discount has narrowed under Risk Rating 2.0, and lenders and buyers increasingly use First Street-style risk scores whatever the FEMA zone says. Floodway land in growth metros may trade at about $1-5k/acre against $50-300k/acre for entitled residential land (estimate). But most of that gap is entitlement plus development cost, not the map change, so the step-up that comes purely from proving is probably 2-10x.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Estimates, unverified (no searches ran). LOMA cost: no FEMA review fee, plus a surveyor's elevation certificate at about $500-2,000. LOMR-F: FEMA fee in the hundreds of dollars plus survey. Physical-change LOMR or floodway revision: FEMA fee of several thousand dollars plus $20-100k+ of engineering, and 6-18 months. My recollection is that most LOMAs FEMA receives are approved, because applicants pre-screen with elevation data. If so, the base hit rate for pre-screened attempts is already high, perhaps 50%+, and the most ML can cut capex is about 2x, not 10x. For floodway removals the hit rate is low, but the cost is set by the hydraulics and the politics, not by discovery.
scored.data: The inputs are public and mostly LEGIBLE: NFHL is structured GIS, 3DEP LiDAR is a standard point cloud, and BFEs are attributes on the map. Comparing a DEM against the BFE is a simple overlay, as the candidate itself admits. The only truly illegible input is the scanned FIS hydraulic backup data. Outcomes are already written into legible fields: LOMC cases are published as points and polygons in the NFHL and the Map Service Center LOMC index. Incumbents already do this routinely: flood-determination vendors, civil engineering firms, LOMA consultants, and developers who fill land via CLOMR-F. FEMA's own Risk MAP restudies keep remapping with the new LiDAR, and these mostly expand the SFHA rather than shrink it.
scored.right_bought: Yes, the right is bought. You can buy fee title or an option from private owners, tax-delinquent sellers or farmers who discount floodplain land, and some of them cannot read the maps. But owners and agents can check a free FEMA flood zone lookup and any surveyor's elevation certificate, so the information gap is thin for the cheap SFHA cases. For floodway land the discount is mostly rational, because development is regulated whatever the parcel's true elevation.
scored.buyer: Production homebuilders (Lennar, DR Horton) buying through lot-banking partners (Millrose, Varde, etc.), BTR funds, and local builders. They are capitalised and buy at volume, but mostly finished or entitled lots with a takedown schedule, not raw land that has only a map revision.
scored.ladder: The ladder is real but crowded and low-margin: land entitlement, then horizontal development and lot banking, then vertical homebuilding or BTR ownership, then property management. Each rung is a mature, competitive industry. Winning the map-revision rung gives no defensible edge on the rungs above, and the market is local, so it does not scale like a trillion-dollar chain.
scored.fatal_flaw: The big step-up is in the floodway-to-buildable case, and there the proving step is not mostly discovery. It needs a hydraulic no-rise re-model, community concurrence, entitlement and site development, much as the bespoke geothermal plant dominated the coal-mine case. The rung where discovery does dominate (an SFHA-to-X LOMA) only yields about 1.2-2x. A DEM-vs-BFE lookup already captures it, the outcomes sit in legible LOMC fields, and the base hit rate is probably already high. So ML has little lever.
scored.one_line_reason: Not excluded but weak (11/25). The ML-findable case (SFHA-to-X) is a ~1.2-2x step-up that a free elevation lookup mostly solves, and the 20-200x floodway case is dominated by engineering, politics and development rather than discovery. These scores come from prior knowledge, because the shared search budget ran out before any search ran.
sources: No web sources: the shared WebSearch budget (200 per turn) was used up before this agent's queries ran. All figures are estimates from prior knowledge and should be checked.
Unverified reference: FEMA LOMC process and fee schedule (fema.gov/flood-maps/change-your-flood-zone)
Unverified reference: FEMA NFHL / Map Service Center LOMC index (msc.fema.gov)
Unverified reference: 44 CFR 60.3(d) floodway encroachment and no-rise requirement

scored.name: Coastal Vested Rights: frozen California coastal lots
scored.one_line: Buy coastal lots trading as unbuildable; ML over Coastal Commission permit archives and pre-1972 records finds valid vested rights or CDPs; secure permits and sell to luxury builders.
scored.unproven_right: Coastal lot believed unbuildable, $10-50k.
scored.proving_step: Vested-rights determination or CDP approval with takings leverage ($50-200k, 1-2 years).
scored.proven_buyer: Luxury spec builders and HNW buyers.
scored.public_data: Coastal Commission permit archive and staff reports, LCPs, pre-1972 maps, assessor unbuildable codes.
scored.frame: The rung is a coastal lot taken from 'unbuildable' to 'entitled', meaning it holds a Coastal Development Permit (CDP) or a vested-rights determination, and is then sold to a builder. Inside that rung, discovery (finding a lot with a hidden valid right) is my estimate of 20-35% of the work. The remaining 65-80% is the proving step itself: geotech, biology/ESHA surveys, septic or sewer, fire access and water-meter availability, plus local and Coastal Commission hearings, appeals and takings negotiation. That is bespoke, political, multi-year entitlement work. It is the same shape as the coal-mine geothermal counter-example: doing the proving is harder than finding the lot. The buyer (luxury spec builders, HNW buyers) is real and capitalised.
scored.step_up: These are my estimates; the web search budget was used up and no live search ran. Substandard or ESHA-constrained lots in places like Malibu's El Nido/Big Rock, Montara, Big Sur and Sea Ranch change hands at roughly $20-150k. Comparable lots with a permit or an approved CDP sell at roughly $1-4M in Malibu and $300k-1.5M elsewhere on the coast. That gives about 10-50x on a hit, and up to ~100x at best. The anchor case is Lucas v. South Carolina Coastal Council (1992), where buildable beachfront lots were valued around $975k. Entitlement costs of $150k-1M+ eat into the multiple, so the net step-up is closer to 5-20x.
scored.hit_rate_capex: My estimates, not sourced. Each proving attempt costs about $150k-1M+ in consultants, studies, legal fees and appeals, and takes 2-5 years, not the 1-2 years the pitch assumes. On lots screened by an experienced entitlement attorney, the base hit rate is plausibly 30-60%. The Commission usually allows some economically viable use to avoid takings liability (for example, approving reduced-footprint homes in ESHA). The cases that fail do so mainly for physical reasons: no water meter, septic infeasible, slope, fire access. ML cannot change any of those. With base hit rates that high, the lever is capped at about 2-3x, not 10x, and ML does nothing to the dominant cost, which is the entitlement process.
scored.data: The signal is partly public and partly illegible. Coastal Commission staff reports from roughly the 1990s on are online as PDFs. Pre-1972 subdivision maps, Proposition 20 (1972) exemption records and pre-1977 vested-rights claims sit in scanned county records and Commission archives, which is a real OCR/ML opportunity. But the outcome is often already legible. LCP land-use designations, ESHA overlays, county 'substandard lot' or merger designations, water-district meter moratoria and a lot's prior permit denials are mapped or recorded fields. That is the same pattern of the answer already being in a status field. Buying the right is plausible: cheap lots are often held by heirs or out-of-state owners. But the sellers are not data-blind. Local land brokers and coastal entitlement attorneys already target exactly these lots.
scored.right_bought: Fee-simple purchase of the lot from heirs, absentee owners or tax-default sales, roughly $20-150k (my estimate). The right is bought, not free first-come, which fits the rubric. Downside: the seller can sue or claim a share if a 'worthless' lot is flipped for millions shortly after. Upside: you hold an option-like real asset even when proving fails.
scored.buyer: Luxury spec builders and HNW end buyers in Malibu, Laguna, Carmel/Big Sur and the Sonoma/Mendocino coast. They are capitalised and pay for entitlement certainty. The market is thin: perhaps tens to low hundreds of qualifying lots a year statewide (my estimate).
scored.ladder: Climbing the ladder means entitled lot, then design and build, then a luxury coastal homebuilder or developer. It is a capped, regulation-bound regional market with no path to a very large company. The rungs above (construction) are bespoke and low-margin compared with the discovery edge.
scored.fatal_flaw: The proving step is discretionary, multi-year, bespoke entitlement and litigation against the Coastal Commission, plus hard physical constraints (water, septic, slope, fire access). It is not a cheap, quasi-mechanical test like an exploratory drill, so discovery is a minority of the work. Base hit rates on screened lots are already moderate, so ML cannot cut capex 10x. This is the same structural failure as the geothermal-in-coal-mines counter-example.
scored.one_line_reason: The step-up is real (~10-50x) and the right can be bought, but proving costs $150k-1M+ and takes 2-5 years of political and legal process that ML does not shorten. Base hit rates are not low, much of the outcome is already in LCP/ESHA/water-moratorium fields, and the ladder ends at a regional luxury homebuilder.
sources: No live web searches ran; the shared 200-call per-turn search budget was used up. All numbers are estimates from prior knowledge.
Lucas v. South Carolina Coastal Council, 505 U.S. 1003 (1992): total regulatory taking of beachfront lots valued around $975k
California Coastal Act of 1976, Pub. Res. Code s.30010 (no taking without just compensation) and s.30608 (vested rights); Proposition 20 (1972) exemptions
California Coastal Commission staff reports archive (coastal.ca.gov/meetings) and Malibu LCP ESHA overlay maps (general knowledge)

scored.name: Ghost Offsets / OffsetBank: unclaimed emission reduction credits from shut-down sources
scored.one_line: Buy for a nominal fee or revenue share the unexercised right to bank NOx/VOC/PM ERCs from closed or curtailed boilers, turbines, kilns and small industrials in nonattainment areas; ML matches shutdowns (ECHO, NEI, WARN, bankruptcies) against ERC registries and reconstructs defensible baselines from scanned permits and stack tests; certify and sell to data-center turbine, peaker, refinery and LNG projects that cannot permit without offsets.
scored.unproven_right: Owner's unexercised ERC banking claim inside a 180-day to ~2-year window, bought by assignment/option for ~$0-25k from defunct plants, estates, hospitals, REIT landlords.
scored.proving_step: Reconstruct 2-of-5-year baseline actuals, show surplus/permanent/enforceable, file before deadline; physical step is only permanent shutdown.
scored.proven_buyer: BTM gas data-center developers (Williams, Crusoe, VoltaGrid-style, hyperscalers), IPPs, refineries, ports, chip fabs, LNG; ERC brokers (Evolution, Element Markets). SJV NOx ~$9.5-20k/t 2025-26; Houston VOC once $125-300k/t.
scored.public_data: TCEQ Central Registry and point-source inventory, TCEQ/SJVAPCD/BAAQMD/SCAQMD/CARB ERC registries and cost logs, EPA NEI, AMPD/CEMS, ECHO/ICIS-Air, EIA-860 retirements, WARN notices, PACER.
scored.rough_step_up: ~25-1000x on capital deployed; base hit rate moderate (~20-40%) so lever ~3-5x; inventory tonnage is legible, edge is eligibility, deadline and baseline.
scored.frame: The rung is turning an expiring, unbanked shutdown claim into a certified, saleable ERC. Inside that rung roughly 85-90% of the work is discovery and paperwork: finding the eligible shutdown, rebuilding the 2-year baseline, showing the reduction is surplus and enforceable, and filing before the deadline. The physical step, permanent shutdown, has already happened at no cost to us. Capitalised buyers exist: gas turbine developers, refineries, LNG plants and chip fabs in nonattainment areas cannot get a permit without offsets. So the frame is real. It is narrow, though, and it only works for sources whose owners missed the deadline or do not know the value. Those are mostly small sources with small tonnage.
scored.step_up: These are my own estimates. All web searches failed because the shared search budget was used up, so no number here was checked live. Price unproven: $0-25k for an assignment or option, as stated in the candidate. Price proven: a typical small to mid shutdown (a boiler, kiln or small turbine) yields maybe 5-50 tpy of NOx or VOC. At SJV NOx of ~$10-20k/t (the candidate's 2025-26 figure, from memory of the district's annual ERC report; some trades run higher) that is ~$50k-$1M. In Houston-Galveston-Brazoria and SCAQMD, scarce VOC/NOx sometimes reaches $100k-300k per ton. Return on capital deployed is ~10-100x, with rare outliers near 1000x. The right is not near-zero in the owner's eyes when the owner knows ERCs exist. The step from 'expiring and unclaimed' to 'certified' is genuinely large, but only for the minority of sources that slip through.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Unverified estimate: the base hit rate is the candidate's 20-40% for moving from 'shutdown identified' to 'credit certified', mostly lost to baseline or surplus disqualification and missed deadlines. Cost per attempt is about $10-50k (my estimate) for consultant baseline work, legal assignment, the district filing fee and any stack-test reconstruction. That makes 1/base hit rate only ~2.5-5x. ML raising the hit rate cannot cut capex 10x. The proving step is not expensive or mostly failing. It is cheap paperwork that mostly succeeds when the source is eligible.
scored.data: Data is partly legible, partly not. Legible already: emissions tonnage (the TCEQ point-source emissions inventory, EPA NEI, AMPD/CEMS), shutdowns (EIA-860 retirements, ECHO permit status) and banked credits (district ERC registries). The registry outcome field already shows who banked. Matching 'shutdown in EIA-860/ECHO with no registry entry' is a join, not an ML problem. Illegible: scanned permits and stack tests for reconstructing baselines, plus surplus determinations. That is real but modest work that consultants already do by hand. The outcome is not hidden. Brokers such as Element Markets and Evolution Markets, plus environmental consultancies, actively canvass large shutdowns. Owners of the valuable large sources are sophisticated and sell through brokers at near full value, minus roughly 5-15% commission (my estimate). So the cheap-purchase condition holds only for small, distressed or bankrupt sources.
scored.right_bought: Yes, the right is bought and not free first-come. It is an assignment or option on the owner's banking claim, or a purchase out of a bankruptcy or estate. It has to be bought before the filing window closes: SJV is about 180 days after shutdown; TCEQ, from memory, allows about 2 years. Both windows are unverified. The window is the constraint. The inventory refreshes only as fast as shutdowns happen in nonattainment areas, and most of the large tonnage is already captured.
scored.buyer: Real, capitalised buyers whose demand is growing: behind-the-meter gas data-center developers, IPPs and peakers, refineries, LNG plants, ports and chip fabs in SJV, SCAQMD, BAAQMD and Houston-Galveston-Brazoria. They can buy directly or through ERC brokers (Element Markets, Evolution Markets). Demand is strong, and scarce offsets block permits.
scored.ladder: Weak to moderate. Possible rungs: ERC origination, then an ERC trading desk or broker, then permitting-ready sites (offsets plus land plus interconnection), then owning gas generation for data centers. Each rung above origination is a crowded, conventional business (brokerage, power development) where discovery is a small share of the work. The ladder does not climb into an increasingly discovery-dominated chain. Total market is limited: ERC trading across all US districts is probably in the low hundreds of millions of dollars a year (my estimate).
scored.fatal_flaw: There is no purchase discount where the value sits. The outcome (who banked) is already in legible public registries, and brokers already canvass large shutdowns. The only cheap rights are small, low-tonnage, short-window sources, so the hit-rate lever is capped near 3x and the opportunity is a niche origination business, not a 10^4 discovery engine.
scored.one_line_reason: Clean paperwork-only frame with real capitalised buyers, but valuable shutdown tonnage is already legible and broker-canvassed, the base hit rate is not low (lever ~3x), and the step-up is mostly 10-100x on small sources, so it is a solid niche, not a Terranox analogue.

scored.name: Chapter 7 Abandoned Causes of Action
scored.one_line: Buy for $1-10k the debtor lawsuits and claims Chapter 7 trustees sell or abandon; ML across PACER schedules flags valuable ones; sell or fund via litigation funders.
scored.unproven_right: Estate causes of action sold by motion for nominal consideration.
scored.proving_step: ML triage plus funder-grade merits and damages memo.
scored.proven_buyer: Burford, Omni Bridgeway, Parabellum, contingency firms.
scored.public_data: PACER/RECAP, Schedule A/B, 363 notices, CourtListener, state dockets.
scored.frame: The rung is "own a purchased estate cause of action and turn it into a funder-grade case". By my estimate discovery and triage are only about 40-60% of the work inside that rung. The rest is court-supervised purchase mechanics (363 motion, notice, overbid), questions over whether the claim can be assigned (legal-malpractice and some personal-injury claims are non-assignable in many states), and above all litigating to realisation. Funders price the claim on expected litigation outcome and years to resolution, not on the memo. Unlike a drill hit, the memo does not make the value real. The physical step, litigation, is neither trivial nor abstracted.
scored.step_up: My estimate, no source verified: a claim bought for $1-10k that turns out good might be worth $100k-1M as a funded or contingency-backed claim, roughly 20-300x on paper. Commercial funders such as Burford and Omni typically want claims with damages in the high seven or eight figures and fund rather than buy outright. Most Chapter 7 claims are small individual or small-business claims, so the realisable step-up is lower and comes years later, discounted by funder share (often 20-40% of proceeds, estimated). That puts it at about 10-100x. It is not 10^3-10^4.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Base hit rate is the candidate's own 1-3% (my estimate and unverified). Each proving attempt costs very little: ML triage is near-free, plus about $5-25k for a merits and damages memo (estimate). Today's capex is not large and mostly failing in the way a $100k-1M exploratory drill is, so a 10x capex cut buys little. The lever cap of 1/hit rate (about 30-100x) exists in theory. In practice the binding constraint is deal flow from trustees, not the cost of evaluating.
scored.data: PACER/RECAP, Schedule A/B, 363 sale notices and CourtListener are public but partly illegible (PDF schedules, scattered dockets). Schedule A/B has explicit lines for claims against third parties, and the trustee, a fiduciary paid partly on recoveries, reviews them in the 341 meeting. So the outcome-relevant judgment is effectively already made by an informed insider. Trustees routinely hire contingency counsel at no estate cost for anything with merit (avoidance actions, D&O claims, undisclosed PI claims).
scored.right_bought: Yes, mechanically. Trustees sell estate causes of action by 363 motion, often for nominal consideration. But the seller (trustee plus counsel) is not an owner who cannot read the data. Sales are noticed and open to overbid, and the defendant is often the natural highest bidder because it is buying peace. Nominal-price sales are mostly claims the trustee judged worthless.
scored.buyer: Litigation funders (Burford, Omni Bridgeway, Parabellum, Longford), contingency-fee plaintiff firms, the defendants themselves (settlement by purchase), and creditors. These buyers are capitalised, but for small claims they mostly fund on a share rather than paying a lump sum up front.
scored.ladder: Claim acquisition, then in-house litigation finance, then a captive contingency law firm, then a balance-sheet litigation fund or distressed-claims platform. This is a real ladder, but it tops out as a specialty finance or asset-management business. Burford's market cap is about $2-3B (from memory, not checked). There is no clear trillion-dollar chain.
scored.fatal_flaw: Adverse selection by an informed fiduciary. The Chapter 7 trustee has a legal duty to maximise the estate, is paid a percentage of recoveries, and can hire contingency counsel at zero estate cost. Any claim with real expected value gets pursued, not sold for $1-10k. What reaches nominal-price sale or abandonment is the residue the expert already rejected, and the sales are open to overbid, with the defendant as the natural bidder. Value is realised only through years of litigation, not at the moment of proving.
scored.one_line_reason: The sellers are informed trustees with contingency counsel, so the claims they sell cheaply are the rejected residue. Litigation is not an abstracted physical step. The step-up is about 10-100x and arrives years later, not as an immediate 10^4 revaluation.
sources: No web sources: the shared web-search budget for this turn was used up before any search ran, so every number above is an estimate from background knowledge and none was verified.

11 U.S.C. 326 (trustee compensation tied to disbursements), from background knowledge

scored.name: Restitution Claim Matcher / Provenance Claims: looted-art restitution
scored.one_line: Buy or fund heirs' restitution claims; ML matches scanned ERR, Linz, CCP and dealer stock records against museum collections and auction listings; collect settlements or sale splits.
scored.unproven_right: Heirs' rights to specific works by assignment or purchase, $1-10k.
scored.proving_step: Provenance match plus heirship proof; claim letter or filing.
scored.proven_buyer: Christie's/Sotheby's restitution departments, museums, possessors' insurers, art-title insurers.
scored.public_data: Lost Art database, ERR project, DHM Linz/CCP database, Heidelberg catalogues, NARA Holocaust-era assets (Fold3), museum APIs.
scored.rough_step_up: ~10^3x on a hit; finite shrinking pool; must be heir-aligned.
scored.frame: The rung is "own or co-own a matched restitution claim and settle it". Matching provenance (ERR/Linz/CCP/dealer stock books against collections) is discovery, and I estimate it at about 40-50% of the work. The rest is not trivial: proving heirship across several generations and countries (genealogy, probate in multiple jurisdictions, getting all co-heirs to sign) and then negotiating or litigating against possessors, often for 2-10 years (estimate, based on known cases like Altmann/Klimt and Welfenschatz). So the "physical step" here is legal and genealogical work. It is bespoke and slow, which is the coal-mine-geothermal pattern, not drilling.
scored.step_up: The unproven right costs a few thousand dollars per assignment, or more typically a contingency share of about 20-40% of recovery (that range is the practice of heir-hunting and restitution firms such as Mondex, from memory, not verified this run). A proven claim on a mid-market work pays roughly $50k-$5M as a settlement or sale split; outliers like the Klimt Adele Bloch-Bauer I were sold for $135M after restitution. Measured on the company's cash outlay (about $5-20k of research and genealogy per claim, my estimate) against its share of a typical settlement (about $100k-$500k), the step-up is about 10-100x. 10^3x happens only on rare blockbusters. Most claims end in a split with the possessor (Washington Principles "just and fair solutions"), and that shrinks the payout further.
scored.hit_rate_capex: I could not verify this: the shared search budget was used up before this agent ran, so every number is an estimate from prior knowledge. Cost per proving attempt (provenance match plus heirship file): about $5-50k. Base hit rate from candidate match to recovery: I estimate 5-15%. The main reason claims fail is not finding the work. It is legal defences (statute of limitations or laches outside the US HEAR Act window, "forced sale" disputes, good-faith purchaser laws in Switzerland and other civil-law countries) and getting heirs to cooperate. ML speeds up the matching but leaves those failure modes untouched, so I estimate the real capex lever at about 2-3x, not 10x.
scored.data: Partly fits. The ERR project (about 30k records), DHM Linz/CCP databases, dealer stock books, Heidelberg auction catalogues and NARA/Fold3 Holocaust-era records are public, and much of it is scanned and messy. The problem is that the outcome is already partly written into legible fields. The German Lost Art Foundation database (lostart.de) lists search and found reports. Museums publish provenance-gap lists (AAM/NEPIP, the German museum PDF lists). The Art Loss Register and the Commission for Looted Art in Europe already match against auctions. NY State's Holocaust Claims Processing Office does this work for heirs for free. Major auction houses screen every consignment. So the open seam is the long tail of mid-value works with no prior report, and that is real but thin.
scored.right_bought: The right can be bought, but at a heavy discount for ethics and law. Heirs can assign claims or sign contingency agreements. However, many heirs are already reached by heir hunters and specialist lawyers. Outright purchase of a claim by a profit-seeking firm hurts how possessors and the German Advisory Commission view it (moral-claim framing). Some jurisdictions restrict champerty or claim assignment. The heirs can usually read the data themselves once someone else points out the match, so there is no information asymmetry to buy into cheaply. In practice the realistic structure is a contingency share, not a cheap outright buy.
scored.buyer: There is a capitalised counterparty: museums, possessors and their insurers, art-title insurers, and auction houses brokering sale splits through Christie's/Sotheby's restitution departments. But they settle reluctantly. They are adversaries, not willing buyers paying a market price for a proven asset the way a mine developer is.
scored.ladder: The ladder is weak. Possible rungs above: owning restituted works and dealing or auctioning them, art-title insurance, a provenance-clearance service. These are small, partly service businesses. The pool is finite and shrinking (WWII-era losses, about 80 years on), so there is no path to a trillion-dollar chain.
scored.fatal_flaw: The work after discovery (multi-generation heirship proof, then years of contested negotiation or litigation against reluctant possessors under limitations, laches and good-faith-purchaser defences) dominates the effort and the failure rate. Discovery is nowhere near 80% of the rung. The pool is also finite and shrinking, and the work is already partly matched by free or nonprofit bodies (HCPO, the Commission for Looted Art in Europe, the Lost Art Foundation, the Art Loss Register).
scored.one_line_reason: This is a legal-collections business dressed as discovery: matching is the easy part, heirship and litigation are the bespoke hard part, the step-up is about 10-100x on the company's share, and the market is shrinking with no ladder.

German Lost Art Foundation database (lostart.de), prior knowledge
ERR Project database (errproject.org), prior knowledge
NY State Holocaust Claims Processing Office (dfs.ny.gov), prior knowledge
HEAR Act 2016 (US); Washington Principles 1998

scored.name: Black Box Publishing / Catalog / Claimant: orphan compositions behind unmatched royalties
scored.one_line: Buy writer and publisher shares from heirs and defunct small publishers whose compositions earn unmatched or unclaimed royalties at the MLC, SoundExchange, PROs and foreign CMOs; ML matches usage to works; register, collect accrued money, resell.
scored.unproven_right: Composition shares or royalty streams, $500-10k.
scored.proving_step: ML matching of unmatched usage to scanned registrations and splits, ownership proof, registration and claims.
scored.proven_buyer: Concord, Reservoir, Round Hill, Spirit, Duetti, Royalty Exchange, SongVest buyers.
scored.public_data: MLC public search and unmatched data, SoundExchange unclaimed, PRS/GEMA/SACEM unidentified lists, CCE renewals, ASCAP/BMI repertories, MusicBrainz/Discogs.
scored.rough_step_up: ~10-250x; MLC itself is matching, so edge contested.
scored.frame: The rung is "own an orphan composition share and get it registered and collecting". Inside that rung, matching usage to works, proving the chain of title and filing the claims is about 70-85% of the work, and nothing physical is involved (my estimate). The catch is that much of the work is legal: tracing heirs, estates and the files of defunct publishers. Matching is only part of it, and an ML model does not get you through probate. Catalog funds (Concord, Reservoir, Round Hill, Spirit) and marketplaces (Royalty Exchange, SongVest) do buy the output. But they price on a 3-year net publisher share (NPS) history, so a newly claimed share with almost no clean history sells at a discount. The frame exists, but it is weaker than Terranox's.
scored.step_up: From memory, not newly searched: small catalogs sell for about 5-12x NPS on Royalty Exchange-type marketplaces, and large catalogs for about 12-20x. Suppose a share bought for $500-10k is actually unclaimed and the pool has, say, $200-2k of accrued money (my estimate for one long-tail work). After the claim you collect that money and the share sells for maybe 6-10x its ongoing annual NPS. Real step-up on the purchase price: about 2-20x, nowhere near 10^3. The reason is that the long tail of unmatched money is spread over millions of works, so very few are worth much. Under the MMA, unclaimed money is eventually paid out by market share, and the date keeps getting extended. A hit is income you can claim. It does not move an asset from about $1 to $10k.
scored.hit_rate_capex: From memory: in Feb 2021 the MLC received about $424M of historical unmatched mechanical royalties from DSPs, and since then it has reported match rates above 90% by dollar value. The money left over is spread thin. The proving attempt is cheap: a database lookup plus a claim filing costs maybe $50-500 per work, and the legal title work costs maybe $1-5k per estate (estimates). So the proving step is neither expensive nor mostly failing in a way that ML would improve 10x. Discovery capex is low already, so the 1/base-hit-rate lever is small. The cost that matters is title and heir clearance, which ML does not cut. Web search budget was exhausted, so no new sources were added.
scored.data: The data is public and partly illegible: Copyright Office renewal records (CCE scans, pre-1978), PRS/GEMA/SACEM unidentified-performance lists, and MusicBrainz/Discogs. However, the MLC's public portal and its unmatched-usage data already mark which recordings are unmatched in a legible field. SoundExchange publishes its unclaimed list in a searchable form. The PROs (ASCAP/BMI) have searchable repertories. So the regulator-style status field that answers "is there money here?" already exists. ML only helps with linking messy metadata, and a whole industry already does that: Songtrust, Sentric, CD Baby Pro, Kobalt/AWAL admin, Music Reports, Audiam/Downtown, royalty-audit and heir-finder firms, and the MLC's own matching team.
scored.right_bought: Yes. Writer and publisher shares can be bought from heirs, estates and defunct small publishers, and buying a writer share is legal and common. But sellers can type the song title into the MLC, SoundExchange or the PRO search and see that money is waiting. Free admin services (Songtrust etc.) market to them directly, so the information gap gets arbitraged away quickly. Heirs who do not know they own anything exist, but finding them is skip-trace and probate work, not reading illegible data.
scored.buyer: Catalog funds (Concord, Reservoir, Round Hill, Spirit, Hipgnosis/Recognition, Primary Wave, Duetti for indie artists) and retail royalty marketplaces (Royalty Exchange, SongVest). They have the capital, but they want cash flow with history and enough scale. Tiny orphan shares only sell once they are bundled.
scored.ladder: The ladder is real but modest: aggregate orphans, become an admin/publisher, then a catalog fund, then possibly a full publisher-plus-label or a rights-data infrastructure company. The music publishing market is about $8-10B a year in global revenue (from memory), with a ceiling around a major publisher, worth tens of billions. That is not a trillion-dollar chain.
scored.fatal_flaw: The outcome is already legible: the MLC, SoundExchange and the PROs publish searchable unmatched and unclaimed status, and the MLC and admin companies are already matching. On top of that, the per-work dollars in the long tail are tiny, so a hit yields roughly 2-20x on a small purchase, not 10^3-10^4. The hard cost is title and heir clearance, which ML does not solve.
scored.one_line_reason: This is a cheap, crowded matching problem: the MLC and PROs already surface unmatched status, the long-tail payouts are small, and the realistic step-up is about 2-20x rather than 10^3+, so it fails C2, C3 and C4 even though a buyer exists.
sources: No new web sources: the web search budget was used up before any search ran. Every figure is from memory or my own estimate and should be checked:
MLC historical unmatched royalties transfer, about $424M, Feb 2021 (themlc.com press releases, from memory)
MLC reported match rates above 90% (MLC annual reports, from memory)
Catalog valuation multiples of about 5-12x NPS for small catalogs and 12-20x for large ones (Royalty Exchange market reports, Citrin Cooperman catalog studies; from memory)
Music Modernization Act 2018: unclaimed mechanicals distributed by market share after a holding period (17 U.S.C. 115(d)(3)(J))

scored.name: Reversion Rights Partners: out-of-print book reversions
scored.one_line: Find genre titles revertible under out-of-print clauses that fit adaptation demand, fund the reversion, co-own the reverted subsidiary rights, sell options.
scored.unproven_right: Revertible subsidiary rights, $1-10k.
scored.proving_step: ML on print status and contract norms, reversion letters, title clearance, option sale.
scored.proven_buyer: Studios, Audible, Podium, game studios, Skybound, Legendary.
scored.public_data: CCE and recorded assignments, publisher catalogues, Internet Archive/HathiTrust, Bowker, probate.
scored.frame: The rung is: obtain the reverted subsidiary (film/TV/audio/game) rights to an out-of-print genre title and sell an option on them. Discovery (finding which titles can be reverted and might be adapted) is maybe 30-40% of the work inside that rung (my estimate). Most of the work is people and selling: persuading the author or estate, getting the publisher to sign a reversion letter (often months, and contested), clearing chain of title, and pitching producers. The hit is decided by a producer's taste, not by a fact hidden in the data. The buyers (studios, Audible, Podium, Skybound) have money, but they buy through a slow, relationship-driven pitch process, not the way a developer buys a drill-proven claim.
scored.step_up: My estimates (web search budget was exhausted, so no live sourcing). Unproven right: $1-10k to fund a reversion plus a co-ownership share. Option sale on a midlist or backlist novel: usually $1k-$25k, about 1-10% of the purchase price. Purchase price if the project is made: about $50k-$500k for midlist, more for a known IP. Backlist audio rights: about $1-5k advances. So an option, the 'proof' event, is about 1-5x the cost. The 10-100x claimed in the pitch only arrives at a purchase-price exercise, which is rare and comes years later. No 10^3-10^4 jump happens straight away.
scored.hit_rate_capex: My estimates from industry folklore, not sourced this run. Commonly cited: under 10% of optioned books (often given as 1 in 10 to 1 in 20) get made. The share of reverted backlist titles that ever get optioned is probably in the low single-digit percent. Each attempt is cheap, though (legal letters plus pitching, about $1-10k), so the expensive proving step that ML could make 10x cheaper does not exist. Predicting adaptation demand is a taste problem with a weak signal. ML might lift option rates a little, but it cannot cut a large capex because there is no large capex.
scored.data: Mixed. Whether a title is in print is fairly easy to see (Bowker/Books in Print, Amazon, publisher catalogues). The CCE, recorded copyright assignments and Section 203 termination windows are public but messy, and there is a real but small edge in reading them. The contract terms that decide reversion (how 'out of print' is defined) are private, not public. Post-2000 contracts usually count ebook or print-on-demand availability as 'in print', which defeats reversion. Incumbents and free help already exist: the Authors Guild runs a rights-reversion service for members, the Authors Alliance publishes a reversion guide, Open Road Media and other backlist digital publishers built businesses on reverted rights, and literary agents and estates mine backlists. Audio publishers (Podium, Blackstone) and IP scouts already comb backlists for adaptation material.
scored.right_bought: Partly. The rights belong to authors or estates, who must agree to revert and then sell or share them. That makes this a negotiated, one-at-a-time acquisition, not buying a claim cheaply from someone who cannot read the data. Owners often have agents and get free reversion help from the Authors Guild, and they hold the leverage once told their book is wanted. There is some information gap: neglected estates and orphaned midlist authors often do not know their rights can revert. But the price rises as soon as you reveal interest.
scored.buyer: Studios and streamers, production companies (Skybound, Legendary), Audible, Podium, Blackstone and game studios. All have money, but they buy through a pitch and development process, and most options lapse.
scored.ladder: Rights aggregation leads to an IP library and packaging (as at Skybound, Wattpad Webtoon Studios or Pocket FM), then audio and graphic adaptations, then production. A real ladder exists, but each rung is a creative, hit-driven business, not a discovery-heavy one, and the top of the chain is a studio, not a trillion-dollar vertical.
scored.fatal_flaw: The 'hit' is a buyer's taste decision found by pitching, not a hidden fact proven by a cheap test. On top of that, options pay only about 1-10% of purchase price, so the step-up at proof is about 2-5x rather than 10^3-10^4. Modern ebook and POD 'in print' definitions also shrink the pool of titles that can be reverted.
scored.one_line_reason: The hit depends on producer taste found through pitching, and an option pays only a few times its cost, so there is no expensive, mostly-failing proving step with a 10^3x payoff for ML to make cheaper.
sources: Web search budget was exhausted this turn (200 calls shared across agents), so no live sources were fetched; every number above is my estimate from prior knowledge and should be checked in a follow-up.
Authors Guild rights reversion service (authorsguild.org), from prior knowledge
Authors Alliance, 'Understanding Rights Reversion' guide (authorsalliance.org), from prior knowledge
Open Road Media backlist business model, from prior knowledge
17 U.S.C. Section 203 termination of transfers, from prior knowledge

scored.name: SEP Essentiality Prover (cellular, Wi-Fi, codec, JEDEC, industrial standards; incl. university SEPs)
scored.one_line: Buy declared-but-unverified or undeclared patents that read on 3GPP, IEEE 802.11, HEVC, JEDEC or industrial standards (OPC UA, TSN, EtherCAT) from small declarants, defunct handset/chip firms and universities at bulk prices; ML aligns claims to spec clauses; independent evaluator certifies; place in pools or sell to licensors.
scored.unproven_right: Declared or undeclared SEP families at $5-100k; only ~8-36% of declared are truly essential.
scored.proving_step: ML claim-to-spec alignment across releases and change requests; independent essentiality evaluation ($5-30k per family).
scored.proven_buyer: Avanci, Sisvel, Via LA, Access Advance, InterDigital, Nokia, Ericsson, Acacia, SEP funds.
scored.public_data: ETSI IPR declarations, 3GPP spec and ~500k contribution archive, IEEE LOAs and drafts, JEDEC disclosures, USPTO/EPO/CNIPA full text, PACER schedules.
scored.rough_step_up: ~10-500x; lever capped ~3-10x by base essentiality rate.
scored.frame: The rung is 'own a declared or undeclared patent family and get it certified essential, then put it in a pool.' Inside that rung, discovery (matching claims to spec clauses) is about 60-70% of the work. The rest is legal: claim construction, an evaluator per jurisdiction, pool admission, and often reissue or continuation prosecution to make the claims read cleanly on the spec. The value is not realised at certification. It is realised over years of royalty distributions or FRAND enforcement, which costs $2-10M+ per case in the US/EU/China. So the 'physical step' is not abstracted the way a drill is. Pools buy the output (Avanci, Sisvel, Via LA, Access Advance), and so do InterDigital, Acacia and SEP funds. But pools admit patents without buying them, so the owner still carries the asset over time. Estimate.
scored.step_up: Estimates from prior knowledge; no live search was possible. Secondary-market patents typically trade at ~$50-250k per asset (Richardson Oliver Law Group market reports have put average ask prices around $100-200k and falling). Undeclared or unverified telecom families from distressed or university sellers might go for ~$10-50k each in bulk. A family certified essential and placed in a pool might be worth ~$100k-1M NPV. That figure depends on remaining life, how many jurisdictions it covers and how pool shares are split; Avanci 4G/5G vehicle royalties of ~$20-32 per car are shared across thousands of families. That makes the realistic step-up ~5-30x, with rare outliers at ~100x. It is far from 10^3-10^4, and it is not immediate: cash arrives over years of distributions.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Base essentiality rate of declared families: about 8-36% across studies (Goodman & Myers 2005 put 3G at ~21%; later LTE/5G studies by Fairfield, Cyber Creative Institute and others fall in the ~15-40% range). Using the candidate's own figure, the ML lever is capped at ~3-10x, and in practice lower, because ML alignment pre-screens are already used. Cost per proving attempt: ~$5-30k per family per evaluator (candidate figure; Avanci/Sisvel-style evaluations commonly run ~$10-20k). Cheap ML pre-screening already exists (IPlytics/LexisNexis, Patentcloud SEP OmniLytics, Unified Patents, Amplified), so the costly human evaluation is already the confirmation step, not the search step.
scored.data: The data is public and large: ETSI IPR declarations, 3GPP specs with ~500k+ contributions and change requests, IEEE LOAs, JEDEC disclosures, and full text from USPTO, EPO and CNIPA. But much of it is already structured and mined. ETSI declarations are a searchable database. IPlytics, LexisNexis and Clarivate sell analytics that combine declarations with contributions. Pools publish their patent lists, so for pooled assets the outcome already sits in a legible field. The remaining edge is in undeclared families (especially from universities and for industrial standards like OPC UA, TSN and EtherCAT, where coverage is thin) and in mapping claims to clauses at the change-request level.
scored.right_bought: Yes, the rights are bought rather than claimed for free. Sellers include small declarants, defunct handset and chip makers through bankruptcy auctions (Nortel, Kodak and BlackBerry style sales), and university tech-transfer offices. However, sophisticated buyers (Acacia, InterDigital, Dominion Harbor, RPX, Intellectual Ventures and SEP funds) already bid at these auctions with the same analytics, so the discount for 'owners cannot read the data' is small except at universities and very small firms.
scored.buyer: Patent pools (Avanci, Sisvel, Via LA, Access Advance), which mostly admit patents rather than buy them. Licensors and aggregators (InterDigital, Nokia, Ericsson, Acacia) and SEP-focused funds do buy, but at prices that discount for remaining life and litigation risk.
scored.ladder: Climbing the ladder means going from SEP aggregator to licensing and enforcement company to pool operator to standards-contributing R&D licensor (the InterDigital model). The top of this ladder is a licensing company worth roughly $5-15B (InterDigital is worth about $5-8B). Each rung is legal or contribution work rather than a physical industrial chain, so there is no path to a trillion-dollar company and no route into owning the underlying industry.
scored.fatal_flaw: The step-up is only about 10x and it is not realised at certification. The value comes from years of royalty distributions or costly FRAND enforcement on a 20-year asset that is shrinking. Meanwhile, well-funded aggregators already run ML claim-to-spec screening at the same auctions, and the 8-36% base rate caps the hit-rate lever at about 3-10x.
scored.one_line_reason: This is a reasonable patent-arbitrage niche but not a Terranox analogue. The step-up is about 5-30x, not 10^4. Proving does not convert straight into cash: value only arrives through litigation or slow pool payouts. Incumbents (IPlytics, Acacia, InterDigital) already mine this data, and the ladder tops out at an InterDigital-sized licensing company.
sources: Web searches were not run because this turn's shared search budget of 200 was used up. All figures are prior knowledge or estimates and should be checked.

Richardson Oliver Law Group patent market reports (secondary-market average ask prices per asset, ~$100-200k range)
Avanci 5G Vehicle program public pricing (~$32 per vehicle; $29 early-bird)
ETSI IPR online database (dipr.etsi.org): declarations are structured and searchable
IPlytics (LexisNexis) SEP analytics; Patentcloud SEP OmniLytics: existing ML essentiality screening

scored.name: Function-Category Arbitrage: US/EU devices into Japan STM reimbursement
scored.one_line: Take Japan rights to cleared devices from small makers; ML maps them onto MHLW function categories with fixed prices; get Shonin approval without new trials; sell to Japanese distributors.
scored.unproven_right: Exclusive Japan marketing rights, $20-100k option.
scored.proving_step: PMDA consultation and Shonin/Ninsho filing with an MAH ($100-300k).
scored.proven_buyer: Japan Lifeline, Century Medical/Itochu, Medikit, Terumo, Olympus.
scored.public_data: MHLW function-category notices (Japanese PDFs), PMDA approvals, FDA 510(k), EUDAMED.
scored.frame: The rung is "Japan rights to a foreign cleared device, taken through Shonin/Ninsho approval with a B (existing function category) reimbursement assignment". Discovery, meaning working out which MHLW function category a device fits and therefore its fixed price, is maybe 15-25% of the work inside that rung (my estimate). Most of the work is regulatory and operational: PMDA consultation, preparing a STED dossier, showing foreign clinical data is acceptable, MO169 QMS conformity audits, setting up an MAH or designated MAH, Japanese labelling, and post-market vigilance. The physical step is not trivial or abstracted. A capitalised buyer does exist (Japanese distributors), but they buy commercial supply rights, not a mapping insight. This sits closer to the coal-mine geothermal counter-example than to Terranox.
scored.step_up: Unproven right: exclusive Japan option, $20-100k (from the candidate, unverified). Proven right: a Japan-approved device with a B-category price, licensed or sold to a distributor. My estimate is $0.5-5M upfront plus a supply margin, depending on category size. That gives roughly 10-50x, not 10^3. Japan also cuts reimbursement prices every two years and applies foreign-average-price adjustments, so the step-up shrinks over time. All numbers are estimates; I found no sourced deal prices.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Cost per proving attempt is $100-300k (from the candidate). In my estimate, $0.3-1M is more realistic for Class III/IV once QMS audits and MAH costs are included. The base hit rate is HIGH, not low. A device with FDA/CE clearance that maps onto an existing B category is usually approved, because Japan accepts foreign clinical data for most such devices, and its category is predictable from the predicate. Failures come mainly from commercial non-uptake, not failed proving. With a hit rate of perhaps 50-80%, the ML lever is capped at about 1.25-2x, nowhere near 10x. This is an estimate: the search budget ran out before any search could run, so I could not source a PMDA approval-rate figure.
scored.data: The data is public and partly illegible: MHLW function-category notices and insurance-coverage (hoken tekiyo) notices are Japanese PDFs. But the outcome is already written into legible fields. Each approved device's function category and fixed reimbursement price are published in the MHLW material price tables, and FDA 510(k) product codes and predicates are structured. Mapping a new device to a category mostly means looking up how its predicate was categorised, which is a lookup table, the same failure mode as the interconnection-queue candidate. Regulatory consultancies and distributor business-development teams already read these notices routinely, so the illegibility is not a moat.
scored.right_bought: Yes, Japan rights are bought through option or licence agreements with small makers, not claimed free. But the sellers are not uninformed. US/EU makers are pitched by Japanese distributors and consultants all the time, and many already hold Japan partners or plan to self-file. The purchase discount comes from the maker's limited bandwidth, not from an information gap ML can exploit.
scored.buyer: Japan Lifeline, Century Medical (Itochu), Medikit, Terumo, Olympus, plus Kaneka, Asahi Intecc and trading-house medical units. They are capitalised, but they in-license devices themselves; that is Japan Lifeline's core business model. So the buyer is also the main competitor, and would rather sign the small maker directly than pay a middleman's step-up.
scored.ladder: The ladder above is moderate: holding approvals as MAH, then own distribution and sales force in Japan, then expanding to other Asia-Pacific reimbursement systems (Korea, Taiwan), then own-brand devices and manufacturing. Japan Lifeline is the precedent, a company of roughly $1B scale built on in-licensed foreign devices. The device market is large, but the climb is commercial and sales-led rather than discovery-led, and it does not plausibly lead to a trillion-dollar company.
scored.fatal_flaw: Discovery is not the bottleneck and the proving step rarely fails. Function-category mapping is largely a predicate lookup, and its answer is published in legible MHLW price tables. Clearing regulatory and QMS steps and winning commercial uptake is most of the work, and approval of a cleared device into a B category succeeds at a high base rate (estimated). So ML cannot cut capex by anything like 10x. The capitalised buyers (Japan Lifeline, Century Medical) already run this exact in-licensing playbook, so they compete with the company rather than pay it a step-up.
scored.one_line_reason: This is regulatory arbitrage with a roughly 10-50x step-up (estimated), a high base approval rate, outcomes already published in MHLW price tables, and incumbent distributors who already do the same in-licensing. It fails the 95-5 discovery frame.
sources: No web sources: both searches I attempted were refused because the shared search limit for this turn (200 calls) was already used up, so no search returned results. All numbers are my estimates from prior knowledge.
Prior knowledge: MHLW medical device reimbursement categories A1/A2/B/C1/C2 and the specified insurance medical materials (STM) price tables (MHLW notices)
Prior knowledge: PMDA Shonin/Ninsho pathways, MO169 QMS requirements, and acceptance of foreign clinical data
Prior knowledge: Japan Lifeline and Century Medical in-licensing business models

scored.name: Dead-Fabless Mask-Set Revival
scored.one_line: Buy GDSII, mask sets, test programs and wafer bank of discontinued ICs from estates; ML proves sole-source installed base in defense, rail, medical and industrial systems; sell or license revival rights.
scored.unproven_right: Product-line IP and wafer inventory, $0-100k.
scored.proving_step: ML over DMSMS reports, DIBBS demand, QPLs, EOL notices and BOMs; wafer-bank or mask validation.
scored.proven_buyer: Rochester Electronics, Lansdale, Teledyne e2v, primes' DMSMS offices, DLA.
scored.public_data: PACER sales, DIBBS, SAM J&As, QPL/QML, DMSMS portal, EOL notices, Octopart, FCC BOMs.
scored.frame: The rung is "buy the dead product line, then show it has a captive sole-source installed base". Finding the demand is maybe 30-40% of the work, and that is my estimate. The physical step is not trivial. You have to find a foundry that still runs the old process node (or port the design), check that the stored wafers and masks still work, rebuild the test program, and requalify parts to QML/QPL. This is the geothermal-in-coal-mines pattern: running the revival is harder than spotting the line. The only rung that is mostly discovery is selling the unvalidated IP bundle, and in that rung the buyer (Rochester) has strong power to set the price.
scored.step_up: My estimate, with no sources found: the IP and wafer bank costs $0-100k from an estate. If it has real sole-source defense or rail demand, the revival rights might sell or license for $0.5-5M, which is about 10-100x. That gain mostly comes after revival and requalification, not right after a data "hit". A bundle that has not been validated would probably sell to Rochester or Lansdale for only about 1-5x what you paid, because they are the natural buyers and their team already does this valuation. The 50-1000x in the candidate pitch is not backed by any source.
scored.hit_rate_capex: I have no sourced numbers because the searches did not run. Estimates: most dead fabless lines have no captive installed base, so maybe 5-15% are worth reviving. Checking demand on paper costs little (analyst time, a few $k). Validating wafers or masks plus requalification costs about $100k-$1M+ per line. ML only speeds up the cheap paper step, so the expensive step is untouched and the lever is about 2-3x on total capex, not 10x.
scored.data: The demand signal is already quite readable. DIBBS posts NSN solicitations with quantities. GIDEP and DMSMS notices, QPL/QML lists and PCNs/EOL notices are structured and kept by the obsolescence data vendors (SiliconExpert, IHS/Accuris, Z2Data). Incumbents already mine these to target last-time buys. The hard-to-read parts (scanned BOMs, J&A text, PACER estate filings) add some edge, mainly in finding estates. Rights are bought, not claimed first-come. But sellers such as OCMs, trustees and IP liquidators already know Rochester is the buyer, so the price discount from sellers who can't read the data is small.
scored.right_bought: You buy the product-line IP (GDSII, masks, test programs) and the wafer or die bank from bankruptcy estates, liquidators or OCMs that are exiting the line. These are bought, not free. Big OCMs often transfer lines to Rochester under authorized-aftermarket deals. Estates of failed fabless companies are cheaper and less contested.
scored.buyer: From my own knowledge, not sourced: Rochester Electronics (says it is authorized by 70+ OCMs and holds billions of devices), Lansdale Semiconductor, Flip Electronics, Innovasic, Micross, Teledyne e2v, the primes' DMSMS offices and DLA. They are well funded, but they are also direct competitors for the same estates, so selling to them gives up the step-up.
scored.ladder: There are real rungs above. Revived-part manufacturing, then QML qualification, then form-fit-function emulation chips (the Innovasic model), then a full obsolescence-management partner for primes. The top is roughly a Rochester-scale business, which my estimate puts near $1B+ revenue, run as a private, fragmented niche. That is a big company but not a trillion-dollar chain. The obsolescence market is bounded by the size of the legacy installed base.
scored.fatal_flaw: Reviving the part (getting a foundry and process match, validating wafers, requalifying) is much harder and costlier than finding which dead lines have demand. That demand signal is already largely readable in DIBBS, GIDEP and vendor obsolescence databases, which incumbents like Rochester mine while also competing for the same estates.
scored.one_line_reason: This is the geothermal-mine pattern. Discovery is the easy, half-readable part, the physical revival is the hard part, and an established authorized-aftermarket player is both the only buyer and a competitor.
sources: No web searches ran: the shared search budget for this turn was used up. All figures are my estimates from prior knowledge and should be checked.
Prior knowledge: Rochester Electronics authorized-aftermarket model (rocelec.com)
Prior knowledge: DLA DIBBS (dibbs.bsm.dla.mil), GIDEP, DoD DMSMS SD-22 guidebook

scored.name: EastWest Rights / PMDA Bridge: ex-Asia rights to drugs approved only in Japan, China or Korea
scored.one_line: ML translates PMDA, NMPA and MFDS review reports to find drugs with strong local data never filed in the US/EU, licenses ex-Asia rights cheaply, and gets FDA agreement on a bridging path. The FDA meeting minutes are the step-up event.
scored.unproven_right: US/EU development and commercial rights from Asian mid-size pharma for small upfronts ($0.5-10M) plus milestones.
scored.proving_step: Dossier translation, FDA pre-IND/Type B minutes agreeing a bridging or ethnic-sensitivity plan, orphan designation where relevant; ~$0.5-2M, possibly a $5-15M PK bridge.
scored.proven_buyer: US specialty and orphan pharma, big pharma BD, royalty/PE funds ($10-300M deals).
scored.public_data: PMDA review reports and Interview Forms (Japanese, scanned), NMPA/CDE reviews, MFDS approvals, jRCT/ChiCTR/JAPIC, CNKI, J-STAGE, Drugs@FDA.
scored.rough_step_up: ~20-100x. Most Asian-only drugs are me-too; ML filters for rare first-in-class ones.
scored.frame: The rung is 'ex-Asia license plus FDA pre-IND or Type B minutes'. Very little of the work in that rung is discovery. Finding the drug is maybe 20-30% of the effort. The rest is physical and regulatory work that is neither trivial nor abstracted: translating the dossier, CMC/manufacturing transfer, negotiating with the FDA, and usually a PK bridge ($5-15M). Most of the time a new US or multiregional pivotal trial is also needed ($30-150M+, my estimate). The FDA rarely accepts single-country Asian data. Radicava/edaravone (2017) is the famous exception, and Mitsubishi Tanabe filed that itself. This is closer to the geothermal-in-coal-mines counter-example: running a US development program is much harder than finding the drug.
scored.step_up: The unproven right costs about $0.5-10M upfront (candidate's figure). It is not near-zero, and the Chinese assets in this space now command $50M-$1.25B upfronts (Pfizer paid 3SBio $1.25B upfront in 2025). A buyer pays for clean data that FDA will accept, not for minutes. FDA minutes that agree a bridging plan might lift the asset's value 2-5x (my estimate). The candidate's own figure is about 20-100x, and that holds only after a successful bridging or pivotal trial, not at the minutes. There is no public market for 'minutes-stage' Asian assets. Comparator: MediciNova (est. ~2000) has used this exact model since in-licensing ibudilast from Kyorin in 2004. More than 20 years later it has no US approval and a market cap of roughly $100M (my recollection).
scored.hit_rate_capex: Base rate: of drugs approved first in Japan, about 70% (80% for Japanese companies) are never approved by the FDA or EMA (Japanese Journal of Health Economics and Policy analysis). The pool of candidates is large, but most of them are me-too or local-standard-of-care drugs. Cost per proving attempt: about $0.5-2M to get minutes, but the step that actually creates value (a bridging or pivotal trial) costs $5-150M per attempt (estimate). ML only cuts the cheap triage part, which is already cheap: a BD analyst plus translators costs perhaps $50-200k per asset. So ML cannot cut total capex 10x. Most of the capex is trial cost, and ML does not touch it.
scored.data: PMDA review reports, Interview Forms, NMPA/CDE reviews and CNKI really are hard to read for Western teams (they are in Japanese or Chinese). But the outcome is already written into legible fields. Approval status, indication and the absence of a US/EU filing are all in English in Cortellis, Evaluate, Pharmaprojects, GlobalData and PMDA's English approval lists. The MHLW/PMDA 'drug loss' surveys count the gaps explicitly (143 US/EU drugs unapproved in Japan as of 2023). The owners can read their own data perfectly well, because they produced it. Chinese and Japanese pharma run active out-licensing teams. Big pharma BD, Jefferies and BioCentury watch Asia closely, and Chinese out-licensing reached about $124-136B in total deal value across 157 deals in 2025 (SCMP/Caixin). There is no information asymmetry to exploit on the seller side.
scored.right_bought: The right is bought, not taken first-come, which fits the rubric's requirement. But it is not cheap for good assets. Strong first-in-class Chinese assets now command upfronts in the tens to hundreds of millions of dollars. Older Japanese assets can be cheap ($0.5-10M), but they are cheap for a reason. Many have weak or expired patents: ibudilast had no composition-of-matter patent, and its US MS use patent expired in 2018. Without exclusivity, the asset may not be worth developing.
scored.buyer: Real, well-capitalised buyers exist: US specialty and orphan pharma, big pharma BD, and royalty funds such as Royalty Pharma ($10-300M+ deals). But they buy de-risked data: Phase 2/3 results that FDA accepts, or an approval. They do not buy pre-IND minutes. At the minutes rung the buyer is weak.
scored.ladder: The ladder is genuine: license, then minutes, then bridging trial, then US NDA, then commercial specialty pharma, then a multi-asset platform. The specialty pharma end state can be very large; Jazz and Horizon are the models. This criterion scores well.
scored.fatal_flaw: The FDA minutes create no step-up that a buyer pays for. The value-creating proving step is a US-acceptable clinical trial costing $5-150M with ordinary drug-development hit rates. So discovery is a small share of the rung, ML does not touch the dominant cost, and the field is already crowded and legible. MediciNova has run this exact model since 2004 with no approval.
scored.one_line_reason: This is drug development dressed as discovery. Proving value takes a trial, not a cheap drill, and both the outcome fields and the sellers are already legible and competitive.
