scored.name: Survivor Genetics / Wild Elite Tree: resistant survivor trees in blight-killed stands
scored.one_line: Buy propagation rights to individual trees that stay healthy where a pest or pathogen killed their neighbours (Florida HLB citrus, Puglia Xylella olives, TR4 bananas, emerald-ash-borer ash, beech leaf disease, butternut, elm). ML on aerial imagery, FIA plots and citizen science finds outliers; PCR, grafting and challenge assays prove resistance; nurseries and growers license the cultivar.
scored.unproven_right: Exclusive propagation/plant-patent rights to specific survivor trees, ~$300-5k per tree or a blanket grove option.
scored.proving_step: Remote vigour ranking, on-site qPCR titre or controlled inoculation/larval bioassay, budwood grafting and genome identity checks, ~$2-20k per candidate over 1-2 years. Base hit rate ~1-5%.
scored.proven_buyer: Citrus nurseries and UF/IFAS-type programmes, juice processors (Alico, Louis Dreyfus), olive nurseries, banana majors (Chiquita, Dole, Fresh Del Monte), wholesale tree nurseries (Bailey, J. Frank Schmidt), utilities and restoration buyers.
scored.public_data: USDA NAIP, Florida citrus inventory and abandoned-grove maps, NASS surveys, SIT Puglia orthophotos and Xylella maps, Sentinel/Landsat, USFS FIA, iNaturalist/GBIF/TreeSnap, state forest health surveys.
scored.rough_step_up: ~10^3-10^4x: a tree worth ~$0-1k becomes a licensed tolerant cultivar worth $0.5-50M in royalties. Grant-funded public programmes compete.
scored.frame: The rung is "own the propagation right to a survivor tree and prove it is resistant." Finding the tree is maybe 30-40% of the work (my estimate). The rest is a slow biological step that cannot be abstracted: budwood indexing, challenge inoculation or larval bioassay, replicated grafted field trials over several years, and in Florida, entry into the state budwood registration programme. Unlike a drill hit, this proof is not a single quick event. The variety with the best Florida proof, N40-16-7-11 Valencia, was validated by 34 years of field survival (FFSP/NVDMC 2025). The buyers (FFSP/NVDMC, nurseries, Italian olive nurseries) are real, but they mostly license from public breeders. Discovery is well under 80% of the work in this frame.
scored.step_up: Unproven: a survivor tree has roughly $0-1k of option value (candidate's figure; no market exists). Proven: no per-tree citrus royalty rates are published. My estimate is the typical woody-plant patent royalty of about $0.50-2 per tree. One large Florida order was 300,000 HLB-tolerant trees (FreshPlaza), which at that rate is about $0.15-0.6M. A good variety might earn about $1-5M over the patent life, received 5-10+ years later. Italy only allows Leccino and FS-17 (CNR-patented) for replanting, which caps demand for new olive selections until regulators accept them. Discounted for time and risk, the realistic gain on a ~$1-5k right is roughly 10-100x, not an immediate 10^3-10^4.
scored.hit_rate_capex: The base rate is low. Penn State found 13 of 1,762 ash trees still alive in 2019, about 0.7%. The 2021 Frontiers study of Puglia olives found 30 paucisymptomatic trees, and 23 of them clustered genetically with Leccino/FS17, so most were already known resistant cultivars rather than new ones. USFS lingering-ash crosses gave 15-40% of progeny with better defence. Cost per candidate is about $2-20k (candidate's estimate, plausible) over 1-5 years. In theory ML could cut capex 10x. In practice, imagery cannot separate genetic resistance from microsite, rootstock, chance escape or treatment history, so better triage gives perhaps 2-3x (my estimate).
scored.data: Orthophotos, NAIP, Sentinel, FIA and Xylella maps are public, but they are not illegible in the Terranox sense. Canopy vigour is visible to anyone, and Puglia's regional mapping already flags asymptomatic trees. Incumbents already mine this source: UF/IFAS (Grosser's survivor and OLL selections), CNR/Uni Bari/Uni Salento, the USFS Northern Research Station and Holden Arboretum for lingering ash, the American Chestnut Foundation, and Dutch elm programmes.
scored.right_bought: This is weak. Commercial citrus, olive and banana orchards are clonal, so a survivor is usually the same genotype as its dead neighbours. Its survival then comes from environment or rootstock, and the tree is not new or distinct enough to qualify for a plant patent. Under 35 USC 161 a plant found in an uncultivated state cannot be patented either, which affects wild forest survivors. Many forest survivors stand on public or state land. Growers walk their own groves and know which trees survived, so they are not owners who cannot read the data. In Florida the Florida Citrus Commission holds statutory first-option rights on UF varieties.
scored.buyer: FFSP/NVDMC and Florida citrus nurseries; juice processors such as Alico and Louis Dreyfus, which are shrinking with the industry; Italian olive nurseries, which are limited by regulation; banana majors, which are mostly working on TR4 through gene editing and Cavendish somaclones (GCTCV). For ash, beech and elm the buyers are restoration bodies and municipalities on grant budgets. Wholesale nurseries such as Bailey and J. Frank Schmidt pay ordinary nursery royalties.
scored.ladder: The rungs above are licensed cultivar, then own nursery, then own replanted groves, then processing. That is a real ladder but a small one. Florida citrus is in structural decline, and forest restoration has little revenue. Competition from CRISPR and transgenics (Soilcea CarriCea T1, NPR1 lines) may skip survivor selection entirely. This is not a trillion-dollar path.
scored.fatal_flaw: Proving a survivor takes years of biological testing (a 34-year field record for the best Florida example), not a quick discrete event. Survivors in clonal orchards are usually not genetically distinct, so there is nothing new to patent and the owner is not a seller who cannot read the data. Public breeding programmes already scout these same survivors for free.
scored.one_line_reason: Low hit rates are real, but proof is slow and biological rather than instant, survivors in clonal crops usually have nothing new to patent, imagery is legible and already used by public breeders, and per-tree royalties of about $1 give at most a 10-100x step-up after years.

scored.name: Bone Rights / Deep Time Rights: private-land vertebrate fossil leases
scored.one_line: Lease or buy fossil rights on Western US ranch land (surface owner owns fossils per Murray v. BEG) for a few dollars per acre; ML over geologic maps, museum localities, old field notes and LiDAR erosion ranks exposures; surface prospecting proves a skeleton or quarry for sale.
scored.unproven_right: Exclusive multi-year fossil-collection lease or deed on Hell Creek, Morrison or Judith River ranch sections, ~$2-20k per section.
scored.proving_step: Drone photogrammetry and ML bone-spotting plus walking crews and a test excavation; excavation and prep ($100k-1M) is routine but real.
scored.proven_buyer: Sotheby's and Christie's natural-history sales (Stan $31.8M, Apex $44.6M), Gulf and Asian museums, Black Hills Institute-type prep houses.
scored.public_data: USGS/state geologic maps, 3DEP LiDAR, Paleobiology Database, iDigBio and museum collections, digitised AMNH/Yale/Carnegie field notes, BLM survey reports, NAIP.
scored.rough_step_up: ~10^3-10^5x on the parcel; niche and heritage/permit risk.
scored.frame: The rung is: hold a fossil right, find a skeleton, sell it. But finding is not the whole rung. Excavation, jacketing, years of prep and authentication cost $100k-1M+ per specimen, and an unexcavated find in the ground has little resale value; it cannot be flipped the way a drill-proven claim can. My estimate is that discovery is about 40-60% of the work in this rung, not 80%+. Buyers with money exist (Sotheby's and Christie's clients, Gulf and Asian museums), but they buy finished, mounted skeletons, not proven ground.
scored.step_up: Unproven: the ranch where Gus the T. rex was found sold for about $6M for 6,537 acres, about $900/acre (Fay Ranches / Hall and Hall listing, my arithmetic). A lease costs around $2-20k per section (the candidate's own figure; I found no published lease rates). Proven: Gus hammered at $43M and sold for about $50M in July 2026; Apex (stegosaurus) $44.6M in 2024; Big John (triceratops) about $7.7M in 2021; Trey (triceratops) estimated at $4.5-5.5M in 2026. So a hit takes a $2-20k lease to a $1-50M sale, nominally 10^2-10^4. But that value only shows up after excavation, prep and sale, not on discovery. The landowner usually takes about 50% (Larson's 50-50 split, Gus proceeds split with Licking). Typical commercial specimens are mostly worth $0.1-2M, not $40M.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Base hit rate: auction-grade, mostly complete skeletons are very rare. My estimate is a handful a year across the whole Hell Creek, Morrison and Judith River region, despite decades of work by commercial and academic crews. Fragments are found all the time. Cost per attempt: a field season of prospecting costs about $50-200k (my estimate), which is cheap. Successful digs go on to cost $100k-1M+ for excavation and prep. The ML lever is limited: bones are mostly found where they erode out each year, and walking crews already cover the known badlands. Drone ML bone-spotting can raise coverage per dollar, perhaps 2-3x (my estimate), but it will not cut capex 10x. The main constraint is how fast erosion exposes new bone, not where to look.
scored.data: Good: the outcome is not summarised in any legible public field, because a discovery is unknown until someone walks the outcrop. Weak: the useful signal (geologic maps, LiDAR, NAIP imagery) is fairly legible, and the strongest signal, exact locality data, is often withheld or restricted in PBDB and museum databases. Old field notes help, but the productive formations are already well known. Incumbents include Black Hills Institute, Theropoda Expeditions, Clayton Phipps and other 'dinosaur cowboys' (Bloomberg 2021), plus dealers who buy ranches outright for fossils.
scored.right_bought: Legal: yes. Fossils on private land belong to the landowner, and Montana HB 229 (2019) presumes they go with the surface estate unless granted expressly (the Murray v. BEJ dispute). Cheap: no. After Sue, Stan and Gus, Hell Creek ranchers know what fossils are worth. Deals are typically a 50/50 split of proceeds rather than a flat fee of a few dollars per acre, and dealers already buy ranches for fossils. The owners are not unable to read the data; they know the upside, which takes away most of the information-arbitrage discount. Severance, title and mineral-estate risk remains (Dueling Dinosaurs).
scored.buyer: Wealthy collectors through Sotheby's and Christie's (Stan $31.8M, Apex $44.6M, Gus about $50M), new Gulf and Asian museums, and private buyers. There are only a few sales over $5M a year (my estimate), so the market is thin and lumpy. Buyers are also exposed to reputational pressure from the scientific community (Society of Vertebrate Paleontology), plus export and heritage risk.
scored.ladder: The rungs above are prep labs, casting and replicas, exhibition and touring, and dealer/auction intermediation. The whole commercial vertebrate fossil market is probably on the order of $100-500M a year (my estimate). That is a niche ceiling, with no path to a very large company, let alone a trillion-dollar one.
scored.fatal_flaw: The market is tiny and lumpy (a few eight-figure skeletons a year), and landowners already know the value and take about 50%. Bones turn up where erosion exposes them, not hidden under data the way uranium is. Excavation and prep come before any value can be realised. ML can make prospecting somewhat cheaper, but not by 10x, and even then there is no ladder to a large company.
scored.one_line_reason: The step-up is spectacular, but this is a lottery rather than a rung. Value is only realised after costly excavation and prep, landowners are savvy and take 50/50 splits, the ML lever is limited by erosion, and the whole end market is a few hundred million dollars.

scored.name: Die Hunter: unattributed coin and stamp varieties
scored.one_line: Image-classify eBay, Delcampe and regional listings for coins and stamps sold as common types that are rare varieties; buy cheap and lock value with PCGS/NGC or expert certificate.
scored.unproven_right: Ownership of a generically listed coin or stamp.
scored.proving_step: Third-party grading or expertization certificate ($30-300).
scored.proven_buyer: Heritage, Stack's Bowers, GreatCollections, Spink, registry-set collectors.
scored.public_data: Heritage archive, PCGS CoinFacts, VAMWorld, Philatelic Foundation archives, Gibbons/Scott, live listings.
scored.rough_step_up: 10-1,000x per hit; variety references are fairly legible and cherrypickers compete.
scored.frame: The rung is buying a coin or stamp listed as a common type, then having it attributed or expertized. Inside that rung, discovery (spotting the die marker or plate variety) is about 90-95% of the work. Proving is trivial: mail it to PCGS/NGC or the Philatelic Foundation. Capitalised buyers do exist (Heritage, Stack's Bowers, registry-set collectors), but the market is thin. Collectors Universe forum posters say most dealers pay little or nothing extra for most VAM (Morgan/Peace dollar) varieties. The frame passes in form, but the buyer side is shallow.
scored.step_up: This is my estimate, not sourced data. A typical attributed hit is worth 1-5x the common-type price. Some low-population VAMs sell for no premium at all, even in an attributed holder (CU forum). Only famous varieties give 100-1000x, for example an 1882-O/S early die state in XF sold for "a couple thousand dollars" against a common Morgan at about $40-60, roughly 40x (CU forum). Famous doubled dies like the 1955 or 1969-S DDO reach 100-1000x+, but they are well known and seldom sold unattributed. The weighted median hit is around 2-10x, nowhere near 10^3.
scored.hit_rate_capex: The proving step is neither expensive nor mostly failing. PCGS variety attribution is an add-on of roughly $18-24 per coin (forum-cited, likely dated) on top of grading. PCGS charges $10 if the coin does not qualify (PCGS variety FAQ). The Philatelic Foundation charges 5.5% of submitted value, with a $27 minimum for US stamps and $35 for foreign (PF FAQ). The cost is in search labour and the purchase price, not in proving. ML speeds up screening, but it does not cut proving capex 10x, because you submit only what you already believe is a hit. My estimate is that the base hit rate on submitted coins is already high (>50%) for experienced cherrypickers.
scored.data: The signal is in listing photos, which are public, huge and scattered across eBay, Delcampe and regional sites. Photos are often low-resolution and miss the die marker, which limits ML. The answer key is legible and codified: Cherrypickers' Guide, VAMWorld, CoinFacts, Scott and Gibbons. The outcome is not summarised in the listing, which is good. But human cherrypickers already compete for the same listings, and AI coin-ID apps already claim DDO, DDR and RPM detection (CoinKnow, CoinValueChecker, Coin Error Expert, 2026). Sellers increasingly self-attribute with these apps, which erodes the edge.
scored.right_bought: Yes. The right is bought cheaply from sellers who cannot read the variety, at the common-type price (my estimate: typically $5-100). It is clean ownership, bought and not free, which is a genuine strength.
scored.buyer: Heritage, Stack's Bowers, GreatCollections, Spink, Siegel and registry-set or VAM specialist collectors. The buyers are capitalised, but demand for any single variety is thin. Most dealers do not pay a variety premium (CU forum).
scored.ladder: The rungs above are dealer, auction house, grading company and reference publisher. The total US numismatic market is roughly $5-10B a year (my estimate), and varieties are a small slice of it. Grading (Collectors Holdings / PCGS) is the largest prize, at about $1-4B scale. That is no path to a very large company, let alone a trillion-dollar one.
scored.fatal_flaw: The pool of mispriced rare varieties is tiny and finite, and both the buyers and the step-up are thin. Most hits are worth 1-5x on items that cost tens of dollars, and the variety references are fully legible to human cherrypickers and to AI ID apps already on the market. It is a capped hobby arbitrage with no 10^3 step-up and no ladder, and proving is already cheap, so ML has no 10x capex lever.
scored.one_line_reason: The frame passes on paper: discovery dominates and proving is a cheap mailing. But the step-up is usually 1-5x, proving costs only $10-60, the references are legible, cherrypickers and AI apps already compete, and the market is too small to climb.

scored.name: Reversion Rights Co: 1875-Act and easement-only rail corridors
scored.one_line: Buy options on adjacent landowners' reversionary interests along abandoned rail corridors where ML over scanned deeds and ICC valuation maps shows the railroad held only an easement; assemble continuous fee title and sell to HVDC and long-haul fiber developers. Rail-corridor-title variant.
scored.unproven_right: Landowner reversionary claims under abandoned rail easements, options at $100-1,000 per parcel.
scored.proving_step: ML title-chain reconstruction (deeds, ICC maps, Brandt v. US status, STB abandonment dockets) classifying easement vs fee and proving continuity; paper only.
scored.proven_buyer: Merchant HVDC developers (Grid United, SOO Green-type, Invenergy), hyperscaler dark-fiber builders, state transmission authorities.
scored.public_data: NARA ICC Bureau of Valuation maps (RG 134), county deed images, STB AB- dockets, BLM GLO land-grant records, USGS historic topos.
scored.rough_step_up: ~100-1000x on option cost when continuity is proven; binary.
scored.frame: The rung is a continuous corridor title package (options on fee or reversionary interests along an abandoned line), sold to a linear-infrastructure developer. Discovery (title-chain classification) is maybe 40-50% of the work inside that rung, by my estimate. The other half is assembly: signing options with hundreds of separate owners per corridor, any one of whom can hold out and break continuity, plus quiet-title and railbanking (16 USC 1247(d)) issues. That assembly step is not trivial or abstracted the way a contracted drill rig is, so this fails the 80%+ test. It looks more like the coal-mine geothermal counter-example than like Terranox.
scored.step_up: The pitch assumes options at $100-1,000 per parcel. But real reversionary claims are already priced far higher in takings litigation. Nickel Plate Trail paid $7.6M to 168 owners (about $45k each, my arithmetic). Covington GA paid $1.5M to 47 owners (about $32k each). Haggart v. US paid about $140M for about 25 miles of BNSF corridor. Informed owners will not sell for $100-1,000. On the buy side, the only developer number found is SOO Green offering about $8,550 per mile for easements, which is a few thousand dollars per parcel. Realistic step-up on an informed option price is about 1-10x, not 100-1000x. 100x or more only happens if owners are uninformed, and contingency-fee plaintiff firms keep informing them.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Base hit rate is high, not low. Brandt (2014) held that 1875 Act rights of way are easements, and many state-law grants are easements too. Plaintiff firms win a large share of rail-trail cases on easement findings. My estimate is that 50-80% of parcels on 1875-Act or condemned corridors are easement-only. Proving cost is paper title work: about $500-2,000 per parcel for an abstract or title opinion, and maybe $100k-500k per corridor (my estimates). With a high base rate and cheap proving, the ML lever is capped at roughly 1.3-2x, not 10x.
scored.data: The underlying data is genuinely illegible: NARA RG 134 ICC valuation maps, scanned county deeds, GLO land-grant records. But the outcome is partly written down in legible places already. STB AB- dockets and NITU/railbanking status are public. Court of Federal Claims rail-trail opinions classify easement vs fee parcel by parcel. State trail inventories (Rails-to-Trails Conservancy) list corridor status. So the edge exists only on corridors that have not been litigated or railbanked.
scored.right_bought: The rights can be bought. They belong to adjacent private owners, so they are not free first-come claims. Two problems. (1) On railbanked corridors, federal preemption blocks the reversion: the owner holds only a takings damages claim against the US, not deliverable fee title, so you cannot assemble a corridor from them. (2) On non-railbanked abandoned corridors, the reversion often vests automatically under state law, and owners can be reached by plaintiff firms (Lewis Rice, Stewart Wald) that run the same title analysis on contingency. Cheap purchase from owners who cannot read the data is therefore unreliable.
scored.buyer: The buyers named are merchant HVDC developers (SOO Green, Grid United, Invenergy) and dark-fiber builders. Their demonstrated model is co-locating on active rail (85% of SOO Green's route was secured through railroad agreements) or highway right of way, and paying landowners for easements at about $8.5k per mile. There is no evidence they pay a premium for assembled fee title along abandoned corridors. Those corridors are often broken by development, so for these buyers the corridors are routing options, not must-haves.
scored.ladder: The ladder is: corridor title holder, then lessor of the right of way, then co-developer or owner of transmission and fiber assets in the corridor, then a utility-scale linear-infrastructure owner (a "land-REIT for linear assets"). That is a real but capital-heavy and slow path.
scored.fatal_flaw: The value is already priced and owned by others. Owners' reversionary claims are worth tens of thousands of dollars per parcel in takings litigation that contingency law firms already pursue using the same title analysis. Railbanking keeps many corridors from reverting at all. Assembling continuity across hundreds of owners with holdout risk is the real work, not discovery. And the named buyers co-locate on active rail and highway right of way, paying only about $8.5k per mile for easements, rather than paying a large premium for assembled abandoned corridors.
scored.one_line_reason: Discovery is cheap, has a high base hit rate, and is already done by rail-trail takings lawyers, while the hard part (holdout-prone assembly) is not abstracted. The real step-up is about 1-10x, not 10^3.

scored.name: StrandRescue: dark fibre bought out of bankruptcies and failed municipal networks
scored.one_line: Buy fibre, IRUs and pole/franchise rights from bankrupt ISPs, failed municipal broadband and smart-grid builds at liquidation; ML reconstructs route, strand count and assignability; OTDR sweep confirms; sell to consolidators.
scored.unproven_right: 363 lots, abandonment motions and municipal surplus declarations sold for cents on the dollar.
scored.proving_step: ML over docket exhibits, IRU and pole contracts, permits; OTDR sweep and splice audit ($1-3k/mile).
scored.proven_buyer: Zayo, Uniti, Brightspeed, Ziply, Metronet, BEAD subgrantees.
scored.public_data: PACER and receivership dockets, PUC filings, municipal surplus resolutions, RUS/BTOP/BIP grantee records, NTIA middle-mile maps.
scored.frame: Rung: buy distressed fibre, IRUs and pole rights, confirm them and resell them to a consolidator. Discovery is maybe 30-40% of the work inside that rung (my estimate). The rest is physical and legal: OTDR sweeps and splice repair at $1-3k/mile across hundreds of miles, re-assigning pole attachments and franchises (pole owners and PUCs must consent), paying make-ready, settling cure costs on contracts the buyer takes over in a 363 sale, and keeping the network maintained while it waits for a buyer. A large share of the assets are also lit networks with customers, which need someone to run them, not just a proving step. That is close to the geothermal-in-coal-mines counter-example: confirming and transferring the asset is as hard as finding it.
scored.step_up: From recalled precedents, not sourced this session: iProvo cost about $39M to build and went to Google Fiber for $1 in 2013 (it carried bond debt). Lake County MN built on about $66M of RUS loan money and sold for about $13M in 2016 (~0.2x of cost). Burlington Telecom sold to Schurz for about $30.8M in 2017. In the 2001-03 telecom bust (360networks, Global Crossing, etc.) assets cleared at 5-20 cents on the dollar. Proven or fair value is roughly 1-5x the distressed price, call it 3-10x at best. In the bust cases the gain came from the market recovering over years, not from an immediate proving event. Nothing close to 10^3-10^4.
scored.hit_rate_capex: The base hit rate of 'is the fibre real and usable' is high, my estimate 70-90%. Fibre that is in the ground or on poles mostly exists and mostly works; the uncertainty is about condition, assignability and demand, not existence. With a hit rate that high, the lever (capped at 1/base rate) is about 1.1-1.4x, not 10x. Each proving attempt costs $1-3k/mile for OTDR (candidate's figure) plus legal diligence. Each 'shot' is a whole lot bought at auction ($100k to $10M+), not a cheap drill.
scored.data: The data is public but semi-legible: PACER (paid per page), receivership dockets, PUC filings, RUS/BTOP grantee records and NTIA maps. But 363 sale motions and asset schedules already list route miles, strand counts and the contracts being assigned, and bidders get a data room. The outcome is effectively summarised in the sale documents and the stalking-horse bid. The ML edge over reading scanned IRU and pole contracts is real but small, and it speeds up diligence rather than revealing hidden value.
scored.right_bought: Yes, the right is bought, not free first-come. But it is bought in competitive 363 auctions or municipal RFPs where the eventual buyers (Zayo, Uniti, regional ISPs, infrastructure funds) bid directly. The sellers (trustees, municipalities) run price discovery with sophisticated bidders, so the purchase discount is not driven by the owner being unable to read the data.
scored.buyer: Capitalised strategic buyers exist: Zayo, Uniti, Brightspeed, Ziply, Metronet, regional ISPs and infrastructure funds such as Macquarie, DigitalBridge and Antin. But they bid for the same distressed lots themselves, so they compete with the middleman rather than need it.
scored.ladder: There is a real ladder: distressed fibre acquisition, then lit services, regional fibre consolidator, then a Zayo-scale network (Zayo itself was built mostly through acquisitions). But every rung above the first is a capital-heavy operating telecom business, and the bottom rung has no discovery-driven edge to climb from.
scored.fatal_flaw: The asset's existence and value are not hidden. Fibre is mostly real (high base hit rate, so little ML lever). Distressed lots are sold in competitive 363 auctions or municipal RFPs that the end buyers attend directly. And the gap between the distressed and proven price is about 3-10x, not 10^3-10^4. Confirming and transferring the asset (permits, pole consent, splice repair, operations) is as hard as finding it, which is the geothermal-in-coal-mines failure.
scored.one_line_reason: This is distressed-asset arbitrage among sophisticated bidders, with a ~3-10x price gap and a high base hit rate. There is no frame in which discovery is 80%+ of the work and no 10^3 jump on a hit.
sources: The web search budget for this turn was already used up, so neither search ran and no sources were retrieved.

All figures are recalled from memory and unverified: iProvo sold to Google Fiber for $1 (2013); Lake County MN fiber (~$66M RUS loan) sold for ~$13M (2016); Burlington Telecom sold to Schurz for ~$30.8M (2017); 2001-03 telecom-bust fibre asset sales at 5-20 cents on the dollar.
Fibre build cost of ~$30-80k/mile (aerial to underground) is an estimate; OTDR at $1-3k/mile is the candidate's figure.

scored.name: Zombie Spectrum / Rebanded: licences in bands about to be repurposed
scored.one_line: Buy legacy narrowband and site-based FCC licences (paging, SMR, 220 MHz, 450-470, 900 MHz, Part 101, 4.9 GHz, EBS/BRS fragments, LPTV) from defunct holders and estates in bands dockets foreshadow converting to broadband; ML proves which are alive and transferable and forecasts incumbent treatment; sell or swap upgraded rights.
scored.unproven_right: Fragmented licences at fractions of a cent per MHz-pop from owners who cannot read docket trajectory.
scored.proving_step: ML over ULS, scanned construction notices, discontinuance evidence, ECFS ex partes, NTIA reports; the FCC realignment order is the proof.
scored.proven_buyer: Utilities (Anterix 900 MHz leases to Ameren ~$47M, Xcel ~$80M), carriers, EchoStar successors, private-LTE operators, spectrum investors.
scored.public_data: FCC ULS, ECFS dockets, NTIA reports, Federal Register, auction PNs, LMS, state dissolution records, PACER.
scored.rough_step_up: ~10-1000x if realignment happens, near zero if not; binary regulatory risk.
scored.frame: Rung: hold FCC licences in a band before a realignment order and sell or lease the upgraded right. The physical step is trivial (a licence transfer, no building), and capitalised buyers do exist (utilities, carriers). But the 'proving' event is an FCC rulemaking, not something the company does. ML only forecasts it, so discovery may be ~50-70% of the work, and the rest is lobbying in the docket, negotiating relocations, and assembling the county-level majority the FCC requires (Anterix's 900 MHz rule needs the broadband licensee to hold most of the band in each county). Own estimate.
scored.step_up: From memory, not verified this run (search budget was used up): Anterix (pdvWireless) bought Sprint's 900 MHz narrowband licences for about $90M in 2014. After the FCC's May 2020 realignment order it leased 3x3 MHz broadband to Ameren (about $47M), Xcel (about $80M), Evergy (about $30M) and LCRA (about $30M). That is roughly a 3-10x gain on purchase price, before Anterix paid narrowband incumbents to relocate or retune. The best precedent was the 2017 broadcast incentive auction: speculators such as LocusPoint and NRJ bought UHF stations for single-digit to tens of $M and some received $100M+ in the reverse auction, about 10-100x. My estimate of a typical hit is 5-100x, not 10^3-10^4. The FCC usually gives incumbents 'comparable facilities' relocation rather than a windfall, so many zombie licences realise about 1x.
scored.hit_rate_capex: My estimate, unverified: the FCC finishes only about 1-3 band-repurposing proceedings a year (examples: 900 MHz 2020, 3.7 GHz C-band 2020, 2.5 GHz EBS 2019, 4.9 GHz band manager 2024, 600 MHz incentive auction). In most of them small legacy incumbents got relocation or nothing (4.9 GHz went to a FirstNet band manager; incumbents got no upside). Buying a licence is cheap, about $1k-$100k each, so the cost per attempt is already low. The expense is time (years) and binary regulatory risk, not discovery spend. ML cannot raise the chance that the FCC acts, and it adds little to forecasting, because docket trajectory is read closely by the trade press, law firms (Wiley, Keller and Heckman) and spectrum brokers. The 10x capex lever does not apply.
scored.data: Data is public, but mostly LEGIBLE. ULS has structured fields for licence status (Active, Expired, Terminated, Cancelled), construction-notification status, expiry dates and frequencies, and Section 1.953 automatically terminates licences after 1+ year of discontinued operation. 'Is it alive' is therefore largely already a status field. ECFS ex partes are free text, but specialists read them, and NPRMs state the direction of travel openly. ML has some edge in spotting silently non-operating licences that are still marked Active, but those are exactly the licences the FCC voids when challenged. The right can be bought cheaply from defunct holders and estates, but FCC application freezes and anti-windfall rules (cut-off dates, rules that award broadband rights only to licensees holding them before the freeze) often cancel out buying after the NPRM.
scored.right_bought: Yes. Licences are bought by assignment (FCC Form 603, with FCC consent), so purchase from estates and bankrupt holders is possible, and prices for orphaned narrowband licences are low. However, freezes usually start at the NPRM, so the buying window closes before the 'proof' arrives.
scored.buyer: Capitalised: utilities (Ameren, Xcel, Evergy, LCRA paid $30-80M each for 900 MHz broadband leases, from memory), carriers (T-Mobile bought 2.5 GHz rights), and private-LTE operators. The existing competitors are Anterix itself (the incumbent aggregator in the cleanest analog, about $0.5B market cap, my estimate), spectrum speculators from the incentive auction (LocusPoint, NRJ, Fortress-backed groups), spectrum brokers (Select Spectrum, Spectrum Financial Partners) and NRTC.
scored.ladder: Ladder: aggregate licences, then the realigned broadband licence, then lease to utilities, then operate a private-LTE network, then become a carrier or wholesale operator. Anterix shows this climbs to about $0.5-1B, not a trillion. Each rung above licensing requires network capex and depends on the FCC, and US spectrum value is concentrated in national auctions that go to AT&T, Verizon and T-Mobile.
scored.fatal_flaw: The 'proof' is an FCC rulemaking outside the company's control, not a discovery. ML cannot raise its base rate, and the FCC deliberately strips windfalls from speculative post-NPRM acquirers with freezes and 'comparable facilities' relocation. Licence liveness is also already a legible ULS status field, with automatic termination on discontinuance.
scored.one_line_reason: The step-up is real but modest (about 5-100x) and binary on regulators. ML forecasts rather than proves, the data is mostly legible, and Anterix and incentive-auction speculators already play this game.
sources: Search budget used up at the first query (shared 200-call cap), so no live sources were retrieved; all figures are from memory or my own estimates
From memory: FCC Report and Order WT Docket 17-200, 900 MHz broadband realignment (May 2020)
From memory: Anterix press releases and 10-K on Ameren (~$47M), Xcel (~$80M), Evergy (~$30M) and LCRA (~$30M) 900 MHz leases
From memory: pdvWireless purchase of Sprint 900 MHz licences (~$90M, 2014)
From memory: FCC Broadcast Incentive Auction 1001 results (2017), speculators LocusPoint and NRJ
From memory: 47 CFR 1.953 (automatic termination on discontinuance); FCC 4.9 GHz Eighth Report and Order (2024, FirstNet band manager)

scored.name: ResidualUnits: unused density in legacy Florida DRIs and PUDs
scored.one_line: ML over scanned development orders and DRI reports finds approved-but-unbuilt units stranded with defunct master developers; buy remnant tracts or allocations and sell entitled pads.
scored.unproven_right: Residual unit/square-foot entitlements held by untracking successors.
scored.proving_step: Trace DO, NOPCs, monitoring reports and conversion matrices; county zoning verification letter.
scored.proven_buyer: Lennar, Taylor Morrison, Pulte, NexMetro ($15-60k per entitled unit).
scored.public_data: Regional planning council DRI files, county development order archives, Florida Commerce records, clerk-recorded orders.
scored.frame: The rung would be: find stranded residual units, secure the right to them, prove they are usable (zoning verification letter), and sell an entitled pad to a homebuilder. Discovery (reading development orders, NOPCs and monitoring reports) is maybe 40-50% of the work by my estimate. The rest is not trivial. You have to secure title to units that in Florida usually run with land inside the DRI/PUD boundary, so you also have to buy the land itself. You have to negotiate with successor master developers, CDDs and HOAs. You inherit traffic, school and utility mitigation obligations tied to the units, and you may face county pushback on buildout-date extensions. Builders do buy entitled lots, but the physical/legal step is not abstracted the way an exploratory drill is.
scored.step_up: My estimate (searches were blocked; no sourced figures): exurban Florida raw or ag land trades at roughly $10-50k/acre. Entitled land at 4-8 units/acre that builders pay $15-60k per entitled unit for comes to roughly $60-300k/acre, a 3-10x step-up. Finished lots run $80-150k but need development capex. The near-zero starting price exists only when a defunct entity holds a pure allocation with clean transferability, which is rare. The typical case is 2-10x, nowhere near 10^3-10^4. The candidate's own 10-100x claim is at the optimistic end.
scored.hit_rate_capex: No sourced numbers (search budget exhausted). My estimate: proving costs a title/land-use attorney review plus a county zoning verification letter, about $5-25k and a few weeks per tract. That is a cheap desk exercise, not an expensive physical attempt that mostly fails. Once a tract is identified, the base hit rate of the verification step is probably moderate (30-60%, my estimate). So the 1/hit-rate cap on the ML lever is only about 2-3x, not 10x. Most of the risk lies in title, negotiation and lapse, not in discovery.
scored.data: The data is public and partly illegible: regional planning council DRI files, scanned development orders, NOPC amendments, land-use equivalency/conversion matrices, and clerk-recorded orders. But the outcome is largely already summarised in legible form. Florida DRIs had to file annual/biennial monitoring reports that tabulate approved vs. built vs. remaining entitlements by land use. Many counties (e.g., Lee, Pasco, Hillsborough, Orange) keep DRI/PUD buildout tracking for concurrency, and the candidate itself admits some counties keep legible spreadsheets. After the 2018 changes to s.380.06, much of this moved to local development orders, but the remaining-units fields persist. This is the same failure mode as the prior hunts: the regulator writes the answer into a status field. My estimate is that roughly half the signal is legible.
scored.right_bought: Mostly no. Residual units are typically not a freestanding, cheaply purchasable right. They run with the land, are allocated by the master developer under declarations/covenants, or revert or lapse at buildout-date expiry. Where a defunct developer holds them, title often passed through bankruptcy to a lender or successor that already knows their value. Remnant tracts can be bought, but sellers price them as land with whatever zoning a buyer can verify for a few thousand dollars, which removes much of the information asymmetry.
scored.buyer: Lennar, DR Horton, Taylor Morrison, Pulte, Meritage and build-to-rent operators (e.g., NexMetro) buy entitled land and lots continuously. This buyer is real and well capitalised; it is the strongest part of the thesis.
scored.ladder: Clear ladder: entitlement arbitrage, then horizontal land development (finished lots), then vertical building or build-to-rent, then master-planned community developer. It is real and large, as Lennar, St. Joe and the Villages show, but every rung above the first is capital-heavy and commoditised, and incumbent land developers already run this with in-house entitlement teams.
scored.fatal_flaw: Florida residual units are neither a cheap stand-alone right nor hidden. They run with the land or the master developer's covenants and appear in mandatory DRI monitoring reports and county buildout tracking. The realistic step-up is 2-10x, and proving is a cheap legal desk check rather than an expensive mostly-failing shot, so ML has no 10x capex lever.
scored.one_line_reason: The buyer and the ladder are real, but the step-up is 2-10x not 10^3, the remaining-units outcome is already in legible monitoring reports, and proving is a cheap title/zoning check, so the Terranox 95/5 discovery asymmetry is absent.
sources: No web sources: the shared web search budget was used up before any search ran (2 attempts, both blocked). All figures are estimates from background knowledge.
Background knowledge: Florida Statutes s.380.06 (DRI program, amended 2018 to end new state DRI review; existing development orders governed locally), estimate
Background knowledge: Florida DRI annual/biennial monitoring report requirement tabulating approved vs. built entitlements, estimate
Candidate description itself notes some counties keep legible spreadsheets

scored.name: AccessProof / Second Egress: proving legal access to landlocked or stranded parcels
scored.one_line: Buy landlocked parcels or fire-zone lots that are unbuildable for lack of access (incl. California 2023 Fire Safe Regs) at deep discounts; ML over scanned road petitions, old plats, survey notes and deeds proves an existing access right (RS 2477 road, easement by necessity, unopened dedication, forgotten easement); sell at full value.
scored.unproven_right: Fee title to parcels with no record access, $50-300/acre or $5-15k per lot.
scored.proving_step: Chain-of-title to common grantor, road books and GLO plats, legal access opinion; declaratory action, county road certification or fire marshal acceptance.
scored.proven_buyer: Renewable developers, land funds, recreational buyers, adjoiners, custom and spec builders.
scored.public_data: BLM GLO plats and field notes, county road petitions and minutes, deed images and subdivision maps, USGS historic topos, CAL FIRE FHSZ, tax-deed lists.
scored.frame: The rung is buying a landlocked or no-egress parcel and turning it into a parcel with insurable legal access. Discovery (finding the common grantor, an RS 2477 road, an unopened dedication or a forgotten easement in scanned records) is maybe 40-50% of the work. That is my estimate. The rest is legal proving: a title opinion, then a quiet-title or declaratory action, a county road certification or fire marshal sign-off. That step is adversarial, since adjoiners and counties contest it, and slow, often 1-3 years. Unlike a drill, it cannot be bought as a commodity. Buyers (adjoiners, recreational buyers, small builders, the occasional renewables developer) are scattered and mostly small. There is no deep-pocketed buyer for this rung the way a mine developer buys a drilled uranium claim.
scored.step_up: No live searches ran because the shared per-turn search budget was used up, so every figure here is my estimate from general appraisal knowledge. Appraisal practice usually values landlocked land at about 10-50% of comparable accessible land, a 50-90% discount. Proving access therefore yields about 2-10x: a $200/acre rural parcel might reach $1,000-2,000/acre. A $10k fire-zone lot might reach $50-150k as buildable, up to ~10-15x at the best. The candidate's own ~5-50x is optimistic at the top. Nowhere near 10^3-10^4.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Estimates only, since no live searches ran. Base hit rate: maybe 20-40% of record-landlocked parcels have a provable access theory. Easement by necessity needs a common grantor and strict necessity, both common in old subdivided land. RS 2477 claims are heavily litigated and seldom won quickly (Utah's RS 2477 cases have run for 10+ years). Cost per attempt: a title and abstract search costs about $500-3k. Litigation costs about $20-100k+ per contested case. ML cuts only the cheap research part. The expensive, slow part is the court or county process, which ML does not touch. Overall capex drops maybe 1.5-2x, not 10x. The lever is capped at about 1/0.3 ≈ 3x.
scored.data: GLO plats and field notes are public and scanned. County road petitions and minutes, old deeds and subdivision maps are scattered, unstructured and mostly unextracted, which is a real ML fit. No legible public field records the outcome (whether an easement exists). Assessor records sometimes flag 'no access', but that only marks the problem, not the answer. Title companies do chain-of-title work, but only one parcel at a time on request, not across a whole county. The CAL FIRE FHSZ map is legible, so the fire-zone screening layer is commodity data.
scored.right_bought: Yes. Rights are bought, not claimed first-come. Parcels come through tax-deed sales and from absentee or heir owners at steep discounts; tax-deed rural land often trades for a few hundred dollars per acre. That part of the rubric fits. Rural-land flippers already buy these parcels in bulk, but they cannot read the old records, so ML gives a real edge on choosing parcels.
scored.buyer: Adjoiners (often the cheapest exit, since a sale to them dissolves the access problem), recreational buyers, small spec builders and land funds. The buyers are fragmented and the deals are small, often $5k-150k each. Renewables developers rarely need an individual landlocked lot, because they assemble land through options and negotiate their own access.
scored.ladder: Weak. Above this rung sit land assembly, entitlement and homebuilding or development. These are capital-heavy, local and low-margin, and none depends on the access-proving skill. There is no clear path from it to a whole-chain trillion-dollar company. The upside stops at a niche land-investing fund.
scored.fatal_flaw: The proving step is adversarial litigation or county approval, which costs tens of thousands of dollars and takes years. It is the bespoke hard part, like building the geothermal plant in the counter-example, while discovery is the easy part. And a win only lifts value about 2-10x on small parcels. ML speeds up research, but neither the bottleneck nor the step-up gets near 10^3.
scored.one_line_reason: The data and the right-buying mechanics fit, but proving access is slow, contested legal work that ML can't speed up. The step-up is only ~2-10x, the buyers are small and scattered, and there is no meaningful ladder above.
sources: No live web sources: the WebSearch budget for this turn was used up, so the search returned nothing
Estimate from general appraisal practice: landlocked land valued at roughly 10-50% of comparable accessible land
General legal knowledge: easement by necessity needs a common grantor and strict necessity; RS 2477 litigation (e.g., Utah v. US cases) has run for more than a decade
General knowledge: CAL FIRE State Minimum Fire Safe Regulations (14 CCR 1270), revised 2023, and the FHSZ maps

scored.name: Heirs' Property Assembler / Heirs Acre
scored.one_line: Buy fractional undivided heirs' interests cheaply; ML over scanned probate and deeds builds the full heirship tree; consolidate or partition/quiet title; sell insurable title to timber REITs, homebuilders or solar/BESS/data-center developers near substations.
scored.unproven_right: Small fractional interests in clouded parcels bought for a few hundred dollars.
scored.proving_step: Heirship reconstruction from wills, probate, obituaries and vital records; partition or quiet title.
scored.proven_buyer: Weyerhaeuser, Rayonier, solar and BESS developers, homebuilders, land funds.
scored.public_data: County deed and probate files, FamilySearch, Find-a-Grave, tax rolls flagging 'heirs of', utility hosting maps, USDA heirs' property studies.
scored.rough_step_up: ~25-100x; slow quiet title; must be fair to heirs (reputational/legal risk).
scored.frame: Rung: buy clouded fractional interests, consolidate them and deliver insurable title. Rebuilding the heirship tree is maybe 20-35% of the work (my estimate). The other 65-80% is the physical/legal step: serving notice on dozens of heirs including unknown ones, service by publication, appraisal, court hearings, buyouts and negotiation. That step is not trivial or abstracted; it is litigation. It is the coal-mine geothermal pattern again: finding the parcel is easy, and building the clean title is the hard part. The capitalised buyers are real (Weyerhaeuser, Rayonier, solar/BESS developers), but they buy clean title, which means the hard part has to be finished first.
scored.step_up: Unproven: a small fractional interest, say a 1/30 undivided share bought for a few hundred dollars (the candidate's figure). On a $150k parcel its pro-rata value is about $5k, so roughly 10-20x per interest on a tiny dollar base (estimate). But under UPHPA (enacted in roughly 20+ states, from memory) the co-tenants can buy you out at fair market value of your share, so the fraction's value is capped at its pro-rata FMV. To capture the whole parcel you have to buy most of the interests, and the blended capital per parcel moves from a clouded value of maybe 30-60% of FMV to a clear value of 100% of FMV, minus $5k-20k+ in legal costs. On capital deployed that is about 2-5x (estimate), nowhere near 10^3-10^4. Clearing title might add a further 1.5-3x if the parcel then sells for solar/BESS/data-center use near a substation, but that is ordinary land assembly economics.
scored.hit_rate_capex: The base hit rate of the proving step is high, not low. Professional genealogists and title attorneys reconstruct most heirship trees (I would put it at 70-90%), so the ML lever, capped at 1/base hit rate, is about 1.1-1.4x. Cost per attempt is mostly legal: partition or quiet title often costs $5k-$20k+ and takes 1-3+ years per parcel (estimates from memory of heirs' property legal-aid literature; not verified this session). ML cuts the genealogy portion, maybe 20-30% of cost, so total capex falls 1.3x at best, not 10x.
scored.data: The data is public and illegible: scanned deeds, probate, obituaries, FamilySearch, Find-a-Grave. But the target list is already legible: tax rolls flag 'heirs of' or 'estate of' owners, USDA ERS and Forest Service studies have mapped about 0.5M heirs' parcels across Southern states (from memory), and substation proximity comes from public hosting maps. So ML mostly helps with genealogy, which commercial heir hunters and title plants already do by hand.
scored.right_bought: The right can be bought: undivided interests are bought from individual heirs, which is the historical speculator playbook. But UPHPA gives co-tenants a right of first refusal at appraised FMV and a preference for partition in kind. That removes the old forced-sale discount and turns the buyer into the target of a sympathetic legal-aid and press narrative. The sellers are often low-income, frequently Black, families, which is a serious fairness and reputational problem.
scored.buyer: Timber REITs (Weyerhaeuser, Rayonier), solar/BESS/data-center developers, homebuilders and land funds buy clean, insurable title at market. That is a real capitalised buyer, but it pays ordinary FMV, not a speculative premium.
scored.ladder: Fraction purchases, then consolidated parcels, then assembling parcels near substations and entitling them, then development, a land fund or a powered-land REIT. The ladder exists but it is generic land development, and each rung is capital- and process-heavy rather than discovery-heavy.
scored.fatal_flaw: Value is gated by legal process and heir consent, not by discovery. The heirship tree is the easy part; serving, negotiating with and buying out dozens of co-tenants through a 1-3 year court process is the hard part. UPHPA caps the step-up at a fair-market-value buyout, and the model is widely seen as predatory dispossession of Black Southern landowners.
scored.one_line_reason: Discovery is a small part of the work: the legal and consent step dominates, the step-up is about 2-5x on capital deployed rather than 10^3-10^4, the base hit rate is already high so ML has little to raise, and UPHPA plus reputational risk close off the cheap-fraction arbitrage.
sources: No live web sources: the shared search budget for this turn (200 calls across all agents) was used up before this candidate's searches ran. Every number here is an estimate from memory, should be treated as unverified, and needs a follow-up search to confirm.
Uniform Law Commission, Uniform Partition of Heirs Property Act (2010): co-tenant buyout at appraised FMV, preference for partition in kind (from memory)
USDA ERS / Forest Service heirs' property studies (about 2022), roughly 0.5M parcels across Southern states (from memory, unverified)

scored.name: Prior-Converted Proof: wetland-encumbered land to buildable land
scored.one_line: Buy metro-fringe parcels flagged wetland at farmland prices; ML change-detection over pre-1985 FSA compliance film, NHAP and LiDAR proves Prior Converted Cropland or no continuous surface connection post-Sackett; get an Approved JD; sell to homebuilders.
scored.unproven_right: Fee or option on parcels valued as undevelopable.
scored.proving_step: ML delineation package, field visit, USACE Approved JD request.
scored.proven_buyer: Lennar, DR Horton, land bankers (Millrose, Varde), logistics developers.
scored.public_data: USGS EROS FSA/NRCS annual compliance photography 1979-2002, NHAP/NAPP, NWI, 3DEP, Landsat 5, USACE ORM2, SSURGO.
scored.rough_step_up: ~30-300x per parcel; state wetland laws and NWI legibility are risks.
scored.frame: The rung is: buy wetland-flagged land, prove it non-jurisdictional, and resell it as buildable raw land. Inside that rung, discovery and proving are maybe 50-60% of the work (my estimate). The rest is legal and regulatory: an Approved JD from USACE often takes 6-12 months (my estimate; the USACE target is about 60 days). State wetland permitting adds more, as do zoning, utilities and fill. The physical step is not trivial. Even a clean JD only gets you to raw land. Homebuilders pay for entitled, serviced lots, so a step of entitlement sits between this rung and the capitalised buyer. Land bankers like Millrose buy entitled or near-entitled land, not raw land that just has a JD.
scored.step_up: The candidate claims 30-300x. My estimate is closer to 2-10x on the encumbered acres. Metro-fringe raw land in Sun Belt growth markets (DFW, Houston, Atlanta, Charlotte) sells for roughly $15-60k/acre (my estimate from general market knowledge). The wetland-flagged part of a parcel might trade at $1-5k/acre, mostly because sellers usually price whole parcels, not acres net of wetland. Re-rated, it becomes ordinary raw land at about $15-60k/acre. That is around 5-15x on those acres, and much less on a whole parcel, since wetland is usually a fraction of it. It does not go from near zero to 10^3. I could not verify any of these numbers this turn.
scored.hit_rate_capex: The proving step is cheap, and it is not mostly failing. A wetland delineation runs about $3-20k per site. An AJD request has no USACE fee, but it needs a consultant package of roughly $5-25k (my estimates). The base hit rate is probably high, not low. After Sackett (2023), most isolated and non-abutting wetlands are already non-jurisdictional under federal law, so a large share of NWI-flagged polygons in non-regulating states probably clear (my estimate: maybe 30-60%). The ML lever is capped at 1/base rate, so roughly 2-3x, not 10x. Also, proving cost is a small slice of land cost, so cutting it 10x hardly changes the economics.
scored.data:
The data is real and illegible in places: scanned FSA compliance slides from 1979-2002 and NHAP film at USGS EROS. Prior-converted-cropland status is not necessarily summarised, but the key evidence is legible already. NRCS makes Farm Bill wetland and PCC determinations (form NRCS-CPA-026), and the landowner usually holds them. The wetland map (NWI), the 3DEP elevation data and the post-Sackett surface-connection test can be read from vector and LiDAR data without ML on old film. The ML edge on legacy film applies only to the PCC route. Even there, the Corps generally relies on NRCS PCC determinations, which already exist for many ag tracts.

On the right: a parcel can be bought or optioned. But metro-fringe farmers sell to land brokers and builders who routinely make a wetland delineation a due-diligence contingency. That means the wetland discount the strategy depends on mostly does not exist at the point of sale. The buyer's diligence finds out the same thing within a 60-120 day option period.

Incumbents doing this already: homebuilder land acquisition teams (Lennar, DR Horton), land brokers, wetland and environmental consultants (WSP, Stantec, Kimley-Horn, ECS and others), and land bankers. Web searches were unavailable this turn (the shared budget was exhausted), so these figures are estimates from general knowledge.
scored.right_bought: The right is fee or option on rural or fringe parcels. It is buyable, but sellers in development paths price toward development value, and buyers already treat wetland risk through contingent options rather than as a discount. Pure-wetland parcels (mostly wet, little upland) can be cheap, but those are exactly the ones least likely to clear, especially in states with their own wetland programs. NJ, NY, MD, PA, MN, WI, MI, MA, CT, FL and CA regulate wetlands independently of the federal rules.
scored.buyer: Homebuilders and land bankers are well capitalised, but they buy entitled or entitle-able lots on option, with diligence periods. A JD-cleared raw parcel is just ordinary raw land to them, worth the regional raw-land price and nothing more.
scored.ladder: There is a real ladder above this rung: raw land, then entitlement, horizontal development (lots), then a land bank or lot-option provider, then homebuilding. This is the classic master-planned community developer chain (Howard Hughes, Five Point, Forestar, which DR Horton owns). It is large but low-margin and cyclical, and incumbents with cheap capital already own every rung. The wetland-proof edge does not compound as you climb, because the higher rungs are capital and execution businesses, not discovery businesses.
scored.fatal_flaw: The proving step is cheap (about $5-20k per site) and already routine in builder due diligence. After Sackett its base hit rate is probably high, so there is neither a low hit rate for ML to lift nor a mispriced unproven right to buy. The wetland discount gets arbitraged away in every option-contract diligence period, and the step-up is about 2-10x on a fraction of the parcel, not 10^3.
scored.one_line_reason: This fails on the core rubric: proving costs little and mostly succeeds after Sackett. Sellers in growth paths do not give a wetland discount, buyers already run the same check during their option periods, and the step-up is about 2-10x on the encumbered acres rather than 10^3-10^4.
sources: Web searches failed this turn because the shared 200-call budget was used up; every number here is my estimate from general knowledge and should be checked.
Sackett v. EPA, 598 U.S. 651 (2023): wetlands must have a continuous surface connection to relatively permanent waters.
33 CFR 328.3 and the 2023 conforming rule: the prior converted cropland exclusion; USACE generally defers to NRCS PCC determinations.
NRCS Food Security Act wetland determinations (form NRCS-CPA-026), 16 U.S.C. 3801 et seq.
USACE Regulatory Guidance Letter 16-01 on approved versus preliminary jurisdictional determinations.
USACE ORM2 / Regulatory Request System public JD listings: issued AJDs are a legible public record.

scored.name: Senior Paper / Pre-1914 Claim Recovery: unrecorded California pre-1914 and riparian surface-water rights
scored.one_line: Buy fallow or marginal ranch parcels or heirs' interests carrying undocumented senior pre-1914 appropriative or riparian surface rights; ML over scanned county notices of appropriation, ditch records and imagery proves priority and continuous use; file statements and transfer petitions; sell or lease to districts and cities. Surface water only.
scored.unproven_right: Parcels or assigned rights priced as dry land ($2-8k/acre) from owners who cannot read 1850-1914 records.
scored.proving_step: Documentary chain plus imagery of continuous use; supplemental Statement of Diversion and Use, transfer petition, possibly quiet title. eWRIMS may encode part of the answer.
scored.proven_buyer: MWD, San Diego CWA, Westlands, Kern agencies, IID-style districts, growers and data centers ($10-40k/AF permanent; $500-2000/AF/yr dry-year).
scored.public_data: County recorder notices of appropriation (1850s-1914), SWRCB eWRIMS, adjudication decrees, USGS water-supply papers and historic maps, curtailment orders, ditch archives.
scored.rough_step_up: ~5-100x on the water component, 10^3x+ against discovery cost on a hit; SWRCB is tightening scrutiny; adjacent to groundwater exclusion but surface-only.
scored.frame: Rung = buy parcel or heirs' interest, prove a senior pre-1914 or riparian right, and sell or lease the water. Finding the documents is maybe 20-35% of the work at most (my estimate). Most of the work is the physical and legal step. For a pre-1914 right that means proving continuous beneficial use, getting through the no-injury test and protests for a change of place or purpose, CEQA, and getting conveyance or wheeling capacity through SWP/CVP or local canals. All of that is often contested and can take years. Riparian rights add a worse problem: they belong to the land next to the stream, and generally cannot be split off and sold to an off-stream city or district. So the "physical" step here is a bespoke legal and transfer project. Structurally that matches the geothermal-in-coal-mines counter-example: delivering the water is harder than finding the right parcel. Buyers with capital do exist (MWD, SDCWA, Kern agencies), but they buy transferable, delivered, defensible water, not a documentary claim.
scored.step_up: No live searches ran: the shared web-search budget was used up before this agent ran. All figures below are estimates from prior knowledge and need checking. Unproven: dry or grazing land at about $2-8k/acre (the candidate's figure). Proven: Central Valley ag land with secure senior surface water at about $10-25k/acre (estimate). Dry-year spot water was about $1,000-2,000/AF in 2021-22, and the Nasdaq Veles CA water index ran roughly $200-1,100+/AF over 2021-23 (from memory). On a duty of about 3 AF/acre, a fully proven, transferable senior right might lift the parcel about 2-5x. A permanent right at the candidate's $10-40k/AF on 3 AF/acre is about $30-120k/acre, so about 5-15x is the ceiling, and only if it is transferable and conveyable. This is nowhere near 10^3-10^4. You pay real land value up front, unlike Terranox's $1/ha mineral claim.
scored.hit_rate_capex: These are estimates; no searches ran. Proving cost: title and records research is about $10-50k per parcel. A contested transfer, change petition or quiet-title action plus engineering is about $250k-$2M+, and it is litigation-shaped. Base hit rate: a valid, unforfeited, transferable senior right sitting on fallow land whose owner does not know about it is probably low, under 5% (estimate). But the expensive, high-failure part is the legal transfer, not the discovery. ML only lowers the cheap records step. The transfer step stays one-off and its cost is not reduced 10x. On top of that, the inputs to Cal. Water Code 1241 forfeiture (5 years of non-use; North Kern v. Kern Delta, 2007) are exactly what ML would surface, so many of its hits would be disqualifying hits.
scored.data: There is public but illegible data: county recorder notices of appropriation from 1872-1914 (recorded under Civil Code 1415), ditch company records, adjudication decrees, and USGS water-supply papers. Much of the outcome is already in legible fields, though. Since SBX7 8 (2009), claimants must file Statements of Diversion and Use in eWRIMS, with amounts, priority year and use. Adjudicated streams have decrees. Curtailment orders list rights by priority. SB 389 (2023) lets the SWRCB investigate whether claimed pre-1914 and riparian rights are valid, which shrinks the illegible edge and adds regulatory risk. Can the right be bought cheaply? Partly: heirs' and fragmented interests can be cheap. But parcels with valuable senior water are usually in irrigation districts or with farmers who know exactly what they hold. Brokers and buyers already cover this market (WestWater Research, Water Asset Management, Vidler, Cadiz, Kern water banks, Somach Simmons-type law firms). That means sellers are mostly not unaware of what they hold.
scored.right_bought: Yes, bought from private owners and heirs (land or assignment). Riparian rights mostly cannot be severed from the land. Pre-1914 appropriative rights can be transferred but are lost after 5 years of non-use. So the target pool of 'fallow' parcels is weighted toward rights that are already forfeited.
scored.buyer: MWD, San Diego CWA, Kern County agencies, Westlands, growers, and possibly data centers. Their pattern is to buy delivered, approved, defensible supply through long-term transfer contracts. They do not buy speculative claims. The 2003 IID-SDCWA conservation transfer took years of negotiation and needed QSA legislation.
scored.ladder: There are rungs above: water rights aggregation, then water banking and storage (Kern-style), then conveyance and wholesale supply, then a water utility. The ladder exists and is valuable, but each rung is heavily regulated and political. Climbing it is slow and depends on litigation, and does not compound.
scored.fatal_flaw: The ML can find the right, but turning it into sellable water means a bespoke legal and transfer project (no-injury review, protests, CEQA, conveyance, possibly quiet title). That project dominates both cost and timeline, which is the geothermal-in-coal-mines failure. Two rules also cut against the 'fallow parcel' thesis. The 5-year forfeiture rule (Water Code 1241) means continuous use is required, so the owner usually knows about the right, and fallow parcels often have already lost it. Riparian rights cannot be split off from the land. eWRIMS statements and SB 389 investigations put much of the answer into legible fields already.
scored.one_line_reason: Discovery is a minority of the work. The real work is a contested legal and conveyance transfer. The step-up is about 2-15x, not 10^3. Forfeiture and riparian non-severability gut the 'undervalued fallow parcel' thesis.
sources: None live: the shared web-search budget was used up before this agent ran, so all figures are from prior knowledge and marked as estimates
Cal. Water Code 1241 (5-year forfeiture of appropriative rights)
North Kern Water Storage Dist. v. Kern Delta Water Dist. (2007) 147 Cal.App.4th 555 (forfeiture of a pre-1914 right)
SBX7 8 (2009) / Water Code 5101 (Statement of Diversion and Use requirement, eWRIMS)
SB 389 (2023) (SWRCB authority to investigate pre-1914 and riparian claims)
Water Code 1706 (change of pre-1914 right subject to no-injury)
Nasdaq Veles California Water Index (NQH2O) 2021-23 range, from memory
IID-SDCWA transfer / 2003 Quantification Settlement Agreement

scored.name: CU Prove / HCU Water / Cooling Water Rights: proving historic consumptive use for municipal or industrial change-of-use
scored.one_line: Buy senior Western surface irrigation rights, ditch shares and small-town effluent rights at ag value because historic consumptive use is undocumented; ML over 40 years of Landsat ET and scanned headgate records proves a large transferable yield in water court; sell changed municipal or data-center cooling water.
scored.unproven_right: Decreed ag rights or ditch shares and effluent rights with unquantified transferable yield ($1-15k/AF).
scored.proving_step: Field-by-field HCU reconstruction (OpenET/Landsat 1984+, digitised diversion books, crop records, aerials) and a water-court change decree ($0.2-1M, 2-5 years, adversarial).
scored.proven_buyer: Aurora, Thornton, Castle Rock, Colorado Springs, St George, data-center developers, augmentation developers (Select Water Solutions/AV Farms precedent).
scored.public_data: CDSS HydroBase and water commissioner field books, water court decrees, OpenET/Landsat, USDA aerials, Arizona ADWR, Utah DWRi, Nevada SE, TCEQ certificates, EPA NPDES DMRs.
scored.rough_step_up: ~3-40x; engineering is the moat, incumbents already do HCU.
scored.frame: Rung: buy a decreed ag right or ditch share, then get a water-court change decree that quantifies its transferable historic consumptive use (HCU). Discovery is maybe 30-40% of the work inside that rung (my estimate). Most of the cost and time is the adversarial litigation, which runs 2-5 years against objectors, plus the dry-up covenants, return-flow and augmentation terms, and terms-and-conditions negotiation. The physical side is not abstracted either: you need revegetation, dry-up enforcement and often storage or augmentation plans before the yield is firm. This is the coal-mine geothermal pattern, where the bespoke legal and engineering build outweighs the finding. A capitalised buyer does exist (Front Range municipalities).
scored.step_up: Estimate from prior knowledge; my web search budget was used up before any query ran, so none of these numbers were checked this session. Undecreed-for-municipal-use ag shares in the South Platte or Arkansas trade at roughly $5-20k per acre-foot of diversion. Firm changed municipal consumptive yield sells or is valued at roughly $30-80k per acre-foot (Front Range tap and raw-water dedication levels; CBT units trade around $80-100k+ per unit). The change decree usually REDUCES the volume to consumptive use only, about 40-60% of diversions. So the net step-up per dollar is about 2-5x, maybe 10x for a mispriced share. That is far from 10^3-10^4. The candidate's own 3-40x range is optimistic at the top.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Change cases almost always end in a decree. The uncertainty is about HOW MUCH yield, not WHETHER there is any, so this is not a low-hit-rate, binary proving step. My estimates of cost per attempt: about $0.2-1M in engineering and legal fees plus 2-5 years. ML on OpenET or Landsat could cut HCU engineering cost, but engineering is a minority of the attempt cost; litigation and time dominate. Lever is about 1.2-2x, not 10x. Unverified (search budget exhausted).
scored.data: The data is public and partly illegible: scanned water commissioner diversion books in CDSS HydroBase, decrees, and aerial photos. But the outcome-relevant signal is already partly legible. HydroBase has digitised diversion records, OpenET publishes field-level ET openly, and every previously changed share in the same ditch sets a per-share consumptive-use factor in a public decree, which works like a legible status field. Ditch shares trade in a fairly liquid, informed market where municipal buyers, brokers and engineers (Applegate Group, Leonard Rice, Martin and Wood, Wright Water, Brown and Caldwell) already price shares by expected HCU. The sellers' information gap is small.
scored.right_bought: Yes, rights are bought from farmers and ditch shareholders, not taken first-come. But the purchase discount is thin because buyers like Aurora, Thornton and Greeley already price on HCU. Colorado's anti-speculation doctrine (High Plains A&M v. Southeastern Colorado Water Conservancy District, 2005; Pagosa Area Water and Sanitation District v. Trout Unlimited) requires a non-speculative intended use, usually a contracted end user, before a change decree. A merchant cannot easily 'prove and flip' on spec. Ditch company bylaws and objector protests also constrain transfers.
scored.buyer: Front Range and Utah municipalities: Aurora, Thornton, Castle Rock, Colorado Springs, Parker, St George. Also data-center cooling and augmentation developers. They are well capitalised but have their own in-house HCU engineering and long-standing buy-and-dry programmes, so they capture the step-up themselves.
scored.ladder: Rungs exist above: storage and augmentation plans, raw-water delivery infrastructure, treatment, and a water utility or water-as-a-service for data centers. That is a plausible path to a sizeable water company, Pure Cycle style, worth about $0.3B. It is not a trillion-dollar ladder, and the politics of buy-and-dry (HB-style anti-dry-up legislation) cap it.
scored.fatal_flaw: The proving step is adversarial litigation with a near-certain but volume-reducing outcome, not a cheap binary discovery. The step-up is roughly 2-5x on a market where informed municipal buyers already price HCU. The anti-speculation doctrine blocks proving rights on spec for resale.
scored.one_line_reason: Discovery is a minority of a slow, adversarial water-court rung, the step-up is about 2-5x not 10^3+, the outcome is not a low-hit-rate gamble, and incumbent municipal buyers already price HCU, so the Terranox structure does not hold.
