Pagosa Area Water & Sanitation District v. Trout Unlimited, 170 P.3d 307 (Colo. 2007) (prior knowledge)
Colorado Decision Support System HydroBase / OpenET (public field-level ET data) (prior knowledge)
Northern Water Colorado-Big Thompson unit market prices ~$80-100k+/unit circa 2023-2025 (prior knowledge, unverified)

scored.name: Severed Wind Estate Co.
scored.one_line: Buy severed or reserved wind/solar rights from heirs who don't know they hold them, where ML shows they sit under top-quartile resource near transmission; sell to developers blocked by the title defect.
scored.unproven_right: Severed wind/solar estates and deed reservations at $10-500/acre.
scored.proving_step: ML over scanned deeds for reservations, probate heirship tracing, resource join; clean title chain.
scored.proven_buyer: NextEra, Invenergy, Apex.
scored.public_data: County deed and probate records, TX/WY severance statutes, NREL WIND Toolkit and NSRDB, EIA-860, USWTDB.
scored.frame: The rung is buying a severed or reserved wind/solar estate cheaply and selling or leasing a clean, cured interest to a developer. Finding it (deed OCR plus a resource and transmission join) is maybe 40-50% of the work. The rest is not trivial: heirship tracing, probate and quiet-title work, persuading dispersed heirs to sell, and then getting a developer who can micro-site around the parcel to pay. Physical capex is near zero, but legal and negotiation work is a large share, well short of the 80%+ that discovery is for Terranox. (My estimate.)
scored.step_up: I could not verify any numbers. The shared web-search budget was used up before this agent ran, so every figure here is my own estimate from prior knowledge. An unproven reserved wind interest held by unaware heirs might be bought at about $10-100/acre. Its proven value to a developer is roughly the capitalised share of lease or royalty income. Wind leases commonly pay low tens of dollars per acre per year across the project footprint, or a few thousand dollars per turbine per year. Capitalised, that is about $200-1,500/acre, and only on parcels that actually get built. That gives about 10-30x on a hit, and nothing on the many parcels a project never uses. Holdout leverage toward 1000x is unrealistic because developers lease the surface and route around a clouded parcel.
scored.hit_rate_capex: There is no expensive, mostly-failing proving step here. A title abstract or heirship search costs roughly $500-5,000 per parcel and quiet title roughly $5-20k (my estimates). Whether the reservation exists is almost deterministic once the deed is read. The real uncertainty is whether a project ever gets sited on the parcel, which is a developer decision, not a discovery problem. If maybe 5-15% of top-resource parcels near transmission get built within a decade (estimate), the cap is about 7-20x, but ML does not move that probability much: siting depends on the interconnection queue, offtake and landowner blocks. So ML has little lever on capex.
scored.data: This criterion is mixed but is the candidate's strongest. Wind and solar reservations are buried in scanned county deed records (Texas has 254 counties with uneven digitisation) and in probate files. The outcome (whether a wind estate was severed, and who the heirs are) is not in any legible public field, which is a real edge over status-field regimes. Resource and transmission data (NREL WIND Toolkit, NSRDB, EIA-860, USWTDB) are legible and widely used, so they give no edge. The weakness is the supply of rights to buy. Wind-estate severance only became common practice around 2005 onward, so most reservations are recent and held by living, aware grantors or companies, not lost heirs. As I recall (not checked), Wyoming's 2011 statute and similar Montana law bar severing wind rights from the surface, which shrinks the inventory further. The rights are bought, not claimed first-come, which fits the rubric.
scored.right_bought: Severed or reserved wind/solar estates, or undivided heir fractions of them, bought by quitclaim or deed from heirs. Mostly Texas, where severance is permitted but case law is unsettled. Whether a severed wind estate is even a recognised property interest is legally uncertain in Texas, so title insurers may not insure it.
scored.buyer: Utility-scale developers such as NextEra, Invenergy, Apex, Pattern and RWE. They are well capitalised, but they buy leases or easements, not fee estates, and they usually avoid clouded parcels rather than paying a premium to clear them. Title-curative firms and land agents already resolve defects for developers on a fee-for-service basis.
scored.ladder: The rungs above are: aggregating cured wind/solar land positions into project-ready packages, then development rights (interconnection queue position, permitting), then owning and operating generation. That is a real ladder in principle, but the upper rungs are dominated by NextEra-scale incumbents. The interconnection-queue rung was already scored weak in prior hunts. The bottom rung's inventory is too small to finance the climb.
scored.fatal_flaw: The asset is scarce, and buyers can easily avoid it. Wind-estate severance is recent, roughly two decades old. As I recall (not checked), it is barred by statute in Wyoming and Montana, so few valuable reservations are held by unaware heirs. And developers simply micro-site or lease adjacent clean land instead of paying a holdout premium, so there is no forced 10^3 step-up and no costly, mostly-failing proving step for ML to improve.
scored.one_line_reason: Rights hidden in scanned deeds are a real data edge, but the inventory is tiny and recent, a proven parcel is worth only about 10-30x, and developers route around clouded parcels, so there is no Terranox-style 10^4 jump.
sources: No live sources: the shared WebSearch budget was used up before this agent ran, so no figures could be checked.
Estimate from prior knowledge, not checked: Wyoming Stat. 34-27-103 (2011), wind energy rights are appurtenant to the surface and cannot be severed.
Estimate from prior knowledge, not checked: Texas wind leases and severance, as discussed in Texas A&M AgriLife (Tiffany Dowell Lashmet) Texas Agriculture Law blog posts on wind leases and severance.
Estimate: wind lease economics of about $20-60/acre/yr or about $3-10k per turbine per year, from general industry knowledge (not checked).

scored.name: Revived Siting Certificates
scored.one_line: Buy shells of approved-but-unbuilt generation and transmission projects whose permits can still be extended or amended; ML across scattered dockets proves survival; sell permit-ready sites.
scored.unproven_right: Dormant project LLCs with seemingly expired permits plus land options, near zero.
scored.proving_step: Determine survival across state siting boards, counties and federal agencies; win extension or transfer.
scored.proven_buyer: IPPs, utilities, data-center developers.
scored.public_data: OPSB, NY ORES/Article 10, Virginia SCC, Texas PUC CCN dockets, BLM MLRS, FAA OE/AAA, county CUP minutes.
scored.rough_step_up: ~10-100x; certificate status often in docket fields.
scored.frame: The rung is "take a dormant development shell to ready-to-build (RTB) and sell it." Inside that rung, finding out whether the permit survived is maybe 20-30% of the work (my estimate). The rest is physical and regulatory work that is neither trivial nor abstracted: filing extensions or amendments and fighting intervenors, re-signing land options that have lapsed, and above all getting back an interconnection position, plus studies and network-upgrade deposits. That fails the 80%+ test and looks like the coal-mine geothermal counter-example: re-entitling a site is harder than finding it.
scored.step_up: From memory of industry valuation norms, not verified this session: early or mid-stage US solar/wind development assets usually trade at about $0.01-0.05/W ($10k-50k/MW). RTB/NTP projects with interconnection agreements trade at about $0.10-0.30/W ($100k-300k/MW). Shells sold by distressed developers are not near zero: sellers price in sunk permit costs. My estimate is about 3-10x on a hit, not 10^3-10^4. A siting certificate alone, without a live interconnection position, adds maybe 1.5-3x (estimate). Treat these as estimates: the web-search budget ran out before any search returned.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Proving cost has two parts. Checking whether the permit survived is cheap: a paralegal docket review costs about $5k-20k per project (estimate). Actually reviving the project costs about $250k-$2M+ per project (estimate): extension or amendment filings, legal fees, refreshed environmental studies, and interconnection re-study deposits (often $1M+ in PJM/MISO cluster processes). ML only speeds up the cheap triage step. It does not raise the success rate of the expensive revival step, which depends on the regulator, the intervenors and grid capacity. So the lever is well under 10x, perhaps 1.5-2x on total cost (estimate).
scored.data: The dockets (OPSB, NY ORES/Article 10, VA SCC, TX PUC, BLM MLRS, FAA OE/AAA) are public and scattered, and county CUP minutes really are illegible. But the outcome is mostly already summarised in legible form. Certificate issue and expiry dates, extension orders, and case status sit in docket fields. FAA determinations carry explicit expiration dates. ISO queue status (active or withdrawn) is a public spreadsheet field, and LBNL's Queued Up dataset aggregates it nationally. This is the same failure as earlier hunts: the regulator writes the answer down. The purchase discount is weak because sellers are sophisticated developers and asset brokers who know their permit status. Specialist secondary-market players and development-asset marketplaces (for example Anza, LevelTen, and boutique M&A advisors; incumbents named from memory) already run this market.
scored.right_bought: Yes, the right is bought: the project LLC, its permits and its land options come through equity purchase or asset assignment. But the sellers can read their own dockets, and the most valuable component, interconnection position, is often already withdrawn or forfeited. That is usually why the project is dormant. Land options have often lapsed and must be renegotiated at current prices. Some permits cannot be transferred without board approval.
scored.buyer: Capitalised buyers do exist and they are hungry: IPPs (NextEra, AES, Invenergy), utilities, and hyperscaler or data-center developers paying premiums for sites with near-term power. That part of the thesis is real.
scored.ladder: There is a reasonable ladder: shell revival, then full greenfield development, then own-and-operate as an IPP, then power marketing or supplying data-center campuses. The top rungs are capital-intensive, utility-like businesses with thin multiples. A large company is possible but crowded, with NextEra-scale incumbents.
scored.fatal_flaw: Value in US generation siting sits mostly in a live interconnection position, plus current land control and community acceptance, not in the siting certificate. Dormant shells have usually lost those, and the certificate's survival is already a legible docket field. So ML discovers little that is not already known, and the expensive step (re-entitling and re-queuing) is bespoke physical and regulatory work, not discovery.
scored.one_line_reason: Real buyers exist, but the step-up is about 3-10x, permit survival is legible in docket fields, and interconnection plus re-entitlement work (not discovery) dominates the rung, so the 80%+ discovery frame fails.
sources: No web sources: the shared web-search budget (200 per turn) was exhausted before either search ran; all figures are estimates from memory of industry norms.
Memory, unverified this session: LBNL 'Queued Up' interconnection queue reports (public queue status and withdrawal rates)
Memory, unverified this session: Ohio Rev. Code / OAC 4906 (OPSB certificates carry construction-commencement deadlines; extensions are docketed orders)
Memory, unverified this session: FAA OE/AAA determinations carry explicit expiration dates in the public record

scored.name: Gas-Tap Sites: parcels at interstate pipelines with deliverability and air-permit headroom
scored.one_line: Option parcels next to pipeline laterals where EBB capacity and air-shed modelling show firm deliverability and attainment headroom; secure tap/precedent agreement and air screening; sell to BTM-generation data-center builders. Midstream delivery only, no exploration.
scored.unproven_right: Farmland options plus first-mover tap request.
scored.proving_step: Pipeline facilities study and AERMOD screening ($50-150k).
scored.proven_buyer: Crusoe, Energy Transfer/Williams co-location deals, hyperscaler BTM projects.
scored.public_data: Pipeline EBB capacity postings, FERC Form 2/567, scanned tariff filings, EPA AirData and designations, county parcels.
scored.rough_step_up: ~10-50x on land, ~10^3x on option; EBB data fairly legible.
scored.frame: The rung would be: option a parcel next to a pipeline, get a facilities study or tap commitment plus an air-screening result, then sell the site to a builder of behind-the-meter (BTM) gas generation. My estimate is that discovery and proving are only about 30-40% of the work needed to make that rung sellable. A buyer values the site only once there is firm gas transportation, a creditworthy shipper's precedent agreement, a turbine delivery slot (GE and Siemens frame and aeroderivative backlogs ran into 2028-30 per 2025 reporting) and a major-source air permit (PSD/Title V, typically 12-18 months). None of those come from reading data. This is the coal-mine geothermal counter-example again: the bespoke build and permitting are the hard part, not finding the parcel.
scored.step_up: These are estimates from prior knowledge because the search budget was exhausted. Farmland in gas-producing or pipeline states sells for about $5-15k/acre (USDA land values). Fully entitled, grid-powered data-center land in hot markets has traded at about $0.5-3M/acre, roughly 50-200x. That premium comes from confirmed power, and a gas-tap study plus an AERMOD screen does not confer it. My estimate for land that is merely gas-adjacent and screened is 3-20x. An option premium of a few $k could reach 10^2-10^3x only if the site carries a signed tap or precedent agreement, and a land speculator usually cannot get one. The candidate's own claim of 10-50x on land is plausible at best and unsourced.
scored.hit_rate_capex: These are estimates and unsourced. The candidate puts a facilities study plus AERMOD screen at $50-150k. A physical tap and meter station is usually customer-funded at about $1-5M+, and a lateral costs about $2-5M+ per mile. The base hit rate of the screening step is not low. Most points on a large interstate mainline can technically be tapped, and attainment status is a public designation. Failures come from capacity, firm-contract and turbine constraints that the data shows directly, or that only the pipeline can resolve. So there is no 1-in-100 drill-hit dynamic, and the ML lever is near 1-2x, not 10x.
scored.data: The outcome is mostly already in legible fields. Pipeline Electronic Bulletin Boards (EBBs) post operationally available and unsubscribed capacity in structured form, as FERC requires. EPA nonattainment designations and AirData monitors are structured. FERC Form 2/567 flow diagrams and tariffs are semi-legible, and county parcels are standard GIS. The real answer is whether the pipeline will commit firm service at this point, and that sits in the pipeline's internal hydraulic models, which are not public. There is little illegible public signal that incumbents fail to extract. Midstream companies know their own systems perfectly.
scored.right_bought: The farmland option can be bought cheaply from farmers who do not read EBBs, which is the one Terranox-like element. But the value-bearing right is a tap, firm capacity or precedent agreement, and it is not a saleable first-mover right. Pipelines award it through open seasons and request queues to creditworthy shippers, usually with security or rate commitments. A pre-revenue land company cannot hold it cheaply. The pipeline can also bypass the speculator by choosing or co-developing its own sites.
scored.buyer: Capitalised buyers exist and are active. They include Crusoe, VoltaGrid, hyperscaler BTM projects (Meta, xAI and others using on-site gas), and midstream co-location programmes such as Williams (Socrates project for Meta in Ohio), Energy Transfer and Kinder Morgan. The midstream players are also direct competitors: they source sites themselves, alongside site developers such as Tract and Fermi America. Named from prior knowledge; not re-verified this run.
scored.ladder: The ladder above is real: site, then tap and lateral, then BTM generation build-own-operate, then power-as-a-service and data-center shell or colocation, then campus operator. Each rung above the land rung is capital-heavy and execution-bound (turbines, EPC, permits), not discovery-bound. That makes for a big company, but an infrastructure developer rather than an ML-discovery compounder.
scored.fatal_flaw: No frame exists where discovery is 80%+. Value is created by the pipeline's firm-service commitment, turbine slots and a major-source air permit. Those are controlled by the incumbent midstream company and by OEMs and regulators, and data cannot reveal or substitute for them. The screening outcome is already legible in EBB and attainment fields, so ML adds little, and the pipeline can go around a land speculator.
scored.one_line_reason: The buyers are real, but proving is not the hard part, the key right is held by the pipeline rather than bought, and the data is already legible. It fails the Terranox test the same way geothermal in coal mines does.

FERC Order 587 series / NAESB standards requiring interstate pipeline EBB capacity postings (prior knowledge)
USDA NASS Land Values summary for farmland $/acre (prior knowledge)

scored.name: Restored Reels: URAA restoration title house
scored.one_line: Buy US rights to foreign 1930s-80s films, photos and music that owners believe are US public domain; ML proves automatic URAA restoration and chain of title; sell title-insured catalogues to FAST/AVOD aggregators.
scored.unproven_right: Restored US copyright in foreign works, a few hundred dollars per title.
scored.proving_step: Legal-data dossier (publication, source-country status 1996, chain, reliance parties), E&O title opinion and registration/NIE.
scored.proven_buyer: Tubi, Pluto, Roku, Shout! Factory, Kino Lorber, Cinedigm, Criterion; enforcement settlements.
scored.public_data: Copyright Office NIE lists, CCE scans, Copyright Public Records System, foreign archives (BnF, BFI), IMDb/Wikidata, foreign registries.
scored.frame: The rung is a title-cleared restored-copyright title (rights bought, then chain of title proven and E&O-insured). Inside that rung, legal discovery (publication history, source-country status on 1996-01-01, heirs and chain of title) is roughly 70-85% of the work (my estimate). The physical step is trivial: a scan or remaster for FAST runs a few thousand dollars, and many titles already exist in circulating PD prints. Capitalised buyers exist (FAST/AVOD aggregators, Kino, Shout, Criterion), but they buy cheap library content. The ceiling on the frame is buyer willingness to pay, not discovery difficulty.
scored.step_up: Unproven: a few hundred dollars per title (the candidate's figure, unverified). Proven: from training knowledge, without a source, obscure foreign library features license to FAST/AVOD on non-exclusive revenue-share or flat fees, often low thousands of dollars per title per year (my estimate). An exclusive catalogue sale might reach about $5k-50k for a typical title, so roughly 10-100x. A few hits (a Kurosawa, Hitchcock-UK or Fellini-tier title) go far higher, but major studios and estates (Toho, Studiocanal, Gaumont, Mosfilm, ITV) already hold and enforce those. The candidate's claimed 10^2-10^3x is optimistic for the median title.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Base hit rate of the proving step is HIGH, not low. Restoration under 17 USC 104A is automatic for any work of non-US origin that was in the US public domain only for formalities (no notice, no renewal) and still protected in its source country on 1 Jan 1996, and most 1930s-80s foreign works meet that rule (Golan v. Holder, 2012, upheld it). So most screened titles qualify, and the lever (capped at 1/base rate) is maybe 1.5-3x. Cost per proving attempt (my estimate): legal dossier and title opinion about $1-5k, E&O cover about $3-10k per feature. The cost is legal labour, not failed shots, so ML gives little leverage. Live web searches failed because the shared search budget was used up, so these numbers come from prior knowledge and are unverified.
scored.data: The data is public and partly illegible: Copyright Office NIE lists (Federal Register, 1996-2000s), Catalog of Copyright Entries scans, foreign registries and archives. But the outcome is mostly decidable with a rule engine. Inputs are country of origin, publication year, US notice/renewal status (the CCE renewal records are already digitised and searchable) and the source-country term (life+70 or similar), and Wikidata/IMDb already carry most of them. That mirrors the interconnection-queue failure, where a lookup table matched the ML. The real difficulty is identifying heirs and proving chain of title, which is detective work, not pattern extraction at scale.
scored.right_bought: Partly. For orphaned or minor works, heirs and small foreign producers who do not know they hold US rights can sell cheaply, so rights are bought, not free first-come. But finding and contracting foreign heirs costs real money per title, and the valuable catalogues are held by sophisticated foreign studios who know about URAA and already license through agents. Reliance parties (existing PD distributors) also keep rights to sell existing copies until an NIE is served plus 12 months, and must be paid off for derivatives.
scored.buyer: Tubi, Pluto, Roku Channel, Samsung TV Plus FAST channels, plus Kino Lorber, Shout! Factory, Cinedigm/Cineverse, Criterion and Film Movement. They are capitalised but price library content very low. The enforcement-settlement income the candidate lists is copyright trolling (Righthaven/Prenda-style), which carries legal and reputational risk.
scored.ladder: Rungs above: restoration and remastering, owned FAST channels, a distribution label, then a global library or rights house (Studiocanal/Kino-like). The ladder exists, but the end state is a niche library business; foreign-classics library deals land in the hundreds of millions, not a trillion-dollar path. Titles also leave the frame as US terms expire (95 years from publication), so 1930s works run out within a few years.
scored.fatal_flaw: Restoration is automatic, applies to most foreign works of the period, and is decided by a near-deterministic legal rule. That gives a high base hit rate and almost no ML lever. The valuable titles are already held and enforced by aware foreign studios, so what is left to buy cheaply is low-value long-tail content whose proven price (low thousands per title on FAST) barely clears legal and E&O costs.
scored.one_line_reason: Clean asset-ownership structure, but the proving step usually succeeds (the URAA rule settles most titles), the outcome comes from a legible rule rather than illegible data, the median step-up is about 10-100x on cheap library content, and the ladder tops out at a niche library business.
sources: 17 U.S.C. 104A (URAA restoration provisions; prior knowledge, not fetched this run)
Golan v. Holder, 565 U.S. 302 (2012) (prior knowledge)
US Copyright Office NIE lists in the Federal Register, 1996 onward (prior knowledge)
Live web searches failed because the shared per-turn search budget was used up; all prices and costs are the author's estimates and are unverified

scored.name: Recapture / Termination Heirs Capital: copyright termination-right arbitrage
scored.one_line: Find heirs of songwriters and authors whose sec. 203/304 termination windows are open, fund valid notices, and buy the recaptured rights as they vest; sell to catalogue buyers.
scored.unproven_right: Statutory termination interests held by unaware heirs (post-notice future rights).
scored.proving_step: ML resolves grant date, work-for-hire, heir class and window from scanned CCE, recorded documents and probate; serve and record notice.
scored.proven_buyer: Primary Wave, Concord, Reservoir, Round Hill, Sony/UMG publishing; studios for book rights.
scored.public_data: CCE scans, Copyright Office recorded documents and termination recordations, Discogs/MusicBrainz, probate, obituaries, SSDI.
scored.rough_step_up: ~10-10^4x on a hit; heirs need real payouts.
scored.frame: Rung: identify the heir class and window, serve and record a valid notice, then own the recaptured US rights. Inside that rung, discovery (grant date, work-for-hire status, the heir class per stirpes, the 2-10 year notice window) is maybe 60-70% of the work (my estimate). The rest is legal: getting a majority of the heir class to sign, serving the notice, recording it, and defending against work-for-hire and derivative-works challenges. That is not trivial or abstracted. The bigger problem is that the company cannot legally hold the rung's output until the effective date, which can be 2-10 years after the notice. Catalogue buyers do exist, but the original grantee has a statutory head start.
scored.step_up: Unproven: an unaware heir's termination interest has near-zero perceived value. Proven: after the effective date, recaptured US rights trade at catalogue multiples of about 10-20x net publisher share (my estimate from public catalogue-deal reporting, not verified this session). The heir's own step-up is large on a hit song, roughly 10-1000x. The company's step-up is far smaller. It cannot buy before vesting (17 USC 203(b)(4) and 304(c)(6)(D) void any earlier further grant, or agreement to make one, to a third party). So it pays a near-market price after vesting, or it is only a lender or finder taking a fee or a share. Realistic company-level uplift is about 2-5x on its funded costs (estimate). Most eligible works earn almost nothing, so the median hit is worth $0-$10k.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Cost per proving attempt: about $1k-$10k in attorney time, research and recording fees per notice (my estimate; Copyright Office recording fees are on the order of $100+ per document). That is cheap, so cutting it 10x saves little absolute capex. Base hit rate on value is not low in a way ML can fix. Which old works still earn money is already legible from public streaming counts and PRO repertoire listings, so a lookup ranks targets as well as a model would. The illegible part (heir identity and grant chain) is a cost centre, not the value signal. Lever is about 2-3x at best (estimate). No searches went through this session, so every number here is my estimate.
scored.data: Part of the data really is illegible: CCE scans, recorded transfer documents, probate files and obituaries are scattered and messy. But the outcome is already legible in two places. First, value: Spotify play counts, Luminate data and BMI/ASCAP repertoire are public. Second, termination status: notices of termination are recorded and searchable in the Copyright Office public records. The edge is genealogy and chain of title, not hidden value. Incumbent publishers watch their own grant dates and renegotiate before notices land. Music lawyers (Lisa Alter, Evan Cohen and others) and startups such as Rightsback already work termination-heir outreach.
scored.right_bought: Fails. Termination rights are inalienable: termination applies 'notwithstanding any agreement to the contrary', and a further grant is valid only if made after the effective date. The one exception is the original grantee, which can contract once the notice is served. So the unproven right cannot be bought cheaply in advance. The company can only fund heirs (litigation-finance or royalty-advance style, open to challenge as a disguised grant) or bid at market after vesting, against the original publisher, which holds the exclusive window.
scored.buyer: Catalogue buyers and publishers: Primary Wave, Concord, Reservoir, Round Hill, Hipgnosis/Recognition, Sony/UMG/Warner publishing. Studios for literary rights. They are capitalised, but the statute gives the original grantee first, exclusive access, and that grantee is usually one of these same buyers.
scored.ladder: Recaptured-rights aggregator, then catalogue owner and publisher, then admin and sync/licensing platform, then full music publisher. That path leads to a multi-billion-dollar publisher (Concord-scale), not a trillion-dollar chain. Only US rights recapture; foreign rights and pre-termination derivative works stay with the grantee, which caps the TAM.
scored.fatal_flaw: 17 USC 203(b)(4) and 304(c)(6)(D) make the unproven right legally unbuyable. A further grant, or an agreement to make one, to anyone other than the original grantee is void before the effective date. So the company cannot own the asset at the near-zero price and capture the step-up itself. It collapses into a fee-for-service or lender model, which is an exclusion, and the original publisher keeps the inside track.
scored.one_line_reason: Heir-finding is real, illegible discovery, but the statute stops anyone buying termination interests before vesting and gives the incumbent grantee an exclusive window. The song's value is already legible from streaming data. The company can neither own the cheap right nor hold a value edge.
sources: 17 U.S.C. 203(a)(5), 203(b)(4) (termination notwithstanding agreement to the contrary; further grant valid only after effective date, except to original grantee) - from statutory knowledge, not fetched this session
17 U.S.C. 304(c)(6)(D) (parallel rule for pre-1978 works) - statutory knowledge
U.S. Copyright Office Public Records System - notices of termination are recorded and searchable (knowledge)
WebSearch budget was exhausted (shared 200-call limit), so no live sources were retrieved; all dollar figures are labelled estimates

scored.name: Story Rights Co.: true-story life rights from court and archival records
scored.one_line: ML over transcripts, opinions and local newspapers finds dramatic true stories; option life rights and underlying articles cheaply; sell packaged rights to studios and streamers.
scored.unproven_right: Life-story rights and underlying copyrights for $1-10k.
scored.proving_step: Narrative scoring and clearance; studio option or purchase.
scored.proven_buyer: Netflix, HBO, Hulu, Apple TV+, Amazon MGM, Blumhouse, Imagine, podcast networks.
scored.public_data: PACER and state dockets, CourtListener, Caselaw Access Project, Chronicling America, Newspapers.com, FOIA rooms.
scored.frame: The rung is 'acquire and package true-story rights, then sell an option or purchase to a studio'. Finding the story is maybe 30-40% of the work in that rung (my estimate). The rest is getting the subject to sign, clearing the rights, writing a treatment, attaching talent or a producer, and pitching. That selling and packaging work is the real bottleneck and is not trivial or abstracted. It is the opposite of drilling: the physical step here is relationship-driven sales into a hits business. Capitalised buyers do exist (Netflix, HBO, Amazon MGM, Blumhouse, podcast networks).
scored.step_up: Unproven: a life-rights option for a non-famous subject costs about $1k-10k, usually against a purchase price (industry convention, my estimate; not verified this turn). Proven: when a studio options the package, the seller typically gets an option payment of about $10k-50k. The full purchase price, commonly cited as about 1-3% of the production budget (roughly $50k-500k, rarely $1M+ for marquee stories), is usually paid only on the first day of principal photography. The immediate step-up on a hit is about 5-20x, and only about 20-100x if the project is produced. That is ~10^1-10^2, not 10^4. All figures are my estimates from known industry practice; the search budget was exhausted, so none were verified.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Base hit rate: industry lore says roughly 1 in 10 or fewer optioned properties ever get produced, and far fewer cold-pitched true stories get optioned at all, perhaps 1-5% (my estimate, unverified). Cost per attempt is low: about $1k-10k for the option plus a few thousand dollars of treatment and clearance work. That is already cheap, so ML has little capex to cut, and the lever falls on the cheap step (finding stories) rather than the expensive one (studio taste). In theory the lever caps at 20-100x, but ML cannot predict studio appetite, so the realistic lever is under 2-3x.
scored.data: The data is public and partly illegible: PACER and state dockets, CourtListener, Caselaw Access Project, Chronicling America. But the outcome (verdict, ruling, disposition) is already a legible field in dockets and opinions, and dramatic cases already get press coverage. The ML edge is surfacing obscure local stories, which is weak, since journalists, true-crime podcasters and scouts already mine this.
scored.right_bought: This is the fatal weakness. Facts in court records and public archives cannot be copyrighted, and a studio can dramatise a public-record story without buying life rights. Life rights mainly buy access, consent and cover for E&O (errors and omissions) insurance, plus protection against defamation and privacy claims. They are not an exclusive property right. Owners (the subjects) can be bought cheaply, but the right does not lock out competitors the way a mineral claim does. Rival producers can option a different participant in the same case, or work from the record alone. Old newspaper articles before 1929 are public domain, and later ones are owned by publishers who already license them.
scored.buyer: Netflix, HBO/Max, Amazon MGM, Apple TV+, Hulu, Blumhouse, Imagine, and podcast networks such as Wondery and Audible. They are capitalised but buy on taste, talent attachment and timing, not on a provable metric. Existing intermediaries already run this exact model: Truly*Adventurous, Campside Media, Epic Magazine, Story Lab-type outfits and countless true-crime producers. (Named from prior knowledge; not verified this turn.)
scored.ladder: Rights packager, then producer, then podcast or doc studio, then scripted studio with its own IP library. The ladder exists, but every rung above is a hits-driven creative business with low margins and talent-driven economics, not a compounding asset business. It is plausible to reach a mid-size production company, not a trillion-dollar company.
scored.fatal_flaw: The 'right' is not exclusive or provable. Public-record true stories can be dramatised without life rights, so the purchased asset does not capture the step-up. 'Proving' is a subjective studio taste call that ML cannot predict, rather than an objective drill hit.
scored.one_line_reason: This is a hits-driven, taste-gated sales business with non-exclusive rights, a ~10-100x contingent step-up, and existing scouts already mining the same public records. It fails the Terranox frame on C1, C4 and C2.
sources: No web searches succeeded: the shared turn search budget (200) was exhausted. All numbers are estimates from prior knowledge of industry practice: life-rights option conventions ($1k-10k option against a purchase price of about 1-3% of budget), option-to-production rates (about 1 in 10 or fewer), and the US rule that facts and public records are not copyrightable (Feist v. Rural, 1991).
Known intermediaries running the model: Truly*Adventurous, Campside Media, Epic Magazine (prior knowledge, unverified this turn).

scored.name: Process-Patent Evidence-of-Use from Air Permits
scored.one_line: Buy manufacturing-process patents from bankrupt battery, solar, materials and chem startups; ML over state air-permit applications, SDSs and TSCA filings proves large plants run the patented process (35 USC 295 burden shift); sell charted patents to funders.
scored.unproven_right: Issued process patents from estates, $1-5k each.
scored.proving_step: Claim chart from permits, SDSs, import records and microstructure literature.
scored.proven_buyer: Burford, Fortress IP, IPValue, Dominion Harbor, infringers.
scored.public_data: TCEQ, Louisiana EDMS, Ohio eDocs air permits; TSCA CDR and TRI; SDS libraries; PatentCenter; PACER; bills of lading.
scored.frame: The rung is "own a process patent and produce a claim chart showing a named large plant uses the process", then sell it to a litigation funder or an aggregator. Inside that rung, finding evidence of use is maybe 50-60% of the work. My estimate is that the rest is validity and prior-art work against IPR risk (roughly 40-60% of instituted IPR claims get cancelled, from memory of PTAB statistics), damages modelling, venue choice, and checking chain of title and maintenance fees on assets out of bankrupt estates. The physical step is not abstracted away. Value is only realised through litigation or the threat of it, which takes $2-5M and 2-4 years (AIPLA survey, from memory). A funder prices the chart at a deep discount for all of that, so discovery never reaches the 80%+ share inside a cleanly sellable rung. Unlike a drill core, a claim chart is an argument, not a fact. The other side contests it.
scored.step_up: Unproven: $1-5k per patent from estates. That figure comes from the candidate. It is consistent with my memory of bankruptcy IP auctions, where clean-tech estate portfolios often clear at about $5-50k per family, but I could not verify it. Proven, meaning charted against a large infringer: brokered secondary-market patents ask about $100-250k per asset (Richardson Oliver Insights market reports, from memory, not verified this session). A funder may pay an upfront $250k-$1M for a strong charted family, or more commonly take a contingent share. That gives roughly 50-300x on a hit, which scores 3 because it sits in the 10-100x band and only sometimes reaches 100x+. The step-up is not immediate. Most of the value is contingent on the litigation outcome, so the money paid in cash at the moment of the hit is lower.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Base hit rate: the candidate gives 1-3% of estate process patents that can be charted against a large US plant, which is my estimate too. Cost per proving attempt today: a manual infringement or evidence-of-use search plus a claim chart from an IP analytics firm costs about $5-20k per patent (my estimate). The lever is real but capped. A 1-3% base rate allows at most 30-100x in theory. In practice, ML gains are limited because air permits redact process details as confidential business information. Permits show equipment, throughput and emissions, not the claimed process parameters (temperatures, ratios, sequences). The real cap is evidence quality, not the speed of finding candidates. So I estimate the realistic cut in discovery cost at 3-5x, not 10x.
scored.data: The data is public and illegible: state air-permit PDFs (TCEQ, Louisiana EDMS, Ohio eDocs), TSCA CDR, TRI, SDS libraries, and bills of lading. Nobody summarises the outcome in a legible field, so this criterion's 'answer not written into a status field' test passes. Two weaknesses. (1) Process-specific details are routinely claimed as confidential business information and redacted in permit applications and CDR. What stays public, such as chemicals, emissions and equipment lists, often fits many processes, so the evidence comes out circumstantial. (2) 35 USC 295 shifts the burden only after the court finds a substantial likelihood the product was made by the process and that the patentee made reasonable efforts to find out. Courts rarely invoke it, and it applies to products imported into, or made, sold or used in, the US, so the claims have to be framed to fit.
scored.right_bought: The right can be bought, often cheaply, from estate trustees, assignees for the benefit of creditors, and liquidators such as Hilco Streambank and Tangible IP, who cannot evaluate it. The weaknesses are competition and quality. Strong estate battery and solar portfolios often go to strategic buyers or Chinese competitors (for example, A123's assets went to Wanxiang), and large aggregators watch these sales. Many estate patents have lapsed maintenance fees or are near expiry. Startup process claims are often narrow and drafted around lab-scale parameters, which makes them hard to read onto a commercial plant.
scored.buyer: The buyers exist and are well capitalised: Burford, Fortress IP, Omni Bridgeway, IPValue, Dominion Harbor, and defensive aggregators such as RPX and Unified Patents (the last two on the defensive side). The funder market for patent litigation is about $1B+ per year (my estimate). But these buyers underwrite the whole case: validity, damages, venue, defendant solvency. Evidence of use alone does not get a patent bought at a high price. They also already pay specialised firms to find assets.
scored.ladder: The rungs above are: running litigation yourself as an assertion entity, licensing programmes, and then perhaps operating the processes yourself. The first two lead to an assertion-entity business: lumpy, adversarial, exposed to reputation and policy risk, and capped at a few billion dollars at best (Acacia, InterDigital-style licensing). There is no natural climb from patent assertion into owning chemical or battery plants, so the trillion-dollar path does not follow. Unlike land, the asset expires after 20 years.
scored.fatal_flaw: The proving step is not a fact the market accepts. A claim chart is a contestable argument, and its value is only realised through years of costly litigation with high invalidation risk. So discovery is never 80%+ of the work in a sellable rung. On top of that, confidential-business-information redaction strips the process parameters out of air permits, so the ML signal is circumstantial and does not prove use.
scored.one_line_reason: Cheap estate patents and illegible permit data are real advantages. But the step-up is contingent and contested through litigation rather than immediate, redaction of process details caps the ML edge, and the ladder dead-ends at patent assertion.
sources: No searches ran: the shared WebSearch budget for this turn was already used up, so every figure below is from memory or is my own estimate.
35 U.S.C. 295 (statutory text): the burden shifts only after a court finds a substantial likelihood of use plus reasonable efforts by the patentee (from memory)
Richardson Oliver Insights secondary patent market reports: asking prices of about $100-250k per asset (from memory, not verified)
AIPLA Report of the Economic Survey: patent litigation costs about $2-5M through trial (from memory, not verified)
PTAB trial statistics: a large share of instituted claims are found unpatentable (from memory)

scored.name: EstateLab: dead battery and materials startup lab estates
scored.one_line: Buy whole intellectual estates (patents, notebooks, cycler data, samples) of failed materials companies; ML over raw cycling and characterisation data finds abandoned winners; rebuild cells; sell chemistry packages.
scored.unproven_right: Estate data rooms and sample libraries, $50-500k.
scored.proving_step: ML over Arbin/Maccor/Neware files and XRD/SEM archives; 50-200 cell rebuild ($50-150k).
scored.proven_buyer: Panasonic, LGES, SK On, GM, Toyota, specialty materials makers.
scored.public_data: PACER and 363 notices, patents; raw data comes with the estate.
scored.frame: The proposed rung is 'buy a failed lab's estate, re-mine its cycler and characterisation data, rebuild 50-200 cells, sell a chemistry package'. In that rung discovery is maybe 30-40% of the work (my estimate). Proving a battery chemistry well enough that a cell maker will pay for it means going from coin or small pouch cells to large-format cells, then cycle life past 1000 cycles, abuse and safety testing, and checks on supply and manufacturability. That takes 2-5 years and $10M or more, and it is the bespoke physical step, exactly like the geothermal plant in the counter-example. A 50-200 cell rebuild is a screening step, not a proving step. There is no sellable frame where discovery is 80%+ of the work and a capitalised buyer pays on a hit.
scored.step_up: From memory, unverified this session: A123's whole company, with plants and a large patent estate, sold to Wanxiang in the 2013 bankruptcy auction for about $257M. Britishvolt's assets went to Recharge Industries in 2023 for roughly GBP 8.6M. Carcasses of failed cell startups (Cuberg, closed by Northvolt in 2024; Natron in 2025; Ambri's 2024 bankruptcy sale) were liquidated at small fractions of the capital invested. The proven side: QuantumScape's licence to VW PowerCo carried a royalty prepayment of roughly $130M, but that came after more than a decade and over $1B of validation, not after a 50-200 cell rebuild. Buying an estate for $50-500k and selling a screened chemistry package for maybe $1-5M (my estimate; cell makers rarely buy unvalidated startup chemistry) is about 3-30x on a hit. The candidate's claimed 50-250x only appears if you assume the package is already validated, which is the expensive part this plan skips.
scored.hit_rate_capex: My estimate: very few failed materials startups hold an overlooked winning chemistry, perhaps 1-5% of estates. Most failed on scale-up, cost or yield, not because they missed a winner in their own data, and their own data teams had already mined their cycler data. A screening attempt costs about $50-150k for the rebuild plus the estate price. Raising the hit rate on screening is possible, but downstream validation (more than $10M per chemistry) dominates capex, so ML cuts total capex maybe 1.5-2x, not 10x.
scored.data: The raw data (Arbin/Maccor/Neware cycler files, XRD/SEM archives, lab notebooks) is illegible and private, and it comes only with the estate, so the edge is a real proprietary dataset, not public. The public parts (PACER, 363 sale notices, patents) only show deal flow. But the outcome is partly legible already: the startup's own investor decks, published papers and patent claims record its best results, and the reason it failed (usually manufacturing or cost) is known. The chance of a winner hidden in raw data that the startup's own scientists never saw is low.
scored.right_bought: Yes. Estates are bought cheaply in 363 sales or assignment-for-benefit-of-creditors processes, often for tens to hundreds of thousands of dollars for IP-only lots (my estimate; Britishvolt-scale whole-company deals ran to millions of pounds). The sellers (trustees, liquidators, patent aggregators) cannot read the cycler data. This is the strongest part of the idea. One caveat: a sample library degrades, and the people who know the work leave, so tacit knowledge is lost.
scored.buyer: In theory: Panasonic, LGES, SK On, Samsung SDI, CATL, GM, Toyota, and materials makers (Umicore, BASF, EcoPro). In practice these companies run large in-house R&D and buy chemistry through acquisitions or JDAs (joint development agreements) only after large-format validation. Unvalidated chemistry packages have a thin market. Lyten picking up Northvolt assets in 2025 was a distressed buy of factories and people, not a purchase of chemistry data.
scored.ladder: There is a real ladder: a chemistry package, then a validated cell, then pilot line, licensing or royalties, then your own cell manufacturing (the Northvolt/QuantumScape path). The upper rungs are capital-intensive with notoriously poor returns: Northvolt burned more than $10B and failed. The ladder exists, but each rung up is the bespoke physical step.
scored.fatal_flaw: The proving step is not the 50-200 cell rebuild. It is multi-year, large-format validation costing $10M or more, the bespoke physical step that dominates the work, just as building the plant does in the geothermal-in-coal-mines counter-example. So no rung has discovery at 80%+ of the work with a capitalised buyer paying on a hit, and cell makers do not pay a step-up for screened, unvalidated chemistry.
scored.one_line_reason: Estates can be bought cheaply and the data is illegible, but the physical validation needed before a buyer pays dwarfs the discovery work, so the Terranox frame does not exist.

scored.name: Binder Archaeology: dormant university antibodies against now-hot targets
scored.one_line: License hybridomas and antibody sequences NIH-funded labs made and shelved; ML ranks binders against targets that became validated ADC or bispecific targets; a $10-30k CRO run proves the binder; license to ADC/bispecific developers.
scored.unproven_right: Exclusive licence/assignment from a TTO, $1-25k.
scored.proving_step: Gene synthesis, expression, SPR, cell binding, internalisation at a CRO.
scored.proven_buyer: Chinese ADC licensors, Merck, AbbVie, Genmab-type buyers ($1-5M upfront, $50M+ milestones).
scored.public_data: USPTO/WIPO sequence listings (PSIPS), DSHB, RePORTER, PMC methods, Open Targets, ClinicalTrials.gov.
scored.frame: The proposed rung is to license a shelved academic binder, run a $10-30k CRO panel (expression, SPR, cell binding, internalisation), then sell the binder. Inside that rung, discovery (matching an old binder to a now-hot target) is maybe 20-30% of the work, not 80%+. That is my estimate. Real ADC and bispecific buyers do not pay for binding data. They pay for an assembled molecule (the antibody plus its linker-payload, or a bispecific format) with developability and CMC data, mouse xenograft efficacy and ideally non-human primate (NHP) tox. Getting from a validated binder to that package costs roughly $1-5M and 12-24 months, my estimate. That physical step is bespoke and much bigger than the discovery step. It is the same failure as the geothermal coal-mine counter-example. A bare-binder rung exists, but its buyers (small biotechs, sometimes CROs) are not well capitalised and pay little.
scored.step_up: Unproven right: TTO exclusive licences for an academic antibody or hybridoma usually cost $5-50k upfront plus royalties. Non-exclusive DSHB-type hybridomas cost about $50-500. Both figures are my estimate from memory; the search budget ran out. Proven, preclinical binder with only in-vitro data: roughly $0.1-1M upfront, often option-style, my estimate. The $1-5M+ upfronts in the pitch match deals for preclinical ADC assets with in-vivo data. The large Chinese ADC out-licences of 2023-2025 (often $50M-$1B+ upfront) were mostly for clinical-stage assets with Phase 1 data. So the realistic step-up on a hit is about 10-100x, not 10^3-10^4.
scored.hit_rate_capex: My estimate: a published binder will probably reproduce binding to its stated target at a CRO more than 50% of the time. The proving step is cheap ($10-30k) and mostly succeeds, so it is not an expensive, mostly-failing step. The low-hit-rate part comes later: whether the binder beats existing clinical binders on epitope, internalisation and developability, and survives in-vivo work. That part costs $1-5M per attempt, and ML ranking from old papers barely moves it. The lever is capped near 1/0.5 = 2x on the cheap step. Competing supply also undercuts the idea. Phage display or immunisation campaigns produce new binders with fresh IP for about $100-300k in 3-6 months. AI de novo antibody design (Absci, Generate, Chai-2, which reported double-digit-percent binder hit rates in 2025) is commoditising binders against any validated target. These numbers are from memory, not searched.
scored.data: The data is public and partly illegible: patent sequence listings, PMC methods sections, RePORTER grants and DSHB. But the outcome is often already written down in legible form. The paper or patent states the target the binder hits, and often its KD and whether it internalises. Matching old binders to hot targets (TROP2, B7-H3, CLDN18.2, CDH6) is a keyword join. It does not need ML over illegible data, which weakens the edge. IP is a second problem. A sequence published in a patent or paper is prior art. Its composition-of-matter patent may have expired or lapsed, or never been filed. So often there is no exclusive right to buy, and anyone can synthesise the sequence. That breaks the 'bought, not free first-come' requirement.
scored.right_bought: Sometimes. A TTO exclusive licence can be bought cheaply ($5-50k plus royalty, my estimate) when a live patent exists. Many shelved binders, though, are unpatented, have lapsed patents, or have sequences that are fully disclosed. Then the 'right' is worth close to nothing, because any buyer can make the sequence themselves. TTOs also run their own marketing and know which targets are hot, though they do not mine their back catalogue very well.
scored.buyer: The capitalised buyers (Merck, AbbVie, Genmab, Chinese ADC players such as Hengrui, Kelun, Duality and Hansoh) buy assembled molecules with in-vivo and clinical data, not bare binders. They also run large internal binder-generation platforms. Few of them pay for a bare in-vitro binder. Plausible bare-binder buyers are small ADC platform biotechs and option-deal partners, at sub-$1M upfront (my estimate).
scored.ladder: The ladder above is strong in principle: binder, then a developed molecule (ADC or bispecific with in-vivo data), then IND, then Phase 1 out-licence ($50M-$1B+ upfronts), then a full pharma company. The rungs worth money start at the developed-molecule stage, though, where capex is $1-5M+. That is where the company would have to start, and there the discovery share is small.
scored.fatal_flaw: Binders against validated targets are a commodity. Phage display or AI de novo design delivers fresh, patentable binders against any hot target in months for about $100-300k. Buyers pay for in-vivo and clinical data, not sequences. So the cheap CRO binding run takes a shelved binder from about $10k to perhaps $100k-1M, not to $10M. The rungs worth paying for need a bespoke $1-5M development step in which discovery is a minor share. Many published sequences also carry no ownable exclusive right.
scored.one_line_reason: This fails the frame test. Binding is cheap to prove and mostly succeeds. Binders are a commodity (phage display, AI de novo design). Buyers pay for developed ADC or bispecific molecules with in-vivo data, which is a $1-5M bespoke step. The real step-up on a hit is about 10-100x, and published sequences often have no ownable right.
sources: No live sources: both WebSearch calls were refused because the shared 200-search budget for this turn was used up. Every number here is my estimate from memory and needs verifying in a follow-up run.
Memory, not verified: big Chinese ADC out-licences in 2023-2025 (e.g. Kelun-Merck, Hansoh-GSK, Duality-BioNTech, Hengrui) were mostly clinical-stage, with $50M-$1B+ upfronts
Memory, not verified: 2025 AI de novo antibody design reports (Chai-2, Absci, Generate Biomedicines) showing double-digit-percent binder hit rates
Memory, not verified: university TTO antibody and hybridoma licensing norms (DSHB non-exclusive fees; exclusive licences of a few $k to tens of $k upfront)

scored.name: Rare-Disease Registry Roll-up to Trial-Ready Cohorts
scored.one_line: License dormant foundation registries, ML-curate them into variant-confirmed cohorts, sell recruitment and data to sponsors entering the indication.
scored.unproven_right: Exclusive data/recruitment rights, $25-250k plus share.
scored.proving_step: Forecast sponsor arrival; LLM curation.
scored.proven_buyer: Rare-disease and gene-therapy sponsors.
scored.public_data: FDA orphan designations, ClinicalTrials.gov, NORD/Global Genes, GARD, Form 990s, SEC filings.
scored.frame: The rung would be "own exclusive rights to a curated, variant-confirmed rare-disease cohort and sell it to a sponsor when they enter the indication." Discovery here means forecasting which indication a sponsor will enter next, plus LLM curation of the records. My estimate is that discovery is 30-40% of the work inside this rung. The rest is physical and relational, and none of it is abstracted: re-consenting patients, collecting genetic tests or medical records, managing the foundation relationship, IRB and HIPAA compliance, and running site recruitment. Unlike drilling, those steps are the hard part. Buyers with money do exist (gene-therapy and rare-disease sponsors), so the frame is real but weak.
scored.step_up: My estimate: the unproven right costs $25-250k (the candidate's figure). A proven right, meaning a sponsor actually needs the cohort, would sell as a data or recruitment deal for about $0.5-3M per program. That is about 5-20x, not 10^3-10^4. For reference, Invitae bought Ciitizen in 2021 for about $325M, and that value disappeared when Invitae went bankrupt in 2024; this is from memory, not checked this run. Value comes in gradually over sponsor contracts rather than jumping at a single proving event.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Unverified. The search budget for this run was already used up, so these numbers are my estimates from prior knowledge. The base rate at which a given dormant registry's indication attracts a sponsor within 3-5 years is probably 10-25%. There are about 7,000 rare diseases and only a few hundred have active programs, but registries exist mostly where interest is already high. Each attempt costs only $25-250k plus curation, so the step is not expensive and the ML lever is at most 4-10x on paper. Sponsor arrival is also largely readable from public sources: ClinicalTrials.gov, FDA orphan designations, and preclinical and academic pipelines. A simple pipeline lookup gets most of the way there, so the real ML gain over that is small.
scored.data: The outcome is largely already written into legible fields. FDA orphan designation and ClinicalTrials.gov entries are structured, searchable records that tell you a sponsor is coming, and sponsors themselves look up registries through NORD IAMRARE, CoRDS, RARE-X and Global Genes. The illegible part is the registry contents: free-text case report forms and scanned genetic reports. But that data is private to the foundation, not public, so there is no public-but-illegible edge. The sellers are not unsophisticated either. Foundations know their registry is their main leverage with pharma, often negotiate directly with sponsors, and patient consent and governance usually block outright exclusivity. Competitors already work this ground (from memory, not checked this run): Citizen Health, PicnicHealth, RARE-X, NORD IAMRARE, IQVIA/Medidata recruitment, COMBINEDBrain, and the former Ciitizen.
scored.right_bought: An exclusive or non-exclusive data and recruitment license from a patient foundation. It can be bought, but it is constrained: patient consent terms and foundation boards limit exclusivity, foundations often keep re-contact rights, and the patients belong to the community rather than to the asset. The licensee cannot fully own it the way a mineral claim is owned.
scored.buyer: Rare-disease and gene-therapy sponsors (Sarepta, Ultragenyx, BioMarin, many small biotechs) and the CROs that run their trials. They have money, but they often go to foundations directly or to incumbents such as IQVIA or Citizen Health.
scored.ladder: Possible path: registry rights, then natural-history and real-world-evidence datasets, then a recruitment and site network, then a rare-disease CRO, then in-licensing or developing therapies yourself (a cohort-first biotech). Each step up needs very different capabilities, and the step from cohort owner to drug developer adds a lot of clinical risk. A ladder exists, but this first rung does not generate the outsized returns needed to fund the climb.
scored.fatal_flaw: There is no physical proving event that creates a 10^3x step-up, and the signal (a sponsor entering the indication) is already legible in FDA orphan designations and ClinicalTrials.gov. What is left is a modest-margin, relationship-heavy data and recruitment service sold to sponsors, under consent rules that prevent truly owning the asset. That is close to the excluded "sell a service to incumbents" pattern.
scored.one_line_reason: Weak fit: the step-up is about 10x at best, the outcome is mostly visible in public FDA and trial records, the physical consent and recruitment work dominates, and foundations are savvy sellers who cannot grant real ownership.

scored.name: CRL Salvage: drugs rejected only on fixable CMC or inspection grounds
scored.one_line: Mine newly published FDA CRLs, 483s and bankruptcy dockets for drugs rejected only for fixable CMC/facility reasons; buy cheaply; fix via a CDMO and resubmit; sell approved NDA.
scored.unproven_right: Abandoned CRL'd NDA/BLA with IP and dossier, $0.5-5M.
scored.proving_step: ML classification of CRL text; Class 2 resubmission with new site ($5-20M, 6-month clock).
scored.proven_buyer: Jazz, Harmony, Amneal, Supernus, Pharming, Royalty Pharma, HCR ($50-500M).
scored.public_data: openFDA CRL database (2025+), 483/warning letters, Drugs@FDA, PACER/Epiq/Kroll, 8-Ks, AdCom docs.
scored.frame: Rung: own a CRL'd NDA/BLA and get it approved. Discovery (picking which CRL is CMC-only and buyable) is roughly 20-30% of the work by my estimate. The rest is physical and regulatory: moving manufacturing to a new CDMO, PPQ/validation batches, 6-12+ months of stability data, a pre-approval inspection, and the Class 2 resubmission (FDA's goal is a 6-month review, but the work before it usually takes 12-24 months). This is the coal-mine geothermal case again: the fix is bespoke and expensive, not trivial or abstracted. A capitalised buyer does exist (specialty pharma, royalty funds).
scored.step_up: Estimate, not sourced (no search budget left): an abandoned CRL asset in a 363 bankruptcy sale or from a wind-down typically goes for low single-digit $M (the candidate's $0.5-5M range is plausible). An approved specialty or orphan NDA sells to specialty pharma or royalty buyers for $50-500M, depending on sales. That is about 10-100x on purchase price. After adding the $5-20M+ fix cost, the multiple on total invested is about 5-30x, and it arrives only on approval, not immediately on a single cheap test.
scored.hit_rate_capex: From memory, not verified this turn: FDA's own analysis of CRLs from 2008-2013 (Lurie et al., BMJ 2015) found about half cited manufacturing/facility issues, and resubmissions that only had to fix quality problems were approved at high rates. My estimate is that well-chosen CMC-only resubmissions succeed about 60-80% of the time. So the proving step does not mostly fail. The low hit rate (~10-15% of CRLs are fixable and buyable) is in screening, which is cheap desk work. The lever is capped near 1/0.7, about 1.4x, on the expensive step. Cost per proving attempt is about $5-20M (candidate's figure, consistent with my CDMO tech-transfer estimates).
scored.data: This fails the "outcome already legible" test. Since July 2025 FDA publishes CRLs (openFDA, then near real-time), and the CRL is a plain-language letter that lists the deficiencies by category (CMC, facility, clinical). A competent reader or a basic LLM pass gets the classification. ML adds little beyond what is written in the letter. 483s and warning letters are also public and readable. The real hidden information (whether efficacy concerns were redacted out, how bad the data integrity problems are, whether the API supplier is viable) is in the confidential dossier, not public data.
scored.right_bought: Yes, the right is bought, not free first-come. It comes through bankruptcy 363 auctions (Epiq/Kroll dockets), wind-downs and licensing from cash-strapped biotechs, and some sellers will sell cheaply. But sellers do read their own CRL (they hold the full dossier, so they know more than any outside reader). Auctions are competitive, and specialist distressed-asset buyers bid, which pushes prices up.
scored.buyer: Specialty pharma (Jazz, Harmony, Amneal, Supernus, Pharming) and royalty or structured-finance buyers (Royalty Pharma, HCR, XOMA) pay $50-500M for approved, launch-ready orphan or specialty NDAs (estimate). Competitors already doing distressed-asset acquisition: Concentra Biosciences (Tang Capital), XOMA Royalty, Eagle Pharmaceuticals-style 505(b)(2) shops and specialty-pharma business development teams.
scored.ladder: The ladder is real: rescue approval, then commercial launch, then owning a specialty-pharma portfolio, then in-house CMC/manufacturing, then a roll-up into a mid-cap pharma. But it is crowded and capital-heavy, and the first rung already needs $5-20M+ and 1-2 years per asset.
scored.fatal_flaw: The regulator writes the answer: published CRLs state the deficiency category in plain text, so discovery is not illegible and ML adds almost nothing. And the proving step (CDMO tech transfer, validation, stability, inspection) is the expensive bespoke physical work, not discovery. The cost sits in the fix, not the find.
scored.one_line_reason: This is a variant of the already-weak stranded-drug-rescue idea. CRL text is now public and legible, the expensive step is manufacturing remediation that already succeeds at a high rate (so the ML lever is about 1.4x), and the step-up is about 10-100x, gated behind 12-24 months and $5-20M per asset.
