scored.name: Shortline Rx / Dormant ANDA Revival: approved generics bought ahead of shortages
scored.one_line: Buy discontinued or never-launched ANDAs for $10k-500k from generic makers; ML on 483s, warning letters, import alerts, DMF status and sole-source maps predicts shortages 6-18 months out (or targets current shortage molecules); revive via CDMO site transfer and PAS, or sell the ANDA when the shortage hits.
scored.unproven_right: Approved but discontinued/unlaunched ANDA (37% of approved generics never launch).
scored.proving_step: Forecast upstream event and confirm active API DMF; site transfer plus prior-approval supplement ($1-3M) by company or buyer.
scored.proven_buyer: Hikma, Fresenius, Amneal, Zydus, Eugia, Gland, Civica Rx, Vizient, Premier, 503B outsourcers.
scored.public_data: Orange Book discontinued section, FDA/ASHP shortage lists, 483 and warning-letter FOIA room, import alerts, DMF list, GDUFA fee lists, Medicaid SDUD, NDC/SPL.
scored.frame: The rung is a dormant or never-launched ANDA, proven by a revival through a site transfer and a prior-approval supplement. Discovery (picking which molecule will go short and confirming a live API DMF) is about 10-20% of the work in that rung (my estimate). The other 80-90% is physical and regulatory work that is not trivial: finding scarce sterile CDMO capacity, tech transfer, exhibit batches, 3-6 months of stability data, a PAS review of about 6-10 months, and a facility that passes inspection. This is the coal-mine-geothermal pattern again, where building the thing is harder than finding it. A smaller rung exists where you buy the ANDA and flip it unchanged during a shortage, so discovery is close to 100% there. But buyers mostly pay for capacity and speed to supply, not for the paper, so the step-up in that rung is small.
scored.step_up: Estimates, not verified: the web search budget ran out before any search returned. A dormant ANDA sells for roughly $10k-500k (the candidate's own figure, consistent with broker deals I know of). A revived, marketed ANDA for a shortage molecule might sell for or earn $1-10M. That is about 5-50x in typical cases. About 100x or more is possible only for deep sterile-injectable shortages, and those spikes are temporary, since competitors return within 1-3 years. Research I recall (not re-checked) found shortage price rises in the tens of percent on average, with rare grey-market cases at 10-80x. Most shortage volume is sold under GPO contracts (Vizient, Premier), which cap price. Score 2.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Estimates, not verified. A proving attempt costs about $1-3M plus 12-24 months: exhibit batches, stability, PAS and API qualification (candidate's figure; I would put it at up to $5M for sterile products). The hit rate at the forecasting stage is moderate rather than very low. Shortages are persistent and clustered: about 100-300 active shortages a year, concentrated in sterile injectables, so a simple rule like 'sole-source injectable plus a recent warning letter or import alert at the maker' probably already catches a large share. The cost of a failed attempt comes mainly from execution (CDMO, inspection, API supply), and ML forecasting does not touch that. Best case the lever is about 2-3x, nowhere near 10x.
scored.data: Mixed. Several key fields are already public and easy to read. The Orange Book discontinued section shows which ANDAs are dormant. The FDA and ASHP shortage lists state the outcome (a shortage) directly in a status field, the pattern that killed the edge in earlier hunts. The DMF list carries an active or inactive status. The genuinely hard-to-read sources are 483s and warning letters (PDFs and FOIA) plus import alerts. The rights can be bought from generic makers that are pruning portfolios. But the sellers are sophisticated (Teva, Viatris, Sandoz), know what their ANDAs are worth, and use brokers, so the discount for the buyer's information edge is thin. Shortage forecasting is already done by Vizient, Premier, the ASPE/FDA models and the USP Medicine Supply Map. Score 2.
scored.right_bought: Discontinued or unlaunched ANDAs, bought for about $10k-500k (estimate) from generic makers trimming portfolios, through ANDA brokers or direct deals. This is a negotiated purchase, not a free first-come filing. The sellers are large and informed. One caveat: if a product has gone short, the seller can relaunch it themselves or ask a higher price.
scored.buyer: Generic and sterile-injectable makers: Hikma, Fresenius Kabi, Amneal, Zydus, Eugia, Gland, ANI. Also Civica Rx, the GPOs Vizient and Premier (which buy supply contracts, not ANDAs), and 503B outsourcers, which compound shortage drugs without needing an ANDA and so compete with this model. Capitalised buyers exist, but they mostly buy finished supply or capacity, not paper rights.
scored.ladder: The chain has real rungs above the first one: own the dormant ANDA, then a CDMO-supplied relaunch, then owned sterile fill-finish, then API backward integration, then a broad generic portfolio or a 'resilient supply' platform. The trouble is that this ladder already exists as an industry. ANI Pharmaceuticals (which acquired Novitium Pharma, whose model was reviving discontinued ANDAs, in 2021, if I recall correctly), Civica, Phlow and Exela have all climbed it. Generics margins are thin, so the endpoint is a mid-cap generics company, not a trillion-dollar one. Score 3.
scored.fatal_flaw: The proving step is execution, not discovery. Turning a dormant ANDA into supply needs scarce sterile CDMO capacity, tech transfer, stability data and PAS approval (about $1-5M and 12-24 months), and ML does not shrink any of that. The shortage signal is also already written into the public FDA and ASHP shortage lists. Incumbents such as ANI/Novitium already run the dormant-ANDA revival play. So no rung exists where discovery is 80%+ of the work.
scored.one_line_reason: A real business model, already run by ANI/Novitium. Value is created by manufacturing and regulatory work, not discovery, step-ups are about 5-50x and temporary, and the shortage outcome is already in public lists, so it fails the Terranox frame.
sources: No web searches completed: the shared per-turn search budget (200 calls) ran out before my first query, so every number here is an estimate from prior knowledge and is flagged as such
Candidate brief (37% of approved generics never launch; $10k-500k ANDA prices; $1-3M PAS/site transfer)
Prior knowledge, not re-checked: ANI Pharmaceuticals' 2021 acquisition of Novitium Pharma (business built on acquiring and relaunching discontinued ANDAs)
Prior knowledge, not re-checked: FDA Drug Shortage Database and ASHP shortage list (public outcome/status fields)
Prior knowledge, not re-checked: USP Medicine Supply Map; Vizient/Premier shortage forecasting programs

scored.name: Breakthrough Shelf: TTO device IP pushed to Breakthrough Designation
scored.one_line: Option unlicensed university device patents ML predicts will win Breakthrough Device Designation; file BDD; sell designated assets.
scored.unproven_right: Exclusive option, ~$5-25k.
scored.proving_step: BDD request ($30-100k, 60-day decision); grant rate ~50-60%.
scored.proven_buyer: Medtech corp dev, device VCs/NewCos.
scored.public_data: Patents, AUTM/TTO, FDA Breakthrough list and De Novo summaries, CMS TCET/NTAP, MAUDE.
scored.frame: The rung is: option a university device patent, file for Breakthrough Device Designation (BDD), sell the designated asset. Discovery (picking which patent) is only about 30-40% of the work in that rung (my estimate). FDA expects a BDD request to show a working device concept and early bench/animal or feasibility evidence that it beats current care for a life-threatening or irreversibly debilitating condition. With an unlicensed TTO patent, that usually means building a prototype and generating bench data first, so the physical step is real, bespoke engineering. This is the geothermal-in-coal-mines counter-example again: the build is harder than the find. A capitalised buyer exists (medtech corp dev, device VCs), but nobody has a standard price for "patent plus BDD, no clinical data".
scored.step_up: Unproven: exclusive option about $5-25k (the candidate's figure; consistent with typical TTO option fees of roughly $5-50k, my estimate). Proven: no public price for a BDD-only asset, since acquirers price on clinical data, 510(k)/De Novo/PMA clearance and reimbursement. My estimate is that a designated, preclinical, single-patent asset licenses or sells for about $0.1-1M, sometimes more if TCET/NTAP reimbursement looks likely. Against the full cost basis (option + prototype + BDD request, about $100-500k), that is about 1-5x on capital. Against the option fee alone it is 10-100x. Both are far below the 10^4 jump in Terranox. Not verified: the web search budget ran out before I could pull deal comps.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Base hit rate: FDA's Breakthrough Devices Program statistics show about 55-60% of decided requests granted, and more than 1,000 designations through 2024 (from memory of FDA's public program stats page; I could not re-check this session). The ML lever is capped at 1/0.55, about 1.8x, so the required ~10x cut in discovery capex is impossible. Cost per attempt: the request itself is cheap, about $30-100k in regulatory consulting with a 60-day decision (candidate's figure, plausible). The real cost is the prototype and bench evidence: about $100k-1M+ per device (my estimate).
scored.data: Inputs are partly illegible: patents are legible, TTO tech listings are scattered and unstructured, and MAUDE and De Novo decision summaries are long-form PDFs. FDA's public Breakthrough list covers only devices that later received marketing authorisation. Designation status itself is confidential unless the sponsor discloses it, so the outcome is not already sitting in a legible field. That is a point in the candidate's favour. Against it: what decides BDD (unmet need, clinical significance, the 'more effective' standard) is largely a clinical-judgment question that experienced regulatory consultants already handle well. The ML edge over that expert baseline is unproven.
scored.right_bought: Yes. Exclusive options and licenses on university patents can be bought cheaply from TTOs, which are motivated sellers with large unlicensed backlogs (AUTM data suggests most university patents are never licensed). The catch: TTOs may want diligence milestones, and inventors are often needed to build the prototype, so the right is cheap but needs co-operation.
scored.buyer: Medtech strategics (Medtronic, BD, Boston Scientific, Stryker corp dev), device-focused VCs and NewCo builders. They pay little for BDD alone; real valuation step-ups come from first-in-human data and clearance.
scored.ladder: The ladder has many rungs: option, then BDD, then feasibility study, then pivotal trial, then De Novo/PMA, then TCET/NTAP reimbursement, then commercialisation, then a platform medtech company. In principle the climb is large (multi-billion medtech outcomes), but every rung above BDD is capital-heavy and clinical. Discovery is a small share of the work on all of them.
scored.fatal_flaw: Breakthrough Device Designation is granted about 55-60% of the time and is not the main value event. That caps the ML hit-rate lever at under 2x, and buyers pay little for designation without clinical data. Before even applying you must build a prototype and generate bench data, so the physical step dominates and the rung is not 80%+ discovery.
scored.one_line_reason: The base hit rate is already about 55-60% (lever under 2x), designation alone does not produce a large step-up in what buyers will pay, and the prototype work needed before filing makes this a build business, not a discovery business.
sources: FDA Breakthrough Devices Program statistics page, https://www.fda.gov/medical-devices/how-study-and-market-your-device/breakthrough-devices-program (cumulative grant/deny counts; cited from memory, not re-verified this session because the web search budget was exhausted)
FDA guidance 'Breakthrough Devices Program' (2018, updated 2023): eligibility criteria and the 60-day decision timeline
AUTM Licensing Activity Survey: university option/license volumes and typical option fees (from memory)
Estimates marked as such in step_up and hit_rate_capex are the author's, not sourced; both web searches attempted returned 'budget used up'

scored.name: Orphan Data Comp: FIFRA data-compensation rights from defunct registrants
scored.one_line: Buy FIFRA 3(c)(1)(F) compensation rights to pesticide studies from dissolved or bankrupt registrants; ML links MRIDs to follow-on registrations that relied on them; arbitrate and collect.
scored.unproven_right: Study ownership and 15-year compensation entitlement, $5-20k.
scored.proving_step: ML/OCR over jackets, DCI responses, data matrices and REDs; demand and FMCS arbitration.
scored.proven_buyer: Generic registrants (Albaugh, UPL, Sharda, Tide) facing cancellation; claims funds.
scored.public_data: EPA PPLS, OPP dockets, RED/IRED bibliographies, FOIA jackets, dissolution records, PACER.
scored.rough_step_up: ~100-1000x on cash outlay; capped by study cost and window.
scored.frame: The rung is buying a FIFRA 3(c)(1)(F) compensation claim and getting paid on it. Matching MRIDs to the later registrations that cited them is maybe 30-40% of the work (my estimate). Most of the work is the proving step itself: chain of title from a dissolved or bankrupt entity, a demand, then FMCS/AAA arbitration that is lawyer-heavy, expert-heavy and slow (often 1-3 years), with a valuation fight over study cost times market share. That step is the hard bespoke part, like the geothermal plant in the counter-example, not a cheap drill. There is a capitalised payer (generic registrants), but they are a counterparty forced to pay through a contested proceeding, not a buyer who wants the asset.
scored.step_up: Unproven right, per the candidate: $5-20k (not verified). Proven value, my estimate: compensation is a share of the original study cost, and FIFRA guideline studies cost about $0.1M to $10M each. A typical recovery on a compensable package might be $50k to a few $M, before arbitration fees and legal costs of roughly $100k-$1M (estimate). So the net multiple is about 10-100x on a hit, not 10^3. It is also capped by study cost, and by the 15-year compensability window counted from original submission.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Base hit rate (the share of defunct-registrant studies that are still inside the 15-year window and were relied on by a solvent follow-on registrant) is unknown. My estimate is low, under 10%, mostly because of the window. The cost of a proving attempt is mostly legal (arbitration plus experts, estimated at $100k+). ML only lowers the screening cost, which is the cheap part, so it does not cut the expensive arbitration capex 10x.
scored.data: Reliance is partly legible already. EPA keeps a Data Submitters List. Follow-on applicants file data-matrix or cite-all certifications (EPA forms 8570-34/35) and must send offer-to-pay letters, which name the MRIDs and the original submitters. So the outcome (who relied on what) is mostly written into required filings. The illegible part is mainly jackets obtained by FOIA, plus tracing who now owns the dissolved company's claims. Agchem data rights also usually move as assets in M&A and bankruptcy, so many orphans already have an heir.
scored.right_bought: Yes, in principle: buy a contract claim from a bankruptcy trustee, liquidator or former shareholders, for an estimated $5-20k. But the supply of claims that are both orphaned and still inside the window is likely thin. Dissolved registrants' data is mostly old, so the 15-year window has usually closed.
scored.buyer: Generic registrants (Albaugh, UPL, Sharda, Tide) pay under compulsion through arbitration, so they are payers, not willing buyers. Litigation and claims funds could buy proven awards at a discount.
scored.ladder: Weak to moderate. Possible next steps: data-compensation claims, then owning data packages or task-force shares, then holding generic registrations as an agchem generic registrant. That top rung is real (Albaugh-scale is plausibly $1B+ revenue, my estimate). But the first rung is legal claims buying, which does not build the regulatory or manufacturing capability the higher rungs need.
scored.fatal_flaw: The 15-year compensability window collides with the age of defunct registrants' data. Most orphaned studies are already out of the window, and those still in it usually passed to an acquirer. On top of that, the proving step is costly contested arbitration, not cheap discovery, and reliance is already listed in the data matrices and offer-to-pay letters.
scored.one_line_reason: This is a niche legal claims-buying play. The proving step is expensive arbitration, the supply is cut off by the 15-year window, and reliance is already semi-legible, so it fails the discovery-is-95% frame.
sources: No web search was possible: the shared WebSearch budget for this turn was already used up (200-call limit). Every number here is an estimate from domain knowledge, not checked against sources.
FIFRA section 3(c)(1)(F), 7 U.S.C. 136a(c)(1)(F): 10-year exclusive use, and compensation for 15 years from original submission
Thomas v. Union Carbide Agricultural Products Co., 473 U.S. 568 (1985): upheld binding arbitration for data compensation
29 CFR Part 1440: FMCS arbitration rules for FIFRA data compensation
EPA OPP Data Submitters List and forms 8570-34/8570-35 (data matrix, certification with respect to citation of data)

scored.name: Revenant Actives: EU-withdrawn crop protection actives revived as new US AIs
scored.one_line: Buy dormant dossiers for actives dropped from EU review for non-defense reasons and never US-registered; ML ranks by resistance-gap value and clean tox; efficacy and EPA gap analysis prove them; license to ag majors or file for 10-year exclusivity.
scored.unproven_right: Abandoned dossiers and know-how, $50-500k.
scored.proving_step: ML over DARs and withdrawal decisions; greenhouse/small-plot efficacy ($50-200k) plus EPA pre-submission gap analysis.
scored.proven_buyer: Bayer, Syngenta, Corteva, BASF, FMC, UPL, AMVAC ($10-100M+).
scored.public_data: EU Pesticides Database, Official Journal decisions, EFSA DARs, HRAC/herbicide-resistance database, expired patents, EPA new-AI list.
scored.frame: The proposed rung is to buy a dossier, rank it with ML, run greenhouse or small-plot efficacy work and an EPA gap analysis, then sell or license the package. Discovery is maybe 40-50% of the work in that rung (my estimate). It is not 80%+, because the step that actually turns a dossier into a sellable US asset is not trivial: a new food-use active ingredient needs a fresh GLP tox, ecotox and environmental-fate package plus EPA review. By the candidate's own figure that costs $10-30M. From memory, a new AI typically costs $20-100M+ in data and takes 2-4 years at EPA. So the physical step is about 50-150x the proving step. This is the geothermal-in-coal-mines problem: finding the right dossier is easy next to the regulatory build. A capitalised buyer exists (Bayer, Syngenta, Corteva, BASF, FMC, UPL, AMVAC). But they buy registered or near-registration assets, not an efficacy readout on an old off-patent molecule.
scored.step_up: Unproven: $50-500k per dossier (candidate's figure, not verified). After greenhouse efficacy plus a gap analysis, the asset is still unregistered and off-patent, and it is missing most of the data a US filing needs. My estimate is that an option or license on that package fetches about $0.5-3M, a 3-10x step-up. The 100-1000x figure ($10-100M+) only shows up after the $10-30M+ registration spend, so the step-up depends on capex and does not arrive immediately on a hit. For reference, AgbioInvestor/Phillips McDougall put the full cost of discovering and developing a new AI at about $300M over about 12 years (2019 study, from memory). The 10-year FIFRA exclusive-use data protection covers only the NEW data the company pays to generate, not the molecule itself.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Base hit rate: no figure found. My estimate is that 10-30% of shortlisted EU-withdrawn actives would show useful efficacy against resistant weeds or pests. These molecules were originally commercial products, so efficacy is often already known, which keeps the hit rate high and leaves ML little room. The ML lever is capped at 1/hit rate, so about 3-10x, and only on the cheap part ($50-200k per greenhouse or small-plot attempt). The expensive, failure-prone part is the tox and ecotox package, which ML cannot shrink 10x. The 1-in-160,000 screening rate for new chemistry (Phillips McDougall, from memory) applies to novel discovery, not to reviving known actives.
scored.data: The data is public and fairly legible: the EU Pesticides Database has a status field (approved / not approved / withdrawn), Official Journal implementing regulations state reasons for non-renewal, EFSA conclusions are published as structured PDFs, the HRAC/IRAC resistance databases are searchable, and the EPA AI lists are online. The outcome (why it was withdrawn, and whether there was a hazard cut-off such as CMR/ED/PBT) is largely written into the regulatory decision, which is the same failure seen in earlier hunts. Most non-defence withdrawals (the 2008-09 91/414 review wave, where hundreds of substances lapsed for non-support) were old, low-margin generics, and many are already US-registered.
scored.right_bought: Weak. The dossier owners are mostly the ag majors and big generic houses that originally developed these molecules. They can read their own DARs better than anyone and chose to drop them, so there is no information asymmetry to buy against. The molecules are off-patent and the EU data protection has expired, so any party can generate new data. The thing bought is non-exclusive raw data and know-how, not a scarce right, and a competitor can pursue the same AI. EPA exclusive use attaches only to new data.
scored.buyer: Ag majors (Bayer, Syngenta, Corteva, BASF, FMC) and specialist old-chemistry revivers such as AMVAC, Gowan and UPL. These companies already run this exact play, picking up and supporting old actives, with in-house regulatory teams. They are both the buyer and the incumbent competitor, and they buy registrations, not efficacy readouts.
scored.ladder: Real ladder: dossier, then efficacy, then the GLP tox/ecotox package, then EPA registration, then formulation and manufacturing via generic tolling, then distribution, then becoming an integrated crop protection company. Climbing it is plausible, as the AMVAC/UPL models show, but it is capex-heavy and slow (2-4 years per registration). The end state is a mid-cap specialty agchem company (AMVAC is roughly $0.5-1B revenue, from memory), not a trillion-dollar path.
scored.fatal_flaw: The value step-up needs the $10-30M+ regulatory data package, not the discovery step, so discovery is a small share of every sellable rung. On top of that, the dossier owners are the sophisticated originators, who already know the data and why they dropped the molecule, so there is no cheap illegible right to buy.
scored.one_line_reason: Finding the right withdrawn active is cheap and easy next to the $10-30M+ US registration spend that creates the value, and the sellers are the people who wrote the data.
sources: No web searches ran: the shared 200-search budget for this turn was already used up. All figures are from memory and must be checked before use.

AgbioInvestor / Phillips McDougall, 'The Cost of New Agrochemical Product Discovery, Development and Registration' (2016/2019 editions): about $286-301M and 11-12 years per new AI; about 1 in 160,000 compounds screened becomes a product (from memory)
FIFRA section 3(c)(1)(F): 10-year exclusive use protection for data supporting a new AI (from memory)
PRIA 5 fee schedule: new food-use AI registration fee about $0.8-1M (from memory)
EU Pesticides Database (ec.europa.eu/food/plant/pesticides/eu-pesticides-database): structured approval status field
Directive 91/414 review outcome: about 67% of roughly 1,000 substances removed, mostly through non-support (Commission figures, from memory)

scored.name: VoucherWorks / VoucherForge: foreign-approved tropical-disease drugs turned into US PRVs
scored.one_line: Buy US rights cheaply to drugs approved abroad (or well studied) for diseases on the FDA tropical-disease PRV list but never approved by FDA. ML reads foreign dossiers to find candidates that can reach an NDA with little new work. Approval yields a transferable voucher (~$100-210M) that big pharma buys at once.
scored.unproven_right: Exclusive US regulatory and commercial rights plus the dossier, licensed for $0.2-2M from foreign generic makers, NGOs, institutes or academics who see no US value.
scored.proving_step: 505(b)(2)/NDA built on foreign clinical, CMC and literature data, possibly with a small bridging or PK study; about $5-25M over 2-4 years. ML triages eligibility traps (active ingredient never approved in the US, data adequacy, refuse-to-file risk).
scored.proven_buyer: Large pharma PRV buyers (Gilead, AbbVie, Novartis, Sanofi, Novo); global-health funders and specialty pharma for the product.
scored.public_data: FDA tropical PRV list, Drugs@FDA/Orange Book, WHO Prequalification and EML, CDSCO/ANVISA/NMPA/PMDA review reports (often scanned, non-English), WHO TDR/DNDi/MSF archives, ClinicalTrials.gov and WHO ICTRP.
scored.rough_step_up: ~100x on the right; ~10x on all-in capex. Small universe and several pairs already taken (miltefosine, benznidazole, moxidectin, fexinidazole).
scored.frame: The rung is "hold US rights to a tropical-disease drug, get it approved, collect the PRV". Finding the candidate (discovery) is maybe 10-20% of the work inside that rung (my estimate). Since FDARA 2017, the application must include new clinical investigations essential to approval, conducted or sponsored by the applicant. So the physical step is a real trial plus a full NDA with CMC and inspections, which is neither trivial nor abstracted. This is the coal-mine-geothermal pattern: finding the drug is easy, and building the approval package is the hard part.
scored.step_up: Unproven right: $0.2-2M (the candidate's figure; I found no market data). Proven: voucher sales of $103M (Valneva, 2024), $150-160M (Zevra, Abeona, Bavarian Nordic, 2025), with historical tropical vouchers at $125M (Impavido, 2014) and $290M (Vaxchora, 2016). That is roughly 50-500x on the right. But all-in proving cost is $15-40M (my estimate, because a new essential trial is now mandatory), so the step-up on deployed capital is about 4-10x. Score 3.
scored.hit_rate_capex: I found no published hit rate for this. For a drug already approved abroad with good efficacy data, I estimate the base success rate of the NDA/trial at 30-60%, so the ML lever is capped at about 2-3x, not 10x. Cost per attempt: $5-25M (candidate's figure); I estimate $15-40M with a new essential trial and the time it takes. The expensive failures come from trial cost and CMC/inspections, which ML does not cut. Only about 10 tropical vouchers were awarded from 2009 to 2019 (PMC table).
scored.data: The main eligibility test is whether the active ingredient (including any salt or ester) was ever approved under 505(b)(1). That answer sits in a legible field (Drugs@FDA/Orange Book). The disease list is a public FDA list. Foreign approvals sit in the WHO EML, WHO Prequalification and the regulators' own registers, which are mostly legible. The most dangerous trap is legal, not hidden in the data: trial reports submitted for approval in India, Brazil, Thailand or any PIC/S country before 27 Sep 2007 are barred, and new sponsor-run trials are required. So the old foreign dossiers that ML would read are largely unusable as the basis for a voucher. The edge from reading scanned foreign review reports is small.
scored.right_bought: In principle the rights can be licensed from foreign generic makers or institutes. In practice the holders are the NGOs and pharma players who know exactly what a PRV is worth: DNDi, WHO TDR, MDGH, Novartis, Sanofi, Bavarian Nordic and Valneva. After about 15 years of publicity and $100M+ sale headlines, owners who "see no US value" are rare. Expect revenue-share demands on the voucher, not a $0.2-2M flat fee.
scored.buyer: Strong and capitalised. Large pharma (Novo, Gilead, AbbVie and others) pays $100-160M+ in cash for a voucher right away. This is the best part of the thesis.
scored.ladder: Weak. Rungs above the voucher are LMIC global-health product supply (low margin, funder-driven) and becoming a specialty pharma company. Tropical PRVs come in single digits per year at most, and the disease list is short (about 25 diseases), so this does not compound into a very large company. The plausible upside is an MDGH-style nonprofit or a small specialty pharma.
scored.fatal_flaw: FDARA 2017 requires new clinical investigations essential to approval, sponsored by the applicant, and bars trial data submitted in India, Brazil, Thailand or PIC/S countries before 2007. That kills the core idea of "foreign dossier plus a little new work". The proving step becomes a real trial whose cost and risk ML does not reduce, and it sits in a small, well-mined universe that MDGH, DNDi and big pharma already work.
scored.one_line_reason: The buyer and the payout are real ($100-160M vouchers), but the law now requires a new sponsor-run trial. That makes this regulatory and clinical execution, not discovery, in a tiny universe with legible data that informed players already work.

scored.name: Ex-US Rare Pediatric Drug to US PRV Arbitrage
scored.one_line: Buy US rights to drugs approved in the EU, Japan, China or India for rare pediatric diseases from foreign holders with no US plan; on approval win a rare pediatric PRV (~$180-210M) plus the US franchise.
scored.unproven_right: US/North American commercial rights to a foreign-approved orphan pediatric product, often $1-5M upfront.
scored.proving_step: Parse EPARs, PMDA and NMPA reviews against Orange/Purple Book to find US NCEs with rare pediatric indications; then a bridging study plus NDA ($10-40M), which is not trivial.
scored.proven_buyer: PRV buyers (AbbVie, Novartis, Sanofi) and US rare-disease acquirers.
scored.public_data: EMA EPARs and orphan register, PMDA review reports, FDA Orange/Purple Book, FDA orphan database, ClinicalTrials.gov, PRV sale prices in press releases and 8-Ks.
scored.rough_step_up: ~40-200x on the rights purchase; ~5-20x all-in. Discovery is ~50-60% of the work.
scored.frame: The rung is: hold US rights to a foreign-approved rare pediatric drug and take it to FDA approval, which earns a PRV. Discovery inside that rung is maybe 5-15% of the work (my estimate). Finding a candidate is a join of the EMA/PMDA approved and orphan lists against Drugs@FDA/Orange Book, which a data team can do in a week. The other 85%+ is the physical step: a bridging or pediatric study, CMC tech transfer, US manufacturing, a pre-NDA meeting, the NDA itself ($10-40M, my estimate; the candidate itself says this is 'not trivial') and 2-4 years. This fails the same way the geothermal-in-coal-mines example does: the bespoke build is the hard part, not the find. There is a capitalised buyer, since PRVs are liquid.
scored.step_up: Unproven right: US rights to a foreign-approved orphan drug at roughly $1-5M upfront plus milestones and royalties (the candidate's figure and my estimate; no public comparable found). Proven right: a rare pediatric PRV sells for $150-205M. Recent sales: Zevra $150M (net $148.3M, Apr 2025), Abeona $155M, Bavarian Nordic $160M (tropical-disease voucher), Rocket $180M (Jun 2026), Jazz $200M (Jan 2026), Ultragenyx $203M. On top of that comes the US franchise. On the rights alone that is about 40-200x. All-in, with $10-40M of proving cost plus a 2-4 year carry, it is about 4-15x, and that is the number that counts.
scored.hit_rate_capex: I found no public base hit rate. My estimate: once a drug already has EMA/PMDA approval with clinical efficacy data, FDA approval odds are high (about 50-80%), because the hard scientific risk is already gone. That caps the ML lever at roughly 1.3-2x, not 10x. The cost per proving attempt is $10-40M (my estimate) plus 2-4 years, and ML does not reduce it, because it is clinical and regulatory spend, not search spend. The real failure modes are that the drug does not qualify (FDA has previously approved the active moiety, or the disease does not meet the RPD definition of serious or life-threatening with most patients under 18) or that FDA demands a new adequate and well-controlled trial. Both can be checked cheaply by hand.
scored.data: The data is public and mostly legible. The EMA orphan register and the union register of EU-authorised medicines are structured, with fields for approval status, orphan status and indication. The 'is it a US NCE' test is a structured lookup in Drugs@FDA/Orange Book. PMDA and NMPA reviews are less legible (Japanese and Chinese PDFs), which is the only real illegibility edge, and the candidate pool is small: studies show only tens of EU-only orphan approvals in total (e.g. 1264 EU designations and 133 approvals as of 2016). The outcome (approved abroad, not approved in the US) is effectively already a legible field. The price signal (PRV $150-200M) is in press releases that every foreign holder reads, so owners are not ignorant of the value.
scored.right_bought: Yes, rights are bought by licence from foreign holders, not claimed first-come. But the sellers are sophisticated pharma companies (Japanese and EU mid-caps, Chinese biotechs) who know what PRVs sell for. They price in the voucher through milestones and PRV-sharing clauses, so a $1-5M upfront that captures most of the voucher is unlikely (my estimate). Incumbents already run this playbook: Eton Pharmaceuticals (in-licenses ex-US rare pediatric products), Zevra (arimoclomol, from Orphazyme's assets; PRV sold for $150M), Leadiant, Recordati Rare, Chiesi Global Rare, Medunik, and BD teams at every rare-disease company.
scored.buyer: PRV buyers are large pharma (often undisclosed; historically AbbVie, Novartis, Sanofi, Gilead, Merck), and the PRV market is liquid at $150-205M. US rare-disease acquirers (Recordati, Chiesi, Jazz, Ipsen) would buy the franchise.
scored.ladder: There are rungs above: US commercial franchise, then a multi-asset rare-disease platform, then your own R&D. It is a credible path to a $1-10B rare-disease company like Recordati or Eton at scale. It is not a trillion-dollar ladder, and the PRV rung is policy-dependent: the Give Kids a Chance Act (P.L. 119-75, Feb 3 2026) only reauthorized the program through Sept 30, 2029. That is about 3 years, barely enough for one bridging study plus NDA cycle per asset.
scored.fatal_flaw: Discovery is not the bottleneck. The candidate set is a small, legible join of the EMA/PMDA approval registers against the Orange Book, and established players already work it (Eton, Zevra, Leadiant, Recordati). 85%+ of cost and risk sits in the bespoke clinical, CMC and NDA step ($10-40M, 2-4 years). That is the geothermal-in-coal-mines failure mode, made worse by a PRV program that sunsets in Sept 2029.
scored.one_line_reason: The PRV price is real and liquid ($150-205M in 2025-26), but finding candidates is an easy, legible join that incumbents already do, and the expensive slow work is regulatory and clinical, where ML gives no leverage.

scored.name: Hidden Sire: genomic elite-animal hunting in untested herds
scored.one_line: Buy calves, heifers or rams from herds and breeds outside genomic programmes (beef, Nelore/Brahman, goats, sheep, alpaca); ML on pedigrees and performance picks herds and dams; a $40 genomic test proves outliers for AI studs.
scored.unproven_right: Ownership of untested animals at commercial prices.
scored.proving_step: Tissue punch to Neogen/Zoetis ($30-50) and genomic breeding values in weeks; top 0.1-1% qualify.
scored.proven_buyer: Genus ABS, Select Sires, ST Genetics, Semex, CRV, Alta, Brazilian CRI, seedstock operators.
scored.public_data: Breed association EPD/pedigree databases, CDCB/Interbull, DHI records, auction catalogues, USDA MARC reports.
scored.rough_step_up: $1.5-3k calf to $100k-1M stud bull, 10^2-10^3x; edge only in under-tested breeds and countries.
scored.frame: The rung is: own a young animal and prove it genetically elite. Inside that rung, finding the animal is most of the work (my estimate is 70-85%), and the $30-50 tissue test is trivial. But the rung only becomes sellable to an AI stud after things that are not discovery. The animal must be registered, its parentage verified, and it must be phenotyped, semen-collected, health-tested, and marketed so breeders actually use it. In beef, an AI stud's money comes from people taking up the semen, and that is a marketing and proof-over-time problem. A test score alone does not deliver it. So the frame partly exists, but its buyer mostly buys from known seedstock programmes, not from untested commercial herds.
scored.step_up: Unproven: a commercial calf or heifer at $1.5-3k (the candidate's figure, roughly consistent with US feeder and weaned calf prices). Proven, typical case: a genomically documented seedstock bull sells for about 2-7x that. Nelore CEIP (certified superior) bulls averaged about R$10.5k (roughly $2k) at CFM's 346-bull virtual auction (comprerural). Australian Angus stud sales average $5.5-14k AUD (Stock Journal, Countryman). Proven, tail case: record bulls reach $44k-$275k AUD (The Land, 2025), and the rare bull bought by an AI stud reaches $100k-1M. That tail is maybe 1 in 1,000 or fewer of tested animals, and it depends on market uptake, not just the test. The expected step-up on a hit is about 3-10x. 10^2-10^3 is the rare outlier.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Base hit rate: the top 0.1-1% qualify, by the candidate's definition (1 in 100 to 1 in 1,000 at random). Cost per attempt: a $30-50 test (Neogen/Zoetis) plus buying the calf. Most of the calf's cost comes back as feeder or slaughter value, so the net cost per failed shot is only about $50-300 (my estimate). Proving is cheap and failure is cheap, so there is little capex for ML to cut by 10x. Pedigree-based pre-screening could at best raise hits about 5-20x, and the cheap test already makes testing everything rational. That is why 75% of 309,926 registered Angus calves were already genotyped in FY2025 (angus.org).
scored.data: This fails the legibility test. In the breeds where genomics proves value (Angus, Holstein, Nelore with Geneplus/ANCP, CDCB dairy), the answer is already written into public, legible EPD and GEBV fields. 75% of registered Angus calves are genotyped, so there is no illegible signal for ML to exploit. Owners can read EPDs, so there is no cheap mispriced purchase. In the under-tested breeds and countries (goats, alpaca, local sheep, unregistered commercial herds), the reference populations are small or absent. Prediction accuracy can be as low as 2-31% in goats until references reach 1,500-2,000 animals (preprints.org 202405.0592; Frontiers 2024). In those breeds the $40 test does not prove anything a buyer will pay for. The data is also not scanned or unstructured: auction catalogues and DHI records are already structured.
scored.right_bought: Yes, animals can be bought at commercial prices from owners, with no first-come filing. But the cheaply bought animals (unregistered, commercial, untested breeds) are mostly ineligible for an AI stud, or cannot be credibly proven. The eligible ones (registered and genotyped) are already priced on their EPDs. Testing before buying needs the owner's consent, and then the owner learns the result.
scored.buyer: Genus ABS (about $2B market cap), Select Sires, ST Genetics, Semex, CRV, Alta, CRI Genetica in Brazil, and seedstock operators. They are well capitalised, but they source young sires through their own contract-mating and genomic-screening programmes on elite females. They rarely buy from unknown herds.
scored.ladder: The rungs above: contract matings and elite donor females (IVF/embryos), owning a semen and embryo distribution business, then a seedstock or genetics company like Genus or STgen. There is real but bounded room above. The global bovine genetics market is a few billion dollars, Genus is worth about $2B, and there is no clear trillion-dollar path. Running a whole beef chain is commodity cattle ranching with thin margins.
scored.fatal_flaw: Catch-22 on legibility. Where genomic proof is valuable and accepted (registered Angus, Holstein, Nelore), testing is already routine (75% of registered Angus calves genotyped) and the answer sits in public EPD fields that owners can read, so nothing is mispriced. Where herds are untested (commercial cattle, goats, alpaca, local breeds), animals are unregistered and reference populations are too small, so the $40 test proves nothing a capitalised buyer will pay 10^2x for. The hit is also cheap to find and to fail, so there is no expensive discovery step for ML to make cheaper.
scored.one_line_reason: Testing is already cheap and routine, and the results already sit in public EPD fields, so there is no illegible edge. In under-tested breeds the test cannot prove value, and the typical step-up is about 3-10x, not 10^3.

scored.name: Fall Rights / Fall Recovery: radar-tracked fresh meteorite falls
scored.one_line: ML on NEXRAD, GLM and fireball networks pinpoints fresh strewn fields; buy recovery rights from landowners (US surface owner owns meteorites) before dealers arrive; drone and ML sweeps find stones for collectors and museums.
scored.unproven_right: Exclusive recovery rights or options on private parcels in the predicted ellipse, ~$500-5k.
scored.proving_step: Radar deconvolution and dark-flight model, then thermal/RGB drone sweep with ML detection; pick stones up.
scored.proven_buyer: Meteorite dealers, Heritage, Christie's, museums and universities.
scored.public_data: NOAA NEXRAD Level II (AWS), GOES GLM, AMS fireball reports, NASA CNEOS, Meteoritical Bulletin, county parcels.
scored.frame: The rung is a recovery right on one parcel inside a fresh strewn field. Inside that rung, finding the fall is about 80% of the work, and picking up a stone is trivial. But speed and getting there first matter about as much as prediction. Drone sweeping and getting landowner permission are real work too, and buyers are thin. My estimate is that prediction is about 60% of the value and getting there fast is about 40%.
scored.step_up: Unproven right: an access or recovery agreement, usually free permission or a finder's split with the landowner. The candidate's $500-5k figure is my estimate; I found no market price. Proven: an ordinary chondrite from a fresh fall sells for about $5-50/g (my estimate). Rare types sell for much more. Aguas Zarcas (CM2) goes for about $200-300/g retail, and the total known mass is 27 kg. Winchcombe pieces sold at Christie's for about $7,400/g (1.7 g) and $2,000/g (15 g), but only 602 g was ever recovered and about 90% of it went to the UK national collection. The Maine museum offered $25k for the first 1 kg in 2023. So per parcel the value goes from about $1k to about $10k-100k, roughly 10-100x. It reaches 1000x only for rare carbonaceous or achondrite falls, which happen a few times a decade.
scored.hit_rate_capex: A museum chair estimated that only 8-10 of the hundreds of meteorite falls each year are recovered. That counts all falls, most of which are unobserved. For radar-detected US falls, my estimate is that hunters already recover something in roughly 30-60% of cases. A search costs about $5-30k per event in travel, drones and labor (my estimate). The lever is capped near 2-3x, not 10x, because NASA's radar strewn-field predictions already exist and most misses come from terrain, vegetation and stone size, not the prediction.
scored.data: NEXRAD Level II, GLM, AMS and CNEOS data are public. But the outcome is already written up in a legible public form. NASA ARES (Marc Fries) runs a radar-meteorite list that posts each radar-detected fall with a predicted strewn field and mass estimates, often within days (NASA did this for the 2023 Maine fall). The AMS also publishes fireball trajectories. Dedicated hunters (Arnold, Farmer, Hupe and others) read these posts and drive out within 24-48 hours. So the illegible-data edge is mostly gone. Rights can be bought from landowners, since the US surface owner owns the meteorites, and owners often can't value them. That part fits the rubric. But dealers already negotiate the same finder's-split deals on the spot.
scored.right_bought: Yes. US meteorites belong to the surface owner, so recovery rights or options can be negotiated parcel by parcel. These are usually cheap (permission or a 50/50 split), but every deal is bespoke and has to be done in a race against rival hunters.
scored.buyer: Meteorite dealers, Christie's/Heritage/Bonhams auctions, museums (e.g. the Maine Mineral and Gem Museum) and universities. The buyers are capitalised but thin: total market value of new US falls is probably about $1-10M a year (my estimate).
scored.ladder: Weak to none. The next rungs would be dealing, auctions, specimen preparation and sample-return-style science supply, all of them niche. There is no path from here to a large company, because supply is set by nature at a few recoverable US falls a year.
scored.fatal_flaw: The outcome is already public: NASA ARES posts radar-derived strewn fields for every detected fall, so the ML edge is mostly racing other hunters to the field. And total annual supply (a few US falls, mostly ordinary chondrites at $5-50/g) caps the market at single-digit millions with no ladder.
scored.one_line_reason: Clean physical step and surface-owner rights fit the rubric, but NASA already publishes the strewn fields, the hit-rate lever is about 2-3x, and the market is a few million dollars a year with no ladder.

scored.name: Trails Act Corridor Interim-Use Arbitrage
scored.one_line: Take assignment of interim trail manager status (with railbanked reactivation rights) from towns and nonprofits that cannot afford maintenance; ML proves continuity and width; sublicense buried transmission or fiber.
scored.unproven_right: Assignment of trail manager status under 16 USC 1247(d), often for assumed maintenance.
scored.proving_step: ML over STB NITU/CITU dockets, trail agreements and deeds; confirm underground licensing is permitted.
scored.proven_buyer: Underground HVDC developers, long-haul fiber carriers, state DOTs.
scored.public_data: STB NITU/CITU dockets, Rails-to-Trails railbanked lists, county deeds, FRA GIS.
scored.rough_step_up: ~100-1000x on cash basis; takings-claim legal risk.
scored.frame: The rung is: take the trail sponsor role on a railbanked corridor and license its subsurface to a linear-infrastructure developer. That rung is discrete in name only. Most of the work is not discovery but legal and physical. You have to get the STB to approve the sponsor substitution (49 CFR 1152.29). You take on maintenance, liability and taxes. Then you must clear, landowner by landowner, whether utility use fits inside the original easement, and do the trenching, permitting and crossings. My estimate is that discovery (finding continuity and width) is about 15-25% of the work in this frame. Continuity is mostly already known from NITU mileposts.
scored.step_up: On a cash basis, an assumed-liability right (about $0 cost, with ongoing maintenance) becomes a recurring license fee. My estimate: long-haul fiber on rail rights of way has historically licensed at roughly $1-10/ft one-time or a few $/ft/yr, about $5k-50k/mile. HVDC corridors could pay more per mile, but buyers such as SOO Green chose active Canadian Pacific rail corridors, not trails. Because the starting cost is about zero, the cash multiple looks very large. The real multiple is limited because the sponsor holds no fee or subsurface title: the underlying fee usually belongs to adjacent landowners (Brandt v. US, 2014). Unverified; search budget ran out before I could get per-mile lease figures.
scored.hit_rate_capex: There is no expensive, mostly-failing proving step. Proving a corridor is cheap desk work (dockets, deeds, GIS), my estimate a few thousand to tens of thousands of dollars per corridor. The hit rate on finding continuous railbanked corridors is high, since NITU/CITU orders already list mileposts. The binding uncertainty is legal: easement scope and takings exposure, decided by courts and not learnable from data. So ML cannot cut capex 10x, because discovery is not the cost driver.
scored.data: The data is public and partly illegible: scanned 1800s deeds and grant instruments decide whether the railroad held fee or easement, and that is real illegible signal. But the outcome that matters is legible and incumbents already watch it. STB NITU/CITU dockets record railbanked status and mileposts. Rails-to-Trails Conservancy publishes railbanked lists. Fiber carriers and state DOTs already map rail rights of way. Takings plaintiff firms (e.g. Arent Fox/Lindsay Brinkmeyer-style rails-to-trails practices) already read these deeds systematically to find fee-vs-easement claims.
scored.right_bought: The right can be had cheaply: sponsor status is often assigned for free to anyone who assumes maintenance, with STB approval. But what you get is a trail-use interest, not a utility or subsurface right. Any non-trail, non-railroad use generally exceeds the easement scope. That exposes the licensee to landowner trespass or takings claims, as in the 1990s-2000s fiber-on-railroad class actions that ended in per-mile settlements with carriers. A for-profit sponsor that sublicenses for profit may also put the railbanking rationale and NITU at risk.
scored.buyer: Long-haul fiber carriers (Zayo, Lumen) and HVDC merchant developers (SOO Green, Grid United) do pay for linear corridors. In practice they buy from active railroads or state DOTs, where title is clean, because trail corridors carry landowner claims. State DOTs mostly take corridors directly. The buyer has capital, but they avoid exactly this title risk.
scored.ladder: In principle you could aggregate corridors, then build and own the conduit or transmission, then become a linear-infrastructure utility or REIT. That is a real ladder, but each rung above is dominated by construction and permitting, not discovery. It also depends on resolving per-parcel landowner title, so it does not compound off a discovery edge.
scored.fatal_flaw: The trail sponsor does not own the subsurface or the utility right. In most corridors adjacent landowners hold the reversionary fee (Brandt 2014), and utility use beyond railroad or trail purposes is a new burden. That creates per-landowner takings and trespass liability, the same pattern as the fiber-on-railroad class action settlements. So the proving step is a legal title fight ML cannot win, not a discovery problem.
scored.one_line_reason: Taking the role is cheap, but the subsurface value belongs to reversionary landowners, discovery is a small share of the work, continuity is already legible in STB dockets, and buyers avoid trail title risk.
sources: https://mslegal.org/?p=11035 (Marvin M. Brandt Revocable Trust v. US case summary)
https://digitalcommons.lmu.edu/llr/vol48/iss2/4 (law review on Brandt: abandoned railroad easements revert to landowners, opening takings claims)
https://www.inversecondemnation.com/category/rails-to-trails/page/13 (rails-to-trails takings litigation)
Estimates (not verified; search budget exhausted): fiber-on-rail license rates of about $5k-50k/mile, SOO Green siting on CP active rail right of way, 49 CFR 1152.29 sponsor substitution

scored.name: LandingRight: permitted subsea cable landing parcels
scored.one_line: Option coastal parcels and beach-manhole easements; ML scores landing permit feasibility and marine route risk; sell permitted landings with backhaul to cable consortia.
scored.unproven_right: Option on a small coastal parcel or easement plus terrestrial backhaul route.
scored.proving_step: ML over bathymetry, AIS anchoring, fishing effort, coastal commission and Corps permit histories; landing permit.
scored.proven_buyer: Google, Meta, Microsoft, Amazon and SubCom-led consortia.
scored.public_data: NOAA NCEI multibeam, MarineCadastre AIS, FCC cable landing licences, coastal commission reports, Corps permits.
scored.frame: The rung would be "permitted, buildable landing (parcel + beach manhole/HDD easement + backhaul) sold to a cable consortium". Discovery is maybe 20-30% of the work in that rung (my estimate). The rest is physical and political. You need horizontal directional drill bores (estimate $1-5M per landing), a beach manhole, a landing station building, a backhaul build, and a 1-3+ year permitting process across FCC/Team Telecom, the Army Corps, state coastal commissions and local governments. Proving a landing means winning permits and building the shore end, not reading data. This looks like the geothermal-in-coal-mines counter-example: building the bespoke landing is harder than finding the site. No frame exists where discovery is 80%+.
scored.step_up: My estimate, not sourced (the search budget was used up before I could run any query). A coastal parcel or easement option costs roughly $50k-$2M. A permitted, open-access landing station is worth a few million to the low tens of millions, realised through landing fees, colocation and backhaul contracts. That is about 3-10x on the parcel, and maybe ~10-30x on the option premium alone. It is nowhere near 10^3-10^4. The candidate's own ~10^2x looks optimistic, and the value comes from the permit and the build, not from a discovery hit.
scored.hit_rate_capex: My estimate, not sourced (no searches were possible). The proving step is not a cheap shot that mostly fails. Cable route feasibility work is a routine consultant job: desktop study ~$50-200k, marine route survey ~$1-5M+. When a landing is pursued seriously, the base hit rate is fairly high (I'd guess 50%+); failures come from political or permit opposition, not from missing data. Lever is about 1/base hit rate, so under 2x, not 10x. ML over bathymetry and AIS anchoring data copies what route engineers (e.g. SubCom, ASN, NEC, and survey firms like Fugro) already do.
scored.data: The data is partly public but mostly legible already. NOAA NCEI multibeam and MarineCadastre AIS are structured and easy to download. FCC cable landing licences are legible public filings. Coastal commission staff reports and Corps permits are semi-structured PDFs, but the outcome (approved, denied, conditions) is written in plain text in the decision, so ML adds little. Incumbent route engineers already merge these layers in GIS. The signal is not illegible in the Terranox sense.
scored.right_bought: Coastal parcels and easements can be optioned from private owners or municipalities, so the right is bought, not first-come. But the owners are not mispricing because they can't read data. Coastal land is priced as coastal real estate, often expensive, and the binding right (beach crossing, tidelands, state submerged lands lease) belongs to the state and is granted through permits, not bought at a discount. Hyperscalers also tend to choose their own landings, often reusing existing stations or campuses.
scored.buyer: Capitalised buyers do exist: Google, Meta, Microsoft, Amazon and SubCom/ASN-led consortia. But volume is tiny (estimate: a few dozen new cables a year worldwide, roughly 3-8 US landings a year). Buyers are concentrated and choose landings based on end markets, terrestrial data centre routes and their own permitting teams. Open-access landing station developers already work in this lane; from memory (not verified this session): DC BLOX at Myrtle Beach, Globalinx and Telxius at Virginia Beach, and neutral landing stations in Europe such as Sines and Marseille.
scored.ladder: There is a real ladder above the rung: landing station, then backhaul and dark fibre, then colocation and data centre campus, then cable ownership and capacity (IRUs). This is the open-access landing station and data centre business, and it compounds. But it is a capital-heavy digital infrastructure ladder already contested by big players (Equinix, Digital Realty, DC BLOX, Telxius), and the bottom rung gives no discovery edge to climb from.
scored.fatal_flaw: Proving is permitting plus construction, not discovery. The value of a landing comes from winning coastal, Corps, FCC and Team Telecom approvals and building HDD bores, manholes and backhaul; reading data adds little. Base hit rates are not low, so ML has almost no 10x capex lever. This repeats the geothermal-in-coal-mines failure.
scored.one_line_reason: Cable landings are a permitting and construction business with few, concentrated buyers and legible data. There is no rung where discovery is 80%+, and no 10^3x step-up on a cheap hit.
sources: No web searches ran: the shared per-turn WebSearch budget (200 calls) was used up before this agent could make any query. Every number above is my own estimate, labelled as such.

Background knowledge, not checked this session: open-access landing station developers (DC BLOX Myrtle Beach; Globalinx/Telxius Virginia Beach; Start Campus Sines; Digital Realty Marseille).

scored.name: LiveMap: zombie tentative tract maps in California
scored.one_line: Buy land priced as unentitled where a tentative subdivision map believed expired is still alive via post-2008 statutory extensions, discretionary extensions and tolling; ML reconstructs map life from scanned approvals; sell entitled lots to homebuilders.
scored.unproven_right: Fee or option on parcels whose tentative/vesting map the seller and GIS treat as dead.
scored.proving_step: Documentary reconstruction of approvals, extensions (SB 1185, AB 333, AB 208, AB 116) and tolling; county confirmation or title endorsement.
scored.proven_buyer: Lennar, DR Horton, KB, Tri Pointe; Millrose/Varde land banking.
scored.public_data: County planning and supervisor minutes (Legistar/Granicus), recorded maps, Map Act extension history, CEQAnet, assessor transfers.
scored.rough_step_up: ~5-20x on land; entitlement $0 to $1-10M per map.
scored.frame: The rung is 'buy land plus a live tentative map, then sell it entitled'. Finding the map is arguably 60-80% of the work, but the physical step is not trivial. You still have to buy fee land at market raw-land prices, which in California is often $50k-$500k+ per acre (my estimate), carry it, take on stale conditions of approval and impact fees, and close a sale to a builder. Discovery is not 80%+ of capital at risk, because almost all the capital goes into the land, not the proving.
scored.step_up: I could not verify this by search (the shared web-search budget was used up). My estimate: California land with a tentative map sells for about 2-4x unentitled land, because a tentative map still needs a final map, improvement plans, bonds and current fees. The asset does not start near zero; the seller already has the land priced at raw value. The candidate's '5-20x' figure looks inflated except in rare infill cases. Realistic step-up is about 2-5x, or 10^0.5, not 10^3-10^4.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Proving means a records reconstruction plus a written confirmation from the planning department. That costs about $2k-$20k per parcel in staff, legal or title work (my estimate), so it is cheap, not an expensive drill that usually fails. Base hit rate is unknown. The candidate pool shrinks every year. The statutory extensions (SB 1185 2008 +12mo, AB 333 2009 +24mo, AB 208 2011 +24mo, AB 116 2013 +24mo, the last for maps approved after 1 Jan 2000) together add at most about 7 years, so nearly every map from the 2000-2008 era ran out by about 2016-2020. That leaves only later relief (AB 1561 2023, an 18-month extension, recalled not verified), discretionary extensions and litigation or moratorium tolling (Gov Code 66452.6). Because the cost per attempt is small next to the land price, raising the hit rate does not cut total capex 10x.
scored.data: The signal sits in public but partly illegible records: Legistar/Granicus minutes, scanned resolutions, recorded maps, and the extension statutes. But the answer usually sits in a legible field. Planning departments track tentative-map expiration dates in their permit systems (Accela, EnerGov, TRAKiT), and owners or lenders can get a definitive status by calling or writing to the planning department. That is the same 'regulator writes the answer into a status field' failure seen in earlier hunts. Who would sell? Sellers holding mapped land are usually developers, land bankers or REO lenders with land-use counsel, and they know the map's status. Unsophisticated heirs rarely hold tentative maps.
scored.right_bought: Yes, the fee or an option is bought from a private seller. But the price is market raw-land value (not $1/ha), and an option costs real carry (my estimate: 5-10% of price per year). Options usually include due diligence that would reveal the map status to the seller as well.
scored.buyer: Capitalised buyers are real and active: Lennar, D.R. Horton, KB Home, Tri Pointe, and land bankers such as Millrose (the Lennar spin-off) and Varde. They pay well for entitled lots in California and run their own entitlement and diligence teams, so they are both the buyer and the competitor.
scored.ladder: The ladder is clear: entitlement arbitrage, then land development (final map, horizontal improvements, finished lots), then vertical homebuilding, then land banking or financing. These are large markets (D.R. Horton and Lennar are worth about $40-60B each). But the bottom rung is not a discovery business, so the ladder grows a land-development firm, not an ML discovery engine.
scored.fatal_flaw: The proving step is a cheap, definitive lookup, not an expensive mostly-failing bet. Each planning department already records the tentative-map expiration date and confirms it on request. Sellers are sophisticated land holders. The pool of 'zombie' maps shrank once the 2008-2013 statutory extensions ran out (about 2016-2020). Even on a hit, already-priced raw land steps up about 2-4x, not 10^3-10^4.
scored.one_line_reason: The status of a California tentative map is a legible, county-confirmable fact held by sophisticated sellers on land already priced at market. Proving is cheap and the step-up is about 2-4x, so it lacks the Terranox mix of near-zero asset, expensive failing proving step and illegible signal.

scored.name: TapRight: dormant utility connection entitlements in moratorium districts
scored.one_line: In water/sewer-constrained districts, buy 'unbuildable' lots carrying forgotten prepaid capacity (old assessment-district EDUs, will-serve letters, legacy meters), prove the entitlement and sell buildable lots.
scored.unproven_right: Vacant lot bought at unbuildable value carrying an unrecognised connection right.
scored.proving_step: Assessment payment records, meter assignments and resolutions, then a district confirmation or will-serve.
scored.proven_buyer: Custom builders and end buyers in constrained coastal/mountain towns.
scored.public_data: Special district minutes, 1911/1913/1915 Act rolls, LAFCO reviews, meter registers (CPRA), assessor vacant rolls.
scored.frame: The rung is buying an 'unbuildable' vacant lot in a water/sewer moratorium district and proving it already holds a connection right (EDU, will-serve, legacy meter). Inside that rung, finding and documenting the right is about 85-90% of the work. The physical step is close to nothing: a records request plus a district confirmation letter. The catch is that the proof is not ours to make. A district board or general manager decides whether to issue the confirmation, so the last step is a political or administrative approval, not a measurement. Estimate: about 85% discovery, but the final gate is outside our control.
scored.step_up: Unverified: the search budget ran out before any search returned, so these are estimates from memory. Cambria CSD (California) has had a connection moratorium since about 2001 with a waitlist. Lots without water there have reportedly traded around $15-50k, and buildable lots with water roughly $250-500k, so about 10-20x. In Bolinas (BCPUD, moratorium since 1971), water meters have reportedly sold on their own for six figures, roughly $200-400k, against lots worth much less without one. The candidate's 20-50x is plausible only at the top end. My central estimate is 10-20x, which scores 3. That is nowhere near 10^3-10^4.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Estimate only, nothing sourced. The base hit rate, meaning the share of moratorium-district vacant lots that hold an unrecognised but valid prepaid entitlement, is likely well under 1-2%. A proving attempt (records requests, a title or records researcher, legal review of 1911/1913/1915 Act rolls) costs maybe $2-10k. But the cost that matters is buying the lot, often $20-50k, and here the lot is the asset bought before proving. So ML mostly saves acquisition capital on lots that turn out to have nothing. The lever looks real on paper (1/hit rate is above 50x), but the hit space is tiny and limited by the supply of lots.
scored.data: This is the fatal weakness. Districts already keep the answer in a legible ledger: meter registers and EDU/connection allocations are tied to the parcel number (APN), and anyone can get them by calling the district or filing a CPRA (California Public Records Act) request. Assessment-district payoffs show on the tax bill and title report as special assessments. In moratorium towns, whether a lot has a meter is the single most price-relevant fact, so owners, local agents and title companies routinely check it. The illegible sources (old board minutes, 1911/1913/1915 Act bond rolls) add an edge only in rare cases. And even when a prepaid assessment is found, many districts treat it as a capacity charge, not a guaranteed right to connect during a moratorium, so finding it does not prove the entitlement.
scored.right_bought: Yes, the right can be bought: vacant lots are bought from owners, often absentee heirs, at unbuildable prices. But sellers in these towns are usually well informed about meter status, and any listing agent will check with the district before pricing. The discount on lots where nobody knows about the right exists only at the thin edge of the market.
scored.buyer: Custom builders and well-off end buyers in constrained coastal and mountain towns (e.g. Cambria, Bolinas, Los Osos, parts of Marin, Montecito during its moratorium). They have money but come one at a time, and there are few of them. There is no institutional buyer like a mine developer who repeatedly buys proven assets at scale.
scored.ladder: Weak. The rungs above are building homes on the lots, then small-scale development, then perhaps owning water supply or desalination in constrained towns. The total market is a few hundred to a few thousand lots across a handful of districts, so it caps at a niche real-estate business. There is no trillion-dollar path.
scored.fatal_flaw: The outcome already sits in a legible public field. Districts record meter and EDU allocations against each parcel number, special assessments appear on tax bills and title reports, and in moratorium towns every party checks water status first. On top of that, the proving step is a discretionary approval by the district (often refused during a moratorium), and the market is tiny. That leaves no information gap for ML to exploit and no 10^3 step-up.
scored.one_line_reason: The step-up is real but modest (about 10-20x, estimated). The answer is mostly already in district meter registers and on title reports, the final proof is a district's discretionary approval, and the market is a niche of a few thousand lots with no path up a large ladder.
sources: No web sources: the shared search budget ran out before any search could run (the one search attempted returned nothing). All figures are estimates from prior knowledge and are unverified.

scored.name: By-Right Parcels: legacy zoning that already permits data centers
scored.one_line: ML over scanned zoning codes, legacy PUD ordinances and old rezoning minutes finds parcels whose forgotten entitlements permit data centers by right ahead of moratoria; option at ag prices, get a zoning verification letter, sell entitled sites.
scored.unproven_right: Options on parcels priced as ag/vacant.
scored.proving_step: Zoning verification letter or vested-rights determination ($500-20k).
scored.proven_buyer: Data-center developers facing rezoning fights; powered-land funds.
scored.public_data: Municode/American Legal ordinances, scanned PUD ordinances and minutes, county zoning GIS, assessor rolls.
scored.rough_step_up: ~10x on land, 10^2-10^3x on option premium; usually needs power too.
scored.frame: The rung is "unentitled parcel to by-right data-center parcel". Inside it, discovery (reading ordinances, PUD text and minutes) is about 85-90% of the work, and the proving step is a cheap letter. The trouble is that buyers do not purchase this rung by itself. Data-center developers buy powered, entitled land. Zoning alone is roughly 10-20% of the work in the smallest frame a capitalised buyer actually pays for, because power, fibre and water dominate it. So the 80%+ discovery frame exists, but no buyer sits at the end of it. (Estimate.)
scored.step_up: I could not verify this: the shared search budget ran out before any query ran. These are estimates from prior knowledge. Agricultural land in data-center counties sells for about $5k-15k/acre. Northern Virginia data-center land traded at about $1M-3M+/acre in 2021-2024 (Loudoun and Prince William deals). Nearly all of that premium comes from power availability and location, not zoning. Industrial-zoned parcels without power trade at about $50k-300k/acre. A zoning-only hit on an unpowered parcel is therefore plausibly 2-5x on land value (estimate). The 10^2x on option premium is leverage from the option itself, not value created.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Not verified (no searches available). From prior knowledge: a zoning verification letter costs about $50-500 in most jurisdictions. A formal zoning-administrator determination or vested-rights determination runs about $500-5k, plus legal fees of $5k-20k. That is cheap, and it is not mostly failing on screened candidates. The expensive, mostly failing step is the power study and utility queue. An interconnection or large-load study costs $50k-500k+ and takes 1-3+ years, and ML over zoning text does not move it. ML can lift the hit rate on candidate screening, but proving capex is already low, so there is no ~10x capex lever. (Estimate.)
scored.data: Mostly legible already. Zoning districts are in county GIS and assessor rolls, and permitted-use tables are on Municode and American Legal. Brokers, site selectors and landowners read these. Real illegibility is limited to scanned legacy PUD ordinances, conditional rezonings, proffers and old minutes. There, an ML edge could exist on a long tail where a vague use such as "communications facility", "utility" or "warehouse/light industrial" might cover a data center. Even then, the answer is an interpretation that a zoning administrator can reject and neighbours can appeal. Outcome legibility is high: the district code is already a field.
scored.right_bought: Yes in form: land options are bought from owners, typically for 1-5% of price per year (estimate). But the information gap is weak. Owners of rural parcels in data-center hot zones are now heavily solicited and price the possibility of a data-center sale in. Parcels that already carry industrial or PUD entitlement are priced as industrial, not agricultural. A truly agricultural-priced parcel with a hidden by-right data-center use is rare. Public moratoria and rezoning fights (for example the Prince William Digital Gateway, and moratoria in several Georgia and Virginia counties) push owners to inflate asks the moment a buyer appears.
scored.buyer: Hyperscalers and their land teams (Microsoft, Amazon, Google, Meta), data-center developers (QTS, Vantage, Stack, CyrusOne, Aligned, EdgeCore) and powered-land funds. All are well capitalised, but they buy on power first. Incumbents doing the zoning discovery already include site-selection consultants, land brokers (CBRE, JLL, Cushman), powered-land developers and zoning-data startups (Zoneomics, Gridics, Regrid zoning layers).
scored.ladder: The ladder is: entitled parcel, then powered land (utility commitment), then a shell with power delivered, then the developer or operator, then the full data-center platform. It is real and very large. But the first rung is not the gating one, and the second rung (power) is capital- and time-heavy and contested by many funded players.
scored.fatal_flaw: Zoning is not what makes data-center land valuable; power is. A parcel that permits data centers by right but has no near-term utility capacity is worth only a modest premium over agricultural or industrial land. Separately, the zoning outcome is mostly already in a legible field (the district code in GIS), so neither of the 10^3-10^4 jumps the model needs exists.
scored.one_line_reason: Discovery is cheap and the proving step is trivial, but the step-up from zoning alone is about 2-5x because power drives value, the zoning field is already legible, and buyers will not buy the zoning-only rung. This is the geothermal-in-coal-mines pattern: the hard part (power) is not the part ML finds.
sources: Not verified: the shared WebSearch budget (200 per turn) ran out before any query for this candidate ran. Every figure is an estimate from prior knowledge.
Prior knowledge: Northern Virginia data-center land deals at about $1M-3M+/acre in 2021-2024 (Loudoun and Prince William counties)
Prior knowledge: Prince William Digital Gateway rezoning litigation and county data-center moratoria (Virginia, Georgia), 2023-2025
Prior knowledge: typical municipal zoning verification letter fees of about $50-500
