scored.name: Reimburse: orphaned Texas MUD developer reimbursement claims
scored.one_line: Buy unpaid MUD developer reimbursement claims from defunct developers, trustees and estates at distressed prices; ML over scanned MUD minutes and TCEQ files finds and validates them; collect face at the next MUD bond issue.
scored.unproven_right: Unpaid reimbursement claim under a MUD financing agreement, bought at 2-10 cents.
scored.proving_step: Prove validity and amount from agreement, engineering report and audit; get included in the next bond application.
scored.proven_buyer: MUD bond issuances funded by muni investors and underwriters (Samco, RBC, Baird).
scored.public_data: TCEQ MUD bond applications, district minutes, EMMA disclosures, county assignments, PACER schedules of 2008-11 failed builders.
scored.frame: The rung is buying an unpaid MUD developer reimbursement claim and getting it paid. There is no physical step, so the work is all paper: legal and audit validation plus timing. My estimate is that discovery is only about 30-40% of that work. The rest is (a) the legal step: proving the claim is valid, that the assignment chain holds and that it has not expired or been released, (b) getting the district board to include it in a TCEQ-approved bond application, and (c) the bond issue itself. Step (c) depends on new taxable value being built in the district, which the claim holder does not control. The 'buyer' is not a buyer of the right. It is the district paying the claim from muni bond proceeds, and only once its debt-to-assessed-value ratio supports a sale. So the payout is set by real-estate absorption, not by proving the claim.
scored.step_up: Proposed purchase price is 2-10 cents, collected at par, which is 10-50x. That ratio is unverified. Searches failed (the shared web-search budget was used up), so all numbers are my estimates. Based on how the market works, a claim whose district has a live tax base and a clear path to bonds would not trade at 2-10c. It would sell for about 40-80c to the developer, the lender or the next landowner. Claims that do trade at 2-10c are cheap because the district has no tax base, the agreement has lapsed, or the claim was already assigned or released. Realistic step-up is about 2-5x on good paper, with heavy duration risk (often 5-15 years to the next bond issue). Interest accrual is capped under the agreement and TCEQ rules.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Estimate only, no sourced figures. Validating one claim costs about $10k-50k (legal review, a reimbursement audit by the district's auditor, and engineering report reconciliation). The audit is normally done at the district's expense when bonds are sold. My guess is that 20-40% of identified orphan claims are collectible. The lever is capped at about 3-5x, not 10x. Most failures come from the legal chain and the district's capacity to issue debt, not from failing to find the claim.
scored.data: The raw documents are public and somewhat illegible: board minutes (often scanned PDFs on district or law-firm sites), TCEQ bond applications (obtainable by open-records request) and PACER schedules. But the outcome is already written into a legible field. MUD annual audited financial statements posted on EMMA normally have a footnote on developer advances, or a 'Commitments and Contingencies' or 'Subsequent Events' note, giving the estimated amount owed to developers and to be reimbursed from future bonds. The bond Official Statements on EMMA also list the developer reimbursement paid from each issue. This matches the earlier pattern where the regulator or issuer summarises the answer, which removes most of the ML edge. Any bond attorney or financial advisor at Samco, RBC or Masterson can see the open balances.
scored.right_bought: The claims are contractual and assignable, so they can be bought. The best sellers are FDIC receivers, bankruptcy trustees and estates of 2008-11 builders. However, most claims from that era were (a) pledged to and foreclosed by lenders, (b) bought together with the land by the next developer, who needs them to make the land deal work, or (c) settled or released in bankruptcy. Sellers who cannot read the data are rare, because lenders and land buyers do diligence on exactly this. The remaining stock of truly orphaned claims with a live path to bonds is probably small: my estimate is tens of millions of dollars of face value statewide, not billions.
scored.buyer: The issuing MUD pays from bond proceeds, which muni investors fund through underwriters such as Samco, RBC and Baird. Payment needs board action and TCEQ approval, and for most districts a ratio of debt to taxable value that supports the sale. Texas MUD bonds are a real, deep market at about $3-5B a year (estimate), but the claim holder has no control over when or whether the district can issue.
scored.ladder: The rungs above are claim buying, then providing developer finance (funding MUD infrastructure ahead of reimbursement, as Hines, Johnson Development and Land Tejas do), then land development, then homebuilding. This is a real ladder in Texas suburban growth. But the next rung up is just real-estate development and lending, a competitive, capital-heavy business with no ML moat. It looks like a niche distressed-credit fund, not a path to a trillion-dollar company.
scored.fatal_flaw: Payment depends on a future bond issue, which only happens when new taxable value is built in the district. That is outside the claim holder's control, so collection is decided by real-estate absorption, not discovery. The amounts owed are also already disclosed in MUD audit footnotes and Official Statements on EMMA, so there is no illegible-data edge and no seller who cannot see what they hold.
scored.one_line_reason: A clever distressed-credit niche, but the outcome sits in EMMA audit footnotes, good claims are not sold at 2-10c, collection depends on future tax-base growth rather than discovery, and the true orphan supply is small.
sources: No live sources: both web searches came back unrun because the shared web-search budget was used up, so every figure here is my own estimate

scored.name: Dormant Permit Perfection: Nevada and Utah permits near cancellation
scored.one_line: Buy approved-but-uncertificated water permits from holders behind on filings; ML over scanned NDWR files and imagery proves beneficial use already occurred; file proof and change applications; sell certificated rights to developers needing will-serve water.
scored.unproven_right: Permits near cancellation sold for cents on the dollar.
scored.proving_step: ML on permit files, Landsat ET and imagery; proof of beneficial use (~$350) or extension; change application.
scored.proven_buyer: Truckee Meadows developers (TMWA dedication), TRIC data centres, Southern Nevada developers ($10-40k+/AF).
scored.public_data: NDWR database and permit images, Utah DWR files, cancellation notices, OpenET, NAIP.
scored.frame: The rung is "acquire an un-certificated NV/UT water permit and convert it to a certificated, transferable right." Inside that rung the work is title/chain review, evidence that beneficial use actually happened by the statutory deadline, a certified water-right surveyor's proof map, filings, and then a change application. That is roughly 50-60% evidence and paperwork and 40-50% legal and regulatory process: State Engineer review, protests, and in over-appropriated basins a near-certain fight over how much water can be changed. My estimate is that discovery (finding the right permit) is under 50% of the rung, because the hard part is what the State Engineer certifies, not finding the permit. There is no physical step, which is good, and capitalised buyers exist (TMWA dedication market, TRIC users, homebuilders). This is not excluded: it is a paper-rights play with no groundwater exploration or drilling. It sits next to the groundwater exclusion, though, because many target permits are groundwater.
scored.step_up: I have no sourced numbers. The web search budget was used up before any query ran, so everything below is my estimate. Certificated, dedicable Truckee Meadows rights have historically traded at roughly $7k-$12k/AF. In Southern Nevada, SNWA serves most development through connection charges rather than developers buying rights, so the candidate's $10-40k+/AF buyer is doubtful outside places like Pahrump or Coyote Springs. Permits in pending-cancellation status should trade at a discount, plausibly $0.5k-$3k/AF. The holders are mostly farmers and LLCs who know that water in Reno is valuable, and the cancellation notice itself tells them the deadline. That makes a realistic step-up about 3-20x, not 30-300x. The proven quantity is also capped at the use actually shown, which is often a fraction of the permitted duty.
scored.hit_rate_capex: These are estimates, not sourced. Each proving attempt costs a few hundred dollars in NDWR filing fees (the candidate cites ~$350), plus $2k-$10k for a certified water-right surveyor's proof-of-beneficial-use map, plus legal costs for a change application (several $k, much more if protested). So one attempt is about $5k-$25k. The base hit rate (did use actually occur, and will the State Engineer certify a material quantity?) is unknown. It is not a mostly-failing, expensive process like exploratory drilling: failures come from use that never happened, which ML cannot create. The cap of 1/base rate is probably only about 2-4x. Capex is already low, so a 10x cut in discovery capex does not move the economics.
scored.data: Partly legible. Old NDWR permit files, proof maps and Utah DWR files are scanned and unstructured. OpenET, Landsat ET and NAIP are huge and public, and ET-based proof of historic irrigation is a real ML use. But the key outcome fields are already legible: permit status (permitted / certificated / pending cancellation / cancelled) and the proof-due dates sit in the NDWR water rights database, and cancellation notices are public. Anyone can filter a list of at-risk permits without ML. The ML edge is only in estimating how much use can be proven, a second-order quantity.
scored.right_bought: Yes, the permits are bought from holders, not claimed first-come. But the sellers are not data-blind. The State Engineer's cancellation notice gives the holder a statutory window (about 30 days, plus extension or petition paths) to file proof or seek an extension themselves at low cost. Reno-area holders and their water-rights brokers know prevailing $/AF prices. Discounts may be modest, and buying a permit during its notice window is a race against the deadline.
scored.buyer: TMWA's will-serve and dedication market (Reno/Sparks homebuilders and commercial developers), TRIC industrial and data-centre users who need dedicated rights, and some rural Southern Nevada developers (Pahrump, Coyote Springs). They are capitalised but the market is thin. Incumbents and competitors: water-rights brokers and consultants in Reno, appraisers such as WestWater Research, and Vidler Water, a water-rights aggregator acquired by D.R. Horton in 2022, which caps how big the pure-play can get.
scored.ladder: The rungs are: perfecting permits, then aggregating and banking water rights, then a water utility or wholesaler for new development (the Vidler model), then land entitlement and development. There is a real ladder, but the top is a regional water and land developer. It is not a trillion-dollar chain: the Vidler exit was a few hundred million dollars (my estimate of scale), and Nevada and Utah paper water is a finite, regulator-capped pool.
scored.fatal_flaw: Proof of beneficial use only certifies water that was already put to use by the statutory deadline. The State Engineer certifies the quantity actually used, and in over-appropriated Nevada basins any change application gets heavy scrutiny. So the step-up is not created by discovery: it is mostly a legal and administrative conversion of value the holder already partly sees. The status that flags the opportunity (pending cancellation) is a legible public field, which removes the ML edge in finding targets.
scored.one_line_reason: This is administrative arbitrage on a legible status field: the step-up is likely about 3-20x, not 10^3-10^4, proving is cheap and rarely fails for reasons ML can fix, and certification is capped by use that already happened. It is a niche water-brokerage business, not a Terranox-shaped rung.

scored.name: Dormant Mill Water / Senior Cooling Water: unforfeited rights at idle factories and retired thermal plants
scored.one_line: Buy idle Western mills and plants or retired coal/gas plants, or just their appurtenant senior surface rights, which owners think have lapsed or are bundled at a discount; ML over scanned state-engineer files, decrees and EIA-923 cooling data proves historic use and non-abandonment; win change of use; sell to hyperscalers, fabs and cities.
scored.unproven_right: Appurtenant industrial/cooling surface rights valued at zero or a bundled discount ($500-2,000/AF).
scored.proving_step: Reconstruct beneficial use and statutory exceptions from scanned filings and diversion logs; change-of-use/place decree or permit.
scored.proven_buyer: Intel, TSMC, Microsoft, Meta and other data centers/fabs in AZ, NV, UT, CO, WA, ID, TX; municipal utilities ($10-50k+/AF).
scored.public_data: WA Ecology WRTS, CO CDSS/HydroBase, UT/ID scans, AZ ADWR, TCEQ, EIA-860/923 cooling data, USGS water use, county deeds.
scored.rough_step_up: ~10-30x typical, 10^3+ where the right comes nearly free with the land; adjacent to killed powered brownfields and some states write forfeiture into status fields.
scored.frame: The rung is "buy a dormant senior industrial or cooling right, then win a change-of-use decree or permit". Discovery (finding rights with defensible use history) is my estimate of 20-35% of the work. The physical step here is the legal one: historic consumptive-use engineering, a water-court or agency change proceeding, objector litigation, and dry-up or return-flow terms. In Colorado that typically takes 2-7 years. This is the geothermal-in-coal-mines pattern again: winning the bespoke change case is harder than finding the right. There are capitalised buyers (cities, fabs), so the frame partly exists, but the 80%+ discovery share does not.
scored.step_up: From my knowledge, not verified this run because the shared search budget ran out. Unchanged senior ag or industrial rights in the West trade at roughly $1-10k per acre-foot (AF) of consumptive use. Firm municipal supply on the Colorado Front Range sells for about $30-80k/AF; Colorado-Big Thompson units have traded at about $80-100k per unit. The candidate's own $500-2k to $10-50k range is about 10-30x after years of legal cost. A 10^3x jump only happens where the right is genuinely missed inside a land sale, which is rare because water is appraised separately in the West. Typical step-up is 3-30x, not 10^3.
scored.hit_rate_capex: These are estimates. Cost per proving attempt (engineering, water attorney, court) is about $150k-1M+ per Colorado change case; Washington and Idaho permits are cheaper but slow. The base hit rate is not low: well-documented thermal and mill rights are usually changed successfully, though with quantities cut back to historic consumptive use. The real uncertainty is how many acre-feet survive, not whether the right exists. So ML has little failure rate to cut: the lever is under about 2x, and legal cost dominates whatever ML does.
scored.data: Mixed. Colorado's HydroBase and the decennial abandonment lists published by the division engineers write abandonment status into a public field. Washington's relinquishment rules (5 years of non-use, with statutory exceptions) are illegible in the scanned Ecology files. Colorado diversion records are already digitised in CDSS. EIA-923 cooling-water data is structured and public, so plant consumptive use is legible to anyone. The true illegible edge is narrow: old mill rights in Washington, Idaho and Utah scans.
scored.right_bought: It can be bought, but the sellers are mostly sophisticated. Retiring coal and gas plants belong to utilities and co-ops (Xcel, Tri-State, PNM, APS, PacifiCorp) that inventory and monetise their water; plant-retirement water deals are negotiated publicly. Idle mills are a better target, but their sellers usually hire water brokers, and Western water is appraised separately from the land. Specialist buyers already work this space: WestWater Research (broker and valuation), Water Asset Management, Vidler Water, Renewable Resources Group and municipal acquisition programmes.
scored.buyer: Municipal utilities (Aurora, Denver Water, Colorado Springs, Front Range districts) are real, capitalised buyers. Hyperscalers and fabs (Intel in Chandler, TSMC in Phoenix, Microsoft, Meta) mostly buy through municipal supply, reclaimed-water agreements or water-replenishment credits rather than owning adjudicated rights. Pricing is set by the municipal market, not a one-off willingness to pay.
scored.ladder: Moderate. Possible rungs: buy rights, then change cases, then storage and recharge, then water utility or wholesale supply, then water-plus-power-plus-land sites for data centers. The top rungs are regulated utilities with capped returns, and this looks like a niche water-asset business (the Vidler/PICO shape, under $1B), not a trillion-dollar path.
scored.fatal_flaw: The value is created in a multi-year adversarial legal change proceeding (consumptive-use quantification, objectors, injury terms), not in discovery. The owners of the valuable rights (utilities, mill owners advised by brokers) already know what they hold, and key status fields (Colorado abandonment lists, EIA-923 cooling use) are public and legible. So there is no frame where discovery is 80%+ and no near-zero entry price.
scored.one_line_reason: This is a mature, brokered Western water market with roughly 10-30x after years of legal work. Proving the right is a bespoke court fight, which repeats the geothermal-in-coal-mines failure rather than a cheap drill hit.

scored.name: Flowage Holdings: dormant reservoir flowage easements for pumped storage
scored.one_line: Acquire century-old flowage/inundation easements granted to defunct power companies for never-built reservoirs; ML proves validity and footprint match; sell to PSH developers as a land-assembly shortcut.
scored.unproven_right: Recorded flowage easements held by dissolved utilities, by nominal quitclaim.
scored.proving_step: ML deed parsing and boundary reconstruction against DEMs; title opinion.
scored.proven_buyer: PSH developers and utilities.
scored.public_data: County recorder scans, FPC/FERC abandoned applications, USGS historic topos, 3DEP.
scored.frame: Rung: own a recorded flowage easement and prove it is valid and fits a reservoir footprint. Inside that narrow rung, discovery (finding the deed, rebuilding the boundary, getting a title opinion) is about 80-90% of the work, and the physical step really is trivial. But the output is only worth something if a pumped-storage project gets built, and that project is a multi-billion-dollar bespoke build (my estimate, from memory: $2,000-4,000/kW, so $2-6B for 1-2 GW). Land is low single-digit percent of that capex (estimate). So the rung's value depends on the hardest physical step in the chain. That is structurally the geothermal-in-coal-mines counter-example, not Terranox.
scored.step_up: Unproven: a nominal quitclaim from a dissolved company's successor or trustee, about $100-$5,000 per instrument (my estimate, no source; web search budget was exhausted). Proven: at most what a developer saves on land assembly and holdout risk. FERC-licensed hydro developers can condemn land under FPA Section 21, so the ceiling is roughly fair-market easement value plus saved litigation time. That is likely 1-3x the land's ordinary easement value, perhaps tens to low hundreds of dollars per acre of rural flood land (estimate). The ratio from quitclaim price can look 100x+, but the absolute dollars are small next to project capex. And the value is only realised if the project reaches license and financing. It is not an immediate, liquid repricing the way a drill hit is.
scored.hit_rate_capex: The proving step is cheap: deed parsing, DEM overlay and a title opinion at about $1-5k each (estimate). Expensive, mostly failing proving attempts do not exist here, so ML has little capex to cut. The real low hit rate is downstream. Very few US pumped-storage projects with FERC preliminary permits ever get built (from memory: dozens of permits, a handful of licenses, roughly 1-2 new major projects in recent decades). Also, a century-old easement footprint matching a modern closed-loop design (different heads, sites and dam heights) is probably rare, under 5% (estimate). ML does not move either of those odds. No live sources: the search budget was used up.
scored.data: The data really is illegible: county recorder scans, old Federal Power Commission (FPC) and FERC applications, historic USGS topo maps, plus 3DEP elevation data as the cross-check. Incumbent title firms do not mine it at scale. The outcome is partly summarised in legible places, though. FERC eLibrary preliminary permits, license applications and the DOE/ORNL hydropower resource assessments already list candidate PSH sites. So the "where is a good site" answer is public. Only "who holds an old easement there" is hidden.
scored.right_bought: Weak. Many of these easements are legally dead or dying: abandonment doctrine (purpose never carried out), marketable record title acts in about 20 states that extinguish unrenewed interests after 30-40 years, and the rule that easements tied to a specific purpose fail when that purpose fails. When they survive, they usually passed by merger into today's utilities (most early power companies were rolled up into current IOUs). Those successors can read their own records and will not quitclaim cheaply once they know a PSH developer is circling. Underlying fee owners also have strong quiet-title claims.
scored.buyer: PSH developers (e.g. rPlus Hydro, the sponsor of the Goldendale project, utilities like Duke and Dominion) are well capitalised but few. The pipeline that actually converts into projects is a handful a decade. They hold federal eminent domain once licensed, so they have little reason to pay a premium for a contested old easement.
scored.ladder: In theory there is a ladder: easement, then site control, then a FERC preliminary permit, then a license, then build and own the PSH plant. But the rung right above is the bespoke multi-billion-dollar build that the rubric says breaks the model. Winning the bottom rung gives no real head start on the top rungs. A better ladder would be 'site-control aggregator for long-duration storage', and that does not depend on old easements.
scored.fatal_flaw: The proven right has almost no step-up a buyer will pay for. Licensed hydro developers can take land by federal eminent domain (FPA Section 21). Abandonment and marketable-record-title laws probably extinguish most century-old unused flowage easements. Surviving ones sit with successor utilities rather than being orphaned. And the asset's value depends on a multi-billion-dollar bespoke plant that rarely gets built.
scored.one_line_reason: The discovery rung is real and the scanned deeds are illegible. But the right is legally fragile and can be bypassed by condemnation, the buyers are few, and the value depends on the hardest physical step (building the PSH plant). That makes it the geothermal-in-coal-mines failure, not Terranox.

scored.name: Dormant Hydro Permit Revival
scored.one_line: Mine surrendered, lapsed and denied FERC hydro/PSH dockets for sites that died for reasons no longer valid, re-secure site control and preliminary permits, reuse prior studies and sell revived sites.
scored.unproven_right: Land options plus newly filed first-come permits and purchased study archives.
scored.proving_step: ML classifies death reasons and re-scores under today's markets.
scored.proven_buyer: PSH and small hydro developers, infrastructure funds.
scored.public_data: FERC eLibrary, FERC permit/licence lists, ORNL HydroSource.
scored.rough_step_up: ~10-100x; permits are free first-come, status fields partly legible.
scored.frame: Proposed rung: a revived FERC preliminary permit plus site control. That rung doesn't prove anything, though. A preliminary permit only gives filing priority for 3-4 years. What creates the value is getting the FERC licence, which takes about 5-10 years of environmental and geotechnical studies, interconnection and offtake work. Inside that rung, discovery (picking the site and the reason it died) is about 10-20% of the work by my estimate; regulatory and engineering proving is the rest. So no sellable frame exists where discovery is 80% or more. The 'ML re-scores death reasons' step is desk analysis, not a proving event that a buyer pays a step-up for.
scored.step_up: From memory, not verified (search budget exhausted): a preliminary permit costs almost nothing to file (no FERC filing fee; consultant time maybe $20-100k, my estimate). Unlicensed PSH permits trade near zero, since sponsors like Premium Energy Holdings hold dozens at once. A licensed, shovel-ready PSH project might sell for a few $M to tens of $M of development premium (my estimate, roughly $10-50/kW on 500-1,000 MW). Permit to licence is maybe 10-100x on the permit-stage spend, but most of that is earned through licensing spend, not on a hit. Revival alone (permit refiled, no new evidence) is about 1-3x.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Base rate (from memory): FERC has issued preliminary permits for well over 100 GW of PSH, but only a handful got licences in the last 15 years (e.g. Swan Lake, Gordon Butte, Eagle Mountain, Goldendale in process). The only big recent build is Bath County's expansion; Rocky Mountain (1995) was the last major new plant. So the permit-to-licence hit rate is maybe under 5-10% (estimate). But each attempt costs about $10-50M+ over 5-10 years, my estimate. Projects die on offtake, interconnection, capital cost ($2-4B+ per GW) and environment, not on site choice. ML can't raise that hit rate by 10x because the failures aren't caused by poor discovery.
scored.data: FERC eLibrary is public and partly illegible (scanned orders, comments). But the outcome is written down in legible form: issuance, surrender and cancellation orders, plus permit status lists, often say why a permit lapsed (e.g. 'failed to file progress reports'). ORNL HydroSource and NPD/PSH resource assessments are already structured. Incumbents read this closely: Rye Development, Premium Energy Holdings (a serial permit filer), Absaroka/Daybreak, FFP and big utilities. Rights aren't bought below value from people who can't read the data. Permits are free and first-come with competing-application rules, so there is no purchase discount and no exclusivity moat. Land options are bought from ordinary landowners, but land isn't where the value sits.
scored.right_bought: Mostly free first-come preliminary permits, which competitors can file too, plus land options at market rates from landowners. Old study archives could be bought from failed sponsors cheaply, which is a modest real edge. But studies go stale: environmental baselines more than about 5 years old usually have to be redone.
scored.buyer: PSH and hydro developers (Rye, NextEra, Brookfield, GE Vernova-backed sponsors), utilities and infrastructure funds. They're well capitalised, but they buy licensed or near-licensed projects with offtake, not revived permits.
scored.ladder: The rungs are real: permit, then licence, then interconnection and offtake, then construction (EPC), then ownership and operation of GW-scale storage. Long-duration storage is a big market. But every rung above the permit is capital-heavy, bespoke civil engineering that takes years, which is the same failure as the geothermal-in-coal-mines counter-example.
scored.fatal_flaw: The proving step isn't discovery. Building PSH means bespoke multi-billion-dollar civil works, with $10-50M and 5-10 years of licensing for each 'shot'. Sites die because of economics, interconnection and offtake, not because nobody found the site. Permits are free first-come and already blanketed by serial filers, and the reasons sites died are mostly written into legible FERC orders. This is the geothermal-coal-mine counter-example in hydro form.
scored.one_line_reason: No rung where discovery is 80% or more: licensing and building dominate, permits are free and contested, death reasons are already legible, and the step-up comes from heavy proving spend, not an immediate hit.

scored.name: Latent / Surplus Interconnection: buying non-operating or weak generators for retained interconnection rights
scored.one_line: Buy mothballed or underperforming small generators (old peakers, PURPA QFs, biomass, LFG, small hydro) near scrap value; ML reads scanned ISAs/LGIAs and QF contracts to find units whose interconnection service is still alive and reusable via surplus/replacement processes; sell the site plus right to BESS, peaker and data-center developers. Rescores killed queue idea; edge must come from terms not in tables.
scored.unproven_right: Ownership of a facility whose IA or legacy QF contract may carry live MW of service on rule-based clocks.
scored.proving_step: Parse agreements, amendments and deactivation dates; file surplus or replacement request and win RTO/utility acceptance.
scored.proven_buyer: BESS and peaker developers, Constellation/Vistra/Talen-style co-location buyers, Crusoe, hyperscalers ($50-500k/MW).
scored.public_data: EIA-860/860M/923, FERC eLibrary QF Form 556 and IA PDFs, EQR, RTO deactivation and surplus postings, state PURPA filings, non-RTO PUC dockets.
scored.rough_step_up: ~5-50x; base feasibility ~30%, EIA fields give part of the answer.
scored.frame: The rung is owning an old generator site whose interconnection rights are still alive, then proving those rights reusable through a surplus or replacement request. Discovery (reading IAs and checking clocks) is maybe 40-50% of the work in this rung (my estimate). The rest is not trivial: you have to buy and hold a physical plant with environmental, decommissioning and O&M liabilities, and the RTO has to accept the request. Under PJM's replacement and surplus rules (FERC Order 845 surplus service, MISO generator replacement) the replacement must usually be at the same point of interconnection and within the existing MW and technology limits, so the right only becomes valuable when it is paired with a buyer's build. Capitalised buyers do exist (BESS and gas developers, Vistra, Talen, Constellation, hyperscalers). But this rung is not one where 80%+ of the work is discovery.
scored.step_up: My estimate, not verified, because the web search budget ran out before any search returned: a mothballed small unit at about scrap or salvage value, roughly $10-50k/MW, versus about $100-300k/MW for an interconnection-ready site sold to BESS or data-center buyers. The candidate's own $50-500k/MW range puts the top case higher. That gives about 3-10x, maybe 20x in the best cases. It is nowhere near 10^3-10^4, because the seller already prices in the land, the substation and the interconnection.
scored.hit_rate_capex: The candidate gives base feasibility of about 30%, so the ML lever is capped at about 3.3x, not 10x. Cost per proving attempt (my estimate): legal and engineering review plus surplus or replacement study deposits of roughly $50k-$500k. The main cost is buying the plant before you prove anything, often $1M-$20M for small units, and better reading does not lower that.
scored.data: Mostly the outcome is already legible. EIA-860/860M carry status, retirement dates and nameplate MW. PJM publishes deactivation requests with dates, and its tariff ends a deactivated unit's capacity interconnection rights about one year after deactivation unless a replacement or transfer is filed (from my recall; not checked this run). MISO's replacement window, about 3 years, is likewise rule-based. So "is the right still alive" is deactivation date plus a tariff clock: a lookup, the same failure as the killed queue idea. Some edge is left in scanned LGIA amendments and legacy QF or state interconnection terms for non-RTO units, but that is a small tail.
scored.right_bought: The right is bought, not claimed first-come, by buying the plant. But sellers are mostly sophisticated IPPs, PE funds and utilities who already know that interconnection is the scarce asset in 2024-26. The biggest owners (Vistra, Talen, Constellation, NRG) are themselves turning interconnection into money through co-location. Small QF and biomass owners are less sophisticated, but their units are often distribution-level with few MW, which suits BESS buyers but not data centers.
scored.buyer: BESS and peaker developers. Large IPPs doing co-location (Talen-AWS Susquehanna, Constellation, Vistra). Hyperscalers and Crusoe-style developers looking for powered sites. Incumbent competitors already working this exact play (from general knowledge, not checked this run): PE-backed roll-ups of brownfield plants for interconnection (e.g. Hull Street Energy, LS Power, Lightstone), plus developers' internal origination teams. These buyers are capitalised and active, but many of them are also the competition.
scored.ladder: The rungs are reasonably clear: a site with a live right, then a developed BESS or peaker on it, then an owned-and-operated IPP fleet, then co-located power for data centers. Becoming an IPP is a large-company path, but a crowded and capital-heavy one. Winning the first rung brings no data moat that carries up the ladder, because the right rests on rule-based clocks everyone can read.
scored.fatal_flaw: The outcome is already in legible public fields (EIA-860M status and retirement dates, RTO deactivation lists, rule-based clocks for retaining the right), and sophisticated owners price the interconnection value into the sale. The step-up is about 3-10x, not 10^3, and the ML lever is capped near 3x by the ~30% base feasibility. It repeats the killed queue-position idea.
scored.one_line_reason: The value step-up is only about 3-10x, the plant must be bought before any proving, the answer is mostly in EIA and RTO tables, and capable incumbents already roll these sites up, so it fails C2-C4.

scored.name: Lost Occurrence-Policy Archaeology / Dormant Shell Coverage
scored.one_line: Acquire insurance rights (or the corporate shells) of dissolved manufacturers cheaply via trustees, receivers or reinstatement; ML reconstructs pre-1986 occurrence CGL and excess policies from scanned 10-Ks, EPA PRP files and court exhibits and matches them to live PFAS, asbestos or Superfund exposure; monetise via buybacks or assignments.
scored.unproven_right: Rights to unknown historical policies of defunct companies, ~$5-50k.
scored.proving_step: Secondary evidence of carrier, years and limits to court standard; notice letter or declaratory action.
scored.proven_buyer: Run-off insurers and legacy buyers (Enstar, Catalina, R&Q successors, AIG/Travelers legacy), PRP groups, asbestos trusts, water utilities in PFAS MDL, funders.
scored.public_data: EPA SEMS PRP lists and site files, CERCLA decrees, EDGAR historical 10-Ks and microfiche, coverage dockets, state dissolution and insurance department records, PFAS MDL 2873, Newspapers.com.
scored.frame: The rung would be: find a lost occurrence policy, prove it, and collect a buyback. Finding the policy (reconstructing carrier, years and limits) is maybe 20-30% of the work by my estimate. The 'physical step' that follows is not trivial. It is coverage litigation or a negotiated buyback: declaratory actions, fights over allocation and exhaustion, and late-notice and lost-policy defences. In US practice this usually costs $0.5-5M+ in legal fees and takes 2-7 years (estimate). So discovery is nowhere near 80% of the rung. This is the same failure as the geothermal-in-coal-mines counter-example: proving the right is harder than finding it.
scored.step_up: Unproven: rights to unknown policies of a defunct company, about $5-50k (the candidate's figure). Proven: the value is not the policy limit. It is the expected indemnity the insurer would actually owe on live claims, discounted for litigation. Buybacks of lost-policy sets usually settle at 10-40% of limits (my estimate), on limits of $1-25M per year-layer. The headline gross multiple could reach 100x or more. But the policy is only worth anything while a liability is attached to it, and those proceeds legally go to claimants and creditors, not to whoever bought the shell (see right_bought). The net step-up to the acquirer is probably 2-10x after legal costs. These numbers are not sourced because no search could be run.
scored.hit_rate_capex: My estimate: once a company is known to have had pre-1986 operations and exposure, insurance archaeologists find evidence of at least one policy in most cases, perhaps 50-80%. The hard part is never finding it. It is proving the policy's terms to court standard and then winning against the insurer. Archaeology costs $25-150k per matter (estimate). Litigation costs 10-100x that. ML can only make the cheap part cheaper, so total discovery cost falls perhaps 1.2-2x, not 10x. And because the base hit rate on finding is already high, the 1/hit-rate cap on the lever is low anyway.
scored.data: The data really is public and illegible: EPA SEMS PRP files, scanned 10-Ks and microfiche, court exhibits, state insurance department filings, and PFAS MDL 2873. That half of C4 holds. But the outcome is often already pieced together by others. For years, asbestos plaintiffs' firms and PRP groups have sued dissolved corporations as 'insurance-only' defendants. California Corp Code 2011 and similar laws in other states allow suits against dissolved corporations up to their insurance. Specialist insurance-archaeology firms already do this reconstruction for policyholders (from memory; not verified this session).
scored.right_bought: The right is weak and contested. Anti-assignment clauses mean you need either a post-loss assignment or an assignment approved by the policyholder or trustee. California allows post-loss assignment (Fluor, 2015), but other states vary. Receivers and bankruptcy trustees have a fiduciary duty to sell for full value, or to pursue the policy themselves for claimants. Buying the shell through reinstatement brings its liabilities with it, and fraudulent-transfer and successor-liability claims follow. Insurance proceeds legally belong to injured claimants, as asbestos trusts and the 524(g) channeling injunction show. So the realisable right is not cheaply purchasable or cleanly owned.
scored.buyer: Run-off and legacy acquirers (Enstar, Catalina, R&Q successors, AIG/Travelers legacy units) do pay buybacks. But they pay to extinguish exposure, and only once a claimant or policyholder can force coverage. PRP groups and asbestos trusts want the proceeds themselves, so they compete with the acquirer rather than buy from it. Litigation funders could finance it, but they price it as litigation risk, not as an asset.
scored.ladder: The rungs above would be a legacy-liability aggregator: buy many dissolved shells, finance PRP cleanups, become a run-off insurer or a claims-resolution vehicle. Enstar is a multi-billion-dollar company built on legacy run-off, so the ceiling is real. But it is a capital-and-actuarial business, and archaeology is not the moat that gets you there.
scored.fatal_flaw: The value appears only when an insurer is forced to pay a live liability, and that payment legally belongs to the claimants and creditors who hold the liability, not to whoever bought the shell or policy rights. Proving it is years of coverage litigation, not a cheap Terranox-style drill. Discovery is a minority of the work, and the step-up is not captured by the owner.
scored.one_line_reason: Finding the policy is the easy, cheap part. Coverage litigation is the expensive, slow 'drill', and the proceeds go to claimants, so no rung exists where discovery is 80%+ and the owner keeps the step-up.

scored.name: PFAS Coverage Assignments for Water Utilities
scored.one_line: Buy coverage rights and shells of defunct platers, finishers and carpet mills near PFAS-impacted water systems; ML locates probable source and reconstructs historical insurers; sell assignments to utilities and plaintiffs.
scored.unproven_right: Historical coverage rights and shells of defunct dischargers.
scored.proving_step: ML over NPDES files, Sanborn maps, directories and UCMR5 for source-to-policy chain.
scored.proven_buyer: Public water systems and counsel, PFAS MDL committees, carriers via buyback.
scored.public_data: EPA UCMR 5, scanned NPDES files, ECHO, Sanborn maps, city directories, EDGAR.
scored.frame: The rung would be: buy a defunct discharger's shell or its coverage rights, then 'prove' it by tying a PFAS plume to that site and finding a pre-1986 occurrence CGL policy. Discovery here (finding the source and the old insurer) is maybe 20-30% of the work by my estimate. The other 70%+ is the physical-equivalent step, which is not trivial. You have to establish causation with fate-and-transport experts. You have to defend against the qualified pollution exclusion (1973-86) and the absolute pollution exclusion (post-1986). You have to win trigger and allocation fights, and coverage cases usually take 3-7 years. Policy reconstruction also often ends in a fight over secondary evidence of the policy. Litigation is the 'bespoke geothermal plant' of this candidate. No frame exists where proving is 80%+ discovery.
scored.step_up: My estimate, not sourced (my search budget was used up before I could search). An unproven defunct-company shell or coverage-assignment right likely costs ~$1k-$50k, since nominal shells are cheap. A proven, collectible claim on a reconstructed CGL tower might settle for $1M-$20M per site. That ratio is ~10^2-10^3, but only after litigation succeeds, not immediately when the source is found. Finding a probable source plus a probable insurer moves value by maybe 3-10x, because a carrier or plaintiff still discounts heavily for exclusion and litigation risk. 3M's ~$10.5-12.5B and DuPont/Chemours/Corteva's $1.185B water-system settlements (2023) set the upstream benchmark. Those came from solvent manufacturers, not from defunct platers' insurers.
scored.hit_rate_capex: These are my estimates. The proposal's own figure is a ~5-15% hit rate. Finding a source is not the expensive, mostly failing step. The expensive step is coverage litigation: roughly $0.5M-$3M+ per contested claim in fees and experts, with a success rate I'd guess at 30-50%. ML raises the source-finding hit rate, but it does not cut the dominant cost, which is legal. So ML cuts total capex maybe 1.2-2x, not 10x. Insurance-archaeology research (manual policy reconstruction) costs maybe $10k-$100k per company. ML could make that piece ~10x cheaper, but it is a small share of total cost.
scored.data: On the data side: EPA UCMR 5 already publishes PFAS detections per water system as a legible field. EPA ECHO/NPDES and state industrial-user lists name the likely dischargers (SIC 3471 platers, carpet mills) in legible fields too. The genuinely illegible part is the historical insurer, pieced together from Sanborn maps, scanned filings, city directories and old broker records. That part has real ML value. On buying the right: anti-assignment clauses are generally unenforceable after a loss (e.g., Fluor v. Superior Court, Cal. 2015). But many states let plaintiffs sue a dissolved corporation directly, up to its insurance limits, without buying anything (e.g., Cal. Corp. Code 2011). So the right is effectively free to whoever sues first. A purchase gives no moat, and the sellers (former shareholders, trustees) are often unreachable.
scored.right_bought: You would buy shells or coverage assignments of defunct dischargers from former shareholders, bankruptcy trustees or state-revived entities. You could also take post-loss assignments of policy proceeds.
scored.buyer: In theory: public water systems and their contingency-fee counsel, PFAS MDL (AFFF MDL 2873) plaintiff committees, and carriers buying policies back. In practice, these buyers already get the same value through direct action against dissolved entities. Contingency counsel does not pay large upfront sums for unlitigated coverage theories.
scored.ladder: The rungs above are weak: litigation finance, then a remediation/treatment contractor (GAC/IX installs), then water-system ownership. These are separate businesses with modest synergy, not a vertically integrated chain that compounds toward a very large company. The ceiling is roughly that of a specialised litigation-finance fund.
scored.fatal_flaw: The step-up comes from winning years of coverage litigation (pollution exclusions, trigger and allocation, missing-policy proof), not from discovery. Plaintiffs can also already sue dissolved insureds directly without buying any right, so owning the asset gives no capture.
scored.one_line_reason: Finding the source and the insurer is a minority of the work. The value is realised through slow, expensive coverage litigation, and the right is reachable without buying it, so the Terranox 95/5 frame does not exist.
sources: No web searches ran: the shared search budget was used up. The figures below are from background knowledge and should be checked.
EPA UCMR 5 data (epa.gov/dwucmr/fifth-unregulated-contaminant-monitoring-rule)
3M PFAS public water system settlement, 2023 (~$10.3-12.5B), In re AFFF Products Liability Litigation MDL 2873
DuPont/Chemours/Corteva $1.185B water system settlement, 2023
Fluor Corp. v. Superior Court, 61 Cal.4th 1175 (2015): post-loss assignment of CGL benefits allowed
California Corporations Code section 2011: suits against dissolved corporations up to insurance coverage
ISO CGL qualified pollution exclusion (1973) and absolute pollution exclusion (1986)

scored.name: Historical Policy Recovery for Revival-Window Abuse Defendants
scored.one_line: Buy coverage rights of dissolved nonprofits sued under abuse lookback windows, ML-reconstruct 1950s-80s policies, monetise via plaintiffs or carrier buybacks. Ethically sensitive.
scored.unproven_right: Coverage rights of dissolved defendant organisations.
scored.proving_step: Secondary policy evidence from diocesan bankruptcy exhibits, minutes, newspapers and broker records.
scored.proven_buyer: Settlement trusts, plaintiff consortia, CNA/Travelers/Chubb legacy units.
scored.public_data: Diocesan Chapter 11 dockets, NY CVA filings, charity registries and 990s, newspaper archives.
scored.frame: The rung is 'prove that a historical CGL policy existed and what its terms were (lost-policy doctrine)'. Inside that rung, discovery (finding secondary evidence: ledgers, broker cards, board minutes, certificates, bankruptcy exhibits) is about 60-70% of the work by my estimate. The rest is not trivial. It is litigation: proving existence and terms to a preponderance or clear-and-convincing standard (depending on the state), winning coverage defenses (expected/intended, number of occurrences, late notice, known-loss), and then getting each underlying abuse claim to judgment or settlement. That legal step is the bespoke-plant problem from the coal-mine counter-example, not drilling. Buyers with capital do exist (settlement trusts, plaintiff consortia, legacy/runoff units), but they buy settlements, not 'proven policies'.
scored.step_up: Estimate, not sourced (search budget was exhausted before any query ran). An unreconstructed policy for a dissolved defendant is worth about $0 to anyone. A reconstructed 1960s-70s primary CGL policy, typically $100k-$1M per occurrence before stacking across years, could be worth roughly $0.1M-$5M+ across a tranche of claims, after legal fees and coverage fights. So a hit takes value from near zero to meaningful dollars. But the price of the 'right' before the hit is undefined, not $1, because there is no seller (see data/right). Benchmark from memory, unverified: the Boy Scouts plan drew roughly $787M from Hartford and roughly $800M from Century/Chubb, showing that insurers pay large sums once policies are proven and claims aggregated. The realised step-up needs years of litigation, not an immediate mark like a drill hit. Scored 3 rather than 5 because the jump is neither immediate nor something you can mark-to-market.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Estimate: insurance-archaeology searches cost about $10k-$100k per organisation (archivist hours plus broker and carrier record requests). Hit rate for finding enough secondary evidence for at least one policy year is moderate, maybe 30-60%, because large orgs (dioceses, Scouts councils) kept records and established firms already do this. Litigating each lost-policy claim costs $100k-$1M+ and takes years, which dwarfs the discovery cost. ML might cut search cost 2-3x, but the dominant capex is litigation, which ML barely touches. Lever capped at about 1/0.4 = 2.5x. Not sourced; the search budget was exhausted.
scored.data: Public but illegible data does exist: diocesan Chapter 11 dockets with coverage charts and archaeology reports as exhibits, NY CVA filings, 990s, newspaper archives. But in the big bankruptcies the outcome is often already summarised in a legible field: debtors and tort committees file schedules of insurance and coverage charts listing carrier, policy period and limits, produced by hired insurance archaeologists. So the highest-value targets have already been mined by incumbents.
scored.right_bought: Very weak. A dissolved nonprofit usually has no officers, board or estate left to sell or assign its coverage rights. Rights usually pass by operation of law (receiver, attorney general, cy-pres successor, or a successor diocese/council). Assigning policy proceeds is often allowed post-loss, but buying abuse-claim coverage raises champerty and public-policy problems, and courts and AGs would look hard at a third party profiting from abuse recoveries. Plaintiffs can also often go after a dissolved corporation's insurers directly (for example, NY Insurance Law 3420 after an unsatisfied judgment, plus state survival statutes), so the plaintiffs' bar has no need to buy from you. The 'cheap purchase from owners who cannot read the data' leg is missing.
scored.buyer: Settlement trusts, plaintiff consortia and mass-tort firms, and legacy/runoff carriers (Chubb/Century, Travelers, CNA, Hartford) through buyback settlements. They are well capitalised, but the carriers are adversaries rather than buyers. They pay only under litigation pressure and at a discount, and the trusts mostly fund their own archaeology.
scored.ladder: Short and ethically capped: archaeology, then coverage litigation, then claims aggregation or funding (litigation finance), then maybe a runoff or legacy-liability acquirer. That at best becomes a niche litigation-finance or legacy-liability shop, which already exists (litigation funders, runoff consolidators like Enstar), not a trillion-dollar vertical. Demand is finite and tied to lookback windows that are closing.
scored.fatal_flaw: There is no cheap, buyable right. Dissolved defendants have no one who can sell their coverage, plaintiffs can reach the insurers directly, and buying abuse-claim recoveries runs into champerty and public-policy limits. The value is realised through years of bespoke coverage litigation, not an immediate mark, so the legal step is the hard part (the coal-mine geothermal failure mode). The big targets (dioceses, BSA) are already mapped by incumbent insurance archaeologists, with coverage charts filed on the dockets.
scored.one_line_reason: Insurance archaeology for abuse defendants is an existing service, the right cannot be cheaply bought from dissolved entities, the payout runs through years of coverage litigation that ML barely touches, and it is ethically fraught with a finite, closing market.
sources: No live sources: the shared WebSearch budget for this run (200 calls per turn) was used up before this candidate's queries ran. All numbers are estimates or recalled from memory and are not verified.
Recalled, unverified: Boy Scouts of America Chapter 11 plan (D. Del. 2022). Hartford roughly $787M and Century/Chubb roughly $800M contributions to the abuse trust.
Recalled, unverified: NY Insurance Law 3420 direct action against insurer after an unsatisfied judgment.
Recalled: established insurance-archaeology firms (e.g., Insurance Archaeology Group, Policyholder Services) retained in diocesan Chapter 11 cases.

scored.name: Lost Reinsurance Recoverables in Run-off Cedents
scored.one_line: Buy run-off books or their recoverable rights from tiny cedents and receiverships; ML reads scanned treaty slips and bordereaux to find unbilled long-tail losses against solvent reinsurers; commute for cash.
scored.unproven_right: Unknown or unbilled recoverables under 1960s-90s treaties.
scored.proving_step: Match paid claims to treaty wordings and panels; billable recoverable.
scored.proven_buyer: Swiss Re, Munich Re, Lloyd's RITC syndicates, Enstar, Compre.
scored.public_data: NAIC historical statements and Schedule F, receivership filings, NOLHGA/NCIGF, Lloyd's records.
scored.frame: The rung is buying a run-off book, or just its reinsurance recoverable rights, and turning unbilled recoverables into cash by billing or commuting them. Finding the recoverable (matching paid claims to the treaty wordings and the panel of reinsurers) is maybe 40-60% of the work. That is my estimate, not sourced. The rest is not trivial or abstracted. Reinsurers on 1960s-90s long-tail treaties routinely push back with late-notice, allocation, follow-the-settlements and aggregation defenses, and they go to arbitration. Collection is the bespoke physical step, much like the coal-mine geothermal counter-example. Many 1960s-90s reinsurers are now insolvent or in schemes of arrangement, so some of what you find cannot be collected. Commuting is the sellable exit and the buyers are capitalised (Swiss Re, Munich Re, Enstar), but a commutation is a negotiated discount, not a market purchase at a step-up.
scored.step_up: I estimate about 2-5x from my own knowledge of how run-off deals and commutations are priced. Nothing was verified, because the web search budget was already used up when this agent ran. A run-off book is bought at a discount to its net reserves, typically 5-20% of reserves. An unknown recoverable inside that book is worth essentially nothing until it is documented, so on paper the step-up looks infinite. Realistically, though, unbilled long-tail recoverables that nobody can see trade at roughly 10-30 cents on the dollar inside a book purchase. Once billed and commuted, they collect perhaps 50-85 cents on the dollar, with reinsurer disputes and present-value discounts taken off. That is about 2-5x, far from 10^3-10^4. The candidate's own 20-100x figure is optimistic, because the purchase price of the book already reflects an expected recoverable.
scored.hit_rate_capex: These are my estimates, not verified. A proving attempt is a recoverables audit of one book: roughly $50k-500k of analyst and claims-forensics time, plus arbitration costs of $0.5-3M when a reinsurer disputes. Recovery audits at legacy firms usually find recoverables in a modest share of files, perhaps 5-20% with any uplift. So base hit rate is not terribly low and the ML lever is capped at maybe 2-5x. Most of the expensive part is arbitration and collection, which ML does not cut.
scored.data: This fails C4. The signal is not in public data. Treaty slips, bordereaux, claim files and ceded-loss histories are the cedent's private records, and you only get them after buying the book or signing an NDA in a receivership. Public NAIC Schedule F shows recoverables by reinsurer in legible fields. That is already the summarised outcome for booked recoverables, the exact pattern the prior hunts flagged as killing the ML edge. Receivership filings are partly public but give aggregates. NOLHGA covers life and health guaranty funds, which is not relevant to P&C long-tail. There is no public, illegible, outcome-unsummarised dataset to mine before buying.
scored.right_bought: The right can be bought, but not cheaply, and not from owners who cannot read the data. Run-off books and receivership assets are sold through competitive processes, often brokered, where sophisticated buyers run their own diligence. Receivers and liquidators have fiduciary duties and use reinsurance collection specialists. Tiny cedents are the one place a discount might exist, but deal size there is small and regulators must approve portfolio transfers (Part VII in the UK, Form A or loss-portfolio-transfer approval in the US).
scored.buyer: For commutations, the counterparty is the solvent reinsurer itself (Swiss Re, Munich Re, Berkshire/NICO). For whole books, legacy consolidators buy: Enstar, Compre, R&Q (Randall & Quilter, distressed), Catalina, Fortitude Re, Marco, and Lloyd's RITC syndicates. These buyers are also the main competitors. Enstar, Compre and Resolute-type claims/TPA firms already run in-house teams for reinsurance recoverable collection and commutation.
scored.ladder: There is a ladder: recoverables collection, then run-off book acquisition, then a full legacy consolidator (Enstar-scale, low-to-mid single-digit billions of market cap, my estimate), then capital and reinsurance provision. It is a real path, but the ceiling is a niche consolidator, not a trillion-dollar chain. The runoff market is large: global non-life run-off reserves are often cited at ~$1T, from PwC's annual run-off survey as I recall it, unverified this run.
scored.fatal_flaw: The discovery signal is in the cedent's private claim files and treaty slips, not in public illegible data. The only public piece (NAIC Schedule F) already writes booked recoverables into legible fields. So there is no pre-purchase ML edge. On top of that, the post-discovery step (collecting from reinsurers disputing old long-tail claims through arbitration) is bespoke and expensive, not trivial. The realistic step-up is about 2-5x, and capitalised incumbents (Enstar, Compre) already do exactly this.
scored.one_line_reason: This is a real business, but it fails the Terranox shape. The data is private, the public field (Schedule F) already summarises the outcome, collection runs through arbitration and is hard, the step-up is about 2-5x rather than 10^3, and sophisticated consolidators own the niche.
sources: No web searches ran: the shared WebSearch budget for this turn was used up (both attempted queries were refused). All figures are estimates from prior knowledge and should be checked.
NAIC Annual Statement Schedule F (Ceded Reinsurance) structure: legible per-reinsurer recoverables fields (prior knowledge)
PwC Global Insurance Run-off Survey (~$1T non-life run-off reserves; prior knowledge, unverified)
Enstar Group, Compre, R&Q, Catalina, Fortitude Re annual reports and press releases on legacy acquisitions (prior knowledge)

scored.name: Orphan Subrogation Buyer
scored.one_line: Buy closed unsubrogated property claim files at 1-3 cents per paid dollar; ML links losses to defective products via recall, complaint and fire data; collect from manufacturers' insurers.
scored.unproven_right: Assigned subrogation rights from small mutuals, MGAs and self-insureds.
scored.proving_step: ML on narratives and photos vs CPSC/NHTSA/UL data; demand letter.
scored.proven_buyer: Product-liability insurers, funders, subrogation firms.
scored.public_data: SaferProducts.gov, CPSC recalls, NHTSA ODI, NFIRS, fire investigation reports, PACER.
scored.frame: The rung is: buy a closed, unpursued subrogation file, then prove product causation well enough that a defendant's insurer pays or a funder buys the claim. ML linking only matches files to recalls and complaints. It is perhaps 20-30% of the work (my estimate). Most of the work is physical and legal. A cause-and-origin expert has to examine the failed product. The evidence has to be preserved and its chain of custody kept. Spoliation defenses have to be beaten, the statute of limitations checked, and the case taken through demand, negotiation or suit. So the physical step is not abstracted. It is the bespoke-plant problem from the coal-mine counter-example, in legal form. Discovery is well below 80% of the work in this rung.
scored.step_up: Unproven: the candidate assumes 1-3 cents per paid dollar. I could not verify any market price for closed unsubrogated files (estimate). Proven: product-defect subrogation settlements often net about 20-50 cents per paid dollar after expert and legal costs. Contingency subrogation firms take about 25-33% (industry norm, estimate). That is roughly 10-30x on a file that hits. But the value is realised over 1-3 years of negotiation or litigation, not immediately on a desk 'hit'. A file that ML has only flagged sells to a funder for perhaps 2-5x what you paid. So the immediate step-up is about 3-10x.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Industry commentary commonly says insurers miss subrogation in about 10-15% of claims that had potential (frequently cited Verisk/Celent-type figures, recalled, not verified this session). So in a pool of closed files, perhaps 1-5% are viable product-defect recoveries (estimate). Proving one costs about $5k-25k for cause-and-origin and engineering experts plus legal work (estimate), not a cheap drill. ML can screen files cheaply. But the expensive step, expert causation, does not get cheaper, and most files fail on spoliation or the statute of limitations, which ML cannot fix. A realistic capex cut is 2-3x, not 10x.
scored.data: The public data is real and illegible: SaferProducts.gov narratives, CPSC recalls, NHTSA ODI complaints, NFIRS and PACER. But the key evidence is private: the insurer's own claim narrative, photos and adjuster notes, which you only get by buying the file. No legible public field records the outcome 'this loss was caused by product X'. That is good for the ML edge. The right can be bought, since subrogation rights are generally assignable. But owners are not unable to read their files. Small mutuals and MGAs already send files to no-cure-no-pay contingency subrogation firms and keep 67-75% of recoveries at zero cost. That puts a floor on the purchase price far above 1-3 cents for any file that is plausibly viable. Incumbents: subrogation firms such as Matthiesen Wickert & Lehrer and Ken Bates (from memory), plus Verisk ClaimSearch/ISO, CCC, Shift Technology and Clara Analytics' subrogation-detection AI.
scored.right_bought: Assigned subrogation rights in closed claims, bought from small mutuals, MGAs and self-insureds.
scored.buyer: Product-liability insurers pay as defendants, not as buyers of the rung's output. Litigation funders and subrogation firms would buy proven claims, but at modest multiples. The capital pool is thin compared with mine developers.
scored.ladder: The rungs above are: subrogation file acquisition, then a contingency subrogation firm, then product-liability litigation finance, then a mass-tort aggregator or a claims-data/insurtech carrier. The climb is legal and financial and capped at the size of the subrogation market (about $15-25B per year in US P&C recoveries, estimate). There is no path from start to finish into a trillion-dollar physical chain.
scored.fatal_flaw: Closed, unpursued files have usually lost the physical evidence (the product was discarded and the scene repaired), and many are past the statute of limitations (often 2-4 years). Spoliation and limitation, not discovery, decide whether a file recovers. ML cannot recover that evidence. On top of that, contingency subrogation firms already take viable files at no cost to the owner, so cheaply priced files are mostly the dead ones.
scored.one_line_reason: The ML linking is real, but recovery depends on physical evidence and litigation the model cannot replace. The step-up comes slowly through litigation, not immediately. And contingency firms already set the purchase price of viable files, so there is no Terranox-style frame where discovery is 95% of the work.
sources: No web searches ran: the shared web search budget for this turn was used up before this agent's queries ran. All numbers are estimates or recalled industry figures, not verified this session.
Recalled, unverified: industry commentary (Verisk/ISO, Celent) that about 10-15% of claims with subrogation potential are missed
Recalled: contingency subrogation fee norms of 25-33%
Public datasets named in the candidate: SaferProducts.gov, CPSC recalls, NHTSA ODI, NFIRS, PACER

scored.name: Dormant Judgment Revival / Revived Judgments
scored.one_line: Buy aged uncollected civil judgments at 1-3 cents from creditors who gave up; ML across scanned county, probate, UCC, deed, officer and registry records finds debtors who have since come into assets; renew, lien and collect, or sell liened judgments at 30-70% of face.
scored.unproven_right: Assigned renewable money judgments.
scored.proving_step: Debtor-asset record linkage, renewal filing and recorded lien/levy.
scored.proven_buyer: The company itself via title payoffs; judgment funds and specialty credit.
scored.public_data: County judgment indexes and abstracts, deed/mortgage scans, UCC, probate, SoS filings, FAA/USCG registries, PACER discharges.
scored.frame: The rung is buying aged judgments and turning them into collectible liens. Finding the debtor's assets is maybe 30-50% of the work (my estimate). The rest is physical and legal work that is not trivial: renewing judgments before state deadlines (5-20 years), recording abstracts county by county, garnishments and levies, debtor exams, homestead and wage exemption fights, bankruptcy discharge checks, plus FDCPA and state collection-agency or debt-buyer licensing. A lien on real property usually pays only when the property is sold or refinanced, and that can take years. So the enforcement and legal step is a big, bespoke share of the work. Structurally this is closer to the geothermal-in-coal-mines counter-example than to the drill hit. The buyers exist but pay low multiples: specialty credit, judgment funds, and the company itself through title payoffs.
scored.step_up: Estimate, not sourced, because my searches were blocked by the shared budget. Aged or 'zombie' consumer judgments and charged-off debt trade at roughly 0.5-3 cents per dollar of face (CFPB/FTC debt-buying studies report about 4 cents for fresh charge-offs and under 1 cent for old paper). A judgment where assets have been found and a lien recorded might sell for 20-50% of face, or collect 50-100% at a title payoff. That is about 10-50x on a hit, and only after years of carrying it, not right away. That is 10-100x territory (score 3), far from 10^3-10^4.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Estimate: about 2-5% of aged judgments recover something meaningful (the candidate's own number, which fits debt-buyer liquidation curves). But each proving attempt is cheap. A commercial skip trace or asset search through LexisNexis Accurint or TLO costs about $1-$25 per debtor, and a renewal or abstract filing costs about $20-$150 in court fees. Discovery is not the expensive bottleneck, so a 10x improvement in hit rate saves little discovery money. Most of the cost sits in enforcement and in carrying the asset over time. Note that the lever's 1/hit-rate cap (20-50x) is high, but that is not where the money is spent.
scored.data: Fatal for the ML edge. The signal is already legible and already commercialised. LexisNexis Accurint, TransUnion TLO, Experian, and title-plant vendors already merge deeds, mortgages, UCC filings, liens, judgments, bankruptcies (PACER), and vehicle, vessel and aircraft registries into searchable debtor reports. Large debt buyers such as Encore Capital and PRA Group, plus law-firm collection mills, run those reports with large-scale analytics and scoring. The outcome itself, a debtor now owning a home, is a legible field in county assessor and deed indexes. Buying the right is cheap and possible: creditors and dormant law-firm files sell or assign judgments readily. But the sellers are not unable to read the data. They gave up because collecting is uneconomic, not because the assets are invisible.
scored.right_bought: Yes. Money judgments can be assigned and are bought from original creditors, small businesses, and law firms, for about 1-10 cents per dollar of face in a competitive judgment-broker market (estimate).
scored.buyer: Mostly the company collects itself through title payoffs at sale or refinance, plus garnishment. Secondary buyers are judgment funds and specialty-credit buyers paying low multiples. The market is mature and crowded: Encore and PRA (each with about $1B or more in revenue), judgment-recovery brokers, and contingency collection attorneys taking 33-50%.
scored.ladder: The ladder is weak. Rungs above this one are debt buying at scale, then collection servicing, then perhaps originating credit. Debt buying is a regulated, reputation-toxic industry with low multiples, so it is not a path to a trillion-dollar company. The CFPB and state limits on suing over or reviving time-barred debt put a regulatory ceiling on growth.
scored.fatal_flaw: The asset-discovery signal is already legible and commoditised through LexisNexis and TLO skip-trace and asset reports that Encore, PRA and collection firms already use. The real bottleneck is legal enforcement and the years of carrying cost, which ML cannot shrink, not discovery.
scored.one_line_reason: Cheap rights and 10-50x step-ups exist, but discovery is cheap and already done by data aggregators, while the expensive, slow part is legal enforcement. That breaks the 95/5 frame and leaves no real ML edge.
sources: No web searches ran: the shared turn search budget was used up, so every number here is an estimate from prior knowledge
CFPB / FTC 'Structure and Practices of the Debt Buying Industry' (FTC 2013): fresh charge-offs about 4 cents per dollar, older paper well under 1 cent (from memory, not re-checked)
LexisNexis Accurint and TransUnion TLOxp product descriptions: commercial skip-trace and asset aggregation of deeds, UCC, liens, judgments and bankruptcies (from memory)
Encore Capital Group and PRA Group annual reports: scale and analytics in debt purchasing (from memory)

scored.name: Orphan Call Rights: pre-2008 RMBS/ABS clean-up calls
scored.one_line: Buy dormant clean-up call rights on 2004-07 trusts from defunct depositor/servicer estates; ML over 10-D exhibits and AVMs finds trusts worth calling; sell the right or fund the call.
scored.unproven_right: Optional-termination right held by defunct estates, $5-25k.
scored.proving_step: Confirm holder and exercisability from PSA; loan-level mark showing par plus margin.
scored.proven_buyer: Mortgage credit funds and dealer call programs.
scored.public_data: EDGAR 424B5, PSAs, 10-Ds, trustee portals, PACER, county data.
scored.frame: The rung is owning a clean-up call right and showing it can be exercised at a profit. Inside that rung, discovery (reading the PSA for who holds the call, checking the pool factor is under the threshold, usually 10% of original balance, and marking the remaining loans against par) is maybe 70-80% of the work. That is my estimate. The physical step is not trivial: to exercise the call you buy the whole remaining pool at par plus accrued interest plus REO value, often $10-100M of capital. You can push that onto a buyer by selling the right, but then the buyer needs that capital and a servicing setup, so the step is partly abstracted at best. A capitalised buyer exists: legacy call aggregators, credit funds and dealers.
scored.step_up: Unproven right: the $5-25k figure is the candidate's own assumption. I could not verify any actual sale prices for orphan call rights. Proven right: the value is roughly (market value of the remaining loans + REO - par - accrued interest - trustee and legal costs). That is my estimate. Example: a 2005 deal with $1B original balance at a 5% factor has $50M left. If seasoned reperforming loans are worth 102-104 because of home price gains since 2012, the call is worth about $1-2M gross before costs and the funding spread. Against a $15k purchase that is about 70-130x, so realistically 10-100x, with 10^3 only on outliers. Many 2004-07 subprime and Alt-A pools still mark below par (high delinquency, modified loans, losses), so their call is worth about zero.
scored.hit_rate_capex: The candidate claims a base hit rate of 5-15%; that is its assumption and I did not verify it. Cost per proving attempt is mainly lawyer and analyst time reading the PSA, and a loan-level mark from Intex/CoreLogic. My estimate is $2-10k per trust. That is cheap, not the expensive, mostly failing step the rubric requires. ML can cut maybe 2-3x off a small cost. The lever is weak because failed attempts cost little in the first place, so this is nothing like a $1M+ drill program.
scored.data: The data is public but only partly illegible: PSAs and 424B5s on EDGAR are long but readable by a good parser. The outcome is largely already in legible fields. Each 10-D gives the pool balance (so whether the call is exercisable is a simple ratio), plus delinquency, REO and losses. Loan-level performance for pre-Reg AB II deals is in Intex and CoreLogic, which every incumbent subscribes to. The ML edge over a factor-and-delinquency screen is probably small, the same failure pattern as the interconnection-queue and powered-brownfield hunts. Tracing a call holder through bankruptcy dockets on PACER is the one truly illegible piece.
scored.right_bought: In principle the right is bought, not claimed first-come. In practice: (1) in many PSAs the call belongs to the master servicer or servicer, and on a servicer default it passes to the successor servicer (Ocwen/Onity, Nationstar/Mr. Cooper, SPS, etc.), not to a defunct estate. (2) The big liquidations (Lehman/LBHI, ResCap, New Century, American Home, Aurora) ran asset sales and plan-trust monetisations that probably already sold or assigned their valuable call rights in 2012-2020; this is from memory and I did not verify it. (3) Where the call holder is the NIM or residual holder, those securities are already traded. Truly orphaned, unassigned, valuable calls that can be bought for $5-25k are probably rare.
scored.buyer: Legacy call-rights aggregators and resecuritisers. From memory (not verified this session), New Residential/Rithm has openly run a 'call rights' strategy since about 2016: collapse legacy trusts and resecuritise the seasoned loans. Mr. Cooper/Nationstar, Ocwen/Onity, PIMCO, Pretium, Waterfall, Lone Star and dealer call desks are also in this space. These buyers are real and well funded, but they are also the competitors already sweeping the same trusts.
scored.ladder: Steps up the ladder: call right, then fund the call, then resecuritise the reperforming loans, then own the servicing, then RPL/NPL whole-loan investing, then origination. The ladder exists, but it climbs into crowded, capital-heavy mortgage finance, where the edge is funding cost and not discovery. The starting pool is also finite and shrinking: 2004-07 trusts are paying down and getting called every year.
scored.fatal_flaw: The outcome is already legible and the market is already swept. Whether a call is exercisable is a ratio of 10-D pool balances, and whether it is in the money comes from delinquency fields plus Intex loan-level data that incumbents subscribe to. A decade of call-rights aggregation (Rithm/NRZ, the servicers inheriting calls, estate sales) has probably taken the valuable calls. The orphaned rights left over are likely out of the money, the proving step is too cheap for ML to add much, and you need tens of millions to exercise.
scored.one_line_reason: This is a real but mature niche: the call trigger is in legible 10-D fields, the valuable rights have mostly sat with servicers or been sold by estates already, proving is cheap so the ML lever is small, and the realistic step-up is 10-100x, not 10^3-10^4.
