scored.name: Dirt Bond Recovery: defaulted land-secured muni bonds
scored.one_line: Buy defaulted Mello-Roos/CDD/MUD/PID bonds at 5-15 cents where ML shows collateral has regained value; drive foreclosure or builder sale.
scored.unproven_right: Defaulted bond positions on EMMA.
scored.proving_step: Reconcile disclosures and delinquency rolls with entitlements and builder activity.
scored.proven_buyer: Homebuilders, land bankers, high-yield muni funds.
scored.public_data: EMMA, assessor and recorder data, delinquency rolls, permits, CDIAC.
scored.frame: Rung: owning a defaulted land-secured bond position (bondholder claim on special-tax/assessment liens) and resolving it through foreclosure or a builder sale. I estimate analysis is about 40-50% of the work inside this rung. The rest is physical, legal and political: bondholder direction and consent across fragmented holders, indenture trustee actions, judicial foreclosure (in California, Mello-Roos foreclosure is a court process that runs 1-3 years), and paying the carry on land while waiting. Unlike drilling, the proving step cannot be abstracted. Value arrives through litigation and a land sale, not in one cheap discrete event.
scored.step_up: From memory, not verified: the 5-15 cent entry is plausible for deeply distressed CDD and Mello-Roos paper in a down cycle such as Florida 2009-2012. The claim is capped at par plus accrued interest and penalties, so the theoretical maximum is about 7-20x and that requires full recovery from a 5-cent entry. Realistic resolved recoveries on land-secured defaults are commonly 30-70 cents (my recollection of rating-agency and CDIAC-era commentary; not verified this run). That gives a realistic step-up of about 2-6x. This is a bond claim with a hard ceiling, not an option on an asset that can be worth 10^4x.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Estimate: the base 'hit rate' is high, not low. Most defaulted dirt bonds recover something meaningful because special-tax and assessment liens sit at parity with property taxes, ahead of mortgages. So 1/hit-rate caps the lever at roughly 1.5-3x. Cost per attempt is the full position cost (millions of dollars) plus legal, foreclosure and carry costs (estimate $0.5-3M per deal). ML picks better positions; it does not make each attempt 10x cheaper.
scored.data: The data is public and partly illegible: EMMA continuing-disclosure PDFs, delinquency rolls, county recorder and assessor data, permits, and CDIAC Mello-Roos annual reports (California). Much of the outcome is already in legible form, though. EMMA material event notices flag payment defaults and draws on the reserve fund. CDIAC reports carry delinquency rates and appraised value-to-lien ratios. Continuing disclosures list absorption and builder ownership. Sellers are institutional high-yield muni desks and distressed funds that read this data professionally. These are not owners who cannot read their own data, and the bonds trade OTC with bid-ask spreads that already price collateral recovery.
scored.right_bought: Yes, positions are bought on the secondary muni market, not claimed for free. But they are bought from sophisticated counterparties: high-yield muni funds, insurers, and occasionally retail via broker-dealers. That makes a large information-asymmetry discount unlikely. The deal flow is also cyclical and small; there are few live defaulted land-secured issues outside housing downturns. Retail-held odd lots could carry some mispricing (estimate).
scored.buyer: Homebuilders (public and private), land bankers (e.g., Millrose-type vehicles, Varde, Lennar's old Rialto platform), high-yield muni funds, and distressed credit funds. These buyers have capital, but several are also direct competitors for the same bonds.
scored.ladder: The ladder is plausible: bondholder, then owner of the land after foreclosure, then entitled land banker, then lot developer, then homebuilder or master-planned-community developer. Rialto Capital (Lennar) ran a version of this after 2008, buying distressed CDD bonds and taking control of land. The ladder is real but it leads into homebuilding, which is a low-multiple, capital-intensive, cyclical business. It is a large company, not a trillion-dollar path.
scored.fatal_flaw: The payoff is capped at par on a bond claim. A realistic step-up of 2-6x (theoretical maximum ~7-20x) is two to three orders of magnitude short of the 10^4 jump. On top of that, the base recovery rate is already high (no low-hit-rate lever), the sellers are sophisticated distressed-muni desks reading the same EMMA and CDIAC data, and the resolution step (foreclosure, holder consent, land carry) is slow and costly rather than trivial.
scored.one_line_reason: This is a distressed-credit strategy with capped upside, high base recovery and a sophisticated seller base. Discovery is not 80%+ of the rung and the step-up is ~2-6x, not 10^4.

scored.name: Orphan Catalog / Chain of Title: dormant legacy media rights cleared for licensing and adaptation
scored.one_line: Buy murky surviving copyrights of defunct publishers, labels, distributors and photo agencies and out-of-print novels and characters by quitclaim; ML over CCE renewals, card catalog, assignments and succession records proves ownership and non-public-domain status; sell E&O-insurable rights to catalogue funds, studios, stock libraries and AI-data licensors.
scored.unproven_right: Quitclaims of uncertain value, $1-50k.
scored.proving_step: Title reconstruction and renewal screening, title opinion and E&O; registration and recorded transfers.
scored.proven_buyer: Concord, Reservoir, Round Hill, Primary Wave, Shamrock, Getty, Netflix, Amazon MGM, Warner, Legendary, Skydance, AI training licensees.
scored.public_data: CCE scans (Internet Archive, Stanford renewals), Copyright Public Records System, Virtual Card Catalog, AFI catalog, SoS records, PACER.
scored.frame: Rung is "buy a quitclaim, then prove title and non-PD status to a standard an E&O insurer will write on". Inside that rung, title reconstruction is perhaps 60-70% of the work (my estimate). Turning the cleared right into money is not trivial: someone has to pitch it, package it and secure an adaptation or sync deal, because catalogue funds and studios pay for demand, not for clean paperwork. So discovery is not 80%+ of the sellable frame. The buyer is capitalised (Concord, Reservoir, studios), but it buys proven commercial IP, and clean title is only a precondition.
scored.step_up: Estimates, not sourced (search budget was used up before I could search). A quitclaim from heirs or a defunct-company successor costs maybe $1-50k. Clearing it adds value only if the work has demand. An obscure out-of-print novel's option or remake right typically trades at $5-100k, so the step-up is roughly 1-10x. Rare hits with a recognisable character or song could reach $1M+, i.e. 20-100x+. Most cleared orphans are worth close to the cost of clearing them. A typical step-up of about 3-10x, with a fat tail, scores 2. Nothing near the 10^4 land step-up.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Estimates and recalled figures, not sourced this run. A copyright title search or report from firms like Thomson CompuMark or clearance attorneys costs about $500-5k per work (my estimate), so proving is cheap, not drill-expensive. The base renewal rate for 1923-1963 US registrations is low, about 7% for books and about 15% overall (recalled from the 1961 Ringer study for the Copyright Office). But a non-renewed work is public domain: the failed screen leaves nothing to own, not a cheaper path to a hit. The scarce thing is commercial value, not provable title, and ML over records does not raise the odds that a work has demand. ML would only cut the cost of an already cheap step, so the lever on what matters is small.
scored.data: From memory, not checked this run. The public records are partly illegible: CCE scans, pre-1978 card catalogue, recorded assignments, state corporate records, PACER. But the key outcome (renewed or not, so PD or not) is already largely extracted into legible form. For books, the NYPL CCE renewal transcription (structured data on GitHub) and the Stanford Copyright Renewal Database cover the renewals. HathiTrust's CRMS has made rights determinations on hundreds of thousands of volumes, and the Copyright Office's Virtual Card Catalog and the CPRS digitisation are making the rest searchable. Chain of succession after corporate death (bankruptcy, asset sales, heirs) is genuinely scattered and illegible, which is the real residual edge. Rights holders such as heirs and liquidators often cannot read their own position, so cheap quitclaims are plausible.
scored.right_bought: Yes, rights are bought, not claimed first-come. Quitclaims or assignments come from heirs, bankruptcy trustees, liquidators and the successors of defunct publishers, labels and agencies, plausibly for low thousands. But a quitclaim conveys only whatever the seller actually holds, and competing heirs or termination rights can undermine it: author or heir termination under 17 USC 203/304 can claw back transfers 35-56 years later.
scored.buyer: Catalogue funds (Concord, Reservoir, Round Hill, Primary Wave, Shamrock) buy cash-flowing catalogues on earnings multiples, not dormant orphans with no royalty history. Studios and streamers option known or adaptable IP at modest option fees. Stock libraries (Getty) buy at low per-asset prices. AI-data licensors pay by volume (cents to dollars per work), not per-title premiums. So the buyer exists but pays for demand, not for clean title.
scored.ladder: The ladder exists: clear rights, then license or option, then develop or produce adaptations (a Boom/Dark Horse-style IP house), then own a studio or catalogue platform. But the upper rungs are creative, hit-driven production, the bespoke and hard part, like building the geothermal plant in the coal-mine counter-example. Winning title clearing does not compound into an edge at producing hits.
scored.fatal_flaw: Value comes from demand, not from finding the title. The works worth owning (known characters, hit songs, notable films) already have identified owners who know what they hold. The truly orphaned, unrenewed or murky works are mostly public domain or commercially worthless. Clearing title is a cheap precondition, not the value-creating discovery, and much of the renewal outcome is already in legible databases (NYPL, Stanford, HathiTrust CRMS).
scored.one_line_reason: Title clearing is cheap, and much of the renewal outcome is already in public databases. Value depends on commercial demand and creative adaptation, not on finding the title, so there is no rung where discovery is 80%+ with a 10^3x step-up.

scored.name: Embedded Dead-Vendor Code Rights
scored.one_line: Buy copyrights in RTOS, TCP/IP, codec and bootloader libraries from defunct embedded vendors; binary fingerprinting over public firmware proves unlicensed shipping use; sell portfolio or settle with OEMs.
scored.unproven_right: Copyright and licence rights, $10-100k.
scored.proving_step: Function-level binary similarity across firmware images; letters to OEMs.
scored.proven_buyer: IP holdcos, litigation funders, OEMs, Wind River/Siemens.
scored.public_data: OEM firmware portals, FCC filings, firmware archives, Copyright Office catalog, SEC filings.
scored.frame: The rung is: own a copyright or licence in dead-vendor embedded code and prove it is used in shipping firmware without a licence. Spotting that the code is present (binary similarity) is maybe 30-40% of the work and is cheap. Most of the work and money goes into the step that is not trivial or abstracted: (a) showing a given OEM has no licence, which depends on private contracts, perpetual buyouts and source licences that carry over when the assets are sold; (b) proving clean chain of title, since dead-vendor IP goes through bankruptcy estates and asset sales; (c) litigation or credible threat of it to collect. That last step is the 'bespoke geothermal plant' of this idea. My estimate: discovery is 20-35% of the work inside the rung, well below the 80% bar.
scored.step_up: My estimate, not sourced (search budget was used up): a dead-vendor RTOS or stack copyright could be bought for $10k-100k (the candidate's own range; plausible for estate or abandoned IP). Once infringement is proven, value is capped by actual damages, because statutory damages need registration before the infringement (17 USC 412), and dead vendors often did not register or registered old versions. Actual damages are roughly lost per-unit royalties, typically cents to a few dollars per unit for embedded stacks. Infringement older than 3 years is also time-barred. A realistic portfolio settlement is $0.1M-5M, so roughly 3-50x on a hit. 100-1000x happens only in rare high-volume cases, and SCO-style failures show the downside.
scored.hit_rate_capex: My estimates, unsourced. Detection: function-level binary similarity (Ghidra BSim, BinDiff, BinaryAI) is already commodity and cheap, about $1k-10k of compute and analyst time per firmware corpus scan, with a high detection rate for statically linked libraries. The expensive, mostly-failing step is collection. A copyright suit through trial typically costs $1M-5M per case (AIPLA survey range, from memory). I guess most targets turn out to hold a valid licence, or have a licence/laches defence, or are not worth suing. ML does not move that hit rate, because the deciding fact (does a licence exist) is not in the binary. The lever on real capex is about 1-1.5x, not 10x.
scored.data: Public: firmware images (OEM portals, FCC equipment authorisations sometimes include internal photos but rarely firmware), firmware archives, Copyright Office catalog, SEC filings. Firmware is huge and hard to read, which fits. But the outcome that matters, whether the OEM has a licence, sits in private contracts and cannot be seen in public data. So ML can show the code is used, not that the use is unlicensed. That is the reverse of what the gold rubric needs. Incumbents already extract the 'used' signal: Black Duck/Synopsys, Finite State, ONEKEY and NetRise do SBOM binary composition, and SFC/gpl-violations do the same for open-source enforcement. Buying the right: yes, you can buy it cheaply from estates or acquirers who do not track it, but chain of title is often murky (SCO v. Novell lost on exactly who owned the Unix copyrights).
scored.right_bought: Copyright plus licensor rights in dead-vendor embedded libraries, bought from bankruptcy estates, liquidators, or acquirers that abandoned the product line. My estimate is $10k-100k. You take them subject to every existing licence.
scored.buyer: Litigation funders and IP holdcos (they fund patent trolls, much less copyright, because damages without registration are small), OEMs paying settlements, and possibly Wind River or Siemens buying defensively. None of these are capitalised buyers who reliably pay a fixed step-up for the 'proven' asset the way a mine developer pays for a drill hit. They price in litigation risk.
scored.ladder: Weak. The rungs above (an embedded software vendor or a compliance/licensing business) do not compound off a troll-style asset base. Enforcing against OEMs also poisons the customer base you would need to climb to. There is no clear path to running the whole chain.
scored.fatal_flaw: The deciding outcome (unlicensed use) is in private contracts, not in public firmware. Binary fingerprinting proves the code is used, which incumbents' SBOM tools already do, but not that the use is unlicensed. Collecting then needs costly litigation, where damages are limited to actual royalties if there was no pre-infringement registration and claims are cut off after 3 years. So the work inside the rung is legal, not discovery.
scored.one_line_reason: Detection is cheap and commoditised. The value sits in proving no licence exists and in litigating, which ML cannot touch, and copyright damages on dead embedded code are small, giving roughly 3-50x with troll-style risk.

scored.name: Fielded-system firmware and ROM rights for obsolete controllers
scored.one_line: Buy firmware, ROM and bitstream IP of defunct industrial, medical and rail board makers; ML finds captive installed bases; sell to OEM successors and MRO firms.
scored.unproven_right: Copyrights and trade secrets from estates for nominal sums.
scored.proving_step: ML over MAUDE/510(k), transit and utility procurement, rate cases for part numbers.
scored.proven_buyer: Industrial MROs, OEM successors, transit agencies, utilities, obsolescence roll-ups.
scored.public_data: FDA 510(k)/MAUDE, procurement portals, PUC rate cases, PACER, Copyright Office.
scored.frame: The rung is "own the firmware/ROM/bitstream copyright for a defunct board and show that a captive installed base depends on it". Finding the installed base is maybe 60-70% of the work (my estimate). The rest is not trivial: tracing title through bankruptcy trustees, estates and asset buyers, recovering the actual source or binaries and toolchains (often lost), and qualifying the parts (FDA design history file, rail SIL, utility qualification). Selling a right doesn't finish the job either. The buyer usually wants a part it can install, so you end up building boards, which is the bespoke physical step the coal-mine geothermal counter-example warns against. A capitalised buyer exists (Rochester-style aftermarket makers, obsolescence roll-ups, OEM successors), but it buys qualified supply, not a bare copyright.
scored.step_up: Unproven: a nominal estate or trustee price, maybe $0-$5k per product line (my estimate, no source; no web search ran). Proven: a licence or sale to an MRO or OEM successor, plausibly $50k-$1M for a line with a real captive base (my estimate). That is roughly 10-200x on paper, but it is illiquid and there is no market price for a proven right. The value only shows up once you add manufacturing and qualification. Realistic immediate step-up on a "hit" is 3-30x (my estimate), not 10^3.
scored.hit_rate_capex: The proving step is desk research over MAUDE, 510(k), procurement and rate-case records. It costs roughly $1k-$10k in analyst time per target (my estimate) and is not an expensive physical attempt like a $200k+ drill hole. Because the base cost is already low, ML has no 10x capex cut to deliver. The real costs are title clearance and requalification, and ML barely touches those. I found no published base hit rate. Every web search this turn failed because the shared search budget was used up, so all figures here are my estimates.
scored.data: The data is public but scattered: MAUDE and 510(k) narratives, transit and utility RFPs that name part numbers, PUC rate cases, PACER bankruptcy schedules and Copyright Office records. It is not summarised in a legible "installed base" field, so there is some ML edge in joining these sources. One weakness: the parties who actually feel the pain (the asset owners themselves, and broker or repair houses like Radwell or EU Automation, named from memory) already know their own installed base without any ML.
scored.right_bought: Rights can be bought, from bankruptcy trustees, estates and asset buyers, often for nominal sums. But the chain of title is often murky (code sold off with other assets, or work-for-hire with the customer owning it) and the source code or binaries may be gone. Firmware copyright is also weak protection: repair shops dump and clone ROMs, and DMCA repair exemptions and interoperability defences undercut enforcement. So the owned asset is hard to defend.
scored.buyer: Authorized aftermarket manufacturers (for example Rochester Electronics, which licenses discontinued IP from many OEMs; from memory), obsolescence roll-ups, OEM successors, and transit agencies and utilities facing qualification or replacement costs. These buyers mainly pay for qualified physical supply or service. Few pay meaningful sums for a bare copyright.
scored.ladder: The ladder above the right is: own IP, then remanufacture and qualify boards, then become an authorized aftermarket supplier, then do life-extension or emulation retrofits, then become an obsolescence-management platform. It is real, but it is a niche ceiling: a likely multi-hundred-million-dollar outcome (Rochester-sized), not a path to a trillion. Each rung is bespoke per product line.
scored.fatal_flaw: A proven right has no liquid buyer that pays a step-up for the right itself. The value appears only after you build and qualify replacement hardware for each product line, and that is bespoke and physical (the same failure as the coal-mine geothermal example). The ML proving step is also already cheap desk research, so there is no expensive, mostly-failing attempt for ML to make 10x cheaper.
scored.one_line_reason: This is a buy-and-build obsolescence play with illiquid 10-100x upside per line. The value comes from building and qualifying replacement hardware, not from discovery, and the proving step is too cheap for ML to give a 10x capex cut. Weak against the rubric.

scored.name: Predictive Generic Domain Acquisition
scored.one_line: Register or buy domains ML predicts startups will want and sell at end-user prices.
scored.unproven_right: Registrations at ~$10/yr or expiring names, first-come.
scored.proving_step: Name-demand model; a funded company asks.
scored.proven_buyer: Startups via Afternic/Dan/Sedo.
scored.public_data: ICANN CZDS, NameBio, Crunchbase/YC, arXiv/GitHub/USPTO text, drop lists.
scored.rough_step_up: 10^3-10^4x per name, low portfolio return; first-come, legible.
scored.frame: The rung is "hold a domain until an end user buys it". Picking the name is close to 100% of the work, and the physical step (registering it) costs about $10 and is fully abstracted. Buyers do exist (startups selling through Afternic, Dan or Sedo), but each is a small, scattered retail buyer, not a capitalised developer paying a known multiple on proof. The "proving" is also not a single event you can control: you wait for an inbound offer that may never come, and you pay renewal fees the whole time.
scored.step_up: From memory, not searched this turn: hand registration costs about $8-12/yr. Aftermarket end-user sales on NameBio for non-premium .com names commonly fall around $1k-5k, with a median in the low thousands. That is roughly a 100-500x step-up per sale (my estimate), not 10^3-10^4. A 10^3x+ result ($10k+) happens only for the rare premium name. Expiring names bought via drop-catch or backorder start at about $59-69 (NameJet/SnapNames/DropCatch minimums) and often go to auction, which cuts the multiple.
scored.hit_rate_capex: From memory, not searched: the commonly cited sell-through rate for domain-investor portfolios is about 1-2% of names per year (Domain Name Wire / Afternic investor commentary). One attempt costs about $10/yr of renewal, so the attempt is cheap and the cost is carrying cost, not an expensive drill. The lever is in theory capped near 50-100x by the 1% base rate. In practice, a good model has to beat thousands of experienced domainers and existing AI name-generation and appraisal tools (GoDaddy appraisal, Estibot), so the realistic gain is perhaps 2-3x (estimate). Capex is small to begin with, so cutting it 10x unlocks little.
scored.data: Nothing here is illegible. Zone files (CZDS), drop lists, NameBio sales comps, Crunchbase/YC launches and USPTO filings are all structured, machine-readable and already mined by drop-catch operators and domainers. The outcome is already summarised in legible fields: NameBio publishes the sale prices, and appraisal tools publish estimated values.
scored.right_bought: No. New registrations are first-come at a fixed registry price, and expiring names go to competitive drop-catch auctions. There is no owner who cannot read their data and would sell you the right cheaply. Names aimed at what specific startups will want also carry UDRP/ACPA cybersquatting risk when they track trademarks or company names.
scored.buyer: Early-stage startups and SMBs buying through Afternic (GoDaddy), Dan.com and Sedo. They are fragmented, price-sensitive and often switch to an alternative name or TLD (.ai, .io, get-prefix) instead of paying.
scored.ladder: Weak. The rungs above are marketplace, registrar and registry, and those are dominated by GoDaddy (which owns Afternic and Dan), Identity Digital and Verisign under ICANN-regulated contracts. The domain aftermarket is about $2-4B a year (estimate), and there is no trillion-dollar chain to climb.
scored.fatal_flaw: The rights are first-come and contested, and the data is fully legible. Thousands of domainers and drop-catchers already work the same structured zone files and NameBio comps, so there is no illegible signal and no ignorant seller to buy from cheaply. On top of that, the assets carry a 1-2% sell-through rate, ongoing renewal costs, and a small market with no ladder above it.
scored.one_line_reason: Discovery is the whole game here, but it is played on public, legible data in a crowded, first-come market, with typical step-ups of about 100-500x, a ~1% sell-through rate and no large chain above, so it fails C4 and C5.

scored.name: Orphaned Consumer Brands and Discontinued SKUs (food, CPG, cosmetics, OTC)
scored.one_line: Buy trademarks, trade dress and formulas of discontinued or orphaned consumer brands and SKUs from bankrupt estates, family owners and conglomerates pruning tails, plus lapsed marks with surviving recall; ML scores residual demand; a co-packed or contract-manufactured limited relaunch proves sell-through; sell or license to CPG and revival buyers.
scored.unproven_right: Trademark, formula and trade-dress packages for $5k-500k, or assignments with goodwill from owners unaware of residual value.
scored.proving_step: Demand score from TSDR, Wayback, Reddit/Change.org, eBay sold, Trends, reviews; legality check against FDA NDC/OTC/MoCRA where relevant; 5-20k unit co-packer pre-order drop.
scored.proven_buyer: Hostess/J.M. Smucker, Utz, Campbell's, KDP, Unilever, Henkel, Church & Dwight, Prestige Consumer Healthcare, B&G Foods, Hometown Food, River West Brands, Retrobrands, Hilco Brands, Authentic/Marquee/WHP.
scored.public_data: USPTO bulk data, TSDR specimens, TTAB, PACER schedules, Wayback, Reddit, Change.org, eBay sold, Amazon/Walmart reviews, Google Trends, FDA NDC/MoCRA listings.
scored.rough_step_up: ~20-500x; nostalgia partly legible and incumbents do it by intuition.
scored.frame: The candidate rung is "own a dormant consumer mark and prove residual demand with a limited relaunch." Inside that rung, discovery (scoring residual demand) is my estimate of only about 20-30% of the work. The other 70-80% is physical and commercial: re-creating or reformulating the product, finding a co-packer with minimum order quantities, packaging and trade dress, FDA/MoCRA/OTC compliance, and then the real proof, which is retail slotting and repeat purchase rather than a one-off nostalgia pre-order. A buyer pays for proven velocity and distribution, not for a pre-order spike. This is the geothermal-in-coal-mines shape: building the bespoke product business is much harder than finding the right dormant mark. There is no rung where the physical step is abstracted the way drilling is for Terranox.
scored.step_up: No new numbers were retrieved because the shared web search budget was used up. The figures below come from my prior knowledge and are labelled as such. Dormant or abandoned marks and bankruptcy-estate IP for small CPG brands usually trade for about $5k-$500k; estate IP auctions run by Hilco and similar firms sometimes reach low millions for recognised names (estimate). Hostess is the famous outlier: Apollo/Metropoulos bought the snack brands for about $410M in 2013, Hostess went public at roughly $2.3B in 2016, and Smucker paid about $5.6B in 2023. But that step-up came from a rebuilt plant, distribution and operations, not from proving demand. A typical revival that reaches about $2-10M in sales might sell at 1-3x revenue, so roughly $2-30M. Over a $25k-250k basis that is about 10-100x on a hit, but only after years of operating. A pre-order drop alone proves little, and the realistic immediate step-up is about 3-10x (estimate).
scored.hit_rate_capex: These are estimates from widely cited industry figures, not verified this run. The commonly quoted figure (attributed to Nielsen and others) is that about 70-85% of new CPG products fail within a year or two. Nostalgia revivals with known demand probably do better, so I estimate a 20-40% base rate of reaching durable sell-through. One proving attempt costs an estimated $50k-$300k: formulation, a co-packer run of 5-20k units with MOQs, packaging, compliance and marketing for the drop. Retail proof costs much more (slotting fees, broker fees, working capital). With a base hit rate of 20-40%, ML can lift hits by at most about 2.5-5x, not 10x. Most of the cost is manufacturing and go-to-market, which ML does not reduce.
scored.data: Mostly the signal is legible. Nostalgia demand already shows up plainly in Reddit threads, Change.org petitions, Google Trends, Facebook groups and eBay sold listings, and incumbents and revival specialists already use these, often by intuition. USPTO TSDR status fields state the outcome directly (live/dead/abandoned/cancelled, plus the filing basis). Some illegibility does remain: specimens, scanned PACER schedules and unregistered common-law rights. Rights can be bought. Dead marks can sometimes be re-filed for nothing, but that is contested ground because of residual goodwill (the Retrobrands litigation history is my recollection, not checked this run). Estate or conglomerate packages that include formulas must be bought. Sellers such as conglomerates pruning their tail SKUs know their sales data better than any outside ML model, so the information asymmetry runs against the buyer.
scored.right_bought: Trademark, trade dress and formula packages bought from bankrupt estates (via Hilco and similar auctions), family owners, or conglomerates pruning tail SKUs, for an estimated $5k-$500k. Alternatively, a fresh intent-to-use filing on abandoned marks, which carries legal risk where goodwill survives.
scored.buyer: The likely buyers are J.M. Smucker (Hostess), B&G Foods, Hometown Food, Utz, Campbell's, Prestige Consumer Healthcare, Church & Dwight, and brand-licensing aggregators such as Authentic, Marquee and WHP. They are capitalised, but they buy proven revenue and distribution at revenue or EBITDA multiples, not pre-order evidence.
scored.ladder: Above the mark, the rungs are: a relaunched brand, then a portfolio brand house (as Hometown Food and B&G Foods are), then owned manufacturing and distribution, then a CPG conglomerate. The path is real, but it is a roll-up and operating business with ordinary CPG margins. It does not compound the way a discovery engine does.
scored.fatal_flaw: The proving step is not discovery. It means rebuilding a physical CPG business (formulation, co-packing, compliance, retail distribution, repeat purchase), and that is where nearly all the cost and failure sits. Meanwhile the demand signal (nostalgia) is already legible and already worked by specialists such as Retrobrands, River West, Hilco and Hometown. This is the coal-mine-geothermal counter-example applied to brands.
scored.one_line_reason: Finding the dormant brand is easy and legible, while relaunching it is the expensive, failure-prone physical work. The step-up is about 10-100x and only after operating, and the hit-rate lever is capped at about 3-5x.

scored.name: Dormant spirits brands from closed craft distilleries
scored.one_line: Buy trademark, COLA history and recipe of dead craft spirits brands; ML scores residual demand; one contract-distilled batch proves depletion; sell to spirits majors.
scored.unproven_right: Mark, COLA history, recipe and goodwill, $5-50k.
scored.proving_step: ML over TTB COLA, license closures, reviews, auctions; 3-6 month single-state depletion test.
scored.proven_buyer: Diageo, Pernod, Sazerac, Campari, Brown-Forman, spirits PE.
scored.public_data: TTB Public COLA Registry, TSDR, state ABC closures, DSP permits, competitions, Unicorn/Whisky Auctioneer.
scored.frame: The rung is "own a dormant spirits mark and prove repeat demand with one contract-distilled batch". Inside that rung, discovery (picking which dead brand still has demand) is maybe 10-20% of the work (my estimate). The other 80-90% is commercial and physical: re-filing the COLA, sourcing and contract distilling liquid (aged whiskey cannot be recreated in 3-6 months), packaging, getting through the three-tier system (distributor, wholesaler, retailer), getting retail placement and paying for marketing to move product off shelves (depletion). This is the same shape as the geothermal-in-a-coal-mine counter-example: building the brand again is much harder than finding it. The physical step is not trivial or abstracted.
scored.step_up: Unproven right: the candidate assumes $5-50k. Many lapsed marks are close to free, since a dead mark can be cancelled for non-use and re-filed for about $350 per class at the USPTO, and bankruptcy brand assets often sell for low five figures (estimate, not verified this run). Proven right: majors pay about $1,000-6,000 per 9L case of annual volume. For example, Casamigos sold for about $1B on roughly 170k cases (from memory, not verified this run). But those prices apply to brands doing 20k-100k+ cases with several years of growth. A 3-6 month single-state test might show a few hundred to about 2,000 cases, which a small roll-up or PE buyer might value at $0.2-2M (estimate). Measured against total cash in (right plus $150-500k launch cost, my estimate), the real step-up is about 1-10x, and only around 10-100x measured against the mark alone. It is not 10^3-10^4.
scored.hit_rate_capex: I estimate the base success rate of reviving a dead craft brand to the point where an acquirer wants it at under 5%. Most craft brands die because of weak demand or distribution failure, and closures were rising in 2024-25 as the craft spirits sector contracted. Cost per proving attempt is about $150-500k (estimate covering liquid, packaging, COLA and state registration, distributor programming, marketing). ML can screen out obviously dead brands, but most of that cost is go-to-market spend that ML cannot reduce. The lever on capex is maybe 1.5-2x, not 10x. No source was verified this run because the shared search budget was exhausted.
scored.data: TTB's Public COLA Registry, USPTO TSDR, state ABC license data and auction results are public. They are messy, but they are mostly structured and searchable rather than truly illegible. The outcome (lapsed mark, surrendered DSP permit, closure) is already written into legible status fields, which is the failure pattern seen in earlier hunts. Residual-demand signals (reviews, secondary-market auction prices) are visible to anyone, and auction prices actually push the price of cult dead brands up (for example, closed-distillery bottles trade at premiums). Owners of dead brands, often bankruptcy trustees or founders, can read this data as well as anyone. There is no illegibility edge.
scored.right_bought: Partly bought, partly free. Rights can be bought from founders or bankruptcy trustees, but abandoned marks can often just be re-filed after cancellation for non-use, so they work more like free first-come rights. The recipe and goodwill have little value without the original aged liquid and distribution relationships.
scored.buyer: Diageo, Pernod, Campari, Brown-Forman and Sazerac are capitalised, but they buy proven velocity at scale (tens of thousands of cases, multi-year growth) or take minority stakes through incubators such as Diageo's Distill Ventures. They do not buy one-state, one-batch tests. The realistic buyers for this rung are small roll-ups and spirits PE, at low multiples.
scored.ladder: The rungs exist: own marks, then contract production, then your own distillery, then a portfolio, then distribution. That is a real path to a multi-brand spirits house (Sazerac and Proximo are examples). But each rung above is capital-heavy, slow brand building, and none of it is discovery-led. And spirits majors top out around $10-50B market cap, not a trillion-dollar path.
scored.fatal_flaw: The proving step is go-to-market (distribution plus marketing spend to drive depletion), not discovery. It costs most of the money, ML cannot shrink it, and building the brand is harder than finding it, the same as the coal-mine geothermal case. Acquirers also do not pay step-up prices for a one-batch, one-state test.
scored.one_line_reason: Finding the dead brand is the easy part. Proving demand means rebuilding a consumer brand through three-tier distribution and marketing spend, so discovery is about 15% of the rung, the step-up on cash invested is about 1-10x, and the ML lever on capex is under 2x.

scored.name: Revival Moulds: toy and consumer tooling plus dormant IP
scored.one_line: Buy injection moulds and lapsed character/brand rights from liquidated toy makers at scrap; ML ranks collector demand; preorder proves it; sell to reissue houses.
scored.unproven_right: Moulds plus brand rights, $1-20k per line.
scored.proving_step: ML on resale and forums, title clearing, preorder campaign.
scored.proven_buyer: Super7, Basic Fun, Funko, Hasbro/Mattel, River West Brands.
scored.public_data: eBay/WorthPoint sold, TSDR abandoned, Virtual Card Catalog, bankruptcy schedules, Kickstarter/Backerkit.
scored.frame: Rung: own a mould plus dormant brand and prove demand with a preorder, then license or sell to a reissue house. Discovery is roughly 30-40% of the work inside this rung (my estimate). The rest is not trivial: clearing the chain of title (character copyrights run 95 years for work-for-hire and usually sit with Hasbro, Mattel or a licensor, not with the liquidated maker), refurbishing old steel tools, paying Chinese factory MOQs, and running the campaign. The physical step is not abstracted the way drilling is.
scored.step_up: Estimate (no search result to back it): unproven mould plus lapsed mark trades at $1-20k, at or near scrap value. A proven line with a funded preorder might sell or license for $50-500k, usually as a royalty of about 8-12% of wholesale with a modest minimum guarantee, not an outright purchase. That is about 10-50x on a hit, and the realised value mostly arrives as royalty stream rather than an immediate revaluation. Nothing like 10^4.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Estimate from prior knowledge: Kickstarter's overall funding success rate is about 40% (Kickstarter public stats). A nostalgia toy preorder costs about $10-50k all in (sculpt/tool refurb, samples, marketing, title legal). Base hit rate of 30-50% caps the ML lever at about 2-3x, not 10x. The expensive part (title and tooling) is not cut by ML.
scored.data: The signal is mostly legible already. eBay and WorthPoint sold prices are structured, searchable price-demand data that every collector, Super7 and Funko scout already reads. TSDR abandonment status is a legible field. Bankruptcy schedules list IP and tooling as assets with values. Kickstarter/Backerkit results are public and legible. ML adds little over a sorted eBay sold-price query. Rights: abandoned trademarks are free first-come to re-file (no purchase moat, and anyone can file). The real rights (character copyright) are not lapsed and are held by sophisticated owners who license directly to Super7. Moulds are often scrapped or lost (e.g. many vintage Kenner tools were destroyed).
scored.right_bought: Moulds can be bought cheaply in liquidation. The brand is either free (abandoned trademark re-filed first-come) or not available (copyright held by a live major). Neither gives a defensible bought right that a non-reader owner is underpricing.
scored.buyer: Super7, Basic Fun, Funko, Hasbro/Mattel, River West Brands. They are capitalised but prefer to license directly from IP owners. Their own scouts already track nostalgia demand, and they pay royalties rather than large upfront premiums.
scored.ladder: Modest. Rungs go IP holding, then licensing, then own manufacturing, then retail brand house (the WHP/Iconix/Authentic Brands model). The ceiling is a mid-size brand-licensing company. Brand aggregators like Iconix struggled, so there is no visible trillion-dollar path.
scored.fatal_flaw: The valuable right (character and brand copyright) almost never actually lapses. It sits with live majors who license directly. What does lapse (trademarks, moulds) is either free first-come or scrap. Demand is already legible in eBay sold prices, so there is no illegible-data edge and no 10^3 step-up.
scored.one_line_reason: Low step-up (about 10-50x, paid out as royalties), high base hit rate that caps the ML lever at about 2-3x, demand already legible in eBay data, and non-bought or non-lapsed rights. A brand-licensing hobby business, not a Terranox analogue.

scored.name: Lapsed Patent Revival (incl. robotics and deeptech)
scored.one_line: Buy patents expired for unpaid maintenance fees within the revival window from small inventors and dissolved companies for $1-5k; ML picks ones reading on current products; petition for unintentional-delay revival and sell charted patents. Intervening rights reduce past damages.
scored.unproven_right: Lapsed but revivable patent and right to petition.
scored.proving_step: ML screening of lapse events by CPC class, EoU chart, 37 CFR 1.378 petition (~$2k).
scored.proven_buyer: Litigation funders, NPEs, RPX/AST, operating companies.
scored.public_data: USPTO maintenance fee events bulk data, assignments, full text, FCC ID photos, teardowns, state dissolution registries.
scored.frame: The rung is "own a lapsed US patent, revive it, chart it, sell it." Inside that rung, finding a lapsed patent that reads on a current product is maybe 70-85% of the work (my estimate). The physical step is cheap: a 37 CFR 1.378 petition plus the overdue fee. But the hard part is legal, not physical, and it does not go away. The petitioner has to state that the entire delay was unintentional. Under MPEP 2590 and 711.03(c), a deliberate choice not to pay is intentional, and a later change of mind, such as a sale to us, does not make it unintentional. Since 2020 the USPTO also requires an extra explanation for delays over 2 years. Most lapses are deliberate cost-cutting, so the pool of patents that can be honestly revived is small. Buying a patent the owner chose to abandon and swearing the delay was unintentional invites inequitable-conduct and unenforceability challenges (Network Signatures v. State Farm is the known fight over this). So, like the geothermal counter-example, the clearance step is the real bottleneck.
scored.step_up: Unproven: a lapsed patent bought from a small inventor or the estate of a dissolved company for about $1-5k (the candidate's figure; plausible, my estimate). Proven: a charted, enforceable US patent in the brokered market. From memory, Richardson Oliver Insights put average asking prices at roughly $100-250k per asset, with only about 20-30% of listed packages selling. On paper that is about 30-100x, which scores 3. But 35 USC 41(c)(2) intervening rights protect anyone who made, bought or started using the product during the lapse, and the products ML would flag "reading on current products" are exactly those. That cuts the proven value well below a normal patent's, so I put the realistic step-up at about 3-30x and score it 2. Nothing is near 10^3-10^4 immediately on a hit.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Base hit rate: about 1-5% of issued patents read on a commercial product and can be licensed (my estimate, consistent with the usual figure that under 5% of patents ever earn licensing revenue). Roughly half of US patents lapse for non-payment before full term (my estimate from USPTO maintenance-fee renewal rates). Cost per attempt: an EoU chart costs about $5-20k from a firm (estimate), petition fee about $2.1k for a large entity and about 40% of that for a small entity (FY2025 schedule, from memory), plus acquisition and back fees. ML could plausibly raise the screening hit rate 5-10x and push charting cost toward the cost of a GPU run, so the lever is real but capped at about 1/0.03 ≈ 30x. The binding constraint is not the hit rate. It is the share of lapses that can honestly be called unintentional, and ML cannot raise that.
scored.data: Lapse events are public and LEGIBLE: the USPTO maintenance fee events bulk file and Patent Center status say "Expired for failure to pay maintenance fees" in a structured field. The full patent text and assignments are public and already structured. The illegible part is product evidence (FCC ID photos, teardowns, manuals), and that is where ML adds something. That is the same infringement-reading work NPEs, brokers and analytics vendors (PatSnap, Unified Patents, Clarivate) already automate. The real outcome is "enforceable and infringed," and that turns on the owner's intent and on intervening rights, which no public data field records. The edge is thin.
scored.right_bought: Yes, mechanically. Small inventors and the estates or trustees of dissolved companies will sell lapsed patents cheaply, and the right is bought rather than claimed first-come. But in most cases the right being bought, revival on an unintentional-delay petition, legally does not exist, because the seller let the patent lapse on purpose. Diligence on the seller's intent is required, and when the answer is honest it usually disqualifies the patent.
scored.buyer: Litigation funders, NPEs and aggregators (RPX, AST, Allied Security Trust). The buyers exist and have capital, but they apply heavy discounts for enforceability risk. A revived patent with intervening-rights exposure and a challengeable unintentional-delay declaration is close to the worst asset class they price. The brokered market has been soft since about 2015, and sell-through is low.
scored.ladder: The ladder is patent monetization, NPE or aggregator, then a litigation finance platform. That is a known ceiling: Intellectual Ventures and Acacia never became trillion-dollar companies, and the model is mostly a legal arbitrage that does not compound into owning a physical value chain. There is no natural rung up into making the robotics or deeptech products themselves. The ladder is weak.
scored.fatal_flaw: The unintentional-delay standard plus intervening rights. Most maintenance-fee lapses are deliberate, so they cannot be honestly revived, and swearing otherwise invites unenforceability and inequitable-conduct challenges. For the minority that can be revived, 35 USC 41(c)(2) intervening rights shield exactly the current products ML would flag, because those makers acted during the lapse. That wipes out most of the step-up.
scored.one_line_reason: Cheap to buy and cheap to petition, but the revival right legally does not exist for most deliberate lapses, and intervening rights strip the value from the hits ML finds. That leaves a 3-30x legal arbitrage in a soft patent market with a low ceiling, not a 10^4 discovery rung.

scored.name: Mandate-Essential: patents that read on coming regulatory mandates
scored.one_line: Buy small-entity patents whose claims ML matches to draft regulations and standards before they become compulsory (FMVSS 127 AEB, GSR2 driver monitoring, NG-eCall, Cyber Resilience Act, FDA cybersecurity); sell to pools and aggregators once the mandate is final.
scored.unproven_right: Maintained patents with no licensing history, $5-30k.
scored.proving_step: Claim-to-requirement mapping over NPRMs, UNECE and standards drafts; mandate finalisation.
scored.proven_buyer: Avanci, Via LA, Sisvel, Access Advance, Acacia, IP Bridge, RPX, automakers and Tier-1s.
scored.public_data: USPTO full text and wrappers, assignments, EPO register, Federal Register and regulations.gov, UNECE WP.29, 3GPP/ETSI, PACER.
scored.frame: The rung is 'own a patent that reads on a mandated requirement, then sell or license it'. Discovery (mapping claims to draft rules) is maybe 30-40% of the work inside that rung (my estimate). The rest is the proving step, which is not cheap or abstracted. A patent is only proven by (a) the mandate going final, which is outside the company's control, and (b) an essentiality evaluation, then licensing or litigation, which survives inter partes review (IPR) at the Patent Trial and Appeal Board (PTAB). That is the bespoke plant in this case: it is the expensive, hard part, as in the geothermal counter-example. The buyers do exist and have money (pools, aggregators, NPEs).
scored.step_up: Unproven price is $5-30k per maintained small-entity patent (candidate's figure; it fits my recollection that the brokered secondary market prices most assets in the tens of thousands to low $100ks). A proven patent reading on a standard sells or yields roughly $100k-$1M+ per family (my estimate from memory of brokered SEP deals and pool payouts). Avanci's 4G vehicle royalty is about $20 per car, but it is split across thousands of patents. That gives about 10-100x for a typical winner. 1000x is reachable only for rare litigated outliers, and it arrives slowly, not on the day of a hit. Note: I could not verify these figures live because the shared web-search budget was used up.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Base hit rate: probably well under 5% of mapped patents end up licensable at a premium (my estimate). Pool essentiality checks reject many submissions. Of claims that reach a final IPR decision, about 60-70% are found unpatentable (my recollection of PTAB statistics). Cost per proving attempt is not the $5-30k purchase. It is the essentiality evaluation (about $10-20k per patent per pool evaluator, my estimate) plus litigation, which costs $2-5M+ per case through trial (my recollection of the AIPLA economic survey). ML cuts the screening cost, which was never the big cost. It does not cut the litigation and validity cost, so the realistic capex lever is about 2-3x, not 10x.
scored.data: The data is public and partly illegible: USPTO file wrappers, UNECE WP.29 drafts, NPRM dockets. But the outcome that matters is often already in a legible field. ETSI's IPR database lists declared standard-essential patents, and pools publish lists of patents found essential. Claim-mapping analytics is a commodity (LexisNexis PatentSight, Clarivate, Amplified, plus in-house tools at RPX, Unified Patents and Acacia). The deeper problem: regulations such as FMVSS 127 (automatic emergency braking), the EU's GSR2 driver monitoring, the Cyber Resilience Act and FDA cybersecurity rules are performance-based and technology-neutral. A patent therefore rarely becomes truly essential to a mandate, because automakers can design around it. Only interoperability standards (3GPP/ETSI, which covers NG-eCall) create real essentiality, and those are already declared and pooled.
scored.right_bought: Yes. Patents are bought, not claimed first-come. Small-entity owners and lapsing portfolios sell cheaply, often through brokers or maintenance-fee lapse lists. This part of the thesis holds.
scored.buyer: Patent pools (Avanci, Via LA, Sisvel, Access Advance) take in patents found essential and pay out royalties; they do not buy them outright. Aggregators (RPX, Acacia, IP Bridge) and NPEs do buy. Automakers and Tier-1 suppliers buy defensively at low prices. The buyers have money, but they pay for proven essentiality or litigation leverage, not for a mapping.
scored.ladder: The rungs run: acquire patent, assert or pool it, run a licensing business, then possibly become a pool administrator. The ceiling is an Acacia-type company (market cap in the hundreds of millions, my recollection) or a pool such as Avanci. None of the rungs lead toward making the mandated product, so there is no path to a trillion-dollar company.
scored.fatal_flaw: Regulatory mandates are performance-based and technology-neutral, so patents do not become essential to them. Real essentiality comes only from interoperability standards, where declarations and pool lists already put the answer in a legible public field. Value is then realised only through slow, expensive licensing or litigation (more than $2M per case, with about two-thirds of IPR-challenged claims lost), not through a cheap, discrete proving step.
scored.one_line_reason: Buying the right is cheap and the buyers exist, but the proving step is litigation rather than discovery. Essentiality to mandates is mostly illusory. Where it is real (3GPP/ETSI), it is already declared publicly. That leaves a 10-100x step-up and an NPE-sized ceiling.

scored.name: ColdAlloy: Cold War alloy and magnet compositions re-patented with modern process claims
scored.one_line: ML mines scanned OSTI/DTIC/NACA reports for rare-earth-free magnets and high-temperature alloys that should perform under AM or rapid solidification; file process/use patents; prove with a coupon; license.
scored.unproven_right: New process/use patents filed by the company ($10-20k), not bought.
scored.proving_step: Extraction and physics-informed screening; $10-30k arc-melt or LPBF coupon plus VSM/tensile.
scored.proven_buyer: Niron, VAC, Proterial, Noveon, aerospace primes, Carpenter, ATI, Höganäs, DoD/DOE programs.
scored.public_data: OSTI, DTIC, NASA NTRS, ASM literature, Materials Project.
scored.frame: The candidate rung is a coupon-proven process/use patent. Discovery (extraction plus screening) is maybe 60-70% of the effort to make a coupon (my estimate). But a coupon is not the rung a capitalised buyer pays for. Magnet makers and aerospace primes buy qualified, scaled processes, and scale-up and qualification are the hard bespoke physical step. Niron's iron-nitride (Fe16N2) magnet descends from a 1972 Kim and Takahashi discovery, and it needed University of Minnesota process work plus roughly $100M+ and about a decade to reach production (from memory). That is the geothermal-in-coal-mines pattern: finding the composition is easy compared with industrialising it. In the sellable frame, discovery is likely below 30% of the work.
scored.step_up: Unproven: a filed provisional or utility application costs about $10-20k (candidate figure; US utility filing to grant usually $30-60k, my estimate). Proven by coupon: a materials patent licensed before qualification typically brings $0 to low six figures upfront plus small royalties (estimate, based on the general AUTM pattern that most licensed university patents earn under $100k). A realistic coupon-proven step-up is about 0-10x. Most such patents earn nothing. The candidate's 30-150x figure assumes a buyer exists, and the coupon does not show one does. No real numbers could be pulled because the shared search budget ran out.
scored.hit_rate_capex: The proving step is already cheap: a $10-30k arc-melt or LPBF coupon plus VSM/tensile testing (candidate figure; plausible). The base hit rate for 'old composition performs well under AM or rapid solidification' is maybe 10-30% (my estimate). That caps the ML lever at about 3-10x on a cost base that is already small. The expensive, mostly failing step is downstream (scale-up and qualification, about $1-10M+ per alloy and 3-10 years for aerospace, my estimate), and ML over old reports does not de-risk it.
scored.data: The data is public and partly illegible: scanned DTIC, OSTI, NTRS and NACA reports. But the outcome (measured properties: coercivity, creep, tensile) is written in the reports themselves, so the answer is already in the text and LLM extraction is commodity. Google GNoME, Citrine Informatics, Materials Project, and newer labs such as Periodic Labs, Lila Sciences, CuspAI and Orbital Materials already mine this literature (from memory). NASA reused its own NTRS alloys for AM itself (GRCop-42/84), which shows that the owners of the data can and do read it.
scored.right_bought: No right is bought. It is created by filing, so there is no seller who cannot read the data and nobody to buy cheaply from. Worse, the public Cold War reports are prior art. Composition claims are anticipated, and 'known alloy made by AM' process claims face strong §103 obviousness rejections, so the right is weak and hard to enforce. Anyone else reading the same reports can design around it or invalidate it.
scored.buyer: Niron, VAC, Proterial, Noveon, Carpenter, ATI, Höganäs, aerospace primes, DoD/DOE. They are well capitalised, but they license or buy qualified processes and freedom to operate, not coupon-stage patents on public-domain compositions. They typically develop in-house or through university collaborations.
scored.ladder: A real ladder exists above: alloy or powder production, magnet or part manufacturing, qualified supply to OEMs (the Niron and Carpenter Additive path). But each rung is capital-heavy manufacturing, and the bottom rung (coupon patents) does not throw off cash to fund the climb.
scored.fatal_flaw: The right is created rather than bought, and it sits on top of the very public prior art the ML reads. So the 'proven' asset is a weak, obviousness-vulnerable patent with no cheap seller and no buyer at coupon stage. All the value sits in scale-up and qualification, the bespoke physical step: the coal-mine geothermal failure mode.
scored.one_line_reason: The coupon is cheap to prove, but the buyer pays for qualification rather than discovery. The patent is weakened by the same public reports it is built from, and no underpriced right is acquired.

scored.name: NCI Compound Rights Desk
scored.one_line: License NIH/NCI intramural compounds in non-oncology fields where ML over NCI-60 and PubChem finds activity; one cheap in vitro/in vivo proof; sell to specialty pharma. Near killed stranded drug rescue.
scored.unproven_right: Field-of-use exclusive licence from NIH OTT.
scored.proving_step: Target assay plus one animal model ($50-200k).
scored.proven_buyer: Specialty and rare-disease pharma.
scored.public_data: NCI DTP archives, PubChem BioAssay, NIH OTT listings.
scored.frame: The rung would be "own a field-of-use licence and prove it with a target assay plus one animal model." Discovery is not 80% or more of the work here. The physical step is wet-lab biology: synthesis or resupply of the compound, PK, a dosing study and one disease model. That costs $50-200k and takes months, and it is the bespoke part, the same failure as the geothermal-in-coal-mine counter-example. More importantly, specialty pharma does not pay for mouse efficacy alone. They price in tox, CMC, formulation and a defensible patent. The work left after this rung (IND-enabling studies at about $2-5M, then clinical trials at $50-500M+) is more than 99% of the value chain. So the rung is not a frame where proving dominates, and the buyer's discount for everything still unproven is very large. Discovery share inside this rung (my estimate): about 20-30%.
scored.step_up: My estimates from prior knowledge (no live search was possible): an NIH OTT exclusive therapeutic licence typically costs $25k-150k up front, plus minimum annual royalties, milestone benchmarks and 2-6% royalties on sales. A non-oncology asset that is preclinical, has only mouse proof of concept and has weak or no composition IP usually sells or out-licenses for $0-2M up front, with most of the value in contingent milestones. Many such assets do not transact at all. Total entry cost including proving is about $100-350k, so a hit realises roughly 3-20x on cash outlay. Even on the licence fee alone it is about 10-100x, nowhere near 10^3-10^4. The headline biobucks in rare-disease deals are milestone-weighted and contingent, not immediate.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Base hit rate, my estimate: computationally predicted repurposing hits from in vitro signal to a significant in vivo effect in one model run at about 10-30%. That is not low enough for a 10x lever: the cap of 1/base hit rate is about 3-10x, and ML lifts it perhaps 1.5-3x. Cost per proving attempt is $50-200k (candidate's figure; consistent with contract research organization pricing for one efficacy model plus PK, my estimate). The real attrition is downstream: about 90% of drugs entering clinical trials fail (widely cited BIO/Informa figure). The buyer carries that risk and prices it in, so it does not show up as a step-up for the rung owner. ML reduces the wrong failures.
scored.data: This fails C4 badly. NCI-60 (about 50k+ compounds across 60 cell lines), the DTP archives and PubChem BioAssay are structured, machine-readable and among the most heavily mined datasets in computational biology. The Connectivity Map, the Broad Drug Repurposing Hub, CellMiner and dozens of academic ML papers already use them. The signal is legible and the outcome (activity values) already sits in a field, so there is no illegible-data edge. Competitors and incumbents already exploit this kind of signal: Healx, Every Cure (ARPA-H funded), BioXcel, Recursion, BenevolentAI, Insilico and academic repurposing groups.
scored.right_bought: The right can be bought, but not from an owner who can't read the data. NIH OTT is a sophisticated licensor with a published technology list. It also requires a commercial development plan and diligence milestones. Under 37 CFR 404, an exclusive or field-of-use licence must be noticed in the Federal Register with a 15-day objection period. Worse, many NSC compounds have no live patent: their structures and activity were published decades ago, which is prior art. That leaves either nothing to licence, or only a weak method-of-use claim that a buyer will discount heavily. There is no information-asymmetry discount like Saskatchewan claim staking.
scored.buyer: Specialty and rare-disease pharma, and later biotech holding companies such as BridgeBio-style hubs. They are capitalised but buy mainly IND-ready or clinical assets with clean IP. They rarely buy mouse-only data on off-patent compounds for meaningful upfront cash.
scored.ladder: The rungs above are long and do exist: IND-enabling studies, Phase 1-3, approval, commercialisation, then a rare-disease platform. That is the BridgeBio and Roivant hub-and-spoke model, which reached multi-billion-dollar scale. Each rung up costs 10-100x more and carries large binary risk. The ladder is real but capital-heavy and well trodden.
scored.fatal_flaw: There is no illegible-data edge and no defensible right. NCI-60 and PubChem are public, structured and already heavily mined by funded repurposing companies. Many NCI compounds have no live composition patent, so the proven asset lacks the exclusivity buyers pay for. On top of that, the proving step is bespoke wet-lab biology that buyers discount steeply, so the immediate step-up is about 10x, not 10^4.
scored.one_line_reason: This is stranded drug rescue with a government licensor. The data is legible and crowded, the IP is weak because the compounds' public disclosure is prior art, the proving step is bespoke biology, and the step-up is about 10x on a hit and mostly contingent milestones. It does not get rescued.

scored.name: Unlicensed Genetic-Target Patent Picker
scored.one_line: Option unlicensed university target/biomarker patents and prove human genetic support via MR, colocalisation and protective LoF evidence; sublicense validated targets to pharma.
scored.unproven_right: Exclusive option/licence, $10-50k.
scored.proving_step: LLM patent-to-gene mapping plus MR against FinnGen, UKB-PPP, gnomAD, All of Us; optional CRISPR at CRO.
scored.proven_buyer: Pharma BD and genetics-first biotechs ($1-10M upfront).
scored.public_data: PatentsView, AUTM/TTO listings, FinnGen R12, UKB-PPP pQTL, GWAS Catalog, gnomAD, Open Targets.
scored.frame: The rung is 'own a target patent and attach human genetic evidence to it'. Inside that rung, discovery and proving (patent-to-gene mapping, MR, colocalisation, LoF lookup) is close to 100% of the work, and compute costs almost nothing, so on paper the rung meets the 80%+ test. It fails on the buyer side. Pharma BD pays for molecules, data packages and exclusivity on an asset. It does not pay for a target patent, because a target can be drugged without a licence: the claims are weak or invalid after Myriad (2013) and Amgen v. Sanofi (2023, enablement), and research use is exempt. So this is a rung with no reliable capitalised buyer, unlike a drilled claim sold to a mine developer.
scored.step_up: Unproven: a $10-50k option, the candidate's own figure. Proven: $1-10M upfront claimed. That is a nominal 20x-1000x, but it is my estimate that standalone target-patent licences with genetic support almost never close at $1M+. Disclosed genetics-target deals (deCODE/Amgen, Regeneron Genetics Center, Maze, Genomics plc, insitro collaborations) are platform deals with per-target upfronts of a few $M, paid for proprietary cohort data and team, not for a university patent. The realised step-up is probably 0-10x on most hits. I could not verify this with live sources because the shared web-search budget was used up.
scored.hit_rate_capex: The proving step is not expensive. MR and colocalisation on FinnGen, UKB-PPP and gnomAD summary statistics cost roughly $100-$1k of compute and analyst time per target (my estimate). An optional CRO CRISPR screen costs about $50-200k (estimate). Genetic support raises clinical success about 2.6x (Minikel et al., Nature 2024) and about 2x (King et al., PLoS Genet 2019). That lift is on the downstream clinical attempt, which costs $100M+ and is not what this company pays for. There is no costly, mostly failing proving step for ML to cut 10x. The base 'hit rate' of finding some genetic support for a target is also fairly high, roughly 5-10% of target-indication pairs (estimate), so the lever, capped at 1/base hit rate, is small.
scored.data: The data is public but already legible. Open Targets Platform and Genetics publish locus-to-gene scores, colocalisation and genetic association scores for every target-disease pair. The GWAS Catalog, gnomAD constraint/LoF tables and FinnGen/UKB-PPP results ship as structured summary statistics. In effect the outcome is already written into a public field, which is the pattern that killed earlier ideas. Patent-to-gene mapping is the only illegible part, and that is cheap: SureChEMBL and PatentsView already gene-tag patents. Big pharma (GSK, Sanofi, BMS, Pfizer, Genentech and others) co-fund Open Targets and run in-house genetics, so there are no incumbents left who cannot read this.
scored.right_bought: An exclusive option or licence on a university target, method-of-treatment or biomarker patent, bought cheaply from a tech-transfer office (likely $10-50k, since many such patents are unlicensed and TTOs discount them). The right is buyable, but it carries little value. Gene and target claims are largely unenforceable or easy to design around, and the genetic evidence that would make the target valuable is public to everyone, so owning the patent gives no exclusivity over the actual value.
scored.buyer: The intended buyers are pharma BD teams and genetics-first biotechs (Alnylam, Regeneron, Maze, Verge, Amgen/deCODE). They are well capitalised, but they buy molecules and data, not target patents, and they already run the same MR and colocalisation analyses in-house on the same public and proprietary data.
scored.ladder: The ladder is real but very capital-heavy: target, then tool compound/hit, then lead, then IND, then clinic, then approval. Each rung above target is a $10M-$1B+ physical and clinical step where discovery is a small share, so the 'win the smallest rung' advantage does not carry upward. Climbing makes this an ordinary biotech. The trillion-dollar ceiling exists (pharma), but the first rung confers no edge.
scored.fatal_flaw: The asset bought (a university target patent) is not what drives value or exclusivity: targets can be drugged without a licence after Myriad and Amgen v. Sanofi, and the genetic proof is already published in legible form (Open Targets L2G and colocalisation scores), so pharma has no reason to pay the step-up.
scored.one_line_reason: Discovery is nearly all the work in this rung, but the bought right gives no exclusivity, the proof is cheap and already summarised publicly in Open Targets, and pharma buys molecules, not target patents.
sources: Minikel EV et al., 'Refining the impact of genetic evidence on clinical success', Nature 2024 (genetic support ~2.6x relative success) - from prior knowledge, not re-verified this run

scored.name: External-Control Arm Foundry
scored.one_line: Buy natural-history and registry datasets from failed rare-disease sponsors and foundations; ML harmonises into regulatory-grade external control arms and matches to active pivotal programs.
scored.unproven_right: Data ownership or exclusive licence, $10-100k.
scored.proving_step: Match terminated observational studies to active trials; LLM CRF extraction and propensity comparability.
scored.proven_buyer: Ultragenyx, Sarepta, BioMarin, PTC ($2-20M per dataset).
scored.public_data: ClinicalTrials.gov, FDA rare-disease dockets, NORD/GARD, PubMed, EMA qualification opinions.
scored.frame: The rung is 'own a harmonised natural-history dataset and license it as an external control arm (ECA)'. Inside that rung, discovery (working out which terminated or orphaned datasets exist and match an active pivotal program) is perhaps 20-30% of the work, by my estimate. Most of the work is the physical-equivalent step: legal title and consent re-use rights, getting patient-level CRFs (often on paper or in old EDC exports), curation to CDISC/SDTM, FDA-grade provenance and audit trails, and then defending comparability (endpoint definitions, eras of standard of care, propensity overlap) with the FDA. That defence is bespoke for each program, the same way the geothermal plant is bespoke in the coal-mine counter-example. A capitalised buyer exists (rare-disease sponsors), so the frame is sellable, but discovery is nowhere near 80% of it.
scored.step_up: Estimates only; I could not verify any of them. Unproven: the candidate's $10-100k for data from a defunct sponsor or a foundation. Proven: ECA or real-world-data licenses for a single indication are, to my knowledge, usually in the low hundreds of thousands to low millions of dollars. The candidate's $2-20M per dataset looks high next to my understanding of licensing norms for Flatiron, Medidata, IQVIA and C-Path data. That gives roughly 10-50x, not 10^3-10^4. The value does not appear immediately when a match is found. It appears only after the buyer's FDA review accepts the comparator, years later and often not at all.
scored.hit_rate_capex: There is no costly, mostly-failing proving step that ML makes cheaper. Matching datasets to trials and extracting CRFs is desk work, on the order of $10-100k per dataset (my estimate). The real gate is regulatory acceptance. FDA has accepted natural-history or external comparators in a handful of rare-disease approvals (Brineura for CLN2 and Zolgensma, from my knowledge) and has criticised them in many others. It issued a 2023 draft guidance on externally controlled trials, which flags bias and comparability concerns. ML does not move that acceptance rate much. So the lever is small, maybe 1.5-2x on curation cost, against the roughly 10x the thesis needs.
scored.data: The signal is mostly private, not public but illegible. ClinicalTrials.gov, the FDA dockets and GARD/NORD only tell you that a study exists. The asset itself (patient-level data) is held by sponsors and foundations, so there is no illegible public dataset to out-read. Which natural-history studies exist is already a legible field: ClinicalTrials.gov tags observational studies and records their status. Incumbents already aggregate in this space: Medidata's Synthetic Control Arm, Flatiron (bought by Roche for about $1.9B), IQVIA, Aetion, TriNetX, Unlearn.AI, and C-Path's Rare Disease Cure Accelerator (RDCA-DAP), which pools rare-disease natural-history data for open use. Buying the right is also shaky. Patient informed consent often limits secondary or commercial use and transfer. Foundations tend to share data through C-Path or directly with sponsors for free, because they want therapies built, and are reluctant to grant exclusive commercial licenses. Assets of a failed sponsor's estate do sell, but the buyers are informed (other sponsors, CROs).
scored.right_bought: Exclusive license or ownership of patient-level natural-history or registry data, from defunct sponsors (bankruptcy estates) or patient foundations. The candidate puts this at $10-100k; I could not verify that figure. Whether the right can be transferred depends on consent scope. Foundation data is frequently non-exclusive or shared openly.
scored.buyer: Rare-disease sponsors running pivotal programs (Ultragenyx, Sarepta, BioMarin, PTC, Biogen, and gene-therapy biotechs). They are well capitalised, but they often commission their own prospective natural-history studies so the comparator is FDA-defensible, and they buy through incumbent real-world-data vendors.
scored.ladder: The rungs are: ECA data asset, then a real-world-evidence / regulatory-science CRO, then in-licensing stranded rare-disease assets whose approval path the company's own ECA unlocks, then becoming a rare-disease sponsor itself. The ladder is real. The top rungs resemble the previously killed 'stranded drug rescue' idea, and Roche's roughly $1.9B purchase of Flatiron suggests a sizeable but not trillion-dollar outcome.
scored.fatal_flaw: There is no immediate step-up on a hit. The asset's value is set later by FDA acceptance of comparability inside someone else's pivotal trial, which is bespoke, slow and often refused. The data is private and governed by consent rather than public and illegible. And open pooling (C-Path RDCA-DAP) plus incumbent real-world-data vendors leave no cheap, exclusive right to arbitrage.
scored.one_line_reason: Discovery is a minority of the work. The 10-50x step-up (my estimate) depends on FDA comparability years later. The data is private and consent-limited, not public but illegible, and C-Path, Medidata and Flatiron already aggregate it. This is a CRO-like service dressed as asset ownership.

scored.name: LCD Flip: non-covered devices made reimbursable
scored.one_line: Buy cleared devices from companies crippled by MAC non-coverage LCDs where ML shows evidence has since crossed the MAC's bar; file reconsideration; sell covered asset.
scored.unproven_right: Device IP and product line at distressed prices.
scored.proving_step: LCD reconsideration dossier ($50-150k, 6-12 months).
scored.proven_buyer: Specialty medtech strategics, roll-up PE.
scored.public_data: CMS Medicare Coverage Database and response-to-comment PDFs, PubMed, ClinicalTrials.gov, Part B PUFs, FDA summaries.
scored.frame: The rung is "buy a cleared device line that Medicare won't cover, get the LCD reconsidered, and sell it as a covered product." Inside that rung, discovery (finding where the published evidence has already met the MAC's bar) is maybe 30-40% of the work. That is my estimate. The rest is not trivial. You have to buy and keep alive a distressed operating company (QMS, FDA registration, supplier contracts, complaint handling, inventory). You have to lobby the MAC medical directors, usually several of them, because there are 7 A/B MACs plus the DME MACs and harmonized LCDs mean you work with all of them. You then wait 1-2+ years. Even after the LCD changes you still need coding and payment rates, and commercial payers lag behind. This is much closer to the geothermal-in-a-coal-mine counter-example than to an exploratory drill: owning and running the asset is the hard part, not finding it. Capitalised buyers do exist (strategics and PE roll-ups).
scored.step_up: I could not pull sourced numbers because the shared search budget was used up before this agent ran. Estimate only: a distressed cleared device line with no coverage might sell for about $1-10M (IP plus inventory, sometimes close to liquidation value). A covered one might sell at 2-5x revenue on revenue that coverage has to grow first. So a realistic step-up when a reconsideration succeeds is about 3-30x, and it arrives slowly as revenue ramps, not immediately. The candidate's claimed 100-1000x assumes the unproven asset is worth close to zero, which is not true of a cleared device with a team, a QMS and inventory. Value also does not jump the day the LCD changes; buyers pay for the coverage-driven revenue that follows.
scored.hit_rate_capex: The candidate gives a 20-30% reconsideration success rate. That is unverified, and so is my estimate below. Using the candidate's own $50-150k dossier cost, the most ML could do is lift the hit rate from about 25% to about 75-100%, which is a 3-4x lever at most, not 10x. The dossier is also cheap next to the asset purchase ($1-10M) and the 1-2 years of running costs, so cutting dossier cost barely changes total capex. Most failures are because the evidence really isn't there (no RCTs, small effect sizes), and ML can't create new trials.
scored.data: The data is public and somewhat illegible: the MCD, response-to-comment PDFs, PubMed, ClinicalTrials.gov and the Part B PUFs. But the outcome is already written down in legible form. The LCD text lists which devices are non-covered and explains the evidence bar in its rationale section. The MCD also publicly tracks reconsideration requests and proposed LCDs. Literature that clears the bar is visible to anyone who reads the trial readouts. The ML edge over a reimbursement consultant reading 20 papers is small.
scored.right_bought: You can buy the right, but not from owners who can't read the data. The device owner, with its reimbursement VP and consultants, is the party best placed to know its own coverage status and evidence. If the evidence had crossed the bar, the owner would file the reconsideration itself (it costs $50-150k) rather than sell cheap. The distressed sellers left over are mostly the ones whose evidence really fails, or who are distressed for reasons other than coverage (clinical adoption, competition, burn rate). That is adverse selection.
scored.buyer: Specialty medtech strategics (for example Boston Scientific, Stryker, Medtronic tuck-ins) and medtech PE roll-ups. They are well capitalised and do pay for covered, growing product lines, but they pay on revenue, not on coverage status alone.
scored.ladder: A ladder exists: device line owner, then a commercial platform, then a multi-product medtech roll-up, then possibly evidence generation (running trials) and manufacturing. But every rung is operationally heavy, and none has a discovery-dominated frame. Medtech roll-ups are a known PE playbook, not a trillion-dollar path.
scored.fatal_flaw: The owner can already read the signal. Coverage status and the evidence bar sit in legible LCD fields, and the device company is the party most motivated and best equipped to file a reconsideration itself for about $100k. Any asset you can buy cheaply has been adversely selected to be one where the evidence does not clear the bar. On top of that, owning a cleared device company is heavy operations, not a trivial physical step.
scored.one_line_reason: Weak. The outcome sits in legible LCD fields, the seller knows more than the buyer (adverse selection), the realistic step-up is about 3-30x and slow, the hit-rate lever is capped near 3-4x, and running the asset is the hard part. Scores rest on estimates because no web searches were possible.
