Worth checking: CMS Medicare Program Integrity Manual Ch. 13 (LCD process, reconsideration timelines)

scored.name: MDR Orphans: legacy CE devices abandoned by small makers
scored.one_line: Buy MDD technical files being dropped before MDR deadlines; ML picks ones whose literature-based evidence passes; recertify and sell to EU roll-ups.
scored.unproven_right: Technical file, lapsing CE certificate, 510(k), trademark.
scored.proving_step: MDR CER and notified-body audit ($150-500k).
scored.proven_buyer: EU medtech PE buy-and-builds, mid-cap strategics.
scored.public_data: EUDAMED, notified-body registries, NANDO, MDCG surveys, FDA 510(k), PubMed.
scored.frame: The rung is 'buy a lapsing MDD file, then get it MDR-certified'. Discovery (picking which file has literature evidence that will pass) is about 10-20% of the work in that rung (my estimate). The other 80%+ is bespoke physical and regulatory work: a gap analysis and rewrite of the technical documentation to MDR Annex II/III, a QMS (ISO 13485) under a legal manufacturer, a CER, PMCF plans or studies, often new bench, biocompatibility and usability testing, and a 12-24 month notified-body queue. This is the geothermal-in-coal-mines pattern: finding the right file is easy, and recertifying it is the hard, expensive part.
scored.step_up: Estimates only; the search budget ran out, so none of these numbers are verified. An abandoned small-maker device line with a lapsing certificate probably sells for about EUR 0-200k, or may simply be given away, because the maker is exiting anyway. Once MDR-certified, a niche class IIa/IIb line with EUR 1-5M in sales might be worth roughly 1-3x revenue to a roll-up, so EUR 1-15M. Against the bare purchase price that is about 10-50x. Against the true basis (purchase plus EUR 150-500k+ recertification plus QMS overhead plus 1-2 years of carry) the step-up is about 3-10x. That is a value-add margin, not a 10^4 discovery jump.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Estimates, unverified (search budget exhausted). Cost per proving attempt: EUR 150-500k for each class IIa/IIb device (the candidate's own range, consistent with industry commentary I recall), and more for class III or implantables. Base hit rate: probably high (50-80%) when the evidence work is done properly. Notified bodies seldom reject outright. What fails is cost, time and missing clinical data, not a hidden binary outcome. With a base rate of about 0.5, the ML lever is capped near 2x, nowhere near 10x. The main cost driver, generating new clinical or bench data, is not reduced by better selection.
scored.data: Mostly legible already. NANDO lists notified bodies. Certificate status and expiry are in NB registries and partly in EUDAMED (rollout still incomplete). FDA 510(k) clearances are a structured public database. MDCG/MedTech Europe surveys report discontinuation rates by aggregate. PubMed is public but not illegible, and every regulatory consultancy already mines it for CERs. Key legal problem: under MDR Art. 61(5), a class III or implantable device can only claim equivalence to a competitor's device with a contract giving access to that device's full technical documentation. Literature-only routes are also heavily restricted for higher classes, so 'literature evidence passes' is a weak signal. The outcome (whether the certificate was renewed or lapsed) is written into a legible status field.
scored.right_bought: Partially. A technical file, trademark and 510(k) can be bought through an asset purchase from an exiting SME, often cheaply. However, an MDD certificate cannot be transferred as a free-standing right. It is tied to the manufacturer and the notified body, so any change of legal manufacturer or substantial change typically forces a new conformity assessment. So you buy paper and IP, not a provable right that keeps its standing. The sellers can read their own data well. They are exiting because they know the recertification cost, not because they are missing a signal.
scored.buyer: Yes, a capitalised buyer exists: EU medtech PE buy-and-builds and mid-cap strategics, who buy certified product lines and small manufacturers. Specialist legacy-device acquirers and regulatory-remediation consultancies (e.g. Qserve, Emergo/UL, and many CRO/regulatory consultancies) already work this space. PE platforms do their own remediation after buying, which competes directly with the proposed arbitrage.
scored.ladder: Moderate. The rungs run: own certified legacy SKUs, then a contract-manufactured portfolio, then an owned QMS and legal-manufacturer platform, then an EU/US commercial roll-up, then R&D on new devices. It is a credible path to a mid-cap medtech roll-up (EUR 100M-1B). A trillion-dollar path is implausible: niche legacy devices are fragmented, low-growth, and capped by the size of each niche.
scored.fatal_flaw: The proving step is not discovery. MDR recertification is EUR 150-500k+ of bespoke regulatory and clinical work per device, has a high conditional pass rate, and runs 12-24 month notified-body queues. ML selection can cut maybe 2x of the waste, not 10x. The step-up over the true cost basis is about 3-10x. And the MDR Art. 61 limits on equivalence and literature-only evidence undercut the core ML thesis.
scored.one_line_reason: This is the coal-mine geothermal counter-example again. Finding the right orphaned file is the easy 10-20%. MDR recertification is the expensive, high-pass-rate, bespoke 80%. The data is mostly legible and the true step-up is about 3-10x.

scored.name: Unlimited Rights Second Source
scored.one_line: Find spare parts whose GPR data rights lapsed to unlimited but are still sole-source; become the qualified second source; sell to roll-ups.
scored.unproven_right: Approved-source qualification earned via SAR (weak bought-right).
scored.proving_step: SAR approval plus first article.
scored.proven_buyer: TransDigm/Heico-style aggregators, defense PE.
scored.public_data: FPDS-NG, DIBBS, cFolders, DFARS markings.
scored.frame: The rung is "become an approved alternate source on a sole-source NSN (National Stock Number)." Inside that rung, discovery (finding the NSN where the data rights lapsed but there is still one source) is only about 10-20% of the work. That share is my estimate. Most of the work is physical and paid for up front: get or reverse-engineer the technical data package, build a SAR (Source Approval Request) package, make the parts, then pass first-article and qualification testing, plus the AS9100/QPL burden for flight-critical items. This is the same shape as the geothermal-in-coal-mines counter-example: the physical step is hard and specific to each part, not trivial.
scored.step_up: There is no market price for an "unproven qualification" because you cannot buy one. It is worth about $0 plus your sunk engineering cost. A proven second-source approval is worth the stream of awards you win on that NSN, and winning as the second source usually pushes the price down 20-50% from the sole-source price (my estimate, from typical DLA competition results). So the value is roughly the present value of a small-margin contract stream. My estimate: if annual demand is $0.2-2M and you take part of it, the approval is worth about 1-3x the SAR cost. The candidate's own ~10-30x is generous, and nothing like 10^3-10^4. I found no sourced figure because web search was unavailable.
scored.hit_rate_capex: I could not run any searches (the shared search budget was used up), so these are from memory and should be treated as estimates. DLA SAR disapproval rates are commonly said to be high, roughly 40-60% returned or disapproved, mostly because the data packages are incomplete. Reviews take about 6-24 months. One attempt costs about $25k-$500k in reverse engineering, test articles and first-article testing; flight-critical safety items cost the most. ML can mainly improve which parts you pick (demand, how strong the data rights are, how hard the part is to make). It cannot make the engineering cheaper or get the package approved, so the capex lever is maybe 1.5-2x, not 10x.
scored.data: The public data is real but partly legible already. DIBBS RFQs and the Federal Logistics data carry the AMSC/AMC acquisition-method codes. These codes directly summarise whether the government has the technical data and whether a part is sole source (for example AMSC C, D or P versus G). That is the "outcome written into a status field" problem. FPDS-NG award histories are structured and already mined by GovSpend, BidLink, Govly and many small reverse-engineering shops and DLA dealers. The parts that really are illegible (DFARS 252.227-7013 restrictive markings on scanned drawings in cFolders/JEDMICS, and when the 'limited rights' terms lapse) are useful but often access-controlled: export-controlled, with JCP certification required. So there is some edge, but it is narrow.
scored.right_bought: Nothing is bought. Source approval is earned through engineering and government review, not bought cheaply from an owner who cannot read its own data. The OEM sole source is the opposite of an ignorant seller: it actively defends its position. So the 'bought-right' piece of C4 fails. The candidate itself calls it a weak bought-right.
scored.buyer: The intended buyer is mismatched. TransDigm and Heico buy proprietary sole-source positions with pricing power. A second source is their competitor, and it destroys exactly the margin they pay for. Heico's PMA model is close, but Heico builds that capability in-house. Realistic buyers are defense lower-middle-market PE roll-ups of DLA job shops. My estimate is that they pay 4-8x EBITDA for a small manufacturer, not a premium for each qualification.
scored.ladder: The ladder is moderate: second-source qualification, then a portfolio of NSNs, then a contract manufacturer, then OEM-level proprietary parts and data rights (the TransDigm model). That is a real path to a multi-billion-dollar company: TransDigm is worth about $70B+ on sole-source aftermarket parts. But each rung up adds manufacturing, so the discovery share keeps falling instead of staying dominant.
scored.fatal_flaw: The proving step is not discovery. It is costly, part-by-part engineering and qualification (reverse engineering, first article, SAR review taking months to years). On a win you get a competitive, lower-price contract stream worth a few times its cost, not a 10^4 step-up. And the named buyers (TransDigm and Heico) value sole-source pricing that a second source destroys.
scored.one_line_reason: The rung is dominated by manufacturing and qualification, the step-up is about 1-3x, AMSC codes already flag sole-source and data-rights status, and the named buyers are the incumbents this company would undercut. It fails the Terranox frame.

scored.name: Nuclear-Grade Salvage: qualified spares from decommissioning and cancelled plants
scored.one_line: Buy decommissioning and cancelled-plant warehouse inventory at surplus prices; ML over ADAMS rebuilds 10 CFR 50 App B/ASME pedigree; sell qualified obsolete spares to the life-extending fleet.
scored.unproven_right: Title to warehouse lots disposed as commercial surplus.
scored.proving_step: Match lots to equipment lists, CMTRs and vendor QA; commercial-grade dedication and light test.
scored.proven_buyer: Constellation, Vistra, Southern, Duke, TVA, parts integrators, restart programs.
scored.public_data: NRC ADAMS (FSARs, LERs, Part 21 reports), PSDARs, GovDeals/liquidator listings.
scored.frame: The rung is buying surplus warehouse lots, then dedicating and reselling them as qualified spares. Discovery (matching a lot to a part number, plant equipment list, CMTR and original vendor) is maybe 30-40% of the work in that rung (my estimate). The rest is physical and regulatory: commercial-grade dedication under your own 10 CFR 50 App B / NQA-1 QA program, critical-characteristic testing, storage and shelf-life verification, and Part 21 liability. That is the coal-mine-geothermal pattern: the bespoke qualification step is harder than finding the part. There is a capitalised buyer (the fleet operators and restart programs), but the rung is not discovery-dominated.
scored.step_up: My estimate, not sourced, because search was unavailable. Liquidator or commercial-surplus lots of nuclear spares clear at roughly scrap to 5-10% of list. A dedicated, qualified obsolete spare can sell at list or several times list when it is the only source (e.g. a $5k surplus valve resold for $50k-200k). That is about 10-100x per item, and 1000x only in rare obsolete-component, forced-outage cases. Per-lot step-up is lower, because most items in a lot are low-value consumables or have no buyer. The candidate's ~100-1000x claim is optimistic.
scored.hit_rate_capex: These are my estimates, not sourced. Dedication succeeds for most items with an identified part number and intact vendor documentation, probably over 50%. The failures are economic: no buyer, an unverifiable storage history, or a failed critical characteristic. Each attempt costs roughly $5k-50k in engineering, testing and documentation per item type, and more for active components that need seismic or EQ (environmental qualification) evidence. The base hit rate is not low, so the ML lever (capped at 1/hit rate) is about 2x at most, not 10x. Most of the cost is in testing and QA paperwork, which ML does not remove.
scored.data: The data that actually establishes pedigree mostly sits in private records, not in ADAMS: the utility's own warehouse and asset-management systems (e.g. SAP or Passport stock codes with a Q/non-Q quality classification), receipt inspection records, and vendor QA files. ADAMS FSARs and LERs give equipment-level design information but rarely item-level traceability. The outcome is also already legible inside the industry. As I understand it (not confirmed this session), the Utilities Service Alliance's RAPID shared inventory database and PIM (Pooled Inventory Management) let utilities list and trade spares, including from plants that are shutting down. Decommissioning owners such as Holtec, EnergySolutions and NorthStar, or the utility before handing the plant over, typically sell safety-related stock utility-to-utility with its pedigree intact before anything is scrapped. So the ML edge is thin, because the outcome is already summarised in fields incumbents read.
scored.right_bought: Lots can be bought cheaply, but adverse selection is severe. Whatever reaches GovDeals or a liquidator has usually already been offered to the fleet through RAPID or direct sales, and it was released as commercial surplus because its pedigree chain was broken. Once that chain is broken, you need full dedication: you cannot recover the original Q status from documents. The sellers (decommissioning companies and utilities) can read their own records, so the core information gap that makes Terranox work is missing.
scored.buyer: Constellation, Vistra, Southern, Duke, TVA, Dominion, and restart programs (Palisades, Crane/TMI-1, Duane Arnold). These buyers are well capitalised and do pay premiums for obsolete qualified parts. But they buy through approved suppliers (Curtiss-Wright, AZZ/Nuclear Logistics, Westinghouse, Framatome, Paragon/Ultra Electronics), so a new entrant has to pass vendor audits before it can sell.
scored.ladder: From salvage dealer, the ladder runs to dedication house, then obsolescence-engineering and reverse-engineering supplier, then an OEM-equivalent parts manufacturer. That is roughly the Curtiss-Wright nuclear segment, a business of a few billion dollars, not a trillion. The top of that ladder ends in component manufacturing and does not climb into owning plants. The market is bounded by about 94 US reactors and a few restarts.
scored.fatal_flaw: The proving step is commercial-grade dedication: a regulated, physical step done under your own App B QA program. It is neither trivial nor discovery. The pedigree information sits in sellers' private records and is already shared industry-wide through RAPID and PIM, so sellers are not blind to value. The surplus that leaks out cheaply is surplus whose pedigree is already broken.
scored.one_line_reason: This is a real but niche arbitrage. The proving step is mostly regulated qualification work, not discovery. The hit rate is not low, so the ML lever is about 2x, not 10x. Incumbents already trade pedigreed decommissioning spares through RAPID and PIM, and the ceiling is a Curtiss-Wright-sized supplier.

Prior knowledge (unverified this session): Pooled Inventory Management (PIM), a pool of large nuclear spares operated for member utilities

scored.name: Orphan Embodied Data: robot and AV datasets from bankruptcies
scored.one_line: Buy teleop, manipulation and AV sensor datasets from estates at hardware-liquidation value; prove clean rights and benchmark lift; sell to labs.
scored.unproven_right: Raw datasets of uncertain licensability, $10-100k.
scored.proving_step: ML over APAs, contracts and privacy policies; cheap fine-tune benchmark.
scored.proven_buyer: Physical Intelligence, DeepMind Robotics, Nvidia, Tesla, Skild, Scale.
scored.public_data: PACER and claims-agent dockets, CA DMV AV reports, CPUC, Wayback policies.
scored.frame: Rung: buy a dataset out of a bankruptcy estate, clean up its rights, and resell it. My estimate is that proving (contract and privacy-policy review plus a fine-tune benchmark) is about 50-60% of the work. The rest is deal sourcing, competing with strategics before the 363 sale, the consumer privacy ombudsman process, and de-identifying faces and plates in AV logs. Those are bespoke legal and engineering jobs, not an abstracted step like a drill. The buyers are well funded (PI, DeepMind, Nvidia), but they buy data under bespoke contracts and mostly collect their own. There is no liquid market that reprices a proven dataset the way a mine developer reprices a proven claim.
scored.step_up: Estimate only; the search budget ran out before any search returned, so none of this is sourced. An unproven estate dataset: $10-100k, the candidate's own figure, and plausible because estates value data near hardware scrap. A proven dataset with clean rights: my estimate is $0.2-2M for a few thousand hours of manipulation or teleop data, if collecting the same data costs roughly $100-300 per hour. That is about 10-50x, not 50-200x. The price is capped at the buyer's cost to collect the data fresh, and capped further because free open datasets exist (Open X-Embodiment, about 1M+ episodes; DROID). Strategics usually take the best datasets before any estate auction (Embark went to Applied Intuition; Argo and Cruise data stayed with Ford, VW and GM).
scored.hit_rate_capex: Estimate: the proving step is cheap, about $5-30k of legal review plus a $1-10k fine-tune benchmark. My guess is the base hit rate (rights clean enough to resell, and data that lifts a benchmark on a target embodiment) is about 20-40%. The ML hit-rate lever is capped at 1/base, so about 2.5-5x. The proving step is neither expensive nor mostly failing today, so a 10x discovery-capex drop does not apply. Unsourced; searches were blocked.
scored.data: PACER and claims-agent dockets (Stretto, Kroll, Epiq), asset purchase agreements, schedules of assets, and Wayback copies of privacy policies are public, scattered and hard to read, so the legibility part holds. The asset itself, the dataset, is private, and its quality cannot be judged from public data before buying. Schedules often lump data into 'IP / intangibles', but the 'outcome' (is it licensable?) is not in any legible field. That gives ML a modest edge on rights triage. CA DMV AV reports and CPUC filings give miles and disengagements, not data value. AV logs with people in them trigger 11 USC 363(b)(1): selling personally identifiable information needs a consumer privacy ombudsman (as in the RadioShack and Toys R Us cases). That adds friction and lets the court, not ML, decide the outcome.
scored.right_bought: Yes. The rights are bought from trustees and estates, who often cannot value data and price it near the hardware liquidation value. That part fits. But the number of deals is tiny: maybe 5-20 robotics or AV shutdowns a year with meaningful data (estimate), and strategics and acqui-hirers often move first. The purchase also brings embodiment-specific data that loses value quickly.
scored.buyer: Physical Intelligence, Google DeepMind Robotics, Nvidia (GR00T), Tesla, Skild, Figure, Toyota Research Institute, Scale, Applied Intuition. They are well funded, but most see self-collected and teleop data as the moat, and scaled collection drives the marginal value of third-party data toward its collection cost.
scored.ladder: Possible path: estate dataset buyer, then a data broker or marketplace, then owned teleop collection fleets, then a foundation model or robot company. The upper rungs are crowded (Scale, Encord, Cortex-style data vendors, every robot lab collecting its own data). The first rung builds little advantage toward them except deal flow. This is weaker than mineral-rights-to-mine, where each rung has its own buyer and price discovery.
scored.fatal_flaw: The proven dataset's value is capped by what it would cost the buyer to collect it fresh, which is falling quickly as labs scale teleop. On top of that, free open datasets and strategics taking the good datasets before auction squeeze it further. So the step-up is about 10-50x on tiny deal sizes, the deal count is single or double digits a year, and there is no 10^3-10^4 jump or expensive, mostly failing proving step for ML to lever.
scored.one_line_reason: The legal-triage part fits the rubric (rights bought from estates that cannot read their own data), but proving is cheap and usually succeeds, the step-up is capped at the buyer's collection cost (about 10-50x), deal flow is tiny, and there is no frame where discovery is 80%+ of the work with a liquid buyer.
sources: No sources: WebSearch returned 'budget used up' (shared limit of 200 per turn) on both attempts. Every number here is an unsourced estimate from model knowledge.
11 U.S.C. 363(b)(1) and the consumer privacy ombudsman rule (11 U.S.C. 332); RadioShack (2015) and Toys R Us PII sale precedents, from memory
Open X-Embodiment (2023, about 1M+ trajectories) and DROID (2024) open robot datasets, from memory
Embark Trucks assets acquired by Applied Intuition (2023); Argo AI shutdown with assets absorbed by Ford and VW (2022), from memory

scored.name: Surplus Physics: mis-listed scientific instruments
scored.one_line: Buy mis-described dilution fridges, magnets, SRF cavities, HTS tape, UHV chambers on surplus auctions; vision/OCR identifies them; test and sell to quantum, fusion and semi buyers.
scored.unproven_right: Lots listed as untested equipment.
scored.proving_step: Nameplate OCR vs grant records, pickup, leak/cooldown test.
scored.proven_buyer: Quantum startups, national labs, fusion companies, refurbishers.
scored.public_data: GSA Auctions, GovDeals, Public Surplus, university surplus, NSF MRI awards, DOE excess listings.
scored.frame: The rung is buying a mis-listed surplus lot, proving it works and reselling it. Spotting the lot (OCR of nameplate, photo ID, matching to the grant) takes maybe 20-30% of the work, by my estimate. Most of the effort is physical. Proving a dilution fridge means rigging and freight of a 1-2 t cryostat, leak checking, a pulse-tube compressor (often missing or needing a service of about $20-40k, estimate) and a He-3/He-4 mixture (He-3 roughly $2-3k per litre STP, so tens of thousands of dollars per fill, estimate). After that comes a multi-day cooldown to under 20 mK, and usually a refurbishment. SRF cavities need a vertical test stand at 2 K, which only labs have. HTS tape needs Ic testing and degrades in storage. This is the geothermal-in-coal-mines pattern: the physical proving and refurbishment is harder than finding the lot. Capitalised buyers exist (quantum startups, labs, fusion companies), but they mostly buy new with a warranty and integration support.
scored.step_up: From memory, not verified (search budget was exhausted): a new dilution fridge (Bluefors or Oxford Triton) costs about $400k-$1M+. A used or refurbished working unit probably sells for about $100-400k. Untested cryostat or 'vacuum chamber' lots on GovDeals, Public Surplus or eBay usually clear somewhere from a few hundred dollars to $20k, often with key parts missing. A mis-labelled lot bought for $2-5k and resold working for $150k would be about 30-75x gross. Net of the $50-100k refurbishment, test and freight, it is about 10-30x. 1000x happens only on rare jackpot lots. UHV chambers and magnets are more like 3-10x. Realistic C2 is the 10-100x band.
scored.hit_rate_capex: I have no sourced base rate. My estimate is that well under 1% of 'untested lab equipment' lots are high-value quantum or fusion hardware that is truly mis-described, and maybe 30-60% of those can be restored economically. Each proving attempt (pickup, freight, leak test, cooldown with He mixture) costs roughly $10-50k per large cryogenic lot, also my estimate. ML raises the share of the right lots spotted, but most of the capex is the physical test and refurbishment, which ML does not reduce. Bidding is cheap compared with testing, so the lever is capped well below 10x.
scored.data: The data is public and somewhat illegible: auction photos, terse titles, and agencies or universities that do not know what they have. Matching against NSF MRI and DOE awards is a real but thin edge. The outcome is often half-legible: titles commonly say 'Oxford Instruments cryostat' or 'Janis'. Specialist dealers and flippers (lab-equipment resellers, eBay cryo sellers, EquipNet/BidSpotter watchers, and lab staff who know their own surplus) already watch these feeds with saved-search alerts. Rights are bought cheaply at open auction, which is good, but the auctions are competitive. Once a lot is spotted, other watchers bid it up. Volume is tiny: probably only tens of dilution fridges or SRF cavities reach surplus worldwide each year (estimate).
scored.right_bought: A surplus auction lot (GSA Auctions, GovDeals, Public Surplus, university surplus, DOE excess) bought at open auction, as-is and untested, often with pickup and rigging required within days.
scored.buyer: Quantum computing startups and university groups that are short of capital, national labs, fusion startups, and refurbishers or dealers. Well-funded buyers mostly buy new from Bluefors, Oxford or Maybell for the warranty and support. That leaves a thin secondary market at a discount.
scored.ladder: Weak. The rungs above (refurbish, then build cryostats, then sell cryogenic platforms) put the company in competition with Bluefors, Oxford Instruments and Maybell as an OEM. That is a manufacturing business, and owning surplus discovery gives no compounding advantage there. The chain ends as a niche used-equipment dealer, not a path to a very large company.
scored.fatal_flaw: The physical proving and refurbishment step (freight, He-3 mixture, compressor, multi-day cooldown, repair) is costly, slow and dominates the work, while discovery is a small share. On top of that, supply is only tens of high-value lots a year, so the TAM is tiny. It is an equipment-flipping business, not a 95-5 discovery rung.
scored.one_line_reason: Rights are cheap and buyers are real, but proving and refurbishing dominate the work (the geothermal-in-coal-mines failure), the net step-up is about 10-30x, and there are only tens of lots a year with no ladder to a large company.

scored.name: SpacingSlot / Roadside Rights: new billboard permit sites
scored.one_line: Option roadside parcels that legally qualify for new Highway Beautification Act billboard permits (incl. along future interstate segments forecast from STIPs and NEPA RODs); win the DOT permit; sell to outdoor operators.
scored.unproven_right: Ground-lease/easement options at $500-5k from farmers.
scored.proving_step: ML over DOT permit files, zoning, traffic, sign imagery, caps and corridor plans; file and win the permit.
scored.proven_buyer: Lamar, Outfront, Clear Channel, regionals ($100k-1M+ per site).
scored.public_data: State DOT outdoor advertising databases, FHWA HPMS, zoning GIS and ordinances, STIPs, NEPA EIS/RODs, ROW maps.
scored.frame: Rung: hold a ground-lease option on a roadside parcel and turn it into a DOT plus local sign permit that you sell to an operator. Discovery (finding a parcel that clears spacing, zoning, cap and visibility rules) is maybe 40-60% of the work inside that rung (my estimate). The rest is not trivial: local zoning and variance politics, neighbour opposition, scenic-byway rules, landowner negotiation, and build-or-lapse deadlines (permits often lapse in 6-12 months if no structure goes up). A capitalised buyer does exist (Lamar, Outfront, Clear Channel, regional operators). But they mostly buy built, cash-flowing structures, valued at a multiple of cash flow, not bare permits. A bare permit is worth much less than a built site.
scored.step_up: All figures are my estimates; the search budget was used up before I could verify any. Unproven right: an option or ground lease at about $500-5k a year, matching the candidate's own range and typical rural billboard ground rents. Proven right: a permitted but unbuilt interstate site probably sells for about $20k-150k. The candidate's $100k-1M+ figure applies to built, leased structures, especially digital, and building one costs roughly $100k-400k of real capex. Step-up on the right itself: about 10-100x. That is far from 10^3-10^4, and the TAM per site is small.
scored.hit_rate_capex: My estimate, not verified. Filing a permit costs roughly $100-2k plus survey and legal, so maybe $2-10k per attempt including the option. Eligibility is a deterministic rule check: commercial or industrial zoning, spacing of about 500 ft on interstates in many states, plus local caps. A good rules-based screen gets hit rates high on its own. Failures come mainly from discretionary local politics and caps, which ML over documents does not predict well. The base hit rate is not low and each attempt is not expensive, so there is no ~10x discovery-capex cut to buy. The lever is about 1.5-3x at best.
scored.data: Mostly legible already. State DOT outdoor-advertising inventories typically list permitted signs with GPS coordinates. Zoning GIS and FHWA HPMS traffic counts are structured. Spacing compliance is geometry. The only illegible piece is the future-interstate angle (STIPs, NEPA RODs), and it carries timelines of 5-15 years and a lot of route uncertainty. Rights can be bought cheaply from farmers, which is the one real positive. But incumbents' real-estate and leasing reps, and independent site developers, already scout exactly these parcels, and ground-lease aggregators such as Landmark Dividend and Radius already buy billboard leases. The outcome (where a sign is permittable) is largely readable from legible spacing and zoning data, so the ML edge is thin.
scored.right_bought: Yes. Ground-lease or easement options from rural landowners at about $500-5k (estimate), bought rather than taken first-come. The catch is that the permit itself is often first-come by filing order within a spacing zone, so it is partly a race and not just a purchase.
scored.buyer: Lamar, Outfront, Clear Channel Outdoor and regional operators. They are capitalised, but they buy mostly built and leased structures valued on cash flow, and they already run in-house site-acquisition teams.
scored.ladder: Permitted site, then build the structure, then become an operator selling ad inventory, then go digital and programmatic. This ladder ends in competing with Lamar and Outfront in a US out-of-home market of about $9B (estimate), with new supply capped by the Highway Beautification Act and local bans. There is a path to a mid-size operator, not a trillion-dollar chain.
scored.fatal_flaw: Whether a site qualifies is a deterministic rule check (spacing, zoning, caps) over mostly legible GIS and DOT inventories, and incumbents' site teams already run that check. What is left of the risk is local politics and regulatory caps, which ML cannot lever. Separately, a permit's value is small until someone pays for a real build (about $100k-400k), so the frame is not 80%+ discovery and the step-up is only about 10-100x.
scored.one_line_reason: Qualifying a billboard site is a rules check on legible data that incumbents already run, and a bare permit is worth only about 10-100x the option before costly construction, so neither the 95/5 frame nor the 10^3+ step-up holds.

scored.name: Pharmacy Location Rules site prospector (Australia)
scored.one_line: Find sites qualifying under Australia's Pharmacy Location Rules, lock lease options, win approval with a pharmacist JV, sell new pharmacies.
scored.unproven_right: Lease option beside qualifying supermarket or medical centre.
scored.proving_step: ML over ACPA decisions; surveyor measurement and application.
scored.proven_buyer: Chemist Warehouse/Sigma, Priceline, TerryWhite.
scored.public_data: ACPA decisions, FOI reports, PBS locations, Healthdirect, GLA data, ABS.
scored.frame: The rung would be: hold a lease option at a qualifying site, then get a PBS approval under Section 90 of the Pharmacy Location Rules. Finding the site is maybe 40-50% of the work (estimate). The rest is not trivial: the applicant must be a registered pharmacist, you need a surveyor and a legal submission, the ACPA has to recommend it, and then you must fit out and open a trading pharmacy (roughly A$0.5-1M fit-out plus stock, estimate) to realise the value. That physical step is not abstracted. Discovery is well below 80% of the work inside this rung.
scored.step_up: Unproven: a lease option, probably about A$5-50k in option fees and holding cost (estimate). Proven: an approved site before it trades may sell for low hundreds of thousands of AUD (estimate). An established pharmacy sells for roughly 25-40% of turnover, about A$1-4M (industry rule of thumb, unverified this run). Most of that value comes only after build-out and trading. The immediate step-up on approval alone is about 10-50x on the option cost, not 10^3-10^4.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Base hit rate: well-prepared ACPA applications are mostly approved, my estimate about 60-80%. That caps the lever at roughly 1.3-1.7x, not 10x. Cost per attempt: surveyor about A$5-15k, consultant or legal work about A$20-60k, plus the application fee (all estimates; I could not verify them because the search budget was used up). The failure mode is not finding a site. It is rule technicalities and objections from nearby pharmacies, which ML over past decisions only partly helps with.
scored.data: ACPA decisions and reasons are public. The rules are deterministic distance and facility tests: 1.5km, 10km, the supermarket floor-area test, and the medical centre prescriber-hours test. Mapping data (supermarket floor areas, PBS pharmacy locations, GP centre rosters) already makes the main signal largely legible. Banner groups' development teams and specialist pharmacy-location consultants already screen for these sites. The prescriber full-time-equivalent count at medical centres is the least legible input and gives some edge. Landlords near supermarkets know pharmacy tenancies are valuable, so lease options are not cheap from naive owners.
scored.right_bought: You can buy a lease option on the premises. But the PBS approval must be held by a pharmacist, and state laws limit pharmacy ownership to pharmacists (with narrow exceptions such as friendly societies). So a non-pharmacist company cannot own the proven asset or capture its step-up directly. It needs a pharmacist JV or nominee structure, which those laws restrict.
scored.buyer: Pharmacist owners, including those in banner or franchise groups (Chemist Warehouse/Sigma, Priceline/API-Wesfarmers, TerryWhite Chemmart). The groups themselves cannot legally own pharmacies; they place pharmacist franchisees. They are well capitalised and do pay for good approved sites.
scored.ladder: Site approval, then opening and running the pharmacy, then a multi-site group, then wholesale and distribution. The pharmacist-ownership laws cap the ladder for a non-pharmacist company, and the Location Rules limit total store count. The market is about A$20B+ per year in Australia (estimate), so the path is bounded and does not look like a trillion-dollar one.
scored.fatal_flaw: Australian law limits pharmacy ownership to pharmacists, and Section 90 approvals must be held by pharmacists. So the company cannot own the proven asset and keep the step-up itself. On top of that, approval is not where the value is realised; a fit-out and a trading business are. The base approval rate is high, so ML gives almost no hit-rate lever.
scored.one_line_reason: This fails on three counts: (1) only pharmacists can own the proven asset, (2) the step-up is about 10-50x, not 10^4, and (3) approval rates are high and the distance rules are legible, so there is little ML hit-rate lever.

scored.name: Shovel-Ready Berths: permitted-but-stalled marine terminal sites
scored.one_line: Option stalled waterfront parcels carrying live or extendable Section 10/404 permits and submerged-land leases; prove validity; sell permitted berths to energy and export developers.
scored.unproven_right: Option on parcel priced as raw industrial land.
scored.proving_step: ML over USACE notices, tidelands leases, CZM files and channel surveys.
scored.proven_buyer: Offshore-wind port developers, ammonia/e-fuel exporters, LNG developers, port authorities.
scored.public_data: USACE ORM2 and notices, channel surveys, submerged-land registries, NOAA ENC.
scored.frame: The rung is 'own a waterfront parcel with valid, transferable USACE Section 10/404 permits and a submerged-land lease, then sell it as a permitted berth.' Inside that rung, discovery (finding the parcel and checking the permits) is maybe 30-40% of the work (my estimate). The rest is legal: permit transfer letters, getting the state lease assigned, extending expirations (standard USACE individual permits usually run about 5 years), and checking that the channel depth still matches the permitted design. Buyers also price in the work they still face: dredging, piling and quay construction ($50M-$500M+ per berth, my estimate), plus FERC/DOE approvals for LNG. Those dominate the value. This looks like the geothermal-in-coal-mines counter-example, because building the bespoke terminal is much harder than finding the site.
scored.step_up: My estimate is 2-5x, not 10-50x. Deepwater-access industrial land already trades at a waterfront premium (very roughly $100k-$1M/acre depending on port, estimate). The permits save a buyer about 2-5 years and a few million dollars of permitting cost. That is a real premium but not orders of magnitude. Reference points from memory, not verified this run: Tradepoint Atlantic bought the Sparrows Point site (about 3,100 acres) for roughly $110M as raw brownfield. Stalled LNG projects that changed hands (e.g. Magnolia LNG, Commonwealth-type sales) were priced mostly on FERC authorizations and offtake, not on USACE permits. I could not run any web search (the shared budget was used up), so these numbers are unsourced estimates.
scored.hit_rate_capex: There is no expensive, mostly-failing physical proving step. 'Proving' means pulling the permit file and a title/lease review, roughly $10k-$50k of legal and survey work per site (estimate). Whether a permit is valid is close to certain once you read the permit document. So the base hit rate of proving is high, and ML has no 10x capex lever to pull. The real uncertainty is buyer demand. The offshore-wind port pipeline shrank sharply after 2025 federal actions against offshore wind, and ammonia/e-fuel export projects are mostly pre-FID. Both are market risk, not discovery risk.
scored.data: The data is public but mostly legible. USACE permits list an issue date, an expiration date and special conditions. ORM2 decisions and public notices are posted by each District, and FOIA covers the rest. State submerged-land leases are recorded instruments with terms. Channel depths are in NOAA ENC and USACE condition surveys, which are structured. So the outcome (is the permit live, when does it expire) is already written in a legible field, the same failure mode as earlier hunts. Incumbents already screen these sites: port-focused industrial brokers (JLL/CBRE port groups), Tradepoint Atlantic-style redevelopers, and the developers' own site-selection consultants. ML adds little over a structured permit query.
scored.right_bought: You can option the parcels, but not at raw-land prices. The owner of a stalled permitted terminal paid millions and spent years getting those permits and knows exactly what they hold. There is no illegible-data asymmetry like a Saskatchewan claim-holder who cannot read assessment files. The few true mispricings would be estates, bankrupt developers or legacy industrial owners whose permits are near expiry, and those permits often lapse or need re-review.
scored.buyer: Real but thin and cyclical. Buyers would be LNG developers (they need FERC more than the berth), ammonia/methanol export developers (mostly pre-FID), port authorities (often use eminent domain or public funds and pay appraised value), and offshore-wind port developers (demand collapsed in 2025-26, estimate). That is a handful of transactions a year nationally, not a repeatable flow.
scored.ladder: There is a plausible ladder: permitted site, then developed berth/terminal, then terminal operator, then logistics or export platform. Terminal operating is a large infrastructure business (e.g. port operators and LNG terminal owners worth billions). But each rung above the first is capex-heavy, bespoke construction, which ML discovery does not help with.
scored.fatal_flaw: There is no illegible discovery problem. Permit validity and expiration are legible fields the owner already knows, so you cannot buy at raw-land prices. The value step-up is about 2-5x because the bespoke terminal build (dredging, quay, FERC) dominates the work. That is the same pattern as the geothermal-in-coal-mines counter-example.
scored.one_line_reason: Permit status is already legible, owners know what they hold, the step-up is only about 2-5x, and building the terminal dwarfs the discovery work, so discovery is never 80% of any sellable rung.
sources: No web searches ran: the shared 200-call WebSearch budget for this turn was used up before this candidate; every number above is an estimate from prior knowledge and needs checking.

Prior knowledge (unverified this run): USACE standard individual permits usually carry an expiration date of about 5 years and can be transferred by a transfer letter signed by both parties (33 CFR 325).
Prior knowledge (unverified this run): Tradepoint Atlantic / Sparrows Point bought for about $110M for about 3,100 acres.
Prior knowledge (unverified this run): the US offshore-wind port pipeline contracted after 2025 federal actions on offshore wind.

scored.name: SlagBank / FlueDust: smelter and roaster residues re-read for Ge, In, Ga, Te, Sb, Bi, Co, Re
scored.one_line: Re-read remedial-investigation assay tables and feed histories at historic Cu/Pb/Zn smelter, antimony oxide and arsenic works to predict slag, flue dust and roaster residue piles rich in unanalysed by-product metals; buy removal rights from PRPs and owners; assay; sell to secondary-feed smelters and DoD-backed processors.
scored.unproven_right: Ownership/removal rights to residue heaps carried as liabilities, $0-50k.
scored.proving_step: Surface/trench grab sampling and ICP-MS full-suite assay, recovery test ($5-150k).
scored.proven_buyer: Teck Trail, Umicore, Nyrstar, Dowa, Mitsubishi Materials, Korea Zinc, US Antimony, Perpetua, DLA stockpile.
scored.public_data: EPA SEMS RI/FS/RODs, RCRAInfo, USGS/USBM Minerals Yearbook plant chapters, state brownfield inventories, Sanborn maps, historic freight tariffs.
scored.rough_step_up: ~100-1000x on a hit; few hundred sites.
scored.frame: The intended rung is to buy the removal right to a residue pile, then sample and assay it, and sell the pile as proven secondary feed. Discovery (finding which piles hold Ge/In/Ga/Te) is maybe 15-30% of the work in that rung (my estimate). The rest is physical and legal. You have to excavate, take responsibility for the hazardous waste (CERCLA owner/operator/arranger exposure, RCRA manifests), transport arsenic-bearing material, and above all prove metallurgical recovery. Ge/In sit in glassy silicate slag or ferrite at roughly 50-500 ppm (estimate, from general slag literature). Recovery is what limits the value, not finding it. This has the same shape as the geothermal-in-coal-mines counterexample: the bespoke processing step costs more than picking the right pile. Unlike Terranox, the rung has no trivial physical step.
scored.step_up: The unproven right is $0-50k per the candidate, and is often negative because the piles are carried as liabilities. A proven pile is worth what a secondary-feed smelter pays: payables are usually a fraction of contained metal, with penalties for As/Pb/Cd plus freight. My estimate is a step-up from near-zero to perhaps $0.5-5M per mid-size pile on a hit. That reads as large in multiple terms only because the base is about zero. On a value-per-tonne basis the multiple versus remediation cost is about 3-10x at best. Many hits will still net out negative after the cleanup obligation. Estimate only; my web search budget ran out, so none of these numbers are verified.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Proving is cheap. Grab/trench sampling plus ICP-MS full-suite costs roughly $5-50k per site (candidate figure; estimate), and recovery testwork is about $50-150k. The base hit rate for 'contains elevated Ge/In/Ga' is probably not low at Zn/Pb smelters, because these metals concentrate predictably by feed type (sphalerite gives Ge/In/Ga; Cu gives Te/Se/Re; Pb gives Sb/Bi). Domain metallurgists can predict that without ML. So the ML lever on discovery capex is under 2-3x, and capex is not the bottleneck anyway. Unverified: search budget exhausted.
scored.data: The data is partly illegible. EPA SEMS RI/FS/ROD assay tables usually report the RCRA-8/priority-pollutant metals (As, Pb, Cd, Zn, Cu, Sb, sometimes Tl) but rarely Ge/In/Ga/Te/Re. That gap is real, and the absence of a legible field is the one edge here. However, the feed histories in USBM Minerals Yearbook plant chapters let an expert infer by-product enrichment fairly directly. The USGS has also published slag characterisation work (e.g. Piatak et al. on historical smelter slags). Known slag-recovery precedents show the opportunity is not hidden from incumbents (named from memory, not verified this session): Gecamines/STL Big Hill slag at Lubumbashi (Ge/Co/Zn), the Tsumeb Ge slag dumps, and Teck Trail and Korea Zinc running secondary feed.
scored.right_bought: Buying the removal right is plausible: PRPs and site owners would happily hand over piles. But for the same reason it is not a cheap option but a liability transfer. Taking ownership of Superfund residue can make the buyer a PRP or arranger unless the deal is structured under bona fide prospective purchaser protections, consent decrees or EPA approval. Those take months to years and require EPA sign-off on the remedy. The 'right' is really a negotiated remediation contract, not a clean mineral-right-style option.
scored.buyer: Real capitalised buyers exist for secondary feed: Teck Trail, Umicore, Nyrstar, Korea Zinc, Dowa, Mitsubishi Materials, and DoD DPA Title III/DLA for Ge/Ga/Sb. But they buy at payables with heavy penalties, and they need proven, consistent feed and a metallurgical flowsheet. They will not pay a 10^4 premium for an assayed pile the way a developer pays for a drill-proven uranium claim.
scored.ladder: There is a real ladder: residue aggregation, then hydrometallurgical by-product recovery (a Ge/Ga/In refinery), then a domestic critical-minerals refiner with DoD offtake. China's 2023-2024 export controls on Ga/Ge/Sb create policy pull. The upper rungs are processing businesses, though, and the moat is chemistry, not discovery.
scored.fatal_flaw: Discovery is not the hard part. For trace Ge/In/Ga in glassy smelter slag, the binding constraint is metallurgical recovery plus CERCLA liability transfer. That is the geothermal-in-coal-mines failure mode: the bespoke physical and legal step dominates, so there is no frame where discovery is 80%+.
scored.one_line_reason: The ML read of RI/FS tables is a genuine gap, but sampling is cheap, enrichment is predictable from feed history, and value is gated by recovery chemistry and Superfund liability, not by finding the pile.

Prior knowledge, not verified this session: Tsumeb smelter Ge-bearing slag dumps, Namibia
Prior knowledge, not verified this session: CERCLA bona fide prospective purchaser provisions (42 USC 9601(40), 9607(r))

scored.name: Breeze Signal: ML bloodstock pinhooking
scored.one_line: Buy weanlings and yearlings at low-tier sales, ML picks latent elite athletes from video and pedigree, prove in breeze-ups or races, sell to breeding operations.
scored.unproven_right: Ownership of unraced young horses, $5-30k.
scored.proving_step: Timed breeze or stakes win; training cost real.
scored.proven_buyer: Coolmore, Godolphin, Juddmonte, Gulf/Japanese buyers.
scored.public_data: Equibase/Racing Post, replays, breeze-up videos, sale catalogues, Jockey Club pedigrees.
scored.frame: The candidate rungs are (a) buying a weanling or yearling and selling it as a yearling or 2-year-old (pinhooking) and (b) buying unraced and racing it to a stakes win. Neither is a discovery-dominated rung. My estimate is that picking the horse is 30-50% of the work. The rest is physical: 6-24 months of feeding, breaking, training and vet care, plus injury and death risk. Development decides the outcome as much as selection does. Training plainly creates value; it is not drilling. The buyers are well capitalised (Coolmore, Godolphin, Juddmonte, Gulf and Japanese buyers), but they buy horses that are already proven. Discovery never reaches 80% in any frame.
scored.step_up: These are estimates from memory, not sourced this run. A typical good pinhook returns about 1.5-5x, for example a $30k yearling resold for $75-150k at a 2-year-old in-training sale such as OBS March or Arqana. A $5-30k horse that becomes a Grade 1 winner and colt stallion prospect can be worth $5M-$30M+, which is 10^2-10^3x. But that happens about 0.1-0.5% of the time and takes 2-3 years. The step-up is also not immediate. The 10^3 step needs years of racing, not a single cheap test, so the expected step-up on the cheap proving step (the breeze) is only about 3x.
scored.hit_rate_capex: These are estimates from memory, not sourced this run. Commonly cited industry figures put stakes winners at about 3% of North American foals, and graded stakes winners under 1%. Industry folklore holds that roughly half of pinhooks lose money once costs are counted. The cost of one proving attempt is the purchase ($5-30k) plus preparation and training to a breeze or race. My estimate for that is $30-60k per horse per year in the US (training fees about $100-150 a day, plus vet, farrier and insurance). Total is about $50-150k a shot. The base hit rate is low, but the lever is mostly unavailable. Most failures come from soundness, temperament and injury after purchase, which video and pedigree cannot predict. So ML cannot cut the cost per shot about 10x; my guess is 1.5-2x on selection at best. Training cost is fixed per horse whatever the model says.
scored.data: The data is public but already legible and heavily worked over. Breeze-up times are published by the sale companies (OBS, Fasig-Tipton, Arqana, Tattersalls). Race results, speed figures and earnings are structured fields in Equibase, Racing Post and Timeform. Pedigrees are structured in the Jockey Club database, and black-type stakes winners are flagged in the sale catalogues. So the outcome is already written into legible fields, which is exactly the failure mode the rubric warns about. The signals that are not yet legible are videos of how a horse moves and biometric data. Incumbents already extract these: EQB (Jeff Seder; heart scans and biomechanics; known for picking American Pharoah), DataTrack, Bloodstock Data/ThoroughBrain, Brisnet, and the agent teams at Coolmore and Godolphin. The most predictive data is private, not public: repository X-rays, scopes, gallop GPS.
scored.right_bought: The asset is bought, which fits the model: horses are purchased at auction (Keeneland November/September, Tattersalls, Goffs, OBS) or privately. But the sellers are breeders and consignors who know the market well and see the same videos, pedigrees and vet records. Prices come from an open-outcry auction where Coolmore, Godolphin and Japanese buyers bid against each other. That leaves little systematic discount, so the asset is not a mispriced right held by owners who cannot read the data.
scored.buyer: Pinhooked 2-year-olds are bought by trainers and racing owners, plus stables like Godolphin, Coolmore, Juddmonte, Japanese buyers and Saudi/Gulf owners. Proven stakes winners and stallion prospects are bought by breeding operations: Coolmore, Darley, Spendthrift, Shadai, WinStar. These buyers are well capitalised, but the whole market is small. My estimate is about $4-6B a year in global thoroughbred auction turnover.
scored.ladder: Pinhooking leads to racing ownership, then standing stallions and breeding (a stallion farm), then the full farm-to-racing operation, which is the Coolmore or Darley model. The rungs are real and Coolmore shows the top of the ladder. But the ceiling is a multi-billion-dollar private bloodstock empire funded by a sovereign or a billionaire, not a trillion-dollar path. The market is hard-capped by the size of racing and its wagering economy, which is shrinking in the US.
scored.fatal_flaw: The proving step is physical and costly, not abstracted. Every horse costs about $30-60k a year to raise and train, with injury and death risk, whatever ML picks. Most failures come from unobservable soundness and temperament, not from things ML could see in the data. The outcomes (breeze times, race results, black type) are already legible public fields that efficient, sophisticated auction buyers price, and EQB-style analytics firms already mine the illegible video and biometric signals.
scored.one_line_reason: Fails the Terranox test: training a horse is the bespoke plant, not the drill. Discovery is under 50% of the rung, outcomes are already legible, sellers are sophisticated, and the market is small.

Estimate (prior knowledge): US training day rates of about $100-150, so roughly $40-55k a year per horse

scored.name: Cohort Strains: exclusive isolate rights over banked human microbiome cohorts
scored.one_line: Buy exclusive commercial isolation rights to frozen stool/tissue biobanks of academic cohorts whose metagenomes and outcome tables are public; ML picks strain-level variants tied to clinical effects; culture the strain, run one mouse model and sell the live biotherapeutic candidate.
scored.unproven_right: Exclusive commercial-use agreement with a university biobank or cohort PI, ~$50-250k.
scored.proving_step: Anaerobic culture, whole-genome confirmation and one mouse model readout, hundreds of thousands of dollars via CRO.
scored.proven_buyer: Nestle Health Science, Danone, Takeda, J&J, Seres/Ferring-type LBP developers, microbiome VCs.
scored.public_data: SRA/ENA metagenomes (HMP, MetaCardis, TwinsUK, LifeLines-DEEP, IBD and oncology cohorts), dbGaP summary tables, UHGG, curatedMetagenomicData.
scored.frame: The proposed rung is "exclusive isolate rights to a cohort biobank -> culture + WGS + one mouse study -> sell candidate." Inside that rung discovery is NOT 80%+ and the physical step is NOT trivial: >70% of human gut species in the UHGG catalogue have no cultured representative at all (Almeida et al., Nat Biotechnol 2021, 39:105-114), so anaerobic isolation of the specific strain the model picked is bespoke R&D with an unknown success rate, not an abstracted commodity step like a contract drill rig. One mouse readout is also not the proving step a buyer prices off; the thing that actually converts a strain into value is human clinical efficacy, which is years and tens of millions away. This is structurally the geothermal-in-coal-mines counter-example: building the "plant" (culture, GMP-able manufacturing, in vivo, IND, trial) is much harder than finding the candidate. There is no capitalised buyer who buys the output of this single rung at the claimed price: the best-documented precedent for a preclinical live biotherapeutic is Takeda/Finch FIN-524 at $10M upfront (2017), and even that was a co-development deal with an operating platform company, not a purchase of a strain with one mouse readout.
scored.step_up: Claimed $50-250k -> $20-200M (10^2-10^3x). Real comparables do not support it, and the sector repriced to near zero. Evelo paid Mayo Clinic US$12,500 for a single Prevotella melaninogenica strain (Evelo 10-K exhibit, Mayo agreement), i.e. raw strain material is a four-figure item, not a scarce right. Preclinical LBP upfronts: Takeda/Finch $10M (2017); OptiBiotix's L. plantarum cholesterol strain licence was a "six figure payment" on signing. Exit economics: Seres sold VOWST - an FDA-APPROVED product with revenue - to Nestle Health Science in 2024 on undisclosed terms sized to clear ~$110M of Oaktree debt, and Nestle later bought out remaining sales milestones for $25M total ($12.5M on 2026-07-01 and 2026-10-01). Kaleido shut down (2023), Evelo failed its primary endpoint and its board resigned, 4D pharma went into administration. So the honest step-up on a culture+mouse hit is roughly $100k -> low single-digit millions in a good case (~10-30x), and it is not immediate: it is realised over years and only if the clinic cooperates. Scored 2-3; I give 2 because the "immediate on a hit" condition fails outright. (My estimate, anchored on the deals above.)
scored.hit_rate_capex: Cost per proving attempt (my estimate from CRO price lists and standard practice): targeted anaerobic isolation + whole-genome confirmation ~$30-150k per strain; one mouse efficacy study at a CRO ~$150-500k including colonisation/germ-free or gnotobiotic housing, which is the dominant cost. So ~$200-650k per attempt, in the candidate's stated range. The problem is the direction of the base rate. The nominal proving step (does the strain do something in a mouse?) has a HIGH base hit rate - the microbiome literature is saturated with positive mouse results - so 1/base-hit-rate caps the ML lever at roughly 2-3x, not 10x. The step with the genuinely low base rate is human efficacy, and ML over observational metagenomes cannot raise it, because the associations are confounded: the canonical case is that the type-2-diabetes gut signature is substantially a metformin signature, with a classifier trained on metformin-exposed T2D samples outperforming one trained on metformin-unexposed samples; a 2025 bioRxiv preprint on confounder-free microbiome phenotype models shows transit time, inflammation and BMI overriding the variance explained by colorectal-cancer case status. ML here buys more shots at a target that is partly an artefact.
scored.data: Public, yes; illegible, no. SRA/ENA metagenomes, HMP, MetaCardis, TwinsUK, LifeLines-DEEP are already assembled, taxonomically profiled and outcome-labelled for you: curatedMetagenomicData ships uniformly processed profiles with study-level disease category and case counts per dataset, and UHGG/MGnify already reconstructed 204,938 genomes across 4,644 gut prokaryote species (Almeida 2021). That is the opposite of scanned Saskatchewan assessment files - it is a tidy matrix with the label column filled in, which is exactly the failure mode the rubric warns about ("the outcome is already summarised in a legible field"): the disease label IS the metadata field, and thousands of published differential-abundance and ML-classifier papers have already run the case-control model on these exact cohorts. The remaining signal is strain-level resolution, which is real but is also the explicit research programme of StrainPhlAn/inStrain academic groups and of every surviving microbiome company. Incumbent extraction is high, not absent.
scored.right_bought: This is where the analogy breaks hardest. A mineral right is excludable by law and geographically unique; a bacterial strain is neither. If the model says "this Akkermansia/Faecalibacterium lineage with these genes drives the effect," a competitor can isolate a conspecific strain from any donor, or order the type strain from DSMZ/ATCC, and does not need your biobank at all. Composition-of-matter patents on an isolated natural strain are narrow (and post-Myriad/Alice shaky on natural products), so even a granted patent does not fence the finding. Layered on top: the $50-250k "exclusive commercial isolation right" is legally fragile - most academic cohort consent is broad-research consent that does not authorise exclusive commercial exploitation of participant-derived material; IRB re-consent, GDPR/HIPAA, and institutional tech-transfer policy routinely forbid granting one company exclusivity over a shared cohort resource, and NIH-funded repositories are generally obliged to distribute material non-exclusively. The owners are also not uninformed: university TTOs and cohort PIs read the metagenomics literature on their own cohort - they publish it. So there is no cheap purchase from a counterparty who cannot read the data, and no step-up captured because there is no exclusion.
scored.buyer: Stated buyers (Nestle Health Science, Danone, Takeda, J&J, Seres/Ferring-type developers, microbiome VCs) exist but are the wrong shape and the wrong vintage. Nestle Health Science is a real buyer but it buys approved, revenue-generating products (VOWST, 2024), and even then it bought out remaining milestones for $25M. Takeda's FIN-524 deal with Finch is the only clean preclinical-strain precedent and sits at $10M upfront in 2017, pre-crash. Since then the buy side for preclinical microbiome assets has largely exited: Kaleido dissolved, Evelo failed and its board resigned, 4D pharma went into administration, Seres sold its product and shrank to a cash-runway story, and the generalist microbiome VC that funded this layer is gone. A capitalised buyer who will pay $20-200M for one strain plus one mouse model does not currently exist.
scored.ladder: Rungs above do exist and are genuinely large: strain -> IND-enabling tox and GMP manufacturing -> Phase 1/2 -> approved live biotherapeutic -> consumer/medical-nutrition brand (the VOWST and Nestle path). Ceiling is real, multi-billion. But climbing any of them requires full biotech capex and 8-12 years, which inverts the Terranox logic: the smallest rung here is not self-funding, so there is no cash-generative base to climb from. Scored 3 on ladder existence, with the caveat that the ladder cannot be climbed out of rung-one proceeds.
scored.fatal_flaw: The asset is not excludable. A bacterial strain is not a mineral title: anyone can re-isolate a conspecific strain from any donor or buy the type strain from a culture collection, so the "exclusive isolate right" purchased from a biobank fences nothing, and no step-up can be captured even if the ML call is correct. Compounding it, the physical step is harder than the find (>70% of gut species have never been cultured) and the public data is already fully legible with the outcome label in a metadata field - the exact condition the rubric says kills the edge.
scored.one_line_reason: Total 8/25: the ML call may be right but you cannot own it - strains are re-isolable by anyone, the data is a tidy labelled matrix thousands of papers have already mined, culturing is the hard part rather than the trivial part, and the preclinical microbiome buy side that would pay the step-up has collapsed.

scored.name: Orphan Enzyme Estates: lapsed enzyme patent families proven against live markets
scored.one_line: Buy enzyme and strain patent families from defunct or disinterested owners for back fees; ML over sequence databases finds dormant claims covering high-performing enzymes for markets that appeared after filing; express to prove the claim is real and sell to whoever needs it.
scored.unproven_right: Patent families and Budapest Treaty deposits bought in bulk for low thousands per family.
scored.proving_step: Order deposited strain or synthesise sequence, express, assay against today's benchmark; cheap.
scored.proven_buyer: Enzyme and ingredient majors and manufacturers whose process falls inside the claim; $1-50M licence or sale.
scored.public_data: Google Patents/Espacenet sequence listings, USPTO maintenance-fee and assignment records, Budapest deposits, NCBI/UniProt, product sequence disclosures.
scored.frame: The rung on offer is "own a dormant enzyme patent family and prove it covers a live commercial process." Discovery here means mapping claims onto the sequences of commercial enzymes, and ML could plausibly do most of that, maybe 30-40% of the total work. The pitch's proving step (express the enzyme and assay it) proves nothing a buyer pays for. A granted patent is already presumed valid, and performance against a benchmark does not create licence value. A licence is worth something only when a third party actually practises the claim and cannot design around it. Showing that means sequencing a competitor's product, sending a demand letter, and in most cases suing or settling. That is litigation, not a trivial or abstracted physical step. So inside the sellable rung, discovery is well under 80% and the hard part is enforcement. This is the coal-mine-geothermal pattern: finding the asset is easier than turning it into value.
scored.step_up: Unproven: a dormant family at roughly $2-20k (candidate's figure; my estimate is low thousands to tens of thousands for small-owner families in a bulk deal). Proven: the median NPE suit resolves for about $0.52-0.55M in combined legal and settlement cost, with a mean of $6-7.6M skewed by a few large cases (RPX NPE cost studies, 2013). On the asking side, Ocean Tomo's average ask per patent was about $150-180k in 2020-21, and 2006-08 live auctions averaged $116k-$622k per lot sold, with about half of lots unsold. A realistic hit is therefore about 10-100x, not 10^3. The $1-50M exit needs a major's flagship process to sit squarely inside the claim, which is rare and is exactly what majors' freedom-to-operate teams already check.
scored.hit_rate_capex: The proving step the candidate names, expressing and assaying, costs about $1-10k per sequence (my estimate for gene synthesis plus expression and assay) and succeeds often, so it is not the bottleneck and ML has little to lever. The real proving step is enforcement. Median litigation cost is about $0.6M through claim construction and $1M through trial for $1-10M at risk, and $1.5M / $3M for $10-25M at risk (AIPLA 2025, as reported by IPWatchdog). Patentee win rates at trial are commonly cited around 25-35% (my estimate from general patent-litigation statistics). ML cannot drop that cost 10x. Legal fees, inter partes review challenges and design-arounds dominate. The lever is capped near 1-2x.
scored.data: The data is public. Google Patents and Espacenet sequence listings, USPTO maintenance-fee and assignment records, and NCBI/UniProt are all searchable. Sequence listings are structured (ST.26 XML), and BLAST against claims is routine work for IP firms. So the data is legible, not hidden. Maintenance status is a legible field. The legible field does not record infringement, but infringement is also not visible in public data, because commercial enzyme sequences are mostly trade secrets. That makes the key signal neither public nor ML-extractable without buying products and sequencing them. On the right itself: a patent that lapsed for unpaid fees is in the public domain and cannot be bought. Only the owner can revive it, within 2 years and only for unintentional delay, and only about 2.5% are reinstated (Patently-O, 2009). Live families from disinterested owners can be bought, but they are near the end of their 20-year term if the market appeared after filing. Incumbents and competitors already work this space: Intellectual Ventures, RPX, IP brokers such as Ocean Tomo, and the majors' own patent-landscaping teams (Novonesis, IFF, DSM-Firmenich).
scored.right_bought: Yes for live families: they are bought from defunct biotechs, universities and bankruptcy estates, often cheaply. No for genuinely lapsed families, which are public domain and therefore not ownable. Budapest Treaty deposits give access to the strain, not an exclusive right.
scored.buyer: The intended buyers are enzyme and ingredient majors such as Novonesis, IFF and DSM-Firmenich, plus industrial manufacturers. They are well capitalised, but they buy defensively and grudgingly. Their typical reaction to an asserted patent is an inter partes review, a design-around (enzymes can be mutated out of a sequence-identity claim) or a nuisance-value settlement, not a $1-50M purchase. The output of the rung reaches them as a litigation threat, not as an asset they want.
scored.ladder: The ladder is weak. The patents expire within years, so nothing compounds. In principle you could step up to manufacturing the enzymes yourself, but that is a capital- and know-how-heavy fermentation business where the majors have about 50%+ share (Novonesis alone), and owning expiring patents gives no moat there. The more natural ladder is toward an NPE or patent-aggregator business, which tops out at a few billion dollars, not a trillion.
scored.fatal_flaw: The step-up is realised through enforcement, not discovery. A patent is worth money only if someone currently infringes it and cannot design around it, and proving that means litigation at a median cost of $0.6-3M per case with low win rates. That is not trivial, ML cannot drop it 10x, and expressing the enzyme in the lab adds no value. On top of that, families that truly lapsed are public domain and cannot be bought, and families that are still live but cover markets that appeared after filing have little term left.
scored.one_line_reason: The value comes from litigating against infringers, not from discovery, so this is a patent-troll model with about 10-100x upside, litigation-dominated costs and expiring assets.

scored.name: Phage Rights: exclusive phage isolates for crop bacterial disease
scored.one_line: Take exclusive commercial rights to deposited phage isolates; ML on phage genomes and pathogen pangenomes predicts which lyse today's field strains of Xylella, Erwinia, Ralstonia, Xanthomonas and Clavibacter; prove on plate and in one greenhouse trial; sell the cocktail right.
scored.unproven_right: Exclusive commercial licences on deposited phages and grower-site sampling, a few thousand dollars each.
scored.proving_step: Host-range plating against current field isolates, then one greenhouse or small-plot trial.
scored.proven_buyer: Certis/Mitsui, Syngenta Biologicals, Bayer, APS Biocontrol-type acquirers, state/industry disease boards.
scored.public_data: INPHARED phage sets, NCBI viral and host genomes, pathogen pangenomes, PADLOC/DefenseFinder, collection catalogues with only propagating-host metadata.
scored.frame: The proposed rung is "isolate + plate-proven host range on current field strains," sold to an ag-biologicals acquirer. Inside that rung discovery (which phage lyses today's strains) is maybe 30-40% of the work at most: the thing a capitalised buyer actually pays for in crop phage biocontrol is a formulated, shelf-stable, field-efficacious, EPA/FIFRA-registered product. Plate host-range is cheap and fast (~$50-200/isolate-strain pair, my estimate from standard spot/plaque assay consumables and labour), but so is it for everyone, and a greenhouse hit does not transfer to field: phage UV/desiccation sensitivity and resistance emergence make field efficacy the dominant uncertainty, which no amount of genome ML resolves. This is structurally the geothermal-in-coal-mine failure mode: building the bespoke deliverable (stable formulation + registration + field data package) is much harder than finding the right phage. There is no established market where someone writes a cheque for a plate-positive, unregistered cocktail right the way a mine developer writes one for a drilled uranium claim.
scored.step_up: Claimed $5-30k to $10-100M (10^3-10^4x) is unsupported by any observable transaction. Price of the unproven right: public culture collections distribute deposited phages for roughly $100-500 per isolate (DSMZ/ATCC-type catalogue pricing; my estimate within that range), and exclusive commercial licences on an already-public deposit are generally not available at all because deposits under Budapest-Treaty/open-collection terms are distributed non-exclusively. Price of the proven right: no disclosed comparables exist. The closest real datapoints found are the Phagelux acquisition of OmniLytics (AgriPhage, the only EPA-registered crop phage product line in the US) with no disclosed value, and EcoPhage, formed 2019 by Bayer with the Bayer-Trendlines Ag Innovation Fund as a seed-stage vehicle rather than an acquisition. Both suggest the whole registered-product company trades at venture-seed to small-M&A scale, not $10-100M for a pre-registration cocktail. Honest estimate for a plate+greenhouse-positive cocktail with no field or regulatory data: $100k-1M in option/milestone terms, i.e. roughly 10-100x on a few thousand dollars of inputs, not 10^3-10^4x.
scored.hit_rate_capex: The proving step is cheap, not expensive, which breaks the C3 lever: a host-range plating campaign against a panel of field isolates costs hundreds to a few thousand dollars, and phage hunters routinely screen dozens of candidates because screening is the cheap part. With a cost per attempt that low there is no 10x capex to cut; ML buys you nothing you could not buy with a bigger plate panel. Worse, the ML itself underperforms where it would need to work: a published benchmark of 11 host-prediction tools using 16 broad-spectrum phages found ML/DL methods are accurate mainly at species or genus level, while at strain level only moderate sensitivity (<80%) is reachable and precision is low (<40%). Receptor-binding-protein models report PR-AUC 73.6-93.8% but only on narrow, well-sampled hosts (E. coli, Salmonella, C. difficile) — not Xylella, Clavibacter or Ralstonia, where phage-host training pairs are sparse. The expensive, mostly-failing step in this business is the field trial and registration package (multi-season, multi-site, my estimate $1-5M and multi-year for a FIFRA biopesticide), and ML on phage genomes does not raise that hit rate.
scored.data: Partly favourable, and the one genuinely good feature of this candidate: collection catalogues record only the propagating host, so the thing you care about (lysis of current field strains) is NOT written into a legible status field — unlike the prior hunts where regulators summarised the answer. INPHARED/NCBI phage genomes, pathogen pangenomes and PADLOC/DefenseFinder defence-system calls are public and genuinely underexploited. But the data is not illegible in the Terranox sense: it is clean FASTA in structured databases that every academic phage lab and every phage startup already mines, not scanned paper nobody can read. And the binding constraint is not data legibility, it is that the ground truth (does this phage lyse the strain in a field) is generated by wet-lab work that is cheap enough for anyone to do.
scored.right_bought: This is where it collapses. There is no excludable, cheaply-purchasable right. Deposited phages in public collections are distributed non-exclusively by design; the depositor, not the collection, would have to grant exclusivity, and for an already-published isolate that exclusivity is close to worthless because anyone can order the same strain. More fundamentally, phages are the least scarce biological asset there is: a new lytic phage against a given plant pathogen can be isolated de novo from soil, sewage or infected plant material for roughly $100-500 of consumables in a week or two (my estimate), which is why every ag-phage programme does its own isolation rather than licensing. Compare uranium: you cannot make a new Athabasca basin. Grower-site sampling access is also non-exclusive in practice and unenforceable as an asset. So there is no owner "who cannot read the data" sitting on something you can buy at $5-30k and revalue — the supply of substitutes is effectively infinite at near-zero cost.
scored.buyer: Named buyers are real companies but not capitalised buyers of this rung's output. Certis/Mitsui (owner of EPA-registered phage products via the AgriPhage lineage; the only agricultural phage franchise with a registration history, acquired by Phagelux at undisclosed value), Syngenta Biologicals and Bayer (which chose to build EcoPhage with Trendlines rather than license isolates) all have in-house isolation capability and no demonstrated practice of buying unregistered plate-proven cocktails. State/industry disease boards fund trials; they do not buy asset rights. There is no equivalent of the mine developer who is "in for $40k/ha and collects $100k/ha" — the buyer's marginal cost after your rung is the entire $1-5M-plus registration and formulation programme, dwarfing anything you can charge for the isolate, so the raw-dollar logic that makes Terranox work for both parties inverts here.
scored.ladder: The ladder itself is genuinely good and is the strongest leg: isolate/cocktail right → formulation and stability → EPA/FIFRA registration and label → branded product with distribution → grower-facing application service and resistance-monitoring subscription → broader ag-biologicals platform spanning multiple crops and pathogens. Each rung has a real incumbent and real revenue, and climbing it is the Bayer/Certis business, so a company that genuinely won the bottom rung would have a legible path to scale. The problem is purely that the bottom rung is not winnable or ownable, so the ladder has no first step to stand on.
scored.fatal_flaw: No excludable right: the asset is infinitely substitutable. A new lytic phage against any of these pathogens can be isolated fresh from the environment for a few hundred dollars in days, and deposited phages are distributed non-exclusively, so there is nothing scarce to buy cheaply from an owner who cannot read the data — and the value-creating step is the multi-million-dollar field-efficacy and FIFRA registration package, not discovery.
scored.one_line_reason: Scores 8/25: real vertical ladder and genuinely non-summarised outcome data, but the proving step is cheap rather than expensive (no 10x capex lever), strain-level host-range ML has <40% precision in published benchmarks, and the "right" is unownable because phages are isolable de novo for a few hundred dollars, so there is no $1/ha-to-$10,000/ha asset to hold.
