scored.name: SportScout: somatic-mutant ornamental plant hunting
scored.one_line: Buy single plants with new somatic sports (variegation, dwarfing, new colour) for $20-200 from growers and hobbyists; a vision model screens listing photos; outsourced tissue culture proves stability; patent and license to wholesale growers.
scored.unproven_right: Ownership of one physical plant showing a new sport, bought before propagation or patenting (within the one-year public-sale bar).
scored.proving_step: Vision screening, then 2-3 generations of tissue culture/cuttings (~$2-5k) and a USPTO plant patent; most sports revert (hit rate ~1-5%).
scored.proven_buyer: Costa Farms, Dümmen Orange, Ball Horticultural, Proven Winners licensing.
scored.public_data: Etsy/eBay/Facebook/Instagram plant listing images, USPTO plant patents, UPOV PLUTO, ICRA lists.
scored.frame: The rung is: own a stabilised, patented sport and license it to a brand or wholesaler. Spotting the sport is maybe 30-40% of the work inside that rung (my estimate). The rest is physical and slow: 2-3 generations of propagation to prove the sport stays stable, multi-season trials to show the plant is distinct, uniform and sells, then patent prosecution. One hosta example took 9 years from selection to grant (Bellingrath). Brands like Proven Winners then do the marketing that actually creates the value. The physical step is not trivial or abstracted. It is the hard part, much like the geothermal-in-coal-mines counter-example. A buyer does exist (brand licensing programmes), but it pays as royalties over time, not as an upfront purchase.
scored.step_up: Unproven: a $20-200 plant (candidate's figure). Hobby sellers who see variegation already list it at $100s-1000s, and variegated Monstera fell to $25-50 retail once tissue culture scaled it up (plantcelltechnology blog). Proven: royalties run about $0.10-2.00 per plant over a 20-year patent (Bellingrath). Proven Winners says it is usually "a few cents" and gives 50,000 plants x $0.02 = $1,000 as its example. Assuming 50k-500k plants a year at $0.05-0.25, a typical licensed sport earns roughly $2.5k-125k a year (my estimate), paid slowly. The candidate's $100k-2M figure fits only rare hits. A realistic upfront-equivalent step-up is about 50-500x on the plant cost, before the $2-5k proving cost, and nothing is realised at the moment of a hit.
scored.hit_rate_capex: The candidate puts the base hit rate at about 1-5% surviving reversion. No measured reversion rate was found; sellers say most tissue-culture plantlets of rare variegates revert to green. Each proving attempt costs about $2-5k for propagation and trials plus about $3k for the patent (Bellingrath), and takes 12-24+ months. ML vision can only rank what a plant looks like in a photo. Whether a sport is stable depends on the chimera's layer structure, which a listing photo cannot show, so ML barely improves the hit rate on the costly step. A 10x capex cut is implausible; my estimate is at most about 1.5-2x from better triage.
scored.data: Listing photos on Etsy, eBay, Instagram and Facebook are public, but the outcome is already legible. Sellers title listings "variegated", "sport" or "albo" and price them at a premium, and hobbyists understand variegation value perfectly well. The legal right also degrades at the moment the data appears: a US plant patent must be filed within one year of the first offer for sale or showing, "even on the Internet" (Bellingrath). So the listing itself starts the clock and is a public disclosure. The patent also has to name the actual discoverer (the hobbyist) as inventor, so each deal needs an assignment. Incumbents produce most sports in their own tissue-culture labs at scale: 'Singing in the Rain' and 'Etched Glass' were found in Zeeland, MI wholesale TC labs and 'American Icon' in a Waseca, MN TC lab (USPTO plant patents PP19565, PP30748, PP17441).
scored.right_bought: Yes, a single plant can be bought cheaply. But the sellers are exactly the people who can read the signal, since variegation is visible and already priced. Brand licence terms often assign sports of patented varieties to the patent holder, which removes much of the supply. The one-year public-sale/Internet bar may already be running when the plant is bought.
scored.buyer: Proven Winners, Ball Horticultural, Dümmen Orange, Costa Farms and Walters Gardens. They buy through royalty-licence programmes worth cents to dollars per plant, not lump-sum purchases. Their own TC labs are where most sports are found.
scored.ladder: The rungs above are: sport hunting, then a breeding programme, then a brand/licensing company, then young-plant propagation and wholesale. Leaders at the top are Ball Horticultural and Dümmen Orange, each with low single-digit $B revenue (my estimate). A ladder exists, but its ceiling is a few billion dollars, not a trillion-dollar path.
scored.fatal_flaw: The value is not illegible and not realised on a hit. Sports are visible and already priced by the hobbyists who list them, and the listing starts the one-year patent bar. Most commercially useful sports come out of incumbents' own tissue-culture labs. Proving stability takes years of physical propagation and trials that ML cannot speed up, and the payoff is cents-per-plant royalties. That makes the step-up small, slow and owned by the licensor.
scored.one_line_reason: Fails the Terranox shape. The physical proving step (stabilisation, trials, patent) is most of the work and ML barely moves it. The signal is already legible and priced by sellers, incumbents find most sports in their own labs, and royalties of cents per plant cap the step-up well below 10^3 at the moment of a hit.

scored.name: War Cargo Title / Cargo Ledger / Underwriter's Wreck: insurer- and government-owned sunken cargo
scored.one_line: Buy salvage contracts or title from governments (UK DfT, MARAD) and underwriters who own war-loss and casualty cargo; ML over scanned manifests, war-risk claims, Lloyd's casualty lists and U-boat/convoy logs shrinks the search box; an AUV/ROV survey proves wreck and cargo; sell to recovery contractors.
scored.unproven_right: Salvage-rights contract or title transfer for a named loss, typically on 75-80% salvor share, ~$10-100k.
scored.proving_step: ML position reconciliation plus one AUV side-scan/magnetometer and ROV identification run, ~$0.1-3M; admiralty arrest.
scored.proven_buyer: Deep-ocean recovery contractors and financiers (Ocean Infinity, Odyssey-type, Smit), metal traders. SS Gairsoppa yielded ~110 t silver.
scored.public_data: UK National Archives BT/MT/ADM series, Lloyd's List and War Losses, uboat.net and KTB logs, UKHO and NOAA AWOIS wrecks, EMODnet/GEBCO/NCEI multibeam, NARA convoy records.
scored.rough_step_up: ~10^3x on the right; recovery is hard and bespoke, so sell before recovery; UNESCO/war-grave limits.
scored.frame: The intended rung is 'located and identified wreck under salvage contract'. There is no evidence that this rung trades on its own. Value is realised only once cargo is recovered and sold. Odyssey's own deals (Gairsoppa with UK DfT, the SS Central America receiver) are search-and-recovery contracts where the salvor takes the whole risk. I found no market for selling a located wreck before recovery. Once recovery is in the frame, discovery is roughly 10-30% of the work (my estimate). Gairsoppa's search and recovery budget was single-digit $M against a 4,700 m-deep lift that needed specialist ROVs. This is the geothermal-in-coal-mines pattern: the bespoke physical step dominates the work.
scored.step_up: There is no observed price for the unproven or the proven right. UK DfT awards contracts by competitive tender, with the salvor bearing search and recovery risk and keeping 80% of net salved value after expenses (Odyssey press release). There is no up-front purchase price, so the '$10-100k right' in the candidate is unsupported. Finding the wreck creates a contingent claim on a cargo whose value is already known, but nobody pays a quoted price for that claim. My estimate is a 3-10x option-value uplift that is illiquid. For scale: Odyssey's entire shipwreck research database and assets sold for $21M in 2015 (net book $13.5M). Total Gairsoppa monetisation was ~$80M over two years against cargo estimates of $121-260M.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Base hit rate per search is unknown. One data point: the 1989 Gairsoppa search by the sole bidder failed to find the wreck, and Odyssey later found it. Cost per proving attempt is ~$0.1-3M for a survey (my estimate, consistent with the 'single-digit millions' total budget). Better positioning from ML could cut search cost, but search is the minority of total project cost. Recovery is tens of $M, so a 10x discovery-capex cut does not give 10x more shots at the full value. Industry economics are poor: of 52 annual reports from listed shipwreck-recovery firms since 1996, only 5 show a net profit, and Odyssey has ~$150M in cumulative losses (secondary magazine source, unverified).
scored.data: The data is public but illegible: National Archives BT/MT/ADM series, Lloyd's War Losses, convoy logs and KTB logs. But the outcome (what cargo and roughly how much) is already summarised in legible insurance and war-risk claim records. That is exactly why governments know to tender these contracts. The ML edge would only cover position, and specialist researchers already do that: Odyssey's research department, the Magellan/Monaco Financial database, Ocean Infinity. Wreck-specific historians also make it a human-scale task, since each target is a single event and not a population to model.
scored.right_bought: Not cheaply bought from owners who cannot read the data. The owners (UK DfT, MARAD, underwriters) know exactly what they lost. They award rights by competitive tender on a net-share basis, not for a cash price. War-grave status, the UNESCO 2001 Convention and sovereign-immunity rules (for naval vessels) limit which rights are available. Admiralty arrest is contestable, as Odyssey's Black Swan loss to Spain showed.
scored.buyer: There is no buyer of record for a located but unrecovered wreck. Monaco Financial/Magellan paid $21M for a whole portfolio database plus assets, and that is the closest comparable. Recovery contractors (Odyssey, Ocean Infinity, Smit) prefer to hold contracts themselves on cost-plus or net-share terms. Metal traders buy only recovered bullion.
scored.ladder: Short. The rungs are research, then search, then recovery, then sale of metal or coins. The top of the ladder is a niche: the global pool of high-value insured metal-cargo wrecks is in the low hundreds, and each is a one-off, so there is no compounding path to a very large company. The Odyssey precedent ended with the company pivoting to seabed phosphate mining.
scored.fatal_flaw: The step-up is not realised at the discovery rung. A located wreck has no liquid buyer, and value comes only after bespoke, deep, legally contested recovery. On top of that, the cargo value is already known to the owners, who award rights by competitive tender and not for a cheap cash price. So there is neither an information-asymmetry purchase nor a sellable 95%-discovery rung.
scored.one_line_reason: The discovery rung isn't sellable: value only comes after hard, bespoke recovery (the coal-mine geothermal failure mode). Owners already know the cargo value and award rights by tender for a net share. And 25 years of Odyssey losses, ending in a $21M sale of its whole database, cap the upside.

scored.name: Sleeper Atelier: mis-catalogued Chinese imperial ceramics and works of art
scored.one_line: Buy under-described Asian ceramics and bronzes at regional sales for $200-2k; image models against palace and museum collections and scanned HK catalogues flag imperial pieces; TL/XRF and specialist vetting prove them for HK sales.
scored.unproven_right: Clear title to an object sold as decorative 20th century.
scored.proving_step: ML triage, purchase, TL/XRF (~$500) and specialist opinion.
scored.proven_buyer: Sotheby's, Christie's, Poly, Bonhams Asian art; mainland and HK collectors.
scored.public_data: LiveAuctioneers/Invaluable/Proxibid archives, Palace Museum and NPM Taipei collections, Met/BM/V&A open access, scanned HK catalogues.
scored.rough_step_up: ~1,000-10,000x on a hit; human runners compete.
scored.frame: Rung = picking imperial pieces out of regional-sale lots and reselling them with an attribution in HK. Discovery (attribution) is roughly 80-90% of the work, and the physical part (buy, ship, consign) is trivial, so the frame looks right on paper. The problem is that 'proving' a Qing imperial piece is mostly a market and specialist opinion, not a measurement. TL tests the age of the clay; it cannot tell an 18th-century piece from a 19th-century or modern copy with confidence, and it can be fooled by artificial irradiation or by genuine shards set into the drilled areas. The capitalised buyers (Sotheby's/Christie's/Poly HK and their collectors) exist, but they do their own vetting.
scored.step_up: The headline cases are real: a Geneva vase estimated at CHF 500-800 made CHF 5M in 2017 (10,000x the estimate); a Keys (Aylsham) lacquer box estimated at GBP 30-40 made GBP 63,000 in 2022; ATG cites plaques estimated at GBP 30-50 that sold for GBP 7,000. In every case the step-up happened AT the regional sale, because mainland Chinese online bidders competed it up, and the gain went to the consignor, not to a buyer. The step-up a buyer can actually capture (hammer price to HK resale) is my estimate at about 1.5-5x, with occasional 10x+. The 10^3-10^4 figure is estimate to hammer, not purchase price to resale.
scored.hit_rate_capex: I found no published price for a TL test; the candidate's ~$500 figure is plausible (my estimate: $300-700 per sample; Oxford Authentication runs about 3,000 samples a year, about 90% of them Chinese ceramics). Base hit rate (my estimate): for a typical 'decorative 20th century' lot, well under 1% is actually imperial. But the cost per attempt is mostly the purchase price, and pieces that look imperial are bid up publicly whatever their status, so ML does not cut the cost of an attempt. It only filters which lots to bid on, and there it competes against thousands of human eyes looking at the same images.
scored.data: The data is public and largely legible: lot photos with descriptions on LiveAuctioneers/Invaluable/the-saleroom, plus open-access museum collections. The outcome is effectively already summarised. Not in a regulator's status field, but by the live global bidding crowd: specialist runners, HK/mainland dealers and online bidders who look at the same photos and set the hammer price. The images are not illegible in the Saskatchewan-assessment-file sense.
scored.right_bought: You buy title at an open public auction, competing against everyone. You cannot buy cheaply from an owner who cannot read the data, because the auction mechanism lets the most-informed bidder set the price. Off-market buying (house clearances, estates) avoids this but cannot scale, and both buyer and seller carry provenance/export scrutiny risk.
scored.buyer: Sotheby's/Christie's/Bonhams/Poly HK Asian art departments and mainland/HK collectors. They are capitalised and active, but they need provenance, and they discount or turn down pieces that surface from regional sales after a public bidding war.
scored.ladder: Short: runner, then dealer, then your own auction house or gallery. There is no industrial chain above it comparable to exploration, then a mine, then fuel. The ceiling is roughly a Sotheby's-scale business; the global Chinese art auction market is a few $B a year (my estimate), not a trillion-dollar path.
scored.fatal_flaw: The step-up is captured at the purchase itself: regional sales of Chinese works are bid globally online (Chinese bidders compete GBP 30-40 estimates up to GBP 63k, and CHF 500-800 up to CHF 5M). The 10^4 jump goes to the consignor, and there is no cheap, unreadable 'right' to buy before proving.
scored.one_line_reason: Low estimates are not low purchase prices: crowd bidding already finds the sleepers, so ML has no information edge and no cheap right to buy, and the proving step is a specialist's opinion rather than a measurement.

scored.name: Unconsummated Abandonment Lines: dormant federally preempted rail corridors
scored.one_line: Buy dormant short-line segments still legally part of the national rail system (discontinued or abandonment never consummated) at salvage value; ML proves preserved ICCTA preemption and continuity; sell as reactivatable rail-served industrial corridors.
scored.unproven_right: Dormant segment at salvage value (~$20-50k/mile) or a lease/option.
scored.proving_step: ML over STB docket PDFs, consummation letters, deeds and imagery.
scored.proven_buyer: Rail-served industrial park developers, transload operators (Watco, OmniTRAX), hyperscaler campuses, Class Is.
scored.public_data: STB e-library, FRA NARN GIS, county deeds, NAIP.
scored.frame: The candidate rung is buying a dormant segment and selling it as a reactivatable, preempted corridor. Proving the legal status (unconsummated abandonment, still under ICCTA preemption) is maybe 10-20% of the work (my estimate). The value comes from three other things. (1) Rehab: anecdotal and project figures run about $64k/mile (Minnesota Prairie Line, 2002, low speed) up to $250k-$1M+/mile for a closed line. (2) An anchor shipper or a developer who actually needs rail. (3) STB acquisition authority (10901/10902 exemption) plus taking on common-carrier obligations. Discovery is well under 80% of this rung. It is the geothermal-in-coal-mines pattern: the physical and commercial step is harder than finding the asset.
scored.step_up: The unproven side is salvage or net liquidation value. East Penn 8.6 mi: county NSV $377,804 (about $44k/mi) vs the railroad's NLV $2.16M (about $251k/mi). Idaho 66.8 mi: NLV $1.8M (about $27k/mi). The proven side is a going-concern short line, which needs traffic: San Luis and Rio Grande, 154 mi for about $7M (about $45k/mi, rural); G&W/Rail Management, about $330k/mi; G&W/Georgia-Pacific, about $445k/mi with a 20-year service contract (per-mile figures are my calculations from deal totals). A dormant line with no traffic sells near salvage no matter how clean its preemption status is. Even the going-concern comps are only 1-10x salvage, and that comes from traffic, not legal status. I found no published rail-served land premium. The listings I saw ($50-70k/acre in Strafford, MO; about $65k/acre in Lubbock) suggest a premium in the tens of percent at most (estimate). So realistically 2-10x, and only after rehab capex is spent. The candidate's ~10-100x claim is not supported.
scored.hit_rate_capex: There is no expensive, mostly-failing proving step. Checking legal status means reading dockets plus a title search, perhaps $5-30k per segment in attorney and title work (estimate). Among segments that are actually dormant, the base rate of 'still legally in the national system' is high, because no consummation notice means authority can lapse and the line stays in the system. So ML has little hit rate to improve. The costly, failure-prone step is finding a shipper and funding rehab ($250k-$1M/mi), and ML over dockets does not touch that. Lever: about 1-2x.
scored.data: The outcome sits in a legible field. Under 49 CFR 1152 the carrier files a notice of consummation in the STB docket, and if none is filed in time the authority expires. The STB e-library docket shows whether that notice exists, and FRA NARN GIS flags active, abandoned and out-of-service links. Scanned county deeds matter for reversionary interests, but preemption status does not hinge on them. On the right itself: dormant segments are owned by carriers (often Class Is or holding companies) who know their own regulatory status perfectly well. That rules out an information-asymmetry discount. Lines leaving the system go through the OFA process (49 USC 10904), a public, NLV-priced, first-come mechanism that rail-trail groups, states and short-line operators already monitor. Buying also requires STB authority.
scored.right_bought: In principle the right can be bought at roughly NLV ($27-251k/mi in the dockets above) or through an OFA. But sellers are sophisticated carriers who know the line's status, so there is no discount from data they cannot read. Buying makes the acquirer a common carrier, with STB filings and service obligations.
scored.buyer: Short-line holding companies (Genesee & Wyoming under Brookfield, Watco, OmniTRAX, RJ Corman), rail-park developers and state DOTs. All are well capitalised. They already buy and reactivate lines themselves and pay for traffic, not for proof of preemption.
scored.ladder: The ladder above is real: corridor, then short-line operator, then transload or industrial park development, then rail-served campuses (data centers, manufacturing), then roll-up into a short-line holding company. G&W sold for $8.4B, which shows the top of that ladder. But the bottom rung is not a discovery rung.
scored.fatal_flaw: The step-up depends on traffic and rehab capex ($250k-$1M/mi) rather than on discovery. And the 'proof' (whether a consummation notice exists, i.e. preemption) is already a legible STB docket field that the selling carrier understands. So there is no illegible-data edge and no discount from uninformed owners.
scored.one_line_reason: Preemption status is a docket lookup and isn't where the value comes from. The value comes from rehab and finding shippers, which is the geothermal-coal-mine trap. Realistic step-up is 2-10x and only comes after heavy capex.

scored.name: RoofBank: rooftop and riser rights in densification hot zones
scored.one_line: Buy long-term rooftop/riser easements from small building owners where ML predicts carrier densification need; RF and structural sign-off; sell portfolios to aggregators.
scored.unproven_right: 20-30 year easement, ~$5-20k upfront.
scored.proving_step: ML ranking plus RF/structural sign-off; value accrues on tenant signings (no binary hit).
scored.proven_buyer: Vertical Bridge, Diamond, Landmark Dividend, Radius Global, carriers.
scored.public_data: FCC ASR and BDC, small-cell permit logs, building permits, lidar.
scored.frame: The candidate rung is "own an easement with no tenant on it". Inside that rung, discovery is maybe 30-40% of the work. The rest is getting the owner to sign, title and easement legal work, structural and RF sign-off, and above all landing a carrier tenant. That last step is a commercial sale that depends on the carrier's own RF plan and capex budget, not a physical step you can treat as trivial. No capitalised buyer exists for this rung's output. Aggregators (Landmark, Radius/EQT, Diamond, Vertical Bridge) price ground and rooftop easements as a multiple of the rent already in place. An easement with no tenant has no cash flow to capitalise, so the sellable rung really starts only after a tenant signs. That moves the proving step outside the company's control. The frame fails.
scored.step_up: My estimate, not checked against sources (search budget used up). Unproven: $5-20k upfront for a 20-30 yr easement with no tenant, per the candidate. Proven: one carrier rooftop lease at roughly $1,500-3,000/month (industry folklore range) is $18-36k/yr. Aggregators buy that at roughly 10-20x annual rent (my estimate), so about $180-700k. That is ~10-40x on a hit, but only after a tenant signs, which can take years. It is not instant like a drill core. In expectation (hit rate times value) the uplift is much smaller.
scored.hit_rate_capex: My estimate. Base rate that a speculative rooftop easement gets a carrier tenant within 5 years is very low, likely under 5%. Carriers pick sites from their own RF search rings, they have many interchangeable rooftops to choose from, and macro or rooftop builds have slowed. Examples: T-Mobile decommissioning ~35k Sprint sites, AT&T and Verizon cutting capex in 2024-25, and EchoStar/DISH exiting its own network in 2025 (general knowledge, unverified this run). Cost per attempt is $5-20k plus legal/RF, roughly $10-30k. In theory a low hit rate gives a big lever. In practice ML cannot raise it much, because the deciding variable is the carrier's private RF plan and budget. The carrier already knows that answer and outsiders do not. The lever is mostly fictional.
scored.data: The public data (FCC ASR, BDC coverage, small-cell permit logs, building permits, lidar) is mostly structured and legible already. FCC ASR and BDC are clean databases, and permits are semi-structured. The signal that matters is carrier search rings and capacity congestion. That is private carrier data, shared with site-acquisition firms under NDA. So the outcome is effectively already decided, just in a private field rather than a public one. Also, densification has moved to small cells on municipal poles and right-of-way. The FCC 2018 order caps those fees at about $270/yr per pole (general knowledge), so they bypass rooftop owners entirely.
scored.right_bought: Yes in form: easements are bought from small owners, not claimed first-come. But the owners are not data-blind in the way that matters. An unchosen owner has no counterparty, and a chosen owner gets approached directly by the carrier's site-acq vendor. Easement aggregators pursue owners aggressively, but only once a lease exists. You can buy cheaply, but you are buying an option on a decision someone else controls, and the carrier can route around you to the next roof.
scored.buyer: Vertical Bridge, Diamond Communications, Landmark Dividend, Radius Global (EQT), DigitalBridge vehicles, and carriers. All of them pay for cash-flowing tenanted leases, not for untenanted easements.
scored.ladder: Modest. The rungs are tenanted easement, then owning the tower or rooftop infrastructure (towerco), then neutral-host or DAS operator. Towercos are large (AMT/CCI/SBAC together roughly $150B+ market cap, my estimate), but the macro tower market is mature and consolidated, and new-site growth is slowing. Not a trillion-dollar path.
scored.fatal_flaw: The proving event (a carrier tenant signing) is decided by the carrier's private RF plan and capex budget, not by discovery from public data. There is no capitalised buyer for an untenanted easement. The rung therefore has no sellable output until a third party decides to use the site, and carriers can substitute any nearby roof or a municipal pole.
scored.one_line_reason: The step-up depends on a carrier's private siting decision, not on discovery. Aggregators only buy easements that already have tenants, data that matters is private, and densification is moving to cheap municipal poles, so the Terranox 95/5 frame does not exist here.
sources: No web searches ran: the shared per-turn search budget was used up before this agent's queries (WebSearch returned budget-exhausted). Every figure is my estimate from general industry knowledge and is unverified.
General knowledge (unverified): FCC 2018 Small Cell Order fee safe harbor of about $270/yr per small cell in the right-of-way
General knowledge (unverified): T-Mobile decommissioning about 35k Sprint sites after the merger; EchoStar/DISH network exit in 2025
General knowledge (unverified): Radius Global acquired by EQT in 2023; aggregators price leases as a multiple of in-place rent

scored.name: Holdout: site-based incumbents inside future overlay auctions
scored.one_line: Buy legacy fixed/microwave licences that block high-value overlay areas in bands the FCC will auction; collect incentive proceeds or buyouts.
scored.unproven_right: Legacy licences bought from small holders on current-use value.
scored.proving_step: ML over ULS/IBFS and NPRMs predicts blocking/incentive-eligible positions; FCC order.
scored.proven_buyer: Overlay winners (Verizon, AT&T, T-Mobile, SpaceX) or FCC incentive pool.
scored.public_data: FCC ULS and IBFS, ECFS dockets, auction notices.
scored.frame: The rung is buying an incumbent licence and holding it until an FCC overlay or incentive auction pays it out. The physical step is close to nothing: you hold paper and maybe keep a link running to meet construction rules. But discovery is not the main work. The real work is predicting what the FCC will do, the rulemaking itself, and waiting 3-6 years. My estimate is that discovery is about 20-30% of the value-creating work. The other 70%+ is regulatory risk the company cannot control. A buyer with capital exists (the overlay winners or the FCC's auction proceeds), but only after the FCC decides to pay. The buyer is not paying because you discovered something.
scored.step_up: From memory, not verified (search budget exhausted). Normal FCC relocation law (Emerging Technologies, AWS-1 and 2 GHz microwave cost-sharing) pays incumbents comparable facilities or their actual relocation costs. That is roughly 1x, not a windfall. The windfall cases are the exception: 39 GHz Auction 103 incentive relinquishment (2019-20), Straight Path's 39/28 GHz licences sold to Verizon for about $3.1B in 2017 after being acquired cheaply, and the C-band Auction 107 accelerated relocation payments of $9.7B to the satellite operators (SES about $4B, Intelsat about $4.9B). Those went to large satellite and mmWave holders, not to small site-based fixed links. Realistic step-up for a small site-based licence: 1-10x (my estimate). It is 10-100x only in rare Straight-Path-like setups, which the FCC now closes off with filing and assignment freezes and pro-rata MHz-pop formulas.
scored.hit_rate_capex: There is no expensive proving step that usually fails. Licences are cheap (my estimate: a few thousand to low hundreds of thousands of dollars per site-based licence). A 'hit' comes from FCC policy, not from a better prediction. Base rate that a given band gets an overlay auction with incentive payments: maybe 10-30% within 5 years for bands already in an NPRM (my estimate). Bands named in the One Big Beautiful Bill Act / upper C-band 3.98-4.2 GHz proceeding are already public knowledge. The FCC usually freezes new applications and assignments once a band is identified, so the window to buy before it is legible is narrow. ML cannot raise this hit rate much, because the outcome is set by politics and lobbying, not hidden in data. The lever is well under 10x.
scored.data: ULS, IBFS and ECFS are public but fully legible: structured licence fields with frequency, coordinates, call sign, expiry and construction status. NPRMs say outright which bands and incumbents are affected, and auction procedures publish pro-rata MHz-pop formulas. The outcome is already written into legible fields and rulemaking text, which is the exact failure mode the rubric warns about. Spectrum lawyers, consultants and speculators (Straight Path-style aggregators, Columbia Capital, Anterix, spectrum brokers) already read these dockets closely.
scored.right_bought: Yes, licences can be bought through ULS assignment (Form 603) from small holders (utilities, municipalities, small carriers) at use value. But small holders file comments in the same dockets and their lawyers tell them about pending auctions, so the information gap is thin. The FCC also often freezes assignments or applies anti-speculation and construction-requirement rules (Straight Path paid a $100M FCC penalty and gave up licences in 2017 over construction filings).
scored.buyer: Overlay auction winners (Verizon, AT&T, T-Mobile, possibly SpaceX/EchoStar spectrum buyers) or the FCC incentive and relocation pool. They have capital, but they pay only under FCC-set formulas or relocation-cost rules, not open-market value for the holdout.
scored.ladder: Weak. The rungs above (holding spectrum, aggregating it, wholesaling it like Anterix or Ligado, then operating a network) do exist. But each rung is regulator-gated, with heavy capex and competition from the big three carriers. Anterix's 900 MHz play has been a slow, sub-scale business, not a trillion-dollar path.
scored.fatal_flaw: The step-up comes from FCC policy, not from discovery. The FCC compensates site-based incumbents at relocation cost under formulas published in legible dockets, and freezes assignments once a band is identified. So there is no hidden signal for ML to find, and no reliable 10^3x jump.
scored.one_line_reason: This is regulatory arbitrage on legible public dockets with cost-based compensation, not a discovery-dominated rung. Low step-up, no ML hit-rate lever, and the outcome is already in structured fields.
sources: Web search budget for this turn was exhausted before any query ran; all figures are from prior knowledge and are unverified
FCC Auction 107 (C-band) public notices: $81B gross proceeds, $9.7B accelerated relocation payments (fcc.gov/auction/107), from memory
FCC Auction 103 (39 GHz) incentive/relinquishment procedures (fcc.gov/auction/103), from memory
Verizon acquisition of Straight Path ~$3.1B (2017) and FCC $100M Straight Path consent decree (2017), from memory
FCC Emerging Technologies / microwave relocation cost-sharing rules, 47 CFR 101.69-101.82 and 27.1160 et seq., from memory
One Big Beautiful Bill Act (2025) spectrum pipeline and FCC upper C-band 3.98-4.2 GHz NPRM (2025), from memory

scored.name: VestedRights: tax-deed parcels with grandfathered entitlements
scored.one_line: Find tax-deed and neglected parcels carrying legacy rights no longer creatable (vested pre-moratorium approvals, nonconforming uses, grandfathered billboard permits, legacy sewer taps, curb cuts); ML proves validity from scanned files; resell as entitled sites.
scored.unproven_right: Valid but forgotten entitlements on parcels priced as raw land.
scored.proving_step: ML over scanned minutes, plat approvals, sewer ledgers and outdoor-advertising files; zoning verification letter or permit transfer.
scored.proven_buyer: Homebuilders in capped markets, billboard operators (Outfront, Lamar, Clear Channel), commercial developers.
scored.public_data: Scanned planning minutes and approvals, DOT outdoor advertising registries, utility allocation ledgers, tax-deed lists.
scored.frame: The rung would be: buy a neglected or tax-deed parcel and get a zoning verification letter, vested-rights determination or permit transfer that confirms a legacy right. Inside that rung, finding and proving the right is most of the work (my estimate is 70-85%), and the physical step is close to nothing because it is paperwork. But the output is a land parcel with a small entitlement attached, not a separate asset class. Buyers (homebuilders, Lamar/Outfront/Clear Channel, developers) buy entitled sites one at a time and price them on comparable sales, not on a discovery premium. Billboard operators usually already hold the permit and only lease the ground, so the landowner often does not own the right being 'discovered'. The frame exists but it is thin and fragmented.
scored.step_up: My estimates, not from sources (the search budget was used up before I could check): a typical tax-deed lot clears at about $2k-20k. If it truly carries a vested approval, a transferable sewer allocation in a moratorium market (tap or capacity fees often $10k-50k per unit in capped markets), or a valid nonconforming billboard site (ground-lease buyout values often $50k-500k for good sites, from industry knowledge, not verified this run), resale is maybe $20k-200k. That is usually 3-30x and rarely 100x+. The 10^3-10^4 claim needs a near-zero parcel with a big right attached, and that is extremely rare. Typical step-up is about 10x.
scored.hit_rate_capex: I could not check either number this run because the search budget was used up. Cost per proving attempt is cheap: a zoning verification letter is about $100-500 and a records request plus attorney review about $1-5k (my estimate). Because proving is already cheap, there is little capex for ML to cut ten-fold. The base hit rate is very low (my estimate is under 1% of tax-deed parcels carry a valid, transferable legacy right). The main cause is law, not search difficulty: most ordinances end nonconforming-use rights after 6-12 months of discontinuance, plat and site-plan approvals usually expire after 1-5 years, and billboard permits typically lapse when the structure is removed or neglected. ML raises recall in the search, but the cost being saved is screening time, not drilling-scale capex.
scored.data: Public data is mixed. State DOT outdoor-advertising permit registries are mostly legible databases that carry permit number, status and owner, so for billboards the outcome is already in a legible field. Utility capacity and tap ledgers are often internal and not public. Scanned planning minutes and plat approvals are illegible and scattered, which is the one real ML edge. But the authoritative answer comes from the zoning administrator's determination, which anyone can request cheaply. So the ML edge is only finding which parcels are worth asking about.
scored.right_bought: Partly bought. Tax-deed parcels are bought at public auction with open bidding, and local investors and auction regulars compete there. Neglected owners can also be approached directly with cheap offers. The catch is that the cheap ones are cheap because the right has usually lapsed through abandonment.
scored.buyer: Homebuilders and commercial developers in capped or moratorium markets buy entitled lots one at a time. Billboard operators (Lamar, Outfront, Clear Channel) buy or lease sites. Billboard-lease buyout funds are also active buyers and competitors, such as Landmark Dividend and Radius Global (named from my knowledge, not verified this run). Buyers have capital but buy at comparable-sales prices, not at a discovery premium.
scored.ladder: Parcel entitlement arbitrage, then land banking and assembly, then vertical development (homebuilding or commercial), then owning outdoor-advertising or real-estate operations. The ladder is real but leads into ordinary real-estate development, where neither ML nor discovery is the bottleneck. Each rung up is more about capital and construction than discovery, so the 95-5 shape vanishes immediately. That is close to the geothermal-in-coal-mines counter-example.
scored.fatal_flaw: The neglect that makes these parcels cheap is the same thing that legally kills the right. Abandonment and discontinuance clauses (typically 6-12 months), approval expiry dates and billboard permit lapse rules mean that most rights on tax-deed or neglected parcels have already expired. Where a right does survive, the answer is usually in a legible registry (DOT billboard permit status) or a cheap zoning verification letter, so ML gives no lasting edge.
scored.one_line_reason: Proving is cheap paperwork, the typical step-up is about 10x not 10^3, rights on neglected parcels usually lapse by law, and billboard and permit status is already in legible registries, so this is a weak entitlement-arbitrage niche, not a Terranox analogue.
sources: No web sources: the web search budget for this turn was used up before any query ran, so every number here is my own estimate and should be checked in a follow-up search.
General zoning law (not verified this run): nonconforming-use abandonment or discontinuance periods of 6-12 months are common in US municipal codes.

General knowledge (not verified this run): state DOT outdoor-advertising permit registries (Highway Beautification Act, 23 USC 131), and billboard ground-lease buyout firms such as Landmark Dividend and Radius Global.

scored.name: Remnant: surplus DOT and government remnant parcels as assemblage keystones
scored.one_line: Buy DOT, municipal and GSA surplus remnants; ML links them to pending assemblages and entitlement filings to find keystones; sell to the developer.
scored.unproven_right: Fee title to irregular remnants valued standalone.
scored.proving_step: ML linking remnant to adjacent ownership, filings, setbacks and FAR; a deed.
scored.proven_buyer: Commercial/multifamily developers, QSR and fuel site teams, hyperscaler land teams.
scored.public_data: DOT surplus lists and ROW maps, GSA disposals, parcel GIS, planning agendas, permits.
scored.frame: The rung would be buying a surplus remnant and flipping it to the developer who is assembling the block. The deed is cheap, so the physical step is trivial. But the "discovery" here is matching a remnant to a known assemblage, and a buyer appears only after a developer has already started assembling and filed publicly. So discovery is maybe 50-60% of the work (my estimate). The rest is negotiation, title cleanup, the DOT's access-control and deed restrictions, and holding risk. The buyer has money, but there is only one buyer per parcel (the assembler), not a market.
scored.step_up: Estimate only; both searches were refused because the shared search budget was used up. Remnants usually sell at an appraised standalone value of nominal to low-five-figure amounts. Sale at fair market value is broadly required for federally funded right of way (23 CFR 710.403, from memory). A keystone in an active assemblage can fetch a holdout premium of maybe 2-10x appraised value. In rare cases it is 10-100x on tiny, near-zero-value strips, but the dollar amounts are small. A 10^3-10^4 jump is not plausible, because any appraiser or adjoiner already sees part of the plottage value.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Estimate only. The proving attempt is buying a remnant: about $5k-$100k plus closing and holding costs, and each one has to be bought. The base hit rate for a remnant becoming a real keystone in a deal that closes is maybe 1-5% if bought blind. But public planning filings show where the assemblages are, so a simple rules-based filter, not ML, gets most of the lift. Each miss is not a sunk cost like a dry drill hole: you still own a resellable remnant at about cost. That means the cost of failing is low, so the ML lever is small.
scored.data: DOT surplus lists, GSA disposals, parcel GIS and planning agendas are public, but mostly they are legible: structured listings and readable agendas. Developers' land teams and local brokers already watch rezoning and site-plan filings, so the outcome (an assemblage under way) is effectively summarised in a public filing before any value is created. The right can be bought, but many states give abutting owners first offer or a direct negotiated sale on uneconomic remnants. Public auctions are open to everyone, and DOTs often keep access-control restrictions. The seller (the DOT) is not a blind owner; it appraises the parcel and may price in assemblage value.
scored.right_bought: Fee title to the surplus remnant, by DOT or GSA auction or negotiated sale, usually subject to the adjoiner's priority and access-control restrictions.
scored.buyer: The single developer assembling the block: multifamily or commercial developers, fast-food and fuel-station site teams, data-centre land teams. Each one is a bilateral holdout negotiation, not a deep market. Developers also design around the parcel (setback variances, redesign, condemnation where a public purpose exists), which caps the premium.
scored.ladder: Weak but real: remnant flipping, then small assemblage aggregation, then land banking or entitlement, then development. Moving up turns it into an ordinary real-estate development business, with no proprietary discovery edge that carries upward.
scored.fatal_flaw: A remnant becomes a keystone only after a developer has publicly started assembling. By then the answer is already in a legible public field (rezoning or site-plan filings) that incumbents and the adjoiner can read. The adjoiner's priority rights and appraisal-based pricing take most of the premium. And the value comes from a holdout negotiation that buyers can design around, not from discovery.
scored.one_line_reason: This is holdout arbitrage, not discovery. The step-up is about 2-10x on small dollars, the signal is mostly legible public filings, adjoiners get first offer, and ML adds little over a filter on planning agendas. Numbers are estimates because the search budget was used up.
sources: No live sources: both WebSearch calls were refused because the shared per-turn search budget was used up. All numbers are the agent's estimates.
23 CFR 710.403 (FHWA rules on disposing of surplus right of way at fair market value), from memory
49 CFR 24.102(k) (Uniform Act rules on uneconomic remnants), from memory

scored.name: HeirShare: lost mutual ditch company shares
scored.one_line: Buy orphaned Colorado ditch and reservoir company shares from heirs who don't know they hold them; ML rebuilds title from scanned ledgers and probate; get certificates reissued and sell to Front Range cities.
scored.unproven_right: Unclaimed certificates whose holder of record is dead or dissolved, quitclaims for $500-10k.
scored.proving_step: Linking ledgers, probate, deeds and obituaries to clean chain of title; rare quiet title.
scored.proven_buyer: Thornton, Aurora, Greeley, Fort Collins, Northern Water utilities, developers (C-BT ~$85k/AF 2025).
scored.public_data: County probate/recorder images, ditch company reports and ledgers in water court filings, HydroBase, change cases, state unclaimed property.
scored.frame: The rung is clearing title on orphaned mutual ditch shares and reselling them. Linking records (ledger, probate, deed, obituary) is maybe 60-70% of the work (my estimate). The rest is not trivial: board approval of the transfer under the company's bylaws, reissuing the certificate (often with a lost-certificate bond), sometimes a quiet-title action, and for a municipal buyer a water-court change case (a 2-5 year process, usually paid by the buyer). Buyers have capital (Thornton, Aurora, Greeley, Northern Water, developers), but they buy a clean, changeable share, not a lead. So the frame exists, but discovery is not 80% of it.
scored.step_up: The share's market value does not change when title is proven. A proven NPIC, C-BT or similar share trades at a known, published price (the candidate cites C-BT at ~$85k/AF in 2025; I could not verify this because the search budget ran out). The 'step-up' only exists against cash paid to uninformed heirs: $500-10k paid for an asset worth roughly $30-100k is about 3-100x, most likely ~5-20x once heirs are told the asset exists, which a valid quitclaim effectively requires. This is information arbitrage on a fully priced asset, not 1 -> 10^4 value creation. My estimate, unsourced.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Proving is cheap per attempt: a few hundred to a few thousand dollars of records research. A quiet title runs maybe $5-25k in legal fees if contested (estimate). The base hit rate is not low because of hard discovery. The constraint is that true orphans are scarce. So ML has little to multiply: lever well under 10x. All numbers are estimates; no web searches ran (shared budget used up).
scored.data: The data is half illegible (scanned probate and recorder images, old ledgers in water-court filings). But the key outcome is legible to the one party that matters. The ditch company's own stock ledger and its annual assessment roll show which shares are unpaid, and under typical bylaws a mutual ditch company can forfeit and resell shares with delinquent assessments (from domain knowledge; I did not verify Colorado's statute or forfeiture rules this run). So abandoned shares mostly go back to the company, not into a findable orphan pool. A share whose assessments are being paid has a live owner who gets bills. HydroBase records decrees and structures, not who holds the shares.
scored.right_bought: Yes in form: heirs can quitclaim or assign their interest. But heirs who are being billed already know they hold the shares. Heirs who are not being billed have usually already been forfeited out. Buying from heirs who do not know what they hold invites heir-hunter or unconscionability challenges, and if any of the asset counts as unclaimed property, Colorado's finder-fee rules may cap the take (I did not verify the cap). The company's board can also refuse to transfer, or hold a right of first refusal.
scored.buyer: Front Range municipal water utilities (Thornton, Aurora, Greeley, Fort Collins, Northern Water member entities) and homebuilders who need raw water dedication. They are real and well funded, and they already run acquisition programmes and use water brokers, and they often contact ditch shareholders directly.
scored.ladder: Short ladder. Brokering shares, then doing change cases, then a water bank or leasing could build a regional water-rights firm. Above that the next rungs are municipal utilities and agricultural dry-up, which are politically constrained (buy-and-dry backlash, anti-speculation doctrine). The total market is a few billion dollars of Front Range ag water, which is real but nowhere near a trillion-dollar path.
scored.fatal_flaw: Proving title does not create value. A ditch share is already priced in a liquid, legible local market, and mutual ditch companies track holders through annual assessments, forfeiting and reselling delinquent shares. So genuinely orphaned, unclaimed shares are rare. The only margin is underpaying uninformed heirs, which is small, legally fragile, and hard to scale.
scored.one_line_reason: This is title-clearing arbitrage on an already-priced asset whose holders the issuer tracks through assessments: there is no 10^3 proving step-up, ML has little to lever, and the orphan pool is thin.
sources: No web searches were completed: the shared WebSearch budget for this turn was used up. Every number here is either the candidate's own figure (C-BT ~$85k/AF 2025, quitclaims $500-10k) or my estimate from domain knowledge.

Domain knowledge (not verified this run): Colorado mutual ditch company bylaws on assessments, forfeiture and resale of delinquent shares; water court change-case practice; Front Range municipal water acquisition programmes; HydroBase (Colorado Division of Water Resources) covers decrees and structures, not who holds shares.

scored.name: Gravel Pit Storage Rights
scored.one_line: Pair old-priority conditional storage decrees from defunct developers with mined-out South Platte gravel pits; ML picks feasible pairs; perfect decrees and sell lined storage to cities.
scored.unproven_right: Conditional storage decrees plus exhausted pits operators want to shed.
scored.proving_step: Diligence filings and absolute decree; slurry-wall liner ($2-6k/AF) is moderate construction.
scored.proven_buyer: Front Range utilities ($15-40k/AF of lined storage).
scored.public_data: Water court diligence and conditional decrees, DRMS permits, CDSS, CGS hydrogeology.
scored.frame: The rung here is turning a mined-out pit plus a conditional decree into lined, decreed storage that a utility will buy. I estimate discovery (choosing the pit-decree pair) is only about 10-20% of the work inside that rung. Most of the work is physical and legal: a slurry wall plus a State Engineer leak test (required under the 1999 liner design standard), a water court change-of-water-right case, and diligence/absolute filings that opposers can contest. Pit locations are already known: DRMS lists every permitted pit and its reclamation status, so nothing about the asset is hidden. This has the same shape as the geothermal-in-coal-mines counter-example, where building the asset is harder than finding it.
scored.step_up: My estimates, from memory; no web searches ran because the shared budget was used up. Unlined mined-out pit land sells for about $5-15k/acre. Lined storage holds about 30-60 AF/acre and Front Range utilities pay roughly $10-40k/AF of capacity, so about $0.5-2M/acre. That is about 50-150x gross. But the liner costs about $2-6k/AF (about $100-300k/acre), and legal and engineering add more, so the net multiple on capital deployed is about 3-10x. The step-up is also not immediate: it arrives only after construction, the leak test, and a water-court decree, which takes years.
scored.hit_rate_capex: My estimate: the proving step does not mostly fail. A competently built slurry wall passes the SEO leak test in most cases (I estimate more than 70% on the first test, with remediation available after a failure). Water court outcomes for change cases are also mostly favorable, just slow. Each attempt costs millions in construction (for example, 1,000 AF at $2-6k/AF is $2-6M) plus about $0.2-1M in legal fees, and that cost is mostly fixed by geometry. ML cannot cut it 10x. Since the lever is capped at 1/base hit rate, it is at most about 1.5x.
scored.data: CDSS/HydroBase publishes every decree with structured fields: priority date, appropriation date, amount, and conditional vs absolute status. Water court diligence filings appear in monthly resumes. DRMS permits list pit location, depth, and reclamation plan. CGS publishes alluvial aquifer maps. The outcome (whether a decree is conditional, absolute, or abandoned) is already in a legible status field, which is the failure pattern seen in earlier hunts. Some judgment is buried in decree PDFs: where the decree lets the storage site move, and opposer stipulations. That is real but small. The incumbents read all of this fluently: water lawyers, engineering firms (e.g. Wright Water Engineers, Leonard Rice — named from memory), and aggregate operators.
scored.right_bought: The pieces can be bought, but with problems. (1) Exhausted pits come from aggregate majors (Martin Marietta, Aggregate Industries/Holcim, Lafarge; names from memory, not verified). They already understand the storage value and often reclaim pits as lined storage themselves and sell to cities, so there is no illegibility discount. (2) Conditional decrees from defunct developers often belong to estates or shells, but conditional rights carry heavy legal risk. Colorado's anti-speculation doctrine (Vidler; Pagosa Area WSD) requires a specific beneficial user and a can-and-will showing. Moving a conditional storage right to a different pit is a contested change. And the old priority date may not survive the move: if the court treats it as a new appropriation, the right becomes junior. Junior South Platte storage fills only in wet years.
scored.buyer: Front Range municipal utilities: Aurora, Thornton, Denver Water, Centennial, Castle Rock, Parker, and South Platte augmentation groups (Brighton/Fort Lupton/Greeley area). They are well capitalised and actively buy lined storage. The buyer side is real.
scored.ladder: Moderate. Lined storage leads to augmentation plans, then to a full water portfolio for growing municipalities (supply, storage, exchange, delivery). That could become a regional water utility or water-rights holding company. It is a large business, but it is capped regionally by Colorado water law and politics. There is no obvious trillion-dollar path.
scored.fatal_flaw: The proving step is construction plus water-court litigation, not discovery. The slurry wall (about $2-6k/AF) and the change-of-right case are most of the work and cost. Discovery is trivial because pits and decree statuses are already public in structured databases, and incumbent aggregate companies already capture the lined-storage step-up. On top of that, the anti-speculation doctrine and the risk of losing priority make the 'pair an old decree with a new pit' trick legally fragile.
scored.one_line_reason: This has the same shape as the geothermal-in-coal-mines counter-example: building the lined storage and litigating the decree outweigh finding the pair. The outcome is already shown in legible CDSS status fields, the net step-up is only about 3-10x, and the hit rate is already high, so ML has no 10x capex lever.
sources: No web searches ran: the shared WebSearch budget for this turn (200 calls) was used up before this candidate. All numbers are estimates from prior knowledge and should be checked in a follow-up.
Colorado State Engineer, Guidelines for Lining Criteria for Gravel Pits (1999), from memory: the source for the leak-test requirement
Colorado Decision Support System / HydroBase (cdss.state.co.us): decree status fields (conditional/absolute)
Colorado Division of Reclamation, Mining and Safety permit database: pit locations and reclamation status
Colorado case law on anti-speculation, from memory: Colorado River Water Conservation Dist. v. Vidler Tunnel Water Co. (1979); Pagosa Area Water & Sanitation Dist. v. Trout Unlimited (2009)
Candidate's own figures: $2-6k/AF liner cost, $15-40k/AF utility price

scored.name: Ridgeline Storage: closed-loop pumped hydro site origination
scored.one_line: Option remote ridge-valley parcel pairs ML ranks as top-decile closed-loop PSH sites, prove with FERC preliminary permit, desktop geotech and water screen, flip permitted packages to PSH developers.
scored.unproven_right: Purchase/easement options on rangeland plus first-to-file FERC preliminary permit.
scored.proving_step: ML over DEMs, geologic and geotech reports, FERC eLibrary; light geotech coring.
scored.proven_buyer: Rye, rPlus, Brookfield, PacifiCorp, APS, TVA, infrastructure funds.
scored.public_data: NREL closed-loop PSH assessment, 3DEP lidar, state geological reports, FERC eLibrary, USGS NWIS.
scored.frame: The proposed rung is a parcel option plus a FERC preliminary permit plus a desktop screen. Finding the site is maybe 5-10% of the work inside that rung (my estimate). The value comes from licensing (5-10 years, roughly $10-50M of studies, NEPA, water rights, interconnection, offtake), not from picking the site. The rung buyers would actually pay for is a late-stage licensed project, and there discovery is well under 10% of the work. This is the same shape as the geothermal-in-coal-mines counter-example: building a bespoke multi-GW civil megaproject is much harder than finding the ridge.
scored.step_up: My estimate (no live search was possible): a rangeland option costs roughly $50-500/acre-equivalent, and a preliminary permit costs almost nothing. An early-stage permitted PSH package with a desktop screen trades at nominal value, often a development fee or earn-out. Licensed, shovel-ready projects might fetch roughly $10-50/kW, which is $10-50M for 1 GW, but only after many years and tens of millions in development spend. Immediate step-up on a 'hit' at the preliminary permit stage: about 3-10x at best, because nothing is de-risked. The candidate's own estimate is 10-100x over 5-10 years.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Base rate from my background knowledge, not verified this session: FERC has issued hundreds of PSH preliminary permits (tens of GW to over 90 GW pending at any time). Only a handful of US PSH projects have been licensed since about 2014: Gordon Butte, Swan Lake, Eagle Mountain, and Goldendale more recently. Even fewer have been built, so permit-to-construction is likely under 5%. But failures come mostly from cost, financing, offtake and transmission, not bad geology, so ML site ranking does little for the hit rate. A preliminary permit costs almost nothing to file. The expensive attempt is licensing ($10-50M+, estimate), and ML does not cut that 10x.
scored.data: The signal is already legible. NREL's closed-loop PSH resource assessment (Rosenlieb et al., about 2022) published ranked, costed site lists nationwide, with GIS layers and cost curves. 3DEP lidar is structured and free. FERC eLibrary is scanned, but permit status and outcomes sit in legible docket fields. Geotech reports are the one illegible input, and they are rarely the binding constraint.
scored.right_bought: Partly. Land or easement options are bought from ranchers, but those owners do not hold the data edge: the site value only appears after licensing, so they cannot capture it anyway, and they get no discount from being unable to read the data. The core right, the FERC preliminary permit, is free and first-come, which the rubric counts as a fail. Permits are also routinely squatted and challenged by competing filers (Rye, rPlus and others hold many). A permit gives priority, not property, and lapses after 4 years, extendable to 8 under the 2018 amendments.
scored.buyer: Real capitalised buyers exist (Brookfield, utilities such as PacifiCorp/APS/TVA, infrastructure funds, Rye/rPlus as developers). But they buy licensed or late-stage projects with offtake paths, not desktop-screened permits. Incumbent originators (Rye Development, rPlus Hydro, Absaroka, Premium Energy) already file permits on NREL-type sites.
scored.ladder: The ladder exists: origination, then licensing, then interconnection and offtake, then EPC, then own and operate long-duration storage. It is capital-heavy and slow (8-15 years to commercial operation, $2,000-4,000/kW capex, estimate). The ladder is real, but every rung above origination is execution-dominated, not discovery-dominated.
scored.fatal_flaw: No rung exists where discovery is 80%+ of the work. NREL has already published ranked closed-loop sites, the key right (the FERC preliminary permit) is free first-come, and PSH value is made by a 5-10 year licensing, financing and civil build process. So ML site-finding moves neither the hit rate nor the price. This is the geothermal-in-coal-mines counter-example.
scored.one_line_reason: Building is the hard part and site discovery is a commodity: NREL already ranks the sites publicly, permits are free and first-come, and value appears only after years of licensing. It fails the 95-5 frame.

FERC hydropower preliminary permit rules (18 CFR Part 4; America's Water Infrastructure Act of 2018 permit term extension to up to 8 years), from background knowledge
FERC licensing records for Gordon Butte, Swan Lake, Eagle Mountain and Goldendale PSH, from background knowledge

scored.name: Upgrade Credit Recovery: stranded network-upgrade refund and transmission-credit claims
scored.one_line: Buy refund, transmission-credit and incremental-rights claims held by dissolved developers and estates under executed ISAs; prove entitlement from scanned agreements and later network-use events; collect or sell.
scored.unproven_right: Contingent claims under ISAs bought by assignment at 1-5% of face.
scored.proving_step: Parse ISAs, cost allocations, true-ups; get transmission owner acknowledgement.
scored.proven_buyer: Transmission owners obligated to pay; claims funds.
scored.public_data: FERC eLibrary ISAs and refund reports, RTO upgrade studies, PJM incremental ARR postings, bankruptcy dockets.
scored.frame: The rung is buying a contingent receivable and proving the entitlement. Almost all of that work is legal and document work (reading ISAs/LGIAs, cost allocations, true-ups, then getting the transmission owner to acknowledge the claim), so "discovery" could plausibly be 80%+ of it. But it is collections, not discovery. The buyer at the end is the obligor (the transmission owner paying out under a tariff), not a capitalised developer bidding for a proven asset. Nothing physical gets built, which is good, but the rung tops out at the claim's face value. My estimate is that the rung itself meets the shape of the test, but it is a debt-collection rung with no developer-style buyer above it.
scored.step_up: The candidate says 1-5% of face goes to 100% of face, which is 20-100x on paper. I could not verify any real trade prices because the web search budget was used up before my first search ran, so every number here is my estimate. Under the FERC pro forma LGIA (Order 2003, Art. 11.4), repayment of funded network upgrades through cash or transmission credits is tied to the generating facility reaching commercial operation, and runs over up to 20 years with interest. A dissolved developer whose project never reached COD usually has no refund stream at all, only a refund of unspent security when it withdraws, which the RTO or transmission owner computes and pays out routinely. Where a stream does exist, it belongs to whoever holds the LGIA, and that is normally the operating plant owner, not an estate that can't read its own files. Once you price in probability and the discount for 20-year payment timing, I expect the real step-up per hit to be about 3-10x (an estimate). It is a discount on a known face value, not a 10^3-10^4 jump.
scored.hit_rate_capex: I have no sourced base hit rate; the search budget was used up. My estimate is that most orphaned claims are worth nothing, because the projects withdrew before COD and their security was already refunded or forfeited under tariff formulas. The cost of each proving attempt is mostly legal and document review: roughly $5k-$50k per claim to parse the agreements, plus the time spent negotiating acknowledgement with the transmission owner (also an estimate). ML can cheapen the document parsing, but the binding cost is legal: getting transmission owner acknowledgement or consent to assignment, and possibly litigating at FERC. ML does not cut that 10x. The lever is small.
scored.data: The documents are public but hard to read. FERC eLibrary holds scanned ISAs/LGIAs and refund reports, and bankruptcy dockets are on PACER. However, the outcome is largely already written down in legible places. Transmission owners and RTOs track credit balances and repayment schedules for billing (for example, SPP's Attachment Z2 crediting process computes and settles sponsor credits). This is from memory; I could not verify it this session. That is the same pattern earlier hunts found: the regulator or obligor writes the answer into an administrative record, which kills the ML edge.
scored.right_bought: In principle the claims can be bought by assignment from estates or dissolved developers, and bankruptcy claims traders already buy estate receivables, so this is not an untouched market. In practice, the LGIA and the rights that come with it usually need the transmission owner's consent to assign, and they generally travel with the generating facility. That makes it hard to buy the receivable on its own at 1-5% of face, and the obligor has every incentive to dispute it.
scored.buyer: The transmission owners and RTOs that owe the money (paying under tariff), plus litigation and claims funds as secondary buyers. Neither is a capitalised buyer paying a premium for a proven asset the way a mine developer does. The obligor pays at most face value, and only grudgingly.
scored.ladder: The ladder is weak. The next rungs would be claims servicing, then funding network upgrades directly in exchange for the credits (upgrade finance), then developing interconnection positions. Upgrade finance is a financing business priced on cost of capital, and development has already been scored as weak (interconnection queue positions). There is no path to owning a large physical value chain.
scored.fatal_flaw: The repayment rights belong to projects that reached commercial operation, and those projects are owned by live plant owners. Orphaned estates mostly hold claims that are worthless or already settled by formula. The value is capped at a face amount that the obligor already computes and tracks, so this is discounted debt collection with no 10^3-10^4 step-up.
scored.one_line_reason: This is collecting a capped receivable with a known face value, not discovering hidden value. Real-world step-up is probably 3-10x after pricing, the obligor already keeps the legible record, and there is no ladder to a large company.

scored.name: QF Attribute Title / Uncaptured Legacy RECs
scored.one_line: Buy REC and capacity-attribute rights from small old PURPA QFs (hydro, biomass, WTE, LFG, CHP) whose contracts are silent on RECs (attributes stay with the QF under American Ref-Fuel unless state law says otherwise); prove title from scanned PUC dockets, register in GATS/M-RETS/WREGIS/NEPOOL and sell RECs to obligated LSEs.
scored.unproven_right: Forgotten or contested attribute claims priced near zero, bought for upfront plus share.
scored.proving_step: ML classifies PPA text and eligibility, legal opinion or PUC ruling, tracking-system registration and meter feed.
scored.proven_buyer: RPS-obligated LSEs and retail suppliers (Eversource, National Grid, Constellation, CCAs), REC brokers, hyperscalers.
scored.public_data: State PUC e-dockets, FERC Form 556, EIA-860/923, tracking-system generator lists (gap = missing QFs).
scored.rough_step_up: ~10-60x; utility litigation risk and state variation.
scored.frame: The rung would be buying a REC/attribute right from a small old QF, proving title, registering it and selling the RECs. Finding the gap is maybe 20-30% of the work, and it is a cheap join of EIA-860 against the GATS, M-RETS, WREGIS and NEPOOL GIS generator lists. The other 70-80% is legal and administrative: a title opinion or PUC ruling, eligibility certification, meter and telemetry feed, registration, and selling RECs for years. So discovery is not 80%+ in any sellable frame. ISO-NE's NEPOOL GIS creates certificates for essentially every generator in the ISO-NE control area, which removes most of the 'missing QF' gap in the highest-priced region (from memory).
scored.step_up: My estimate, not sourced, since searching was blocked. Pre-1997/1998 hydro, biomass, waste-to-energy (WTE) and landfill gas (LFG) plants mostly qualify only for the 'existing' tiers: MA Class II or WTE, CT Class II, PJM Tier 2, at roughly $1-15/MWh. They mostly do not qualify for MA/CT Class I (~$30-40/MWh, alternative compliance payment (ACP) around $40), because of vintage cutoffs. Worked example: a 5 MW hydro at 50% capacity factor makes ~22,000 MWh/yr. At ~$5-10/MWh that is $110-220k/yr, worth maybe $0.5-1.5M NPV. Against a near-zero bought claim that is maybe 5-30x on the contracted price. That is not a 10^3 jump, and part of the value goes back to the QF owner through the revenue share.
scored.hit_rate_capex: My estimate, unsourced. The proving step is a legal and registration process, not a mostly-failing probabilistic shot. Cost is ~$25-150k in legal opinion, PUC filing and metering per facility. Once a real contract-silent QF is identified, the hit rate is fairly high (maybe 30-60%). The main risk is utility litigation under state law that gives RECs to the utility; many states settled this after American Ref-Fuel (FERC 2003) and the Wheelabrator Lisbon v. CT DPUC 2d Cir. 2008 decision, some of them for the utility. With a base hit rate of ~0.3-0.6, the ML lever is capped at ~2-3x, nowhere near 10x.
scored.data: The data is mostly legible. EIA-860/923, FERC Form 556 and tracking-system generator registries are structured and downloadable, so the 'missing QF' gap is a SQL join, not an ML problem. The scanned PPA text in PUC e-dockets is the only illegible part, and it settles only the contract-silence question. Many states have already decided REC ownership for legacy QF contracts in generic dockets, so the outcome is often written into a legible ruling. Also, many 1980s PURPA contracts (typically 15-30 years) have expired, so the QF already holds its attributes outright.
scored.right_bought: In principle the right can be bought (upfront plus a share) from the QF owner. But owners are not unable to read the data. Small hydro and WTE operators know about RECs, and brokers and aggregators already sign up small generators routinely (Karbone, 3Degrees, Sterling Planet, Evolve, Mass. small-hydro aggregators, from memory). So there is no real information discount to buy against.
scored.buyer: Buyers exist and have capital: RPS-obligated LSEs and competitive suppliers (Eversource, National Grid, Constellation, CCAs), REC brokers, and corporate and hyperscaler buyers. The catch is that hyperscalers want new-build additionality, not 1985-vintage Class II RECs, and LSEs buy those cheaply in bulk.
scored.ladder: The ladder is modest. It could go from REC aggregation to buying the small QFs themselves (small hydro roll-up) and on to repowering. But that is a mature, low-margin small-hydro/WTE roll-up path (Eagle Creek and similar exist), not a path to a trillion-dollar company.
scored.fatal_flaw: Old QFs mostly qualify only for low-price 'existing' REC tiers (~$1-15/MWh, my estimate), the gap shows up in structured registries and is filled by existing brokers, and state law has often already given REC ownership to one side. That leaves no illegible-data edge, no 10^3 step-up and no low-hit-rate shot for ML to improve.
scored.one_line_reason: This is really a legal and administrative REC-aggregation business with low-value existing-tier RECs and a ~2-3x maximum ML lever, not a discovery-dominated rung.

scored.name: Foam Bank: CFC-11 in pre-1993 building and cold-storage insulation
scored.one_line: ML over assessor, permit and demolition data predicts buildings holding CFC-blown foam; buy the foam as waste at demolition, core-test, recover and destroy under ODS protocols, sell offsets.
scored.unproven_right: Title to insulation foam in buildings slated for demolition (negative-value waste).
scored.proving_step: Lab core test, then panel removal and transport piggybacking on paid demolition.
scored.proven_buyer: WA CCA and California cap-and-trade compliance entities, voluntary buyers, ODS aggregators.
scored.public_data: Assessor use codes, permit/demolition portals, GCCA refrigerated warehouse directories, NAIP/USGS aerials, EPA SNAP history.
scored.rough_step_up: ~100-1000x+ from negative value; weak ODS prices and registry eligibility.
scored.frame: The rung would be: hold title to CFC-blown foam in a building scheduled for demolition, and prove it contains CFC-11. Discovery is maybe 10-20% of the work inside that rung (my estimate). The real work is physical: separating panels at demolition, handling bulky low-density foam, transporting it, extracting or incinerating it at an approved destruction facility, and getting the destruction certified and verified. A buyer does not pay for foam that has only been proven. Credits come into existence only after destruction and verification. So no rung exists where discovery is 80% or more. This is the same structure as the coal-mine geothermal counter-example: knowing which building has the foam is easy, and recovering it is hard.
scored.step_up: Unproven: the foam is waste with a disposal cost, roughly -$1 to -$5/m2 (my estimate). Proven, my estimate: 30-40 kg/m3 polyurethane, about 10 cm thick, about 3-4 kg of foam per m2, and roughly 5-8% residual CFC-11 after decades of off-gassing. That leaves about 0.15-0.3 kg of CFC-11 per m2. At GWP 4,750 (AR4) that is about 0.7-1.4 tCO2e per m2. At ODS offset prices of roughly $5-15/t voluntary and about $15-25/t for CARB compliance (from memory of 2023-2025 ranges, not verified this session), gross value is about $5-30/m2 before recovery and destruction costs, which take a large share of it. A cold-storage warehouse of about 10,000 m2 of panel would gross about $50k-300k. Going from negative to positive makes the multiple look unbounded, but the realised gain is about 10x in absolute terms, and nothing is gained at the moment of a hit, only after destruction.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Proving is cheap: a core sample plus GC lab analysis costs roughly $100-500 per building (my estimate). The base hit rate is high for the target set. For cold storage and commercial roofs insulated with PUR/PIR before about 1993, the chance of CFC-11 is likely 40-70% (my estimate; CFC-11 was the dominant PUR blowing agent until the Montreal Protocol phase-out in 1993-96). Since the lever is capped at 1/base hit rate, ML can improve the hit rate by about 1.5-2.5x at most. A cheap test that mostly succeeds already leaves little discovery capex to cut. No searches could be run (the shared search budget was exhausted), so these numbers are not verified.
scored.data: There is some illegible public data: assessor use codes, year-built fields, demolition permit portals, the GCCA warehouse directory and aerial imagery. However, year-built plus a 'refrigerated warehouse' use code is already a legible proxy that gets most of the way, so ML adds a small edge over a simple filter. Rights are cheap: owners will give the foam away to avoid disposal costs. But that is because the foam has no value until it is destroyed, not because owners cannot read the data. The bigger problem is registry eligibility. The CARB U.S. ODS Compliance Offset Protocol, as I recall it, covers refrigerants and foam blowing agent recovered from appliances. Building insulation foam is not eligible for compliance credits. Voluntary methodologies (CAR/ACR/Verra) are narrower or untested for building foam, and ODS credits face additionality and quality discounts in the voluntary market. Who already does adjacent work: A-Gas, EOS Climate, Tradewater, Recoolit, and the appliance recyclers ARCA and JACO. In the EU and Japan, foam recovery is regulated and handled by waste contractors.
scored.right_bought: Title to the insulation foam at demolition, given away for free or paid for by the owner as avoided disposal cost. It is cheap because the foam is a waste liability, not because the owner lacks information.
scored.buyer: Voluntary carbon buyers and ODS aggregators. CARB compliance entities likely cannot use building-foam credits because the protocol is restricted to appliance foam (from memory, unverified). The WA CCA uses ARB-type protocols with the same restriction. The buyers do have capital, but the volume is small and prices are low.
scored.ladder: Possible rungs are demolition-stage foam recovery, then a destruction facility, then a full ODS/HFC bank-management business, then refrigerant lifecycle services. The ceiling is modest. The global ODS bank in foam is large (several GtCO2e in total), but it is dispersed, declining through off-gassing, and set to shrink further as buildings are demolished. This is not a trillion-dollar path.
scored.fatal_flaw: Discovery is not the bottleneck. Proving is cheap and usually succeeds, so the ML lever is under about 2x. The value appears only after costly physical recovery, transport and certified destruction (the coal-mine-geothermal failure mode), and building insulation foam is likely not eligible under the CARB/WA compliance ODS protocol, leaving thin voluntary prices.
scored.one_line_reason: Finding a CFC-foam building is easy and cheap. Monetising it means physically recovering and destroying the foam for low-priced, possibly ineligible offsets, so no discovery-dominated rung exists and there is no 10^3x hit.
