From memory: Climate Action Reserve U.S. ODS Project Protocol v2
From memory: IPCC AR4 GWP for CFC-11 = 4,750
From memory: TEAP/UNEP reports on ODS banks in building foams

scored.name: Superfund Forensics: CERCLA cost-recovery claim assignments
scored.one_line: Buy cheap assignments of CERCLA 107/113 claims from landowners and towns stuck with orphan contamination; ML over declassified CORONA/Hexagon, historic aerials and Sanborn maps identifies the solvent historical polluter or successor; sell to funders or settle.
scored.unproven_right: Assigned claims worth near zero while the PRP is unknown.
scored.proving_step: Imagery time-series detection linked to directories, permits and successor chains; attribution dossier.
scored.proven_buyer: Litigation funders (Burford, Omni Bridgeway, Parabellum), PRP insurers.
scored.public_data: USGS EarthExplorer CORONA/Gambit/Hexagon, NHAP/NAPP, historic aerial archives, LoC Sanborn, EPA SEMS/Envirofacts, state spill/UST files.
scored.rough_step_up: ~$0 to $1-20M funded claims; slow litigation, thinner ladder.
scored.frame: The proposed rung is "attribution dossier plus assigned claim", but it is not a discrete, sellable rung where discovery is 80%+ of the work. A CERCLA §107 claim is only worth the necessary response costs the claimant has actually incurred, consistent with the NCP (statutory requirement, from my own knowledge). A town or landowner stuck with orphan contamination usually has not spent much yet. So the physical steps come first and dominate: site investigation (RI/FS), the cleanup itself, and years of litigation. My estimate is that naming the PRP is 10-25% of the work behind a recovered dollar. This is the same shape as the geothermal-in-coal-mines counter-example: the hard part is everything after you find the target. Funders do buy cases, but they are buying litigation economics, not a proven asset.
scored.step_up: Estimate, unsourced (the search budget was used up before any search ran). An assigned claim with no known PRP is worth close to $0. Once a solvent PRP is named, a funded claim is still worth only what the court is likely to award times the recovery rate, minus fees: roughly 20-50% of incurred costs. It also takes 3-8 years and needs the costs to be spent first. If you buy at 5-15% of face and the claim is funded or settles for 30-60% of face, the step-up is about 3-10x and arrives slowly, not 10^3-10^4x right away. The candidate's own "$0 to $1-20M" counts an unknown PRP as $0, but most of that value comes from cleanup spending, not from discovery.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Estimate, no source. A manual PRP search or historical forensics study (EPA contractor PRP searches, consultants working from aerials and Sanborn maps) costs roughly $20k-$150k per site. My guess is it names a viable, solvent PRP at maybe 20-40% of orphan sites; the rest are dead or dissolved companies, and §107 needs a successor that still exists and has money. ML could cut the cost per attempt a lot. But the lever is capped at about 3-5x (1/base hit rate), and the binding limit is whether the polluter is still solvent, which imagery cannot fix.
scored.data: Partly favourable. CORONA/Hexagon declassified imagery, NHAP/NAPP aerials and Sanborn maps are public, huge and hard to read by machine. But reading them is already a commodity in environmental due diligence. EDR (now part of LightBox) sells Sanborn maps, historical aerials and city directories as standard inputs to ASTM E1527 Phase I site assessments. At NPL and larger sites, EPA's SEMS records and PRP search reports often already name the PRPs. State spill and UST files usually list a responsible party in a legible field. So the edge is limited to true orphan sites that are small and below EPA's attention, and most of those have insolvent polluters.
scored.right_bought: This is weak. Courts are split on whether a §107 cost-recovery claim can be assigned (from my own knowledge, not verified here). Insurer subrogation is allowed under §112(c). A §113 contribution claim can only exist after the holder has been sued or has settled, so it cannot be bought in advance. The assignor is a current owner, which makes it a PRP itself and leaves it exposed to counterclaims. Champerty rules vary by state. Limitation periods are short: 3 years for removal actions, 6 years from the start of remedial construction, 3 years for §113 after a judgment or settlement. The right is technically something you buy, but it is legally fragile and sellers are few.
scored.buyer: Litigation funders: Burford, Omni Bridgeway and Parabellum are the candidate's named examples; I have not checked their real appetite for environmental claims, and environmental cost recovery is a niche for them. Others: the PRPs' historic CGL insurers, through settlements; and environmental litigation firms such as the plaintiffs' bar that does PFAS and MTBE cases. All are capitalised, but they pay for expected litigation value, not for a dossier.
scored.ladder: This is thin. The possible steps up are: brownfield acquisition and remediation (owning the land and capturing the uplift once it is cleaned), environmental remediation contracting, and insurance archaeology (tracing historic insurance policies to recover from them). Each is a fragmented, low-margin services business. There is no clear path to a very large company. Insurance archaeology plus funded claims is the most credible extension, but incumbents already do it.
scored.fatal_flaw: The claim's value is set by response costs actually incurred and by litigation, not by discovery. Naming the polluter does not turn the asset into money. Someone still has to pay for cleanup and spend years in court, and the polluter has to be a solvent successor that still exists. The physical steps are much harder than finding the PRP, the same failure as geothermal in coal mines. On top of that, Phase I research (EDR/LightBox) and EPA PRP searches already make most of the attribution readable.
scored.one_line_reason: Discovery is a small slice of the value of a CERCLA claim. Value depends on incurred cleanup costs, polluter solvency and slow litigation, so the step-up is about 3-10x over years, not an instant 10^4x.
sources: No live sources: all three WebSearch calls were refused because the shared per-turn search budget was used up. All figures are estimates from prior knowledge and should be checked.
Statute, from my own knowledge (not fetched): CERCLA 42 U.S.C. 9607 (cost recovery, NCP consistency), 9613(f)/(g) (contribution and limitation periods), 9612(c) (subrogation)
Industry, from my own knowledge: EDR/LightBox historical Sanborn maps, aerials and city directories used in ASTM E1527-21 Phase I site assessments
Agency, from my own knowledge: EPA SEMS and PRP search practice at NPL sites

scored.name: Zombie Vertical Software Rescue: dead-vendor installed bases in government and utilities
scored.one_line: Buy code and IP of defunct small vertical-software vendors (permitting, courts, water billing, CAMA); LLM over council minutes, budgets and audits finds agencies still running it; sign maintenance and sell the book. Generalises killed orphaned ICS idea.
scored.unproven_right: Source, copyright and contract novation rights, $10-100k.
scored.proving_step: LLM over minutes, RFPs and inventories; convert use to maintenance contracts.
scored.proven_buyer: Constellation/Harris, Tyler, Jonas (1-3x recurring revenue).
scored.public_data: Granicus/Legistar/CivicPlus minutes, procurement portals, auditor reports, USAspending, Wayback client lists.
scored.frame: The rung would be "own the IP of a dead vendor plus a confirmed list of agencies still running it". Inside that rung, finding the agencies is maybe 15-25% of the work (my estimate). The rest is the hard physical-equivalent step. That means rebuilding a support organisation for old code (old stacks, missing build environments, security and CJIS/SOC2 compliance), getting each government agency to approve a contract novation or a new sole-source award, and keeping the book alive. That makes it the geothermal-in-coal-mines pattern: delivering the asset is harder than finding it. The buyer cannot purchase the 'discovered' state on its own. Harris or Constellation pay for signed, retained recurring revenue, not for a list of agencies.
scored.step_up: Unproven: code and IP rights from a defunct vendor or bankruptcy trustee at $10-100k (the candidate's figure; plausible for asset sales out of liquidation). Proven: Constellation/Harris-style buyers pay roughly 1-3x recurring revenue for small VMS books (from my memory of Mark Leonard letters and roll-up commentary; I could not verify it this run). Example (my estimate): $50k for IP; 20 agencies at $15k/yr maintenance gives $300k ARR, which sells for about $300-900k. That is about 6-18x, and it only happens after months of contracting and support, not right away on a 'hit'. It is nowhere near the 10^3-10^4 jump.
scored.hit_rate_capex: The proving attempt is cheap today: a records request, a phone call to the IT department, or a search of the agency's check register for the vendor name. That costs maybe $100-1,000 per agency (estimate). The real cost is converting and servicing each agency, which ML does not touch. Base hit rate is unclear but not the bottleneck. Many installs of a dead vendor's software are already known to the bankruptcy trustee or former employees through the old customer list, so the hit rate given a good lead is high. ML's lever on discovery capex is small, maybe 2x at best, not 10x. No sourced numbers: the web search budget ran out this run.
scored.data: The data is public and fairly illegible: Legistar/Granicus minutes, procurement portals, annual audit reports (ACFR/single audits), check registers, USAspending, Wayback client lists. But the outcome is legible to the one party that matters, the agency itself, which knows exactly what it runs and who it pays. Vendor names also show up in plain text in payment registers and budget line items. The defunct vendor's own customer list, which comes with the IP purchase, mostly is the answer. That kills most of the ML edge: the asset seller is the party holding the legible list.
scored.right_bought: Partly yes. IP, source code and copyrights can be bought cheaply from trustees, founders or heirs. But the right that actually holds the value is the contract with the agency, and it is not buyable. Government contracts usually need the agency's consent to assign or novate, and expired licences often need a new procurement. Many perpetual licences mean the agency owes no maintenance at all. Owning the code does not oblige anyone to pay you.
scored.buyer: Harris Computer (a Constellation unit, which specialises in exactly this: buying mature or declining public-sector software books), Tyler Technologies, Jonas, N. Harris, Volaris, Civica, CentralSquare, Caselle. They are capitalised, but they buy proven ARR, and they already source this deal flow themselves through relationships and vendor-founder outreach.
scored.ladder: The ladder would run from rescuing dead books, to rolling up live small VMS vendors, to running a multi-vertical public-sector software platform, i.e. a Constellation clone. A real ladder, but the top is already occupied by Constellation (about $60-70B market cap, from memory) and Tyler. The trillion-dollar path is weak, and the bottom rung is not discovery-dominated.
scored.fatal_flaw: The value comes from servicing and re-contracting old government software, not from discovering it. Finding agencies still running a dead vendor's software is cheap and largely given away by the vendor's own customer list. Turning them into paid maintenance needs agency consent and new procurement, plus a real support operation. Buyers like Harris pay 1-3x for proven ARR only, and they already work this niche. So there is no discrete rung where discovery is 80%+ and a hit immediately gives a 10^3x step-up.
scored.one_line_reason: This fails the core test: finding the installed base is cheap and partly handed over with the asset, while servicing and re-contracting is most of the work. The step-up is about 6-18x over months, not 10^3x on a hit, and Harris/Constellation already work this space.
sources: No live sources: the shared WebSearch budget (200 calls per turn) ran out before this agent could search, so every figure here is from memory or is my estimate and is marked as such
Mark Leonard / Constellation Software shareholder letters (from memory): small VMS acquired at roughly 1-3x revenue, with hurdle rates on proven recurring revenue
Harris Computer Systems (Constellation): stated strategy of buying mature public-sector and utility software (from memory)
General public-procurement practice (from memory): government contract assignment and novation needs agency consent

scored.name: Dormant App Installed-Base Acquisition
scored.one_line: Buy abandoned apps and developer accounts for $1-10k; ML finds rebootable user bases; update and sell to app rollups.
scored.unproven_right: App listing, bundle ID and history via transfer.
scored.proving_step: Ship update and measure reactivated MAU (moderate engineering).
scored.proven_buyer: Bending Spoons, Apalon/IAC, Tiny-style holdcos.
scored.public_data: App Store/Play listings, AppBrain, Sensor Tower free tiers, Wayback, reviews.
scored.frame: The rung is buying a dormant app plus its listing and bundle ID, shipping an update, and showing reactivated MAU and revenue. Discovery (choosing the app) is maybe 25-35% of the work inside that rung. That is my estimate. The rest is operating work: rebuilding for current iOS/Android SDKs, passing store review, re-engaging users, adding monetisation and doing ASO. This is the coal-mine-geothermal pattern, where the bespoke work after you find the asset is harder than the finding. No frame gets discovery to 80%+.
scored.step_up: No searches could be run: the shared WebSearch budget for this turn was already used up, so every figure here is my estimate from prior knowledge. Dormant apps with no revenue usually sell on Flippa or Acquire.com for about $500-$10k, and the candidate itself assumes $1-10k. A revived app is priced on earnings, at roughly 2.5-4x annual profit (my recollection of the range Flippa and Acquire.com publish). For a typical win, say $3-5k MRR revived from a $3-5k purchase, that means a sale price of about $100-200k. That is about 20-50x on the purchase price but only about 5-15x once you count engineering and marketing spend. It is not an immediate step-up on a hit like a drill core: the value has to be earned over 6-12 months of revenue history before a buyer will pay.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Estimates only, no searches. Each proving attempt costs about $1-10k for the purchase plus $10-50k of engineering and marketing. I estimate 10-20% of revived dormant apps reach meaningful sellable revenue. The users of an abandoned app have mostly uninstalled it, an update only reaches devices that still have it installed, and push tokens and consent are fragile. So the lever is capped at about 5-10x. ML only helps pick which apps to buy, while most of the cost sits in engineering and growth work that ML does not shrink 10x, so discovery capex falls by maybe 2x.
scored.data: The data is mostly legible already, and the outcome largely is too. App Store and Play listings show the last-updated date, rating counts, review history and download bands (Play shows install bands directly). Sensor Tower, data.ai, AppMagic and AppBrain sell clean download and MAU estimates per app, so the core signal (a large installed base, recent decay, a good rating) is a structured field incumbents already query. Wayback and the review text add only a little. There is no scanned, illegible corpus that only ML can read.
scored.right_bought: Yes, it can be bought: developers can transfer apps through App Store Connect and Play Console, and abandoned apps can be bought cheaply from indie developers who have stopped caring. But sellers are not blind. The same sales metrics are visible to them and to the brokers, and marketplaces like Flippa, Acquire.com and app-flipping communities price these apps competitively. The discount comes from the owner's neglect, not from data the owner cannot read.
scored.buyer: Possible buyers include Tiny-style holdcos, Apalon/IAC, small app rollups and Flippa or Acquire.com buyers paying about 2.5-4x profit. Bending Spoons mostly buys large established products (Evernote, WeTransfer, Vimeo, about $1B+ deals), not revived micro-apps, so it is not a real buyer for this rung. The real buyers are fragmented, small-ticket and price strictly on trailing earnings.
scored.ladder: Weak. The path is: revive single apps, become a portfolio rollup, then a Bending Spoons-style operator of acquired software. That is horizontal aggregation, not vertical integration, and the top of the path is a crowded holdco model rather than a chain where each rung adds a discrete step-up. Bending Spoons shows the model can get to about $10B+, but its edge is operating excellence, not discovery.
scored.fatal_flaw: Proving is operating, not discovery. The value comes from months of engineering, growth and monetisation work that is then priced at 2.5-4x earnings, and the selection signal (installs, ratings, decay) is already in legible app-intelligence fields that every app flipper uses. There is no immediate 10^3 step-up and no illegible-data edge.
scored.one_line_reason: This is a coal-mine-geothermal case: picking the app is easy and legible, while rebooting it is bespoke operating work that sells at earnings multiples, not as a discovery step-up.

scored.name: US rights to foreign heritage food brands with diaspora pull
scored.one_line: License exclusive US trademark and import rights from foreign food brands with no US presence; prove velocity through ethnic grocers; sell US rights back or to distributors.
scored.unproven_right: Exclusive US licence or TM assignment, royalty-only or small upfront.
scored.proving_step: ML over bills of lading, grey listings and diaspora data; one container through 50-200 grocers.
scored.proven_buyer: Parent company, House of Spices, GreenLeaf, Jetro, McCormick-type CPGs.
scored.public_data: CBP bills of lading, USPTO and Madrid Monitor, FDA facility and import refusals, Amazon listings.
scored.frame: The rung is "exclusive US licence plus one proving container". Discovery (choosing the brand) is maybe 20-30% of the work inside that rung (my estimate). The other 70-80% is physical and regulatory: FDA food facility registration, FSVP importer compliance, US-compliant labels and nutrition panels, a customs broker, freight, warehousing, getting into 50-200 grocers (slotting fees or DSD relationships), and working capital tied up for 60-120 days. That is the coal-mine-geothermal pattern: running the distribution is harder than finding the brand. The buyer exists (diaspora distributors, CPG roll-ups), but what they pay for is the running distribution business, not a proven right.
scored.step_up: My estimate, not sourced. The unproven right costs about $0-50k: royalty-only (typical food royalties around 3-8%) plus a small upfront. A proven US licence with $1-3M of revenue might sell for 0.5-1.5x revenue, so $0.5-4M. That is roughly 10-100x on the upfront. But it is not an immediate step-up on a hit. Value builds slowly with sell-through, and the cost basis also includes $50-150k per container of inventory and launch spend. Counted against total capital at risk, the step-up is roughly 3-30x. The parent can also refuse to renew or can buy back at a low price, so the value sits mostly with the licensor.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Both numbers are my estimates; I found no sourced figures. Base hit rate: roughly 20-40% of diaspora-brand container tests reach repeat velocity. Diaspora pull is easy to see in advance (grey imports and Amazon reseller listings already exist), so the base rate is not tiny. Cost per proving attempt: about $50-150k (one 40ft container of product at $20-60k, freight and duty, FDA/FSVP and labelling setup, broker and slotting or promo spend, sales labour). With a base hit rate of 20-40%, ML can improve hit rate by at most about 2.5-5x, well short of 10x, and it does nothing to the fixed physical cost of each attempt.
scored.data: The data is public and largely legible already. CBP bills of lading are packaged by commercial vendors (Panjiva, ImportGenius, ImportYeti) into searchable, structured form. USPTO and Madrid Monitor are structured databases. FDA import refusals are a published database. Amazon listings, ratings and BSR are legible and scraped by many tools. The outcome (whether US demand exists) is close to summarised in visible fields: grey-import volume on bills of lading and Amazon reseller sales rank. Incumbent diaspora importers (House of Spices, Patel Brothers' supply chain, GreenLeaf, Jetro/Restaurant Depot buyers) already read this through trade relationships. There is little hidden, ML-only edge.
scored.right_bought: Yes, the right is bought, through a negotiated licence or TM assignment. But the sellers are not illiterate about the asset. Foreign brand owners know their diaspora market, and many already sell through US importers. A licensor can protect itself with term limits, minimum-volume clauses and buyback options. Squatting on an unregistered US mark is not a safe alternative: Belmora v. Bayer (4th Cir. 2016) allowed Lanham §43(a) false-association claims by a foreign brand owner, and Paris Convention 6bis well-known-mark protection also applies. The licensee holds a revocable, time-limited right, not a durable asset like a mineral claim.
scored.buyer: The parent brand (most likely, and it holds the bargaining power at renewal), diaspora distributors (House of Spices, GreenLeaf/Swad, KeHE ethnic division, UNFI), and occasional CPG acquirers. They buy distribution businesses at about 0.5-1.5x revenue (my estimate), not proven rights at a large premium.
scored.ladder: Rungs above: master import licensee → multi-brand diaspora distributor → private label or US co-manufacturing → acquiring the brands outright. It is a real but modest path; the end state is a mid-size specialty food distributor (the KeHE/UNFI-type ethnic segment), low margin, not a trillion-dollar chain. The core problem is that you never own the brand IP, so each rung up still depends on licensor goodwill.
scored.fatal_flaw: The proving step is mostly physical distribution, not discovery. FDA/FSVP compliance, labels, freight, inventory capital and grocer slotting make up most of the work and capital, and that fixed cost does not fall with ML. On top of that, the "proven" asset is a revocable licence that the foreign parent can reclaim or reprice at renewal. That moves the step-up to the licensor, and the demand signal is already legible in commercial bill-of-lading tools and Amazon ranks.
scored.one_line_reason: This is an import-distribution business in disguise. Discovery is about 25% of the rung, the proven asset is a revocable licence worth about 0.5-1.5x revenue, the demand signal is already legible, and the ML lever is capped around 3-5x by a 20-40% base hit rate.

scored.name: CatalystShelf: pruned catalyst and porous-material patent families for new uses
scored.one_line: Buy non-core zeolite, MOF and catalyst families pruned by majors; ML scores example tables against SAF, e-methanol, DAC and PFAS targets; contract-lab test proves new use; sell to licensors and project developers.
scored.unproven_right: Pruned families at $5-50k each.
scored.proving_step: ML on example tables; $20-60k reactor or isotherm test.
scored.proven_buyer: Topsoe, Honeywell UOP, Axens, JM, Climeworks, Heirloom, e-fuel developers.
scored.public_data: PatentsView, EPO, USPTO assignments, file wrappers.
scored.frame: The rung would be "own a catalyst patent family and prove one new use with a lab test". Inside that rung, discovery is maybe 30-40% of the work (my estimate). The rest is physical: a $20-60k reactor or isotherm test is only a screening result. Licensors (Topsoe, UOP, Axens, JM) and DAC developers buy process guarantees backed by pilot data: thousands of hours on stream, attrition, regeneration, scale-up of synthesis, cost per kg. That is the geothermal counter-example again. Scaling a bespoke material from grams to tonnes is much harder than finding it, and MOFs show this clearly. So there is no rung where discovery is 80% or more and a capitalised buyer pays for the output.
scored.step_up: Unproven: the candidate assumes $5-50k per pruned family (not verified; web search budget was exhausted). Pruned families can also simply lapse into the public domain for $0. Proven: catalyst and sorbent licences are usually bundled with know-how and paid as running royalties or $1-10M+ upfront (my estimate). A lab test alone does not earn that. A realistic price for "family plus one lab result" might be $100k-1M. That is about 10-100x, and only on the rare hit.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Cost per proving attempt is $20-60k per the candidate (plausible for a contract-lab fixed-bed or isotherm run; my estimate, not verified). That is already cheap, so dropping it 10x saves little. The expensive, mostly failing step is pilot scale-up ($1-10M+; my estimate), and ML on patent example tables does not touch it. Base hit rate of a repurposed material beating the state of the art at the target: perhaps 1-5% (estimate). There is also heavy existing computational screening: CoRE MOF and hypothetical-zeolite databases, and academic and national-lab high-throughput work. So ML adds little over the screening that already happens.
scored.data: Patent data is about the most legible data there is: full-text, classified, searchable in PatentsView, EPO, Google Patents and Lens, with OCR'd file wrappers. The example tables (composition, conversion, selectivity, uptake) are structured and already mined by academic NLP groups and commercial tools (e.g. CAS SciFinder). The outcome is effectively already summarised. The sellers are majors who can read their own data and who pruned because they know the family's value. There is no illegibility edge.
scored.right_bought: The right does not capture the step-up. An old composition patent covers the material and its disclosed uses, not the new use you find. The new-use value would sit in a new method-of-use patent and your own test data. Anyone can file those without buying the old family, and the old family itself counts as prior art against broad claims. Pruned families also usually have only 5-10 years of term left (estimate), and abandoned ones are free to use. So buying the family is mostly unnecessary, and its purchase price is not the gate.
scored.buyer: Topsoe, Honeywell UOP, Axens, Johnson Matthey, BASF, Clariant, Climeworks, Svante, Heirloom, e-fuel developers. They are well capitalised, but they buy proven process packages or acquire companies (e.g. BASF and Svante's MOF sorbent work), not patents plus lab data. Startups like Mosaic Materials (acquired by Baker Hughes) and Nuada show the value is realised only after scale-up.
scored.ladder: In principle there is a ladder: material IP, then pilot-proven sorbent or catalyst, then licensor of process packages, then the operator of SAF, e-methanol or DAC plants. Each rung above the first is dominated by capex, scale-up and process guarantees, not discovery, so the ML edge disappears immediately. There is a path to a large company, but it is the ordinary hard-tech path, not the Terranox one.
scored.fatal_flaw: The step-up does not attach to the right you buy, and the physical step is not trivial. A new use of an old material is protected by a new method-of-use patent and your own data, which needs no purchase of the pruned family. And buyers pay for pilot-scale proof costing millions, not for a $40k lab test. That is the geothermal-in-coal-mines failure: building and scaling the material is far harder than finding it.
scored.one_line_reason: Patent data is fully legible and already mined, the bought family does not capture the new-use value, and buyers pay only after expensive pilot scale-up, so no rung exists where discovery is 80% or more.

Background knowledge: Richardson Oliver Insights brokered patent market reports (typical asking prices ~$100-300k per asset, mostly tech/SEP; chemicals rarely traded).
Background knowledge: CoRE MOF database and IZA hypothetical zeolite databases (existing computational screening).
Background knowledge: Baker Hughes acquisition of Mosaic Materials (2022); BASF-Svante MOF sorbent manufacturing partnership.

scored.name: Orphaned Consented Cohorts: bankruptcy biobank roll-up
scored.one_line: Buy consented genomic and biospecimen collections from bankrupt genomics, DTC and CRO companies for cents per participant; prove rare-variant carrier enrichment; license to pharma target discovery (GSK-23andMe precedent).
scored.unproven_right: Trustee sale of samples, data and consent/recontact permissions.
scored.proving_step: Parse PACER schedules and consents; impute or low-pass sequence and run burden tests.
scored.proven_buyer: GSK, Regeneron Genetics Center, AbbVie, Novo, Truveta, Tempus.
scored.public_data: PACER, EDGAR, ClinicalTrials.gov and dbGaP registrations, IRB consents, 23andMe/TTAM record.
scored.frame: The rung is buying a consented cohort out of bankruptcy and licensing it to pharma. Inside that rung, finding the asset is easy: bankruptcies are announced and the trustee runs a marketed auction. The hard part is legal and operational. You have to clear consent scope and transferability, deal with state genetic-privacy laws, objections from attorneys general and the patient ombudsman, deletion requests, and storing and re-sequencing the samples. My estimate is that discovery is about 20-30% of the work in the rung, not 80% or more. A capitalised buyer does exist (pharma target-discovery groups), but they can bid at the auction directly.
scored.step_up: The facts below are from memory up to mid-2025, not from new searches in this run. 23andMe went through Chapter 11 in 2025. Regeneron bid about $256M, and TTAM (Wojcicki) won at about $305M for roughly 15M customers. That is about $20 per participant, not cents. On the proven side, GSK paid $300M in 2018 for a 4-year exclusive drug-discovery deal when 23andMe had about 5M customers, about 80% of them consented. That is roughly $60-75 per consented participant over the term. GSK extended for $50M in 2022. So unproven is about $20 per participant and proven is about $60-100 per participant, a step-up of about 3-5x. Smaller CRO or DTC collections may sell for less, but they are also worth less to pharma because they lack scale, phenotypes and recontact. The candidate's claim of ~100-1000x is not supported.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Proving is computational and cheap. Low-pass sequencing or imputation costs about $20-50 per sample (my estimate), and burden tests are close to free. That makes the proving cost about $0.5M-5M per cohort (estimate), against purchase prices that range from $1M to $300M. The purchase dominates capex, not the proving. There is also no clear binary low hit rate, because most consented cohorts have some licensing value. ML has little hit rate to raise, and the lever is likely under 2x.
scored.data: PACER schedules and asset purchase agreements are public but messy. However, the key facts are written into legible fields or filings: cohort size, consent scope and genotyping platform appear in sale motions and in reports by the consumer privacy ombudsman. dbGaP and ClinicalTrials.gov registrations are structured. The asset's value is not hidden in illegible data that sellers cannot read. Sophisticated bidders (Regeneron, TTAM) already price it. These are competitive 363 auctions with stalking-horse bids, so the asset is not sold cheaply by owners who cannot read the data.
scored.right_bought: The right is bought at a court-supervised 363 auction, from trustees advised by bankers. In the 23andMe case, 28+ state attorneys general objected, and about 1.9M+ users requested deletion (memory, approximate). Consents are often non-transferable or limited to the original purpose. State genetic-privacy laws (e.g., California, Illinois GIPA, newer 2025 state laws) can require fresh consent before a transfer. The right exists, but it is competitively priced and can shrink after purchase.
scored.buyer: Pharma and genetics groups such as GSK, Regeneron Genetics Center, AbbVie, Novo, and data aggregators like Truveta and Tempus. These buyers also compete directly at the auctions: Regeneron bid for 23andMe itself. Incumbents and competitors include Regeneron, TTAM Research Institute, Tempus, Truveta, Helix and Nucleus.
scored.ladder: There are plausible rungs above: a cohort roll-up, then a recontact and phenotyping platform, then target discovery, then in-licensed drug development (a Regeneron-like path). The ladder exists, but the bottom rung does not offer an edge from discovery.
scored.fatal_flaw: The asset is neither hidden nor cheap. Orphaned cohorts are sold in public, competitive 363 auctions where the eventual pharma buyers bid directly (23andMe went for about $20 per participant, vs. about $60-75 per consented participant in the GSK deal, a step-up of about 3-5x). Consent and genetic-privacy law can also destroy or shrink the right after purchase through deletions, re-consent requirements and attorney-general objections. There is no illegible signal that ML can extract and incumbents miss.
scored.one_line_reason: Bankruptcy biobank sales are public, competitive auctions that the end buyers already bid in, and consent and privacy limits erode the right. The step-up is about 3-5x, not 10^3, and ML has little hit rate to improve.
sources: Web search budget for this run was exhausted (0 of 5 searches returned); all figures below are from memory up to mid-2025 and should be re-verified
23andMe Chapter 11 (E.D. Mo., 2025): Regeneron ~$256M bid; TTAM Research Institute won at ~$305M; ~15M customers (news coverage and court filings, mid-2025)
GSK-23andMe 2018 collaboration: $300M equity investment, 4-year exclusive drug target discovery; extended 2022 for $50M (GSK and 23andMe press releases)
State attorney general objections and consumer privacy ombudsman report in the 23andMe bankruptcy (2025), ~1.9M deletion requests (approximate, from memory)
Estimate: low-pass sequencing/imputation cost ~$20-50 per sample

scored.name: Closed-Hospital Tissue Archive Rescue
scored.one_line: Take custody of FFPE archives from closing hospitals, scan and AI-triage for rare subtypes, sell annotated cohorts to oncology pharma, CDx and pathology-AI firms.
scored.unproven_right: Title/custody of de-identified archives at $0 to nominal.
scored.proving_step: Rank archives by case mix; scan ($5-10/slide) and AI triage.
scored.proven_buyer: Oncology translational teams, Roche Tissue Dx, Agilent, Foundation Medicine, pathology-AI ($500-5k per case).
scored.public_data: CMS HCRIS, Provider of Services file, Sheps closure list, state filings, SEER.
scored.frame: The rung would be taking custody of a closed hospital's archive and turning it into sellable annotated cases. Inside that rung, discovery is maybe 10-20% of the work (my estimate). The bulk is physical and legal: negotiating custody with the bankruptcy trustee or records custodian, moving and storing hundreds of thousands of blocks, pulling and recutting them, de-identifying them under HIPAA and the Common Rule, checking state law and the IRB position, and handling QC and fulfilment. This is the coal-mine-geothermal pattern: running the operation is harder than finding the asset. A capitalised buyer does exist (pharma translational teams, CDx companies, pathology-AI firms).
scored.step_up: Unproven: blocks sitting in storage under a 10-year CAP retention duty are worth about $0, or less, because storage costs money (CAP retention rule is from memory, not searched). Proven: commercial biospecimen vendors list remnant FFPE blocks at roughly $150-600 each. Rare subtypes or cases with outcome annotation can reach about $1-3k (my estimate from memory of vendor quotes; no search possible). A single sale of a good case can be 30-100x the cost of handling it. But the value is per unit and is earned through processing and selling, not revalued on a hit. Only a small fraction of any archive is ever sold. Blended across the archive, the step-up is about 10-100x.
scored.hit_rate_capex: The proving step does not mostly fail. Every hospital archive holds thousands of cancer cases. Rare subtypes are a known few percent, and you can find them by reading the pathology reports. Scanning at $5-10 a slide plus about $10-30 a block to retrieve and recut (estimate) is a processing cost, not an exploration bet with a 1-5% hit rate. ML adds little: ML triage would replace a text search of reports that already exist. The 1/base-hit-rate cap is about 2-5x at most, and the real lever is less than that.
scored.data: This fails the legible-outcome test. Each block's diagnosis and subtype is already written in its surgical pathology report and laboratory information system (LIS), as ICD-O/SNOMED codes, and it also goes to state cancer registries (and on to SEER). So the outcome sits in a legible field for whoever holds the archive. The public files listed (HCRIS, the Provider of Services file, the Sheps closure list) only tell you which hospitals are closing and their rough case mix. That is a lead list, not an illegible signal that incumbents fail to extract. ML on whole-slide images adds marginal value, such as morphology-defined subgroups, but buyers usually need molecular confirmation anyway.
scored.right_bought: The archive can be had for $0 to a nominal sum, but it is not a clean, buyable title. Blocks are linked to protected health information (PHI). When a hospital closes, records and specimens go to a successor provider or a designated records custodian, often under state rules and bankruptcy court oversight. HIPAA bars selling PHI, so you can only sell de-identified material. Patients can request their blocks back. Some states restrict commercial use of tissue without consent (consent risk, as the candidate itself notes). Sellers are not illiterate about the asset. Their problem is liability, and that liability moves to you.
scored.buyer: Oncology translational and biomarker groups, CDx developers (Roche Tissue Dx, Agilent, Foundation Medicine), and pathology-AI firms building training sets. Real demand, but buyers mostly want molecularly characterised, outcome-annotated, consented cases with a reliable supply. They do not want one-off batches from a closed rural hospital.
scored.ladder: Possible rungs above: a biospecimen broker, then a multi-site prospective biobank, then a real-world data and outcomes business (linking tissue to claims and EHR), then a CDx or companion-diagnostic partner. Incumbents already hold each rung. Discovery Life Sciences (multi-million-block FFPE archive), BioIVT, iSpecimen, Precision for Medicine, Indivumed, Cureline, Proteogenex, Tempus and Caris, plus academic-centre honest brokers. The ladder exists but is crowded, and nothing about the first rung gives you a unique edge for climbing it.
scored.fatal_flaw: There is nothing to discover. The answer for each block (its diagnosis and subtype) is already written in that block's own pathology report and LIS code. The real work is physical, legal and consent logistics for PHI-linked tissue, which is the coal-mine-geothermal failure pattern. Established biobank brokers like Discovery Life Sciences already aggregate remnant FFPE at scale.
scored.one_line_reason: Each block's subtype is already in its pathology report. The work is custody, de-identification and consent logistics rather than discovery, there is no low-hit-rate step for ML to improve, and established brokers already resell remnant FFPE.

scored.name: Material Threat Voucher Hunter: medical countermeasures
scored.one_line: Buy shelved countermeasure candidates from defunct biodefense contractors and BARDA-abandoned programs with near-complete animal-rule packages; file NDA/BLA; win material threat PRV and stockpile contracts.
scored.unproven_right: Rights at $0.1-2M.
scored.proving_step: ML over BARDA/NIAID awards, DTIC, MTDs and animal studies; NDA/BLA ($10-30M).
scored.proven_buyer: Big-pharma PRV buyers, BARDA/SNS procurement.
scored.public_data: USAspending, SAM.gov, DTIC, DHS MTDs, PubMed, Drugs@FDA.
scored.frame: The rung would be buying a shelved countermeasure and taking it through to FDA approval and a voucher. Finding the asset is maybe 10-20% of the work inside that rung. The other 80%+ is the physical and regulatory step: GMP manufacturing, process validation, re-running stability on expired lots, pivotal animal efficacy under GLP in usually two species, and a human safety database. This is the geothermal-in-coal-mines counter-example again. Finding the right shelved program is easy (the BARDA/NIAID portfolio is public and short). Finishing the BLA is the bespoke plant. A capitalised buyer does exist: big pharma for the voucher, BARDA/SNS for procurement.
scored.step_up: Unproven right: $0.1-2M as the candidate states it (my estimate; no sourced comps). Proven right: a priority review voucher has historically sold for roughly $80-160M (SIGA's TPOXX material-threat voucher sold for about $80M in 2020; rare pediatric vouchers sold for about $100-158M in 2023-2025, from memory, not re-verified this run). Add any SNS procurement on top (TPOXX contracts were around $600M over years). So the right goes up about 50-150x on approval, but only after the $10-100M+ proving spend. All-in, that is about 2-8x. The voucher's existence is also a sunset risk: the material-threat voucher under FD&C 565A covered approvals before Oct 1, 2023 unless PAHPA reauthorized it. I could not confirm reauthorization status as of Oct 2026.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Cost per proving attempt: the candidate's $10-30M is optimistic. My estimate is $30-150M once you add GMP re-manufacture, pivotal animal studies and a human safety cohort; BARDA-funded animal-rule programs have typically consumed $100M+. Base hit rate: only about 15-20 products have been approved under the Animal Rule since 2002 (from memory). Shelved late-stage programs usually failed for a known scientific, manufacturing or funding reason. My estimate is a 20-40% approval rate from a near-complete package. ML cannot change that much: failure comes from the biology and the manufacturing, not from picking the wrong candidate. And with only tens of candidates, the lever is capped at about 1/0.3, or 3x, and in practice is close to 1x.
scored.data: USAspending, SAM.gov, the BARDA portfolio, clinicaltrials.gov, Drugs@FDA and DHS material threat determinations are all structured and legible. DTIC and the animal-study literature are partly unstructured, but there are few of them (tens of programs, not millions of files). The outcome is already written into legible fields: approval status in Drugs@FDA, trial status on clinicaltrials.gov, and contract termination or option-not-exercised in USAspending. That leaves no edge from reading illegible data.
scored.right_bought: Rights can be bought, from bankruptcy estates, defunct contractors' assignees and university licensors. But sellers are not illiterate about the value. Voucher values are widely publicised, and biodefense business development teams (Emergent, SIGA, Soligenix, Chimerix-style acquirers, royalty funds) watch this small universe closely. A near-complete animal-rule package will not go for $0.1M. Expect a multi-million upfront plus milestones and royalty, or a seller who has already shopped it. A government-funded program may also carry government-purpose license rights, which encumber it.
scored.buyer: Big pharma buys vouchers (historically about $80-160M each). BARDA/SNS buys under Project BioShield procurement contracts. Both are well capitalised, but the SNS budget is about $1B/yr in total and is lumpy and political.
scored.ladder: The ladder runs from in-licensing shelved assets, to running your own development, to GMP manufacturing, to a full MCM company. The ceiling is set by the government MCM budget. Emergent BioSolutions peaked around $1.5-2B in revenue, and SIGA is about $0.1-0.2B in revenue. This is a niche, not a trillion-dollar path.
scored.fatal_flaw: The proving step is a $30-150M+ manufacturing and regulatory build (GMP, animal-rule pivotals, human safety), not a cheap abstracted drill. The work is in finishing the package, not finding the asset. On top of that, the outcome is legible in Drugs@FDA, clinicaltrials.gov and USAspending, and the voucher's eligibility may have sunset (565A, Oct 2023).
scored.one_line_reason: This fails the frame test the same way the geothermal-in-coal-mines idea does: the candidate list is small, public and legible, and the value is created by an expensive, bespoke BLA and GMP effort that ML cannot shrink. The government-capped ladder also limits how big the company can get.

scored.name: DMF Orphan Rescue: pairing dormant API DMFs with abandoned 505(b)(2)s
scored.one_line: Buy dormant Type II DMFs and never-launched 505(b)(2) NDAs whose missing piece was API supply or CMC; pair, file and sell approved differentiated products with exclusivity.
scored.unproven_right: Dormant DMFs and approved/tentative NDAs, $50k-2M.
scored.proving_step: ML cross-matching fee lapses, tentative approvals and exclusivity windows; DMF reactivation plus CMC supplement ($1-5M).
scored.proven_buyer: Eton, Azurity, Exela, Slayback-type acquirers.
scored.public_data: FDA DMF list, GDUFA lists, Drugs@FDA, Orange Book, NDC directory.
scored.frame: The candidate rung is buying a dormant DMF plus a stalled 505(b)(2) NDA, pairing them, and getting a CMC supplement approved. Discovery inside that rung is about 10-20% of the work (my estimate). The rest is physical and regulatory execution: tech transfer to a working API site, registration and validation batches, 6-12 months of stability data, a prior-approval supplement, and often a pre-approval inspection. A Type II DMF is only a file describing one manufacturing site's process. A dormant DMF usually means the site, process or holder has gone away, so 'reactivating' it means rebuilding the supply chain. In Terranox's terms this is the coal-mine geothermal pattern: building the thing is harder than finding it.
scored.step_up: The candidate claims ~10-30x and I could not verify any of it, because the web search budget was used up before a single search ran. My estimate: discontinued or never-launched small NDAs change hands for roughly $0.5-5M; a relaunched niche 505(b)(2) with 3-year exclusivity sells or is valued at roughly $10-50M in Eton/Azurity-type deals. Adding $1-5M+ of CMC spend puts the realised step-up on total cost at about 3-10x. That is not 10^3 and not immediate: the value only arrives after FDA approval of the supplement and a launch, 12-24 months later.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Estimate, no source (search budget exhausted). Each proving attempt costs $1-5M+ (tech transfer, batches, stability, PAS filing fee, consultants) and takes 12-24 months. The base failure mode is not a low hit rate on a hidden signal. It is execution risk (CMC deficiencies, complete response letters, a failed inspection) and commercial risk (a small market, or a generic arriving after the 3-year exclusivity ends). ML matching fee lapses to tentative approvals does nothing to lower tech-transfer or stability costs, so the capex lever is close to 1x, not 10x.
scored.data: The data is public but already legible. FDA publishes the DMF list as a structured spreadsheet with holder, subject, type and an Active/Inactive status field. The GDUFA 'available for reference' list marks Type II DMFs that passed the completeness assessment. The Orange Book has a discontinued-products section and structured exclusivity and patent-expiry fields. Drugs@FDA lists approval status and letters. The outcome (dormant, discontinued, exclusivity window) is written into status fields, which is exactly the failure pattern the rubric warns about. What is missing (why a product stalled, whether the API site still exists) sits in private CMC files, not public data.
scored.right_bought: Yes, NDAs and DMF letters of authorization can be bought or licensed from holders, often small or distressed sponsors. But the sellers are not unable to read the data: they know exactly why their product stalled. Brokers and specialty pharma business-development teams already run this market, so there is no information-asymmetry discount. A DMF bought without the manufacturing site is close to worthless.
scored.buyer: Real, capitalised buyers exist: Eton, Azurity, ANI, Amneal, Exela, Slayback, Harrow and Assertio-type specialty pharma companies, plus royalty and PE funds. They are also the direct competitors, because acquiring and relaunching dormant or discontinued NDAs is already their business model (ANI and Eton in particular).
scored.ladder: There is a moderate ladder: relaunch a product, then build a specialty pharma portfolio, then add your own API and finished-dose manufacturing and a commercial organisation. ANI and Amneal show this can reach multi-billion-dollar scale. It is a crowded, low-margin roll-up path, not a trillion-dollar one.
scored.fatal_flaw: The proving step is CMC and manufacturing execution (tech transfer, stability, FDA supplement review, inspection), not discovery, and the data that would locate targets is already legible in FDA status fields (DMF Active/Inactive, Orange Book discontinued and exclusivity). There is no frame where discovery is 80%+ and no ML hit-rate lever. Incumbents like ANI and Eton already do this deal type.
scored.one_line_reason: Pharma's version of geothermal-in-coal-mines: finding the stalled DMF/NDA pair is easy and already in FDA spreadsheets, while rebuilding the supply chain and getting CMC approval is the real, multi-million-dollar, multi-year work. The step-up is roughly 3-10x and competitors already run this.

scored.name: DormantDossier / UK REACH Dossier Bank: orphaned REACH data ownership
scored.one_line: Buy REACH study data and lead-registrant positions from insolvent or exited registrants; ML matches substances to forced buyers (new registrants, tonnage up-bands, UK REACH 2029-31 deadlines) lacking cheap letters of access; sell LoAs or dossiers.
scored.unproven_right: Data-ownership title to study summaries and reports, €5-20k to low five figures.
scored.proving_step: ML over ECHA dissemination/IUCLID, HSE DUIN lists, insolvency registers and consortium tariffs; chain of title plus committed buyers.
scored.proven_buyer: EU and UK importers/manufacturers, Only Representatives (£20-200k per LoA; Defra est. up to £2bn total).
scored.public_data: ECHA dissemination database, CoRAP/SVHC, Comext, HSE UK REACH lists, BODACC/Insolvenzbekanntmachungen.
scored.frame: The rung is 'own REACH study data or a lead-registrant position, then sell letters of access (LoAs)'. Most of the work inside it is legal and commercial, not discovery. You need chain of title out of insolvency estates, consortium agreements and negotiated cost-sharing under Implementing Regulation (EU) 2016/9. My estimate is that discovery is about 30-40% of the work. The physical step (title transfer and negotiation) is not trivial. There are capitalised buyers: registrants and Only Representatives.
scored.step_up: From memory, not verified this run because the search budget was used up: the candidate assumes title costs €5-20k and an LoA sells for £20-200k. But REACH Art. 27 and Reg 2016/9 require 'fair, transparent and non-discriminatory' cost sharing, which means a pro-rata share of the actual study cost plus a capped admin fee. If talks fail, ECHA can grant 'permission to refer' (Art. 27(6)/30(3)). Under Art. 25(3), anyone may cite study summaries submitted 12 or more years ago for free, and most 2010/2013 dossiers are already past that line. So the LoA price is capped by regulation, not by what the market will pay. My estimate of a realistic step-up is about 2-10x on a portfolio that has to be split across many co-registrants, with no 10^3 jump.
scored.hit_rate_capex: There is no proving step that is expensive and mostly fails. 'Proving' is title diligence (roughly €5-30k of legal work per substance, my estimate) plus finding buyers. ECHA's dissemination portal publishes which substances are registered at which tonnage bands, so buyers can already be identified. My estimate of the base hit rate is that buyers exist for maybe 20-40% of acquired dossiers. That caps any ML lever at about 3-5x, and title risk, not discovery, is what decides each deal.
scored.data: The data is mostly legible. ECHA dissemination lists registrants, tonnage bands, lead registrants and study endpoints in structured form. HSE publishes the UK REACH DUIN and registration lists. Insolvency notices (BODACC, Insolvenzbekanntmachungen, the Gazette) are searchable. The outcome (who needs which data, and by when) is close to a legible field: the deadline lists plus the DUIN holders who lack a full registration. The one hard-to-read part is who actually owns the data inside a consortium, and that is in private contracts, not public data.
scored.right_bought: Partly. Data rights can be bought from liquidators, but they are often shared with, or held through, consortia that have pre-emption or joint-ownership terms. The 12-year free-reference rule (Art. 25(3)) erodes the value of the right over time. Owners such as liquidators can read the data. They simply value it low, correctly, because the cost-sharing rules cap what it can earn.
scored.buyer: UK REACH registrants and Only Representatives facing deadlines in Oct 2029, 2030 and 2031, and EU new entrants or companies moving up a tonnage band. But Defra's proposed Alternative Transitional Registration model (ATRm) is designed to cut how much full hazard data UK registrants must hold. That would shrink much of the roughly £2bn LoA cost Defra estimated. Competitors are well entrenched: consortium managers (ReachCentrum, Penman/Cefic sector groups), REACHLaw, Only-Representative firms and UK data-sharing consortia.
scored.ladder: The ladder is weak: data brokerage, then Only Representative / regulatory consultancy, then perhaps chemical distribution. None of those steps leads to owning a chain worth $1T. Regulatory compliance data is a finite market that expires on a deadline.
scored.fatal_flaw: REACH data sharing is regulated, so the step-up cannot exist. Art. 27 and Implementing Reg 2016/9 force cost-based, pro-rata pricing. ECHA can grant permission to refer when talks fail. Data older than 12 years can be cited free (Art. 25(3)). And Defra's ATRm aims to remove the UK REACH data demand this plan relies on. An orphaned dossier cannot be repriced from €10k to a monopoly LoA.
scored.one_line_reason: The asset is a regulated, cost-capped, time-decaying data right whose demand is legible from public lists, so there is no 10^3 step-up and no real discovery lever.

scored.name: Registro Bank: dormant Brazilian pesticide registrations
scored.one_line: Buy granted-but-uncommercialised Brazilian registros and sell to entrants avoiding the 5-8 year queue.
scored.unproven_right: Granted registros, $100-300k.
scored.proving_step: Validate transferability and demand gaps; signed transfer.
scored.proven_buyer: UPL, Albaugh, Nufarm, Sumitomo, Chinese technical suppliers.
scored.public_data: MAPA AGROFIT, Diário Oficial, ANVISA, IBAMA.
scored.frame: The rung is owning a granted Brazilian pesticide registro and transferring it. It is discrete and sellable, because transfer of titularidade at MAPA is a recognised process. But discovery is not 80% of the work. Every registro is already listed by name, holder, active ingredient and crops in AGROFIT and the Diário Oficial. Most of the work is deal-making: negotiating with the holder, legal checks on transferability, data-protection and technical-source (equivalence) issues, and finding a buyer. My estimate is that discovery is about 20-30% of the work. The physical step (paperwork) is cheap, but the work is mostly brokerage, not finding things.
scored.step_up: From the candidate's own framing, the purchase price is $100-300k and the resale is perhaps $0.5-1.5M. That is roughly 3-10x, on my estimate (unverified; my search budget was used up before any search ran). The ceiling is set by the cost of a fresh registration: dossier, studies and fees, which I estimate at about $0.5-2M, plus the time value of the queue. Law 14.785/2023 sets about 2 years as the statutory target for a decision, which shrinks the queue premium over time. Nothing here goes from near zero to 10^3x. The asset already has a known floor price.
scored.hit_rate_capex: There is no expensive proving step that mostly fails. The 'proving step' is a legal and commercial check plus a signed transfer. My estimate is a hit rate of 30-60% for deals that close once a dormant registro is found and its holder is willing. Cost per attempt is legal diligence of roughly $10-50k (my estimate). A low-hit-rate step where ML would cut capex 10x does not exist. The lever is capped at about 2-3x.
scored.data: The data is public and mostly legible. AGROFIT is a structured searchable database (product, holder, registration number, status). The Diário Oficial publishes grants and transfers. The one partly hidden signal is whether a registro is actually commercialised. IBAMA's annual sales reports are aggregated by active ingredient, so per-registro sales cannot be seen directly. But that signal can be inferred cheaply: check whether the product's label or brand is in distributor catalogues, or simply ask the holder. The asset itself, the registro, is written down in a legible field, so the ML edge is small. Holders are agrochemical firms that know exactly what they own. They are not owners who cannot read the data. Specialised regulatory consultancies already broker these deals (for example AllierBrasil, Regulatory-type firms, and Agrolink-network brokers; named from memory, not verified).
scored.right_bought: Yes, registros are bought and transferred by negotiated deal. But sellers are sophisticated regulatory-literate firms (often Chinese or Indian generic houses and local formulators), so there is no information discount like the $1/ha land the uranium play buys. The discount comes only from a holder needing liquidity or being a failed entrant.
scored.buyer: The buyers are capitalised: UPL, Albaugh, Nufarm, Sumitomo/Ourofino, Rainbow, Tide, CropChem, Chinese technical suppliers moving downstream, and local formulators. They buy registrations and whole portfolios, usually in M&A bundles rather than one registro at a time.
scored.ladder: There is a real ladder: registration bank, then own-brand registrant that sources the technical active ingredient from China, then formulation, then a distribution and retail network in Brazil, the world's largest pesticide market at about $15-20B/yr. Albaugh and UPL show how big a generic agchem company can get (multi-billion), which would be the end point. But the trillion-dollar ceiling is not plausible: it is a commodity-margin business.
scored.fatal_flaw: The asset and its status are already written in a legible public registry (AGROFIT/DOU), and the holders know what they own. So nothing is hidden for ML to find, the step-up is only about 3-10x and capped by the cost of a fresh registration, and Law 14.785/2023's roughly 2-year target erodes the queue premium the thesis depends on. This is regulatory arbitrage and brokerage, not discovery.
scored.one_line_reason: Legible registry, sophisticated sellers, a step-up of about 3-10x shrinking under the 2023 law, and no low-hit-rate proving step: brokerage, not Terranox-style discovery.

scored.name: QPL Revival: dormant Qualified Products List slots
scored.one_line: Buy exiting manufacturers listed on mil-spec QPL/QML slots with few qualified sources; requalify; sell to component consolidators.
scored.unproven_right: QPL/QML listing plus product line.
scored.proving_step: Requalification test lot at contract labs.
scored.proven_buyer: Amphenol, TE, Glenair, defense PE.
scored.public_data: ASSIST QPL/QML, DLA Land and Maritime notices, DIBBS/FPDS.
scored.frame: The rung would be: buy an exiting QPL/QML-listed manufacturer, requalify it, and sell the qualified line. Discovery is roughly 5-15% of the work inside that rung (my estimate). Finding a QPL slot with only one or two qualified sources takes a simple query against ASSIST QPL, which lists every qualified source by part number and plant. The rest of the work is operational: keep or move a mil-spec production line, keep certified processes and staff, pass DLA Land and Maritime qualification audits, build and test a qualification lot, then keep the qualification alive with periodic retention testing. QPL qualification belongs to a specific manufacturing site, so moving the line forces requalification. The physical step is the whole business, not a trivial one. This is the geothermal-in-coal-mines counter-example: finding the asset is easy and running it is hard.
scored.step_up: Estimate only; no deal data was retrieved. A distressed or exiting small mil-spec component maker probably sells for about 0.3-1x revenue, or 3-6x EBITDA. Qualified niche defense component lines go to strategic buyers (Amphenol, TE, TransDigm, HEICO, Arcline-backed platforms) for about 2-5x revenue, or 10-20x EBITDA. On a successful requalification that is roughly a 3-10x step-up. The candidate's claimed 10-50x would only hold if the slot were bought for near zero, which is unlikely when the seller has revenue and inventory. The jump does not come from a proving event like a drill hit. It is earned by restarting production and winning DIBBS awards over quarters to years.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Estimate only; no lab quotes were retrieved. A qualification test lot under a MIL-PRF connector or component spec probably costs $50k-$500k at a contract lab, plus several months of a running compliant line and an audit. If the product is built to the spec's drawings and processes, base pass rates are high, probably 70-90% after one or two iterations, because the spec tells you exactly what to build. At that pass rate the ceiling on any hit-rate lever is 1/0.8, about 1.25x, nowhere near 10x. Little of the cost is a gamble that ML could make cheaper; the cost is production capex and compliance work.
scored.data: The outcome is already written into legible public fields. ASSIST QPL/QML lists each qualified manufacturer, plant (CAGE) and part number with qualification status. DLA Land and Maritime publishes notices when sources are removed or their qualification lapses. DIBBS shows open solicitations, award prices and how many bidders each one gets. FPDS shows contract history. Anyone can see which slots have one or no active source with simple queries and no ML. This is the same failure mode as earlier hunts: the regulator records the answer in a status field. DMSMS and obsolescence firms already mine this data (Rochester Electronics for authorised semiconductor continuation, Lansdale, Source Engineering, plus aftermarket and PE roll-ups). The owners of exiting manufacturers are sophisticated about their own QPL value and sell through M&A brokers. They are not owners who cannot read their own data.
scored.right_bought: The right can be bought, but only by acquiring the operating company or its product line, assets, drawings and plant. A QPL listing cannot be transferred on its own: it is tied to the qualified facility and processes, so a new owner at a new site must requalify. The sellers are informed (founder-owned defense suppliers using brokers), so there is no read-the-data discount. The purchase price reflects the known QPL scarcity.
scored.buyer: Real, capitalised buyers exist and pay up for qualified sole-source mil-spec lines: Amphenol (Military and Aerospace), TE Connectivity, Glenair (private), TransDigm and HEICO (whose models depend on sole-source aerospace and defense parts), and defense and industrial PE firms such as Arcline and Arlington. This is the strongest part of the candidate.
scored.ladder: There is a ladder above it: run component lines, then consolidate many sole-source slots into a TransDigm-style aftermarket platform with pricing power, then move into assemblies, harnesses and subsystems. TransDigm, at about $80B market cap, shows the top of the ladder is worth a lot. But the ladder is a PE roll-up and operations ladder, not a discovery ladder, and the top is already occupied by TransDigm, HEICO, Amphenol and Arcline.
scored.fatal_flaw: There is no illegible discovery problem. The ASSIST QPL source counts and DLA notices already say which slots are thin, and the value is realised through mil-spec manufacturing and qualification operations, not through finding something. This is a known PE and TransDigm roll-up play run by informed buyers and informed sellers.
scored.one_line_reason: The buyer is real but the frame fails. Discovery is a simple lookup in ASSIST QPL, while making and qualifying the product is most of the work. Requalification usually passes, so ML has little to raise. The step-up is roughly 3-10x and comes from operations, not a 10^3x jump on a hit.

scored.one_line: Buy small vendors holding national cooperative purchasing awards; route ML-detected agency demand; sell to category strategics.
scored.unproven_right: Cooperative contract award with large ceiling.
scored.proving_step: ML over minutes and budgets; first $1-5M of sales.
scored.proven_buyer: Category strategics, public-sector distribution PE.
scored.public_data: Sourcewell/OMNIA/NASPO/TIPS lists, municipal minutes, procurement portals.
scored.frame: The rung is "own a small vendor that holds a cooperative contract and push it to its first $1-5M of sales." Discovery (finding agencies that are about to buy) is maybe 15-25% of the work inside that rung (my estimate). Most of the work is selling (agency relationships, demos, quotes, piggyback paperwork) and fulfilling (making, shipping, installing and servicing the product). That physical step is the business itself, not a trivial or abstracted one. This is the coal-mine-geothermal pattern: knowing which agency will buy is easier than winning and delivering the order. A capitalised buyer exists (category strategics, public-sector-focused PE), but it pays for revenue and EBITDA, not for a proved right.
scored.step_up: No live searches ran (the shared per-turn search budget was used up), so every number here is my estimate from general knowledge. Lower-middle-market vendors with under $1M EBITDA usually sell for about 3-5x EBITDA. Bigger platforms that public-sector PE buys trade at about 8-12x EBITDA. That is roughly 2-3x of multiple arbitrage, plus whatever revenue growth the operator adds. Taking a $0.5M-revenue vendor to $5M of contract revenue is about 10x revenue, but that growth is paid for with sales spend and working capital, not unlocked by one discovery event. The award on its own is worth close to nothing, because it is non-exclusive. Sourcewell, OMNIA and TIPS award several vendors per category, and the award is usually not assignable without the cooperative's consent. So there is no step from $1 to $10,000 at a single moment. The pitched "10-50x" looks inflated; about 2-5x on capital is more realistic.
scored.hit_rate_capex: These are my estimates, not sourced. Many awarded co-op vendors book little or nothing through their contract; I would guess a large share sit near zero. But the cost per attempt here is the cost of buying a company (about $0.5-5M) plus 1-3 years of sales effort, not a cheap drill. ML can make outreach better, but the base rate is limited by product fit, price and incumbent relationships, not by not knowing who needs what. A plausible gain is 1.5-2x sales efficiency, not 10x lower capex.
scored.data: This is from my own knowledge, with no live verification. Co-op award lists (Sourcewell, OMNIA, NASPO ValuePoint, TIPS, BuyBoard) are public and legible, and some co-ops publish spend or usage reports. Municipal minutes and budgets are scattered and unstructured, but several funded companies already mine them: Starbridge (minutes and budgets for public-sector sales), GovSpend, Deltek GovWin and Pavilion (a search engine for co-op contracts). The outcome (which agency bought what from whom) increasingly shows up in purchase-order and spend data that GovSpend and others aggregate. As for the right itself: you buy a whole operating company at an operating-business price, not a mispriced right. Sellers know their own revenue, so there is no information gap like a landowner who cannot read assessment files. The award is not a separable asset, and it is re-bid every 4-5 years or so.
scored.right_bought: A small private vendor that holds one or more national cooperative purchasing awards. It is bought as an operating company at roughly 3-5x EBITDA or about 0.5-1x revenue (my estimate). The award itself is not assignable without the co-op's consent and is non-exclusive.
scored.buyer: Category strategics (for example, public-sector-focused distributors in furniture, playground equipment, fleet, technology and facilities) and public-sector PE roll-ups. They pay on EBITDA multiples (about 8-12x for scaled platforms, my estimate), not for a proved right.
scored.ladder: There is a moderate ladder: a single-category vendor, then a multi-category public-sector distributor, then a procurement platform, possibly a co-op administrator (an OMNIA- or Sourcewell-like aggregator earning admin fees), then manufacturing. That is a real path to a large public-sector distribution company, but it is a classic PE roll-up path with heavy competition, not a discovery-led one.
scored.fatal_flaw: The proving step is sales and fulfilment execution, not discovery. The co-op award is non-exclusive, effectively not assignable, re-bid every few years and close to worthless on its own. Value comes only from selling and delivering product, at operating-business multiples. There is no rung where discovery is 80% or more of the work, no step-up of 10^3 or more, and the demand-signal data is already mined by Starbridge, GovSpend and GovWin.
scored.one_line_reason: This is a PE roll-up with ML-assisted lead generation, not a discovery play. Value comes from selling and delivering product (about 2-5x through multiple arbitrage and growth), the award itself is non-exclusive and near-worthless, and incumbents already mine the minutes and budgets data.

scored.step_up: My estimate, unverified because the search budget ran out: dormant STCs from defunct holders change hands for roughly $5k-$50k, which matches the candidate's own figure. Live STCs with demand and a complete data package sell as product-line deals, usually $100k to a few $M for niche GA or avionics STCs. Large freighter-conversion STC programs are worth tens of $M or more, but those are not orphaned and their value comes from the conversion capability, not the certificate. That gives a realistic step-up of about 3-30x on hits, not 100-1000x. A step-up only comes once the data package and production capability have been rebuilt, not the moment a match is found.
scored.hit_rate_capex: My estimate, with no sourced figure: the "proving" step is ML matching plus a desk check that the data package is complete. That costs roughly $1k-10k per candidate. There is no expensive, mostly-failing physical test like an exploratory drill. The step that is expensive and fails a lot is rebuilding the package and getting it re-approved, roughly $100k-$1M+ per STC, and ML does not reduce that cost. A cheap screen can't produce a 10x capex reduction, because the screen was never the bottleneck.
scored.data: The STC record is already legible. FAA DRS lists each STC's number, holder, approved models/eligibility and status, and the registry master file and AD database are structured and easy to download. So the "which aircraft does this fit" answer sits in a legible field, the pattern the rubric says kills the ML edge. Demand signals (ADs, mandates, obsolescence) are also published in structured form. Only the dissolution and successor-of-interest chain (state corporate records, PACER) is messy and scattered, and that tells you who to buy from, not whether the asset is worth anything. The asset itself, the design data package, is private and often lost. The right can be bought cheaply from estates or trustees, so that half of C4 holds.
scored.right_bought: The STC plus its data package is bought from a defunct holder, a bankruptcy trustee or an estate, by FAA transfer letter, for roughly $5-50k (estimate). The right is bought, not claimed first-come. But a certificate whose data package is missing has little value, and the package is often what's missing.
scored.buyer: Operators facing an AD or mandate, MROs, conversion houses (AEI, Mammoth, Precision), avionics dealers. Several of them are themselves STC developers who can engineer a fresh STC rather than buy a revived orphan. That caps what they will pay at about the cost of a new STC, which is typically $250k-$2M for mid-complexity mods (estimate).
scored.ladder: Orphan STC acquisition, then kit manufacture (PMA), then an installation/MRO network, then an in-house STC design office (ODA), then full conversion programs (e.g. passenger-to-freighter conversions). The ladder exists, but it climbs into a mature, low-margin aftermarket full of entrenched players. It does not lead to a trillion-dollar chain. The orphan rung serves a shrinking population of aging aircraft.
scored.fatal_flaw: The value is in the private engineering data package and in production and continued-airworthiness capability, not in the public certificate. Any buyer can also design a new STC for a capped cost. So the ML discovery step is cheap, legible and not the bottleneck, and the certificate does not jump in value on a match.
scored.one_line_reason: Discovery is a small share of the work. The STC eligibility data is already legible in FAA DRS. Reviving an STC is mostly engineering and production work, so there is no 10^3x step-up on a match and no 10x hit-rate lever.

scored.name: Slot Futures
scored.one_line: Win cheap slots and gates at airports before Level 3 coordination and sell slot pairs to network carriers.
scored.unproven_right: Historic slots or long gate leases.
scored.proving_step: Predict coordination; operate under 80/20 rule (heavy).
scored.proven_buyer: IAG, Delta, Lufthansa.
scored.public_data: IATA WSG list, coordinator declarations, NOTAMs, master plans, schedules.
scored.frame: No rung exists where discovery is 80%+ of the work. Predicting which airport goes Level 3 is maybe 5-10% of the work (my estimate). The other 90%+ is physically flying aircraft at 80% utilisation for the whole season under use-it-or-lose-it so the series earns historic precedence. That means holding an air operator certificate and running an airline. It is the coal-mine-geothermal counter-example: the bespoke physical step dwarfs the finding.
scored.step_up: Unproven: slots at Level 1/2 airports, and new-entrant slots at Level 3 airports, are allocated free under EU Reg 95/93 and IATA WSG. Proven: Heathrow daily slot pairs have sold for about $60-75M (from memory: Oman Air paid about $75M to Air France-KLM in 2016; similar prices since). Gatwick and other congested pairs sell for roughly $1-15M (my estimate). So the paper step-up is very large, on the order of >=10^3x over a near-zero cost basis. But the cost basis is not near zero. It includes a full season of operating losses on the route, which I estimate at $5-30M per daily pair. Net that out and the real step-up is about 1-10x, and only at the very few airports that become Heathrow-like.
scored.hit_rate_capex: The base hit rate on predicting Level 3 designation is fairly high and not where the money is. Designations creep up slowly and are flagged years ahead in master plans, capacity studies and the published WSG list, so ML gives little lift; the lever is capped near 1/base rate, maybe 2-3x (my estimate). The cost of a proving attempt is a season of flying, roughly $5-30M per slot series per airport (my estimate, not sourced). ML does not reduce that cost.
scored.data: The IATA WSG airport level list, coordinator declarations and capacity declarations are public, legible and already summarise the outcome (the airport's level and its declared capacity). The answer is written into the status field. Schedules (OAG/Cirium) are legible commercial data that every airline network planner already uses. Master plans are the only illegible part, and they are weak signals.
scored.right_bought: No. The right cannot be bought cheaply from owners who cannot read the data. Under EU Reg 95/93, UK and most WSG regimes, slots are allocated free by the coordinator, only to air carriers, and earn grandfather rights only through use. Before coordination there is no tradable slot at all. Secondary trading and leasing exists only at Level 3 airports and is priced by sophisticated airlines. Long gate leases at US airports are held by airlines under use agreements, mostly preferential or common-use with recapture clauses. A non-airline cannot hold them speculatively.
scored.buyer: Real and well capitalised: network carriers (IAG/BA, Delta, Lufthansa, United, Qatar) do pay tens of millions for a Heathrow pair. The buyer is fine; supplying the rung is the problem.
scored.ladder: Slot portfolio, then a niche airline, then a network carrier or airport ownership. Airlines are a low-margin, capital-heavy industry, so climbing the ladder means becoming an airline, which is a poor trillion-dollar path. Airport concession ownership is the more valuable rung, but it is bid competitively by infrastructure funds.
scored.fatal_flaw: Only an air carrier can hold slots, and a slot becomes valuable only after a full season flown at 80% use. The proving step is running an airline, not a cheap, abstracted drill. The outcome (the airport's coordination level) is also already published in the IATA WSG list.
scored.one_line_reason: The buyer and the headline price are real (about $75M for a Heathrow pair), but the right is allocated free and only to airlines, and it is proven only by flying for a season under use-it-or-lose-it. Discovery is a tiny share of the work and ML gives no capex lever.
