scored.name: Bankruptcy-Estate EV Pack Arbitrage
scored.one_line: Buy condition-unknown packs from bankrupt EV/e-bus makers; ML ranks health; certify for second life.
scored.unproven_right: Bulk battery lots priced as disposal liability.
scored.proving_step: ML on dockets and recalls; diagnostic and UL 1974 assessment.
scored.proven_buyer: Redwood Energy, B2U, Moment, Smartville, recyclers.
scored.public_data: Claims-agent dockets, PACER, NHTSA, Copart/IAA, EPA certificates.
scored.frame: The rung is buying lots of packs from a bankruptcy estate and selling certified second-life packs. Discovery is about 20-30% of the work inside that rung (my estimate). Most of the work is physical: hauling hazmat (UN3480 Class 9), storing it, pulling the modules apart or repacking them, getting BMS access when the maker is gone, fire insurance, and UL 1974 assessment followed by UL 9540/9540A integration. That is a bespoke physical step, much like the geothermal-in-coal-mines counter-example. It is not abstracted like a contract drill.
scored.step_up: About 2-5x at best (my estimate). Unproven lots sell for roughly -$5 to +$15/kWh. LFP has a net disposal cost of about $1-4/kg, and NMC is worth a little for its black mass. Certified second-life packs sell for about $40-100/kWh. That ceiling is being squeezed by new LFP stationary cells at about $50-60/kWh and new containerised BESS at about $100-150/kWh (2025 figures). These numbers are from memory, not checked this run. The candidate's own ~3-10x figure is optimistic. Nowhere near 10^3.
scored.hit_rate_capex: The base hit rate is high, not low. Most fleet packs from failed OEMs are young, at roughly 80-95% state of health (SOH), so about 60-80% of a lot is usable (my estimate). Each proving attempt is cheap: a BMS readout or a capacity and impedance test costs about $100-1,000 per pack (my estimate). Formal UL 1974 evaluation costs more, but it is paid once per pack design, not per pack. With a 1/base-hit-rate cap of about 1.3-1.7x, ML cannot cut capex 10x.
scored.data: The dockets (Proterra 2023 Ch.11, Lion Electric 2024-25 CCAA, Arrival, Lordstown, Fisker, Nikola) are public but low-signal. Health is not in the dockets. It sits in the BMS, which a direct readout or a test reveals cheaply, so the outcome is effectively legible to anyone holding the pack. NHTSA recalls are already structured fields. Copart/IAA listings show damage codes. The estates sell through professional liquidators (Hilco, Tiger, Gordon Brothers) to informed bidders: recyclers and second-life firms already bid on these lots. Rights can be bought, but there is no reliable illegibility discount. Fisker's estate, for example, sold to an informed buyer. Proterra's battery business went to Volvo for about $210M as a going concern, not as distressed scrap (from memory).
scored.right_bought: Title to physical lots of packs or vehicles, bought through 363 sales or liquidator auctions in Chapter 11/7 or CCAA proceedings. The lots are bought, not claimed first-come, and they come with hazmat liability.
scored.buyer: B2U Storage Solutions, Moment Energy, Smartville, Element Energy and Connected Energy for second life, and Redwood Materials (Redwood Energy), Li-Cycle (now owned by Glencore) and Ascend Elements as recyclers. Most of these are thinly capitalised startups, and several of them buy the same lots directly.
scored.ladder: Climb: second-life aggregation, then BESS integration, then owning grid storage projects (IPP), then recycling/black mass, then cell supply. The ladder is real, but every rung is capital-heavy and has low margins, and the second-life rung itself is being undercut by cheap new LFP.
scored.fatal_flaw: The proving step is cheap, passes most of the time, and gives a direct answer (a BMS/SOH readout), so ML adds almost nothing. The step-up is only about 2-5x and is capped by falling new LFP prices. Most of the work is physical hazmat handling and repackaging, not discovery.
scored.one_line_reason: Fails the Terranox test: the physical repack/certification step dominates, the hit rate is high and testing cheap so ML has no lever, the step-up is about 2-5x rather than 10^4, and informed liquidators and buyers already price these lots.

scored.name: Relocation Credit Bank: billboard cap-and-replace credits
scored.one_line: Buy forgotten nonconforming structures, dead permits and relocation rights from small sign owners in cap-and-replace jurisdictions; prove they still count as credits; sell bundles to majors converting to digital.
scored.unproven_right: Old structures and permit claims, $1-20k.
scored.proving_step: ML over ordinances, minutes and condemnation files; credit recognition filing.
scored.proven_buyer: Lamar, Outfront, Clear Channel.
scored.public_data: Municode/Legistar, DOT condemnation files, local permit histories, URA claims.
scored.frame: The rung is 'own a recognised removal/relocation credit in a cap-and-replace jurisdiction and sell it to a digital converter.' Inside it, maybe 50-60% of the work is discovery (finding surviving rights in ordinances, minutes and condemnation files). The rest is legal: a recognition filing, often a fight with zoning staff, and transferability problems. Many ordinances tie credits to the operator who takes down its own faces, so a third party's banked credit may be unsaleable or need a council vote. The physical step is trivial, but the legal proving step is bespoke for each jurisdiction. My estimate, not sourced.
scored.step_up: Candidate claims ~10-100x ($1-20k forgotten claim to a credit a major would pay for). Estimate only, since no search ran: in big metros a digital-conversion credit or a permitted static location might be worth ~$50k-$500k to a major. A truly dead permit is worth ~$0 because it is legally extinguished, not undervalued. Realistic step-up on the rare hit: ~10-30x, not 10^3. No sourced price for an unproven versus proven credit was found.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Unsourced estimates. Cost per proving attempt is low: ~$2-20k of land-use attorney time plus a filing fee. The base hit rate on 'forgotten' credits is probably low (<10%), because most nonconforming-sign statutes end the right after 6-24 months of discontinuance or abandonment. ML could help triage, but with each attempt already cheap, a 10x capex cut saves little in absolute dollars. The lever is weak.
scored.data: Mostly legible. Under the Highway Beautification Act, state DOTs keep outdoor-advertising permit inventories with status fields (active, revoked, nonconforming). Cities keep sign permit registries. That means the outcome is largely already written in a legible field. Municode ordinances are searchable text. Legistar minutes and condemnation/URA files are less legible, so there is some edge there. On whether the right can be bought: small sign owners are lobbied all the time by majors' real-estate teams and specialist billboard brokers, so they know what a live permit is worth. The truly forgotten rights are mostly legally dead.
scored.right_bought: In principle yes: structures, ground leases and permits are bought from small operators and landowners, typically at ~8-15x cash flow for live structures (rough recollection of industry multiples, not sourced here). The cheap ($1-20k) end is cheap because the right is lapsed or not transferable. That is not information asymmetry.
scored.buyer: A three-firm oligopoly (Lamar, Outfront, Clear Channel Outdoor), plus regional players. They have in-house real-estate and permitting teams who already roll up small operators and manage credit banks with cities. That leaves a monopsony buyer with strong bargaining power, and the market is fragmented by jurisdiction.
scored.ladder: Credits, then owning static structures, then digital conversion, then becoming a regional outdoor operator. The top of the ladder is the US out-of-home market, roughly $9-10B a year (estimate). Lamar's market cap is ~$10-13B (estimate). That is a real ladder, but it is capped well below trillion-dollar scale, and regulation shrinks inventory over time.
scored.fatal_flaw: The 'forgotten' rights mostly do not legally exist. Nonconforming sign rights end by statute after discontinuance or abandonment. Live permits already show in legible DOT and city permit status fields. Credits are often tied to the removing operator and cannot be transferred. The only buyers are three majors who already run in-house acquisition and credit-banking teams. So there is no illegible-data edge and no 10^3 step-up.
scored.one_line_reason: The physical step is trivial and there is a capitalised buyer. But the proving step is a cheap legal filing on rights that usually lapse by statute, the outcome sits in legible permit registries, the step-up is ~10-30x at best, and the buyer is a sophisticated oligopoly that already does this.

scored.name: Dormant home health and hospice CON agencies
scored.one_line: Acquire dormant CON-protected agencies whose authorization survives CHOW; sell to post-acute consolidators.
scored.unproven_right: Shell agencies, $50-300k.
scored.proving_step: ML over CON files and surveys; CHOW.
scored.proven_buyer: Enhabit, Amedisys/Optum, AccentCare, Gentiva, PE roll-ups.
scored.public_data: CMS POS/Care Compare, HCRIS, CON archives, survey reports.
scored.frame: The rung is buying a CON-protected home health or hospice agency and transferring it through a change of ownership (CHOW). Discovery is maybe 30-40% of that work (my estimate). Finding a dormant agency is easy, because state CON registries and the CMS Provider of Services (POS) file list every licensed and certified agency with its status. Most of the effort is regulatory and operational: state CHOW approval, CMS 855A enrollment, accreditation or survey, and keeping a minimum census and staff so the license stays active. Like the coal-mine geothermal case, the bespoke step is harder than the finding.
scored.step_up: My estimate is about 1.5-4x, not 10^3. In CON states the license is already priced as scarce. The candidate says shells cost $50-300k. Agencies sold to consolidators with real census are valued on EBITDA (roughly 5-12x for home health and hospice, from memory of broker reports by firms like VERTESS and Mertz Taggart). A pure shell with no census sells for a license premium, which I estimate at a few hundred thousand to about $1M in high-barrier CON states. The asset is never near zero: sellers know what a CON is worth, and the candidate's own 10-30x figure looks too high.
scored.hit_rate_capex: There is no expensive, mostly-failing proving attempt. The CHOW either clears or doesn't on a known checklist, which I estimate at more than 70% when the right is still valid. Cost per attempt is legal and consulting fees plus carrying the agency, roughly $50-150k (my estimate). The lever (1/base hit rate) is therefore at most about 1.5x. ML has nothing to raise.
scored.data: The outcome is already in legible public fields, which is the pattern the hunt says kills the ML edge. The CMS POS file has certification and termination status. Care Compare and PECOS show active enrollment. Claims volume and HCRIS cost reports show whether an agency is operating and its census. State CON registries list license holders. Incumbent brokers and buyers screen these tables as routine. Survey reports are partly unstructured, but they bear on quality, not on whether the right exists.
scored.right_bought: Yes, the right is bought, not claimed free. But the owners are healthcare operators who know what their CON is worth, so there is no information gap to buy into. Rules also cap the value of a dormant agency. CMS deactivates billing privileges after 12 consecutive months with no claims (42 CFR 424.540). The 36-month rule (42 CFR 424.550(b)), which covers home health agencies and was extended to hospices from 2024, means a majority ownership change within 36 months forces new enrollment and survey. Many state CONs lapse if services aren't provided. These are from memory and not re-verified this run.
scored.buyer: The buyers are capitalised: Enhabit, Amedisys (now part of Optum/UnitedHealth), AccentCare, Gentiva, BrightSpring, Addus and PE roll-ups. They buy census and EBITDA, not empty licenses, and Optum in particular faces antitrust and CON scrutiny.
scored.ladder: There is a moderate ladder: license, then operating agency, then a regional platform, then a value-based post-acute network. The upper rungs are labour-intensive care delivery with thin margins and heavy reimbursement risk (Medicare home health rate cuts, hospice fraud enforcement). A large consolidator could be built, but this is not a path to a trillion dollars.
scored.fatal_flaw: Dormancy destroys the right. CMS deactivates Medicare billing after 12 months with no claims, the 36-month rule blocks quick flips of home health and hospice enrollments, and many state CONs lapse if unused. So a truly dormant agency has little transferable value. An agency that is still active is listed in legible CMS and state fields and priced by brokers. There is neither a 10^3 step-up nor an ML discovery edge.
scored.one_line_reason: This is a regulatory and operational CHOW business with outcomes already listed in public CMS and state status fields. Its step-up is only about 1.5-4x, and the dormancy that would make shells cheap is what voids the right.

scored.name: Register-Ready: historic tax credit eligibility
scored.one_line: Buy unlisted older buildings, prove NPS eligibility, sell HTC-eligible buildings.
scored.unproven_right: Building priced as tear-down.
scored.proving_step: ML on SHPO surveys and Sanborn maps; National Register nomination and Part 1.
scored.proven_buyer: Rehab developers and HTC investors.
scored.public_data: NPS NRHP/NPGallery, SHPO surveys, Sanborn maps, TPS data.
scored.frame: Rung is: own a building priced as a tear-down, prove it is eligible for the National Register (NPS Part 1 or a nomination), then sell it as an HTC-eligible building. The rung exists, but discovery is not 80%+ of the value. The federal HTC is 20% of qualified rehabilitation expenditures (IRC s.47; since TCJA 2017 it is paid out over 5 years), so the credit only exists once someone spends heavily on a certified rehab (NPS Parts 2 and 3). That makes the bespoke rehab the physical step and most of the work, the same failure as the geothermal-in-coal-mines counter-example. My estimate is that eligibility work is about 5-10% of a typical HTC deal's effort and cost.
scored.step_up: Candidate's own figure is about 1.2-2x on acquisition price. My estimate, with no fresh source because the search budget was used up: the credit is roughly 20% of rehab spend (plus 10-25% state credits in about 35 states), and its present value after syndication pricing (about $0.85-0.95 per credit dollar) goes mostly to whoever does the rehab. A buyer will pay a premium on the land and shell only up to part of that value. For example, a $1M shell with $5M of QREs carries about $1M of federal credit, with NPV around $0.8M. If the developer captures half of that, the shell goes from $1M to about $1.4M. That is roughly 1.4x, not 10^3-10^4x.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Proving cost, my estimate: a Part 1 for a building inside an already listed district is about $2k-10k of consultant time. An individual National Register nomination is about $5k-25k and takes 6-18 months through the SHPO and state review board. Base hit rate is high, not low: buildings that are candidates for Part 1 are pre-screened with the SHPO, and I believe NPS approves the large majority of Part 1s (estimate over 85-90%, not verified this run). The proving step is cheap and usually succeeds, so ML has nothing to multiply: 1/base hit rate is about 1.1x, nowhere near 10x.
scored.data: Sanborn maps (Library of Congress, scanned), SHPO architectural survey forms (often paper or PDF, uneven by state) and NPGallery nominations are public and partly illegible, so the illegible-data condition holds in part. But the outcome is often already summarised in a legible field: NRHP listing status, and contributing versus non-contributing status within listed districts, sit in SHPO GIS and inventory databases in many states (for example Virginia's VCRIS, Ohio's OHI, California's BERD). Being 50+ years old is just a year-built field in county assessor data. The remaining signal is integrity and significance judgement, which a SHPO reviewer decides subjectively, so ML cannot certify it.
scored.right_bought: Yes, the right is bought: you buy fee title to the building on the open market. But there is little mispricing to exploit. Sellers and their brokers in older downtowns routinely market 'historic tax credit eligible' properties, and contributing status in a district is a public lookup. Buildings that are truly priced as tear-downs usually have integrity problems that are also why they fail Part 1, or that make rehab uneconomic. Partial credit only.
scored.buyer: Capitalised buyers do exist: HTC rehab developers (for example Historic Restoration Inc., Brinshore), HTC equity investors and syndicators (big banks such as US Bancorp Community Development Corp, plus Enterprise and other syndicators), and opportunity-zone funds that layer HTC with LIHTC. But these buyers pay mainly for the rehab economics, and many of them source deals themselves with in-house historic consultants.
scored.ladder: The ladder is plausible: eligibility, then Parts 2 and 3 certified rehab, then credit syndication, then a rehab developer and operator, then a large owner of historic adaptive-reuse buildings. But each rung above the first is ordinary capital-heavy real estate development with thin, competitive margins. It is not a path where discovery compounds into a trillion-dollar company, and the market is small: NPS certifies on the order of 1,000-1,300 completed projects a year, about $6-7B in QREs (estimate based on recent NPS annual reports).
scored.fatal_flaw: The HTC is a percentage of rehab spend, not a property of the building, so the value is created by the bespoke physical rehab rather than by discovering eligibility. Proving eligibility is cheap, usually succeeds, and is often already recorded in SHPO inventory fields, so the step-up is about 1.2-2x and ML has no hit-rate lever.
scored.one_line_reason: Fails the Terranox test like geothermal-in-coal-mines: the rehab is the work and the source of the credit, eligibility proving is cheap and high-hit-rate and often already a legible SHPO field, and the step-up is under 2x.

scored.name: Tidefield: geoduck-grade private tidelands
scored.one_line: Buy overlooked private Puget Sound tidelands; ML over 1890s-1910s tideland records and substrate/eelgrass/PSP data finds farmable parcels; survey and pre-application; sell or lease to geoduck growers.
scored.unproven_right: Fee title to private intertidal parcels.
scored.proving_step: Substrate cores, eelgrass delineation, SSDP/NWP-48 pre-application ($10-30k).
scored.proven_buyer: Taylor Shellfish, Seattle Shellfish, Chelsea Farms.
scored.public_data: WA DNR tideland sale records, county assessor data, WDFW/DOH classifications, SVMP eelgrass, Ecology Coastal Atlas, NOAA bathymetry.
scored.frame: The rung is a permitted or permit-ready private intertidal parcel leased or sold to a geoduck grower. Inside that rung, discovery is only about 20-30% of the work (my estimate). Finding sandy or muddy low-intertidal ground with no eelgrass, in an Approved DOH growing area, is fairly easy: growers already do it from boats and county maps. Most of the work is permits: a county Shoreline Substantial Development or Conditional Use permit, Corps NWP-48 or an individual permit, then Shoreline Hearings Board appeals and organised opposition from neighbours (Coalition to Protect Puget Sound Habitat and similar groups). That is the coal-mine-geothermal counter-example: the bespoke step, here a contested permit, is harder than the find.
scored.step_up: My estimates; web search budget was exhausted, so none of this is verified. Unproven private tidelands, often attached to an upland lot, sell or are assessed for very little, roughly $1k-$20k per acre. Growers usually do not buy the land. They lease it, paying the owner a royalty of about 10-20% of harvest or a flat rent. Farmed geoduck grosses roughly $100k-$300k+ per acre over a 5-7 year cycle. So a permitted, leasable parcel is worth roughly $20k-$60k per acre to the owner on a royalty NPV basis. That is about 3-10x over unproven value, not 10^3-10^4. Neighbour litigation can wipe out the uplift.
scored.hit_rate_capex: My estimates, unverified. The proving cost per attempt is about $10-30k for cores and eelgrass delineation, as the candidate says. Add permitting and legal costs of $50k-$300k+ and 1-5 years where a permit is contested; Pierce and Thurston county geoduck SSDPs have repeatedly gone to appeal. The physical suitability hit rate on pre-screened parcels is probably already high, about 30-60%, because substrate, elevation and DOH classification are easy to screen. The low-success part is political or permit risk, and ML cannot raise that. The lever is capped at about 2-3x, not 10x.
scored.data: The 1890s-1910s DNR tideland sale records are illegible, but they mostly establish ownership, which county assessor GIS already makes legible. Suitability is largely written into legible public fields: DOH Shellfish Growing Area classifications (Approved, Conditionally Approved, Restricted, Prohibited) are a published GIS layer. SVMP and county eelgrass maps, the Ecology Coastal Atlas and NOAA bathymetry are all already structured. So the outcome is largely summarised in legible fields, which is the known killer of the ML edge. The biggest unknown, permit outcome, is not in any dataset.
scored.right_bought: Yes, fee title or a lease can be bought from upland owners. About 60-70% of Puget Sound tidelands are private, sold off by the state from 1889 to 1971 (from memory, not verified). But the owners are waterfront homeowners. Many will not sell or lease because they oppose aquaculture, and their neighbours fight permits. Growers such as Taylor Shellfish already run direct-mail and outreach campaigns to these owners, so there is little information asymmetry left to arbitrage.
scored.buyer: Taylor Shellfish, Seattle Shellfish, Chelsea Farms and a handful of smaller growers. It is a small, concentrated buyer pool. They are capitalised, but they prefer royalty leases to buying land, and they do their own siting. The WA farmed geoduck market is small, probably under $100M a year farmgate (my estimate). Export demand depends on China, which has imposed tariffs and import bans in the past.
scored.ladder: Land, then permitting, then seed and hatchery, then grow-out with 5-7 year cycles, then harvest, processing and live export to Asia. Real rungs exist, but the total addressable market is small (a niche shellfish species in one sound, plus a little in BC), so the ladder tops out as a mid-sized shellfish company, nowhere near trillion-dollar scale. Moving into oysters and clams adds some breadth, but those have the same permit bottleneck.
scored.fatal_flaw: The proving step is a contested, multi-year shoreline and Corps permit fight, not a discovery problem. Physical suitability is already legible in DOH, eelgrass and bathymetry layers, and growers already know where the good ground is. ML improves the cheap part, while the expensive, failing part (permits and neighbour litigation) is political. This is the same structure as the geothermal-in-coal-mines counter-example.
scored.one_line_reason: The bottleneck is permitting, not discovery. The step-up is about 3-10x (my estimate), suitability is already in legible public GIS fields, and the market is small.

scored.name: Concesiona: idle Chilean salmon concessions
scored.one_line: Buy idle or caducity-threatened concessions; ML proves biological viability; survey and file operating plans; sell to majors blocked by the moratorium.
scored.unproven_right: Existing concessions, $100-500k.
scored.proving_step: INFA/CPS survey and production project filing ($50-200k).
scored.proven_buyer: AquaChile, Mowi Chile, Cermaq, Blumar, Australis.
scored.public_data: SERNAPESCA INFA and ACS data, SUBPESCA registry, SHOA, IFOP HAB, Copernicus, SEIA.
scored.frame: The rung is 'idle concession turned into a fileable, operable concession'. Very little of the work in that rung is discovery. My estimate is under 20%. Most of the work is regulatory: SEIA/RCA environmental approval, the INFA aerobic-status requirement, the sanitary rotation rules of the ACS (neighbourhood) system, stocking-density (PRS/SIEP) allowances, ECMPO indigenous-claim overlaps and caducity litigation. Whether a site is biologically viable is mostly known already, from the concession's own production history and its ACS. The buyer is real and has money (AquaChile, Mowi, Cermaq, Blumar, Australis), but those buyers are paying for regulatory capacity, not for a discovery.
scored.step_up: No live data; the search budget was exhausted, so these are my estimates. An idle concession of roughly 5-10 ha in Los Lagos or Aysén trades for about US$0.3-2M. A permitted, producing concession with stocking allowance is valued at about US$2-10M in M&A, and much of that value sits in the attached production allowance, not the concession title. My estimate of the step-up is about 3-10x, and only when regulatory and ECMPO risk clears. The candidate's own 5-30x figure looks optimistic. Nothing near 10^3.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Estimate, not sourced. The proving step costs about US$50-200k for an INFA/CPS survey plus a production-project filing, as the candidate states. It does not fail mostly for biological reasons. When it fails, the cause is permitting delay, ECMPO claims, an anaerobic INFA in a saturated ACS, or a density cap. ML cannot change those outcomes. The ML lever is roughly 1-2x, not 10x.
scored.data: The data is public and mostly legible. SERNAPESCA publishes INFA results as an aerobic/anaerobic status per concession. That status is the outcome written into a field, which is exactly the failure mode the rubric warns about. The SUBPESCA registry lists every concession with its holder, status and ACS, and ACS production and density data are published every period. Copernicus, SHOA and IFOP HAB data are useful but are also used by the majors' own environmental teams. The universe is small (on the order of ~1,300-1,400 salmon concessions in the south, my estimate), and every major tracks all of it. Nothing about it is illegible to incumbents.
scored.right_bought: The rights can be bought. Concessions are transferable, and their holders are small operators, heirs or companies in distress. But the sellers can read the same registry and INFA data as everyone else, so they cannot be priced below fair value for lack of information. The ones at risk of caducity are discounted for legal reasons that are already visible to all parties. Magallanes concessions inside national-park waters are exposed to political relocation risk.
scored.buyer: The salmon majors (AquaChile/Agrosuper, Mowi Chile, Cermaq/Mitsubishi, Blumar, Australis, Multi X, Salmones Camanchaca). They do buy concessions. They also run their own concession-acquisition and regulatory teams, so a middleman adds little.
scored.ladder: There is a ladder: concession, then smolt, then grow-out, then processing, then export. But every rung above the concession is capital-heavy biology and operations, with sea lice, algal blooms and SRS disease. The majors already own the whole chain end to end. Climbing is possible in principle, but it means competing as just another salmon farmer in a sector in political retreat (moratorium, the Lafkenche/ECMPO law, park-relocation pressure).
scored.fatal_flaw: A concession's value comes from regulation and politics (permits, density allowances, ECMPO, the moratorium), not from discovery. Its biological viability is already written into public legible fields (INFA aerobic/anaerobic status, ACS production history) that every major already tracks, across a universe of only about a thousand sites. So there is no illegible signal for ML to extract and no 10^3 step-up.
scored.one_line_reason: This is regulatory arbitrage on a small, transparent universe of concessions. The outcome sits in INFA status fields, the step-up is about 3-10x, and permits rather than discovery set the value, so it fails C1, C3 and C4.

scored.name: AshSeam / AshPond Critical: coal ash ponds traced to REE/Ge/Ga-rich seams
scored.one_line: Join EIA-923/FERC 423 mine-to-plant shipments to COALQUAL seam chemistry and posted CCR documents to rank closing ash impoundments for REE, Ga, Ge, Sc; take ash under beneficiation/offtake agreements at negative cost; sample and sell to processors.
scored.unproven_right: Ash removal/offtake rights from utilities paying $10-40/t to close.
scored.proving_step: Vibracore/auger sampling, ICP-MS and acid-leach test ($20-300k per pond).
scored.proven_buyer: REE separators and DOE-funded coal-byproduct projects (Ramaco partners, MP feed, Energy Fuels, Ucore), cement makers for residue.
scored.public_data: EIA-923, FERC Form 423, USGS COALQUAL, utility CCR compliance PDFs, NETL REE sampling, MSHA IDs.
scored.rough_step_up: ~10-100x in dollars, >10^3 on near-zero basis; processing economics unproven.
scored.frame: The rung would be "own pond ash with a proven assay and sell it as REE/Ge/Ga feed". It is not on the hard-exclusion list, because this is sampling an industrial waste pile, not exploring the ground. But it is close to landfill mining, which was killed earlier. My estimate is that discovery is about 10-20% of the work. The rest is extraction: acid leach or roasting, getting the REE out of a glassy aluminosilicate matrix, separation, and managing the residue. That processing is the unsolved, capex-heavy part. There is no mature buyer who pays for an assay result alone. This is the same shape as the geothermal-in-coal-mines counter-example: the bespoke plant is harder than finding the right pond.
scored.step_up: There is no observed market price for a proven ash right, so these are my estimates. Unproven: ash in place, worth roughly -$10 to -$40/t to the utility (its closure cost). Separately, well-characterised fly ash that can be harvested sells to cement at about $30-60/t (estimate; there is a fly-ash shortage). Proven REE-grade ash: total REE of about 300-600 ppm (Taggart et al. 2016, Duke: Appalachian average ~591 mg/kg, Illinois ~403, PRB ~337) works out to about $20-100/t of contained oxide at basket prices (estimate). Recoverable value is maybe 30-60% of that after leach yield. So a hit moves the right from roughly -$20/t to maybe +$10-40/t of net value, and only if a processor exists to take it. That is a 2-5x swing in dollars, not 10^3. The ">10^3 on a near-zero basis" in the pitch is an artefact of dividing by zero, not a price anyone pays.
scored.hit_rate_capex: The base hit rate is high, not low. Most Appalachian and Illinois Basin ash already beats DOE's 300 ppm REE screening threshold (Taggart et al. 2016, from memory), and you can largely predict it from basin and seam using COALQUAL alone. Cost per proving attempt is $20-300k per pond (the candidate's figure; my estimate is $20-80k for coring plus ICP-MS, with leach tests at the high end). That is cheap next to the processing capex, which is likely $100M+ per plant (estimate). If the hit rate is about 50-70%, the ML lever is capped at about 1.5-2x, nowhere near 10x. Ge and Ga hits are rarer in US coals, so the lever there is bigger, but the deposits are also much smaller. Note: the search budget ran out before any search returned, so the numbers here come from memory of published literature, not fresh searches.
scored.data: The data really is public and partly illegible: EIA-923 and FERC 423 mine-to-plant shipments, USGS COALQUAL seam chemistry, and utility CCR compliance PDFs. But the CCR PDFs report groundwater chemistry and structural stability, not the REE content of the ash. And COALQUAL plus basin averages already gives a legible first-order answer, which Duke/NETL/USGS have published at national scale. So the ML edge over a basin-level lookup table is probably small. This is similar to the interconnection-queue finding, where a lookup table matched ML.
scored.right_bought: Utilities closing ponds under the CCR rule do sign removal and beneficiation contracts. But established ash marketers and beneficiators already compete for those contracts for cement use: SEFA Group (STAR units), Eco Material Technologies, Charah Solutions, Boral/Eco legacy, Waste Management/EnviroSource. Removal also carries liability and permitting obligations. So the right is bought, but it is contested, and the price is set by cement value rather than ignorance of REE content. Utilities and DOE already know their ash may hold REE, so there is little to arbitrage.
scored.buyer: The capitalised buyer is weak or largely absent. US REE separators (MP Materials, Energy Fuels, Ucore) run on concentrated mineral feed (bastnaesite, monazite) and do not buy 300-600 ppm ash at scale. Coal-byproduct REE efforts are mostly DOE/NETL-funded pilots (e.g., the West Virginia University AMD work, Ramaco Brook Mine, which is coal rather than ash, and university pilots like Rice's flash Joule heating). Cement makers will pay for clean residue, but that is a commodity price with no step-up.
scored.ladder: There is a real ladder: ash rights, then assay and concentrate, then leach/MREO production, then separation, then metals and magnets, with residue to cement. It is policy-favoured (DOE critical minerals, IRA 45X). But every rung above the first is a hard chemical-processing business, and climbing it is the whole game rather than a later extension.
scored.fatal_flaw: Discovery is not the bottleneck. Ash REE grades are low, well-mapped and mostly above threshold already, and the value depends on unproven, capex-heavy extraction. So no capitalised buyer pays a step-up for a proven assay. This is the geothermal-in-coal-mines counter-example again.
scored.one_line_reason: Grades are widely known and high-hit-rate, and the hard part is processing, not finding. A proven ash pond is worth only a few x more than an unproven one, to a buyer who barely exists.
sources: Taggart, Hower, Dwyer, Hsu-Kim (2016), 'Trends in the Rare Earth Element Content of U.S.-Based Coal Combustion Fly Ashes', Environmental Science & Technology 50(11) (cited from memory; the search budget ran out before any search returned)
US DOE/NETL Rare Earth Elements from Coal and Coal Byproducts program, 300 ppm screening threshold (from memory)
USGS COALQUAL database (from memory)
EPA CCR Rule 40 CFR 257 public posting requirements (from memory)
Industry knowledge: SEFA Group, Eco Material Technologies, Charah Solutions ash beneficiation contracts (from memory, not verified this turn)

scored.name: RadiumRescue: legacy Ra-226 as Ac-225 feedstock
scored.one_line: Take title to disused Ra-226 (medical needles, dial stocks, static eliminators, lightning rods, standards) from holders counting it a disposal liability; ML over NRC ADAMS and agreement-state files locates and grades it; gamma assay and licensed transfer; supply Ac-225 producers.
scored.unproven_right: Title to uncharacterised radium items acquired free or with the holder paying.
scored.proving_step: Entity resolution across scanned inspection and transfer records; gamma spectroscopy and OSRP-style pickup.
scored.proven_buyer: NorthStar/QSA Global, Actineer (CNL+ITM), Niowave, Eckert & Ziegler, BWXT Medical, DOE Isotope Program; TAT pharma behind them.
scored.public_data: NRC ADAMS, agreement-state licence files, CRCPD SCATR, NARM registries, FUSRAP files, IAEA Ra-226 initiative, OSRP reports, hospital histories.
scored.rough_step_up: Effectively >10^3 from negative basis; finite global pool (tens-hundreds of grams).
scored.frame: The rung would be: acquire legacy Ra-226 items, characterise them, and hand them to an Ac-225 target maker. Inside that rung, discovery is roughly 10-20% of the work (my estimate). Most of the cost and risk is physical and regulatory: an NRC or agreement-state licence to possess byproduct/NARM material, Type A/B shipping, opening sealed sources, chemical recovery of Ra from Pt/Au needle capsules and luminous paint, and purification to target grade. Those steps cost far more than finding the item. This is the same shape as the coal-mine geothermal counter-example. The buyer exists (Ac-225 producers) but buys purified, characterised Ra-226, not raw needles.
scored.step_up: Unproven: zero or negative basis. Holders pay for disposal; my estimate is $10k-$50k+ per source for licensed disposal, and OSRP/CRCPD SCATR pick up for free or subsidised. Proven: a few mg of purified Ra-226 target material. Producers do value it highly, but I could not verify a price (search budget exhausted). My estimate is low thousands to tens of thousands of dollars per mg once purified, and much less as raw sealed sources that still need recovery chemistry. Going from a negative basis to positive is a large multiple on paper. But most of that value is created by the recovery and purification work, not by discovery, so I scored it 3.
scored.hit_rate_capex: I could not verify numbers; web search was unavailable (the shared budget was used up) and all figures below are my estimates. Finding licensed radium is not a low-hit-rate step. Holders are licensees whose possession is already recorded. Base hit rate per inspected record is probably high (>30%, estimate). Cost per attempt is a records review plus a site visit and a gamma survey, likely $1k-$10k (estimate). Because 1/base hit rate is small, ML can cut capex by about 2-3x at most, not 10x. The expensive failure mode is chemistry and regulation, and ML does not touch that.
scored.data: The data is public but mostly legible already. Since the 2005 Energy Policy Act, NARM radium falls under NRC and agreement-state licensing. Licences list the radionuclide and possession limits, so the outcome sits in structured licence fields. CRCPD SCATR and DOE/LANL OSRP keep inventories and collect actively. The IAEA's Ra-226 initiative already matches donor countries' disused sources to producers. Unlicensed historical items (dials, lightning rods) are scattered and poorly recorded; that is real illegibility, but it is also the low-grade, high-cost-to-recover tail. Title is cheap or free, but it is not bought from owners who cannot read the data: holders know exactly what they have and that it is a liability.
scored.right_bought: Title to disused radium sources: acquired free, or with the holder paying a disposal fee. Possession needs an NRC or agreement-state radioactive materials licence. Competing free takeback exists (OSRP, SCATR, IAEA initiative), so this is not an information-asymmetry purchase.
scored.buyer: Ac-225 makers using the Ra-226 route: Niowave (photonuclear), NorthStar, BWXT Medical, Eckert & Ziegler, Actineer (CNL+ITM). The DOE Isotope Program also supplies Ra-226 itself. Total demand is a few grams to tens of grams of Ra-226, a tiny, concentrated buyer set. Several of them use Th-229 generators or Th-232 spallation and do not need Ra at all.
scored.ladder: Rungs above: Ra-226 purification and target fabrication, then Ac-225 production (cyclotron or electron linac), then radiopharmaceutical supply. Each rung up is capital-intensive (accelerators, hot cells, GMP), and the Ac-225 rung already has well-funded competitors. Ac-225 is a real growth market, but the radium-feedstock rung is a small, finite pool (tens to hundreds of grams worldwide, my estimate) and does not compound.
scored.fatal_flaw: Discovery is not the bottleneck. Legacy radium is already recorded in licence files and is actively collected for free by OSRP/SCATR and the IAEA initiative. The value comes from licensed recovery chemistry and purification, which are hard, bespoke physical steps (the coal-mine-geothermal pattern). And the total feedstock pool is tiny and finite.
scored.one_line_reason: The value is made in licensed recovery and purification, not in discovery. The holdings are already legible in licence records and collected free by government programmes, and the finite gram-scale pool does not support a compounding Terranox-style rung.

scored.name: Stranded Enriched Isotopes
scored.one_line: Find forgotten gram-scale enriched stable isotopes (Yb-176, Ni-64, Zn-68, Mo-100, Ge-76, Ca-48) in labs and retired experiments via papers and DOE distribution history; ICP-MS certify; sell to radiopharma precursor buyers.
scored.unproven_right: Title to unlabeled vials bought nominally.
scored.proving_step: ICP-MS/TIMS assay, optional repurification.
scored.proven_buyer: Eckert & Ziegler, ITM, SHINE, NorthStar, Curium, ASP Isotopes, cyclotron radiopharmacies, physics experiments.
scored.public_data: NIDC/ORNL calutron history, Web of Science/arXiv methods, NSF/DOE awards, EHS inventories, theses.
scored.frame: Rung: find, acquire and certify stranded vials of enriched stable isotope and resell them. Inside that rung, finding the vials is maybe 60-70% of the work (my estimate). The assay itself is cheap and outsourced. The rest is not trivial: institutional property and surplus transfer, hazmat and export paperwork, repurification, and building the provenance and quality paperwork a buyer needs. The best-paying buyers are radiopharma GMP users of Yb-176 for Lu-177 and Ni-64 for Cu-64. They need full chain of custody, a certificate of analysis from a qualified supplier and a supplier listed in their regulatory filings. A vial of unknown history cannot enter that supply chain. Only research and physics users would buy it, at a discount and in small amounts. So the capitalised buyer exists, but mostly does not buy this rung's output.
scored.step_up: Estimates; no source pulled because the web search budget was used up. Proven enriched material at list price: Ni-64 roughly $20-50k/g; Yb-176 (high enrichment) roughly $10-30k/g; Ca-48 roughly $100-250k/g; Mo-100 roughly $1-3k/g; Ge-76 roughly $50-100/g at kg scale. The unproven vial is not really near zero, though. Most of this material came from DOE/NIDC with a certificate of analysis and a label, and the institution holding it knows what it is or can find out cheaply. Ungraded material sold for non-GMP research would likely fetch 20-50% of list. So the real step-up is about 3-10x over what a knowing owner would accept, not 10^3x. A 10^2-10^3x step only appears for vials that are truly unidentified and that the owner would otherwise pay to dispose of, which is a rare subset.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Estimates; not verified by search. One proving attempt (outsourced ICP-MS or MC-ICP-MS isotope ratio) costs about $100-1,000 per sample, while the material is worth $10k+ per gram. The proving step is cheap, not expensive and mostly failing. Most of the cost is outreach and acquisition (legal and EHS transfer, shipping hazmat or controlled items), and ML does not shrink that. The base hit rate on vials you actually locate is probably high (they mostly turn out to be the isotope the label says). So the lever, capped at 1/hit-rate, is about 1-2x, not 10x.
scored.data: Papers and theses do reveal who bought which enriched isotope (methods sections cite ORNL/NIDC supply), and they are unstructured. But NIDC/DOE distribution and lease records are not public at the level of individual customers. Lab environmental-health-and-safety (EHS) inventories are internal or behind FOIA. The answer is already written in a legible place: the vial label and its NIDC certificate of analysis. DOE also historically leased some stable isotopes (calutron inventory, Ge, Ca-48 for experiments), so those are not sellable by the holder at all. The owners are isotope-literate scientists, not counterparties who cannot read the data. Buying title cheaply runs into university and federal property disposal rules (surplus, sometimes a DOE right of return). The edge from reading illegible data is weak.
scored.right_bought: Partly. Universities can transfer surplus material, but it goes through property and EHS offices. They often will not sell high-value material for a nominal price once they know its value, and DOE-leased material is not theirs to sell. Small rights bought one at a time, with heavy friction per transaction.
scored.buyer: Research and physics users (accelerator targets, double-beta-decay R&D) at a discount. GMP radiopharma buyers who would pay a premium (ITM, Eckert & Ziegler, SHINE, NorthStar, Curium) source qualified, documented supply from NIDC, Isoflex, Urenco, JSC Isotope or ASP Isotopes, and will not take material of unknown provenance. Their annual need for Yb-176 (on the order of tens of kg) also dwarfs any stranded gram-scale stock.
scored.ladder: In theory: scavenging, then repurification and recycling of irradiated target material, then enrichment capacity (laser or centrifuge, as ASP Isotopes and Urenco do), then precursor and isotope supply to radiopharma. But scavenging builds no enrichment capability or edge. The credible ladder actually starts at target recycling (recovering Yb-176 and Ni-64 from spent targets under contract), which is a service to incumbents and a separate business. The rung is finite and does not lead naturally to the rungs above it.
scored.fatal_flaw: The supply is finite and small, owners know what they hold (labelled vials with NIDC certificates, often DOE-leased), and the high-value buyers need GMP provenance that recovered vials cannot provide. Discovery is neither hard nor where the value sits. The real constraints are title, chain of custody and quantity, and ML does not move those.
scored.one_line_reason: Cheap assay, owners who already know what they have, GMP buyers who refuse material without documented history, and gram-scale finite supply: there is no 10^3x hidden step-up and no 10x hit-rate lever.

scored.name: Restart Option Co: shut reactors in early decommissioning
scored.one_line: Buy or option shut reactors in SAFSTOR/early DECON with intact major components; ML over decommissioning filings proves restartability; sell to hyperscalers and utilities. Rescores nuclear site banking.
scored.unproven_right: Ownership/option on a plant valued near zero net of trust.
scored.proving_step: Records-based restartability assessment; buyer does ~$1-2B restart.
scored.proven_buyer: Microsoft, Google, Amazon, Meta, Constellation, NextEra, Holtec, Vistra.
scored.public_data: NRC ADAMS decommissioning dockets, ISO interconnection records, PUC proceedings, EIA-860.
scored.rough_step_up: 10^3x+ on paper; fewer than ~5 assets, so weak C3.
scored.frame: The rung is "own or option a shut reactor and prove it can be restarted." Records-based proving is perhaps 20-30% of what it takes to get that rung to a buyer. Most of the work is licensing (re-entering operating status under 10 CFR 50, getting exemptions, re-establishing the operating license basis), re-hiring and training licensed operators, fuel procurement, and refurbishing steam generators and other large components. That costs about $1.5-2B (estimate, based on Palisades and Crane), and the buyer does it, but in practice it IS the proving step. A paper restartability study does not hold value on its own. A buyer pays only once the NRC path and the component condition have been physically checked. So discovery is well under 80% of this rung, and the physical step is not trivial. This is the geothermal-in-coal-mines failure pattern: finding the plant is easy, and bringing it back is the hard part.
scored.step_up: From memory, because no searches were available: Holtec bought Palisades in 2022 for a nominal price, with the plant valued near zero or negative once the roughly $550M decommissioning trust was netted against liabilities. Restarting it took about $2B, backed by a $1.52B DOE loan plus state and USDA money. Crane/TMI-1 cost Constellation about $1.6B to restart, backed by Microsoft's 20-year PPA and a roughly $1B DOE loan (2025). Duane Arnold is being restarted by NextEra with a Google PPA (announced Oct 2025, target around 2029). A restarted ~800 MWe unit with a hyperscaler PPA is plausibly worth $2-5B in equity value (estimate). Going from about $0 net to billions is a large multiple on paper (more than 100x), but only after $1.5-2B of physical capex. The step-up is not immediate when a record review comes back positive.
scored.hit_rate_capex: From memory and estimates; the search budget was exhausted. There are about 3 viable candidates (Palisades, Crane, Duane Arnold) and all three are already taken by Holtec, Constellation and NextEra. Nearly every other shut US unit (Indian Point, Pilgrim, Vermont Yankee, Oyster Creek, SONGS, Fort Calhoun, Kewaunee, Zion, Crystal River) is in active DECON. Their reactor vessels and internals are segmented, or their licenses are effectively surrendered, so the remaining hit rate is near 0. A proving attempt (engineering condition assessment plus NRC pre-application) costs perhaps $5-30M (estimate). No large population of mostly-failing shots exists for ML to improve, so the lever is about 1x.
scored.data: The outcome is already written in legible public records. NRC ADAMS PSDARs, Decommissioning Trust Fund reports, and license amendment and component-removal notifications state outright whether the vessel, steam generators and turbine have been removed or segmented. Industry press and DOE reports tracking restart candidates have published lists, and 3-4 people could make the list by hand in a day. The owners (Holtec, EnergySolutions, NorthStar, Constellation, NextEra) are the most sophisticated readers of these records anywhere, and in several cases they are also the buyers. There is no cheap right to buy from someone who cannot read the data. Owners know exactly what restart optionality is worth after Palisades.
scored.right_bought: In principle, ownership or an option bought from a decommissioning owner, usually transferred with the trust fund. In practice the few viable plants were captured by sophisticated owners in 2022-2025. The rest are physically dismantled, and Holtec has said, for example, that Indian Point cannot be restarted. There is no information asymmetry to buy against.
scored.buyer: Hyperscalers (Microsoft, Google, Amazon, Meta) buy through PPAs. Operators that buy or restart plants include Constellation, NextEra, Holtec and Vistra. The buyers are well capitalised, but they deal directly with the owners.
scored.ladder: The ladder is real: restart, then uprate and operate, then new reactors at the same sites (Palisades SMR-300 plans), then a fleet operator. Holtec is the template. But the first rung is billions of dollars of operator work, not a discovery rung, so the climb never gets started cheaply.
scored.fatal_flaw: No illegible-discovery frame exists. The candidate set is about 3-5 plants, already identified and mostly captured by Holtec, Constellation and NextEra. Restartability is written into NRC decommissioning filings (component removal status). The real proving step is a $1.5-2B licensing and refurbishment effort, not a records analysis. ML adds no hit-rate lever and buys no right at a discount.
scored.one_line_reason: This fails the same way geothermal-in-coal-mines does: finding the 3 restartable reactors is trivial and already done by incumbents, and restarting them takes $1.5-2B of physical and licensing work, so there is no 95%-discovery rung to win.

scored.name: Starter Rights: phage-resistant wild fermentation microbes
scored.one_line: Sign exclusive commercial rights to farms', dairies' and fermenters' house cultures where ML on public food metagenomes, CRISPR arrays and phage receptor loci predicts strains resisting the phages that crash industrial starters; prove with one phage challenge and fermentation, sell to the culture oligopoly.
scored.unproven_right: Exclusive commercial-use and benefit-sharing agreement over one producer's cultures, low thousands plus royalty.
scored.proving_step: Isolate, sequence, phage challenge panel and bench fermentation; standard dairy lab work.
scored.proven_buyer: Novonesis (Chr. Hansen), dsm-firmenich, Lallemand, IFF Danisco, Sacco.
scored.public_data: SRA/MGnify fermented-food metagenomes, CRISPRCasdb, INPHARED phage genomes, dairy phage depositions.
scored.frame: The rung would be: hold the right to a house culture and prove it resists phages. Discovery (picking which producer's cultures) is maybe 40-50% of the work. The rest is wet-lab isolation, sequencing, a phage panel and a bench fermentation, followed by long buyer qualification. The buyer wants a strain that resists phages AND acidifies, makes texture and flavor, and scales, so a phage challenge is not the full proving step. Scale-up and regulatory work (QPS/GRAS dossier, Nagoya compliance) sit inside the rung. That puts discovery below 80% (my estimate).
scored.step_up: The claimed $5k right to a $5-50M licence is not supported by any public deal. Real benchmark: Chr. Hansen paid EUR 73M for Valio's culture business in 2016. That included more than 3,000 dairy cultures, LGG probiotic IP and a manufacturing plant, so it works out to under ~EUR 24k per strain even before taking out the plant and LGG. The DIAL strain collection was also bought in bulk (price not disclosed). No disclosed licence for a single phage-resistant wild strain was found. My estimate for a proven, distinctive strain is $50k-$1M in one-off or royalty value, about 10-100x on a $5k right, and most proven strains would be worth less, nearer 3-10x.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Proving cost per strain is my estimate: about $5-30k for isolation, WGS, a phage panel and bench fermentation, before scale-up. The base hit rate for the phage-resistance trait itself is not low. Incumbents create phage-resistant strains on demand: they challenge their own strains with phage and select BIMs that gain CRISPR spacers, the routine Danisco/Barrangou method, with one new spacer being the most common outcome (Deveau/Barrangou 2008, 30 BIMs analysed). So a resistant strain is not rare and has no big discovery premium. The real bottleneck is technological fit plus a novel phage-resistance mechanism, and nobody has published a base rate for that. Because resistance can be made in-house, the ML lever is well under 10x (my estimate: ~2x).
scored.data: Partial fit. Public metagenomes (SRA/MGnify), CRISPRCasdb and INPHARED are large and somewhat illegible. But incumbents are the world's best readers of exactly this data: Danisco/IFF found CRISPR immunity in S. thermophilus, and Chr. Hansen holds tens of thousands of strains (about 40k, from memory) plus phage-resistance patents. Metagenomes rarely tie back to a specific producer's culture that can be bought, and they do not show phenotypes such as acidification or flavor. Rights can be bought cheaply from farms. However, Nagoya ABS rules require provider-country prior informed consent and mutually agreed terms for genetic resources, and some countries (for example India) restrict LAB strains. That adds friction and may let the state claim benefit share. The outcome is not written into any legible public field, which is the one plus.
scored.right_bought: Exclusive commercial-use and benefit-sharing agreement with a farm, dairy or fermenter over its house culture. Low thousands of dollars plus a royalty (candidate's figure, plausible). It is subject to Nagoya-protocol PIC/MAT where the provider country requires it. Exclusivity is weak: the producer keeps the physical culture, and anyone who gets a sample can re-isolate it.
scored.buyer: The culture oligopoly: Novonesis (Chr. Hansen + Novozymes), IFF (Danisco), dsm-firmenich, Lallemand, Sacco. These are concentrated, capitalised buyers. But they buy collections in bulk at low per-strain prices (Valio, DIAL) and make phage resistance internally, so they have little need to pay a premium for single strains.
scored.ladder: There are rungs above: own strain IP, then make cultures (fermentation, freeze-drying, blending), then sell direct to dairies, then the dairy products themselves. That is a real ladder, but the cultures market is only about $1.5-2B a year and dominated by Novonesis, and the climb requires manufacturing that incumbents already do at scale. There is no clear trillion-dollar path.
scored.fatal_flaw: Phage resistance is not a scarce trait you have to find. Incumbents routinely create it from their own strains by selecting BIMs and CRISPR-immunising them with phage (Danisco/IFF's own invention), and they buy whole strain collections for well under ~EUR 24k per strain (Valio: EUR 73M for 3,000+ cultures plus a plant). So a proven wild strain gets no 10^3-10^4 step-up and the discovery lever is small.
scored.one_line_reason: Cheap rights and an oligopoly buyer exist. But the buyer can manufacture phage resistance itself, buys strains in bulk for tens of thousands of euros each at most, and wet-lab work plus technological-fit validation dominate the rung, so the step-up is about 10x, not 10^4.

scored.name: Orphan PVP Certificate Roll-up
scored.one_line: Buy in-force US PVP certificates and breeding archives from defunct small seed companies; ML over scanned exhibits and genotype panels finds certificates protecting valuable traits or lines majors use as parents; sell or license proven certificates.
scored.unproven_right: In-force PVP certificates and archives, ~$10-100k each.
scored.proving_step: Seed-stock phenotype/genotype validation and SNP comparison for essential derivation or trait value, ~$5-20k per variety.
scored.proven_buyer: Major seed companies needing FTO or parental lines; PE-backed seed consolidators.
scored.public_data: USDA AMS PVP database and certificate PDFs, Federal Register, state seed certification, university trials, Panzea/HapMap.
scored.frame: Rung: own an orphan in-force PVP certificate, show by genotype that a major's line derives from it, then sell or license it. Discovery (screening certificates and SNP matching) is maybe 20-30% of the work (my estimate). Most of the work is the physical and legal step: getting seed of the accused line, proving essential derivation in court, and suing or negotiating. That is a lawsuit, not a cheap drill. The PVP Office does not enforce; the owner must sue (UPOV/USDA enforcement slides). So this is not a rung where discovery is 80%+.
scored.step_up: No market prices found for PVP certificates. The best data point: Cornell hedonic study puts the price premium from a PVP certificate on NY soybean seed at about 2.3% (0.7 cents/lb), which says certificates carry little standalone value. The one big US germplasm award (Pioneer v. Holden, $46.7M, 1993-94) was won on trade secret law, not PVP or essential derivation. A certificate bought for $10-100k (candidate's estimate) that turns into a rare settlement might reach 10-30x. That is a litigation lottery, not an immediate market re-pricing. Typical outcome is about 1x or less, because the clock keeps running down the 20-year term.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Base hit rate: unknown; my estimate is well under 1% of orphan certificates protecting germplasm a major uses in a way that infringes. The candidate's $5-20k per variety proving cost is inflated: a SNP chip genotype costs about $20-100 per sample (my estimate). Proving is already cheap, so ML has little capex to cut. The real cost is litigation, roughly $1-5M per case (my estimate), and ML does not reduce that. Lever about 1-2x, not 10x.
scored.data: The data is public and only partly illegible. The USDA AMS PVP database (active and expired certificates, searchable by owner) has legible status, owner and expiry fields, though PVPO disclaims accuracy of status dates. Certificate exhibits are scanned PDFs, and NCRPIS publishes genotype data for ex-PVP lines. The answer (which major's line derives from yours) is not in any public field, which is good. But it is also unknowable without the major's proprietary seed and pedigree, which only come out in discovery during a lawsuit. Rights can be bought cheaply from defunct companies or bankruptcy trustees (plausible, unverified). Incumbents already compare germplasm by genotype routinely.
scored.right_bought: Yes in principle: in-force certificates can be assigned and bought from defunct small seed companies or their estates, probably cheaply (candidate says $10-100k; no transaction data found). But the right is weak. Under 7 USC 2544 the breeders' exemption lets anyone use a protected variety to breed and sell new varieties. Protection against essentially derived varieties exists only for post-1994 certificates and has barely been tested in US courts. Majors protect their inbreds, hybrids and traits with utility patents, which have no such exemption. And within 20 years the variety goes public free via NPGS/NCRPIS.
scored.buyer: Majors (Corteva, Bayer, Syngenta, BASF) and PE-backed seed consolidators. They would pay mainly to settle or clear freedom to operate, not to buy an asset at a market price. Ex-PVP corn inbreds are already available free from USDA, which caps what anyone will pay for old germplasm.
scored.ladder: Weak: orphan certificate roll-up, then germplasm library, then licensing parental lines, then an independent seed or breeding company. A seed company is a real but modest business against a concentrated four-major market. A trillion-dollar path is implausible, and the starting rung is enforcement, not ownership of a productive asset.
scored.fatal_flaw: US PVP certificates are weak, time-limited rights: the breeders' exemption allows derivative breeding, US case law on essentially derived varieties is thin, and certificates expire into free public access. Majors protect valuable germplasm with utility patents and trade secrets instead. So a 'proven' certificate is a speculative lawsuit, not an asset re-priced by a capitalised buyer, and the expensive step is litigation, which ML does not shrink.
scored.one_line_reason: A patent-troll economy on a weak right: proving by genotype is already cheap, the value only shows up through costly litigation, and certificates show a ~2% premium and expire into free USDA access.

scored.name: Bud-Sport Hunter: orchard mutation discovery
scored.one_line: Pay growers small blanket fees for rights to naturally mutated limbs; ML on aerial imagery and colour/phenology anomalies finds them; grafting and genotyping prove new clones that club-variety managers and nurseries buy.
scored.unproven_right: Contractual rights to bud sports found in commercial orchards, ~$1-5k per orchard.
scored.proving_step: Graft the limb, 2-3 years of fruiting evaluation and a genetic stability check.
scored.proven_buyer: Stemilt, Washington Fruit, Zespri-style programmes, PVM, nurseries, wine clone nurseries.
scored.public_data: NAIP and state orthoimagery, Planet/Sentinel phenology, USPTO plant patents; best signal needs grower drone imagery.
scored.rough_step_up: ~10^3-10^4x on a hit; public data is weaker here.
scored.frame: The rung is a contractual right to a mutated limb in an orchard, proven by grafting and evaluation and then sold or licensed to a nursery. Finding the limb is maybe 10-20% of the work (my estimate). The other 80%+ is grafting, 2-3+ years of fruiting trials, a stability check, a plant patent or PBR filing, and then a nursery spending roughly 5-10 years on propagation and marketing. The physical and time-bound step is the bulk of the work, which is the coal-mine-geothermal pattern. Buyers exist (Willow Drive bought exclusive rights to Royal Red Honeycrisp from grower Larry Jones; Tru-Cape manages the Bigbucks Gala sport), but they are small nurseries and marketing desks. They are not capitalised in the way a mine developer is.
scored.step_up: Unproven: a $1-5k blanket fee per orchard (the candidate's figure), and the limb itself is worth about $0. Proven: no finder payment is disclosed for any sport. The ceiling benchmark is Honeycrisp, the most successful US apple ever, which earned the University of Minnesota a total of more than $8M, mostly at $1.30 per tree over its patent life (Good Fruit Grower). A typical red sport probably earns a few $10k-$100k's in royalties spread over a decade (my estimate). Per hit that is roughly 10-100x on the orchard fee, paid slowly over years, not immediately. The claimed 10^3-10^4 is not supported.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Base hit rate: no source found. My estimate is that most observed sports are chimeras, unstable or not better than existing strains, so perhaps 1-10% have any commercial value. Cost per attempt: grafting plus trial rows costs about $1-10k over 3 years (my estimate). Because each attempt is already cheap, a 10x hit-rate gain saves little capex. The binding constraints are time and market demand, not capex. The lever is weak.
scored.data: Public NAIP imagery is about 0.6 m and Sentinel is 10 m, which is too coarse to resolve a single limb's colour or phenology anomaly. The usable signal needs private drone imagery from growers, so the data is not public. The outcome is also visible to the people closest to it: growers and pickers routinely spot colour sports by eye at harvest, which is how Royal Gala, Brookfield and Royal Red Honeycrisp were found. Existing proven sports are legibly listed in USPTO plant patents (more than 20 Gala sports are patented), and that also shows the red-sport niche is crowded.
scored.right_bought: Mixed. Under US law a sport of an open-release variety belongs to the owner of the orchard it is found in (Good Fruit Grower), so it can be bought. Sports of club or managed varieties (Cosmic Crisp, SweeTango, Envy and most new plantings) are typically assigned to the variety owner by licence contract, so they cannot be bought from growers. Growers already know that sports in their open varieties are valuable, so blanket rights would not come at an information-asymmetry discount.
scored.buyer: Nurseries such as Willow Drive and Van Well, and club-variety managers such as PVM, Stemilt, Zespri and Tru-Cape. They pay small upfront sums and per-tree royalties around $1-1.30 per tree. Wine-clone nurseries are smaller still.
scored.ladder: There is a ladder: sport discovery, then nursery propagation, then managed-variety or club licensing, then breeding programmes, then orchards and fruit marketing. But it climbs into a low-margin, slow-cycle apple and fruit industry. The best variety in history produced about $8M in royalties, so the ceiling is a mid-sized horticulture company, not a trillion-dollar path.
scored.fatal_flaw: Finding the limb is not the bottleneck. Proving it takes years of grafting, trials and nursery commercialisation, the payoff is small and slow (tens of $k to low $M per sport), and growers can already see colour sports by eye. Public imagery cannot resolve limbs, and sports in club varieties belong to the licensor.
scored.one_line_reason: Low score: proving and commercialising the sport dominates the work, the payoff is small and slow, the lever is weak because attempts are already cheap, the public data is too coarse and rights in club varieties go to the licensor, so it fails C1, C3 and C4.

scored.name: Wild Hop and Crop-Relative Flavour Discovery
scored.one_line: Exclusive collection and propagation agreements with private landowners where ML over herbarium records and imagery predicts distinct wild hop or flavour landrace populations; GC-MS and pilot brewing prove a new aroma variety for hop merchants.
scored.unproven_right: Exclusive collection and plant-patent rights to wild populations on private ranches, ~$1-10k.
scored.proving_step: Collection, chemotype GC-MS, propagation and pilot brewing, ~$20-50k per candidate.
scored.proven_buyer: Yakima Chief Hops, Hopsteiner, John I. Haas, Barth-Haas.
scored.public_data: GBIF/SEINet herbarium labels, iNaturalist, GRIN Humulus accessions, hop chemistry trial reports.
scored.frame: Rung: "an exclusive right to a wild hop population whose chemistry has been proven, sold to a hop merchant." Finding the plant is maybe 10-20% of the work inside that rung (my estimate). Merchants do not buy wild plants. They buy varieties that have been through years of agronomic trials. Even the wild neomexicanus success stories needed a decade or more of selection after collection: Todd Bates spent decades selecting before CLS Farms commercialised Medusa (and still expects it to stay niche), and Sabro and Talus are bred crosses, not wild plants as found. Most of the work is propagation, testing yield, disease and storage stability, and scaling acreage. The opposite of drilling being trivial.
scored.step_up: Unproven: collection agreement about $1-10k (candidate's estimate). There is no observable market for a "proven wild chemotype." What merchants pay for is a commercial variety. Citra reached about 12k acres and 18.4M lb in 2021, and brewers paid about $16/lb for it. But Citra took 18 years from cross to release (1990 to 2008), and royalties are not public. A GC-MS plus pilot-brew result alone might sell as a germplasm license for roughly $20-200k (my estimate), about 10-50x. It is not an immediate 10^3-10^4 jump. The big value only arrives after 7-15 years of breeding and agronomy, which is the developer's work, not discovery.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Proving cost is about $20-50k per candidate (candidate's estimate). GC-MS itself costs a few hundred dollars per sample. Breeding funnels discard 80-90% of seedlings in year one and keep only an elite line by year ten (Crafty Pint, The Breeder). So the failure rate is high, but the bottleneck is agronomic performance and brewer acceptance, which herbarium and imagery data cannot predict. ML could help pick where to collect a novel chemotype, but sampling is already cheap, so cutting capex 10x saves little money in absolute terms.
scored.data: GBIF, SEINet and iNaturalist records are already legible structured fields: species, coordinates, date. Humulus neomexicanus/lupulus accessions are catalogued in USDA GRIN and distributed to researchers for free, and wild neomexicanus has already been collected and worked by Bates/CLS, Hopsteiner, YCH (Talus) and the Hop Breeding Company (Sabro). On rights: a US plant patent (35 USC 161) explicitly excludes plants found in an uncultivated state. The wild genotype itself is not patentable until you breed or select it in cultivation. Wild hops also grow on public and BLM land and roadsides, so a landowner exclusive does not stop rivals collecting the same population nearby. The right being bought is weak and can be routed around.
scored.right_bought: The landowner collection exclusive is cheap, but it gives no real exclusivity. A US plant patent cannot cover a plant found in the wild. The species occurs widely, including on public land, and GRIN already distributes wild germplasm.
scored.buyer: Yakima Chief Hops, Hopsteiner, John I. Haas, Barth-Haas, and the Hop Breeding Company (the private breeding joint venture behind Citra and Sabro). They are capitalised, but they run their own in-house breeding and wild-germplasm programs and buy finished varieties, not raw chemotypes. The whole US hop crop is worth about $600M a year (USDA NASS, 2022 value of production $618M).
scored.ladder: Germplasm, then breeding, then a licensed variety with royalties, then growing, then merchant/processor. Each rung exists. But the top of the ladder is the global hop market, about $1-2B in total, so the trillion-dollar path does not exist. The idea could extend to other flavour crops, but the rungs stay small and each one has a long agronomic cycle.
scored.fatal_flaw: The physical step dominates: a wild chemotype is worth little until 7-15 years of breeding and agronomic trials (Citra took 18 years from cross to release), and plants found in the wild cannot get a US plant patent, so the cheap landowner right protects nothing. On top of that the market is about $600M a year.
scored.one_line_reason: This is a geothermal-in-coal-mines analogue. Finding the plant is easy and already done by incumbents; turning it into a commercial variety takes a decade of agronomy, the wild genotype cannot be patented, and the market is tiny.

scored.name: Venom Vault: peptide leads from private venomous-animal collections
scored.one_line: Buy venom/tissue access rights from private breeders of rare snakes, cone snails, spiders and scorpions; ML over venom transcriptomes and literature ranks toxins against validated targets (Nav1.7, Kv1.3, GLP-1R, ASIC); synthesise and screen, then license leads.
scored.unproven_right: Contractual access and benefit-sharing to venom from specific captive animals, plus composition-of-matter patents on new peptides.
scored.proving_step: Peptide synthesis ($1-3k each), contracted ion-channel/receptor panels, mouse PK/efficacy on the best; ~$0.5-2M with in vivo.
scored.proven_buyer: Novo, Lilly, Amgen, Vertex, Takeda BD ($5-50M upfront for preclinical leads).
scored.public_data: UniProt ToxProt/VenomZone, ArachnoServer, ConoServer, SRA venom-gland transcriptomes, toxinology literature, breeder trade records.
scored.rough_step_up: ~10^4x on the right itself; but published sequences are not owned and in vivo proof is costly.
scored.frame: The proposed rung is "venom access contract + composition-of-matter patent on a ranked toxin, sold to pharma BD." Inside that rung discovery (ranking toxins by target fit) is maybe 10-20% of the work; the physical step is NOT trivial or abstracted — selectivity engineering, med-chem analoguing, formulation and mouse PK/efficacy dominate. This is structurally the coal-mine-geothermal failure: building the bespoke asset (a de-risked preclinical candidate) is far harder than finding the right animal. A capitalised buyer does exist (Novo/Lilly/Amgen/Vertex pay $10-20M upfront for preclinical pain/metabolic assets — e.g. Astellas paid Chromocell $15M upfront plus >$500M milestones for a Nav1.7 antagonist), but the buyer only pays after the expensive non-discovery work is done, so the sellable rung is above, not at, the discovery step.
scored.step_up: Unproven side: a venom/tissue access and benefit-sharing contract with a breeder is worth roughly $1k-50k/yr (animal husbandry and sample-collection scale; my estimate — no public comparables found), and crucially is non-exclusive over the molecule: the peptide sequence is not the breeder's property. Proven side: $10-20M upfront for a validated preclinical ion-channel asset (Astellas/Chromocell $15M upfront on CC8464, >$515M biobucks). That looks like 10^2-10^3x, but the denominator is wrong — the step-up is not paid for the right, it is paid for the $0.5-2M+ of synthesis/panel/in vivo work plus 2-4 years of med-chem, and the historical analogue deals for pure venom libraries were small screening-access deals with undisclosed, modest upfronts (Xenome/MedImmune 2009, >2,000 venom-derived peptides, terms confidential). Scoring C2 as 3-10x on the right itself, because the right carries almost none of the value.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Proving step cost: peptide synthesis $1-3k/analogue, contracted ion-channel panel ~$5-20k, mouse PK/efficacy $100-500k, so $0.5-2M per serious candidate as the candidate states (consistent with CRO list pricing; my estimate for the panel line). Base rate: venom peptide programmes that reach a licensed clinical asset are vanishingly rare — of the ~20 venom-derived drugs ever approved versus tens of thousands of characterised toxins, and of the Nav1.7 field specifically, every spider-toxin programme (GpTx-1, Pn3a, ProTx-II, Amgen/Genentech/Janssen efforts) has failed on selectivity or PK, not on discovery. So the hit rate is low, which superficially suggests a big ML lever, but the failures are NOT discovery failures — they are selectivity/PK/clinical-translation failures that ML over transcriptomes does not touch. The lever is capped by where the attrition sits, and it sits downstream. 2024 Advanced Science work on hNav1.7 spider peptides states development "has been impeded by limited selectivity," i.e. the bottleneck is engineering, not finding.
scored.data: Data is public and largely ALREADY LEGIBLE, which is the kill shot on C4. UniProt ToxProt is a manually curated, expert-annotated subset (~7,000 toxin entries) in which the target family is written into annotation fields; ConoServer and ArachnoServer are purpose-built, target-annotated toxin databases. That is exactly the failure mode the rubric names: the outcome is summarised in a legible field by curators. SRA venom-gland transcriptomes are genuinely raw and large, but the academic toxinology community mines them continuously and publishes the hits — so the illegible fraction is being harvested by thousands of publishing labs, not ignored by sleepy incumbents. Breeder trade records are illegible but contain no target-pharmacology signal.
scored.right_bought: What can actually be bought cheaply is physical access to animals, not the asset. Nobody owns a wild-type venom peptide sequence; composition-of-matter claims require a novel analogue you invented, which means you must do the expensive engineering before you own anything. There is no owner "who cannot read the data" sitting on a transferable, exclusive right — the breeder has no right to the molecule to sell you, and a competitor can clone the same toxin from a published sequence or another specimen of the same species. Nagoya Protocol / ABS law adds provenance liability on top (source-country consent needed for genetic resources), which raises rather than lowers acquisition friction.
scored.buyer: Real and capitalised: Novo Nordisk, Lilly, Amgen, Vertex, Takeda, Astellas (Astellas/Chromocell: $15M upfront, >$515M total, for a Nav1.7 antagonist). But they buy de-risked preclinical candidates with in vivo efficacy and selectivity data, not ranked sequence lists. Vertex's own success (suzetrigine) came from internal small-molecule chemistry, not venom mining, which is the market's verdict on this input.
scored.ladder: Rungs above do exist — IND-enabling, Phase 1, Phase 2, commercial — and they are enormous, so a winner could in principle become a large pharma. But each rung costs 10-100x the one below and takes 2-5 years, so "win the smallest rung and climb" collapses: the smallest rung here is not self-funding on a short cycle, unlike a drill hit that monetises in months. No compounding flywheel.
scored.fatal_flaw: There is no ownable, cheaply-purchasable unproven right. A breeder cannot sell you exclusivity over a peptide sequence, published toxins are unowned, and the only ownable thing (a composition-of-matter patent on a novel analogue) exists only AFTER you have done the expensive med-chem and in vivo work. So the company cannot buy an asset for ~$0 and realise a step-up on a hit — it has to fund the whole hard, downstream, non-discovery part, where all the actual attrition lives (selectivity and PK, not finding the toxin). Discovery is roughly 10-20% of this rung, not 80%+.
scored.one_line_reason: Fails C1 and C4: the proving step is slow, costly bespoke pharmacology (the coal-mine-geothermal failure mode), the signal lives in already-curated, target-annotated public databases that thousands of academic labs actively mine, and no exclusive right over a venom peptide can be bought from anyone, so there is no near-zero asset whose step-up the company can capture.
