scored.name: Hoard Lease: UK/EU farmland detecting rights ranked by LiDAR and find-spot ML
scored.one_line: Buy exclusive search rights from farmers; ML over EA LiDAR, cropmarks, tithe maps and PAS find densities ranks fields; a detector and magnetometer sweep proves hoards; Treasure Act rewards and non-Treasure sales pay.
scored.unproven_right: Exclusive written search agreements on arable fields, ~£100-1k per field.
scored.proving_step: Detector, magnetometer and GPR sweep; shallow digging.
scored.proven_buyer: UK museums via the Treasure Valuation Committee, Spink, Noonans, Baldwin's.
scored.public_data: EA National LiDAR, Historic England aerial archive and NMP, PAS database (1.6M+ records), tithe/enclosure maps, HER records, place-name gazetteers.
scored.rough_step_up: ~10^2-10^3x; high heritage and ethics risk, weak ladder.
scored.frame: Rung: hold an exclusive search agreement on a field, detect it, and sell what you find. Finding the right field is about 70-85% of the work (my estimate), and the physical step is cheap (a detector, a magnetometer, shallow digging). But the "asset" is not the right. The right is spent when you find something, and the field keeps no resaleable value afterwards. The output is a set of loose objects, and the main buyer is museums with tight budgets, acting through the Treasure Valuation Committee. They are not a capitalised developer buying an asset that has been proven.
scored.step_up: Unproven: a search agreement, typically free or a share of finds; the candidate's estimate is £100-1k per field. Proven, typical case: the median treasure valuation was £270 and the mean £2,671, across 241 valued cases totalling £643,683 (2016 data, Sunday Telegraph 2018). The mean is driven by rare outliers, such as the £325k Leekfrith torcs. The proceeds are also split: landowner and finder take 50:50 of any Treasure reward (Code of Practice), and the landowner owns non-Treasure finds outright in England and Wales (NCMD suggests 50/50 above £500). So the typical step-up is under 3-10x. Only a rare hoard reaches 10^2-10^3x, and that happens to a few cases a year.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Base rate: in 2023 the public recorded 74,506 finds, of which 1,358 were Treasure cases; 2024 had 1,540, the record (PAS Annual Report 2023; British Museum). Tens of thousands of detectorists produced those, which means far below one hoard per field-season (my estimate). Cost per attempt: about £100-500 per field-day (my estimate; hobbyists do it unpaid). Attempts are already almost free, so there is no 10x discovery capex for ML to cut. ML could only shorten the search time, and the total payout pool is too small for that to matter.
scored.data: The PAS database (1.6M+ records) is already structured and public. Its find spots are coarsened, and it is exactly the legible outcome field, the past answers, that the rubric warns about. Detectorists already mine EA LiDAR through free viewers, along with HER data and tithe maps, so this layer is crowded, not illegible. Known sites in the HER are often scheduled monuments, and detecting on those is illegal. The policy trend also works against deliberately targeting archaeology. Rights are cheap but rarely exclusive in a way that matters, and the landowner keeps about 50% of value by default.
scored.right_bought: A written, time-limited search agreement with the farmer. It is cheap, often given free or for a 50/50 share of finds. Land agents advise defining area, season and crops (Strutt & Parker; FWI). The landowner owns non-Treasure finds and splits the Treasure reward 50:50, so the right cannot be bought at a deep discount to its proven value. The farmer keeps half the upside.
scored.buyer: Museums acquire through the Treasure Act, with the reward set by the Treasure Valuation Committee at market value. They are budget-constrained, often rely on rewards being waived, and the sector is debating high scheme costs (Museums Association, Aug 2026). The secondary market is auctioneers (Spink, Noonans, Baldwin's) selling coins to collectors. None of these is a capitalised buyer who pays an asset step-up and then develops it further.
scored.ladder: There is essentially none. No higher rung exists: no development of the field, and no industry downstream of finding the objects, beyond being an auction house or dealer, which is a small collectibles business. The total pool of UK Treasure rewards is on the order of £1M a year (2016: £644k from 241 valued cases), so this caps out as a lifestyle business, not a path to a trillion-dollar company.
scored.fatal_flaw: There is no asset to step up and no capitalised buyer. Each hit is a one-time pull of objects from a shared, tiny pool: about £0.6-1M a year in Treasure rewards, with a £270 median find, and half goes to the landowner. Thousands of free hobbyists already search with the same LiDAR and PAS data, and heritage law and ethics constrain targeting known sites.
scored.one_line_reason: Discovery-heavy and physically trivial, but the proven "asset" is a set of loose objects. They are sold mostly to museums with tight budgets out of a roughly £1M/yr reward pool, the landowner takes about 50%, the data is already legible and used by hobbyists, and there is no ladder.

scored.name: Chassis Ledger: lost works race cars proven from period records
scored.one_line: Buy cars sold as replica or unknown history; ML matches chassis/engine numbers and features against digitised race archives and factory build sheets to prove works or famous-race chassis; registry acceptance; sell via RM Sotheby's or Gooding.
scored.unproven_right: Title to a vehicle or bare chassis whose seller cannot connect it to period history, $30-150k.
scored.proving_step: OCR/vision over entry lists and photos, physical stamping inspection, marque registry acceptance.
scored.proven_buyer: RM Sotheby's, Gooding/Christie's, Bonhams Quail, Pebble Beach-tier collectors.
scored.public_data: Revs Institute Digital Library, Motorsport Images, scanned race programmes and entry lists, accessible title records.
scored.frame: The rung is: buy a car of unknown or replica history, attribute it to period works or race history, and sell it at a top auction. Discovery/attribution is perhaps 50-60% of the work in that rung (my estimate). The physical step is far from trivial. You have to inspect stampings and bodywork forensically. A proven car usually needs a $100k-1M+ correct restoration before RM or Gooding will put it on the block at a proven price. Expect registry politics, and often litigation over title. Example: the Cunningham Corvette sold below its $0.9-1.3M estimate because of its non-original state, and only after a court-ordered ownership split. The buyer is real and capitalised (RM Sotheby's and Pebble-tier collectors), but provenance is judged by a few human gatekeepers, not by the data.
scored.step_up: Best documented case: the #1 1960 Briggs Cunningham Le Mans Corvette (chassis 00867S103535). Bought for $75,000 in 2012 and sold at RM Sotheby's Amelia Island for $785,500, about 10x before restoration and legal costs (Motor Authority). The Bonhams 2016 C-Type (EUR 7.2M) was a re-identification inside an already-known works car, so it was not a near-zero start. Typical step-up is about 3-10x on a running car worth $30-150k. It reaches 10-100x only for a bare chassis that proves out, which is rarer still. Nowhere near 10^3-10^4.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Base hit rate is very low: probably well under 1 in 100 'unknown history' cars of the right marque are actually works or famous-race chassis (my estimate). The universe is tiny, a few thousand works chassis across all marques. Most of them are already located, and their numbers are tracked by registries and historians: Massini reportedly knows the histories of 20,000+ Enzo-era Ferraris, and Cunningham historian Lawrence Berman kept the Corvette's VIN on file for years. Each proving attempt costs the purchase of the car itself ($30-150k), not a cheap drill. So ML cannot cut capex much. You still have to own each car to test it, and the screen for 'is this number a known works number' is a lookup, not ML. The lever is far below 10x on capex. In practice it is a lookup-table edge, which is the same failure as the earlier grid-queue candidate.
scored.data: Period sources (Revs Digital Library, Motorsport Images, scanned entry lists and programmes) are public and partly illegible. But the outcome is effectively already summarised in a legible field: the chassis/VIN number, cross-referenced by marque registries, factory archives (Ferrari Classiche, Jaguar Heritage, Porsche build sheets) and named historians. The Cunningham car was identified by a Google search of its VIN. The right can be bought, but owners of high-end marques are rarely naive, since asking the registry is free and routine before any sale. The edge remains only in obscure marques or works cars that were re-stamped or re-bodied, where value is low anyway.
scored.right_bought: Yes, title to the car is bought outright on the open market ($30-150k per candidate). But title disputes are common on rediscovered cars: the Cunningham Corvette went to court and the proceeds were split.
scored.buyer: RM Sotheby's, Gooding/Christie's, Bonhams and Pebble Beach-tier collectors. They are capitalised and active, but they price on registry and historian acceptance and on originality, not on data.
scored.ladder: Weak ladder. Rungs above are restoration shops, a dealership or auction house, and a provenance registry or certification service. That is a niche luxury market of roughly $2-5B a year at the top end (my estimate). There is no path to a trillion-dollar company, and the supply of undiscovered works chassis is finite and shrinking.
scored.fatal_flaw: The answer is already in a legible field. Chassis/VIN numbers of works and race cars are tracked by registries, factory archives and named historians, so discovery is mostly a lookup, not ML. Meanwhile the physical step (correct restoration, authentication politics, title fights) is bespoke and expensive, and the step-up is about 10x, not 10^4. It has the same shape as the geothermal-in-coal-mines counter-example.
scored.one_line_reason: Rare ~10x hits (Cunningham Corvette: $75k to $785k) on a finite, already-catalogued set of chassis numbers. Bespoke restoration and provenance politics dominate, so there is no 95/5 discovery frame and no 10^4 jump.

scored.name: Successor Shares / Certificate Chain: old certificates that still convert
scored.one_line: Buy old stock and bond certificates at collector prices; ML over scanned Moody's/Fisher manuals, Capital Changes reporters, charter records and EDGAR traces each issuer through mergers to a live successor or escheated distribution; redeem with transfer agent or state.
scored.unproven_right: Title to physical certificates or assigned dormant holdings, $5-50 each.
scored.proving_step: Corporate-lineage reconstruction, then mail certificate to transfer agent or file unclaimed property claim.
scored.proven_buyer: Successor issuers via Computershare/Equiniti/EQ; state unclaimed property programs (obligated to pay).
scored.public_data: Scanned Moody's/Mergent manuals (HathiTrust, Internet Archive), Fisher Manual of Valuable and Worthless Securities, EDGAR and pre-EDGAR microfiche, state dissolution registers, NAUPA databases.
scored.rough_step_up: ~100-10,000x on hits; base hit rate ~1-3%; modest ceiling.
scored.frame: The rung is tracing a certificate's issuer to a live successor and redeeming it. The physical step is trivial: mail the certificate or file a claim. Discovery (the lineage research) is about 90% of the work inside that rung, so the frame exists. But there is no capitalised buyer paying for a step-up. The transfer agent or state just honours an existing claim, and only for the registered owner. The real gating work is legal rather than discovery: endorsement, a medallion signature guarantee, affidavits of loss and probate. That pushes the discovery share of the true rung down to about 40-50% (my estimate).
scored.step_up: Unproven: collector paper at about $5-50 (the candidate's figure; cancelled scripophily typically sells for $5-50). Proven: whatever the successor shares are worth, which on the rare hits is likely $100s-$10,000s (my estimate), so up to roughly 100-1000x per hit. But most collector-market certificates are cancelled (punched or stamped) and redeem for $0. Expected value across the pool is about 2-10x at best (my estimate). No source gives a distribution of redemption values.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Base hit rate is about 1-3%, which is the candidate's own unsourced estimate; I found no published figure. Cost per proving attempt is already tiny: Scripophily.com / RM Smythe's Old Company Research Service traces lineage for $49.95 per company (earlier $39.95, no charge if nothing is found). Replacement or transfer via Computershare costs about $50 plus a 2% surety bond (Ford and Marathon FAQs). ML can cut a cost that is already about $50, so the capex lever is small in absolute dollars. There are no expensive failing shots like a $500k drill hole.
scored.data: The data is public and illegible: scanned Moody's/Mergent and Fisher manuals on HathiTrust and the Internet Archive, Capital Changes reporters, and pre-EDGAR microfiche. But the outcome is already summarised. The Fisher, Scudder, Smythe and Herzog obsolete-securities manuals exist precisely to record valuable-vs-worthless status. Those archives and their publishing rights are owned by Scripophily.com/Smythe, which sells the answer for $49.95. NAUPA and state unclaimed-property searches are legible databases keyed by owner name. The ML edge over existing legible answers is thin.
scored.right_bought: Fatal. Buying the paper does not buy the shares. A registered certificate transfers only with the registered owner's endorsement and a medallion signature guarantee whose signature matches the name on the face of the certificate. A collector holding someone else's unendorsed certificate cannot redeem it. Escheated shares are paid by the state to the owner or heirs, not to whoever holds the certificate. The legitimate route is buying assignments from heirs, which is the heir-finder / unclaimed-property locator business, with fees capped by statute: CT 10%; DE the lesser of $1,000 or 10%; RI and about 14 other states 10%; AZ and NJ 20%. Several states (DE, NJ) also void agreements made within 24 months of escheat. So the owner of the right cannot be cheaply bought out of most of the step-up.
scored.buyer: There is no capitalised buyer paying a premium. Successor issuers (via Computershare, Equiniti or EQ) and state unclaimed-property programs only honour claims at par value, and only for the proper owner. There is no secondary market of developers paying for proven rights.
scored.ladder: The ladder is weak. Next rungs would be general unclaimed-property recovery, heir finding, and lost-shareholder search services, which transfer agents already outsource. All are fee-capped, fragmented, low-ceiling service businesses with no path to a very large company. The total pool of dormant securities is real (states hold billions), but the realisable share is capped at about 10-20% by statute.
scored.fatal_flaw: The right cannot be bought. Owning a physical certificate does not confer the shares without the registered owner's endorsement and a medallion guarantee, escheated value goes to owners or heirs, and buying assignments from heirs is statutorily capped at 10-20% finder fees. The outcome is also already sold as a $49.95 lookup by the Fisher/Smythe successor service.
scored.one_line_reason: Inside the rung, discovery is most of the work. But buying the paper does not transfer the shares, fee caps keep most of the step-up from the buyer, and the lineage answer already sits in purpose-built obsolete-securities manuals sold for about $50, so neither the ML edge nor the step-up comes through.

scored.name: LatencyLine: low-latency microwave geodesic waypoints
scored.one_line: Find scarce parcels and structures on the straight-line path between emerging compute and exchange hubs, option them, prove line-of-sight and licensing, sell the path to HFT firms and hyperscalers.
scored.unproven_right: Rooftop, tower-space or ground options at waypoints, a few thousand dollars each.
scored.proving_step: ML over lidar DSMs, FCC Part 101 paths, FAA heights and zoning; path survey and frequency coordination.
scored.proven_buyer: Jump/New Line, McKay Brothers, Anova, Vigilant, hyperscalers and neoclouds.
scored.public_data: FCC ULS Part 101, USGS 3DEP lidar, FAA DOF, county zoning.
scored.frame: The candidate rung is "an optioned waypoint plus a proven line-of-sight path". It is not a discrete sellable frame. A single waypoint is worth nothing unless the whole end-to-end path exists, and that means 20-40 hops for Chicago-NJ (about 1,200 km at hop lengths of roughly 30-60 km; my estimate). Each hop needs tower or rooftop rights, FCC Part 101 coordination, FAA clearance, and then radio hardware, power and maintenance. Discovery, meaning finding geodesic-adjacent sites with clear LOS, is maybe 20-30% of the work (estimate). The rest is assembling and running the network, so it is a bespoke build, like the geothermal-in-coal-mine counter-example. Finding the site is not the hard part. Securing every link and operating it is.
scored.step_up: No live numbers: the shared web-search budget was used up before this agent ran (0 of 5 searches returned), so all figures are from memory or estimates. A commercial tower-space or rooftop lease runs about $1-3k per month per antenna position (industry norm, estimate). The proven-path value sits at the network level, not the waypoint level. Spread Networks spent about $300M on Chicago-NJ fiber (2010) and was sold to Zayo in 2017 for about $127M (reported, from memory). Microwave networks reportedly cost tens of millions per route. Per waypoint, a key choke-point site might get a 3-10x premium over a normal tower lease, and only if it is truly unique and on the geodesic. That is nowhere near 10^3. The ~10^2-10^3x claim in the pitch is not supported.
scored.hit_rate_capex: The proving step is LOS and path engineering: desktop analysis with Pathloss or similar tools on lidar/DSM data, then a path survey costing about $5-20k per hop (estimate). Success is high once a candidate site exists, plausibly over 50% (estimate). That caps the ML lever at about 2x, not 10x. The expensive failures come from landlord holdouts, zoning denials and frequency conflicts, and ML does not fix those.
scored.data: The data is mostly legible, and the outcome is already published. FCC ULS Part 101 licences list exact coordinates, antenna heights and frequencies for every existing HFT path. Hobbyists (for example the 'Sniper in Mahwah' blog) and competitors already map every network's route from ULS. The FAA DOF lists obstacle heights. USGS 3DEP lidar is large but standard, and RF engineers already use it routinely. The best geodesic-adjacent sites on established routes (Chicago-NJ, NJ-Toronto, London-Frankfurt) are taken, and the record of who holds them is in a public registry. That is exactly the 'regulator writes the answer into a field' failure mode.
scored.right_bought: Partly, yes. Rooftop and ground options can be bought from landowners who do not know their site is on a geodesic, so there is some information asymmetry. But most usable high sites are owned by tower REITs (American Tower, Crown Castle, SBA), and they price tower space by standard schedule and know exactly what HFT tenants are worth. Raw-land options are cheap, but then you have to build a tower and get it permitted, which is the physical step.
scored.buyer: The buyers are a small, shrinking oligopoly: Jump/New Line, McKay Brothers/Quincy, Anova, Vigilant, plus a few firms such as Optiver, IMC and Citadel. All of them run in-house path engineering teams and buy sites directly. The trade is close to the physical limit, the Chicago-NJ microwave paths are within microseconds of the geodesic, and the HFT latency race has been consolidating since around 2016. Hyperscalers and neoclouds do not buy microsecond-latency microwave between compute hubs. They use fiber, and AI training and inference between data centers is bandwidth-bound, not latency-bound at the microsecond level. So the buyer for 'emerging compute hubs' does not really exist.
scored.ladder: The ladder is weak. It goes waypoint, then full path, then operated network sold as latency or bandwidth to traders (the McKay/Anova model), then possibly the trading itself. The top rung is HFT market-making, which is a large business, but the network rung is a niche of a few hundred million dollars total (estimate). It does not compound toward a trillion-dollar chain.
scored.fatal_flaw: A waypoint has no standalone value. Value only appears when a complete end-to-end path is assembled and operated, which makes this a bespoke network build, not a discovery problem. On top of that, every existing path is already published in FCC ULS, and the handful of buyers do this routing in-house.
scored.one_line_reason: This fails the frame test. Discovery is a minority of the work, a single waypoint is not a sellable asset, the outcome is already legible in FCC ULS, the buyers are a few in-house HFT teams, and the hyperscaler demand is not real.
sources: No web searches succeeded: the shared web-search budget for this run was used up before this agent's queries ran, so every figure here is from memory or my own estimate
FCC Universal Licensing System, Part 101 microwave licences (public coordinates and paths): https://wireless2.fcc.gov/UlsApp/UlsSearch/searchLicense.jsp
Spread Networks Chicago-NJ fiber (~$300M build, 2010) and sale to Zayo (2017), widely reported; cited from memory
Sniper in Mahwah blog, which maps HFT microwave networks from FCC ULS: https://sniperinmahwah.wordpress.com (from memory)
Lease, survey, hop-count and network-size figures are my own estimates

scored.name: Dirtwave: AM tower-farm land arbitrage
scored.one_line: Buy small AM stations at radio multiples where the licensee owns 10-75 acres of tower land in growth corridors, move the signal, rezone and sell land to homebuilders or data-center developers.
scored.unproven_right: Dying AM licence plus fee tower parcel priced at $50-500k on radio revenue.
scored.proving_step: ML joins FCC filings to parcel, zoning, utility and growth data; FCC modification and local entitlement (non-trivial).
scored.proven_buyer: Homebuilders (Toll paid $74.1M for WMAL site), industrial and data-center developers, land funds.
scored.public_data: FCC LMS/CDBS, ASR, county assessor/GIS and deeds, zoning maps, utility capacity maps.
scored.rough_step_up: ~5-30x; edge is the long tail of small owners.
scored.frame: The rung is buying an AM licence with its tower land, then selling entitled land. Finding the parcels is maybe 10-20% of the work (my estimate). The other 80%+ is physical, regulatory and political. You have to move or diplex the signal, which needs an FCC minor modification plus a new site or a lease on another station's tower. Then you need rezoning, which means public hearings and possibly environmental review. Ground-radial and soil checks can be needed too, and the whole thing takes 1-4 years. Toll Brothers buying the WMAL site shows the entitlement and permitting step is the real work. This has the same shape as the geothermal-in-coal-mines counter-example: the hard part is the bespoke step, not the search.
scored.step_up: From memory, not verified this run (search budget exhausted): Cumulus sold the roughly 75-acre WMAL tower site in Bethesda to Toll Brothers for about $74.1M, around $1M per acre. In that case the owner, a large group, captured the value itself. Small AM stations trade for about $50k-$500k (my estimate from typical small-market AM sales). But a seller who owns fee land usually prices it, or a broker values the real estate separately. The realistic step-up from the station price to the price of entitled land is about 3-30x, and most of it comes from the rezoning, not from discovery. On the cost basis of the land alone the step-up is often only 2-5x, because the seller knows the land is worth more than the radio business.
scored.hit_rate_capex: I found no measured base hit rate; these are my estimates. Screening is cheap: ML or GIS joins of FCC antenna records to county parcels cost a few thousand dollars per region. The expensive, mostly-failing step is entitlement, at roughly $100k-$1M+ per attempt in legal, engineering, FCC work and carrying cost over 1-4 years. Entitlement success depends on local politics, not on information, so ML barely moves the hit rate. The capex lever is maybe 1.2-1.5x, not 10x.
scored.data: The data is public and mostly legible. FCC records (LMS, CDBS, the ASR tower registry) give tower coordinates and licensees in structured form. County assessor and GIS data give parcel acreage, ownership and assessed value. Zoning maps are online. So the outcome, land value and size, is already summarised in legible fields: assessed value and comparable sales. The real unknown, whether a rezoning succeeds, is not in any dataset. Joining FCC data to parcel data is a weekend GIS job, not illegible-data extraction.
scored.right_bought: The right can be bought, from small owner-operators and estates through radio brokers. But those owners can read the data that matters: they know their acreage and local land prices, and brokers market tower land as real estate. The big groups (Cumulus, iHeart, Audacy, Salem) have already been systematically selling tower land. The long tail of small owners is likely partly priced, and some of those owners will sell the land and keep a leased tower. Exclusion check: this is not a mineral, oil, gas, geothermal or groundwater play and is not Terranox, so no hard exclusion applies.
scored.buyer: Capitalised buyers exist: homebuilders (Toll Brothers paid about $74.1M for the WMAL site, from memory), industrial and data-center developers, and land funds. They buy entitled or entitleable land in growth corridors.
scored.ladder: The ladder is weak and runs sideways. It goes land arbitrage, then entitlement, then possibly vertical development (homebuilding or a data-center powered shell). Development is a mature, crowded, capital-heavy industry where this company has no data edge. There is no natural chain to a trillion-dollar company. The radio licences themselves are a dying asset.
scored.fatal_flaw: Discovery is not the bottleneck. Tower land is legible in assessor and FCC records, and both owners and brokers already price it. The step-up comes from rezoning and moving the signal, which are bespoke, political, multi-year and the same for everyone. That makes it a geothermal-in-coal-mines case: execution, not finding, holds the value, so ML has no 10x lever.
scored.one_line_reason: This is ordinary real-estate entitlement arbitrage with data that is easy to read. The work is in getting the land rezoned, not in finding it, so ML adds little and owners already know what the land is worth.

scored.name: MoveIn / AM Move-In: broadcast allocation-chain solver
scored.one_line: Buy cheap rural FM/AM licences or CPs and use a constraint solver plus ML over the full FCC table and terrain to find legal chains of city-of-licence, class and channel changes that bring the signal over a metro; win the FCC grant and sell to broadcasters.
scored.unproven_right: Rural FM/AM licence or CP worth $25-300k.
scored.proving_step: Combinatorial search over spacing, contours, treaty limits and Rural Radio priorities including multi-station swaps; FCC grant; leased tower and transmitter.
scored.proven_buyer: iHeart, Audacy, Salem, EMF/K-Love, Hispanic and ethnic broadcasters, cluster owners.
scored.public_data: FCC LMS/CDBS engineering data, FM Table of Allotments, USGS terrain, Census urban areas, ECFS allotment dockets.
scored.rough_step_up: ~10-100x; radio is declining and 2011 Rural Radio Order limits move-ins; data is legible so edge is combinatorial.
scored.frame: Rung: own a rural FM/AM licence or CP, then win an FCC allotment and city-of-licence modification that puts a usable signal over a metro, and sell the upgraded licence. Inside this rung, finding a legal chain is maybe 50-60% of the work (my estimate). The rest is not trivial: rulemaking petitions, counterproposals from competitors, Tuck/Section 307(b) showings under the 2011 Rural Radio Order, multi-party consent and reimbursement agreements for swapped stations, then site acquisition, tower lease and construction. Moving tower and transmitter is cheap ($50-300k, my estimate), but the regulatory step is slow (often 1-3+ years) and contested, so it is not abstracted the way a drill contractor is. Capitalised buyers exist but are weakening (see buyer).
scored.step_up: Estimates, not sourced; the web search budget ran out before any search returned. Unproven rural FM: $25k-300k (the candidate's own range, consistent with rural station trades). Proven rim/metro-reaching FM: perhaps $0.5M-5M in mid and large markets today, against $10M-50M+ before 2008. Historical move-ins in the 1990s and 2000s did reach about 10-100x. In the post-2011 Rural Radio regime, with metro FM values down roughly 70-90% since 2006 (my estimate), a realistic hit is about 3-20x. Also, a rim-shot signal from a Class A/C3 often reaches only the edge of a metro, and that sells at a discount to a full-market stick.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Estimate (unsourced). The search step is cheap: a consulting-engineer allocation study costs about $5k-50k, and software like V-Soft Probe/ComStudy runs spacing studies in minutes. The expensive part is FCC and legal prosecution: about $50k-250k per contested rulemaking plus reimbursement of other stations' costs. Hit rate is not set by discovery. It is set by legal feasibility (Rural Radio presumption, last-local-service rules) and by competitors' counterproposals. Most good chains in the dense eastern US were mined out in the 1990s and 2000s. ML does not raise the success rate of the costly step (the FCC decision), so the capex lever is maybe 1.5-2x, not 10x.
scored.data: The data is fully legible. FCC LMS/CDBS engineering records, the FM Table of Allotments, contour data, the Census urbanized areas used for the Rural Radio presumption, and USGS terrain are all structured, machine-readable and already loaded into commercial engineering tools. The 'outcome' (whether a channel and site are allowed) is a deterministic spacing/contour calculation, so the only edge is combinatorial search over multi-station chains. Washington engineering firms (e.g. du Treil Lundin & Rackley, Cavell Mertz, Kessler & Gehman, Hatfield & Dawson) and brokers have done exactly this for 30 years. Owners are often sophisticated or broker-advised, and a rural licence's upgrade potential is sometimes already priced in. Rights must be bought: there is no free first-come entry except FCC auctions of vacant allotments, and those are competitive.
scored.right_bought: A rural FM/AM licence or construction permit bought from small owner-operators, about $25k-300k (estimate). Some deals also need options or consents from neighbouring stations whose channel or class must change in the chain, plus reimbursement of their costs.
scored.buyer: iHeart, Cumulus, Audacy, Salem, Townsquare, EMF/K-Love, Spanish-language and ethnic broadcasters, and religious non-profits. Several are distressed or deleveraging. Audacy and Cumulus went through restructuring around 2024, iHeart is heavily indebted, and Salem has been selling stations (from memory, not verified this session). EMF and religious broadcasters remain active buyers of metro-reaching signals, but at low prices.
scored.ladder: Weak. The rungs above (owning and operating stations, clusters, ad sales) are a structurally declining industry, with US radio ad revenue flat to down for about 15 years (estimate). There is no credible trillion-dollar path. At best a mid-size spectrum-arbitrage or station-group business.
scored.fatal_flaw: The data is fully legible and 30 years of consulting engineers and brokers have already mined the combinatorial space, so ML adds little. The 2011 Rural Radio Order and the collapse in radio values cap the step-up at about 3-20x. And the costly, mostly failing step is a contested FCC proceeding that ML cannot speed up.
scored.one_line_reason: This is legible-data spectrum arbitrage in a declining industry: incumbent engineers already run the search, Rural Radio rules block most move-ins, the step-up is about 3-20x rather than 10^4, and there is no real ladder.

scored.name: HopGraph: FM translator relocation chains
scored.one_line: Buy cheap rural FM translators and find multi-hop minor-modification paths into markets where AM owners pay for FM fill-ins.
scored.unproven_right: Secondary FM translator licence, ~$5-25k.
scored.proving_step: Graph search plus interference model, FCC grant; commodity transmitter.
scored.proven_buyer: AM owners needing FM simulcast, HD2 operators, religious networks.
scored.public_data: FCC LMS translator data, ECFS complaints, terrain.
scored.frame: Rung: own a secondary FM translator licence and get an FCC-granted relocation into a market where an AM station wants an FM fill-in. Inside that rung, finding a legal path through the interference rules is maybe 50-60% of the work (my estimate). The rest is FCC filing, waiting on and fighting objections and interference complaints (ECFS), leasing tower space, and the transmitter. There is a real buyer (AM owners, HD2 programmers, religious networks), but the work is regulatory engineering, not discovery. Per hop the physical step is cheap (commodity transmitter, about $5-15k installed, my estimate). The hidden cost is many months of filing per hop.
scored.step_up: From memory, no searches ran. Rural or unbuilt translators trade around $5-30k. Translators that put a signal into a metro market traded around $100k-$500k+ in the 2016-2018 AM-revitalization windows, and some top-market ones were reported higher. That is roughly 10-50x at the peak, and less since then because AM is shrinking and many AMs already got translators in the 2016-2018 windows. Score 2: it sits nearer the low end now, and the multi-month path to proving it dilutes the jump.
scored.hit_rate_capex: From my own knowledge; I could not verify. A proving attempt costs about $3-10k in consulting-engineer fees plus FCC filing per hop (my estimate). Whether a given chain works is mostly predictable with standard FCC contour and interference tools (the 60 dBu contour-overlap test for a minor change, plus spacing and contour-protection rules). Base hit rate for an engineered filing is high, maybe 50%+ (my estimate). Failures come from petitions to deny, interference complaints and FCC hop restrictions, not from failing to discover a path. ML cannot gain much when the base rate is already high: the lever is capped near 2x, not 10x.
scored.data: Fatal: the data is legible. FCC LMS/CDBS gives every translator's coordinates, channel, power, antenna pattern and status in structured, downloadable form, and terrain data is public. Path search over contours is a classic graph search with deterministic FCC formulas, which consulting engineers already run (FCC tools, V-Soft Probe, Radiosoft). The outcome (grant or no grant) is itself a legible LMS status field. ECFS complaints are semi-structured but small in volume. Nothing illegible is left to extract.
scored.right_bought: Yes, translators can be bought from owners such as small religious and translator-network operators (a few large translator networks hold thousands), and sales need FCC assignment approval. But the sellers are not data-blind: brokers and engineers price relocation potential in. New translators come only through occasional FCC filing windows (mutually exclusive applications settled by auction), not first-come.
scored.buyer: AM owners needing FM simulcast (a declining, cash-poor group), HD2 and multicast programmers, and religious networks (EMF/K-Love, CSN, Calvary Chapel). These buyers are thinly capitalised compared with a mine developer, and the market is shrinking.
scored.ladder: Short. The next rungs are full-power FM stations and radio groups, and terrestrial radio is in secular decline (station values have collapsed since around 2008). There is no path to a very large company.
scored.fatal_flaw: The signal is not hidden. Translator facilities and grant outcomes are structured FCC LMS fields, and the routing is deterministic contour math that broadcast consulting engineers and brokers already run. So there is no ML discovery edge, and the step-up sits in a shrinking, low-capital AM radio market with FCC limits on serial hopping.
scored.one_line_reason: This is regulatory arbitrage on fully legible FCC data, already worked by consulting engineers and brokers, with an estimated 10-50x step-up into a declining industry and a short ladder.

scored.name: Dormant MSS Spectrum Roll-up for direct-to-device
scored.one_line: Buy MSS and adjacent spectrum licences from dormant or bankrupt satellite operators, prove D2D usability via coexistence analysis and FCC modification, sell to SpaceX, AST, Apple-Globalstar or carriers. Overlaps killed ITU idea.
scored.unproven_right: Licences tied to dead or aging satellites marked near zero.
scored.proving_step: ML over IBFS/ECFS and ITU coordination records; petition for rule modification; lobbying-heavy.
scored.proven_buyer: SpaceX (~$17B EchoStar AWS-4/H-block), AST SpaceMobile, Apple/Globalstar, T-Mobile, AT&T.
scored.public_data: FCC IBFS/ICFS, ULS, ECFS, ITU SNL/BR IFIC, UCS satellite database, CelesTrak.
scored.frame: The rung would be: buy a dormant or bankrupt MSS licence, get FCC terrestrial/D2D flexibility, sell it. Discovery is maybe 5-10% of that work (my estimate). The universe is a few dozen US MSS licensees, all named in IBFS/ICFS, so there is almost nothing to find. About 90% of the work is regulatory and political: rulemaking petitions, coexistence fights with incumbents such as GPS/DoD in Ligado's case, and buildout milestones. That physical and political step is the hard part. This is the geothermal-in-coal-mines shape, not the Terranox shape.
scored.step_up: From memory, because the shared web search budget was exhausted before any query ran. The best precedent is EchoStar, which already ran this exact play. In 2012 it bought bankrupt DBSD (~$1.4B) and TerreStar (~$1.38B), about $2.8B for 2 GHz MSS. The FCC then granted AWS-4 terrestrial rights in 2012, and SpaceX paid ~$17B in Sept 2025 (half cash, half stock) for AWS-4 plus H-block. That is roughly 6x over 13 years, with H-block and buildout capital added. Ligado (L-band) is a negative precedent: it went bankrupt in Jan 2025 after the 2020 FCC terrestrial approval was fought by DoD/GPS. AST's L-band arrangement in Ligado's bankruptcy was in the hundreds of millions, not a 10^3 jump. Realistic step-up is 3-10x, which scores 2.
scored.hit_rate_capex: This is my estimate, not sourced, because searches were unavailable. One proving attempt is a multi-year FCC rulemaking or licence modification costing about $10-50M in legal, engineering and lobbying, plus the licence purchase (hundreds of millions to billions). Success depends on politics and incumbent opposition (Ligado lost to DoD despite winning the FCC order), not on hidden information. Only about 2-5 meaningful attempts have happened in 15 years. ML does not raise the hit rate of a political process, so the lever is about 1x.
scored.data: IBFS/ICFS, ULS and ECFS are public and mostly legible. They show licensee, bands, satellite status, milestone compliance and pending modifications. Whether a licence is dormant or tied to a dying satellite is visible in structured fields, CelesTrak and the UCS database. ECFS dockets are large but are read closely by every spectrum lawyer and by analysts (New Street Research, LightShed). The outcome (terrestrial authority granted or not) is written straight into the licence terms and FCC orders. No illegibility edge.
scored.right_bought: Rights are bought, but not cheaply from naive owners. Sellers are bankruptcy estates and sophisticated operators (Ligado, Globalstar, Iridium, Inmarsat/Viasat, Omnispace) advised by spectrum bankers. Bids are competitive and include strategic players (SpaceX, AST, Apple, EchoStar). Dormant licences also tend to be cancelled by the FCC for missed milestones rather than becoming cheap to buy. No information asymmetry to buy against.
scored.buyer: Strong, well-capitalised buyers exist: SpaceX (~$17B to EchoStar, plus a further AWS-3 deal reported at ~$2.6B), AST SpaceMobile, Apple (prepaid ~$1.1B to Globalstar and took a ~20% stake), T-Mobile, AT&T and Verizon. Buyer demand is the one strong part of this idea.
scored.ladder: Rungs exist above it: spectrum, then satellite constellation, then D2D service, then carrier partnerships. EchoStar shows the endpoint can be ~$17B+. But each rung above spectrum costs billions in capex (AST has raised billions; Starlink is the incumbent), so climbing is capital-bound, not discovery-bound. Score 2.
scored.fatal_flaw: There is nothing to discover. The few dozen MSS licences are fully legible and already watched by every strategic buyer and spectrum analyst. Value is created by winning FCC/political fights over terrestrial and D2D authority (Ligado shows this can fail even after an FCC win), not by reading illegible data. ML gives no hit-rate lever, and the step-up is about 6x over a decade (EchoStar), not 10^4.
scored.one_line_reason: Charlie Ergen already ran this play (about $2.8B to $17B over 13 years). The value comes from lobbying over fully legible public licences, so it fails C1, C3 and C4 for the same reason geothermal-in-coal-mines does.

scored.name: Teleport Siting: ground-station-ready land plus earth station licence
scored.one_line: Buy RF-quiet, clear-horizon rural parcels near fiber and power that ML ranks as top gateway sites, obtain the FCC earth station licence and coordination, sell or ground-lease to ground-station operators and LEO constellations.
scored.unproven_right: Farmland at ag prices.
scored.proving_step: DEM horizon, ULS microwave interference, FAA and fiber analysis; Comsearch coordination and licence grant.
scored.proven_buyer: AWS Ground Station, KSAT, SSC, Viasat RTE, Leaf Space, Starlink and Kuiper gateways.
scored.public_data: FCC ULS microwave and earth stations, 3DEP/Copernicus DEM, broadband map and fiber filings, FAA DOF, ITU.
scored.rough_step_up: ~30-300x on parcel; siting rarely fails, so weak C3.
scored.frame: The rung is a site already cleared for a gateway: land plus coordination plus licence. Desk siting (horizon from DEM, checking microwave paths in ULS, FAA, fiber, power) is perhaps 40-60% of the work in that rung (my estimate). The rest is physical and slow: bringing power and fiber to the site, zoning or a conditional use permit, fencing, pads. More important, a meaningful FCC earth station licence is tied to the operator's own antennas, satellites, frequencies and power. A landowner cannot hold a licence that carries over to a buyer. So the thing that can actually be sold is a coordinated, zoned piece of land, and the coordination usually has to be redone with the buyer's real parameters. The buyers are well funded (Starlink, Kuiper, KSAT, AWS), but they mostly choose and coordinate their own sites, or rent space at existing teleports.
scored.step_up: No web searches ran (the shared search budget was used up), so every figure here is my estimate from prior knowledge. Unproven: US cropland is roughly $4-6k/acre (USDA land values, about $5.5k/acre cropland in 2024), so a 2-10 acre gateway parcel is about $10-60k. Proven: Starlink and Kuiper gateway leases are reported in local news at around $10-30k a year for a few acres. Capitalised at 8-10%, that is a lease worth about $100-400k, or roughly 3-10x the farmland value, and at most about 30x at the extreme. That is far below the candidate's claimed 30-300x. The uplift is a premium on a ground lease, not a jump from near zero.
scored.hit_rate_capex: No searches ran, so these are estimates. Base hit rate: high. Most flat, RF-quiet rural parcels near fiber are workable, and Starlink alone has licensed roughly 100+ US gateway sites with little sign of siting failure. Cost per proving attempt: desk siting costs a few thousand dollars. A Comsearch-type frequency coordination is roughly $5-20k (estimate). The FCC earth station filing fee is a few thousand dollars (FCC fee schedule, from memory). If the hit rate is around 70-90%, the most ML could improve it is about 1.1-1.4x, not 10x. Proving is cheap and rarely fails, so there is almost no capex to cut.
scored.data: The data is public, but it is already legible and structured. FCC ULS microwave and earth station records are queryable databases, 3DEP is a clean DEM, the FCC broadband map is structured, and the FAA DOF is a CSV. Existing earth stations are written straight into ULS/IBFS fields. Comsearch, Ligado-era coordinators and the operators' own RF teams already run this analysis routinely. Nothing is locked in scanned or unstructured files that only ML can extract.
scored.right_bought: Yes, farmland can be bought or optioned cheaply at ag prices. But the landowner is not missing anything the data would reveal, because almost any suitable parcel works. Supply of usable land is effectively unlimited, so the scarcity premium is small. Also, the licence and coordination are not a durable right that can be transferred independently of the buyer's system.
scored.buyer: Well funded but vertically integrated. SpaceX/Starlink and Amazon Kuiper run their own site acquisition and file their own FCC applications. KSAT, SSC, AWS Ground Station, Viasat RTE and Leaf Space either own their teleports or co-locate at existing ones. There is a small market for land-banked sites (some tower and data-center style developers, for example teleport REITs and Telespazio/Goonhilly-type operators), but buyers pay lease rates, not a discovery premium.
scored.ladder: Moderate. The next rungs would be building and owning a teleport, offering ground-station-as-a-service, and then a network like KSAT or AWS Ground Station. KSAT and SSC are worth hundreds of millions to low billions of dollars. That is real, but the market is crowded and capex-heavy, and there is no trillion-dollar chain above it.
scored.fatal_flaw: There is no rare discovery. Suitable gateway land is abundant, siting rarely fails, and the data is already structured and used routinely by incumbent RF coordinators. On top of that, the FCC licence depends on the operator's own system, so it cannot be built up in advance and sold. There is no low hit rate for ML to improve and no 10^3 step-up to capture: proving earns a 3-10x lease premium on cheap farmland.
scored.one_line_reason: This is commodity site acquisition, not discovery. The hit rate is high, the data is already legible, the licence is tied to the operator and cannot be transferred, and the step-up is about 3-10x, so it fails C3 and C4 outright.

scored.name: Lazarus Orbital: salvage title to insured-loss satellites
scored.one_line: Buy salvage title from space insurers to written-off satellites at near zero; ML over TLEs, light curves and RF picks recoverable buses; revive via servicer docking and sell or lease capacity.
scored.unproven_right: Insurer-held salvage rights (AsiaSat 3/HGS-1 precedent).
scored.proving_step: ML ranking from Space-Track, photometry, SatNOGS; physical step is MEV-class docking, not trivial.
scored.proven_buyer: SES, Intelsat, Eutelsat, sovereign and military users.
scored.public_data: Space-Track TLE/SATCAT, ESA DISCOS, Seradata loss notices, FCC filings, SeeSat/SatNOGS.
scored.rough_step_up: >1000x on title; servicing capex dominates, weak frame.
scored.frame: This is the coal-mine-geothermal counter-example again. The only sellable rung is a satellite that has actually been revived, and reviving it takes a servicer docking (MEV-class) or a bespoke orbit-raising campaign. By my estimate discovery (ML ranking) is under 10% of the work in that rung; the physical step is roughly 90%, is not trivial, and cannot be abstracted. A ranked list of 'recoverable' dead satellites has no capitalised buyer on its own. Operators buy working capacity, not salvage title plus a hypothesis.
scored.step_up: Unproven: insurer-held salvage title to a written-off satellite. My estimate is roughly $0 to low single-digit $M; there is no public market price. Precedent from memory: AsiaSat 3 (1997, stranded in GTO, about $200M+ insured loss) was bought back by Hughes from underwriters and rescued with lunar flybys as HGS-1, under a profit-sharing deal with insurers, not a cash price. Proven: a revived GEO satellite under lease. My estimate is $10-50M/yr of capacity revenue, less after the servicing fee (MEV-1/Intelsat 901 was reported at about $13M/yr, from memory). The step-up on title is nominally over 1000x, but it only arrives after servicing capex of tens of $M. ML ranking alone gives no immediate step-up. Net multiple on all-in capital is about 1-3x.
scored.hit_rate_capex: I could not verify any of these numbers. The web search budget was used up, so all figures are from memory or my own estimates. The failure mode of a written-off satellite is mostly already known; the open question is whether it can be fixed. Most insured losses (power, payload, deployment or anomaly failures) cannot be fixed by docking. The fixable class, wrong orbit or propulsion/fuel failures, I estimate at 10-20% of losses. Insurers and manufacturers already identify that class from their own telemetry. Cost per proving attempt is a servicer mission: MEV build and launch is reportedly $100M+ per vehicle, or $10-15M/yr per lease (estimate). ML does not cut the expensive step, so the lever is close to 1x.
scored.data: The public data (Space-Track TLE/SATCAT, ESA DISCOS, SatNOGS, amateur photometry, FCC filings) is legible and already well mined, and Seradata is a paid commercial database. The outcome is effectively summarised already: loss cause is reported in insurer claim and loss notices and trade press, and the owner and manufacturer hold the full telemetry. The owner (operator plus underwriters) can read far better data than any outsider, so there is no illegibility arbitrage. Salvage title can be bought, but there are complications. Outer Space Treaty liability stays with the launching state, so transfer needs regulator approval. Spectrum and orbital-slot rights (ITU/FCC) belong to the operator, not to the hardware.
scored.right_bought: Insurer-held salvage rights to written-off satellites. Precedent: AsiaSat 3 / HGS-1. The usual structure is profit-sharing with underwriters, not an outright cheap purchase.
scored.buyer: SES, Intelsat, Eutelsat, and sovereign or military capacity users. They buy working capacity or leases, not unproven salvage title.
scored.ladder: The rungs above are satellite servicing (refuelling, life extension), then owning a capacity fleet, then building satellites. But these rungs are capital-heavy and crowded. Northrop SpaceLogistics (MEV/MRV), Astroscale, Starfish Space and Orbit Fab are already there, and GEO capacity revenue is in secular decline as LEO constellations take share.
scored.fatal_flaw: The proving step is a physical docking or rescue mission costing tens of $M, not an information problem. The few recoverable failures are already known to the owner and insurer from private telemetry. ML over public TLE and photometry data neither cuts the dominant cost nor finds hidden value. This is the geothermal-in-coal-mines failure: the bespoke fix is far harder than finding the right satellite.
scored.one_line_reason: Discovery is a small slice of the work, the servicing capex dominates, the owner and insurer hold better data, and recoverability is already known. The frame fails C1 and C4.

scored.name: GhostPlat / LotRecord: assembling antiquated paper subdivisions
scored.one_line: Buy scattered $50-5k lots in 1920s-70s ghost subdivisions (Lehigh Acres, Golden Gate Estates, Rio Rancho, Deming, AZ/TX plats) from tax-deed sales and absentee heirs; ML maps ownership, vested plat rights and assemblability; vacate paper streets and replat; sell assembled tracts.
scored.unproven_right: Fee title to fragmented unbuildable paper lots.
scored.proving_step: ML over plat books, deed chains and tax rolls for ownership and holdouts plus buyer-spec matching; vacation/replat or vesting confirmation.
scored.proven_buyer: Solar/BESS developers (NextEra, Invenergy), hyperscaler land teams, homebuilders and BTR operators.
scored.public_data: County scanned plats and deeds, tax-deed lists, parcel GIS, special district maps, HUD ILSA archives.
scored.rough_step_up: ~10-300x on purchase; assembly and title-clearing is the binding constraint (partly counter-example pattern).
scored.frame: The rung would be: buy scattered paper lots, then assemble and replat them into a tract a developer can use. Discovery (finding which lots and owners exist) is perhaps 10-20% of the work inside that rung (my estimate). The other 80%+ is the physical and legal part: contacting and negotiating with hundreds to thousands of owners per tract, getting past holdouts, quiet-title and curative work, county hearings to vacate paper streets, replat engineering, and special-district or utility obligations. This is the geothermal-in-coal-mines counter-example: finding the subdivision is easy, and assembling it is the hard bespoke work. Capitalised buyers do exist (solar and BESS developers, BTR operators), but they buy the assembled output, and the assembled output is mostly not a discovery result.
scored.step_up: I could not verify these numbers this run because the shared web search budget was used up. They are estimates from prior knowledge and are unsourced. Deming NM and Rio Rancho-area paper lots trade at about $1-5k per 0.25-1 acre lot on eBay and land-flipper sites, which is roughly $2-10k/acre. Assembled raw desert acreage for solar in NM/AZ sells for about $1-10k/acre, or leases for about $300-1,000/acre/yr. Retail fragmentation means per-acre lot prices are often equal to or higher than assembled acreage prices, so the real step-up is about 1-3x, not 10-300x. Lehigh Acres and Golden Gate Estates lots (about $10-40k per quarter acre in Lehigh, $50-150k per Golden Gate tract, my estimate) are already individually buildable and priced by the retail market, so there is little assembly premium there either. The 10-300x only appears if you buy tax-deed scraps at about $50-500 and somehow realise acreage value, and that happens on single lots, not on assembled tracts.
scored.hit_rate_capex: These are estimates only, not verified this run. There is no expensive, mostly-failing proving shot like a drill hole. The failure mode is assembly failure: one holdout or one unclearable title blocks the tract. My estimate is that assembling about 100-500 lots costs about $500k-$5M in acquisition plus legal and curative costs, plus 2-5 years. The chance of full assembly is probably 10-30%, and it is driven by human holdouts, not by information. ML can rank which subdivisions have the fewest owners or the most tax-delinquent owners. That is a lift of maybe 1.5-2x, not 10x, because the binding constraint is negotiation and legal process, not knowing who owns what.
scored.data: The data is public: county scanned plats, deed chains, parcel GIS, tax-deed lists, and HUD ILSA archives. The key outcome (who owns each lot, the owner's mailing address, delinquency status, assessed value) is already in the legible tax roll and parcel GIS fields. Land-flip operators already buy and mail at scale using exactly these fields: Land Geek (Mark Podolsky), Jack Butala's Land Academy, and DataTree/PropStream-driven mailers. The illegible parts (old plat restrictions, unvacated streets, special-district liens) matter, but they are cleared through legal process, not just extracted. That gives only a modest ML edge.
scored.right_bought: Yes. Fee simple title can be bought cheaply from absentee heirs and at tax-deed auctions, sometimes for $50-500 at Florida tax-deed sales (my estimate). However, the sellers are not unable to read the data: they know they own an unbuildable lot, and that is why the lot is cheap. Many are retail owners who emotionally overvalue their lot, and that creates the holdout problem.
scored.buyer: Utility-scale solar/BESS developers (NextEra, Invenergy), BTR and homebuilders (Lennar, Pulte in Lee County), and hyperscaler land teams. They are well capitalised, but they generally avoid fragmented-title sites. Solar developers usually lease contiguous ranchland from a single owner at much lower friction, so their willingness to pay a premium for an assembled antiquated subdivision is limited (my estimate).
scored.ladder: There is a plausible ladder: assemble land, then entitle it, then develop (solar, BTR, data-center campus), then own and operate. The entitlement-plus-development rungs are the conventional real-estate developer ladder. It is capital-heavy and has no discovery leverage, so it does not look like a trillion-dollar path.
scored.fatal_flaw: The rung is mostly assembly, not discovery. Turning a fragmented paper subdivision into a sellable tract is bottlenecked by holdout negotiation, quiet-title and curative work, and county vacation/replat process. ML cannot abstract that away, which is the coal-mine-geothermal counter-example. Ownership is already in legible tax-roll fields that land flippers use, and assembled per-acre value often does not exceed fragmented per-acre retail lot value, so there is no 10^3-10^4 step-up.
scored.one_line_reason: The hard part is assembly and holdout clearing, not discovery. Ownership is already in legible tax-roll fields, and the assembled step-up is roughly 1-3x per acre, not 10^3.
