Unverified prior knowledge: eBay/land-flip listings for Deming NM (Luna County) and Rio Rancho/AMREP paper lots
Unverified prior knowledge: Lee County FL Lehigh Acres lot market and Collier County Golden Gate Estates tract prices
Unverified prior knowledge: Land Geek / Land Academy land-flip operating models using tax-roll mailing data
Unverified prior knowledge: Florida tax-deed auction results (Lee, Charlotte, Collier clerks)

scored.name: TDR Mint / Flood Sending-Zone TDR Harvester
scored.one_line: Buy near-worthless unbuildable or flood-zone parcels in jurisdictions with TDR programs (NJ Pinelands, Montgomery MD, King County, Palm Beach/Collier/Miami-Dade, TRPA); ML checks eligibility and prior severance in scanned rules and deeds; certify and sell credits to receiving-zone developers.
scored.unproven_right: Dormant, unsevered development-right allocations on parcels priced as worthless.
scored.proving_step: Eligibility and credit yield computation, certification application and recorded easement.
scored.proven_buyer: Receiving-zone developers, Tahoe resorts, county TDR banks.
scored.public_data: Pinelands PDC Bank records, county TDR registries, TRPA commodities ledger, FEMA NFHL, tax-deed lists, scanned deed restrictions.
scored.rough_step_up: ~5x-10^3x; some registries have legible status fields.
scored.frame: The rung is: buy a sending-zone parcel, have the credits allocated, record the easement, sell the credits. Paperwork is most of that work and there is no physical step, so the frame does exist (estimate: about 70% legal and administrative work). But the 'discovery' part is small. Credit allocation in these programs is a published formula in the rules (for example, Pinelands gives 1 Pinelands Development Credit (PDC) per 39 upland acres, a lower rate for wetlands, and 1 PDC = 4 rights). The sending zones are mapped. So there is little hidden to find. The rest is applications, title work and finding a buyer, which are friction rather than discovery. Buyers (receiving-zone developers, county TDR banks, Tahoe land banks) are few, and demand is weak and swings with the cycle.
scored.step_up: From memory, not verified this run (the search budget was used up): Pinelands sending-zone land trades at roughly $1k-3k per acre (estimate). The PDC credits severed from it are worth roughly $1k-3k per acre's worth of credits (a PDC has historically sold for about $20k-40k, i.e. about $5k-10k per right, at 39 acres per PDC). So the step-up is about 1-3x, not 10^3. Montgomery County MD TDRs once sold for about $10k-15k each but are mostly illiquid now that receiving demand has collapsed (estimate). TRPA residential development rights and land coverage can sell for $100k+ per unit or $25-50 per sq ft (estimate). Sensitive Tahoe parcels that hold them are already priced on that value, or bought by the California Tahoe Conservancy and Nevada state lands at prices that include it. The market already prices the credit value into the land.
scored.hit_rate_capex: The proving step is not expensive and rarely fails. Eligibility follows from zoning and the sending-zone maps, and the allocation follows a deterministic formula. Estimated cost per certification (title search, survey, LOI or certificate application, easement recording) is about $5k-25k, and most eligible parcels succeed, likely over 70% (estimate). The lever is capped at 1/base hit rate, so about 1.3-2x. ML cannot cut capex 10x when the base hit rate is already high.
scored.data: Mostly legible, which removes the ML edge. Sending zones are mapped GIS layers. Allocations are issued in recorded documents (the Pinelands Letter of Interpretation, the TDR certificate). Severance is recorded as a deed restriction or easement and tracked in the PDC Bank and county TDR registries. The TRPA commodities ledger and parcel tracker hold the outcome as legible fields. The only illegible part is old scanned deeds that may show prior severance. That is a title-risk check, not a source of hidden value.
scored.right_bought: Yes, the right is bought, since it comes with fee title or can be bought separately. But owners in active programs usually know their land carries credits: counties and the Pinelands Commission do outreach, and land trusts and brokers already pitch them. Owners who don't know (heirs, tax-deed parcels) do exist, but the discount is small because the credit is only worth about 1-3x the land.
scored.buyer: Receiving-zone developers. They buy only when density bonuses are binding, and many programs see few sales a year (estimate: Pinelands sees roughly tens of PDC transactions a year). County and state TDR banks and Tahoe land banks such as the California Tahoe Conservancy also buy. The market is thin, illiquid and driven by policy.
scored.ladder: Weak. The next rungs up are TDR brokerage, then a land-conservation developer, then receiving-zone real estate development. These are commodity real-estate rungs with no compounding data moat, and the market is capped by a few dozen US TDR programs with small volume (estimate: well under $1B a year in total US TDR transactions).
scored.fatal_flaw: The credit value is already set by a published formula and recorded in legible public registries, so the market prices it into the land. The step-up is about 1-3x, not 10^3-10^4. The proving step already succeeds most of the time. And buyers are few and erratic, since demand depends on policy.
scored.one_line_reason: TDR credits are allocated by a public formula and recorded in registries, the land is priced with the credit value in it, the step-up is about 1-3x, the proving step mostly succeeds, and buyers are scarce, so there is nothing for ML to discover.
sources: The shared web search limit was used up before any query ran, and both direct fetches of NJ Pinelands Commission pages (nj.gov/pinelands/pdc/, nj.gov/pinelands/landuse/pdc/) returned 404. Every number in this assessment is the model's estimate from prior knowledge and has not been verified with a source.
NJ Pinelands Comprehensive Management Plan, N.J.A.C. 7:50-5.43 (PDC allocation formula: 1 PDC per 39 acres, 1 PDC = 4 rights), cited from prior knowledge
Pinelands Development Credit Bank annual reports (PDC sale prices), cited from prior knowledge
TRPA Code of Ordinances, Chapter 51 (transfer of development rights and commodities) and the LT Info parcel tracker, cited from prior knowledge
Montgomery County MD Agricultural Reserve TDR program literature (falling TDR demand), cited from prior knowledge

scored.name: Clearfield: FUDS stigma removal
scored.one_line: Buy rural parcels near Formerly Used Defense Sites at steep stigma discounts; ML over Archive Search Reports, declassified range maps and imagery proves they lay outside impact footprints; drone EM/mag sweep confirms; resell clean.
scored.unproven_right: Fee simple at a 50-90% discount.
scored.proving_step: Drone magnetometer/EM survey plus USACE or state no-further-action concurrence.
scored.proven_buyer: Homebuilders, solar/data-center aggregators, timber REITs.
scored.public_data: USACE FUDS inventory and ASRs, DERP reports, CORONA/KH imagery, historic aerials, assessor data.
scored.frame: The rung is buying a discounted parcel near a FUDS footprint, showing it is clean, and reselling it. Discovery (reading Archive Search Reports and range maps) is maybe 40-50% of the work (my estimate). The physical proving step is not trivial: a geophysical survey (drone magnetometry works for ferrous items, but buried UXO usually needs ground-based EM/DGM on cleared ground), any anomaly digs, then a regulatory sign-off that a private owner cannot reliably get. USACE does not issue "no further action" letters to private buyers on request; it works on its own DERP priority schedule. Liability and title-insurance work also sits inside the rung. So the regulator and the physical survey, not discovery, are the bottleneck. This is closer to the geothermal-in-coal-mines counter-example than to Terranox.
scored.step_up: Unproven: rural land near a FUDS, where the candidate claims a 50-90% discount. I could not verify that claim because the search budget was used up. From what I know of the literature, stigma discounts near contaminated sites are typically 10-30%, and most FUDS acreage is cheap rural or agricultural land priced around $1-10k/acre (estimate). Proven: ordinary market value of the same parcel. That gives a realistic step-up of about 1.2-3x, or up to 10x only in rare cases of a deep discount next to a growth corridor. This is nowhere near the 10^4 step from $1/ha to $10,000/ha in the rubric. The candidate's own estimate of ~2-10x, and its own comparison to the killed powered-brownfields idea, agree.
scored.hit_rate_capex: My estimates, not verified this run. Most land adjacent to a FUDS is in fact clean, because munitions concentrate in impact areas and the Archive Search Reports already outline them. So the base rate of a parcel turning out clean is high (likely over 70%), and since the lever is capped at 1/base hit rate, ML can improve the hit rate by at most about 1.4x. Cost per proving attempt: survey roughly $200-1,500/acre for drone or ground DGM plus anomaly reacquisition (estimate), plus legal and regulatory work. The expensive part is the regulatory concurrence and liability, not finding the right parcel, so ML does not cut proving capex 10x.
scored.data: The data is public but partly legible. USACE publishes the FUDS inventory and a GIS layer with property boundaries, munitions response site (MRS) polygons, and status fields: NDAI (No DoD Action Indicated), Response Complete, and the project phase. Archive Search Reports and DERP annual reports are public PDFs. Under the gold rubric's test, the outcome largely sits in a legible field already, because regulators have drawn the footprint polygons and status codes. The illegible ASR scans add some value at polygon edges. The right can be bought, since parcels are fee simple from private owners, but owners and their brokers can look up the same FUDS GIS layer, so the information asymmetry is thin.
scored.right_bought: Fee simple purchase of private parcels inside or next to FUDS boundaries. This can be bought, but the discount is unverified and probably modest. Owners near clean FUDS areas often see no discount at all, because the status is already NDAI in public records.
scored.buyer: Homebuilders, solar and data-center site aggregators, and timber REITs are well capitalised. But they buy on ordinary land comps and will still demand their own Phase I and UXO due diligence and an indemnity, so they will not pay a big premium for a startup's survey.
scored.ladder: Weak. Possible rungs above: entitlement and development of the parcels, or becoming a UXO remediation contractor. Both are crowded, low-margin service businesses already served by contractors such as Parsons, Tetra Tech and the USA Environmental/Weston-style firms. There is no clear path to a trillion-dollar company.
scored.fatal_flaw: The step-up is roughly 1.2-3x on land that is already cheap. The answer to the hunt is already written into the public USACE FUDS GIS polygons and NDAI/Response Complete status fields, which removes both the information edge and the purchase discount. On top of that, the proving step depends on a regulator sign-off (USACE or the state) that a private buyer cannot get on demand. This repeats the powered-brownfields failure.
scored.one_line_reason: This is a stigma-arbitrage version of the killed brownfields idea: a small, unverified discount, an outcome already in public USACE status fields, a high base clean rate, and a regulatory bottleneck instead of a discovery bottleneck.
sources: No live sources: the shared web search limit (200 per turn) was already used up when this agent started, so neither of my 2 attempted searches ran. Every number here is my estimate from prior knowledge and is labelled as one.
USACE FUDS program and public FUDS GIS/inventory with NDAI and status fields (prior knowledge; https://www.usace.army.mil/Missions/Environmental/Formerly-Used-Defense-Sites/)
DoD Defense Environmental Restoration Program annual reports to Congress (prior knowledge; https://denix.osd.mil/derp/)
General hedonic literature on property stigma near contaminated sites, typically 10-30% discounts (prior knowledge, not verified this run)

scored.name: Levee Re-Accreditation Land Bank
scored.one_line: Assemble land behind de-accredited levees that are physically sound; ML over USACE inspection reports and geotech ranks recertifiable levees; fund 44 CFR 65.10 certification and LOMR; sell developable land.
scored.unproven_right: Options or fee on ag/industrial land carrying AE stigma.
scored.proving_step: Levee engineering certification and FEMA LOMR ($0.5-3M per system).
scored.proven_buyer: Industrial/logistics developers, homebuilders, data-center site developers.
scored.public_data: USACE National Levee Database, FEMA levee layers and PAL lists, levee district records, 3DEP.
scored.frame: The rung would be: option land behind a de-accredited levee, get the levee certified and a LOMR issued, then sell the land as out of the floodplain. Proving is mostly not discovery. Picking the levee is maybe 20-30% of the work (my estimate). The rest is physical and political: geotech borings, freeboard and seepage analysis, very often actual repairs (raising crowns, relief wells, closures), an O&M plan adopted by the levee sponsor, and FEMA review that takes 1-3 years. Like the coal-mine geothermal counter-example, the bespoke build-out (here, recertifying and often fixing a public structure) is harder than finding the right levee. The company also cannot run the proving step on its own: 44 CFR 65.10 certification has to be submitted by or through the community or levee sponsor, which is a public levee or drainage district.
scored.step_up: My estimate (no search budget left to verify): ag or industrial land in an AE zone behind a non-accredited levee might trade at roughly $3k-15k/acre. The same land shown as Zone X (protected) next to metro logistics corridors might bring $30k-150k/acre. That is about 3-10x, and much less where the land stays agricultural, since flood-zone status hardly affects farm value. Land behind levees also often trades at only a small stigma discount, because buyers already price in a likely re-accreditation or LAMP remap. This is far from the 10^3-10^4 step-up the rubric wants.
scored.hit_rate_capex: These are estimates, not looked up. Cost per attempt: the candidate's own $0.5-3M per levee system for certification engineering and the LOMR, before any physical repairs, which often run $10M-100M+ per system. Base hit rate: I estimate that of the levees de-accredited since FEMA's Map Modernization era (about 2005-2013), only 20-40% could be recertified without capital works. So the ML lever is capped at about 2.5-5x, not 10x. Also, most of the cost is the engineering and repairs on the levee you pick, not wasted shots on wrong levees.
scored.data: The outcome is already in legible fields. The USACE National Levee Database publishes inspection ratings (Acceptable / Minimally Acceptable / Unacceptable), a Levee Safety Action Classification risk class, and the FEMA accreditation status. FEMA's NFHL publishes accredited, provisionally accredited (PAL) and non-accredited levee layers. FEMA's LAMP process already gives partial credit to sound non-accredited levees. Levee districts, engineering firms and local governments know their own levees well. Any remaining edge in unstructured inspection PDFs is small. That matches the prior pattern where regulators write the answer into status fields.
scored.right_bought: The land can be optioned from farmers, but the asset that actually gets proven is the levee, and that belongs to a public district. Certification lifts every parcel behind the levee, not only the ones the company holds, so neighbours ride free. Once the district starts a certification effort, the news is public and land prices adjust before the LOMR is issued. The company cannot hold the step-up exclusively.
scored.buyer: Industrial and logistics developers, homebuilders and data-center site developers are well capitalised and do pay for Zone X land. But many of them would buy AE land anyway and elevate the pad (fill is cheap, roughly $5-20/cubic yard, my estimate), which caps how much certification is worth to them.
scored.ladder: The rungs above would be horizontal land development, then vertical development, then becoming a levee operator or private flood-infrastructure owner. That is a real path into land development, which is a large but fragmented, low-multiple industry. It is not a trillion-dollar chain. The levee-operator rung runs into public ownership and liability limits.
scored.fatal_flaw: The proving step is not discovery. It is engineering, often repairs, on a public structure the company does not own, and it needs the levee sponsor to cooperate. The resulting value goes to every landowner behind the levee, and the outcome is already published in NLD and FEMA status fields. The step-up is only about 3-10x.
scored.one_line_reason: This fails like the coal-mine geothermal counter-example: recertifying (and often fixing) a public levee is harder than finding it. The company cannot own the levee or the uplift, the step-up is only about 3-10x, and NLD and FEMA fields already summarise the outcome.
sources: Web search budget for this turn was exhausted (shared 200-call limit); no searches returned results. All numbers above are estimates from prior knowledge and should be verified.
44 CFR 65.10 (FEMA mapping of areas protected by levee systems) - https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-44/chapter-I/subchapter-B/part-65/section-65.10
USACE National Levee Database - https://levees.sec.usace.army.mil
FEMA Levee Analysis and Mapping Procedures (LAMP) - https://www.fema.gov/flood-maps/living-levees

scored.name: Burn-Lot Rebuild Rights
scored.one_line: After wildfires, buy burned lots from owners who think they cannot rebuild; ML over scanned permit histories proves legal-nonconforming or like-for-like rights; sell permit-ready lots.
scored.unproven_right: Burned lot at salvage land value.
scored.proving_step: Permit-history reconstruction plus rebuild permit ($10-30k).
scored.proven_buyer: Rebuild and modular developers, institutional SFR, returning owners.
scored.public_data: County permit microfiche, assessor sketches, emergency rebuild ordinances, CAL FIRE DINS.
scored.frame: The candidate rung is a permit-ready burned lot. Discovery (rebuilding the permit history) is maybe 20-40% of the work in that rung; the rest is entitlement processing, debris clearance, surveys, soils and fire-hardening review. Discovery is not the bottleneck either. After the January 2025 LA fires, the state order (Newsom EO N-29-25, CEQA and Coastal Act suspension for rebuilds up to about 110% of the old footprint) and the city order (LA Mayor Executive Order 1) gave blanket like-for-like rebuild rights. Most California zoning codes already let owners rebuild disaster-destroyed nonconforming structures. The value comes from vertical construction, which is the hard bespoke step, so this has the same shape as the geothermal counter-example. Estimate from memory; no search this run.
scored.step_up: From memory, not verified this run: Palisades burned lots traded at roughly $1.5-4M against pre-fire home values of about $3-5M+, and Altadena lot listings ran about $0.5-1M. A burned lot sells at land value, and land is about 60-80% of total value in these markets. A permit-ready lot might fetch about 1.1-1.5x a raw burned lot. Taking it all the way to a rebuilt home is about 2-3x on land cost, but that needs $500-1,000+/sqft of construction. On the rung itself the step-up is under 3x, so C2 = 1.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Estimates: the proving step costs about $10-30k (the candidate's figure; permit-history pull plus expediter and plan check). The base hit rate is high: most burned lots in the Jan 2025 burn areas can rebuild like-for-like under the emergency orders, which I estimate at 80%+. With a hit rate that high the lever (capped at 1/hit rate) is about 1.2x, not 10x. ML would only help on edge cases: unpermitted additions, ADUs, hillside or coastal lots.
scored.data: The data is partly illegible: county permit microfiche and assessor sketches are scanned and scattered. But the outcome is already written down in legible form. Emergency ordinances give blanket like-for-like rights. CAL FIRE DINS publishes damage status per parcel. LA County and City run public rebuild portals and Recovery Permit Centers that pull permit history for owners for free, and assessor records give square footage. On buying the rights: lots can be bought, but after the fires California restricted unsolicited lowball offers on burn-area property for a period (Newsom executive order; I don't remember the number). Owners also became flooded with investor offers and are price-aware, so the information gap is small. The discount mostly reflects time and construction cost, not misread rights.
scored.right_bought: A burned residential lot in fee simple at salvage land value. It is ownable, but there is little purchase discount: burn-area pricing is public and heavily competed, and state anti-predatory-offer rules apply.
scored.buyer: Capitalised buyers exist: rebuild and modular builders (e.g. production builders and prefab firms active in Altadena and the Palisades), institutional SFR funds, and returning owners. They pay land value plus a small premium for entitlement certainty, not a multiple.
scored.ladder: The ladder is plausible: permit-ready lots, then a modular rebuild GC, then a build-to-rent or for-sale homebuilder, then a fire-hardened community developer, then insurance or recovery finance. The upper rungs are ordinary homebuilding with thin margins, and they are where the value sits. Supply is episodic and tied to disaster events.
scored.fatal_flaw: Rebuild rights are handed out wholesale by emergency order, and the money is in construction, not discovery. Emergency ordinances (state EO N-29-25 and LA Mayor EO 1) and standard nonconforming-rebuild clauses already grant like-for-like rights to nearly every burned lot, and DINS plus the county rebuild portals make that legible. ML has nothing hidden to find, the step-up on the rung is under 3x, and the real value sits in bespoke vertical construction.
scored.one_line_reason: Weak: rebuild rights are near-universal and already granted by emergency order, the hit rate is high so ML adds little, and the step-up is about 1.1-1.5x on the rung, with value tied up in construction, like the geothermal counter-example.

City of Los Angeles Mayor Executive Order 1 (Jan 2025) - expedited like-for-like rebuild permitting (from memory)
CAL FIRE Damage Inspection (DINS) public parcel-level data (from memory)
California executive order restricting unsolicited below-market offers on fire-area property, Jan 2025 (from memory)

scored.name: SeniorWater / Tax-Sale Mining Water: senior surface rights on tax-forfeited parcels and patented claims
scored.one_line: In CO/UT/NM/ID/MT, ML reads 1870s-1950s decrees, ditch ledgers and BLM patents to find tax-deed parcels and patented mining claims whose senior surface rights or ditch shares were never abandoned; buy for a few thousand, perfect and change the right in water court, sell to cities, ski towns and fabs. Surface water only.
scored.unproven_right: Dormant senior rights or ditch shares attached to $1-20k parcels.
scored.proving_step: Extract priority, flow and diversion point, link to parcel, screen forfeiture via historic imagery and abandonment lists; water-court change case.
scored.proven_buyer: Front Range and Utah municipalities, mountain districts and ski resorts, data centers and fabs, water trusts ($20-100k+/AF).
scored.public_data: Colorado CDSS/HydroBase and scanned decrees, State Engineer abandonment lists, Utah DWRi and NM OSE files, BLM GLO patents, county tax-lien lists, NAIP.
scored.rough_step_up: ~10^2-10^3x on hits; most old rights are abandoned.
scored.frame: The rung is "buy the dormant right, then perfect it and get the change decree," and that is mostly a legal and engineering step, not discovery. My estimate: finding the right is only about 20-30% of the work. The other 70-80% is the water-court change case: a historic consumptive-use (HCU) engineering study, objectors, and a 2-7 year trial or settlement. This is the geothermal-in-coal-mines pattern: making the right usable (the 'bespoke plant') is much harder than finding it. It is not a separate, sellable rung where drilling is trivial.
scored.step_up: Unproven: the parcel price, $1-20k (the candidate's figure). Proven: Front Range consumptive water sells for roughly $25-60k per acre-foot (AF), and C-BT units have traded around $70-100k per unit. These figures are from memory of 2023-24 reports; I could not check them this run. A hit worth about 20 AF of firm transferable consumptive use would be $0.5-1.2M, so about 50-500x on purchase price. But under the HCU rule, a right that has been dormant transfers almost no yield, so the true step-up on dormant rights is close to 1x. The hits that do transfer are rights with a documented diversion history, and those are already known and priced.
scored.hit_rate_capex: My estimate: the base hit rate for a dormant senior right surviving abandonment and the HCU analysis is under 5%. Cost per proving attempt (HCU study plus water attorney plus change case) is roughly $100k-$1M+ and takes 2-7 years. That is from general knowledge of Colorado practice and was not verified this run. ML can only lower the cost of screening documents, which is a small share of that spend. The lever is well under 10x because each attempt's cost is legal and adversarial, not search.
scored.data: The outcome is already in legible public fields. Colorado HydroBase/CDSS holds structured fields for appropriation date, adjudication date, priority admin number, decreed amount, diversion structure location and decades of diversion records. The State Engineer publishes decennial abandonment lists (most recently around 2020) that name the rights it considers abandoned. Utah DWRi and NM OSE also keep digitised water-right databases. Diversion records are the very evidence used for HCU and abandonment, so the answer is already written down. The illegible layer (scanned old decrees, ditch-company ledgers) adds only a little on top.
scored.right_bought: Partly. Colorado water rights can be severed from land and are often reserved or conveyed separately, so a tax deed may not carry the water. Ditch shares are company stock, transferred in company records, not by the parcel deed. Rights that can be bought cheaply are cheap because they lack use history. Sellers who still hold valuable rights are approached by brokers and cities (Aurora, Thornton, Greeley, Castle Rock) and by water funds such as Water Asset Management, so they rarely sell at a discount.
scored.buyer: The buyers are real and well capitalised: Front Range municipalities (Aurora, Thornton, Castle Rock, Parker), Utah Wasatch Front cities, ski districts, data centres and fabs, and water trusts. But they mostly buy decreed, quantified consumptive use with a change decree done or nearly done, not dormant paper rights.
scored.ladder: Limited. The rungs above are water-rights aggregation, storage and augmentation plans, and wholesale water supply or utility. That is a large regional business but heavily regulated and politically constrained (buy-and-dry backlash, anti-speculation doctrine, Colorado's 2022-23 water speculation scrutiny). It is not a clear path to a trillion-dollar company.
scored.fatal_flaw: The historic consumptive-use and anti-speculation rules. In Colorado (and in Utah and NM, with forfeiture after 5-7 years of non-use), a change case can only move the water that was historically used, quantified over a representative study period. So a dormant right, which is exactly what this strategy targets, yields close to zero transferable acre-feet even if no one formally abandoned it. The rights that do carry value have diversion records already in HydroBase and are already priced by the market.
scored.one_line_reason: Proving is a multi-year adversarial water-court case, not cheap discovery. The outcome is already in HydroBase diversion records and the abandonment lists. And the HCU rule means dormant rights transfer almost no water, so the 10^2-10^3x step-up mostly does not exist.

scored.name: Dormant Vintages: unissued credits on lapsed registered carbon projects
scored.one_line: Buy rights to unverified 2021+ vintages on dormant registered projects that kept running; prove operation with ML plus satellite and grid data; commission verification; sell (CORSIA-eligible where authorised).
scored.unproven_right: Rights to unverified reductions written off by developers.
scored.proving_step: ML estimate of continued operation, VVB verification ($30-80k).
scored.proven_buyer: CORSIA airlines, compliance and voluntary buyers, traders.
scored.public_data: Verra/Gold Standard documents, CDM database and A6.4 transition list, grid data, Sentinel/Landsat.
scored.frame: The rung would be buying unissued vintages and getting them verified and issued. Discovery is maybe 10-20% of that work (estimate). Finding dormant projects is a simple registry filter, because Verra, Gold Standard and CDM all publish status and last-issuance dates. The real work is getting the owner's monitoring records (meter or grid-export data, as the approved methodologies require), passing a VVB site audit, and, for CORSIA, getting a host-country Letter of Authorization with a corresponding adjustment. A satellite or ML estimate of 'it kept running' cannot stand in for the monitored data the methodology requires. So the physical and bureaucratic step is not trivial, and the frame fails C1.
scored.step_up: These numbers are my estimates from prior knowledge, not checked this run because the search budget was used up. Unverified reductions on a dormant project are worth about $0-0.5/t, assuming an owner sells at all. Once verified, legacy renewable or cookstove VCUs sell for about $1-5/t. CORSIA Phase 1 eligible units with an LoA have traded around $15-25/t. That is at most about 10-50x, and only on the CORSIA path, which LoA scarcity limits, not verification. On the common path it is about 3-10x. Nothing like Terranox's $1 to $10,000/ha jump.
scored.hit_rate_capex: These are estimates and could not be verified because search was unavailable this run. A VVB verification costs about $30-80k (the figure given with the candidate; my prior range is $15-60k). Add $5-20k for monitoring reconstruction and registry fees. The base hit rate for 'the plant kept running' is already high, perhaps 50-80% for grid-connected hydro, wind or solar, and it can be checked from public grid or generation data without ML. Failures come from missing monitoring data, a lapsed crediting period, methodology changes, or no LoA, none of which ML fixes. Because the lever is capped at 1/base hit rate, it is only about 1.3-2x.
scored.data: The data is public but mostly legible. Registry status, crediting periods and last issuance date are structured fields in Verra, Gold Standard, CDM and the A6.4 transition list. Plant operation shows up in grid-operator generation data, and satellite images add little. The outcome (still operating, eligible for issuance) is close to already summarised, which removes the ML edge. Not the scanned, illegible archive that gives Terranox its edge.
scored.right_bought: The right is weak. The project proponent keeps the issuance rights and holds the monitoring data. A third party cannot verify without the owner's cooperation, and the owner can see the same registry and grid data, so there is no information gap to buy cheaply against. Owners who stopped did so because the economics were poor (low prices, verification cost, integrity scrutiny on large renewables, which Verra and Gold Standard excluded for non-LDCs from about 2019-2020). They did not stop because they misjudged the value. Some brokers and aggregators already do 'reactivation' deals (e.g., carbon trading desks and CDM-to-A6.4 transition consultants; I did not check this run who is active in 2026).
scored.buyer: There are capitalised buyers. Airlines need CORSIA Phase 1 (2024-2026) units, and voluntary and corporate buyers and traders also buy. But CORSIA demand only takes authorised units with corresponding adjustments, and the binding constraint is host-country LoAs, not verified supply of old vintages. Voluntary demand for legacy renewable credits is weak and low-priced.
scored.ladder: The ladder is modest. Next rungs would be project development and origination, owning a carbon project developer, and trading and retirement services. It is a mid-sized commodity market (voluntary market about $0.5-1B a year in recent years, my estimate) with integrity risk. Not a trillion-dollar chain: the top of this ladder is a project developer or trader, not a mine-scale capital asset.
scored.fatal_flaw: Proving needs the owner's own monitoring data and a host-country Letter of Authorization, which ML cannot supply. The 'is it still operating' signal is already legible in registry and grid data. So there is no information gap to buy against and no step-up near 10^3.
scored.one_line_reason: Finding dormant projects is a registry filter. The hard part is the owner's meter data, a VVB audit and an LoA, and the price uplift is about 3-30x on credits whose value buyers are already discounting for integrity concerns.

scored.name: Deep Peat Finder: Peatland Code rights on upland grazing
scored.one_line: Buy carbon rights or land on drained eroding deep peat priced as rough grazing; ML over legacy soil surveys, LiDAR and Sentinel proves depth and condition; grant-funded drain blocking; sell Peatland Code units.
scored.unproven_right: Peatland carbon rights or freehold at £1.5-5k/ha.
scored.proving_step: ML prediction plus probe survey (£20-50/ha), validation; cheap grant-funded restoration.
scored.proven_buyer: UK corporates, natural-capital funds (Gresham House, Aviva), water utilities.
scored.public_data: Scottish and EA LiDAR, Soil Survey of Scotland maps, 2016 Carbon and Peatland map, UK Land Carbon Registry, RoS/HMLR.
scored.frame: The rung is "registered Peatland Code project with validated Pending Issuance Units (PIUs)." Discovery (finding deep peat that is drained or eroding) is roughly 10-20% of the work inside that rung. That is my estimate. Most of the effort goes elsewhere: agreeing a 30-100 year land-use commitment with the owner, getting a validator to sign off on a restoration plan, physically blocking drains and reprofiling gullies with diggers on remote upland, then monitoring and verifying for decades. Restoration is not trivial. It is the main physical step, and it is grant-funded only when Peatland Action or Nature for Climate budgets allow. Credits are issued as ex-ante PIUs that turn into verified units over time, so most of the value only arrives after restoration and verification. Capitalised buyers do exist: UK corporates, natural-capital funds and water utilities.
scored.step_up: From memory, because the search budget had run out. Upland rough grazing in Scotland or northern England sells for about £1.5-5k/ha, and is already priced up by natural-capital demand since 2021. Claimable reductions on actively eroding or drained peat come to roughly 100-400 tCO2e/ha over the project life, after the risk buffer (estimate). PIUs trade at about £15-30/t, so gross credit value is about £2-10k/ha, before restoration, validation and monitoring costs. The upside is about 1.5-3x the land price, and nowhere near 10^3. Land prices already include the carbon option: the Scottish market saw a 'natural capital premium' in 2021-23 sales.
scored.hit_rate_capex: The base hit rate is high, not low. Deep peat (Class 1/2 on the 2016 Carbon and Peatland map) and its broad condition (erosion and drainage are visible on aerial imagery and LiDAR) are already mapped. A field probe survey costs about £20-50/ha (from the candidate brief, consistent with consultant rates), and I estimate that over 50% of map-identified Class 1 sites confirm as eligible. With a hit rate that high, the ML lever is capped below about 2x, not 10x. Restoration costs about £1-3k/ha (Peatland Action range, estimate), and that dwarfs the cost of proving.
scored.data: The signal is public and already legible. NatureScot's Carbon and Peatland 2016 map, the Soil Survey of Scotland, the EA and Scottish LiDAR, and the UK Land Carbon Registry are all structured, published and used as standard by consultants. The outcome (deep peat, plus a modified or eroding condition) is essentially a mapped field already. ML adds only marginal refinement, such as finer depth and condition estimates. Landowners and agents (Savills, Strutt & Parker, Galbraith) actively market the carbon potential, so sellers do not lack this information.
scored.right_bought: Freehold or a long carbon lease or option can be bought from estates and farmers. They are not free first-come, but they are not mispriced either. The natural-capital boom has priced upland peat as carbon land, and land agents advertise Peatland Code potential, so the information asymmetry needed for a cheap purchase is largely gone.
scored.buyer: UK corporates buying PIUs for insetting or net-zero claims, natural-capital funds (Gresham House, Aviva, Par Equity, Highlands Rewilding investors), water utilities (catchment benefits) and the Scottish Government's blended-finance pilots. The buyer pool is real but thin, and PIU prices are soft. Competitors and incumbents are numerous: Forest Carbon, Nature-based Solutions developers, Scottish Woodlands, the Peatland Code project developers listed by IUCN UK, and estate-owner consortia.
scored.ladder: Modest. The rungs above are restoration contracting, stacking biodiversity and water payments, and owning and operating an upland natural-capital estate portfolio. It is a capped, policy-dependent market: UK upland peat is about 2-3 Mha, with roughly 80% degraded, and the credits are voluntary-market. The chain leads to a decent natural-capital fund, not a trillion-dollar company.
scored.fatal_flaw: The thing to be discovered is already legibly mapped (2016 Carbon and Peatland map, LiDAR) and already priced into upland land values. On top of that, the physical restoration step, plus 30-100 years of permanence and monitoring, dominates the rung. So there is no 80%+ discovery frame, no low hit rate for ML to lever, and only about a 1.5-3x step-up.
scored.one_line_reason: Peat is already mapped and priced, and restoration, not discovery, is the work. The step-up is about 2-3x with a high base hit rate, so the Terranox mechanism does not apply.

scored.name: Species Bank: eDNA-proven endangered-species conservation credits
scored.one_line: Option rangeland where ML over EIR/EIS appendices and museum records predicts undocumented listed species, prove with eDNA, entitle a conservation bank, sell credits to mitigating developers. Near killed wetland bank idea.
scored.unproven_right: Option or fee at $3-10k/acre.
scored.proving_step: eDNA ($300-800/sample) and protocol surveys, 2-5 year bank entitlement.
scored.proven_buyer: Caltrans, HSR, PG&E, solar/transmission developers, homebuilders.
scored.public_data: CEQAnet, EPA EIS database, USFWS ECOS, RIBITS, GBIF/VertNet, NAIP.
scored.frame: The candidate rung is "own rangeland, prove a listed species is there, sell conservation credits." Discovery is only about 10-20% of the work in that rung (my estimate). Most of the work is the bespoke regulatory build: a 2-5+ year USFWS/CDFW bank agreement, a permanent conservation easement, a non-wasting endowment (often $1-5k/acre, estimate), a long-term management plan, habitat restoration, and staged credit release. That is the geothermal-in-coal-mines counter-example again, where entitlement is much harder than finding the right parcel. Nobody buys the output of the discovery step alone, i.e. a parcel with eDNA-confirmed presence but no entitlement. Developers buy only agency-released credits inside a service area that has demand.
scored.step_up: These are recalled from memory, because the shared web search budget was used up before this run and no searches returned results. Unproven: Central Valley or foothill rangeland at about $3-10k/acre (the candidate's figure, consistent with USDA/ASFMRA pasture values I remember). Proven: released credits at roughly $20-80k/acre for California tiger salamander or giant garter snake, and about $100-300k+/acre for vernal pool preservation in the Sacramento region (recalled Westervelt and Wildlands price ranges, not verified). Gross that is about 5-30x. Net of endowment, easement, restoration, legal costs and 3-7 years of carry, I estimate 2-8x on capital, realised slowly as credits are released and sold. It is not an immediate step-up on a hit.
scored.hit_rate_capex: eDNA costs about $300-800 per sample (candidate's figure; I remember commercial lab pricing in the same range), and protocol surveys run about $5-30k per site-season (my estimate). Both are cheap compared with the entitlement cost. The base hit rate is not low: banks are sited inside known ranges and critical habitat mapped by CNDDB, where I estimate presence probability is high (above 30-50%). So the lever (at most 1/hit rate) is under 3x, and it acts on a cost line that is a small share of total capex. ML cannot cut overall capex anywhere near 10x.
scored.data: The outcome is already in legible public fields. CNDDB/BIOS occurrence points, USFWS critical habitat shapefiles, ECOS species ranges, and RIBITS bank locations, service areas and credit ledgers are structured and used routinely by consultants. EIR/EIS appendices add a little marginal signal, but surveyed parcels are usually already logged in CNDDB. The value driver is credit demand within a service area, which RIBITS and pipeline projects make legible, not hidden species presence. The prior hunt pattern applies: the regulator has already written the answer down.
scored.right_bought: The land can be bought or optioned, but at market rangeland prices, so there is no illegibility discount. Ranchers often understand that listed-species presence is a regulatory liability (Section 9 and CEQA exposure), and many have already been approached by bankers. Optioning for a multi-year entitlement period is possible, but sellers will want a share of the bank upside once they understand it.
scored.buyer: The buyers are capitalised and compelled by regulation: Caltrans, California HSR Authority, PG&E, solar and transmission developers, homebuilders. But they buy only agency-released credits, and only in service areas with active projects. Demand is lumpy and concentrated. Incumbent bankers include Westervelt Ecological Services, Wildlands Inc., Ecosystem Investment Partners, RES and Land Veritas, who already compete on siting.
scored.ladder: The ladder is short. Bank → full-delivery permittee-responsible mitigation → turnkey environmental permitting for infrastructure → possibly a land-and-entitlement platform. The total US compensatory mitigation market is roughly a few $B/year (my estimate, recalled figures of about $3-5B/yr for wetland plus species). Even winning it all is not a path to a trillion-dollar company.
scored.fatal_flaw: Discovery is not the bottleneck. Credit value comes from a bespoke, multi-year regulatory entitlement plus an endowment and a permanent easement, priced against service-area demand. Species presence is mostly already legible in CNDDB and critical habitat maps. This is the coal-mine geothermal counter-example, and the same flaw that killed wetland banks.
scored.one_line_reason: This is a wetland-bank clone. Entitlement and endowment, not discovery, make up 80%+ of the work and set the value. Species presence is already in legible public fields, the step-up is about 2-8x net and slow, and the ladder caps out at a few-$B market.

scored.name: Medicare Secondary Payer Claim Assignments
scored.one_line: Take assignments of conditional-payment recovery rights from small MA plans and IPAs; ML proves a primary payer; collect double damages. MSP Recovery is the cautionary precedent.
scored.unproven_right: Assigned MSP recovery rights.
scored.proving_step: Link trauma diagnoses to accident and court records.
scored.proven_buyer: Primary P&C insurers, funders.
scored.public_data: PI court dockets, crash reports, OSHA logs, CMS PUFs; core claims data private.
scored.frame: The rung would be holding an assigned MSP recovery right on one claim and proving a primary payer owed it. Discovery (matching a trauma claim to an accident, a tortfeasor and an insurer) is maybe 30-40% of the work in that rung. The other 60-70% is the physical step, and it is not trivial: litigation or demand letters against large P&C carriers who fight every claim. MSP Recovery's history shows collection, not discovery, is the bottleneck. There is also no capitalised buyer of a 'proven' claim before it is collected. Litigation funders buy only at deep discounts. P&C insurers 'buy' only by settling, and they are the adversary. This is closer to the geothermal-in-coal-mines counter-example: finding the claim is easier than collecting it. (Estimate.)
scored.step_up: The unproven right is usually assigned for a contingent split, often about 50% of recoveries, with little or no cash up front (recalled from MSP Recovery's assignment structure; I could not verify it here). So the 'price' is near zero, but that is a profit share, not a $1/ha purchase. A proven-but-uncollected claim is worth its face amount times the odds of collecting it. Double damages give at most 2x the conditional payment. Paid amounts on trauma claims run roughly $5k-$50k (my estimate). The headline step-up is large only because the starting price is near zero. The realistic proven-claim value is about 3-10x the expected value of an unproven one, not 10^3-10^4. MSP Recovery's own record (recalled, not verified): it booked tens of billions in 'paid value' and collected single-digit to low tens of millions, i.e. pennies on the dollar.
scored.hit_rate_capex: I estimate the base hit rate is low: perhaps 5-15% of trauma-coded claims have an identifiable liable primary payer. That leaves an ML lever of up to about 10x on discovery in theory. But identifying the claim is not the expensive step. Proving it is: attorney time, filings, and fighting causation and coverage, plausibly $5k-$50k+ per contested claim (estimate). ML does not cut that cost. Discovery itself is already cheap: it is database matching. All figures are estimates; my web search budget ran out before I could source them.
scored.data: This criterion largely fails. The core signal (who was treated, diagnosis codes, amounts paid) is private, HIPAA-protected claims data, not public. Personal-injury dockets and crash reports are public but scattered. The main problem is that the outcome is already partly written into a legible field. Under MMSEA Section 111, P&C, no-fault and workers' comp insurers must report to CMS every settlement, judgment or ongoing medical responsibility involving a Medicare beneficiary. CMS's recovery contractor (BCRC/CRC) then recovers for traditional Medicare. That reporting is the legible field that kills the ML edge. MA plans do not get Section 111 data directly, which is MSP Recovery's whole thesis. But recovery vendors such as Rawlings, Optum/Cotiviti, Conduent/HMS and Equian already run subrogation for most MA plans. As for buying the right cheaply: small MA plans and IPAs can and do assign, but the case law is messy. Humana v. Western Heritage (11th Cir. 2016) and In re Avandia (3d Cir. 2012) allow MA private double-damages suits. Many MSP Recovery suits were then dismissed for failing to tie a specific assigned claim to a specific beneficiary, or on assignment-chain standing.
scored.right_bought: An assignment of the MA plan's or IPA's MSP recovery rights (42 USC 1395y(b)(3)(A) double-damages claim plus subrogation), usually for a contingent share of recoveries.
scored.buyer: There is no clean buyer. P&C carriers pay only when forced to settle, and they are the defendants. Litigation funders may finance portfolios at heavy discounts. The original MA plan could buy back, but it already has incumbent vendors working on contingency.
scored.ladder: The rungs above are thin. You could go from assignments to a full payment-integrity or subrogation platform, then to owning risk (becoming an MA plan or IPA yourself). That is a services business or an insurer, not a trillion-dollar vertical stack. Becoming an MA plan does not get better because you won recovery claims.
scored.fatal_flaw: The value is captured by collecting from adversarial, well-funded insurers, not by discovery. The outcome is already partly summarised in Section 111 mandatory insurer reporting to CMS, and incumbent subrogation vendors already work the MA side. MSP Recovery/LifeWallet is the empirical proof: it booked tens of billions in assigned 'paid value', collected pennies, and its equity collapsed more than 99% from its SPAC valuation.
scored.one_line_reason: Discovery is cheap database matching and collection is expensive litigation, which inverts the 95/5 frame. The core data is private PHI, Section 111 reporting already legibly records primary payers, and MSP Recovery's collapse shows the step-up does not materialise.

scored.name: Antitrust Claims of Dead and Small Businesses
scored.one_line: Buy unfiled shares in large antitrust and class settlements (interchange, broilers, pork, beef, seafood, generic drugs) from dissolved and small businesses for a few hundred dollars or 5-10 cents; ML reconstructs purchase volume from public records; file accepted claims.
scored.unproven_right: Assignable direct-purchaser and settlement claims.
scored.proving_step: Class membership and volume reconstruction to claims-administrator acceptance.
scored.proven_buyer: Claims-trading funds (Chicago Clearing, Spectrum, Vintage), funders, opt-out aggregators (50-80% of payout).
scored.public_data: SoS dissolutions, PACER schedules, USDA/AMS records, procurement awards, settlement notices, health permits, UCC filings.
scored.rough_step_up: ~5-1000x depending on claim; crowded, partly legible process.
scored.frame: The rung is 'buy an unfiled claim, establish membership and volume, get the claims administrator to accept it.' Most of the work in it is legal and operational, not discovery: tracing who is entitled to act for a dissolved entity, getting the assignment signed, checking the claim is assignable, and filing. My estimate is that only about 30-40% is finding claims and reconstructing volume. In the biggest settlements discovery is barely needed at all. In MDL 1720 (interchange), the administrator pre-filled claim forms with interchange paid, using Visa and Mastercard transaction data. In the protein direct-purchaser cases (broilers, pork, beef), payouts are computed from the defendants' own sales data. There is a capitalised buyer: claims-trading funds such as Chicago Clearing Corp and Spectrum.
scored.step_up: Estimate, not sourced. An unproven claim sells to an aggregator for about 5-20% of its expected payout, typically as an upfront payment on interchange. Once the administrator accepts it, it trades at about 50-80% of payout, per the candidate's own figure. That is a 3-10x step-up. It reaches 100x+ only for tiny claims bought for nominal sums, and those are capped at a few hundred to a few thousand dollars each. Nowhere near 10^3-10^4 on meaningful dollars.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Estimate. Filing costs very little: a claim form, roughly tens to hundreds of dollars of labour each. Acceptance rates for legitimate members are high, likely more than 70%. The real constraint is the low share of eligible members who file. Class-action claim rates are often in the single digits, per the FTC's 2019 consumer class action report, which put the median at about 4-9%. That gap is about reaching owners, not about proving claims. So the ML lever on proving cost is small: the base hit rate is already high, and 1/hit-rate is at most 1.5x. No web numbers were gathered because the shared search budget was exhausted.
scored.data: The outcome is largely already summarised in legible data the administrator holds. In interchange, card networks and acquirers supplied merchant-level fee data and the forms came pre-populated. In protein direct-purchaser classes, the defendants' transaction records define volume. Public but illegible sources (SoS dissolutions, UCC filings, health permits, USDA/AMS records) mainly help find dead or small claimants. They help much less in proving volume, and indirect purchasers still need receipts or other evidence. Rights can be bought. But claims of dissolved entities need someone with authority to act (a former officer, trustee or successor), and some settlements restrict or scrutinise third-party filers. The MDL 1720 court has issued warnings about claims-filing companies.
scored.right_bought: Yes. Direct-purchaser claims are generally assignable and are bought for a few hundred dollars or 5-20 cents on the dollar. For dissolved businesses, getting valid authority to sell is the hard, non-ML part. Courts and administrators are increasingly scrutinising third-party filers.
scored.buyer: Settlement-claims funds and traders (Chicago Clearing Corp, Spectrum Settlement Recovery, Vintage-type buyers), litigation funders, and opt-out aggregators. They are capitalised, but they are also direct competitors that already run outbound campaigns to the same claimants.
scored.ladder: Weak ladder. The rungs above are opt-out direct actions, litigation funding, and eventually originating antitrust cases as a plaintiff-side firm or fund. That is a niche of a few billion dollars a year, it is regulated (the practice of law and champerty rules), and it does not climb into owning a physical value chain. It is a financial niche, not a trillion-dollar ladder.
scored.fatal_flaw: The outcome is already legible. In the largest settlements, the administrator computes each claim's value from defendant or card-network transaction data and pre-populates or allocates it. Proving is therefore close to free, has a high hit rate, and is not driven by discovery. What is left is a crowded race to reach and contract owners, already run by established claims-trading funds, with step-ups of only about 3-10x.
scored.one_line_reason: This is a crowded claims-aggregation arbitrage. Administrators already know claim volumes from defendant data, filing is cheap and rarely fails, and the step-up is about 3-10x rather than 10^3-10^4, so ML has almost no discovery lever.

scored.name: Revenant Corp / Zombie Entity Recovery
scored.one_line: Buy residual interests in dissolved companies for token sums, reinstate, and claim assets still owed (state unclaimed property, settlement shares, refunds, escrows, remnant parcels, court registry funds).
scored.unproven_right: Equity or residual-asset assignment of a dissolved entity, $100-2k.
scored.proving_step: Entity resolution across 50-state UP databases, claimant lists, parcel rolls and dockets; reinstate and file.
scored.proven_buyer: State UP programs, claims administrators, adjoiners; the company realises value itself.
scored.public_data: MissingMoney/NAUPA, SoS dissolved lists, assessor rolls titled to defunct corps, settlement notices, 28 USC 2042 registry funds.
scored.rough_step_up: ~20-1000x on hits; UP fields partly legible, finder-fee caps.
scored.frame: The rung is: buy the residual or assignment interest of a dissolved entity, reinstate it, and file claims. Inside that rung, finding assets is about 70-85% of the work. The physical steps are cheap: reinstatement fees are typically $50-1,000 plus back franchise taxes (my estimate), and filing is paperwork. But nobody buys this rung's output for more than it is worth. The 'buyer' is a state unclaimed-property (UP) program or a claims administrator paying a fixed amount it already owes. That is collecting a debt, not re-pricing an asset. Adjoiners buying remnant parcels are the only real buyers, and they are thin. Contested equity and title steps (proving you are the successor in interest to the claim) can easily be 30%+ of the work.
scored.step_up: Unproven: residual interest bought for $100-2,000 (candidate's figure). Proven: the cash claim itself, at face value. Most corporate UP holdings are small. Typical UP accounts are under $100, and NAUPA reports that states hold about $70B+ in total (from memory, not verified this session). Hits worth $10k-100k exist but are rare. On a hit the multiple is about 5-50x, not 10^3-10^4, and finder-fee or assignment limits in many states (roughly 10-35%, from memory, e.g. CA 10%, FL 20%) can cap the share you keep if the deal is treated as a finder agreement rather than a true equity purchase. No search numbers verified.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Estimates only; searches were unavailable. A proving attempt is cheap: database searches cost close to nothing, and reinstatement plus filing is about $500-3,000 including legal time. Because the main UP data is searchable, the hit rate on targeted deals is high once you pre-screen (estimate 30-60%). Low capex and a high base hit rate mean ML has little to cut: the lever is at most about 2-3x, not 10x.
scored.data: The core signal is already legible. MissingMoney/NAUPA and state UP portals publish owner name, holder and often an amount band in searchable fields. That is exactly the 'regulator wrote the answer into a status field' failure. Secretary of State (SoS) dissolved lists and assessor rolls are also structured. The more illegible pieces are scanned court dockets, 28 USC 2042 federal court registry funds and settlement notices. That is a real but narrow edge: registry funds total low billions nationally (estimate) and are spread across 94 districts.
scored.right_bought: Yes, the right is bought. Former officers or shareholders of dissolved companies will sell residual interests cheaply. But the sellers can search MissingMoney themselves for free, so the information gap is weak. Rules also make ownership hard to prove: who holds a dissolved entity's claims (shareholders after the winding-up period, survival statutes such as DGCL 278's 3-year survival period), anti-assignment rules, and state rules against assigning UP claims or limiting finder agreements. Any of these can void the purchase or turn it into a capped-fee agreement.
scored.buyer: State UP programs and claims administrators, who pay fixed amounts already owed and add no premium. Adjoining landowners for remnant parcels, a small market at low prices. Overall there is no capitalised buyer paying a large premium for a proven asset.
scored.ladder: Weak. The obvious next steps are buying distressed claims (bankruptcy claims trading, which already has many capitalised players), litigation-finance-style recovery, and tax-deed or remnant real estate. Each is a separate collection or arbitrage business, not higher rungs of one production chain. There is no 'whole mine' to integrate up to; the ceiling looks like a niche recovery firm in the tens of millions, not a path to a very large company.
scored.fatal_flaw: The outcome is already written in a legible public field. MissingMoney/state UP databases list owner and holder, so anyone, including the selling shareholder, can see the prize for free. And the 'proven' value is a fixed debt owed to you, not an asset that a capitalised buyer re-prices 10^3x. It is collection arbitrage with finder-fee caps and murky ownership of dissolved entities, not a discovery step-up.
scored.one_line_reason: Cheap rights and cheap proving, but the answer is already searchable, the payout is a fixed debt rather than a 10^3x re-pricing, the ML lever is small, and there is no ladder up a real production chain.

scored.name: Newsroom Morgue Holdings: defunct-newspaper photo archives
scored.one_line: Buy negatives and copyrights of defunct newspapers and photographers; scan; ML identifies subjects and proves copyright status by linking to published pages; license proven collections.
scored.unproven_right: Copyright plus negatives, $5-20k per archive.
scored.proving_step: Bulk scanning, face/event ID, notice and renewal checks.
scored.proven_buyer: Getty, Shutterstock, AP Images, Alamy, documentary producers, AI training licensees.
scored.public_data: Chronicling America, CCE periodical renewals, NYPL/Stanford renewal datasets, newspaper bankruptcy dockets, ArchiveGrid.
scored.frame: The rung would be: buy an archive, then scan it, identify what is in it and settle its rights. Discovery is maybe 20-30% of the work in that rung (my estimate). Most of the work is physical and has to be done for every image: cleaning, scanning and captioning millions of negatives at roughly $1-5 per frame (my estimate from memory of scanning-bureau rates). Applying ML to identify subjects comes after that cost has been paid; it does not reduce it. This is the coal-mine geothermal failure pattern: the physical step dominates. There is a capitalised buyer (Getty, AP), but it buys the whole collection or individual licences, not a proven right.
scored.step_up: Unproven: $5-20k per archive (the candidate's own figure; it matches my memory of eBay and estate sales of press-print morgues, unverified). Proven: an archive is worth its licensing income. Stock licence prices have collapsed (my memory: Alamy's average fee is in the tens of dollars per sale, and most archive images never sell). A well-captioned regional archive might be worth $50-300k as a library, or bring in a few $k-$10s of k a year (estimate). That is about 3-15x before scanning cost, and roughly 1x after it. AI-training licences pay cents per image (estimate). Nowhere near 10^3-10^4.
scored.hit_rate_capex: There is no low-hit-rate proving step to improve. Almost every archive 'hits' in the sense of holding some licensable images, so the base hit rate is high and 1/hit-rate gives ML little room. The cost of each attempt is the scanning, which is proportional to the number of frames: about $0.5-2.5M for a 500k-negative morgue at $1-5 per frame (estimate). ML captioning reduces labour, but not by 10x on the dominant cost, which is physical handling.
scored.data: The data is public but partly legible already. The renewal outcome is summarised in machine-readable datasets: the NYPL CCE renewal transcription and the Stanford copyright renewal database. These cover the 1923/28-1963 renewal question, which is the "outcome already in a legible field" problem. Chronicling America OCR is public, and LoC and others already do image-to-page linking. The ML edge is mostly face/event identification on images nobody has scanned, but that requires scanning first. Owners (heirs, bankruptcy trustees, small papers) do sell cheaply, so the rights can be bought (satisfied).
scored.right_bought: Yes. The physical negatives plus whatever copyright the paper held, bought from defunct papers, bankruptcy estates and photographers' heirs for roughly $5-20k. There is a catch: for photos published 1928-1963 without a renewal, which is the majority for periodicals (my estimate, over 90% unrenewed), there is no copyright to buy. Only the unpublished outtakes and the physical originals carry exclusivity.
scored.buyer: Getty Images (it has a long history of buying archives such as Hulton), AP Images, Shutterstock/Getty after their merger, Alamy (contributor-royalty model, not an acquirer), documentary clearance houses, and AI training licensees (which pay low per-image rates). Incumbents already in this business: Getty, Historic Images LLC (resells newspaper press prints), university and historical-society archives that take morgues as donations, and Shorpy-style curators. The space is crowded and margins are thin.
scored.ladder: Weak. The rungs above would be a large historical stock library (a Getty or Corbis competitor), media and documentary production, and AI-training data licensing. Corbis is the warning: Bill Gates spent heavily and sold it to Visual China in 2016 for a reported price under $200M (from memory). Historical stock imagery is a shrinking market. It does not lead to a trillion-dollar chain.
scored.fatal_flaw: Proving does not create the step-up; it often destroys value. Checking notices and renewals mostly proves that published images are in the public domain, so anyone can copy them. The remaining value sits in unpublished negatives, and getting at it requires costly per-frame physical scanning, which is the dominant cost. That makes this the coal-mine geothermal case, at roughly 10x gross and about 1x net of scanning, in a stock-photo market with collapsing prices.
scored.one_line_reason: Scanning is the dominant cost and discovery is a small part of the work. The step-up is about 10x before costs and about 1x after. Copyright checks mostly prove images are in the public domain. Historical stock licensing is a crowded, shrinking market.

scored.name: Orphan Typeface Rights + Usage Discovery
scored.one_line: Buy font libraries of defunct foundries and estates; ML detects the fonts across web, PDFs and apps to prove an unlicensed commercial base; sell to consolidators.
scored.unproven_right: Font software copyright and name trademarks, $5-50k.
scored.proving_step: Glyph classifiers over Common Crawl, HTTP Archive, EDGAR PDFs and APKs.
scored.proven_buyer: Monotype and similar consolidators.
scored.public_data: Common Crawl, HTTP Archive, EDGAR PDFs, APK mirrors, USPTO marks, Wayback foundry catalogs.
scored.frame: The rung would be: own a defunct foundry's font library and prove an unlicensed commercial user base. Finding the users is not 80%+ of the work. In the US, typeface designs cannot be copyrighted (37 CFR 202.1(e); Eltra v. Ringer, 1978). Only the font software can be. So spotting a glyph shape in a PDF or on a rendered page proves nothing legally, because the user may be running a legal clone. Turning a detection into money takes a demand letter, a forensic match on the font file, settlement talks and sometimes a lawsuit. That legal work is the hard, bespoke step, much as building the plant is in the geothermal counter-example. My estimate: discovery is 20-30% of the work and enforcement is 70%+.
scored.step_up: Unproven: orphan or estate font libraries change hands for about $5k-$50k (the candidate's own figure, not verified). Proven: consolidator deals I recall without checking: Monotype paid about $50M for Bitstream's font business (2012) and about $15M for FontShop (2014), and Monotype as a whole went private for about $825M (HGGC, 2019). Those prices are for libraries with brand names and live licensing revenue, not orphans. My estimate: a small library with a documented unlicensed base might sell for 3-10x its purchase price, or bring a few hundred thousand dollars in settlements. That is nowhere near 10^3. The candidate's 100-1000x is not supported.
scored.hit_rate_capex: The proving step is a cheap compute scan, not an expensive attempt that usually fails. Crawling HTTP Archive or Common Crawl for a font costs a few dollars to a few thousand dollars of compute (my estimate). So ML has no costly step to make more likely to hit, and there is no 10x capex cut to buy more shots. The real cost and risk is converting each hit into a payment, which works like copyright enforcement. My estimate: well under half of demand letters pay, and the money depends on legal process, not on detection accuracy.
scored.data: Legibility kills the ML edge. Web fonts are named outright in HTTP Archive and Common Crawl: CSS @font-face rules give the family name and the font file URL, so a string match finds them. Embedded fonts in EDGAR PDFs carry the font name in the PDF's /FontName field (BaseFont, often with a subset prefix). APKs bundle .ttf/.otf files whose name tables hold the family, foundry and copyright strings. So the outcome is already written into fields anyone can read. Glyph classifiers only add value against renamed or rasterised use, and that use is also the hardest to win in court. Monotype and others already run font-compliance audits and letter campaigns. Rights can be bought from estates (this part fits), but the sellers are not uninformed about anything ML would reveal.
scored.right_bought: Font software copyright plus any registered name trademarks, bought from defunct foundries or designer estates for about $5k-$50k (candidate's estimate, not verified). Weaknesses: the US gives the design no protection; the trademark covers only the name, which a clone can avoid; and chain of title from defunct foundries is often murky, which hurts enforcement.
scored.buyer: Monotype (private, HGGC-owned) and smaller aggregators. They buy libraries for their brand and recurring licensing revenue. They do not obviously pay a premium for a list of infringers, and they already run their own compliance enforcement.
scored.ladder: The rungs would be: orphan library, then a licensing storefront, then a type foundry or consolidator, then a typography platform. The top is small. The global font market is roughly $1-2B (my estimate), and Monotype was valued at about $825M when it went private in 2019. There is no trillion-dollar chain.
scored.fatal_flaw: Typeface designs cannot be copyrighted in the US, so detecting a glyph does not prove infringement, and the font name is already readable in the CSS, PDF and APK metadata. That leaves ML with no discovery edge. What remains is a litigation-heavy enforcement business in a market of about $1B with no 10^3 step-up.
scored.one_line_reason: Cheap, legible detection plus a hard legal step to monetise each hit, in a small market, makes this a weak copyright-enforcement play rather than a Terranox-style discovery play.

scored.name: Bankrupt-Brand Digital Asset Revival
scored.one_line: Buy domains, trademarks and handles of dead DTC and consumer-software brands in bankruptcy/ABC sales; ML measures residual traffic and search demand; sell proven bundles to revival rollups.
scored.unproven_right: IP bundle at $1k-25k.
scored.proving_step: ML over schedules plus Common Crawl links, Trends, Wayback; auction purchase and transfer.
scored.proven_buyer: Marquee Brands, Authentic Brands, Retrobrands, DTC aggregators.
scored.public_data: PACER/RECAP, trustee notices, TSDR, Common Crawl link graph, Wayback, Google Trends, zone files.
scored.frame: The rung would be "own the dead brand's IP bundle and prove it still has demand." In practice proving is not most of the work. The residual traffic and search demand of a dead brand are read in hours with off-the-shelf tools (Ahrefs, SimilarWeb, Google Trends). The hard part is the physical/operating step: relaunching product, sourcing and marketing. That is the geothermal-in-a-coal-mine pattern: finding the right dead brand is easy, rebuilding the business is hard. My estimate is that discovery is 10-20% of the work at this rung, not 80%+. A buyer does exist (brand licensing aggregators), but they buy at auction against the same data.
scored.step_up: From memory, not verified this run (the web search budget was used up). Large bankrupt-brand IP sales clear in the low millions to tens of millions at competitive auction: Bed Bath & Beyond IP went to Overstock for about $21.5M (2023); Pier 1 IP went to Retail Ecommerce Ventures for about $31M (2020); Modell's IP went for about $3.6M. Those prices come out of a marketed auction, so they are fair value, not near-zero. Small dead DTC brands sold through assignment-for-benefit-of-creditors processes probably clear at $5k-250k (my estimate). Resale of a bundle "proven" by traffic data is maybe 2-10x the purchase price at best, and often under 2x, because the buyer looked at the same traffic. The candidate's 40-400x has no comparable behind it.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Each proving attempt costs very little: roughly $0-500 of SEO/traffic tooling plus the auction bid (my estimate). Because nothing about proving is expensive or mostly failing, ML has nothing to cut. Base hit rate on a "does residual demand exist" check is high and observable before buying. Caveat: the real failure point comes after purchase, in the relaunch, and ML does not change that. So the 1/base-hit-rate cap gives roughly a 1-2x lever, nowhere near 10x.
scored.data: PACER/RECAP schedules, trustee notices and Wayback archives are partly illegible. But the outcome variable (residual traffic, backlinks, search volume, follower counts) is already summarised in legible commercial fields: Ahrefs Domain Rating, SimilarWeb visits, Trends indices, social follower counts. Auction agents such as Hilco Streambank and Gordon Brothers routinely put traffic, email-list size and social stats in the data room and sales flyer. The sellers are therefore not data-blind; their bankruptcy advisors market exactly this signal. A further problem: trademarks that are no longer in use risk abandonment, which may weaken what is bought.
scored.right_bought: Yes, the right is bought: it goes through a section 363 bankruptcy sale or an assignment-for-benefit-of-creditors sale. But it is bought at a competitive, court-supervised, broker-marketed auction, so there is no structural information discount. Expired domains are first-come drops, already fought over by drop-catch firms (DropCatch, SnapNames).
scored.buyer: Marquee Brands, Authentic Brands Group, WHP Global, Retrobrands USA and Hilco-affiliated revival vehicles, plus DTC aggregators. Retail Ecommerce Ventures (owner of Pier 1, RadioShack and Modell's) itself ran into financial distress, which suggests the revival buyer pool is thin and prices the asset tightly. These buyers bid directly at the same auctions, which competes away any arbitrage.
scored.ladder: The ladder exists in principle: IP flipping, then brand licensing, then relaunch operations, then a brand-management house in the style of Authentic Brands (about $20B+ in system-wide sales, my estimate of a commonly cited figure). But the incumbents already sit on every rung, and the bottom rung has no edge to start from.
scored.fatal_flaw: The proving signal (residual traffic and search demand) is already legible: Ahrefs, SimilarWeb and Trends measure it, and auction agents like Hilco Streambank put it in front of the very revival buyers who bid at the same 363 auctions. There is no information discount to capture and no expensive, mostly-failing proving step for ML to cheapen. The real work, and the real risk, is operating the relaunch, which repeats the coal-mine geothermal failure.
scored.one_line_reason: This fails the gold rubric: the right is bought at fair value in a marketed auction, demand proof is cheap and legible to everyone, the realistic step-up is 2-10x rather than 10^3x, and the value is realised by operating the brand, not by discovering it.
