scored.name: Installed-Base Rescue: discontinued robot lines
scored.one_line: Buy IP, firmware, spares and trademarks of discontinued robot/AGV lines for scrap; ML locates the hidden installed base; sell proven service franchise.
scored.unproven_right: Line IP, signing keys, tooling and service rights.
scored.proving_step: ML over bills of lading, OSHA logs, job posts, listings; pilot support contract.
scored.proven_buyer: Field-service roll-ups, integrators, competing OEMs.
scored.public_data: Customs manifests, OSHA injury data, job archives, FCC ID, auctions.
scored.frame: The candidate rung is buying a dead robot line's IP, keys and spares, then proving there is a service franchise in it. Discovery, meaning locating the installed base, is roughly 10-20% of the work inside that rung (my estimate). The other 80-90% is physical and engineering work: keeping old firmware alive, re-tooling or remanufacturing end-of-life parts, certifying, staffing field technicians and carrying service-level liability. That is the geothermal-in-a-coal-mine failure pattern, where building the bespoke operation is far harder than finding the asset. No version of this rung has proving at 80% or more.
scored.step_up: Unproven: assets of failed robot companies tend to go to a single strategic buyer or a liquidator at token prices, low single-digit millions or less. Past examples from memory, not checked this session: Rethink Robotics' assets went to HAHN Group in 2018; Jibo's to NTT Disruption; Anki's to Digital Dream Labs in 2019. Proven: field-service businesses are typically valued at about 0.5-2x revenue or 6-10x EBITDA (estimate). If the base supports $2-5M a year of service revenue, the proven franchise is worth about $2-10M. That is roughly 3-10x on the purchase price, below the candidate's 10-50x claim and far from 10^3. The step-up also builds up over months of service delivery rather than arriving on a single hit.
scored.hit_rate_capex: There is no expensive, mostly-failing proving attempt like a drill hole. The proving step is a pilot support contract that costs maybe $50-250k in engineering and technician time (estimate). Whether a line has a live installed base is known with fairly high probability before purchase: the OEM's CRM, warranty records and serial-number registry usually come in the data room. The base hit rate is high, so the lever (capped at 1/hit rate) is small, maybe 1.5-2x, not 10x. No sourced hit-rate figure exists. All numbers are my estimates.
scored.data: The public data is real but noisy. Customs bills of lading (sold commercially by Panjiva and ImportGenius) show shipments of robots; OSHA injury records sometimes name robots; job posts mention specific robot models; FCC IDs and auction listings exist. But the decisive outcome, who owns the units and runs them, is already written down in a private, legible place: the OEM's own customer and serial records, which the asset buyer inherits. So ML over public scraps mainly re-derives a list the buyer already has. Incumbents with the same idea: HAHN Group (Rethink), Digital Dream Labs (Anki), United Robotics Group (the Aldebaran/SoftBank robots), and third-party maintainers and refurbishers such as RobotWorx. No web searches ran because the shared search budget was exhausted; these points come from prior knowledge and are unverified.
scored.right_bought: Partly. The rights can be bought cheaply from bankruptcy trustees and liquidators, but the sellers can read the customer data perfectly well; they just cannot afford to serve it. The sale is a competitive 363 auction, which removes the information-asymmetry discount. Signing keys and firmware rights can come with licensing and export-control complications.
scored.buyer: Field-service roll-ups (private-equity-backed industrial service platforms), systems integrators and competing OEMs who want to win the customers over. They are capitalised but pay ordinary service-business multiples. A competing OEM may pay only for the customer list, which you could not show came from ML rather than from the inherited CRM.
scored.ladder: Modest. The path runs from service franchise, to a refurbishment and retrofit business, to an aggregator of orphaned automation across many dead lines, to a multi-brand robot maintenance and re-manufacturing platform. That could be a solid company worth $100M to low billions (estimate). It does not lead to building and owning the whole robot value chain; the top rung is competing with ABB, FANUC and others as an OEM, which is a different business.
scored.fatal_flaw: Discovery is not the bottleneck. The installed base comes with the acquired CRM and serial records, and the real work and risk is the physical, engineering-heavy job of supporting obsolete hardware. Proving is a small share of the rung, the base hit rate is high, and the step-up is about 3-10x at service multiples, not 10^3-10^4.
scored.one_line_reason: This fails the rubric the same way geothermal in coal mines does: finding the installed base is easy, since it comes in the acquired customer records, and keeping orphaned hardware running is hard. The proven franchise sells at about 3-10x the purchase price at ordinary service-business multiples.

You could sell a 'proven attention' dormant mark with no revenue, but roll-ups like Marquee, Authentic Brands and Dotdash Meredith buy royalty streams, usually at about 4-8x royalty EBITDA (my estimate from known deals). They do not buy attention scores. So the buyer exists for the rung above, not for the discovery rung.
scored.step_up: Unproven: an abandoned mark costs a USPTO filing fee of about $350 per class plus legal fees, so roughly $1-5k all-in. Residual goodwill from a defunct publisher runs roughly $1k-50k (my estimate). Proven, with no revenue: there is no market price, and a mark with only search or attention signals resells at maybe 2-10x (my estimate). Proven with revenue: brand IP from bankruptcy has sold for $5-30M+, for example Hilco Streambank and Gordon Brothers auctions of retail brands. That jump needs a relaunch and years of operating, not one proving test. On a pure discovery basis the step-up is about 3-10x. Note: I could not verify this live because the web search budget was used up. Figures are from prior knowledge or are estimates.
scored.hit_rate_capex: I estimate that 5-15% of revived dormant brands reach meaningful licensing revenue, from the anecdotal record of River West Brands and Retrobrands-style revivers. Each attempt costs about $50k-$1M+ (product, marketing, legal; my estimate). The expensive, mostly failing part is the relaunch itself. ML can rank which marks carry latent attention, but it does not cut the relaunch cost, so the lever on total capex is well under 10x. The cheap part (filing fees) is the only part ML touches, and it is already cheap.
scored.data: USPTO TSDR and bulk data is fully legible and structured. Mark status ('Abandoned', 'Cancelled Section 8', 'Dead') is written into a status field, so the outcome is already summarised. Google Trends, Wikipedia pageviews and search volume are legible attention proxies that anyone can query. The Internet Archive and LoC newspaper directories are the only illegible data, and they show historical prominence, not today's commercial value. Incumbent revivers and brand-IP liquidators already screen for this by hand.
scored.right_bought: Mostly not bought. A truly abandoned US mark (3 years of non-use is presumed abandonment under 15 USC 1127) is free to whoever files an intent-to-use (ITU) application first. That is first-come, which the rubric penalizes, and anyone can copy the filing once it publishes. Where the right must be bought (residual goodwill from a living defunct publisher or a bankruptcy estate), it goes through Hilco Streambank or Gordon Brothers auctions, where sellers and bidders are sophisticated and prices are competitive. Call letters belong to the FCC and lapse back into the pool; they are not sellable IP of value. There is also litigation risk from residual-goodwill doctrine.
scored.buyer: Marquee Brands, Authentic Brands Group, WHP Global, Bluestar Alliance, Dotdash Meredith and similar roll-ups are well capitalised. They pay for cash-flowing licensing revenue or known brands with distribution, not for dormant marks with attention scores. The only buyers for unproven dormant marks are small revivers (River West Brands, Retrobrands USA), and they pay little.
scored.ladder: The rungs are: dormant mark, then relaunch or licensing, then a brand-management roll-up (an ABG-scale company is worth $10B+). The ladder is real at the top. But the bottom rung has no discovery-dominant sellable output, so you would have to start on the operating rung, which removes the ML edge.
scored.fatal_flaw: No proving test turns a dormant mark into a buyer-priced asset. Value only appears after a bespoke relaunch, so discovery is a small share of the work. On top of that, abandoned marks are free first-come ITU filings, not cheap purchases, and the outcome (status, attention) is already in legible fields.
scored.one_line_reason: This fails the frame test, much like geothermal in coal mines. Relaunch is the real work, roll-ups buy royalties not attention, and the right and the outcome are both legible and free to copy.

scored.name: Expiring-Exclusivity Biologic Patent Picker
scored.one_line: Buy obscure process/formulation patents from small biotech and CDMO owners that read on blockbuster manufacturing or that biosimilar entrants must clear; prove from FDA/EMA reviews and BPCIA filings; sell to originator or entrant.
scored.unproven_right: Peripheral process/formulation patents not listed in Orange/Purple Book.
scored.proving_step: ML over approval packages, EPARs and DMF summaries matched to claims.
scored.proven_buyer: Originators, biosimilar entrants, pharma funders.
scored.public_data: Drugs@FDA reviews, EPARs, Purple Book, PACER BPCIA filings, USPTO.
scored.frame: The rung would be "own a peripheral biologic process or formulation patent and prove that it reads on a commercial product". There is no rung where discovery is 80%+ of the work. Matching claims to public data might be 10-20% of the effort (my estimate). What actually makes a patent valuable is enforcement: claim construction, infringement discovery, surviving an IPR at the PTAB, and then trial or settlement. That is the expensive physical step, and it is slow and hard, like building the bespoke plant in the coal-mine counter-example. A buyer will not pay a proven-asset price after desk analysis alone, only after the patent has survived validity and infringement challenges.
scored.step_up: These are my estimates; no live search was possible. On the secondary patent market (brokered lots tracked by Richardson Oliver Insights), a typical patent asks roughly $100k-$300k. Obscure biologic process patents held by small biotechs or CDMOs probably trade at $10k-$200k, or for the cost of the maintenance fee if abandoned. A proven patent that reads on a blockbuster can settle for a royalty-bearing licence worth $10M-$100M+; AbbVie's Humira patent thicket of about 130 patents produced entry-delay settlements worth billions. That is a 100-1000x step-up only in rare cases, and it arrives after years of litigation, not at the moment of the hit. The expected step-up per patent bought is far lower, about 3-10x after costs (estimate).
scored.hit_rate_capex: Again my estimates; no live search was possible. Patent assertion has a low base hit rate. Pharma and biologic patents challenged at the PTAB are found wholly or partly unpatentable about 40-60% of the time once instituted. Process-patent infringement on biologics is rarely shown. Cost per proving attempt: the AIPLA economic survey puts patent litigation with more than $25M at risk at roughly $4M+ through trial, plus about $0.5M per IPR. ML only improves the cheap screening step, choosing which patents to buy. It cannot raise the hit rate of the expensive step, because infringement depends on confidential manufacturing (CMC) details. So the 10x capex cut does not apply. At best ML cuts screening cost, which is maybe 5% of total capex.
scored.data: The public data is Drugs@FDA reviews, EPARs, DMF summaries, PACER BPCIA filings and USPTO records. It is partly illegible, which is good. The fatal problem is that the CMC and process details needed to prove infringement are redacted as confidential in FDA reviews and EPARs, and DMFs are closed to the public apart from summaries. So the signal that matters is not in the public data. On the other side, the outcome is increasingly written into legible fields: since the 2021 Purple Book Continuity Act, BPCIA patent lists exchanged in the "patent dance" are published in the Purple Book. Litigated patents are therefore already named, and patents left unlisted are mostly the ones originators judged weak. Incumbents already mine all of this: originator and biosimilar IP teams, Big Law firms, and analytics vendors such as DrugPatentWatch, Evaluate, Clarivate/Cortellis and LexisNexis PatentSight.
scored.right_bought: Yes, patents can be bought from small biotechs, CDMOs, universities and bankruptcy estates, often cheaply (estimated $10k-$200k), and buying is not first-come-free. But sellers are not blind. Brokers and NPE aggregators (Acacia, IP Navigation-type firms, litigation funders) already price these assets. Buying a patent also carries hard legal limits: you cannot sue earlier than the patent's own validity allows; licence encumbrances, prior licences, and exhaustion where the original owner was a CDMO serving the very originator; and standing rules. The CDMO case matters a lot, because a CDMO's process patents are often already licensed to its own clients, the blockbuster makers.
scored.buyer: On paper the buyers are originators (to defend a patent thicket), biosimilar entrants (to clear their path) and litigation funders (Burford, Fortress). They are well capitalised but adversarial. Entrants buy freedom to operate cheaply or simply file an IPR, at about $0.5M, instead of paying a premium. Originators already hold more than 100 patents per franchise and do not need peripheral ones. In practice the only real buyer is the defendant, in a settlement, which makes this NPE-style patent assertion rather than selling a proven asset to someone who wants it.
scored.ladder: The ladder is weak. Rungs above, such as becoming a biosimilar developer or a CDMO, are unrelated businesses and do not follow from owning patents ($100M-$250M and 7-8 years per biosimilar programme). Patent aggregation as a business has a ceiling: Acacia and Intellectual Ventures plateaued in the low billions, and the business is unpopular with regulators and courts. There is no path to a trillion dollars.
scored.fatal_flaw: Proving value depends on infringement and validity litigation, not discovery. That costs about $4M+ per case over 2-4 years, and its key evidence (confidential manufacturing and CMC details) is not in public data. ML can only pick which patents to buy; it cannot cheapen or de-risk the step that creates the step-up. Since 2021 the Purple Book also publishes BPCIA patent lists, which legibly flags the patents that matter. This is patent-troll economics with a better screen, not a Terranox-style frame.
scored.one_line_reason: Litigation is the proving step, it is expensive and slow, and the evidence it needs is confidential, so discovery is far below 80% of the rung. The only buyer is the defendant in a settlement, and the Purple Book now publishes the patents that matter.

scored.name: Prior-Art Priority Owner: early university patents reading on commercial biologics and devices
scored.one_line: Take exclusive licences with right to sue on university patents whose priority and claims cover later commercial products; prove infringement and validity; settle or sell to funded licensors.
scored.unproven_right: Exclusive licence with enforcement, $10-100k plus share.
scored.proving_step: Claim construction, infringement chart vs labels and BLA reviews, validity screen ($50-150k).
scored.proven_buyer: Burford, Fortress, patent buyers, infringers.
scored.public_data: USPTO full text and PEDS, Orange/Purple Book, FDA labels and BLA reviews, DailyMed.
scored.frame: The rung would be: hold an exclusive licence with the right to sue on a university patent, and prove it reads on a commercial product. Discovery (finding the patent and charting it against the product) is maybe 10-20% of what it takes to realise the value (my estimate). The other 80-90% is adversarial legal work: a Markman claim-construction ruling, surviving an IPR at the PTAB, expert discovery and trial. That legal phase is the physical step, and it is neither trivial nor abstracted, so the frame fails in the same way as the geothermal-in-coal-mines counter-example. A $50-150k claim chart does not create a sellable proven asset the way a drill hit does. Funders do buy charted, litigation-ready assets, but they pay little until a court or PTAB milestone.
scored.step_up: Unproven: exclusive licence for about $10-100k upfront plus a revenue share (from the candidate brief, not verified). Proven, meaning it has survived Markman and IPR: settlements on biologics or devices can reach $10M-1B. Precedents from memory, not searched this run: Carnegie Mellon v. Marvell, $1.17B verdict, settled for $750M; Caltech v. Apple/Broadcom, $1.1B verdict, later vacated. That is roughly 100-1000x on a hit, but only after 3-5 years and litigation. Right after the proving step this candidate proposes (a claim chart), the market value of the asset rises maybe 2-10x (my estimate).
scored.hit_rate_capex: Base rates from memory, not verified this run. Patent holders win at trial roughly a third of the time (PwC patent litigation studies). The PTAB invalidates all or some challenged claims in a majority of IPRs that reach a final decision. AIPLA economic surveys put median cost through trial for cases with more than $25M at risk at about $4M or more. The $50-150k chart is a cheap screen; the expensive step ($3-5M+) is litigation. Its outcome depends on judges, juries and prior art, which ML can only partly predict. ML can lower screening cost, but screening is not where the cost sits. Realistic lever: under 2x on total cost to reach a proven asset.
scored.data: USPTO full text and PEDS are legible and structured, and they are already mined by PatSnap, Clarivate, RPX, Unified Patents, contingency-fee firms and university tech transfer offices. Drug patents are listed in a legible public field: Orange Book patent listings, and Purple Book patent lists for biologics since 2021, which grew out of the BPCIA "patent dance". Infringement evidence such as labels and BLA reviews is public and searchable. Some signal is still illegible, such as reading claims against the text of BLA reviews. But the outcome itself (validity, infringement) is not in any field and is only settled in court, which is an adversarial step, not a discovery step.
scored.right_bought: The right is technically bought, from university tech transfer offices. But those offices are sophisticated sellers: they track their own portfolios, often enforce directly (WARF, Caltech, CMU, the UC system) and work with contingency firms and funders. Many early university patents expire before the product makes much money, because the 20-year term runs from priority. The owners can read this data, so there is no information asymmetry to buy cheaply into. Granting enforcement rights also requires an exclusive licence with all substantial rights, or the university joined as a party, to have standing; that gives the university leverage on price and terms.
scored.buyer: Litigation funders (Burford, Fortress, Parabellum), patent aggregators (Acacia, IP Investments Group), and infringers paying settlements. They are capitalised, but they price on litigation milestones, not on claim charts.
scored.ladder: Weak. The rungs above (litigation, then licensing programs, then aggregation) all lead to being a patent assertion entity, not to making biologics or devices. There is no path from enforcing a patent to running the product chain. The ceiling is roughly Acacia or IV scale (single-digit billions), and the work is reputationally toxic in pharma. Growth is not self-sustaining because each asset is a bespoke multi-year lawsuit.
scored.fatal_flaw: The proving step is litigation, not discovery. Turning the licence into a proven asset takes $3-5M+ and 3-5 years of adversarial work (Markman, IPR, trial) with roughly coin-flip-or-worse odds. Discovery, which ML would speed up, is a small part of that cost and work, and the sellers (university tech transfer offices) already read the same data.
scored.one_line_reason: Discovery is not 80%+ of any sellable rung, because value only appears after expensive adversarial litigation. The data is legible and already mined, university sellers are sophisticated, and the ladder only leads to patent assertion.

scored.name: Lazarus PMA: orphaned Class III approvals
scored.one_line: Buy still-valid PMAs and technical files from bankrupt device makers; ML confirms legal life and reimbursement volume; restart via site-change supplement; sell to strategics or PE.
scored.unproven_right: PMA plus DHF from estates, $10k-500k.
scored.proving_step: Confirm no withdrawal; 180-day site-change supplement at a CM ($0.3-1.5M).
scored.proven_buyer: Medtronic, BSX, Integra, Teleflex, medtech PE.
scored.public_data: FDA PMA and supplements, Federal Register withdrawals, PACER, 8-K/15-12G, CMS PUFs, MAUDE.
scored.frame: The rung is buying an orphaned PMA plus its DHF and restarting production at a contract manufacturer (CM). Inside that rung, discovery (checking the PMA is still valid and has demand) is my estimate of 10-20% of the work. The other 80-90% is physical and regulatory: tech transfer to the CM, rebuilding the supplier base, process validation, a 180-day site-change supplement with a likely pre-approval inspection, and setting up the quality system and complaint/MDR handling. The candidate's own figure of '~50-60% discovery' is too high. This is the coal-mine geothermal pattern: finding the asset is easy and the bespoke restart is the hard part.
scored.step_up: Unproven: the candidate says PMA plus DHF from an estate costs $10k-500k (my estimate agrees that dormant regulatory files sell cheaply in 363 sales). Proven: a strategic buyer pays for revenue and share, not for the approval. A restarted Class III line with no installed base, no surgeon relationships and lapsed reimbursement momentum is probably worth 1-5x restart cost, so about $2-10M (my estimate). Gross step-up on purchase price is about 10-100x. Net of $0.3-1.5M proving cost plus $1-3M of validation and inventory (my estimate), the step-up on capital deployed is about 2-5x. Nothing like 10^4. Medtech acquirers usually buy at about 3-6x revenue, so value tracks restarted sales, not the restart itself (my estimate). Search budget was exhausted, so none of these are sourced figures.
scored.hit_rate_capex: The proving step does not mostly fail at random. If the device is unchanged and the CM is competent, a site-change supplement probably gets approved more than 50% of the time (my estimate). So the ML lever (capped at 1/hit rate) is under 2x. The real reason an attempt fails is economic: the product was orphaned because it lost commercially, clinically or on liability, and that cannot be read from filings. Cost per attempt: the candidate gives $0.3-1.5M. From memory, the FDA 180-day supplement user fee is about 15% of the PMA fee, roughly $80k in FY2025-26. Validation and inspection readiness add more, my estimate $0.5-2M all-in. ML does not cut that cost 10x, because it is manufacturing work, not search.
scored.data: The outcome is already in legible public fields. FDA's PMA database is structured and lists approval status and every supplement. Withdrawals are published in the Federal Register. CMS PUFs give HCPCS/DRG volumes in tabular form. The legal life and demand signals are a database join, not an illegible-data problem. The useful parts that are hard to read are DHF quality, supplier availability and why the product failed, and those sit in private estate files, not public data. PACER and 8-K filings flag device-maker bankruptcies clearly. Incumbents are already there: bankruptcy brokers and liquidators (e.g. Gordon Brothers, Hilco IP), medtech-focused distressed buyers, and the strategics themselves, who see these 363 auctions.
scored.right_bought: Yes. A PMA can be transferred by letter to FDA, and estates sell it with the DHF in Section 363 sales. But the sale is an open auction run by investment bankers who market to the strategics, so the sellers are not unable to read the data. Any discount comes from the asset's distressed condition, not from information asymmetry.
scored.buyer: Strategics (Medtronic, Boston Scientific, Integra, Teleflex) and medtech PE do have capital. But they buy products with revenue, evidence and reimbursement traction, not freshly restarted dormant PMAs. They often skipped the same asset at the original bankruptcy auction.
scored.ladder: The rungs above are commercialising restarted lines, then a roll-up of revived Class III products into a specialty device company, then R&D on next-generation versions. That is a real path to a mid-size medtech company (for example a roll-up the size of Integra, about $1-2B in revenue). It is not a trillion-dollar chain, and each rung adds manufacturing and commercial work rather than leverage from discovery.
scored.fatal_flaw: Adverse selection plus a physical restart. Orphaned PMAs are orphaned because the economics, clinical results or liability failed. Proving value means rebuilding manufacturing (the hard 80%), not discovering something. And the legal status the ML would 'confirm' is already a structured field in FDA's PMA database.
scored.one_line_reason: Discovery is a database lookup and the value comes from bespoke restarts of commercially failed devices, so there is no 95/5 frame, no 10^3 step-up and only a weak ML lever.

scored.name: Article 95 Rescue: abandoned EU biocide dossiers
scored.one_line: Take over withdrawn BPR active substance/product-type dossiers in ECHA's window; ML picks those near approval; complete and hold Article 95 listing that formulators must license.
scored.unproven_right: Dossier and data ownership via takeover, €50-300k.
scored.proving_step: ML over CA reports and BPC opinions; positive approval.
scored.proven_buyer: EU formulators and distributors, Arxada, Lanxess.
scored.public_data: ECHA Article 95 list, review programme withdrawals, CA reports, BPC opinions, CLH registry.
scored.frame: The rung would be "take over a withdrawn active substance/product-type (AS/PT) dossier and carry it to approval plus Article 95 listing". Inside that rung, discovery (picking which dossier to take) is maybe 10-20% of the work (my estimate). The other 80%+ is the physical step: producing the missing tox, ecotox and efficacy studies, answering Competent Authority (CA) questions, paying ECHA fees and getting through the Biocidal Products Committee (BPC) over 2-5 years. That step is bespoke and is not trivial or abstracted. It has the same shape as the geothermal-in-coal-mines counter-example. Taking over the role does not hand over the old participant's data, so you either rebuild it or pay for a letter of access.
scored.step_up: Unproven: the candidate claims a takeover costs about EUR 50-300k. Proven: a listed AS/PT earns letter-of-access income, and those letters typically sell for tens of thousands to a few hundred thousand EUR per product supplier (my estimate from industry knowledge; I could not check it). Most of the value has to be built by spending millions on studies, so this is a cost-plus regulatory asset, not a value jump on a single hit. Realistic step-up is about 2-10x on total capital invested (my estimate), not 10^3-10^4.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Base hit rate: approval once a full dossier reaches the BPC is fairly high, so failure is not the main cost. Dossiers usually get withdrawn for economic reasons or because hazards trigger exclusion criteria (CMR or endocrine disruptor), and both are visible in public CLH and BPC records. Cost per attempt: completing an active substance dossier is commonly put at about EUR 1-5M+ in studies, plus ECHA approval fees in the low hundreds of thousands of EUR per substance (my estimates from industry knowledge; I could not check them). Because the base hit rate is already high, ML can raise it very little (the lever is capped at 1/base hit rate), so the 10x capex cut does not happen. The cost is study generation, not choosing badly.
scored.data: The data is public: ECHA's Article 95 list, the review programme notices about withdrawals and open invitations to take over, CA assessment reports, BPC opinions and the CLH registry. But it is already legible and read closely by regulatory consultancies, and the outcome is effectively written into status fields (approval/non-approval decisions, BPC opinions, CLH classifications). That is the failure pattern seen in earlier hunts, where the regulator writes the answer into a status field. ML has little edge over a regulatory affairs specialist reading the CA report.
scored.right_bought: The right is not really bought from owners who cannot read the data. Taking over a role in the review programme is a first-come notification answering ECHA's public invitation (Reg. 1062/2014). You are not buying it at a discount from an uninformed seller. The original participant's data stays theirs and needs a letter of access. Also, data protection for review-programme AS/PT combinations ended on 31 Dec 2025 under BPR Art. 95(5) (from memory; I could not check it), which weakens the licensing moat.
scored.buyer: EU biocidal product formulators and distributors who need an Article 95-listed supplier, plus the large active substance holders (Arxada/Lonza, Lanxess, Troy/Arxada, BASF). The buyers have capital, but each one pays little, and the big holders are competitors more than buyers.
scored.ladder: There are some rungs above: become an Article 95-listed substance supplier, then a product authorisation holder, then make the active substance (toll or own manufacture), then formulate biocidal products. That leads to a mid-size specialty chemicals company, not a trillion-dollar chain. The EU biocides active substance market is a few billion EUR (my estimate).
scored.fatal_flaw: The proving step is not discovery. It is millions of EUR of bespoke study work and years of regulatory process. Approval outcomes and hazard blockers already sit in legible BPC and CLH fields. And the review-programme data protection that would make an Article 95 listing licensable expired on 31 Dec 2025 (from memory, unverified). So no frame exists where discovery is 80%+ of the work, and ML has no hit-rate lever.
scored.one_line_reason: The coal-mine-geothermal pattern again: finishing a biocide dossier costs millions in tox studies and takes years, while choosing the dossier is easy and already legible from ECHA status fields. The step-up is only about 2-10x on capital, against the 10^3-10^4 the rubric needs.

scored.name: Alternate Label: pesticide registrations bought ahead of EPA cancellations
scored.one_line: Buy dormant registrations and data-compensation rights for alternatives that become must-have when EPA cancels or restricts a dominant AI (forecast from risk assessments, biological opinions, vacaturs); sell to ag-chem companies.
scored.unproven_right: Section 3 or 24(c) registrations, $20-100k.
scored.proving_step: Forecast cancellations and label-slot fit; cancellation order.
scored.proven_buyer: AMVAC, UPL, Albaugh, Corteva, Syngenta, FMC, Nufarm ($1-50M).
scored.public_data: EPA PPLS, registration-review dockets, PRIA records, ESA biological opinions, FIFRA court dockets, CA DPR/NPIRS.
scored.frame: The rung would be: hold an EPA registration for an alternative active ingredient (AI) before a cancellation and sell it after. Inside that rung, forecasting is perhaps 60-70% of the work (my estimate). The physical part is not trivial: a registration has little value without a supply of technical-grade AI, a formulation, a label that fits the right crops and pests, state registrations in roughly 50 states, and distribution. Each of those is a serious piece of work. The buyers (AMVAC, Albaugh, UPL and others) are well capitalised, but they buy products with market share, not bare registrations.
scored.step_up: No transaction comps found, because the search budget ran out. My estimate from FIFRA mechanics: a dormant Section 3 me-too registration of an off-patent AI is worth about its replacement cost. That is a PRIA fee, roughly $5-15k with a 4-8 month decision, plus annual maintenance fees of about $4-5k per product. After a competitor's AI is cancelled, a buyer could pay a time-to-market premium of perhaps $100k-$1M for a label already in hand. Starting from a $20-100k cost basis, that is about 3-10x at best, not the 30-500x claimed. The $1-50M deals in this sector are for product lines with sales, not bare registrations.
scored.hit_rate_capex: There is no expensive, mostly-failing proving step. The 'proof' is an EPA action that happens or does not, on a public timeline. Registration review runs on a 15-year cycle with a published schedule, proposed interim decisions are posted for comment, and cancellations usually take years and are telegraphed (chlorpyrifos: petition in 2007, tolerances revoked in 2021). The cost per attempt is about $5-15k in fees plus maintenance (estimate). Base predictability is high, so ML has little room to raise the hit rate, and the 1/base-hit-rate cap on the lever is small.
scored.data: The data is public, but the outcome is already summarised legibly: Federal Register notices, proposed and interim decisions, docket comments, and lists of mitigation and cancellation requests in EPA dockets. The buyers themselves (regulatory affairs teams, CropLife, consultancies such as Exponent and CSI) watch these dockets closely, because this is their core competency. ESA biological opinions and court dockets are long documents, but the industry reads them. The ML edge over incumbents is small.
scored.right_bought: The right is not scarce. For an off-patent alternative AI, anyone can file a me-too registration citing existing data under FIFRA 3(c)(1)(F) with an offer to pay data compensation; it is effectively first-come and cheap. Data-compensation rights belong to the original data submitter (usually a major or a task force), which is unlikely to sell them cheaply to a forecaster. Dormant registrations can be bought from small registrants, but the buyer can replicate them in months.
scored.buyer: AMVAC, Albaugh, UPL, Nufarm, Corteva, Syngenta and FMC are capitalised, but each has its own regulatory team. Each can file its own me-too registration or already holds alternative labels, so it pays a premium only for time-to-market or for exclusive data.
scored.ladder: There is a plausible ladder: registration holder, then formulator and generic AI marketer (the Albaugh/AMVAC model, a multi-billion-dollar generic ag-chem business), then sourcing technical-grade AI and owning manufacturing. That ladder is mostly a sourcing, manufacturing and distribution business, not a discovery business, and generic ag-chem is low-margin and commoditised.
scored.fatal_flaw: The right is not scarce and the outcome is legible. A me-too registration for an off-patent alternative costs about a PRIA fee and a few months. Cancellations are telegraphed for years in public EPA dockets that buyers' own regulatory teams already watch. So there is no hidden information to extract, and buyers replicate the right instead of paying a 10^3 premium.
scored.one_line_reason: FIFRA lets anyone cheaply register an off-patent alternative, and EPA cancellations are slow, public and closely watched, so there is no step-up, no low-hit-rate proving step and no illegible-data edge.

scored.name: Vehicle Vault: dormant IDIQ/GWAC seat holders
scored.one_line: Buy small firms holding unused seats on big contract vehicles; ML-target task orders; sell with backlog.
scored.unproven_right: Contract-vehicle seat inside a dormant firm.
scored.proving_step: Win first $5-20M of task orders.
scored.proven_buyer: Mid-tier integrators and gov-services PE.
scored.public_data: FPDS/USAspending, SAM.gov holder lists, eBuy, forecasts, GAO protests.
scored.frame: The rung is "dormant small-business vehicle seat, turned into a seat with $5-20M of task-order backlog". Inside that rung, discovery (working out which task orders to chase) is maybe 10-20% of the work (my estimate). The other 80%+ is proposal writing, building past performance, key-personnel commitments, pricing, and then actually delivering the labor-based services. Unlike drilling for Terranox, the physical step is neither trivial nor abstracted: you only prove the seat by winning the work and performing it. A buyer with capital exists (mid-tier integrators and gov-services PE), but it buys revenue and EBITDA, not seats.
scored.step_up: From my own knowledge, because the web search budget was used up (no numbers fetched this run). A dormant small firm holding a seat but no revenue sells for roughly the cost of its paperwork, about $0.1-0.5M (estimate). Govcon services firms usually sell at about 0.5-1.5x revenue or about 8-12x EBITDA (industry-typical, estimate). With $5-20M of backlog and maybe 8-10% margins, the firm might be worth $2-10M. That is a 5-30x step-up at best, nowhere near 10^3-10^4. And much of it comes from performing the contracts (revenue), not from the seat being proven.
scored.hit_rate_capex: From knowledge, not searched. Yes, many seat holders win little or nothing: GSA cancels MAS schedules with under $25k of sales over 5 years, and a large share of small seats on multiple-award vehicles sit idle (estimate: 30-60% show negligible obligations). But the failures come from missing past performance, BD capacity and incumbency, not from bad targeting. A competitive task-order proposal costs roughly $50-300k in BD and proposal labor (estimate), and pWin for a new entrant without incumbency is about 10-25% (estimate). ML targeting might lift pWin modestly, maybe 1.5-2x. It cannot deliver 10x, because the binding limits are past performance, price and incumbency, which public data does not fix.
scored.data: The data is fully legible, which kills the ML edge. FPDS/USAspending lists every task order by vehicle, holder UEI, amount and date in structured fields. SAM.gov lists vehicle holders. The outcome (did this seat win anything) is already a clean public field. Forecasts and eBuy are structured too, though eBuy is only visible to holders. A whole incumbent industry already extracts this: GovWin/Deltek, Bloomberg Government, HigherGov, GovSpend, GovTribe. There is no illegible signal that only ML can read.
scored.right_bought: The right can be bought by acquiring the firm, but it does not survive the transfer to the people who would pay for it. Under 13 CFR 121.404(g), a firm must recertify its size within 30 days of a merger or acquisition. Once it is affiliated with a mid-tier integrator or PE platform it is no longer small, and under SBA's 2024 rule changes it cannot take set-aside orders on small-business vehicles. 8(a) seats (e.g. 8(a) STARS III) need SBA approval for an ownership change, and only to an eligible disadvantaged owner. Novating a contract also requires government approval. The owners selling dormant seats can read FPDS as well as anyone, so there is no information discount. On top of that, OASIS+ and MAS have continuous or periodic on-ramps, so the seats themselves are not scarce.
scored.buyer: Mid-tier government services integrators (e.g. firms of the Amentum or Parsons tier) and gov-services PE platforms. They pay for revenue, backlog, cleared staff, past performance and margins. They do not pay for the seat itself, and they cannot keep small-business status after buying.
scored.ladder: There are rungs above: subcontractor, then prime on task orders, then full-and-open vehicle holder, then mid-tier integrator, then large integrator. That is a real roll-up path, but it is ordinary services M&A, valued at 0.5-1.5x revenue. Every rung is labor-heavy delivery, and none has a discovery-dominated frame. The upside is a Booz Allen or Leidos style business, not a trillion-dollar one.
scored.fatal_flaw: The asset does not hold its value through a sale. Size-status seats lose set-aside eligibility once acquired by a non-small buyer (13 CFR 121.404(g) recertification; SBA approval needed for 8(a) ownership changes). And the "proving" step is winning plus performing labor-based services, not discovery. On top of that, the outcome of each seat is already a legible FPDS field that GovWin and similar tools index.
scored.one_line_reason: Proving a seat is sales and service delivery rather than discovery. The step-up is about 10x at most and tied to revenue, the outcome is already legible in FPDS, and size or 8(a) status, which is the value of the seat, disappears when it is sold to the stated buyer.

scored.name: Orphan FMS Sustainment
scored.one_line: Buy orphaned OEM IP and support rights for legacy US systems still fielded by FMS customers; win sustainment cases; sell to sustainment primes.
scored.unproven_right: Orphaned product-line IP and support rights.
scored.proving_step: ML over DSCA notices and SIPRI; first sustainment contracts.
scored.proven_buyer: Leonardo DRS, Sierra Nevada, VSE, Heico.
scored.public_data: DSCA notifications, SIPRI, foreign tenders, FPDS FMS awards.
scored.frame: The smallest rung that can be sold is "own the IP and support rights for an orphaned product line, and hold an awarded sustainment contract." Inside that rung, finding the line is perhaps 10-20% of the work (my estimate). The rest is physical and regulatory: DDTC/ITAR registration, getting the line approved as a qualified source (DLA SAR or service engineering approval), rebuilding tooling and test sets, sorting out the technical data package and data rights, and then delivering parts. That is the geothermal-in-coal-mines pattern again: running the bespoke line is much harder than finding it. No rung exists where discovery is 80% or more.
scored.step_up: My estimate, not sourced, because the shared web search budget ran out before any search returned. Orphaned or licensed legacy aerospace and defense lines usually change hands at roughly 0.5-2x revenue (licensing deals or small carve-outs). Aftermarket consolidators value proven sole-source lines at roughly 3-6x revenue, or about 15-25x EBITDA in TransDigm and Heico-style deals. That is about 3-10x, and you only get it after years of running the line. The candidate's own "10-50x" looks optimistic. Nothing jumps immediately when a hit lands; the value builds up through contract awards and margin.
scored.hit_rate_capex: There is no single costly proving attempt that usually fails. The cost of each attempt is the cost of buying and requalifying the line: by my estimate $1-10M and 1-3 years for each line, covering acquisition, tooling, first article testing and ITAR setup. The base hit rate is fairly high (my estimate 30-60%) when you pick lines with known demand, because DSCA notices and FPDS awards already show which systems are still fielded. Since the lever is capped at 1/base hit rate, ML can improve it by about 2-3x at most, not 10x. Capex is set by requalification, not by discovery.
scored.data: The data is public and largely legible. DSCA major arms sale notifications are structured press releases naming the system, quantity and dollar value. FPDS FMS awards are structured fields: NAICS, PSC, vendor and dollar value. SIPRI's arms transfer database is already a curated, structured register of fielded systems by country. The outcome, meaning which countries still field which legacy US systems and who holds the sustainment contracts, is mostly written into these fields already. That is the same failure as the queue-position and regulator-status hunts. Foreign tenders are scattered and the only somewhat illegible source.
scored.right_bought: The rights can be bought, but the sellers are not uninformed. The owners are OEMs (Honeywell, Collins/RTX, L3Harris, Northrop) and they can read the demand data perfectly well. They divest or license tail lines on purpose to specialist buyers. Ontic (CVC-backed), for example, is built on licensing legacy aerospace lines from OEMs. So there is no information discount to capture: the sellers price in the demand, and they often keep the right to approve the buyer because of ITAR and customer relationships.
scored.buyer: The capitalised buyers are real: Leonardo DRS, Sierra Nevada, VSE, Heico, TransDigm and AMETEK. But they are mostly competitors that buy orphaned lines directly (Heico, TransDigm, Ontic, VSE). They are not buyers waiting for someone else to prove a line, so a startup would be competing with them at the auction rather than selling to them.
scored.ladder: The ladder is reasonable: own the support rights, then become the sustainment prime, then do upgrades and modernisation, then become the OEM for derivative systems, then roll up into a TransDigm-style aftermarket platform worth over $70B. The top of the ladder is large and proven, which is why C5 scores 3. But no ML discovery edge feeds the rungs.
scored.fatal_flaw: Discovery is not the bottleneck. The proving step is the bespoke manufacturing, qualification and ITAR sustainment of the line, and the signal (DSCA, FPDS, SIPRI) is already legible and already used by well-capitalised incumbents who buy these lines (Ontic, Heico, TransDigm, VSE). That leaves no information edge, no purchase discount and no step-up of 1,000x or more.
scored.one_line_reason: This is the coal-mine-geothermal pattern in defense: finding an orphaned fielded system is easy from structured DSCA, FPDS and SIPRI data, while qualifying and sustaining the line is the real cost. The step-up is about 3-10x over years, and incumbents like Ontic and TransDigm already buy these lines.

Background knowledge, not checked: Ontic (CVC) business model of licensing or acquiring legacy aerospace product lines from OEMs.

scored.name: Decontrol Arbitrage: ITAR-to-EAR commodity jurisdiction
scored.one_line: Buy ITAR-encumbered niche product lines at domestic-only valuations, predict which will move to EAR, file CJ requests, sell export-open lines.
scored.unproven_right: ITAR product line or IP.
scored.proving_step: DDTC CJ determination ($10-50k).
scored.proven_buyer: Teledyne, FLIR, Hexcel-type strategics.
scored.public_data: DDTC CJ summaries, USML/CCL histories, BIS rulings, DTIC.
scored.frame: The rung is "own an ITAR-controlled product line, get a commodity jurisdiction (CJ) ruling, sell it as an export-open line." Inside that rung, figuring out which lines will come out as EAR is maybe 40-60% of the work (my estimate). The rest is buying a real operating business (diligence, staff, customers, ITAR registration, maybe moving production) plus the cost of holding it, and none of that is trivial. Filing the CJ is cheap and abstracted, but the asset is a working company, not a bare right, so this fails the Terranox test of a trivial physical step.
scored.step_up: About 1.2-3x, and on revenue multiples, not from near zero. This is my estimate from memory: no live search was possible because the search budget for this run was used up. An ITAR-only niche defense line might trade at about 1-2x revenue or 6-10x EBITDA. The same line free to export might reach about 1.5-3x revenue, and only if real foreign demand exists, which takes years of sales work to capture. The candidate itself claims about 2-10x. Even the top of that range is about 10^1, three orders of magnitude short of the 10^4 benchmark. A new export license does not change the earnings on day one, so a strategic buyer will not pay the uplift up front.
scored.hit_rate_capex: The CJ filing costs roughly $10-50k in counsel fees (the candidate's figure, which matches my understanding), and DDTC answers in about 60 days to a year. That cost is tiny next to the price of buying the product line, which is likely $1-20M (my estimate). So the expensive "attempt" is the acquisition, not the ruling. My recollection, which I could not verify here, is that after the 2013-2016 Export Control Reform a large share of CJ rulings, possibly a majority, came out EAR, because the order-of-review and "specially designed" release rules (22 CFR 120.11 / 120.41) make outcomes fairly predictable for experienced export-control counsel. If the base hit rate is about 30-60%, the most a better predictor could improve it is about 2-3x (1/base rate), not 10x. Capex does not fall 10x either, because the acquisition dominates and ML does not make it cheaper.
scored.data: The inputs are public and largely legible. DDTC publishes a list of final CJ determinations (product, applicant, ITAR or EAR), USML and CCL revision histories are in the Federal Register, and BIS rulings and advisory opinions are public. So the answer to "what moved to EAR" is already written into a public status field. That is exactly the pattern that killed earlier hunts: the answer is already published, so ML adds little. DTIC technical reports are messy but marginal to the decision. The order-of-review logic is rule-based and is what export-control law firms already sell. On owners: small ITAR firms usually employ or retain export-compliance counsel, so they are not unable to read their own jurisdiction status. Most could file a CJ themselves for $10-50k rather than sell at a discount.
scored.right_bought: The right can be bought, but not cheaply or in isolation. You would be buying an ITAR-registered product line, its IP, or a whole small company through negotiated M&A at going-concern prices. There is no ~$1/ha equivalent. ITAR also requires a CFIUS/DDTC notice when control changes (the 60-day prior notice under 22 CFR 122.4), which adds friction. My estimate is that the purchase price is set on current earnings, with perhaps a 10-30% discount for ITAR-only status, and no near-zero option value.
scored.buyer: Capitalised strategic buyers exist: Teledyne (which bought FLIR for about $8B in 2021), Hexcel, TransDigm, HEICO, Amphenol, and defense-focused private equity. They have money and regularly buy niche defense and dual-use lines. But they price on earnings and synergies, and they can run a CJ themselves, so they will not pay a big premium just for an EAR ruling.
scored.ladder: There are moderate rungs above: become a roll-up of export-open dual-use component lines, then move into international distribution and manufacturing. HEICO and TransDigm show that roll-ups of niche aerospace and defense parts can become companies worth tens of billions of dollars. But that ladder is a buy-and-build M&A model, not a discovery-led climb, so there is no rung where discovery stays the main lever.
scored.fatal_flaw: The step-up is a small multiple, about 1.2-3x on the value of an operating business (2-10x at best), not 10^3-10^4 from near zero. The CJ outcome is also predictable from published rules and the public DDTC list of CJ determinations, and owners or their counsel can file it themselves for $10-50k. So the arbitrage is small and has no data edge.
scored.one_line_reason: The value uplift is roughly 2x on companies bought at full price, the rulings are rule-predictable and already published, and the main cost is the acquisition, which ML does not cut. This is not a Terranox-shaped frame.

scored.name: Franchise Seats: dormant exclusive municipal service franchises
scored.one_line: Buy small operators holding exclusive waste, towing, ambulance or concession franchises whose exclusivity is buried in minutes; confirm and reset rates; sell to consolidators.
scored.unproven_right: Exclusive franchise within a family operator.
scored.proving_step: ML over minutes and ordinances; legal confirmation and rate reset.
scored.proven_buyer: WM, Republic, GFL, GMR, Clear Channel, JCDecaux.
scored.public_data: Granicus/Legistar archives, PUC filings, RFP archives.
scored.frame: The rung would be buying a family hauler, tow or ambulance operator and confirming its exclusivity. Discovery is maybe 10-20% of the work (my estimate). Most of the work is buying a business that runs day to day, keeping the trucks and crews going, rate-reset negotiations with the city council, and the risk of re-bidding when the franchise ends. Unlike drilling, the physical side is the business itself, not a small step inside it. Consolidators (WM, Republic, GFL, GMR) are well-funded buyers, but they buy cash flow, not discovery.
scored.step_up: About 1.3-2x on enterprise value (my estimate, not sourced: the search budget ran out before I could check). Small private haulers typically sell for roughly 4-7x EBITDA. Consolidators pay roughly 7-10x for tuck-ins, and public majors trade around 12-15x. Exclusive franchise routes do command a premium over open-market routes, but it is a multiple uplift, nowhere near 10^3. The candidate's own "~2-10x" is generous. A rate reset can lift EBITDA, but cities have to approve it and often cap it at CPI-linked formulas.
scored.hit_rate_capex: There is no expensive proving attempt that usually fails. Confirming exclusivity means a lawyer reads one franchise agreement and ordinance, about $5k-25k per target (my estimate). The base rate of "hidden exclusivity" is probably high among operators that hold a contract, so ML has little to improve. The real cost is the acquisition itself, about $1M-20M per small operator (my estimate), and ML does not cut that tenfold.
scored.data: The minutes and ordinances are public on Granicus/Legistar and somewhat hard to read. But the outcome is already legible: the franchise agreement is a signed contract that both the city and the operator hold, and it is usually posted on the city website or recorded in the ordinance. The operator knows they hold an exclusive franchise because it is their core revenue, so it is priced into any sale. Sellers are not unable to read their own franchise. Consolidators' M&A teams and brokers already map franchise areas, for example California's franchised-hauler lists and CalRecycle jurisdiction data (from memory, not checked this run).
scored.right_bought: The right is bought: you acquire the operator, often with change-of-control consent from the city. But it is not cheap compared with what you discover, because the seller knows what the exclusivity is worth. Many franchise agreements also need council approval to transfer, which brings scrutiny and sometimes a rebid.
scored.buyer: WM, Republic, GFL, Waste Connections, Casella (waste); GMR/Global Medical Response (ambulance); Clear Channel, JCDecaux, Outfront (concessions). They are well-funded active acquirers that already roll up tuck-ins with their own sourcing teams.
scored.ladder: The ladder above is reasonable: route density, transfer stations, landfills (where the real moat sits), MRFs, and so on. Waste Connections shows that an exclusive-franchise rollup can build a company worth more than $40B. But this ladder is ordinary private-equity roll-up, not one driven by discovery.
scored.fatal_flaw: There is no information asymmetry. The exclusive franchise is a signed contract the seller knows about and that the city publishes, so it is already in the purchase price. The step-up is a 1.3-2x multiple arbitrage that PE roll-ups and consolidators' own M&A teams already capture, not a jump of 10^3 or more.
scored.one_line_reason: This is a standard waste or ambulance roll-up dressed up as discovery: exclusivity is a signed, known, published contract, operations dominate the work, and the step-up is about 2x, not 10^4.

scored.name: Dormant Type Certificate Holdco
scored.one_line: Buy orphan TCs for out-of-production aircraft; ML finds large AD-stranded fleets; sell support, approvals or the TC.
scored.unproven_right: Orphan TC and data, $10k-500k.
scored.proving_step: ML over TCDS, ADs, SDRs and registry; FAA transfer.
scored.proven_buyer: TransDigm-style roll-ups, Textron Aviation, Mahindra, type clubs.
scored.public_data: FAA DRS TCDS, Orphaned TC list, AD/SDR databases, registry, NTSB.
scored.frame: The candidate rung is buying an orphan type certificate (TC) and its data, then selling support, approvals or the TC itself. Inside that rung, finding the TC worth buying is about 10-20% of the work (my estimate). The other 80%+ is physical and regulatory work that is neither trivial nor abstracted: you have to become the FAA-accepted holder, take on continued-airworthiness obligations (writing AD responses and service bulletins, engineering support, usually through an ODA/DER relationship), certify parts production (PMA or PC), and carry product liability. This is the coal-mine geothermal failure pattern: picking the TC is easy and running a certified OEM support business is hard. A capitalised buyer does exist (Univair-style support houses, parts roll-ups, type clubs), but it buys a running support business, not a proven discovery.
scored.step_up: I could not find any priced deals: web search budget was exhausted, so every number below is my estimate from background knowledge. Unproven: dormant GA and light-twin TCs reportedly change hands for roughly $10k-$500k, often as part of an estate or bankruptcy (the candidate's own range). Proven: a TC with a live fleet and a parts business sells as an operating company at about 1-3x revenue. Small TC-holder support businesses (Univair-type, or the holders of the Aerostar, Lake, Ercoupe and Stinson TCs) are plausibly $1-20M businesses. There is no hit event that moves value 1000x immediately. Value builds slowly through parts sales and support contracts, so a realistic step-up is about 3-10x over years, not 10^4 on a hit. The candidate's own ~10-100x is optimistic.
scored.hit_rate_capex: There is no expensive, mostly failing proving step like an exploratory drill. The proving step is a TC transfer through FAA paperwork, which costs roughly tens of thousands of dollars in legal and engineering work (my estimate) and almost always succeeds once a deal is agreed. The risk is commercial (will the fleet buy parts and support?), and the commercial facts are mostly knowable in advance. Because the base hit rate of the proving step is already high, ML can only raise it slightly: the cap of 1/base rate is about 1-2x, nowhere near 10x.
scored.data: The outcome is already summarised in legible public fields, which kills the ML edge. Fleet size by make and model is a structured field in the FAA Aircraft Registry, which is downloadable monthly. ADs are structured and searchable by TC or model in the FAA DRS. The TCDS names the holder. The FAA keeps an explicit list of orphaned aircraft and TCs. SDRs are structured. The only illegible signal left is in free-text SDRs, NTSB narratives and type-club forums (what parts are short and which ADs strand the fleet), and that is marginal. On the right itself: orphan TCs can be bought from estates, bankrupt OEMs or retired holders who know little about their fleets, so the purchase is a real negotiated sale. But the people who matter (Univair, type clubs, parts houses) can read the registry just as easily, so there is no information asymmetry to exploit.
scored.right_bought: Yes, the right is bought, not free: an orphan TC and its data package come from estates, bankruptcy trustees or retiring holders, at an estimated $10k-$500k. The catch is that the TC holder takes on liability and continued-airworthiness duties. GARA's 18-year statute of repose helps on old airframes, but installing new parts restarts the clock for those parts.
scored.buyer: Possible buyers: Univair-style orphan-TC support houses, parts roll-ups (TransDigm-type, though they want high-margin proprietary parts on large fleets, not GA orphans), Textron Aviation or Mahindra only for their own legacy lines, type clubs, and owners of grounded fleets. None of them is a deep, liquid buyer paying 10^3x for a proven asset.
scored.ladder: TC holding, then a parts manufacturing approval (PMA/PC), then an MRO/support network, then possibly restarting production of a type (as with Aerostar, Mooney and Lake). Each rung up is capital-heavy certification work, and the whole addressable pool (legacy GA and commuter fleets) is shrinking. There is a path to a $100M-$1B niche aerospace aftermarket holdco, but not a trillion-dollar chain.
scored.fatal_flaw: Discovery is not the bottleneck. Fleet size, AD burden and TC holder are already legible in the FAA registry, DRS and the FAA's orphaned-aircraft list, and the value of the asset comes from running a certified airworthiness-support and parts business with liability attached. There is no proving event that produces an immediate 10^3x step-up. This is the geothermal-in-coal-mines pattern: finding the asset is easy and operating it is hard.
scored.one_line_reason: The fleet data is already in structured FAA records, the step-up is a slow 3-10x from operations rather than an instant jump on a discovery hit, and most of the work is certification, support and liability rather than discovery.

Discovery (the records audit) is perhaps 10-20% of the work and value in that rung (my estimate). A321 feedstock runs about $12-15M; a converted A321P2F is worth about $25-30M after about $6M of conversion. The net step-up is about 1.2-2x, not 10^3-10^4. The candidate's own figure of ~2-5x is optimistic.

scored.data: The public data (registry, ADs, SDRs, NTSB/ASN, SEC lease filings) is mostly structured and legible already, and services like Cirium, IBA and Aviation Week Fleet Discovery sell it summarised. What decides eligibility is the back-to-birth maintenance records, LLP status and corrosion/structural repair history. Those are private records held by the lessor or operator, not public filings. The outcome is effectively written into fields incumbents already track (type, MSN, age, cycles, operator). The data edge is weak.
scored.right_bought: The airframe is bought on the open market, but the sellers are sophisticated lessors and airlines (AerCap, SMBC, Avolon, airline fleet teams). scored.buyer: Real, capitalised buyers exist: converters and cargo lessors (EFW, IAI Bedek, Mammoth, AEI, ATSG, Vx Capital, Air Lease, Merx, Aircastle Cargo), plus integrators like DHL, Amazon, FedEx and UPS. But they already source feedstock directly through their own technical and asset-management teams, and several converters run feedstock-plus-conversion programs themselves.
scored.ladder: There are real rungs above: feedstock, then owning conversion slots or STCs, then freighter leasing, then an ACMI cargo airline. Moderate size: freighter leasing is a large, multi-billion-dollar asset class. But each rung is capital-heavy, and the incumbents (ATSG, AerCap Cargo, Vx) are already vertically integrated.
scored.fatal_flaw: The value comes from a $4-6M physical conversion, roughly the price of the airframe itself, that waits on scarce converter slots. This is the geothermal-in-coal-mines counter-example in aviation form. Finding the right airframe is the easy, high-hit-rate, already-solved part; the bespoke physical step is the hard part. The step-up is also only about 1.2-2x, the sellers are sophisticated, and the deciding data is private, not public.

scored.name: Retired-Iron Grid Bank: decommissioned large power transformers
scored.one_line: Locate retired LPTs, GSUs and breakers at closed plants via rate cases and retirement filings; buy at scrap; DGA/test; sell or lease to data centers and utilities facing 3-4 year lead times.
scored.unproven_right: Title to units booked at copper scrap.
scored.proving_step: ML location and nameplate matching; DGA, Doble, FRA tests; refurbishment outsourced.
scored.proven_buyer: Hyperscalers, colos, utilities, IPPs.
scored.public_data: PUC dockets, FERC Form 1, EIA-860 retirements, demolition RFPs, WARN.
scored.frame: The rung is buying a retired large power transformer (LPT) or generator step-up (GSU) unit, testing it and reselling it. Discovery is roughly 10-20% of the work inside that rung (my estimate). The rest is physical and bespoke: de-energising and draining oil, heavy rigging, permits for oversize loads, heavy-haul trucking or Schnabel railcar moves (often $0.3-1M+ per unit, estimate), refurbishment or rewind, and matching voltage, impedance, MVA and footprint to a buyer's spec. This is the geothermal-in-a-coal-mine pattern: finding the unit is easy, while making it usable at a new site is the hard part. A capitalised buyer does exist (utilities, IPPs, data centers).
scored.step_up: Unproven: a ~100-300 MVA unit sold for scrap is worth about $0.1-0.4M (estimate: roughly 20-40 t of copper plus steel and oil). Proven: a refurbished used LPT probably sells for $1-4M, against $3-10M+ new. The new-price range rests on the DOE 2014 LPT report ($2-7.5M), raised for the roughly 60-80% price inflation since 2020; both figures are from memory, not verified this run. The gross gain is about 3-15x, and closer to 2-5x net once $0.5-1.5M of haul, rigging and refurbishment is subtracted (estimate). The candidate's own claim of 10-50x is too high. That puts this far below the 10^3-10^4 band.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Proving a unit means a DGA oil sample (about $100-500), Doble power factor tests, FRA and turns-ratio tests (roughly $5-30k per unit on site), all my estimates. Proving is cheap. The base hit rate is probably 30-60% of retired units being serviceable, but many are 40-60 years old and were retired near end of life (estimate). Because proving is already cheap and fails less than half the time, ML can cut proving capex by at most about 2-3x, nowhere near 10x.
scored.data: The signal is mostly legible already. EIA-860 has structured retirement and planned-retirement fields for each generator, with dates. GSUs map one-to-one onto the generators listed there. FERC Form 1 and utility rate cases are semi-structured. Matching nameplate data (MVA, voltages, impedance) does need unstructured documents, which is a small ML edge, but the outcome of interest ('this unit is free to sell') is close to the public retirement status. Used-equipment dealers and utility spare-sharing programs already work this inventory (EEI STEP and the Grid Assurance spare pool, plus brokers and rebuilders such as Maddox and Sunbelt Solomon; named from memory, not verified this run). Owners are sophisticated utilities who know a working LPT is worth more than scrap. Many keep units as internal spares or reuse the GSU and interconnection for gas, storage or solar repowering through surplus interconnection service. So a scrap-price purchase is unlikely except in distress or demolition-contractor cases.
scored.right_bought: Title to the physical unit, bought from the plant owner or the demolition contractor. Sometimes demolition contracts already assign the scrap and salvage value to the contractor. Purchase is possible, but rarely at copper-scrap price for a unit that tests healthy.
scored.buyer: Utilities, IPPs, hyperscalers and colocation operators facing 2-4 year lead times for new LPTs. Wood Mackenzie and NREL reported about 120-210 weeks in 2024; this is from memory, not verified this run. Demand is real, but buyers need units matched to their spec, which shrinks the usable pool.
scored.ladder: Rungs above exist: refurbishment and rewind shops, then transformer manufacturing, then a substation or powered-site developer. That is a plausible climb into a large equipment and infrastructure business, but each rung is capital-intensive manufacturing, not discovery-led, and the lead-time shortage that drives demand may ease as manufacturers add capacity by 2027-2029.
scored.fatal_flaw: Inside the rung, the physical step dominates: rigging, heavy haul, refurbishment and spec-matching are bespoke and cost about as much as the gain. Finding the units is easy, because retirements sit in legible EIA-860 fields and dealers and utilities already canvass them. The step-up is about 3-10x, not 10^3.
scored.one_line_reason: The real lead-time shortage makes this a reasonable used-equipment brokerage, but it inverts the Terranox rubric: discovery is cheap and already legible, the physical step dominates, and the step-up is only single-digit.

scored.name: Vested Fuel-Use Rescue: dormant gas stations as EV charging sites
scored.one_line: Option closed gas stations whose grandfathered fueling use and large service have not lapsed; prove with zoning and utility letters; sell to fast-charging operators.
scored.unproven_right: Purchase/lease option on a station parcel.
scored.proving_step: ML over permits, UST closures, business licences and hosting maps; zoning verification and will-serve.
scored.proven_buyer: Tesla, Ionna, bp pulse, Electrify America, Mercedes HPC.
scored.public_data: EPA UST Finder, state UST databases, permit archives, utility ICA maps, AFDC, gas-station bans.
scored.frame: The rung is "an optioned parcel with confirmed charger zoning and utility capacity, sold or leased to a charging operator". Inside that rung, discovery is roughly 30-40% of the work (my estimate). The rest is physical or bureaucratic: the utility capacity study, line extension or transformer upgrade (often months and six figures), UST removal and environmental clearance, and site-host negotiation. Unlike a drill, the proving step does not resolve a hidden physical fact. It requests answers that the utility and the zoning office produce on their own timelines. The buyers exist and have capital (Tesla, Ionna, bp pulse, Electrify America), but they usually lease sites or take landowner deals rather than paying a premium for options.
scored.step_up: No price data was retrieved because the shared web search budget was used up. All figures here are my estimates. A closed-station parcel in a secondary market might trade at about $300k-1.5M. A charger-ready version would gain perhaps 1.1-1.5x as land, since charging operators typically pay site-host rent (about $10k-50k per year per site, my estimate) or revenue share, not a land premium. An option might go from about $10k to about $50-150k assignment value (5-15x) in the best case, but option assignments to CPOs are not an established market. The candidate's own "1.5-3x on parcel" is the honest figure. That is far below 10^3.
scored.hit_rate_capex: My estimates, unsourced because search was unavailable. A zoning check costs about $1-5k (a letter or a review by an attorney). A utility will-serve or capacity study costs about $5-25k and takes 3-12 months. The base hit rate for "commercial parcel near a highway can get charging zoning" is high, perhaps 70-90%, because EV charging is a permitted or accessory use in most commercial zones and several states (for example California AB 1236) require streamlined approval. The hit rate for "existing service is enough for 1+ MW DCFC without upgrade" is low, but that is fixed by spending on upgrades, not by discovery. A 1/base-hit-rate cap of about 1.1-3x means ML cannot cut capex 10x.
scored.data: The public data is partly illegible: EPA UST Finder, state UST closure records, scattered permit archives and business licences. But the answers that matter are legible or are not in data at all. Utility ICA and hosting-capacity maps already publish feeder capacity. AFDC lists existing chargers. Zoning tables state whether charging is allowed. Charging operators and their site-acquisition firms already use these layers, and platforms like Volta and ChargePoint site tools did this kind of siting. An ML edge over a planner with GIS is small. On the right: station owners are not unable to read the data. Closed-station sellers are often oil-company or jobber portfolios that know their sites well, and the UST liability discount works against the buyer.
scored.right_bought: Yes, parcels and options are bought from private owners, not claimed first-come. But there is no information asymmetry to buy cheaply against. A closed gas station is priced as contaminated commercial land, and the seller's discount reflects real UST remediation liability, which the buyer inherits.
scored.buyer: Tesla Supercharger, Ionna, bp pulse, Electrify America, Mercedes HPC, Walmart and Buc-ee's partnerships. Most prefer leases or host agreements on operating retail sites (amenities, dwell time) over dormant stations, so demand for bare closed-station options is thin.
scored.ladder: Option, then entitled site, then owning chargers, then operating a CPO network, then energy and storage. The rungs exist, but the higher ones are low-margin, capital-heavy, commoditised and dominated by Tesla. That gives a path to a mid-size infrastructure company, not a trillion-dollar chain.
scored.fatal_flaw: The "vested fueling use" premise does not hold up. EV charging generally does not need the grandfathered gasoline-dispensing right, because it is permitted or accessory in commercial zones and states are streamlining it. So the lapsing right protects nothing the buyer needs. The real constraint is grid capacity, which the utility decides and partly publishes in hosting maps, and which is cured with capex, not found by discovery. There is no 10^3 step-up and no low-hit-rate proving step for ML to lever.
scored.one_line_reason: Physical and utility work outweighs discovery. The step-up is 1.5-3x on the parcel. Zoning and grid capacity answers are legible or utility-controlled. And charging does not need the vested fuel right, so the core asymmetry is illusory.

scored.right_bought: Bought, yes: salvage title at open auction. scored.buyer: Rebuilders and exporters (e.g. many Copart international buyers), EV pack remanufacturers and salvage specialists (e.g. Gruber Motor Co., independent Tesla rebuild shops), second-life storage integrators, and recyclers such as Redwood Materials and Li-Cycle successor operators. scored.name: Dormant CON bed rights bank
scored.one_line: Buy banked or delicensed beds in CON/moratorium states from estates; ML proves validity and relocatability; sell to health systems, REITs and operators.
scored.unproven_right: Banked bed authorizations, $0-2k/bed.
scored.proving_step: Chain of title from CON decisions, need tables and surveys; relocation approval.
scored.proven_buyer: Health systems, Welltower, Omega, Sabra, SNF operators.
scored.public_data: State CON archives and bed inventories, CMS POS, HCRIS, survey records.
scored.rough_step_up: ~10-100x+; some inventories legible, some states ban sale.
scored.frame: The rung is: buy a banked or delicensed nursing-home bed authorization, confirm it is still valid and can be moved, and resell it. Inside that rung, finding the right and proving it is maybe 60-70% of the work (my estimate). The rest is not trivial. Moving beds needs a state CON approval or a transfer filing, which can take months and can be contested. Most states also require the beds to be placed into an operating or planned facility, so a buyer can only use them if it is already building or expanding a home. Buyers do exist and have money (SNF operators, health systems, and REITs such as Omega, Sabra and Welltower through their operators). But they buy beds tied to a project, not as a separate asset class.
scored.step_up: I could not check numbers: the shared web-search budget ran out before I made any query. What follows is my estimate from background knowledge. In moratorium or CON states (for example Ohio, Michigan, Kentucky, North Carolina, New York), SNF bed rights are reported to trade at roughly $5k-$30k per bed through brokers and in operator deals. An estate or closed operator that knows what its beds are worth sells near market. The candidate's '$0-2k/bed' entry price would only hold for distressed or unaware holders, which gives about 3-10x at best (I scored C2 a 1, toward the low end, because most holders know the price). It does not go from near zero to 10^3-10^4. In many cases beds that have lapsed or expired are simply void, so their value is zero rather than a mispriced option.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Estimate, not sourced (no searches ran). Proving means a legal and regulatory check: chain of title, whether the banking period has run out, and whether the state will allow relocation. It costs roughly $5k-$50k in lawyer and consultant time per transfer (estimate). This is not an expensive, mostly-failing shot in the way an exploratory drill hole is. Once a bed shows as banked or licensed in the state inventory, the base hit rate is probably over 50%. So the 1/base-hit-rate lever is capped at about 2x, not 10x.
scored.data: The data is mostly legible, which removes the ML edge. States with CON or moratorium rules publish bed inventories and need tables that list licensed, banked or reserved beds by facility and owner (for example Ohio ODH bed records, NC State Medical Facilities Plan inventory tables, Michigan bed inventories). CMS POS and HCRIS give certified bed counts in structured form. The answer to 'does this bed right exist and who holds it' already sits in a status field. The illegible part, old CON decision PDFs used to rebuild chain of title, matters only for edge cases. Sellers are mostly operators and their lawyers, who know the brokered market, not owners who cannot read the data.
scored.right_bought: Partly. Where the state permits it, bed rights are bought from operators or estates, not claimed free on a first-come basis. But several states forbid selling beds apart from a facility, or let unused or banked beds revert to the state when the time limit passes. In those cases the right cannot be held as a standalone, stockpiled asset. Health systems and operators with an active project are the natural buyers, and they already source beds through brokers and their CON counsel.
scored.buyer: SNF and post-acute operators, and health systems that are expanding (capitalised, but buying only for specific projects). REITs (Omega, Sabra, Welltower) mostly gain exposure through operators and do not buy loose bed rights. Demand is limited by declining SNF occupancy trends, Medicaid reimbursement pressure, and states repealing or loosening CON rules, which pushes bed-right value toward zero.
scored.ladder: The rungs above are: develop or relocate a facility, then operate SNFs, then own the real estate (a REIT-like model). Climbing them means building and running facilities and carrying heavy regulatory and staffing risk. That is the bespoke physical-execution problem the geothermal-in-coal-mines counter-example warns about. The total market is also capped and shrinking, since SNF bed rights are a policy artifact that disappears where CON is repealed. That rules out a trillion-dollar path.
scored.fatal_flaw: There is little discovery to do. Whether a bed right exists and who holds it is already in legible state bed-inventory and need-table status fields and in CMS POS/HCRIS. Holders and brokers already price these rights in a known market. So there is no near-zero-to-10^4 mispricing for ML to unlock. On top of that, the asset can be made worthless by policy, through CON repeal or expiry of banked beds.
scored.one_line_reason: The outcome is already a legible regulatory status field, the market is brokered and priced, the step-up is about 3-10x at best, and proving is legal paperwork with a high hit rate rather than a costly, low-hit-rate shot. It is a weak fit for the rubric.
