That is the pattern the rubric says kills the ML edge.
scored.right_bought: The right can be bought in principle: distressed social-equity licensees do sell stakes. But transfers are restricted. Social-equity licences often carry holding periods, ownership-percentage rules (for example majority SE ownership) and change-of-control approval by the regulator. MSOs often cannot legally hold them, or are already at licence caps. The sellers are not unable to read the data. They are short of capital and local support, and they know exactly why their licence is stranded.
scored.buyer: Named buyers: Curaleaf, Trulieve, Green Thumb (GTI), Verano. These MSOs have been cutting back since 2022: share prices are down sharply, debt is heavy, they are closing or selling stores, and they face per-entity licence caps in states like Illinois. Their appetite for buying new licences is weak and the buyer pool is shrinking. The pending Schedule III rescheduling could help through 280E tax relief, but it does not legalise interstate commerce.
scored.ladder: The rungs above are licence, then site, then build, then operate retail, then cultivation and processing, then multi-state. The chain exists but it is fragmented by state, capped by state licence limits, and stays legally grey while cannabis remains federally illegal. Price compression (wholesale flower prices down sharply in mature markets) erodes the top of the chain. Federal legalisation would open a national market, but it would also wipe out the scarcity value of the licences themselves. That gives a ceiling of maybe a mid-size company, not a trillion-dollar path.
scored.fatal_flaw: The proving step is not discovery. Compliant parcels are easy to find with legible GIS and ordinance text, and are already mapped by cannabis real-estate brokers. What strands a licence is municipal SUP and opt-out politics, landlord refusal, buildout capital and transfer restrictions on social-equity licences, and ML touches none of these. The licence status is already a public field, and the MSO buyers are retrenching.
scored.one_line_reason: This is the geothermal-in-coal-mines failure: siting is about 15% of the work while permits, capital and politics are about 85%, the outcome sits in legible regulator fields, the step-up is roughly 5-15x and needs a costly buildout, and the MSO buyers are shrinking.

scored.name: Revivable pocket liquor licences
scored.one_line: Buy inactive pocket/escrowed quota licences in NJ/MA/PA; ML proves revivability; sell to restaurant and grocery groups.
scored.unproven_right: Inactive licences of uncertain status, $20-100k.
scored.proving_step: Renewal-chain reconstruction, special ruling and transfer.
scored.proven_buyer: Restaurant groups, Wawa, ShopRite, Wegmans, developers.
scored.public_data: NJ ABC database and rulings, council minutes, MA ABCC, PLCB.
scored.frame: The rung is "acquire an inactive/pocket licence, get it renewed, and transfer it to an operator". Inside that rung, discovery (finding which inactive licences are revivable and whose owners will sell) is perhaps 40-50% of the work (my estimate). The rest is legal and process work: N.J.S.A. 33:1-12.39 special-ruling petitions, municipal renewal and place-to-place or person-to-person transfer hearings, objector risk, and broker negotiation. That work is not trivial or abstracted. It looks like the coal-mine geothermal counter-example: proving the licence takes about as much work as finding it.
scored.step_up: The candidate claims about 5-20x ($20-100k in, up to a full market licence out). All figures below are my estimates from memory; none were verified this run. NJ plenary retail consumption licences in quota-constrained towns trade around $300k-$1M+, and pocket licences already trade near that because buyers price the 12.39 risk. MA Boston and suburban all-alcohol licences trade around $300-600k. PLCB auctions of expired restaurant licences (Act 39, 2016) have cleared at about $100k-$700k+ depending on county. A truly distressed licence with an unclear renewal chain might trade at a 30-70% discount to full value, so the realistic step-up is about 2-5x. That is nowhere near 10^3.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Estimate, not verified: the base hit rate looks high, not low. NJ ABC routinely grants 12.39 rulings when good cause is shown (for example, an active search for a site or a pending sale), so most licences that are actually alive get revived. Each attempt costs about $5-30k in legal fees plus 3-12 months of time (estimate). With a base hit rate around 50-80%, the ML lever is capped at about 1.3-2x, not 10x. The real constraint is supply and owner pricing, not the hit rate.
scored.data: The data is public but mostly legible. NJ ABC's POSSE licence lookup lists each licence's status (active, inactive/pocket, expired) and renewal term. Municipal clerks publish renewal resolutions. PLCB's public licence search shows status, including safekeeping and expired, and PLCB auctions expired licences itself. MA ABCC and local boards publish quota counts. The outcome (whether the licence is renewable) sits largely in a status field plus whether a 12.39 ruling was issued. That matches the pattern seen in earlier hunts, where the regulator has already written down the answer. Holders of pocket licences are often sophisticated (restaurant families, estates using liquor-licence brokers), and municipal quota scarcity is widely known. Little information asymmetry is left to buy cheaply. Some edge may remain in messy renewal-chain gaps (estates, bankruptcies, foreclosures), but that pool is small.
scored.right_bought: Yes, the licences are bought, not claimed free. They come through private sales via brokers, estate and bankruptcy sales, and in PA a state auction. They are not cheap, though: sellers and brokers price them near market. Distressed pricing is mainly available in bankruptcy or estate situations with a broken renewal chain.
scored.buyer: Restaurant groups, grocery and convenience chains (Wawa, ShopRite, Wegmans, Total Wine, Stew Leonard's), and mixed-use developers. They are well capitalised and do buy licences. But the market is thin: a few hundred to a few thousand transactions a year across NJ, MA and PA (estimate).
scored.ladder: Weak. The rungs above (owning the restaurants or stores, or the real estate) are ordinary hospitality and retail businesses where a licence edge gives no lasting advantage. Total addressable value is capped by statutory quotas: NJ has about 10-12k retail licences in total, roughly $3-10B of licence value at most (estimate). This is a brokerage and arbitrage niche, not a trillion-dollar path.
scored.fatal_flaw: The outcome is already legible and priced in. Licence status sits in public regulator databases (NJ POSSE, PLCB licence search, which shows safekeeping and expired), and the 12.39 revival is a routine, mostly-granted legal process. So there is no low-hit-rate proving step for ML to improve, and owners and brokers already price pocket licences near market value. That leaves a step-up of about 2-5x, not 10^3-10^4.
scored.one_line_reason: This is legal arbitrage on a regulator-legible status field, with a high base revival rate and only a 2-5x step-up. Neither the discovery-dominant frame nor the ML hit-rate lever applies.

scored.name: Landmark Air: landmark transferable development rights
scored.one_line: Option unused development rights of small landmarks; ML proves transferable FAR and receiving sites from scanned zoning lot declarations; sell to developers.
scored.unproven_right: Unused floor area options, $0.1-1M.
scored.proving_step: ACRIS declarations, prior mergers, LPC reports; legal certification.
scored.proven_buyer: SL Green, Extell, JDS, Vornado.
scored.public_data: NYC ACRIS, LPC reports, PLUTO, Zoning Resolution, other city TDR programs.
scored.frame: The rung is "option unused landmark floor area, certify it as transferable, sell it to a developer." Discovery is maybe 20-30% of the work inside that rung (my estimate). Most of the effort and the value come from two other things. First, finding a receiving site that legally qualifies: for a landmark transfer under ZR 74-79 it must be adjacent or across the street, and East Midtown has its own subdistrict rules. Second, getting the transfer approved, which means an LPC report, a CPC special permit and often ULURP, taking 1-3 years with land-use counsel. That approval step is like building a bespoke plant, not like drilling, so it fails the "physical step is trivial" test. There are capitalised buyers (SL Green, Vornado, Extell, JDS), but they buy deals already tied to a receiving site, not an abstract proven right.
scored.step_up: No new data: the shared web search budget was used up before any search ran, so these figures are from memory and estimates. Manhattan air rights have generally traded at roughly $150-$450/sf of buildable area. Landmark transfers have historically cleared at a discount to as-of-right merger rights. In East Midtown (2017 rezoning), landmark transfers carried a minimum contribution to a public fund, set around $61.49/sf, and reported sales such as St. Patrick's Cathedral to JPMorgan were reported in the low hundreds of dollars per sf. The key point is that the unproven right is not near zero. Owners already know they hold unused FAR and price an option at a large share of the proven value. My estimated step-up from option to certified sale is about 1.5-3x, not 10^3. It only gets bigger where the owner is unaware or distressed, and that is rare for Manhattan landmarks.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Estimate, not sourced. Telling whether a landmark has unused FAR is close to free and nearly always right, because PLUTO lists maximum FAR and built FAR. The expensive, uncertain step is the legal one: title and zoning-lot work at roughly $25k-$150k per lot, plus a special permit that costs $0.5-2M in counsel, consultants and time. Approval odds once a receiving site is lined up are moderate to high, perhaps 50-70%. The base hit rate on discovery is therefore already high, so ML's lever (capped at 1/hit rate) is under 2x, not 10x. ML does not shorten the approval process.
scored.data: The core signal, unused floor area, is already a legible public field: PLUTO has BuiltFAR plus residential, commercial and facility maximum FAR, and commercial tools (PropertyShark, Reonomy, CoStar) compute unused air rights from it directly. That is the "outcome already in a status field" failure that killed earlier hunts. The genuinely illegible part is the scanned ACRIS zoning lot declarations (ZLDs) and light-and-air easements showing that floor area was already transferred or merged away. ML on those could correct PLUTO's overstatements, which is a real but small edge: mostly it removes false positives rather than finding hidden value. Incumbents already do this deal by deal: brokers (Avison Young, Cushman & Wakefield, Meridian; per CRE coverage, not checked here), zoning consultants and land-use firms (Kramer Levin, Slater & Beckerman, Akerman), and developers' in-house teams. Rights can be bought by option, but landmark owners (churches, institutions, small owners) are usually well advised and know what their air rights are worth, so the discount on purchase is thin.
scored.right_bought: Rights are bought, not free first-come, through an option or purchase agreement on the floor area. The purchase discount is small, though, because unused FAR is legible and widely marketed. Sellers often hold out for the specific adjacent developer, who has monopsony-like power because only a few sites can legally receive a landmark's floor area. That bilateral lock means a middleman holding the option has little leverage over either side.
scored.buyer: Manhattan developers and REITs (SL Green, Vornado, Extell, JDS, Related, Silverstein, JPMorgan in East Midtown). They are well capitalised, but each one buys only for its own receiving site and usually negotiates directly with the landmark owner.
scored.ladder: The possible climb is: options on floor area, then assembling zoning lots and sites, then co-developing or developing towers, then a full NYC and multi-city development platform. The rungs are real and lead to a large business (a Related or Extell scale developer). The bottom rung, though, is a thin brokerage-like margin with little ML edge, so it may not fund the climb. TDR programs in other cities (Seattle, San Francisco, Chicago, Miami) are small and illiquid.
scored.fatal_flaw: The outcome is already summarised in a legible public field (PLUTO built FAR versus maximum FAR), and owners already know and price their air rights. Value comes from the adjacency of a receiving site and a slow discretionary approval (LPC, CPC, ULURP), not from discovery. So there is no near-zero-to-10^3 jump: the step-up is about 1.5-3x, and ML's lever on a high base hit rate is under 2x.
scored.one_line_reason: The unused floor area is already visible in PLUTO and known to owners, and the hard part is legal approval tied to a specific adjacent site. That makes it a thin brokerage-style arbitrage with a 1.5-3x step-up, not a Terranox-style discovery rung.

scored.name: Reclass: closed shellfish areas proven clean
scored.one_line: Buy leases in Prohibited/Restricted shellfish waters whose pollution sources are gone; fund NSSP sampling to upgrade to Approved; sell to oyster growers.
scored.unproven_right: Closed lease bottom at $0-50/acre.
scored.proving_step: ML screen; 15-30 sample NSSP series and sanitary survey (12-24 months).
scored.proven_buyer: Commercial oyster growers and consolidators.
scored.public_data: State shellfish sampling databases and reports, NSSP files, ECHO/NPDES, septic permits, NLCD, historic oyster plats.
scored.frame: The rung is "lease in a closed area, reopened by reclassification." Within it, discovery (working out which closed areas are clean now) might be 50-60% of the work. The proving step is not cheap or abstracted. NSSP classification needs a sanitary survey plus at least 15 (systematic random) or 30 (adverse pollution) sample results, collected over 12-24 months and analysed or accepted by the state shellfish authority's certified lab. The authority (for example VDH Division of Shellfish Safety, WA DOH) makes the call. A private party cannot prove the area itself; it can only petition and pay for the work. Reclassification often also comes with conditional or management-plan requirements. The buyer, an oyster grower, is a small, thinly capitalised business, not a mine developer. Most of this is my estimate from knowledge of the NSSP Model Ordinance.
scored.step_up: Estimate, not verified this run (no searches were available). Virginia VMRC leases state bottom at about $1.50/acre/yr, assigned by application. An unproven closed lease is worth about $0-50/acre. Proven Approved leased ground in productive Chesapeake areas plausibly trades at about $500-5,000/acre. WA private tidelands with good oyster ground could reach about $10k-50k/acre, but most of those are already Approved and owned by growers. Realistic step-up is about 10-100x in raw terms, but in small absolute dollars per acre, and the buyer gets it only after it adds the real work of seeding and growing for 2-3 years.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Estimate. A sampling series plus sanitary survey costs about $20k-100k per area (about $100-300 per sample run over 15-30+ runs, plus staff and boat time over 12-24 months). The base hit rate for a closed area passing is low where the closure has a reason (WWTP outfalls, marinas and nonpoint runoff persist). Closures are largely driven by nonpoint sources and rainfall, which do not go away. The state already samples its classified waters routinely (NSSP requires annual reviews and triennial re-evaluations), so the easy wins are captured by the regulator for free. The ML lever is capped by state monitoring already surfacing the improving areas.
scored.data: This fails the rubric's key test. The outcome is already written into a legible public status field. Every NSSP state publishes classification maps (Approved, Conditionally Approved, Restricted, Prohibited) and growing-area annual reports with fecal coliform statistics (geometric mean, 90th percentile) for every station. The data is structured and read by the regulator itself, which changes the classification. ECHO/NPDES and NLCD are already legible. Rights also fail. Leases on state bottom are first-come applications at nominal rent, not rights bought from owners who cannot read the data. In many states you cannot lease, or the lease has no value, in Prohibited waters.
scored.right_bought: Mostly not bought. State-bottom leases (VA, MD, NJ, LA and others) are applied for from the state at nominal rent, about $1.50/acre/yr in VA (from memory), first-come and often with residency or use requirements and shellfish-planting obligations. Private tidelands (WA) are bought, but owners there are growers who know the classification. There is no information-asymmetry seller.
scored.buyer: Commercial oyster growers and consolidators, for example Taylor Shellfish (WA) and Chesapeake lease holders. They are small and fragmented, with limited capital. US oyster farm-gate value is about $300M/yr, an estimate from memory of NOAA/USDA aquaculture census figures. This is not a buyer that pays $10k/ha on proof.
scored.ladder: Weak. Lease, then grow oysters, then process and distribute. A vertically integrated oyster company tops out at roughly $100M-scale revenue, and the whole US market is small. No trillion-dollar path. The adjacent ladder (water-quality remediation and nutrient credits) is a different business.
scored.fatal_flaw: The proving step belongs to the state regulator, and its result is already published. State shellfish authorities sample every growing area routinely and publish the classification and fecal-coliform statistics, so the outcome sits in a legible public field. The proof cannot be run privately to capture an asymmetry, and the unproven right is a near-free first-come state lease rather than something bought cheaply from uninformed owners.
scored.one_line_reason: This fails C4 hard. Regulators already sample these waters and publish the classification, the right is a nominal first-come state lease, and the step-up is about 10-100x in small dollars sold to thinly capitalised oyster growers with no big ladder above.

scored.name: Riparian: NJ tidelands-claim title clearing
scored.one_line: Buy NJ parcels clouded by wrong state tidelands claims; ML georectifies 19th-century T-sheets against claim maps; obtain Statement of No Interest; sell clean title.
scored.unproven_right: Clouded fee parcels at 10-40% of value.
scored.proving_step: Overlay analysis, surveyor report, NJDEP application ($5-25k).
scored.proven_buyer: Waterfront developers, industrial REITs, homebuyers.
scored.public_data: NJDEP Tidelands Claim Maps, NOAA T-sheets, NJ historic aerials, MOD-IV, deeds, grant index.
scored.frame: The rung is a clouded NJ waterfront fee parcel, turned into an insurable fee parcel by getting a Statement of No Interest (SNI) or buying a riparian grant. Discovery here means showing the claim line is wrong by georectifying T-sheets against the NJDEP claim maps. My estimate is that this is only about 30-50% of the work. The rest is survey, legal argument, review by the Tidelands Resource Council and NJDEP, and months to years of waiting. That is not trivial or abstracted: it is the bureaucratic equivalent of building the bespoke plant. Buyers exist (developers, REITs, homebuyers), but they mostly buy clean title as it is, not the rung's output at a premium.
scored.step_up: Estimate, not sourced, because the search budget was used up. In the clouded parcels that trade (through a title exception or a seller who must get a grant), the discount is usually small. Buyers price in the cost of a riparian grant or an SNI, roughly in the thousands to low six figures, not a wipeout of the whole parcel's value. The candidate's '10-40% of value' purchase price is plausible only for parcels that are fully or mostly claimed and undevelopable. The realistic step-up is about 1.2-3x, and 2-10x is the optimistic ceiling. That is nowhere near 10^3-10^4.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Estimate. The proving cost per attempt is about $5-25k (survey, title or riparian counsel, and the NJDEP application fee, which is in the hundreds to low thousands). Hit rate: on parcels where a claim looks clearly wrong after the historical analysis, SNIs are probably granted more often than not, at a guessed 40-70%. With a base hit rate that high, ML can improve the hit rate by at most about 1.5-2.5x. The proving step is not expensive and mostly failing; the cost is time and the legal process.
scored.data: The NJDEP Tidelands Claim Maps are already published as a public GIS layer (NJ GeoWeb). NOAA T-sheets are scanned and partly georeferenced already. Grants and SNIs are recorded in the grant index and deeds. So the outcome (claimed or not, granted or not) already sits in fairly legible public layers, and every NJ title search pulls a tidelands search as standard. The one illegible part is re-reading the historical mean high water line from T-sheets and old aerials, and riparian surveyors already do that by hand. The ML edge is modest. The one real piece of illegibility is that the claim maps from the 1970s-80s are known to be over-inclusive.
scored.right_bought: The fee parcel can be bought, so this is not first-come. But owners are not unable to read the data. Their title company flags the tidelands exception at closing, and specialised riparian attorneys and surveyors (an established NJ niche) clear it for them. Motivated sellers clear the cloud themselves, or price only the grant cost into the sale. A deep discount exists only on parcels that really are mostly claimed, and there the state's claim is often valid, so it ends as a grant purchase rather than a step-up.
scored.buyer: Waterfront and residential developers, industrial and logistics REITs on the Hudson and Delaware waterfronts, and homebuyers. They are well capitalised, but they buy clean land at market price. Nobody pays a premium specifically for proven tidelands clearance beyond removing the discount.
scored.ladder: Weak. From title clearing you could move into waterfront land assembly or redevelopment. That is ordinary real-estate development with no compounding discovery edge, and the market is one state's tidelands, a finite and small parcel set (my estimate: thousands of materially clouded parcels, not millions). It does not lead to a very large company.
scored.fatal_flaw: The step-up is tiny (about 1.2-3x realistically) because the clouded discount equals roughly the cost of a riparian grant or SNI. Clearing is a routine, legible service that NJ title companies and riparian attorneys already provide, so there is no 10^4 jump and no information asymmetry to exploit.
scored.one_line_reason: This is title-cure arbitrage. Discounts are small, the hit rate is already moderate, the state claim layer and grant index are already legible and checked at every closing, a slow legal and bureaucratic step dominates the work, and the market is finite and stuck in one state.

Background knowledge, not fetched: NJ GeoWeb's public Tidelands Claim layer from NJDEP
Background knowledge, not fetched: NOAA historical T-sheets (shoreline surveys) as scanned public archives

scored.name: Canopy Title: timber on heirs' and absentee parcels
scored.one_line: LiDAR/FIA ML finds unknown merchantable timber on cheap absentee parcels; buy, cruise, sell stumpage or land. Calibration counter-example.
scored.unproven_right: Timber deeds or fee at bare-land prices.
scored.proving_step: Timber cruise ($5-15/acre), rarely fails.
scored.proven_buyer: Mills, TIMOs/REITs, carbon developers.
scored.public_data: 3DEP LiDAR, FIA, parcel and tax rolls, probate, NAIP.
scored.frame: Rung: buy a parcel or timber deed, cruise it, sell stumpage or the land. Most of the work is not discovery. Merchantable timber shows up in free NAIP aerial imagery and in 3DEP LiDAR canopy height, so finding it is maybe 20-30% of the effort (my estimate). Heirs' property can only be bought by locating and getting agreement from many fractional heirs, or through a partition action. That title clearing costs much more than finding the trees, which makes this the same kind of failure as the geothermal-in-coal-mines counter-example. Buyers with capital (mills, TIMOs, REITs) exist, but they buy timber because it is visible, not because they have been told where it is.
scored.step_up: Estimate, not sourced, because the search budget was used up before any search ran. Southern US bare or cutover land sells for about $1,500-2,500/ac. Timberland with a merchantable pine stand sells for about $2,500-4,500/ac, and the stumpage on a mature stand is worth about $1,000-3,000/ac. So proving the timber takes an asset worth ~1x to ~1.5-3x. Nothing in this goes from near zero to 10^3. The land always has bare-land value, so the floor is high and the uplift is small. That fits the candidate's own "~2-4x" figure.
scored.hit_rate_capex: A cruise costs about $5-15/acre (from the candidate brief, and consistent with standard forestry consulting rates). Once imagery has been checked, the cruise almost always confirms the timber, so the base hit rate is roughly 80-95% (my estimate). The rubric caps the ML lever at 1/base hit rate, which here is about 1.1-1.25x. There is no 10x drop in capex to win. The expensive and uncertain part is acquisition and title, not proving.
scored.data: The data is public, but most of it is legible. NAIP imagery, 3DEP LiDAR canopy height models and FIA plots are already turned into forest-type and biomass rasters (USFS, plus commercial products such as Pachama and NCX/Renoster-style canopy maps). County tax rolls often record the answer directly through current-use or forestry classifications. The illegible part is probate and heirs-title records, which tell you about ownership complexity, not hidden value.
scored.right_bought: Absentee owners can be bought out, but timber buyers and loggers already mail and knock on doors across this exact population. A timber discount does exist, mostly because unadvised sellers take low lump-sum bids, but it is a negotiation and information edge of maybe 20-50%, not hidden geology. Heirs' property needs consent from every heir or a partition sale, which takes slow and expensive legal work and carries reputational and policy risk (heirs' property loss is a known equity issue in Black land loss).
scored.buyer: Regional sawmills and pulp mills buy stumpage. Weyerhaeuser, PotlatchDeltic, Rayonier and TIMOs such as Hancock/Manulife and Campbell Global buy timberland. Carbon developers such as Finite Carbon buy at small scale. All of them have capital. None of them pay a premium for being told where the timber is.
scored.ladder: The rungs are parcel aggregation, then timber management or TIMO, then logging and hauling, then sawmill or pulp, then wood products and mass timber, plus carbon. The ladder is real (Weyerhaeuser and Rayonier are worth $10-25B). But it is a low-margin commodity chain, and winning the smallest rung gives you no information moat to climb with.
scored.fatal_flaw: Timber is visible from the sky. Merchantable stands show up in free NAIP imagery and LiDAR, and existing forest maps already summarise them, so there is no hidden discovery. Proving rarely fails (hit rate about 90%), so the ML lever is about 1.1x. Because the land always has bare-land value, the step-up is only about 2-3x. The real bottleneck is title clearing on heirs' property, which is the physical-step-dominates failure from the geothermal counter-example. It works well as a calibration counter-example.
scored.one_line_reason: Discovery is cheap and almost never fails because the timber is visible, the step-up is about 2-3x rather than 10^3, and the hard part is acquiring the title, so it fails C2, C3 and C4 and stands as the calibration counter-example.

scored.name: AMD Sludge Rights / Sludge Royalty
scored.one_line: Predict REE- and Co-rich acid-mine-drainage treatment sludge from discharge chemistry and source seams; sign zero/negative-cost offtake; assay; sell feed contracts to REE separators.
scored.unproven_right: Multi-year sludge and legacy pond rights.
scored.proving_step: Lab assay ($2-40k per site).
scored.proven_buyer: REE separators, DOE/NETL AMD-REE partners, MP/USA Rare Earth-style buyers.
scored.public_data: OSMRE AMLIS, PA/WV DEP DMRs and Datashed, ICIS-NPDES, USGS NURE, COALQUAL.
scored.frame: The rung would be 'hold a sludge or pond right, then prove its grade'. Discovery is well under 50% of the work there, roughly 10-20% by my estimate. Grade is not the hard part. The hard parts are physical: dewatering, acid leaching and pre-concentrating sludge that is only about 20-30% solids, then transporting it. WVU's DOE-funded Mt. Storm pilot needed a purpose-built leach and solvent-extraction plant to get to a ~2-4% REE pre-concentrate (recalled, not verified). This is the geothermal-in-coal-mines counter-example again: processing the feed is harder than finding the right sludge.
scored.step_up: Unproven: sludge is a disposal liability today. Treatment operators and states pay to landfill or bury it, so it is worth about $0/t or less (estimate, roughly -$5 to -$30/t wet for disposal). Proven: AMD sludge runs about 300-1,000+ ppm TREE on a dry basis (WVU/Ziemkiewicz literature, recalled). At a ~$30-50/kg oxide basket that is roughly $10-50 of contained value per dry ton. A separator pays only a fraction of that for low-grade, wet, chemically variable feed, likely a few $/t at most (estimate). The step-up goes from a small negative to a small positive. It is roughly 1-10x on a near-zero base in a tiny dollar amount, nowhere near 10^3-10^4, and the candidate's own '~10-100x' is generous.
scored.hit_rate_capex: The proving step is cheap and mostly succeeds. A commercial ICP-MS REE panel costs about $50-300 per sample (estimate from typical lab pricing), so even a thorough multi-sample site characterisation is a few $k. The candidate's $2-40k range overstates it. The hit rate is not low: the literature shows REE enrichment follows simple chemistry. Low-pH, high-Al, high-Mn discharges concentrate REE, and all three are already reported in DMRs. If the base hit rate is about 30-50% with a pH/Al screen, the ML lever is capped at about 2-3x on an already trivial cost. There is no expensive failing shot for ML to make cheaper.
scored.data: The data is public but fairly legible: DMRs, ICIS-NPDES and PA's Datashed give pH, Fe, Al, Mn and flow, and USGS NURE and COALQUAL give seam REE. REE itself is not usually a reported field, which is mildly good. But the proxy (low pH and high Al) is a two-variable lookup that academics such as WVU, Penn State and the NETL-funded teams have already published, so an ML edge over a simple rule is unlikely. This repeats the interconnection-queue failure, where a lookup table matched the ML.
scored.right_bought: Sludge rights can be had at zero or negative cost from treatment operators, watershed groups and state AML programs, so acquisition is cheap. But the owners can read the data as well as anyone, so this is not an information-asymmetry purchase. And many AMD treatment systems are state-run or bond-forfeiture sites, where any contract goes through public procurement rather than a private purchase.
scored.buyer: Few buyers with capital, and none committed. US separators (MP Materials, Energy Fuels' White Mesa, USA Rare Earth, and the DOE/NETL CORE-CM and MREC demo programs) want concentrate or mixed REE oxide feed, not wet sludge. Today the realistic 'buyer' is DOE grant programs, not a market paying for feed. Incumbents and competitors in AMD-REE include WVU's Rare Earth Extraction Facility (with Rare Earth Salvage/partners), TechConnect/NETL partners, Penn State, Virginia Tech and Phoenix Tailings-style waste-to-REE startups (from memory, not verified this session).
scored.ladder: There is a ladder on paper: sludge aggregation, then pre-concentrate, then mixed REE oxide, then separation, then metals and magnets. But every rung above the first is a capital-heavy chemical plant. The total resource is also small: Northern Appalachian AMD REE potential is estimated at only on the order of hundreds to ~2,000 t/yr TREE (recalled from Vass et al.). Even if fully captured, that is a niche business, not a trillion-dollar path.
scored.fatal_flaw: Discovery is not the bottleneck. Proving grade costs a few hundred dollars by ICP-MS and is largely predictable from pH and Al that DMRs already report. The value sits in processing low-grade wet sludge into concentrate, which is bespoke chemical engineering. That is the same failure as the geothermal-in-coal-mines counter-example, and the proven asset is still only worth about $10-50 of contained REE per dry ton.
scored.one_line_reason: Cheap, high-hit-rate assays and a published pH/Al proxy leave ML no lever. The step-up is from a small disposal liability to a small positive value, and processing, not discovery, dominates the work.
sources: WebSearch budget was used up for this workflow turn (shared limit), so no live searches ran. Every figure is from memory or my own estimate and is labelled that way.

Ziemkiewicz, Vass et al., West Virginia University Water Research Institute, AMD-REE characterisation and recovery papers (Minerals/Mine Water and the Environment, 2016-2021), recalled: ~300-1,000+ ppm TREE in dry AMD sludge; Northern Appalachian AMD REE potential estimates
US DOE/NETL Critical Minerals and Materials program (CORE-CM, MREC) funding of the WVU Rare Earth Extraction Facility at Mt. Storm, recalled
Estimate: commercial ICP-MS REE panel pricing of ~$50-300/sample
Estimate: AMD sludge disposal cost of ~$5-30/wet t; REE oxide basket of ~$30-50/kg

scored.name: Dormant Research-Reactor Irradiation Rights
scored.one_line: Lease unused capacity of underused university research reactors, amend licences for medical isotope targets, contract to radiopharma.
scored.unproven_right: Lease of Part 50 research reactor flux time.
scored.proving_step: Neutronics/licensing analysis and NRC amendment.
scored.proven_buyer: Novartis, ITM, Eckert & Ziegler, Curium, NorthStar.
scored.public_data: ADAMS RTR dockets, TRTR data, IAEA RRDB.
scored.frame: The rung would be a leased block of research-reactor flux time, licensed for isotope targets and sold under contract to a radiopharma company. Inside that rung, discovery is roughly 5-10% of the work (my estimate). Which reactor can do the job is already known: power level and flux are written into the licence and the IAEA Research Reactor Database. The other 90%+ is physical and regulatory. That means target design, neutronics and safety analysis, an NRC amendment, hot-cell and shipping set-up, GMP-compatible handling, and running the irradiations. This is the coal-mine geothermal counter-example again: the bespoke physical and regulatory work is much harder than finding the asset.
scored.step_up: All of these are my estimates from domain knowledge, not checked sources; no searches ran because the budget was used up. Unproven: a lease of spare flux time at a small university TRIGA reactor, plausibly tens to low hundreds of thousands of dollars a year. Proven: a supply contract for irradiated targets worth perhaps $0.5-5M a year, and only if the reactor has enough flux. That is roughly 3-30x on the lease and about 1x on the reactor itself. Nothing jumps 10^3-10^4 the moment a 'hit' happens. Value builds slowly through capex, licensing and operations.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Again my estimates, unverified. There is no low-hit-rate search here. Whether a given reactor can make a given isotope is decided mainly by flux, which is in a public field. Commercially useful Lu-177 (Lu-176/Yb-176 routes) and Mo-99 by neutron capture need high flux, around 10^14 n/cm2/s or more. That is found at MURR (10 MW), MIT (6 MW), NIST, HFIR and ATR. Most of the roughly 30 US research reactors are TRIGA-class units under 1 MW, with flux around 10^12-10^13, which is too low for commercial quantities. The proving step itself is an NRC licence amendment plus engineering, probably $1-5M and 1-3 years each, and it mostly succeeds once flux is adequate. With a base hit rate that is high and already knowable, ML has close to zero lever (the cap is 1/base rate, around 1-2x).
scored.data: The data is public and largely legible. ADAMS RTR dockets, annual operating reports (which give MWh run, so utilisation is visible), TRTR materials and the IAEA RRDB all state power, flux and operating hours in structured or semi-structured form. The outcome, whether a reactor is suitable, is effectively summarised by the power and flux fields. That is the failure pattern seen in earlier hunts. Incumbents (MURR, NorthStar, Curium, Eckert & Ziegler, ITM sourcing) already know every reactor that could do this.
scored.right_bought: The right is not bought cheaply from owners who cannot read the data. University reactor owners know their own flux and spare capacity. Most leases are bespoke negotiations governed by university and DOE/NRC licence conditions, and the licensee, the university, must stay the operator, so a third party cannot really own the asset. The highest-value reactors, MURR and MIT, already sell irradiation services commercially, priced at what the market pays.
scored.buyer: The capitalised buyers are real: Novartis (Pluvicto, Lu-177), ITM, Eckert & Ziegler, Curium and NorthStar. They mainly buy from high-flux sources: MURR, European reactors, and power reactors through Bruce Power/Isogen and BWXT, which make Lu-177 and Co-60 in CANDU units with far more capacity than any university TRIGA. Other routes compete too: accelerator and fusion-neutron sources from SHINE, Niowave and Nusano.
scored.ladder: There is a real ladder above this rung. It runs target fabrication and enrichment, then irradiation, radiochemical processing, GMP API supply, radiopharmaceutical development and ownership of a therapeutic franchise. Eckert & Ziegler, ITM, NorthStar and SHINE show the climb is possible. But the rung at the bottom has no discovery edge to win it with.
scored.fatal_flaw: There is no discovery problem to solve. Whether a reactor is suitable is decided by flux and power, which are already legible public fields. Most 'dormant' university reactors are idle because their flux is too low to be commercially useful, not because nobody has read the data. The rung is mostly physical and regulatory work: licence amendments, hot cells, GMP handling and logistics. It is also crowded out by high-flux and power-reactor supply (MURR, Bruce/Isogen) and by accelerator routes. At heart it sells irradiation services to radiopharma incumbents.
scored.one_line_reason: This is the coal-mine-geothermal pattern: suitability is already legible from flux and power fields, the proving step is heavy licensing and physical work with a high, knowable success rate, and the step-up is only about 3-30x, so ML has nothing to discover.
sources: No web searches ran: the shared turn search budget (200 calls) was already used up. Every number here is an estimate from domain knowledge and should be checked before it is relied on.
IAEA Research Reactor Database (RRDB), https://nucleus-apps.iaea.org/rrdb, gives power and flux for each reactor (cited from knowledge, not fetched)
NRC list of operating research and test reactors, https://www.nrc.gov/reactors/non-power.html (cited from knowledge, not fetched)
Bruce Power / Isogen CANDU Lu-177 production agreement with ITM (public press releases 2022-2023, from knowledge)
MURR as the main US supplier of irradiation for I-131, Lu-177 and Mo-99 (NorthStar) (from knowledge)

scored.name: Deadhead Timber / Sunken Stock: sunken old-growth log-drive logs
scored.one_line: Lease state submerged-log recovery permits and riparian rights where ML over scanned log-drive company records, mill tallies and bathymetry locates dense sinker-log fields; sonar and test pulls prove them; sell to tonewood and specialty mills.
scored.unproven_right: State/provincial bottomland salvage permits (WI, MI, FL, ME, ON, BC) and private lakebed rights, ~$1-10k.
scored.proving_step: Side-scan and sub-bottom sonar plus diver/ROV test lifts, ~$20-60k per stretch.
scored.proven_buyer: Luthiers and tonewood dealers, veneer and architectural millwork houses, reclaimed-wood distributors.
scored.public_data: State historical society log-mark and boom-company records, USACE/NOAA bathymetry, DNR lakebed maps, historic topos and Sanborn maps, permit registries.
scored.rough_step_up: ~10^2-10^3x on a field; fragmented buyers, partly first-come permits.
scored.frame: Rung = holding a state submerged-log permit and proving a log field. Discovery is maybe 10-20% of the work inside that rung (my estimate). Most of the work is the physical and regulatory side: approvals from BCPL plus DNR, the State Historical Society and USACE in WI; Part 326 plus a USACE permit in MI; then lifting, 6 months of air-drying or weeks in a kiln, milling and grading. Nobody buys a 'proven field' as a separate thing. Buyers only buy dried lumber.
scored.step_up: Unproven: a WI permit costs a $500 application fee plus a bond of at least $10k (2011 MI analysis citing WI; 1999 BCPL handbook). Proven: no market for a proven permit or field. Value only shows up as lumber. Sinker cypress sold for about $7-10/bf wholesale and dried in 2012 (forum quotes), against roughly $1-3/bf for fresh rough cypress. That is about 3-5x per board foot, not 10^3. The state owns the logs and keeps 30% of stumpage value.
scored.hit_rate_capex: I found no published base hit rate. Logs sit in known places (boom sites, sorting gaps, river mouths, mill ponds), and side-scan sonar finds them cheaply (my estimate: $20-60k per stretch, as the candidate states, unverified). Finding them is not the bottleneck, so the ML lever is probably below 2x.
scored.data: Boom-company and log-mark records are scanned and hard to read, so the data side partly fits. But the state application already asks for estimated species, log count and Scribner board feet, so the outcome is self-reported and checked at permitting. The rights are not bought cheaply from owners who can't read the data. The state owns the logs by statute, issues the permits, and limits WI to 6 named waters with a 160-acre cap per permit. Michigan paused new permits from about 2003 to 2011 (PA 218 of 2011 reopened them).
scored.right_bought: A permit from the state for a contiguous area of up to 160 acres. The state keeps title and 30% of stumpage. Permits are granted on application, not bought from private owners who can't read the data. Private lakebed rights exist but are small and scattered.
scored.buyer: Scattered buyers: luthiers, tonewood dealers, millwork shops and reclaimed-wood distributors. None of them is a capitalised developer that pays a premium for proven ground. Sellers keep prices secret (MI legislative analysis).
scored.ladder: Short. Recovery leads to drying and milling, then specialty lumber or finished products. That is a niche market worth tens of millions at most (my estimate), with no path to a very large company.
scored.fatal_flaw: Wisconsin BCPL's own program document says every entity that applied for a submerged logging permit has gone out of business, most administratively dissolved or bankrupt. The hard part is recovery, permitting, drying and milling, not finding the logs (the geothermal-in-coal-mines failure pattern). On top of that, the state owns the logs and takes 30%.
scored.one_line_reason: Finding the logs is cheap and their locations are already known. The physical, regulatory work and the scattered market killed every Wisconsin permittee, and there is no ~10^3 step-up or capitalised buyer for a proven field.

scored.name: Ghost Spur Track Easements
scored.one_line: Buy dormant industry-track agreements and spur easements from dissolved industrial owners; ML proves which still bind the railroad and servient land; sell rail-served status to manufacturers and fab developers.
scored.unproven_right: Assignment of dormant spur easements and track agreements, nominal cost.
scored.proving_step: ML over deeds, track charts and Sanborn maps; survivability and connection check; buyer relays spur.
scored.proven_buyer: Site selectors, megasite industrial developers, state economic development agencies.
scored.public_data: Sanborn maps (LoC), county deeds, FRA GIS, archived track charts.
scored.frame: The candidate rung is owning a dormant spur easement or industry-track agreement (ITA) and proving it still delivers rail-served status. Discovery is not 80%+ of the work inside that rung. Even if ML shows that a right legally survives, rail service only happens if the Class I or short line agrees to serve the site. That means a commercial negotiation, car-volume commitments, track rehab and the railroad's own engineering approval. Rebuilding the switch and turnout is real construction, not something trivial or abstracted. My estimate is that discovery is 20-30% of the work and railroad consent plus physical relay is 70-80%. This is the geothermal-in-coal-mines pattern: finding the right spur is easier than getting it served.
scored.step_up: From memory, as no searches ran: new industry track costs roughly $1-3M per mile including turnouts (each turnout roughly $150-300k). Those figures are commonly cited by railroads and economic-development agencies. Rail-served industrial land typically sells at a modest premium over truck-only land, my estimate 10-50%, not orders of magnitude. The unproven easement costs close to nothing to assign. But the proven easement is not worth much on its own, because the value sits in the land plus the railroad's willingness to serve. The realisable uplift to an easement holder is maybe the avoided cost of a new right-of-way corridor, $10k-$500k (estimate). In ratio terms against a $0 basis the multiple looks huge, but against the land value it lifts it is under 3x. On honest terms that is C2 = 1.
scored.hit_rate_capex: The proving step today is a title search plus an inquiry to the railroad. That is cheap, roughly $2-10k per site for an abstract and attorney review (estimate). It is not an expensive, mostly failing physical shot like a drill hole. The base rate of a dormant ITA still binding the railroad is likely very low (estimate <5%). ITAs are usually terminable by the railroad on 30-90 days' notice and usually cannot be assigned without railroad consent. Under 49 U.S.C. 10906, spur and industry track can be removed without Surface Transportation Board (STB) abandonment approval, which makes it unlikely that dormant rights survive. ML does not raise that rate, because survival is a legal fact that depends on the railroad, not a hidden signal. There is no 10x capex lever on a step that is already cheap.
scored.data: Library of Congress Sanborn maps, county deeds, FRA GIS track lines and archived track charts are public. Deeds and Sanborn maps are illegible, scanned and scattered, so that part fits. But the decisive outcome, whether a railroad will serve a site, is held privately by the railroad: its ITA files, its industrial development department, and its certified-site programs (BNSF Certified Sites, UP site selection, CSX Select Sites, Norfolk Southern site programs). The railroads do read their own data. The FRA network GIS already shows where active and inactive track exists, which is a legible field that summarises much of the physical answer.
scored.right_bought: Partly. Dissolved industrial owners' contract rights can sometimes be bought cheaply from successors or bankruptcy estates. But the ITA counterparty is the railroad, and most ITAs forbid assignment without its consent, so the right cannot really be bought from someone who cannot read the data. The railroad is the gatekeeper and reads its own files. Spur easements over servient land are often appurtenant to the old industrial parcel, so they transfer with that land and not separately.
scored.buyer: Site selectors, megasite developers and state economic development agencies have capital. But they buy land and railroad commitments, not bare easements. In practice they go straight to the railroad's industrial development team, which certifies sites for free in order to win carload volume.
scored.ladder: Thin. Possible rungs above are site assembly, industrial developer, short-line operator and rail-served industrial parks. That path is real, but it is a capital-heavy real-estate and rail-operations business, contested by Class I railroads and by short-line roll-ups such as Genesee & Wyoming and OmniTRAX. Winning the easement rung gives no edge on those rungs.
scored.fatal_flaw: The railroad, not the easement holder, decides whether a site is rail-served. Industry-track agreements are typically terminable by the railroad on short notice and cannot be assigned without its consent. Spur track can be removed without STB abandonment approval (49 U.S.C. 10906). So a 'proven' dormant right does not deliver rail-served status, and the railroad gives that status away for free through its own site programs to win carload volume.
scored.one_line_reason: The value sits with the railroad's consent and the land, not the dormant easement. Proving is cheap legal work, ML adds no hit-rate lever, and the realisable step-up is a 10-50% land premium, not 10^3-10^4x.
sources: No live searches: this turn's shared WebSearch budget (200 calls) was used up before this candidate could be searched. All figures come from prior knowledge and are labelled as estimates.
49 U.S.C. 10906 (spur, industrial, team, switching or side tracks exempt from STB construction and abandonment authority) - prior knowledge
BNSF Certified Sites, Union Pacific site selection, CSX Select Sites, Norfolk Southern site programs - railroad-run free site certification, prior knowledge
Library of Congress Sanborn Fire Insurance Maps collection; FRA North American Rail Network GIS - public data sources named in the candidate

scored.name: Terroir Proving: AVA petition land
scored.one_line: Buy ranch land whose soil and climate match elite wine regions, prove distinctiveness via a TTB AVA petition and test plantings, sell or lease at AVA vineyard prices.
scored.unproven_right: Rangeland/dry farmland at $3-10k/acre.
scored.proving_step: TTB AVA petition plus test plantings (planting is not trivial).
scored.proven_buyer: Constellation, Gallo, Treasury, Jackson Family.
scored.public_data: SSURGO/gSSURGO, PRISM, historic TTB petitions, USGS geology; mostly legible.
scored.frame: The rung would be 'land with a proven terroir premium', but no rung exists where discovery is 80%+. Finding land with the right soil and climate is maybe 5-10% of the work (my estimate). The other 90%+ is physical and slow: securing water rights, planting at roughly $30-60k/acre over 3-5 years before a commercial crop, then 10-20+ years of winemaking and brand building before buyers pay a regional premium. A TTB AVA petition is an administrative filing, not a proving event. It defines a boundary using climate, soil and name-usage evidence and says nothing about wine quality. This is the coal-mine-geothermal failure pattern: the bespoke build-out dominates the discovery.
scored.step_up: From memory, not verified in this run: California rangeland or dry farmland sells for about $3-10k/acre (USDA/ASFMRA ranges). Planted vineyard values range from about $20-60k/acre in Paso Robles and Lodi, to $100-150k in Sonoma, to $300k-1M+ on the Napa valley floor. The gap between rangeland and Napa looks like 10-100x, but almost all of it comes from planting capex, decades of brand equity and scarcity. An AVA designation alone does not cause it. New AVAs such as Petaluma Gap (2017) and the 11 Paso Robles sub-AVAs (2014) brought no documented immediate land repricing that I know of. The immediate step-up from the AVA alone is estimated at under 2x on unplanted land. Also from memory: the 2024-25 grape oversupply has pushed down vineyard values in Sonoma, Lodi and the Central Coast, and growers are removing vines.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Approval of TTB AVA petitions is high. From memory, nearly all well-documented petitions are eventually approved (about 275+ US AVAs), though it takes 1-4 years and costs about $20-100k in consultants (my estimate). With a base hit rate near 1, the ML lever is capped near 1x. Test plantings cost about $30-60k/acre and take 3-5 years for vines, and a quality verdict takes longer. These are not cheap, repeatable shots. ML on soil and climate cannot cut that cost 10x, because vines still have to grow.
scored.data: The data is legible and already used. SSURGO/gSSURGO and PRISM are clean, gridded and free. Viticulture consultants and university suitability models already map grape suitability from them (for example UC Davis work and the Winkler/GDD indices). Historic TTB petitions are structured Federal Register notices. There is no illegible-data edge. The unproven right (land) is bought from ranchers, but sellers and brokers price land by water access and proximity to known regions, which already capture most of the suitability signal. Water rights matter more than soil, especially under California's SGMA groundwater limits and the Paso Robles basin restrictions.
scored.right_bought: Yes, fee-simple land is bought, not claimed first-come. But the buy discount is small, because brokers and growers already screen the obvious terroir and water signals.
scored.buyer: Constellation, Gallo, Treasury, Jackson Family and Duckhorn exist as buyers. From memory, many of them were divesting vineyards and lower-priced brands in 2024-26 as wine volumes fell, which makes them weak buyers for unproven new regions. They buy established reputation, not new suitability claims.
scored.ladder: Land, then vineyard, then grower contracts, then winery, then brand and distribution. A real ladder exists, but every rung above land is capital-heavy and decade-slow, and the end market (US wine) is shrinking. This is not a trillion-dollar path. The whole US wine industry is roughly $70-100B in retail sales (from memory).
scored.fatal_flaw: No discrete proving event creates value. An AVA petition is a near-certain administrative filing that adds little immediate value. The real premium comes from planting capex plus decades of brand reputation, so physical build-out and time, not discovery, are 90%+ of the work. That is the coal-mine-geothermal failure pattern.
scored.one_line_reason: This fails the rubric: soil and climate data are already legible, AVA approval is near-certain and adds little value, and the 10-100x premium comes from planting plus decades of brand building, sold to buyers who are shrinking.

Federal Register notices for Petaluma Gap AVA (2017) and Paso Robles sub-AVAs (2014), from memory
Industry press 2024-25 on California grape oversupply, vine removal and falling vineyard values, from memory

scored.name: Head Rights: senior water rights at non-powered dams
scored.one_line: Buy dormant hydropower/mill water rights and small non-powered dam parcels; ML proves seniority and non-abandonment from scanned decrees; sell bundled site plus right plus FERC exemption eligibility to small-hydro and data-center buyers.
scored.unproven_right: Pre-1914 or early-adjudicated power/milling rights at old dams, $1-50k.
scored.proving_step: ML extraction of priority and flow, USGS flow joins, legal opinion and energy model; turbine is a later rung.
scored.proven_buyer: Small-hydro IPPs, data-center developers, utilities short on clean firm capacity.
scored.public_data: State water rights databases and scanned decrees, ORNL NHAAP non-powered dam inventory, USACE NID, USGS NWIS.
scored.rough_step_up: ~50-500x; status fields and hydro build are risks.
scored.frame: The proposed rung is "proven senior power right plus dam parcel plus FERC-exemption eligibility," and discovery is a small share of the work inside it. My estimate is about 10-20% of the value-creating work. The rest is the build: turbine, interconnection, FERC exemption or licence, fish passage and 401 water-quality certification. Small non-powered dam (NPD) builds usually run around $4,000-10,000/kW by my recollection of DOE Hydropower Vision and ORNL cost work; this is not re-verified. The buyer underwrites that build, not the paper right. This is the same shape as the geothermal-in-coal-mines counter-example: building the bespoke plant is harder than finding the site. The "proven right" alone is not a discrete product that a capitalised buyer buys at a step-up.
scored.step_up: I could not get real numbers because the shared web-search budget was used up, so everything here is my estimate. Unproven dormant mill/power right plus parcel: $1-50k, per the candidate. A proven, adjudicated, non-abandoned non-consumptive power right at a small NPD (most are under 1 MW) is plausibly worth about $50-250k, because the asset only pays after $4-10M/MW of construction. A typical 300 kW site makes about 1.3 GWh/yr, roughly $65-100k/yr in revenue at $50-80/MWh. That cannot carry a large premium for the right. Realistic step-up is about 2-10x, not 10^3-10^4. The value sits in the energy project, not the right.
scored.hit_rate_capex: My estimate, not re-searched: a seniority and non-abandonment check is a title-and-records exercise. A water-rights attorney or engineer opinion costs about $5-30k, and ownership records plus decree search are cheap. The base hit rate is not the problem: many old rights are on record. What usually kills these projects is economics (head, flow, build cost), not whether the right is valid. Proving is neither very expensive nor mostly failing, so ML gives at most a 2-3x cost cut on paralegal work, far short of 10x.
scored.data: These are known facts from memory, not re-verified. Western state systems record priority date, decreed flow, use type and often status in legible fields: Colorado CDSS/HydroBase, Idaho IDWR, Washington WRTS, Oregon WRIS, Utah. Colorado also publishes decennial abandonment lists. ORNL NHAAP, USACE NID and USGS NWIS are structured and widely used by developers. This is the "regulator wrote the answer into a status field" failure. Scanned decrees add only marginal edge, mostly in unadjudicated pre-1914 claims, such as California statements of diversion. The largest NPD potential (Mississippi/Ohio locks and dams) is federally owned and cannot be bought. Eastern riparian states have no separable water right to buy at all.
scored.right_bought: Partly. Dam parcels and associated rights can be bought from private owners, mill-dam heirs and towns, often cheaply; many owners want to be rid of dam-safety liability. But the right is tied to the parcel and the point of diversion, so changing it needs state approval. Much of the potential sits at USACE and Bureau of Reclamation dams that are not for sale, where FERC permits or Lease of Power Privilege go first-come to applicants. Low-impact certification and FERC permits are a race, not a purchase.
scored.buyer: Small-hydro IPPs (e.g. Rye Development, Enel Green Power NA small hydro, Eagle Creek/Ontario Teachers', Hull Street Energy), which already screen NHAAP and NID in-house. Utilities seeking firm clean power buy built projects or PPAs, not rights. Data-center developers want 50-500+ MW, and almost all private NPDs are under 1-5 MW, so they are not realistic buyers.
scored.ladder: Rungs above the right: develop or own small hydro (Rye, Eagle Creek and Hull Street have done roll-ups), then O&M, then storage and pumped hydro. The ladder exists, but the total US NPD opportunity is about 12 GW (ORNL 2012), with most of it at federal dams. Private-dam potential is a few GW, which caps this as a niche IPP roll-up, not a trillion-dollar path.
scored.fatal_flaw: The value is in building the hydro project (about $4-10k/kW, licensing and fish passage), not in proving the right. Seniority and status are already recorded in legible state water-rights fields. So the step-up on proving is about 2-10x, not 10^4, and incumbent IPPs already screen the structured NPD inventories. It is the geothermal-in-coal-mines counter-example again.
scored.one_line_reason: Discovery is a minor share of a build-dominated small-hydro project; the right's status is already in legible state databases, so the step-up on proving is roughly 2-10x and there is no 80%+ discovery rung with a buyer paying 10^3x.
