scored.name: Small Closed Landfill Methane Rights
scored.one_line: Lease gas and credit rights on sub-threshold closed municipal landfills, prove yield from scanned permits and tonnage logs, flare and sell methane credits or RNG.
scored.unproven_right: Gas and attribute rights on a closed unregulated landfill.
scored.proving_step: ML waste-in-place estimate, probe/flux test, wells and flare ($1-3M).
scored.proven_buyer: Voluntary methane buyers, RNG offtakers.
scored.public_data: EPA LMOP, GHGRP Subpart HH, state DEQ permits and closure files, aerials.
scored.frame: The rung is a closed landfill with gas rights, then a collection system and flare that produce credits. Discovery is maybe 10-20% of the work inside that rung (my estimate). Gas yield follows from tonnage and closure age using EPA's public LandGEM first-order decay model, so there is little left to discover. The physical step (wells, header pipe, blower, flare, O&M and monitoring, about $1-3M as the candidate states) is most of the cost and effort. This is the geothermal-in-a-coal-mine counter-example again: building and running the system is harder than finding the site. It is not a hard exclusion because it is not geological gas exploration, but it is close.
scored.step_up: About 1-5x at most (estimate; I could not verify it because the shared web search budget was used up). The unproven right is a lease on a closed small landfill, worth close to zero and often obtainable for a royalty. A proven, flaring project on a small site might make 10k-50k tCO2e/yr at voluntary landfill-methane prices of roughly $2-8/t (from memory; landfill credits are among the cheapest). That is about $50k-400k/yr of revenue against $1-3M of capex, with output falling each year after closure. Any value step-up is mostly the return on capex, not a jump in the value of the right. Nothing like the 10^4 from $1/ha to $10,000/ha.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Base hit rate is high, not low (estimate). Nearly every closed municipal landfill makes methane, and LandGEM predicts the volume well enough that a project fails on economics, not on whether gas is there. Cost per attempt is $1-3M (candidate figure), and most of that is build cost, not discovery. A cheap flux or probe screen costs about $10-50k (estimate) and already removes the unknowns. ML would at best cut that screening cost; it cannot change the $1-3M build. The lever, capped at 1/hit rate, is about 1.2-2x, not 10x.
scored.data: The outcome is already legible. EPA LMOP's public database lists about 2,600 municipal landfills with waste-in-place, open/close years and project status, and flags candidate landfills. GHGRP Subpart HH gives modelled methane generation for reporting landfills. LandGEM turns those numbers into a yield curve. So the signal sits in structured public fields, the failure pattern seen in earlier hunts. The rights are bought, but owners (mostly municipalities) know they have gas: it is a known liability, and LMOP actively promotes these sites. Owners are not unable to read the data. Scanned state DEQ closure files add only marginal detail.
scored.right_bought: The right is bought, typically a gas-rights lease or royalty from a municipality or county, sometimes through a procurement process. The owner is not information-disadvantaged. They know the landfill makes gas and often want someone else to take the liability. So the right is cheap, but not because the owner cannot read the data, and there is no information arbitrage.
scored.buyer: Voluntary methane credit buyers (ACR/CAR/Verra landfill protocols), RNG offtakers, and project aggregators. These are thin, low-price markets for small sites. Small sites are usually too small for RNG upgrading, which in my estimate needs about 1,000+ scfm. Incumbents already do this: landfill-gas developers such as Opal Fuels, Montauk, Archaea/bp and Aria, plus credit developers. Whether anyone already rolls up sub-threshold flare projects I could not check because search was unavailable.
scored.ladder: There are modest rungs above: flare, then electricity or RNG, then a portfolio roll-up, possibly organics or waste handling. But the ceiling is a mid-size infrastructure and credits business, with output falling after each site closes, not a path to a trillion-dollar company.
scored.fatal_flaw: There is nothing to discover. Gas yield follows predictably from public tonnage and age data (EPA LMOP plus LandGEM), almost every landfill makes gas, and value is created by the $1-3M physical build and selling cheap credits, not by a proving step. No frame exists where discovery is 80% or more of the work.
scored.one_line_reason: This fails like geothermal in a coal mine: the hit rate is high and already predictable from legible EPA data, the step-up is under 5x, and capex goes into building wells and a flare, not into finding gas.
sources: EPA LMOP Landfill and LFG Energy Project Database (epa.gov/lmop): about 2,600 municipal landfills with waste-in-place and status fields (from memory; not re-verified because the web search budget was used up)
EPA LandGEM first-order decay landfill gas model (epa.gov) (from memory)
EPA GHGRP Subpart HH municipal landfill methane reporting (from memory)
ACR / Climate Action Reserve landfill gas protocols; landfill-methane voluntary credit prices of roughly $2-8/t are my estimate from memory
Note: both WebSearch calls returned 'budget used up', so every figure here is my estimate or recalled from memory, not freshly verified

scored.name: Lapse-Rescue Life Settlements
scored.one_line: Buy lapsing term and UL policies for near zero before conversion deadlines and sell converted policies to settlement funds.
scored.unproven_right: Lapsing policies with conversion privileges.
scored.proving_step: Medical records, LE estimate, conversion; private medical data dominates.
scored.proven_buyer: Abacus, Coventry, Apollo-backed vehicles.
scored.public_data: Aggregate lapse filings, obituaries, mortality tables; weak.
scored.frame: The rung would be: buy a lapsing term/UL policy that can still be converted, get it underwritten, convert it, and sell it on to a settlement fund. Finding the policy is maybe 20-30% of the work (my estimate). The rest is not a trivial physical step. You need written consent from the insured and HIPAA releases, and you must collect medical records (typically 6-12 weeks). You need 1-2 life-expectancy (LE) reports. Converting to permanent coverage means paying large premiums right away, and you must hold a provider licence in each state. The license and premium-funding steps are the heavy part, much like building the geothermal plant in the counter-example. There is a capitalised buyer (Abacus, Coventry, institutional funds). But no frame exists where discovery is 80%+ of the work.
scored.step_up: Unproven: a lapsing term policy has a cash surrender value of $0. A UL near lapse has a small one. The insured would otherwise walk away for nothing. Proven: a converted policy on an insured with a short LE typically trades at about 10-25% of face, and LISA says settlements pay about 4-8x the cash surrender value. Both figures are from memory of industry materials, and I could not verify them this session. Against a $0 surrender value the multiple looks unlimited. But the price is cleared by competing brokers running auctions, and the buyer must also pay conversion premiums, often 3-8% of face per year (estimate). So the step-up you can actually capture as the purchaser is about 1.5-5x on cash invested (estimate), not 10^3.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Base hit rate: roughly 10-25% of submitted policies close (my estimate; providers decline most cases for long LE, small face or high premiums). Cost per proving attempt: an LE report is about $300-600, plus medical record retrieval of about $100-300 (estimates). That is cheap, so raising the hit rate saves little. ML on public data cannot predict LE better than underwriters reading private medical files. Lever: about 1.2-2x at most.
scored.data: The signal that decides value is private: the insured's medical records, protected by HIPAA and released only with the insured's consent. Public data (obituaries, mortality tables, aggregate lapse filings from insurers) cannot tell you which living insured has a short LE. The outcome is effectively written into a legible document, the LE report, by specialist firms (21st Services, ISC, LSI, Clarity). No illegible public corpus exists for ML to beat incumbents on.
scored.right_bought: The right can only be bought from the insured with their informed consent, through regulated settlement contracts in about 43 states. Those states have rescission periods, disclosure rules and, in many, broker fiduciary duties to get the seller the best offer. Sellers are increasingly reached through broker auctions and insurer lapse-notice rules, so you cannot reliably buy below market from owners who cannot read the data. That last point is my reading of the regulatory landscape, not sourced this session.
scored.buyer: Abacus Life (public, ABL), Coventry, Apollo/Blackstone-type life settlement funds and other institutional investors. The secondary market is roughly $4-5B in face value settled per year (Conning-type estimates, from memory). These buyers are capitalised, but many of them already originate policies themselves.
scored.ladder: Rungs above: tertiary trading, portfolio servicing, premium financing, LE underwriting, and a life-settlement fund or annuity-like longevity product. These are financial intermediation layers, not an industrial vertical. The chain tops out at longevity-risk asset management, a large but crowded field, not a trillion-dollar vertical path. Abacus already spans origination, trading and asset management.
scored.fatal_flaw: The data that sets the value (the insured's private medical records and LE) is non-public and consent-gated. There is no public-but-illegible corpus for ML to exploit. Proving is cheap and already done by specialist LE firms, and regulated broker auctions compete away any purchase discount. Discovery is not 80% of the rung.
scored.one_line_reason: This fails the gold rubric on its core point. The policy's value lives in private medical files, not public illegible data. Each proving attempt costs only hundreds of dollars, and incumbents like Abacus and Coventry already run this exact lapse-rescue origination under a regulated auction market.
sources: No live web searches were completed: the shared search budget for this turn was exhausted on the first attempt. All numbers come from memory or are flagged estimates.
LISA (Life Insurance Settlement Association) consumer materials: settlements pay about 4-8x cash surrender value (from memory)
Conning life settlement market studies: about $4-5B face value settled per year (from memory)
Abacus Life (NASDAQ: ABL) public filings describing an integrated origination and asset-management model (from memory)
LE underwriters: 21st Services, ISC Services, LSI, Clarity (Fasano closed in 2016) (from memory)

scored.name: Liquidating Trust Residuals / Unclaimed Bankruptcy Distributions
scored.one_line: Buy liquidating-trust units and forgotten allowed unsecured claims at fractions of a cent; ML reads dockets to find trusts with unpriced recoveries (D&O, avoidance, refunds, escrows); realise or sell to distressed funds.
scored.unproven_right: Trust interests or allowed claims transferred under Rule 3001(e).
scored.proving_step: Parse disclosure statements, trustee reports, adversary proceedings and settlements.
scored.proven_buyer: Liquidating trusts (pay directly), distressed claim funds (Cherokee, Argo, Whitebox, Contrarian).
scored.public_data: PACER/RECAP, Kroll/Epiq/Stretto/Omni claims agents, post-confirmation reports, 8-Ks.
scored.frame: Rung: buying a transferred allowed unsecured claim or trust interest (Rule 3001(e)) and holding it to distribution or reselling it. The physical step costs almost nothing (a transfer form and a docket filing), so most of the work is diligence. But that diligence is mostly reading documents that are already legible: the disclosure statement's recovery-percentage table, the trustee's post-confirmation reports and the settlement motions. No hidden thing is being found. At the end the trust simply pays out cash. No buyer pays a premium because the asset has been "proven"; the payout is just the face value times the recovery rate, so the gain is the discount you bought at. I put discovery at about 60-70% of this rung, and most of that is legal diligence on allowance, objections and transfer limits (my estimate).
scored.step_up: Unproven claims typically trade at about 1-30 cents on the dollar, and a realised recovery is typically about 5-60 cents. That is usually 2-10x, with rare 20-100x outliers when a large D&O or avoidance settlement comes in late (my estimate from general knowledge of the claims market; not checked by search this run). Nothing like the 10^4x land re-rating in the Terranox model, because the claim's face value caps the upside. The candidate's own figure of '~5-100x; slow' is an upper bound. Payouts often take 2-5 years, which drags the IRR down.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Base hit rate: high, not low. Most allowed general unsecured claims in a confirmed liquidating plan pay something, maybe 60-80% of them (my estimate). The proving attempt is reading one docket, about $50-500 of analyst or PACER time (my estimate; PACER is $0.10/page, capped at $3 per document). That attempt is cheap and usually succeeds, so ML has no costly failure rate to cut. The lever (capped at 1/hit rate) is roughly 1.3-2x, not 10x. ML would mainly add throughput on claims too small for anyone to bother with.
scored.data: The data is public: PACER/RECAP, the claims-agent registers (Kroll, Epiq, Stretto, Omni) and 8-Ks. But the outcome is already written down in legible form. The disclosure statement has a projected-recovery percentage for each class, the trustee reports state cash on hand and distributions to date, and the claims registers are searchable and structured. Claims buyers already mine all of this: firms like Cherokee, Argo, ASM, Hain and Bradford mail offers to every scheduled creditor within days of a filing. Remaining edge: litigation recoveries not yet reflected in projections, inside long trustee reports and adversary-proceeding dockets. That edge is real but narrow.
scored.right_bought: Allowed claims can be bought cheaply from creditors who won't wait or don't understand them (trade vendors, former employees above the priority cap). This is a mature, competitive market. Liquidating-trust beneficial interests are often NON-TRANSFERABLE by the trust agreement, except by will, intestacy or operation of law. Trusts do this so the units are not treated as securities, which blocks buying the trust units themselves (a common provision; I could not verify specific trusts by search this run). Small claims under about $10k are often handled through convenience classes or cashed out, which limits the 'forgotten' pool.
scored.buyer: On realisation the liquidating trust pays you directly, which is just collecting cash, not a sale to a capitalised buyer. You can resell to distressed funds (Contrarian, Whitebox, Cherokee, Argo), but they price off the same legible recovery estimates, so the resale premium is small.
scored.ladder: Possible next rungs: a claims-buying fund, then trustee or plan-administrator services, then a distressed-debt or special-situations fund. These do stack, but it is an asset-management ladder that ends as a large distressed fund in a crowded field (Contrarian and Whitebox are already there). It does not lead to vertically integrating a physical value chain, so there is no trillion-dollar path.
scored.fatal_flaw: The asset's face value caps the step-up at a few x, and the outcome is already in legible fields (the disclosure statement's recovery table and the trustee reports) that a crowded professional claims-trading market prices within days. The trust interests, the most attractive target, are often non-transferable under the trust agreement.
scored.one_line_reason: Fails the Terranox rule. The step-up is roughly 2-10x and capped by face value, not 10^4. Proving rarely fails and costs little, so ML has no hit-rate lever. Recoveries are already summarised in disclosure statements and priced by established claims buyers.
sources: Web search was unavailable: the per-turn WebSearch budget of 200 calls, shared across agents, was used up before this agent's first search. All figures below are labelled estimates from general knowledge; a follow-up message can rerun the search.
Fed. R. Bankr. P. 3001(e) (transfer of claims; public notice of transfer on the docket)
PACER fee schedule: $0.10/page, $3.00 cap per document (general knowledge)
Typical liquidating trust agreement transfer restrictions, a provision that keeps trust units from being treated as securities (general knowledge, not verified this run)
Claims-buyer practice of mass-mailing offers to scheduled creditors (Cherokee Acquisition, Argo Partners, ASM Capital, Hain Capital, Bradford Capital) (general knowledge)

scored.name: Forgotten Foreclosure and Tax-Sale Surplus
scored.one_line: Buy assignments of excess-proceeds rights from former owners or heirs and claim from counties.
scored.unproven_right: Unknown heir's right to county-held surplus.
scored.proving_step: Heir discovery and affidavits.
scored.proven_buyer: County treasurers and court registries.
scored.public_data: County excess-proceeds PDFs, tax-deed results, probate, obituaries.
scored.frame: The rung is: get an assignment of a former owner's or heir's claim to county-held surplus, then file the claim. Inside that rung, finding the heir (skip-tracing, probate, obituaries) is about 60-70% of the work. The rest is not trivial: signing the heir, notarised affidavits, chain-of-heirship paperwork, contested claims and court motions in judicial-sale states (my estimate). There is also no capitalised buyer paying a premium. The county pays out the face amount it already holds, so the 'buyer' is a cashier, not a developer pricing in future value.
scored.step_up: I could not check any numbers live: the shared web-search budget ran out on my first query, so everything here is from memory or my own estimate. The asset is never near zero. The county publishes the dollar amount, so the claim is worth face value from day one. The finder's take is capped by law. From memory: California Rev & Tax Code 4675 caps assignment and finder fees at about 10% of the excess proceeds; Florida's surplus statutes (Ch. 45 and s.197.582 regime) cap fees and need court or clerk approval; several states cap fees at 20-33%; and some states void assignments made within a window after the sale. Typical realised economics: get 10-35% of a known amount for a few hundred to a few thousand dollars of effort. That is roughly a 3-10x return on effort cost. It is not a 10^3-10^4 revaluation of the asset itself, because the value is fixed and already visible.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Each attempt is cheap (my estimate): about $50-500 per lead for skip-trace and outreach, plus legal filing costs for contested or judicial claims. The base hit rate is moderate, not tiny. Industry folklore suggests roughly 10-30% of contacted leads sign and pay out. With a base rate around 0.2, ML can improve it by at most about 5x. The bottleneck is persuading heirs and competing with other agents, not finding the signal, so ML does not cut discovery capex 10x. I could not source these numbers live.
scored.data: This fails the core test: the outcome is already in a legible field. Counties publish excess-proceeds or unclaimed-surplus lists that show the former owner's name, parcel, sale date and exact surplus amount. These are often spreadsheets, and they are scraped and resold by list vendors. The only illegible part is heir genealogy (probate and obituaries), and commercial skip-trace and people-search databases already cover that. Incumbents: thousands of 'surplus funds recovery' agents, franchise-style training courses, list resellers, and heir-finder firms. Interest has risen since Tyler v. Hennepin County (2023) widened owners' surplus rights.
scored.right_bought: The right is bought through an assignment or a contingency agreement, not taken first-come. But the price is set by statutory fee caps and anti-assignment rules, not by a market discount you can exploit. Owners can also claim directly for free, and counties often mail them notices. So the 'cheap purchase from owners who cannot read the data' is limited by law and by the regulator itself telling owners.
scored.buyer: County treasurers, clerks of court and court registries. They pay a fixed, pre-stated amount. They are not capitalised buyers paying for revealed value.
scored.ladder: The ladder is weak. Possible rungs above: buying tax liens or tax deeds directly, and a broader unclaimed-property and heir-finding business. These are separate, crowded, low-margin businesses, not a vertically integrated chain that compounds toward a very large company. Total US surplus is perhaps low billions of dollars per year (my estimate), and the realisable share is capped at 10-30%.
scored.fatal_flaw: The outcome, meaning who is owed and how much, is already printed in public county surplus lists, and statutory fee caps of about 10-33% limit the step-up. So there is no hidden value for ML to reveal and no 10^4 revaluation: it is a crowded collections business.
scored.one_line_reason: This fails the rubric. The value is known and legible ahead of time, fees are capped by law, the buyer is a county paying face value, the hit-rate lever is small, and there is no ladder up to a very large company.
sources: Web search was unavailable (the shared search budget ran out on the first query), so no claim here was checked live; these are references from memory
California Revenue and Taxation Code section 4675 (assignment and finder fee cap on excess proceeds, about 10%) - from memory
Florida Statutes s.197.582 and Ch. 45.032-45.033 (surplus distribution, limits on assignments and fees) - from memory
Tyler v. Hennepin County, 598 U.S. 631 (2023) (owners' right to surplus from tax sales)
Hit rates, cost per lead and market size are my own estimates, not sourced

scored.name: Food-contact substance notification (FCN) arbitrage for PFAS-free packaging
scored.one_line: Acquire small firms or their FCNs for PFAS-free barrier chemistries, prove performance on fibre, sell to packaging majors facing PFAS bans.
scored.unproven_right: Effective FCNs and know-how (non-exclusive).
scored.proving_step: ML matching FCN memos and patents to use cases; Kit/TAPPI tests.
scored.proven_buyer: Graphic Packaging, Huhtamaki, Pactiv Evergreen, Smurfit Westrock, Solenis, Kemira.
scored.public_data: FDA FCN inventory and FOIA memos, terminations, Federal Register, patents, Safer States tracker.
scored.frame: Rung: own an effective FCN plus barrier chemistry know-how and prove it on fibre (Kit/TAPPI/grease, water and heat-seal tests). Discovery (matching an FCN or patent to a PFAS-free use case) is maybe 20-30% of the work (my estimate). Most of the value sits in formulation, coating-line trials, converting runs, scale-up and customer qualification over 6-18 months, which is the bespoke physical step. This is the geothermal-in-coal-mine pattern: finding the chemistry is easy, making it run on a paper machine is the hard part.
scored.step_up: Estimate, not sourced (the search budget ran out): an unproven small-firm FCN plus know-how might change hands for about $0.1-1M. Getting a new FCN through FDA is commonly quoted in the industry at roughly $50k-$300k plus 120 days. A proven PFAS-free barrier with a major converter's qualification might be worth $5-30M as a licence or acqui-hire. That is about 10-30x at best, nearer 3-10x against the cost of simply filing your own FCN. The step-up is capped because FCNs are non-exclusive for the substance and a competitor can file its own in about 120 days.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Estimate: a Kit/TAPPI bench test costs about $200-$2,000 per sample at a contract lab, and a pilot coater trial about $10-50k. Bench hit rates are not low, because many PFAS-free chemistries (PVOH, latex/acrylic dispersions, waxes, biopolymers) already pass Kit 8-12 at the right coat weight. The binding problems are cost per tonne, repulpability and heat resistance, not finding the needle. With a base hit rate perhaps above 20%, the lever is capped at about 5x, on a step that is already cheap.
scored.data: From my knowledge (not re-verified this turn): the FDA Inventory of Effective FCNs is a structured, downloadable table with FCN number, substance, notifier, manufacturer, intended use, limitations/specifications and effective date. That is the outcome, already written into legible fields, the same pattern that killed earlier hunts. FOIA memos add detail but the main signal is already summarised. Patents are legible and already mined by Solenis, Kemira, BASF, Dow and the like. The right is not cheaply buyable as a discrete asset. An FCN covers only the notifier's and named manufacturers' substance, and other suppliers can file their own. The owners are specialty-chemical firms that read this data better than anyone. Safer States is a legislative tracker, not an asset signal.
scored.right_bought: Non-exclusive FCN, effective only for the notifier and its named manufacturers, plus formulation know-how, usually bought through an acqui-hire of a small chemistry firm. It is not exclusive, not a scarce title, and can be replicated by filing a new FCN in about 120 days.
scored.buyer: Graphic Packaging, Huhtamaki, Pactiv Evergreen, Smurfit Westrock as converters, and Solenis, Kemira, BASF, Dow as chemical suppliers. They are well capitalised, but they buy qualified supply at commodity-plus prices, not speculative rights at a 10^3 premium. Several of them already run in-house PFAS-free barrier programmes.
scored.ladder: FCN or chemistry, then dispersion manufacturing, then coating-as-a-service, then a barrier-board converter, then branded packaging. A ladder exists, but every rung is capital-heavy specialty chemicals and converting at about 5-15% margins, with entrenched incumbents. It is a mid-size specialty-chemical outcome, not a trillion-dollar path.
scored.fatal_flaw: There is no illegible, scarce, cheaply buyable right with a big step-up. FCNs are non-exclusive and replicable in about 120 days. The FDA inventory already states the substance and its intended use in legible fields. The work is in formulation, scale-up and converter qualification, not discovery. So the 95-5 discovery frame does not exist, and the step-up is roughly 10x rather than 10^3-10^4.
scored.one_line_reason: Discovery is a small share of the work, the right is non-exclusive and replicable, and the FDA inventory already exposes the outcome. This is the geothermal-in-coal-mine failure applied to packaging chemistry.

scored.name: Recontactable Protective-Variant Carrier Network
scored.one_line: License recontact rights to small cohorts whose published case reports imply rare protective LoF carriers; re-consent and phenotype; sell validation packages.
scored.unproven_right: Data-use and recontact agreements, $20-100k.
scored.proving_step: LLM over case reports, ClinVar submitters and dbGaP; recontact and blood panels.
scored.proven_buyer: Regeneron, Amgen, Novo, Lilly.
scored.public_data: PMC full text and supplements, ClinVar, dbGaP, gnomAD, consanguineous-cohort papers.
scored.frame: The proposed rung is "find published small cohorts implying rare protective loss-of-function carriers, obtain recontact/data-use rights, re-phenotype, sell a validation package to a large pharma." Discovery (literature/variant mining) is arguably 60-80% of the intellectual work, but the physical step is the opposite of trivial or abstracted: it requires the original investigator's cooperation, an IRB amendment at the holding institution, consent that permitted recontact in the first place, and in many cases a foreign-jurisdiction ethics approval. That is bespoke, per-cohort, human-institution work — structurally the geothermal-plant-in-a-coal-mine failure mode, not the drilling-is-abstracted case. Note: no web searches were completed for this candidate (my first search attempt was blocked), so every number below is an explicit estimate from domain knowledge, not a sourced figure.
scored.step_up: Estimate, unsourced. The "unproven right" is quoted at $20-100k for a data-use/recontact agreement. A validated protective-target package (human genetic LoF evidence plus phenotyped carriers) is worth somewhere in the $1-20M range as a pharma deal, which on paper is ~10-100x. But that comparison is unsound: the $20-100k agreement is not the asset — it is permission to attempt work, and the proving step (re-consent, blood draws, deep phenotyping on 5-50 geographically scattered people, assay development) is itself a seven-figure, multi-year cost that dwarfs the right. Net of true proving cost, the step-up is roughly 3-10x at best, and the holder of the asset (the academic cohort owner) captures most of it because they can re-trade with any buyer. Scored 1-2; I give 1 because there is no moment at which a "hit" revalues a thing you own.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Estimate, unsourced. Base rate of a published rare-LoF observation becoming a validated, pharma-purchasable protective target is very low — single-digit percent at best, which superficially looks like a good ML lever. But the cost per proving attempt is dominated by non-ML, non-parallelisable items: IRB amendment and local ethics (months of calendar time, not dollars you can throw 10x more of at), investigator goodwill (a strictly rationed, non-purchasable input), and clinical phenotyping. ML can raise the shortlist quality — the literature-mining part is genuinely automatable — but the binding constraint is consent and institutional access, so cutting the discovery step 10x buys you almost no extra shots. The lever caps on the scarce input, not the base hit rate. Also the main buyers (Regeneron Genetics Center, Amgen/deCODE, Novo, Lilly) already run exome/genome biobanks in the hundreds of thousands to millions of participants with recontact consent built in at enrollment — they have solved the access problem structurally rather than deal-by-deal.
scored.data: PMC full text plus supplements, ClinVar, dbGaP and consanguineous-cohort papers are genuinely public and genuinely illegible — unstructured supplementary tables, PDFs, inconsistent variant nomenclature — and that is the one real strength here, roughly a 3 on the data half of C4 on its own. Two problems sink the combined score. First, legibility of the outcome: for the protective-variant class that matters, the answer is largely already written into legible fields — ClinVar clinical significance, gnomAD constraint/pLI and allele-frequency fields, and the published abstract itself typically state "homozygous LoF, healthy carrier" explicitly. The hits that make headlines (PCSK9, ANGPTL3, ASGR1, SLC30A8, LPA) were found and worked by pharma genetics groups reading the same literature; the summarisation-kills-the-edge failure mode the rubric warns about applies directly. Second, and decisive: the right cannot be bought. A data-use/recontact agreement is non-exclusive, non-assignable, revocable, contingent on an IRB and on participant re-consent, and worthless without the original investigator's continuing cooperation. The sellers are not naive owners who cannot read the data — they are the authors of the paper, i.e. the single best-informed readers of it on earth. There is no information asymmetry to arbitrage.
scored.right_bought: What is nominally bought is a $20-100k data-use and recontact agreement. What is actually bought is a revocable permission slip, not an asset: it conveys no exclusivity, cannot be held on a balance sheet, cannot be resold, and dies if the IRB or any individual participant declines. Human subjects cannot be owned, optioned, or exclusively contracted, so there is no equivalent of the mineral title that makes Terranox work. The candidate's own one-liner concedes "weak legal right," and that concession is the whole story.
scored.buyer: Buyers are real and deeply capitalised — Regeneron, Amgen, Novo Nordisk, Lilly all pay large sums for validated human-genetics protective targets. But they do not buy the output of this rung. They buy either (a) a target with a tractable chemistry/biology program attached, or (b) biobank-scale platforms. A "validation package" on 5-50 carriers is a service deliverable, which also brushes the rubric's sell-a-service-to-incumbents exclusion: the company never owns the asset, so it never realises the step-up and has no leverage in the negotiation. Worse, the counterparty is also the best-resourced competitor: Regeneron Genetics Center and Amgen/deCODE do exactly this in-house at vastly greater scale, with consent-at-enrollment recontact rights they already hold.
scored.ladder: Rungs above are real and enormous (target to tool compound to clinical asset to approved drug), but not climbable from here: each rung is 10-100x more capital and rung one produces no owned asset and no retained economics to fund the next step.
scored.fatal_flaw: The right cannot be bought, owned, or made exclusive — human research participants are not mineral title. A recontact agreement is revocable, non-assignable and contingent on IRB approval and individual re-consent, so there is no asset that revalues on a hit and nothing to hold while it appreciates. Compounding this, the counterparty you buy from (the paper's own authors) is the single best-informed reader of the data, so the information asymmetry the model depends on does not exist, and the buyers you would sell to (Regeneron Genetics Center, Amgen/deCODE) already run this exact play in-house with consent-at-enrollment recontact rights across million-person biobanks.
scored.one_line_reason: Genuinely illegible public data, but no ownable right, no asset that revalues on a hit, a bespoke non-abstracted proving step gated on IRBs and individual re-consent, and the buyers already do it in-house at biobank scale — it is a service business dressed as an asset play.
sources: No external sources: my first WebSearch for Regeneron/recontact cost figures was stopped by a safety classifier before returning results, and I did not retry on that topic. Every number in this scoring is explicitly my own estimate from domain knowledge, not a sourced figure.

Unsourced background relied on, flagged as recall and not verified this session: Regeneron Genetics Center and Amgen/deCODE operate exome/genome biobanks at the 10^5-10^6 participant scale with recontact consent obtained at enrollment; canonical protective-LoF targets (PCSK9, ANGPTL3, ASGR1, SLC30A8) were identified by pharma and academic genetics groups from the same public literature; ClinVar clinical-significance and gnomAD pLI/allele-frequency fields already summarise the protective-carrier outcome for most such variants.

scored.name: Indication Expander: new-indication 510(k)s on dormant clearances
scored.one_line: Buy dormant 510(k)s; ML over MAUDE, off-label case series and claims finds devices already used for higher-value indications; file new-indication 510(k); sell.
scored.unproven_right: Transferable 510(k) and files, $5-50k.
scored.proving_step: 510(k) filing ($100-250k) relying on real-world use.
scored.proven_buyer: Strategics in aesthetics, neuromodulation, women's health, wound care.
scored.public_data: 510(k) database and scanned letters, MAUDE, PubMed, CMS PUFs, Open Payments.
scored.rough_step_up: ~10-100x; predicates can be cited without owning.
scored.frame: The rung would be buying a dormant 510(k) and filing for a new indication. Discovery (finding devices that are already used for a higher-value indication) is maybe 20-30% of the work at most (my estimate). The physical step is not trivial: FDA usually wants clinical or performance data for a new indication, often a prospective study, or it pushes the device to De Novo/PMA. MAUDE complaints and off-label case series rarely count as valid scientific evidence, so the filing and regulatory work are most of the cost. This looks like the coal-mine geothermal counter-example: finding the device is the easy part.
scored.step_up: Estimates, not sourced (the shared web-search budget was used up before this agent could search). Dormant 510(k)s with no revenue usually change hands as part of small asset sales, often well under $50k, and many are simply abandoned. A cleared new indication with no sales, no quality system and no reimbursement probably sells to a strategic for $0.3-3M at most, about 10-60x the candidate's own $5-50k figure, and only if the indication is defensible. The value is not exclusive: once you are cleared, any competitor can file its own 510(k) citing your device as the predicate. So the proven asset is a reference point anyone can copy, not a scarce right. Strategics pay for revenue, IP and data, not for clearance letters.
scored.hit_rate_capex: These are estimates from general knowledge; no web search was run. The FDA user fee is about $24-26k (FY2025/26 standard), and a full submission costs about $100-250k without a clinical study, or $1-10M+ with one. Most 510(k) submissions that reach a decision are found substantially equivalent, roughly 70-85% after AI rounds, with withdrawals as the main failure. So the proving step does not mostly fail today. The low hit rate is in commercial value, not regulatory success, and ML over MAUDE has nothing to raise. The lever is capped near 1/0.75, about 1.3x, not 10x.
scored.data: The data is public and partly illegible: scanned 510(k) summaries and letters, free-text MAUDE narratives, PubMed case series, CMS PUFs, Open Payments. But the outcome (cleared indications) is written into a legible field, the 510(k) database's indications-for-use statement and product code. The off-label signal is also widely mined already: strategics' medical-affairs teams, CROs and regulatory consultancies (for example Emergo/UL and NAMSA) read MAUDE and the literature all the time. MAUDE is known to be noisy, under-reported and full of litigation-driven reports, so it is a weak signal for value.
scored.right_bought: A 510(k) can be transferred by asset purchase and the owner updates the FDA registration listing, so it can be bought cheaply. But owning it confers almost nothing: a new-indication submission does not need the original holder's clearance, because predicates can be cited without owning them, as the candidate itself admits. The bought right has no exclusivity, so there is no reason to buy it.
scored.buyer: Device strategics in aesthetics (Allergan/AbbVie, InMode), neuromodulation (Medtronic, Boston Scientific), women's health (Hologic) and wound care (Smith+Nephew, Solventum). They buy commercial traction, IP, reimbursement codes and clinical data, rarely a bare clearance. Many buy small device companies only once revenue is above $5-20M (estimate).
scored.ladder: There is a ladder: clearance, then contract manufacturing, a quality system, commercial launch, reimbursement, then a platform device company. Each rung up needs a lot of sales and clinical capital, and the device market is fragmented by indication, so a path to a trillion-dollar company is implausible. A roll-up of niche devices (like Integra or the Teleflex model) is the realistic ceiling.
scored.fatal_flaw: A 510(k) gives no exclusivity: anyone can cite any cleared device as a predicate without owning it, and a new indication usually needs clinical data rather than MAUDE or off-label evidence. So the bought right has no scarcity value, the proving step rarely fails, so ML has no hit-rate lever, and the cleared output is easy for competitors to copy, which leaves no 10^3-10^4 step-up.
scored.one_line_reason: Fails the core rubric. The right is non-exclusive and not needed, the regulatory and clinical work is most of the cost rather than discovery, 510(k)s mostly succeed so there is no hit-rate lever, and the step-up is about 10x at best and can be copied.

scored.name: Predicate Bank: dormant surgical and medical-robot 510(k) clearances
scored.one_line: Buy 510(k)s for surgical, rehab and pharmacy robots from defunct medtech; ML proves validity and SE mapping to a buyer's architecture; sell to strategics avoiding De Novo.
scored.unproven_right: Transferable 510(k) plus DHF, $20-200k.
scored.proving_step: ML over summaries, MAUDE, recalls and design files; SE mapping.
scored.proven_buyer: Medtronic, J&J/Ethicon, Stryker, Zimmer Biomet, robotics startups.
scored.public_data: FDA 510(k) and De Novo databases, MAUDE, recalls, registration, FOIA 483s.
scored.frame: The intended rung is "own a dormant 510(k) plus its design history file (DHF), prove it is valid and maps substantially equivalent (SE) to a buyer's architecture, then sell it." Discovery is not 80%+ of the work in this rung. Finding a cleared robot device is a filtered query on the public 510(k) database. The real work is physical and regulatory: rebuilding or verifying the DHF, re-establishing design controls and a QMS, and filing a new 510(k) for any significant change under 21 CFR 807.81(a)(3). That work is the expensive part, which is the coal-mine-geothermal pattern again. My estimate is that discovery is about 10-20% of the work in this frame.
scored.step_up: I could not verify this. The web search budget was used up before any query ran, so these numbers are my estimates and are not sourced. The candidate claims an unproven 510(k)+DHF costs $20-200k. A clearance on its own, separated from a manufacturing operation, sells for very little because the buyer cannot use it for a different device. Clearances that do sell usually go inside distressed asset or IP sales and are priced on the technology, team and inventory, not the clearance. A "proven" mapping adds nothing a buyer cannot get for free. Any legally marketed device can be cited as a predicate by anyone, with no ownership or license required (21 CFR 807.92/807.100). My estimate of the step-up is 1-3x, and it is not a 10^2 to 10^4 jump. Avoiding De Novo is worth roughly the gap between De Novo and 510(k) costs: FY2025 MDUFA fees of about $160k versus about $24k, and program costs of about $1-3M versus about $0.2-1M (estimate). That saving comes from the public predicate, not from owning the clearance.
scored.hit_rate_capex: The proving step does not fail often. My estimate, from memory of FDA reporting, is that about 75-85% of 510(k) final decisions are SE, so the hit-rate lever is capped near 1/0.8, about 1.25x, and is nowhere near 10x. Cost per attempt is about $24k in FDA fee plus testing and consulting, which I estimate at $200k-1M for a robotic system. ML predicate-selection tools already exist and target the same step: Basil Systems, RegDesk, and many regulatory consultants. None of this was verified, because the search budget was used up.
scored.data: The data is mostly legible. The 510(k) database has structured fields for decision (SEKD/SESE), product code, predicate and applicant, and the summaries are public PDFs. MAUDE and recalls are structured. The outcome, whether a device was cleared, is already written into a legible decision field. That is the same failure mode as earlier hunts where regulators write the answer into a status field. The illegible part is the DHF, which is private and held by the owner, not public. ML would read summaries that every regulatory affairs (RA) consultant already reads.
scored.right_bought: The clearance can be bought cheaply from defunct companies or bankruptcy estates, and transfers are allowed with updated registration and listing. The problem is that the right does not give the buyer anything exclusive. A strategic can cite the same device as a predicate for free. Owning the clearance only lets you market that exact device, and the bought DHF and QMS are often too stale to support continued marketing without remediation.
scored.buyer: The capitalised buyers are Medtronic, J&J/Ethicon, Stryker, Zimmer Biomet and robotics startups. They buy companies, IP and teams, not bare clearances, because they can cite any predicate without buying it. Robotic surgery product codes such as NAY already have many predicates, including da Vinci, Hugo, Mako and Senhance. This last point is my own knowledge and was not searched.
scored.ladder: In principle, the company could start by buying clearances, then remanufacture or relaunch dormant devices, then become a contract or own-brand surgical robot maker. Each rung above the first is ordinary hardware manufacturing and selling into hospitals, with no discovery advantage. The ladder exists, but nothing carries the edge up it.
scored.fatal_flaw: Predicate status is a free public good. Anyone may cite any legally marketed device in their own 510(k) without owning or licensing it. A strategic avoiding De Novo therefore gets the whole benefit from the public database for free. The bought 510(k) is worth something only for marketing the identical device, and that device is the defunct product that already failed. On top of that, the SE outcome is already a legible public field.
scored.one_line_reason: Owning a 510(k) gives no exclusive right, because predicates can be cited by anyone for free. The SE outcome is already public, about 80% of 510(k) decisions are SE so the hit-rate lever is roughly 1.25x, and the hard part is DHF and QMS work, so there is no 10^3 step-up or discovery-dominated rung.

scored.name: HCPCS Ghost Codes: DMEPOS codes with dead suppliers
scored.one_line: Find well-paying HCPCS codes whose verified products are from defunct makers; buy the 510(k) and PDAC verification; restart via CM; sell reimbursed SKUs to DME distributors.
scored.unproven_right: Dormant 510(k) plus PDAC verification, near free.
scored.proving_step: PDAC re-verification and paid claims ($50-200k).
scored.proven_buyer: AdaptHealth, Medline, Cardinal, Owens & Minor/Apria.
scored.public_data: DMEPOS fee schedule, PDAC DMECS, FDA registration, CMS DME PUFs.
scored.frame: The proposed rung is "dormant 510(k) plus PDAC coding verification, made into a reimbursed SKU." There is no rung here where discovery is 80%+ of the work. Finding a well-paying HCPCS code with few verified products is one filter over the public fee schedule joined to the public PDAC DMECS product list. That is days of work (my estimate). Everything after it is the real work: a contract-manufacturing tech transfer, an FDA establishment registration and quality system, a PDAC submission, then winning distributor shelf space against competitive-bid prices. On my estimate discovery is under 10% of the work in this rung. The physical step is the hard part, the same way it is in the geothermal-in-coal-mines counter-example.
scored.step_up: I estimate about 1-5x on the right itself. The candidate's own guess is 10-30x, and I could not support that. Live web searches were refused because the shared search budget for this turn was exhausted, so the numbers below are from my own knowledge and are not sourced. Distributors such as AdaptHealth and Medline buy products at a markup over manufacturing cost. They do not pay a premium for a coding verification, because the verification is not exclusive. The step-up happens only through operating margin on units sold, not through the asset being repriced as soon as a hit lands. A dormant 510(k) for a low-risk DME device probably trades in the low tens of thousands of dollars or less (my estimate). Many DME items are 510(k)-exempt Class I or II devices (manual wheelchairs, many orthoses, canes), so the 510(k) often carries little value at all.
scored.hit_rate_capex: I put the base hit rate of PDAC verification at high, likely over 70% for a product that truly matches a code's description (my estimate). Rejections are usually fixed by resubmitting. The cost of a PDAC review is close to zero: as I understand it there is no application fee, only staff time. The $50-200k in the candidate is mostly manufacturing restart and quality-system cost, not proving cost, and ML does not lower it. Since the lever is capped at 1/base hit rate, it is about 1.4x at most. That is not 10x. These figures are not sourced (search budget exhausted).
scored.data: The data is fully legible. The DMEPOS fee schedule is a structured CSV, the PDAC DMECS product classification list can be searched by HCPCS code, the FDA 510(k) and registration-listing databases are structured, and the CMS DME supplier and utilization public-use files are tabular. The answer this idea is looking for, "which codes have no live verified products," can be read straight off DMECS joined to FDA registration status. That is the "outcome already summarised in a legible field" failure that killed earlier hunts. ML has no edge over a SQL join.
scored.right_bought: A dormant 510(k) can be bought from a defunct or exiting maker, sometimes almost free in an asset sale. But the economically relevant right, eligibility to bill a HCPCS code, cannot be owned or held exclusively. Any manufacturer can apply to PDAC to have an equivalent product verified under the same code, and for exempt devices it needs no 510(k) at all. So buying the right gives no moat and is not what creates value.
scored.buyer: DME distributors and suppliers such as AdaptHealth, Medline, Cardinal Health, and Owens and Minor (Apria). They are well capitalised, but they buy inventory at cost-plus, not rights at a step-up. Competitive bidding and the fee schedule cap what they will pay.
scored.ladder: There is a modest ladder: contract-made SKU, then own brand, then own manufacturing, then a DME supplier or billing arm. Integrated players already exist (Medline, Drive DeVilbiss, Invacare's remnants), the margins are thin, and the market is a low-growth, reimbursement-capped niche. There is no trillion-dollar path.
scored.fatal_flaw: A HCPCS code is not an exclusive right. Any maker can get an equivalent product verified by PDAC, at low cost and with a high hit rate. The "ghost code" gap is visible in public structured data (DMECS joined to FDA registration). So there is no hidden discovery to do, nothing scarce to own, and no step-up on a hit. What is left is ordinary manufacturing and distribution work.
scored.one_line_reason: The answer can be read off structured public lists (DMECS plus FDA), the right is not exclusive, proving is cheap and usually succeeds, and the value comes from making and selling the product, not from discovery.

scored.name: Stalled PMN Rescue: abandoned TSCA new-chemical submissions
scored.one_line: Buy stalled PMN dossiers and test data; ML predicts quick-clear cases; re-file; sell cleared substances.
scored.unproven_right: Test data and PMN dossier, $50-200k.
scored.proving_step: EPA determination and Notice of Commencement.
scored.proven_buyer: Specialty chemical makers (electrolytes, PFAS replacements, semi chemicals).
scored.public_data: EPA TSCA tracker, Section 5 determinations and orders, SNURs, Inventory.
scored.frame: The rung would be 'own a TSCA-cleared new chemical substance'. Inside it, getting through EPA review is maybe 30-50% of the work at most (my estimate). The rest is synthesis and scale-up, application/customer qualification (semiconductor and battery electrolyte qualification cycles run 1-3 years), and the commercial pull that makes a cleared substance worth anything. Clearance is a regulatory gate, not a discovery. The submitter already knows the molecule, its use and the hazard data. The physical and commercial steps are not trivial or abstracted, which is the coal-mine-geothermal failure pattern.
scored.step_up: Unproven: a stalled dossier plus test data at the candidate's assumed $50-200k (not verified). Proven: a cleared PMN is not a separately traded asset with a market price. Once the Notice of Commencement is filed, the substance goes on the public TSCA Inventory and any company can make it for non-exempt uses, subject to any SNUR or consent order. So the cleared right is mostly non-exclusive. The value that can be captured comes from CBI-masked identity, know-how and customer qualification, not from the clearance. My estimate is a 1-5x uplift on dossier cost for a resale to a specialty maker. The candidate's own ~10-30x looks optimistic, and it already notes weak ownership after listing. Nowhere near 10^3-10^4.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Base hit rate: most PMNs eventually clear. Historically about 80-90% end with a 'not likely' determination or with an order/SNUR; the remainder are withdrawn, often after EPA signals concerns. This is from memory and could not be checked (searching unavailable). Cost per attempt: EPA PMN fee is about $37,000 (2024 fee rule; about $6,480 for small businesses) plus about $20k-$500k+ of testing when EPA asks for data (my estimate). Review takes 1-2+ years against a statutory 90 days. Because the base hit rate is high, the lever (capped at 1/base) is only about 1.1-1.5x. The real pain is delay, not failure, and ML does not shorten EPA's queue.
scored.data: There is public data: the EPA TSCA new-chemicals status tracker, Section 5 determination documents, consent orders, SNURs and the Inventory. But the outcome is written into legible public fields: the case status, the determination category, and the order/SNUR text listing the risks EPA identified. That is exactly the pattern where regulators write the answer down and kill the ML edge. Chemical identities are often CBI-masked under generic names, which makes data less available, not more extractable. Who already does this: regulatory consultancies (e.g. Bergeson & Campbell, Ramboll, Exponent, ToxStrategies) and the large in-house teams at chemical makers, who already predict EPA outcomes with QSAR and EPI Suite / analog methods, the same tools EPA uses.
scored.right_bought: In theory you can buy test data and a dossier from small or failed submitters. The PMN itself cannot really be transferred as an exclusive right. Unlike FIFRA, TSCA gives almost no data-compensation exclusivity outside Section 4 test rules. The sellers are sophisticated chemical firms or their consultants, who read the EPA data better than an outsider, so there is no illegible-data discount when buying.
scored.buyer: Specialty chemical makers (battery electrolytes, PFAS replacements, semiconductor chemicals). They are well capitalised, but they buy molecules that perform and are qualified with customers, not regulatory clearances. Usually they would rather file their own PMN, about $37k, than pay a premium for someone else's.
scored.ladder: Cleared substance, then toll manufacturing, then own production, then a specialty chemicals business. The ladder is real but conventional: each rung needs chemistry, plant capex and customer qualification. The first rung gives no discovery edge to build on.
scored.fatal_flaw: The proven asset is not ownable and is not a discovery. Clearing a PMN puts the substance on the public TSCA Inventory, where anyone can make it. Most PMNs clear anyway, so ML adds only about 1.1-1.5x, and the determination is already written into legible EPA fields. There is no 10^4 step-up to capture.
scored.one_line_reason: A regulatory-delay play, not a discovery play. The base clearance rate is high, the outcome is public and legible, ownership after listing is weak, the step-up is about 1-5x, and scale-up and customer qualification dominate the work.

scored.name: Predicate Bank (tobacco): grandfathered nicotine product status
scored.one_line: Buy dormant pre-2007 tobacco/nicotine product lines and records; ML over scanned trade, tax and archive records proves grandfathered status or SE predicates; sell to makers needing pathways.
scored.unproven_right: Dormant pre-2007 product line and records, $10-50k.
scored.proving_step: Assemble FDA-acceptable evidence; grandfather or SE acceptance.
scored.proven_buyer: PMI/Swedish Match, Altria, BAT/Reynolds, ITG, Turning Point.
scored.public_data: FDA CTP SE/NSE orders, UCSF Truth Tobacco Documents, MSA directories, trade publications, TTB permits.
scored.frame: The rung would be "own a documented grandfathered (pre-Feb 15, 2007) product, prove its status, and sell the predicate". Assembling evidence is most of the work here, maybe 70-80% (my estimate), and the physical step (an FDA submission) is cheap. But what comes out of the rung is not an exclusive asset. Under FD&C Act sec. 905(j) and 910(a)(2), any applicant may cite any grandfathered or SE-cleared product as a predicate without owning it (this is my understanding of FDA SE guidance; I could not check it this run). They only have to characterise it, for example by testing samples or using public specifications. So there is little to sell. The large makers (PMI, Altria, BAT/Reynolds, ITG) already hold big internal predicate libraries and would not pay for one.
scored.step_up: Unverified estimate. The candidate says a dormant pre-2007 line plus its records costs $10-50k. A proven, documented predicate is worth roughly the cost a buyer avoids by not doing a PMTA instead of an SE: PMTA $1-10M+ (FDA's own deeming-rule cost estimates, from memory) versus SE about $50-300k. That puts the ceiling for a proven predicate at maybe $100k-$1M, but only where no substitute predicate exists. That is about 3-20x, not 100-1000x. And because predicates are not exclusive, the price falls toward the cost of producing the evidence (consultant fees).
scored.hit_rate_capex: Unverified estimate. Proving a predicate is not a low hit-rate gamble. Documents like invoices, catalogues, TTB permits and state MSA listings either exist or they do not, and checking costs about $5-30k in consultant and legal time. FDA's NSE and refuse-to-accept outcomes mostly come from differences between the new product and its predicate or from missing data, not from failing to find a predicate. For example, in 2021 FDA refused large batches of applications covering millions of deemed products on content grounds (from memory). Base hit rate on predicate status is probably above 50% when records exist, so the ML lever is capped at about 2x. It is not a 10x lever.
scored.data: There is public, partly illegible data: UCSF Truth Tobacco Industry Documents (14M+ scanned documents), old trade publications, and TTB records. But the outcome is already written into legible fields. FDA publishes SE marketing orders and NSE lists, plus product lists from the grandfathered-determination process (this is my recollection; I could not verify the determination list this run). Most of the evidence that matters (invoices, sales records) is private, held by the original manufacturer, not public. Major makers' pre-2007 portfolios are fully documented internally.
scored.right_bought: You can buy dormant brands and trademarks from small defunct makers cheaply. But grandfathered status attaches to the product's characteristics, not to the owner, and it cannot be exclusively owned. Anyone with the same specs and evidence can use it as a predicate. What you buy is a trademark plus a records archive, not a gatekeeping right.
scored.buyer: The large makers named in the candidate already own most of the relevant predicates and do not need to buy. Realistic buyers are small cigar, hookah, pipe and smokeless makers. They are thinly capitalised and squeezed by user fees and compliance costs. ENDS/vape makers, the high-value segment, mostly have no grandfathered predicates (e-cigarettes were barely on the US market in 2007), so they must file a PMTA either way. Existing competitors are regulatory consultancies that already do predicate searches as a service.
scored.ladder: There is a weak ladder: predicate bank, then SE filings, then contract manufacturing, then owning tobacco brands. The category is shrinking under regulation, and the rungs above are a declining, ethically fraught industry. There is no path to a trillion-dollar company. ESG-restricted capital also limits who will fund or acquire it.
scored.fatal_flaw: Predicates are non-exclusive. The law lets any applicant cite any grandfathered or SE-cleared product without owning it, so proving status creates no ownable asset to sell for a step-up. The price falls to the cost of producing evidence, which makes it a consulting service, not an owned asset. The high-value buyers (big tobacco) already have predicates, and the segment with the strongest demand (ENDS) has none.
scored.one_line_reason: Proving grandfathered status creates no exclusive, ownable asset, and the step-up is about 3-20x, not 10^3. In practice this is regulatory consulting to a shrinking industry.

scored.name: Coastwise Hulls: Jones Act eligibility in scrap-bound hulls
scored.one_line: Buy US-built hulls headed for scrap; prove coastwise eligibility survived via USCG rebuild rules; sell for conversion.
scored.unproven_right: Old US-flag hulls priced as steel.
scored.proving_step: Build/rework history reconstruction and USCG rebuild determination.
scored.proven_buyer: Crowley, Edison Chouest, Harvey Gulf.
scored.public_data: USCG PSIX/NVDC, MARAD lists, FOIA rebuild letters, breaker notices.
scored.frame: The rung would be: buy a scrap-bound US-built hull, prove it is still coastwise-eligible, sell it. In practice proving eligibility is maybe 5-15% of the work (my estimate). Most of the value is unlocked by the physical step: drydock, reactivation or conversion, and re-certifying the hull with USCG and ABS, the vessel classification society. That physical step is large and bespoke. This is the geothermal-in-coal-mines counter-example again: finding the right hull is easy, and converting it is the hard part.
scored.step_up: Estimate only; my search budget ran out, so none of these numbers are sourced. A hull bought at scrap value (light ship weight x roughly $300-500/LT for US domestic scrap) might be worth 1.5-3x that as a coastwise-eligible hull before conversion. The candidate's ~10-50x step-up appears only after a multi-million-dollar conversion, and that is a build margin, not a discovery step-up. Remember that the 2016-2021 OSV downturn sent many fully coastwise-eligible US Gulf OSVs to scrap or cold stack. That suggests eligibility alone carries little premium when the conversion or operating economics fail.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Estimate. The base hit rate is high, not low. Most US-built, US-flag hulls headed for scrap still have their coastwise endorsement, because losing it takes a foreign rebuild, foreign registry or sale to a non-citizen under 46 USC 12132 and 46 CFR 67.177, and those events are uncommon and recorded. A proving attempt costs a records review plus a USCG rebuild determination request, maybe $5k-50k in counsel and survey time. Because the lever is capped at 1/base hit rate, ML can improve it by about 1.2-2x at most, not 10x.
scored.data: This is the killer. The outcome is already written into a legible field. The USCG NVDC Certificate of Documentation lists the endorsement (coastwise, registry or fishery), and PSIX and the NVDC vessel lookup show build country and documentation status for free. Rebuild determinations go through the USCG NVDC with published criteria. Ship brokers and owners like Crowley, Edison Chouest and Harvey Gulf read this data every day, so there is no illegible signal for ML to extract.
scored.right_bought: The hull can be bought, from scrap sales, MARAD obsolete-fleet disposals, bankruptcy auctions and cold-stacked OSV fleets. But sellers already know whether the hull is coastwise-eligible, because it is printed on their own COD. So there is no information asymmetry to buy at a discount. Distressed scrap pricing happens because the hulls are old and uneconomic, not because sellers misread eligibility.
scored.buyer: Possible buyers are Jones Act operators: Crowley, Edison Chouest, Harvey Gulf, Hornbeck, and offshore-wind support-vessel builders. They are well capitalised but prefer newbuilds or reactivating their own cold-stacked fleets. They buy converted, classed hulls, not eligibility opinions.
scored.ladder: There are rungs above (hull acquisition, conversion yard, Jones Act operator, offshore-wind vessel provider), and that is a real but limited path in a protected niche market. US shipyard capacity and cost (US builds run roughly 3-5x foreign) cap how far it scales. It is not a trillion-dollar ladder.
scored.fatal_flaw: Coastwise eligibility is already a public, legible endorsement field on the USCG Certificate of Documentation, and it is usually intact (high base hit rate), so discovery adds almost no value. The step-up comes from heavy, bespoke conversion capex, which is the geothermal-in-coal-mines failure mode.
scored.one_line_reason: The answer is already printed on the hull's COD, sellers know it, and the value lies in shipyard conversion rather than discovery, so there is no 95/5 frame and no ML lever.

scored.name: Obsolete IC Surplus Lots matched to military demand
scored.one_line: Buy surplus electronics lots by weight; vision/OCR on photos finds EOL parts DLA and primes cannot source; authenticate and sell into solicitations.
scored.unproven_right: Unidentified component lots at scrap.
scored.proving_step: Marking OCR cross-matched to DIBBS and EOL notices; AS6081/AS6171 testing.
scored.proven_buyer: DLA, primes, Rochester, Smith, Converge.
scored.public_data: DIBBS RFQs and awards, SAM.gov, GovDeals/GSA listings, PCN/EOL notices, FLIS.
scored.frame: The rung would be "buy an unidentified surplus lot, identify the parts in it, authenticate them, sell them into a DoD solicitation." Discovery (finding the part) is maybe 20-30% of the work inside that rung. That is my estimate. Most of the work and cost goes elsewhere: AS6081/AS6171 authentication, establishing provenance, sorting and handling, quality-system certification, and passing DLA/prime supplier approval. Reading the part number off a chip is not hard, because it is printed on the package. The hard part is proving the part is genuine and traceable, and testing cannot fully do that for parts with no chain of custody. The physical and compliance step is the main work, which is the same failure as the coal-mine geothermal counter-example. The buyer has capital, but rules restrict what it may buy (DFARS 252.246-7007/7008 require buying from the original manufacturer or authorized distributors first, and extra controls on independent distributors).
scored.step_up: My estimate, no searches ran. Scrap e-waste and mixed surplus boards or reels sell for roughly $1-20/lb. Authenticated EOL military-grade ICs can sell for about $20-500+ per unit, and some rare line items for more. Per hit line item the multiple can be 100x or more, but averaged over a lot it is closer to 10-100x. Most of a typical lot is commodity or worthless parts, and the testing cost of about $1k-5k per part number (estimate) comes out of the gain. The 100-1000x figure only holds for the rare item. The asset's value does not jump because of identification alone: unidentified-provenance parts trade at a discount even after they are identified.
scored.hit_rate_capex: My estimate, no sources. Identification is cheap and already common: brokers and harvesters read markings by eye or with basic OCR and check them against NetComponents, IC Source and ERAI. Lots are bought for a few hundred to a few thousand dollars, and identifying what is inside costs labor-hours, not drill-level capex. The expensive and often-failing step is authentication: AS6171 test suites cost about $1k-5k+ per part number (estimate), and non-traceable lots often fail or come back inconclusive. ML on photos does not raise the authentication pass rate, because whether a part is counterfeit or a reclaimed pull is decided by lab tests (X-ray, decap, XRF), not by the markings. The lever on the costly step is about 1-2x, not 10x.
scored.data: The data is public but already easy to read. DIBBS RFQs are structured: they list the NSN, the approved CAGE/part number and quantity, and brokers already scrape them. FLIS links NSNs to part numbers. PCN/EOL notices are aggregated by SiliconExpert, IHS/Accuris and Z2Data. Chip markings are printed text, and GovDeals/GSA listings often name the contents. The outcome (does this part match a solicitation?) is effectively already sitting in a legible field, the part-number match. Rights can be bought cheaply at auction or by weight, but sellers such as e-waste recyclers and liquidators already pull out the high-value ICs, and Shenzhen-style harvesting markets do this at scale.
scored.right_bought: Surplus or scrap electronics lots bought by weight or at auction (GovDeals, GSA Auctions, liquidators, e-waste streams). They are cheap, but they lack the one thing the buyer values: chain of custody back to the original manufacturer.
scored.buyer: DLA Land and Maritime (via DIBBS), defense primes and their supply chains, and authorized aftermarket or independent distributors (Rochester Electronics, Smith, Converge, Fusion). DFARS counterfeit rules limit how much they will buy from a non-traceable independent source. DLA's Qualified Suppliers List for Distributors (QSLD) also requires traceability.
scored.ladder: The ladder is weak. Possible rungs above: independent broker, then certified authorized-aftermarket distributor (Rochester's model, which depends on licenses and die/wafer transfers from the manufacturers, not on discovery), then re-manufacturing or emulating EOL parts (die bank, re-packaging, FPGA emulation, as GDCA and Rochester do). Those upper rungs are won through original-manufacturer licensing relationships, not through the discovery edge. The market is also a niche of a few billion dollars (estimate). There is no path to a trillion-dollar company.
scored.fatal_flaw: Provenance, not identification, is what creates the value. Military buyers discount parts with no traceability back to the original manufacturer, and DFARS 252.246-7007/7008 plus DLA QSLD restrict buying them. Reading the markings (the ML step) is easy and already widespread among brokers and harvesters. Authenticating parts with no chain of custody is the expensive step, ML on photos does not improve it, and it is the main counterfeit risk area that the rules exist to keep out.
scored.one_line_reason: This is a crowded broker business. The discovery step (reading printed part numbers against structured DIBBS data) is already easy and done by others. The value depends on traceability and authentication testing, which ML cannot supply, and DoD counterfeit rules work against untraceable surplus.

scored.name: Shuttered Cleanroom Shells
scored.one_line: Buy closed fab shells at industrial prices; ML proves revivable cleanroom and utilities; recertify; sell to CHIPS-funded fabs. Powered-brownfields-like weakness.
scored.unproven_right: Fab shell at warehouse price.
scored.proving_step: ML over permits and filings; particle recertification; bespoke utility work.
scored.proven_buyer: Specialty and defense fabs, semi REITs.
scored.public_data: Building permits, ECHO/TRI, air/wastewater permits, SEC closures.
scored.frame: The rung would be buying a closed fab shell and proving it can be brought back into service. Discovery is maybe 5-15% of the work in that rung (my estimate). Most of it is physical: requalifying the cleanroom, rebuilding the UPW/HVAC/exhaust/gas/abatement systems, and replacing tools. This is the geothermal-in-a-coal-mine counter-example: refitting a bespoke facility is far harder than finding the right one.
scored.step_up: About 1.5-3x, maybe 3-10x in the best case (my estimate). Closed fabs do not sell at warehouse prices because the buyers already know what a fab is. From memory, not searched this run: TI bought Micron's Lehi fab for about $900M in 2021; ON Semi bought GlobalFoundries' East Fishkill fab for about $430M; TI bought Qimonda Richmond tools for about $172.5M in 2009. Prices like these already include most of the revival value. I could not verify any warehouse-price fab sale.
scored.hit_rate_capex: The proving step has no low base hit rate. Whether a known fab can be revived is mostly decided by a site visit and engineering review, so the hit rate is already high (estimate: more than 50% of marketed fabs are revivable at some cost). That puts the lever near 1/0.5 = 2x at most. The real cost of proving is a recertification and utilities refit, roughly $10M-$100M+ (my estimate), and ML does not lower that cost.
scored.data: The data is public but already legible. Every fab is a known, named facility listed in SEMI World Fab Watch and in TRI/ECHO and air permits. Closures are announced in SEC filings and press. Brokers who specialise in fabs (for example Cushman, JLL semiconductor groups) and buyers like TI, ON, Polar, SkyWater and Bosch already track every shell. The outcome, whether this is a working cleanroom fab, is effectively written in the name of the asset.
scored.right_bought: The right can be bought outright. The owners, though, are sophisticated semiconductor firms who know exactly what they are selling and often strip the tools first or price in the fab premium. Nobody is selling unaware of the cleanroom's value, so there is no information gap to capture.
scored.buyer: The buyers are well capitalised: CHIPS-funded specialty, analog and defense fabs, IDMs, and foundries such as TI, ON, SkyWater, Polar and Bosch. They buy fabs directly from the closing owners, which cuts out a middleman.
scored.ladder: The ladder is real: shell, then refurbished cleanroom, then tool install, then operating a specialty foundry. Each rung above is dominated by capex and execution, not discovery, so the ML edge does not compound as the company climbs.
scored.fatal_flaw: There is no information gap and no discovery-dominated rung. Fabs are a small, fully catalogued set of assets whose owners and buyers know their value. Proving revivability is a bespoke physical refit, not a cheap test that mostly fails. This is the coal-mine geothermal pattern, plus the powered-brownfields problem of no purchase discount.
scored.one_line_reason: This fails C1-C4. Fab shells are a few hundred known, legible assets sold by sophisticated owners at fab-aware prices, so the step-up is under 3-10x, the hit rate is already high, and the hard part is the physical refit, not discovery.
