scored.name: Stalled NEVI Award Rescue
scored.one_line: Buy stalled NEVI/CFI site packages from small awardees; ML picks those nearest energization; finish and flip.
scored.unproven_right: Assignment of sub-award, lease and interconnection application.
scored.proving_step: Utility energization date confirmation ($20-50k/site).
scored.proven_buyer: Pilot/GM, Love's, Tesla, EVgo.
scored.public_data: DOT NEVI awards and reports, FHWA plans, Joint Office data, utility dockets, permits.
scored.frame: The rung would be buying a stalled NEVI/CFI award package and taking it to confirmed energization. Discovery here means picking which stalled sites will energize soon, and I estimate it at no more than 10-20% of the work. Most of the work and money is the physical and administrative build: utility make-ready, a transformer, switchgear, four 150 kW DC fast chargers, Buy America compliance and the state DOT's consent to transfer the grant. From my own knowledge (unverified this run), a NEVI site costs about $0.8-1.5M in total. Federal funds cover up to 80% of that, and the awardee must fund the rest. This is the coal-mine-geothermal pattern: finishing the asset is much harder than choosing it.
scored.step_up: My estimate (no sources were reachable this run): a stalled package of an award, a site lease and a pending utility application might trade at about $25-150k, with heavy uncertainty, because there are no sold comps. A site that is energized or ready to build might sell to a charging operator for about $150-400k as a developer premium, on top of reimbursing what has been spent. That is roughly a 2-5x step-up. It is not 10^3, and it only shows up after the build capital has been spent. The step-up is also politically fragile: FHWA suspended state NEVI plan approvals in February 2025, and courts and new guidance in 2025 only partly undid that.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Most awarded sites probably do energize in the end, so failures mean delay rather than a dry hole. I would guess well over 50% eventually energize. With a base hit rate that high, the lever is capped at under about 2x, because the maximum is 1/base hit rate. The candidate puts the cost of the proving step at $20-50k per site (its own number, unverified). However, the money that is actually at risk is the roughly $1M build, and better site selection does not reduce that.
scored.data: The data is public and fairly legible: state DOT NEVI award lists and quarterly reports, the Joint Office and AFDC station locator, the EV-ChART reporting that FHWA requires, and utility interconnection dockets. Status (awarded, under construction, open) is already written into those status fields and dashboards. Utility energization queue dates are partly in dockets but are often private between the utility and the developer. This matches the failure seen in prior hunts: the answer is already sitting in a legible field. The ML edge over simply calling the utility and the DOT is small.
scored.right_bought: The right can be bought only in part. Federal sub-awards are not freely assignable: a transfer needs the state DOT's approval, a new compliance review and assumption of the cost share and the obligation to operate and maintain the site for 5 years. Small awardees such as convenience stores and local developers might sell, but they know their own sites' status better than outside data does, so they are not owners who cannot read the data.
scored.buyer: Charging operators and site hosts: Pilot/Flying J with GM, Love's, EVgo, Electrify America, Tesla, ChargePoint, BP Pulse and others. These are real buyers with capital, but they mainly develop their own sites or buy networks that are already operating. Tesla in particular rarely buys third-party award packages. Demand for half-built NEVI packages from outsiders is unproven.
scored.ladder: From site rescue the ladder goes to owning and operating chargers (becoming a charging operator), then a regional network, then energy and storage services. That is a real but modest ladder. The charging-operator business is crowded and low-margin, and most operators are losing money, so there is no clear trillion-dollar chain.
scored.fatal_flaw: The proving step is not discovery. The value is unlocked by about $1M of physical construction per site plus a non-assignable federal grant needing state DOT approval, and the site status is already published in legible NEVI reports. That leaves no hidden-signal arbitrage and a step-up of only about 2-5x, which is politically fragile.
scored.one_line_reason: Fails the Terranox test: the build, not the discovery, dominates; the step-up is about 2-5x; site status is already in public status fields; and grant assignment is gated by the state DOT.
sources: No web sources: the shared search budget for this turn (200 calls) was already used up before this candidate could search, so these numbers come from my own knowledge, are estimates and are unverified. A follow-up message can rerun the search.

Background knowledge (unverified this run): FHWA NEVI formula program of about $5B with up to 80% federal share; FHWA suspended NEVI state plan approvals in February 2025, partly undone by courts and new guidance in 2025; typical NEVI site of four 150 kW ports costing about $0.8-1.5M; EV-ChART reporting and the AFDC station locator publish site status.

scored.name: Curb-Power Rights: municipal curbside charging franchises
scored.one_line: Buy dormant curbside/streetlight charging permits from pilot operators; rank by grid capacity and demand; energize and sell portfolios.
scored.unproven_right: Assignment of encroachment/concession permits (consent needed).
scored.proving_step: DNO connection offer plus pilot utilisation.
scored.proven_buyer: Char.gy, ubitricity/Shell, Itselectric, Voltpost, Connected Kerb, Zouk.
scored.public_data: Council concession records, UK DNO capacity maps, NYC DOT permits, housing surveys.
scored.frame: Rung = holding a curbside charging concession/permit and getting it energised. Inside that rung, discovery (picking which streets have grid headroom and demand) is about 10-20% of the work (my estimate). Most of the work is physical: civils, DNO connection works, buying hardware, highway permits, and running and maintaining the chargers. This is the same shape as the geothermal-in-coal-mines counter-example, where building the asset is harder than finding the site. A buyer only pays for energised, utilised sites, so no rung exists where discovery is 80%+ of the work.
scored.step_up: Unproven: a dormant pilot permit or encroachment consent is worth roughly $0 to a few hundred dollars per site (my estimate; it is a revocable licence, not property). Proven: an energised lamppost or kerbside charger is typically valued at roughly replacement cost plus a modest premium. That is about £3-6k hardware plus installed cost for a lamppost unit and £8-15k for a kerbside post (my estimate, from UK industry figures recalled from memory, not verified this session). Once you count the capex you spend to get there, the value gained is about 1-3x the money put in, not 10-30x. The candidate's 10-30x compares against the permit's nominal cost and leaves out the build cost.
scored.hit_rate_capex: The proving step (DNO connection offer plus utilisation) is not mostly failing. Most low-power lamppost and kerbside connections are approved, because the load is 3-7 kW and runs off existing street-lighting or LV supply. Utilisation risk is real (UK on-street average utilisation is often cited at roughly 5-15%; estimate, not verified), but a failed site loses the hardware cost, about $5-15k (estimate), not a cheap probe. If the base hit rate is about 50%+ (estimate), the ML lever is capped at under 2x. The expensive step is the build, not the guess.
scored.data: The data is mostly public and legible. UK DNO network capacity and heat maps (UKPN, SSEN, NGED) are published as structured, machine-readable maps. Charger demand is already modelled from DfT and ONS off-street-parking and housing data, and by tools such as the Field Dynamics and Zapmap utilisation datasets. Council concession awards are published tender notices (Find a Tender / Contracts Finder). There is no meaningful illegible-data edge.
scored.right_bought: No cheap purchase route. UK on-street rights are mostly awarded through competitive council tenders, notably LEVI-funded concessions of about 10-15 years (from memory). They are not dormant rights held by owners who cannot read the data. Assignment needs council consent, and change-of-control clauses are typical. Pilot permits usually expire or are tied to the pilot operator. NYC DOT curbside pilots (such as itselectric and Voltpost) are revocable revocable consents/permits, not tradable property. The counterparty, the council, already knows the value and runs the auction.
scored.buyer: Buyers are capitalised: Shell (bought ubitricity in 2021), Char.gy (Gresham House-backed), Connected Kerb (Aviva and Gresham House funding, from memory), Zouk-managed funds, Believ, and infrastructure funds. But they buy energised, contracted portfolios, or they bid directly in council tenders themselves. They do not need to buy unproven permits from a middleman.
scored.ladder: Some ladder exists: concession, then build, then operate, then aggregate and sell portfolios to infrastructure funds, then expand into fleet or depot charging and energy services. It is a low-margin, crowded utility-style business, not a trillion-dollar chain. Incumbents (Shell, BP Pulse, Char.gy, Connected Kerb) already hold the upper rungs.
scored.fatal_flaw: The asset's value comes from building and operating it, not from discovering it. Getting a curbside site energised needs hardware, civils and grid works at roughly 1x the proven value, and rights are allocated by competitive council tender, not bought cheaply from owners who cannot read the data. That leaves no 80%-discovery rung, no 10^3 step-up, and no illegible-data edge.
scored.one_line_reason: This is build-heavy infrastructure. Rights are tendered and non-assignable, grid and demand data are legible, and the step-up is about 1-3x once build capex is counted. It repeats the geothermal-in-coal-mines failure.

scored.name: Latent Permit: dormant limited-entry fishing permits
scored.one_line: Buy latent fishing permits ahead of catch-share programs and sell allocated quota.
scored.unproven_right: Latent permits at $1-10k.
scored.proving_step: Council adoption and NMFS allocation (slow, uncontrollable).
scored.proven_buyer: Integrated harvesters and quota banks.
scored.public_data: NOAA permit lists, Federal Register, council transcripts, FOIA permit histories.
scored.rough_step_up: ~10-100x; holders can read their own history.
scored.frame: The rung is: buy a dormant limited-entry permit, then hold it until a catch-share program allocates quota to it. Almost none of the work in that rung is discovery. The 'proving' step is a council and NMFS rulemaking that usually takes 5-15 years and that the company cannot run, speed up or repeat. Finding which permits are dormant is easy, because the latent permit lists come out of NMFS landings data and council analyses. So the rung is mostly waiting on a political process, which makes it the geothermal-in-coal-mines failure pattern (the hard part is not the finding) rather than the Terranox pattern. This is my judgement. The web search budget was used up, so no live sources were checked.
scored.step_up: This is my estimate from general knowledge and is not verified. Latent permits trade for about $1-10k. A permit with heavy catch history going into a catch share can turn into quota worth $100k to several million dollars (for example Gulf red snapper IFQ shares, Pacific trawl IFQ, Alaska crab rationalisation). But allocation is almost always based on catch history in qualifying years, so a permit with no recent landings gets about zero, or at most a small equal-share slice. For the permits this strategy can actually buy, the expected step-up is about 1-3x, or a loss if the permit is cancelled. The rare upside of 10-100x mostly goes to permits with history, and their holders already know that and price it in.
scored.hit_rate_capex: There is no repeatable proving attempt that ML could make cheaper. Each fishery gets one allocation decision, made by council vote. Cost per 'attempt' is the permit price plus holding costs (annual renewal fees, about $100-1k per year, my estimate) over 5-15 years. Councils publish control dates specifically so that history built up after the date does not count, and they often remove latent licences outright: the Alaska groundfish and crab LLP latent licence actions of about 2008-2011 are examples, from memory and not verified. So the base 'hit rate' for a latent permit getting a meaningful allocation is low, but it is set by policy, and better prediction does not raise it. The ML lever is about 1x.
scored.data: The outcome is already written down in legible form. Allocation depends on landings history, which NMFS and the states record as structured fish-ticket and logbook data. The permit holder can see their own history, and council analyses publish allocation-distribution tables and latency counts. Permit lists are public and structured. Council transcripts are unstructured, but they only help you guess whether and when a program happens, not which permit wins, and that is plain political reading that any industry participant already does. This is the regulator-writes-the-answer-into-a-field problem flagged in earlier hunts.
scored.right_bought: The permits can be bought, since most limited-entry permits are transferable. But sellers are not blind: holders know their own landing history and follow council action closely. Many councils also limit who can own permits (owner-on-board rules, citizenship and vessel-linkage requirements, ownership caps), which restricts a financial buyer that does not fish.
scored.buyer: Integrated harvesters, processors and community quota entities or quota banks, all of which buy quota shares once allocation happens. The buyer is real, but transfer and ownership-cap rules limit it (for example the Pacific trawl IFQ accumulation limits).
scored.ladder: The rungs above are: quota aggregation (permit bank), leasing quota to fishermen, owning vessels and processing, then seafood distribution. This is a real but modest ladder. Ownership and accumulation caps in most US catch-share programs block consolidation by design, so the path to a very large company is legally capped.
scored.fatal_flaw: The value is set by a slow political allocation that rewards catch history the seller already knows about. A dormant permit almost by definition has no history, so it gets near-zero quota. Control dates and latent-licence removal exist precisely to stop this kind of speculation, and no discovery problem exists that ML could solve.
scored.one_line_reason: The 'proving' step is uncontrollable rulemaking, not discovery. Allocation is history-based and already legible to holders and regulators, and latent permits are what councils deliberately cut out, so there is no 95-5 frame and no hit-rate lever.

scored.name: CatalystCell: buried refinery catalyst landfills
scored.one_line: Buy closed refinery/petchem landfill cells booked as liabilities; ML over RCRA permits, manifests and unit inventories finds buried pre-1990s Pt/Re/Pd/Ni-Mo-Co catalyst; test pits and assay prove it; sell to PGM refiners. Industrial waste, not mineral exploration.
scored.unproven_right: Title or excavation rights to a cell at $1 or negative.
scored.proving_step: Test pits/auger grabs, XRF, fire assay/ICP-MS ($20-50k).
scored.proven_buyer: Johnson Matthey, Heraeus, Umicore, Sabin, BASF.
scored.public_data: RCRAInfo, state manifest archives, closure plans, TRI, SEMS, 1960s-80s Oil & Gas Journal unit inventories.
scored.frame: The rung would be "own a closed refinery waste cell and prove it holds recoverable catalyst metal." Discovery is maybe 10-20% of the work inside that rung (my estimate). Finding a refinery landfill is easy: the refinery and its RCRA unit are on the public record. The hard, bespoke and expensive part is excavating hazardous waste, segregating it, treating it to Land Disposal Restriction standards, shipping it and processing it. That is the coal-mine-geothermal counterexample again. No buyer purchases an in-place proven cell, so there is no sellable rung.
scored.step_up: My estimates, not sourced. Unproven: a closed cell carries 30-year post-closure care plus CERCLA liability, so its value is negative, roughly -$1M to -$10M. Proven: Ni-Mo/Co-Mo hydroprocessing catalyst is worth about $500-3,000/t of contained metal, depending on the Mo price (~$20/lb). It is diluted in mixed sludge, soil and debris. Excavation, hazardous handling and transport cost about $150-400/t before any metal processing. Net value of a proven cell is roughly break-even to modestly positive, not $1-10M per hit. Starting from negative, the move is "less negative," far below 10^3x. Pt/Re/Pd reforming catalysts (0.3-0.6 wt% Pt) were almost always reclaimed under refiner metal-management or leasing accounts, so the PGM upside rarely sits in landfills.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Proving cost $20-50k per cell for test pits, XRF and assay (the candidate's figure; plausible). My estimate is that the base hit rate for "this refinery cell contains catalyst" is fairly high, perhaps 30-60%, because refineries landfilled spent hydrotreating catalyst on site routinely before EPA listed it as K171/K172 hazardous waste in 1998. The rate of hits that are economic after excavation is very low, but ML cannot fix that, because it is set by grade and treatment cost, not by locating the material. The lever is capped at about 1/0.4, roughly 2-3x, not 10x. Proving is also not the expensive step.
scored.data: The data is partly legible, partly absent. The federal manifest system only started in 1980. From then on, RCRAInfo, Biennial Reports and closure plans record waste codes and quantities in structured fields, so for post-1980 disposal the outcome is already summarised in a legible field. Before 1980 the records are mostly missing, not just hard to read. Oil & Gas Journal unit inventories tell you catalyst throughput, not where the spent catalyst went. That is a weak illegible-signal edge.
scored.right_bought: No real purchase market. Closed RCRA cells sit with the refiner (ExxonMobil, Chevron, Marathon etc.) under post-closure permits. A refiner keeps its CERCLA liability even if it transfers title, and a buyer becomes a potentially responsible party on top. The refiner is not an owner who cannot read the data: it holds the manifests and knows what it buried. Re-excavating creates newly generated hazardous waste, which triggers permit modification and corrective action. A $1 transfer is legally possible, but it means paying to take on liability. You cannot buy a cheap option on upside here.
scored.buyer: For recovered Ni/Mo/Co/V: spent-catalyst reclaimers such as Gulf Chemical & Metallurgical/Eurecat, Moxba, AMG Vanadium and Treibacher. For any PGM: Johnson Matthey, Heraeus, Umicore and BASF. Those buyers want processed concentrate, not a proven cell in the ground. No capitalised buyer pays a step-up for an in-situ proven landfill cell.
scored.ladder: The ladder exists in principle: cell rights, then excavation and remediation, then pyro/hydromet catalyst reclamation, then metals trading and supply to catalyst makers. Spent-catalyst recycling is a niche market, likely low single-digit $B a year (my estimate), with established reclaimers. It is not a path to a trillion-dollar company.
scored.fatal_flaw: The valuable PGM catalysts were reclaimed, not buried. What sits in refinery landfills is low-grade Ni-Mo-Co diluted in hazardous mixed waste. Excavating and treating it costs about as much as the metal is worth or more. The cell cannot be bought as a cheap right without inheriting CERCLA and RCRA post-closure liability. So discovery is not the bottleneck and there is no 10^3-10^4 step-up.
scored.one_line_reason: Fails the frame test, like coal-mine geothermal. Finding the catalyst is easy and already partly recorded in RCRA manifests. Excavation, hazardous treatment and inherited liability are most of the cost. What is buried is low-value Ni-Mo-Co, not PGM, so the step-up is near break-even from a negative start.

scored.name: Sweeps: precious-metal recovery from decommissioned industrial buildings
scored.one_line: ML over TRI, plating permits, directories and Sanborn maps ranks demolition-bound plating, jewelry, dental, mint and contact plants holding Au/Ag/PGM in floors, drains and ducts; buy salvage rights; swab-assay; sell to refiners.
scored.unproven_right: Salvage/demolition rights or the building at negative value.
scored.proving_step: Floor, drain-trap and duct swabs plus fire assay ($5-15k).
scored.proven_buyer: Heraeus, Sabin, Metalor, Asahi Refining.
scored.public_data: EPA TRI, state electroplating and discharge permits, Sanborn maps, city directories and Thomas Register, demolition permits.
scored.frame: The rung is buying salvage rights to an industrial building and selling its precious-metal residues to a refiner. Inside that rung, finding the site is maybe 10-20% of the work (my estimate). The other 80-90% is physical recovery: tearing out floorboards, pulling drain traps and sewer laterals, scraping ducts, burning carpet and wood, and handling cyanide, chromium and nickel plating sludge as RCRA hazardous waste before anything goes to a refiner. Swabbing tells you a building has metal in it, but swabs are not the saleable product. Refiners pay on recovered, assayed lots, so the hard physical step cannot be skipped. This is the coal-mine geothermal pattern: recovering the metal is harder than finding the building.
scored.step_up: I have no sourced numbers, because the shared search budget ran out before my first query and no search ran. Estimates: salvage rights to a demolition-bound plating or jewelry building cost roughly $0 to slightly negative. A large old jewelry or dental plant might recover maybe $20k-$500k of Au/Ag/PGM, and a small plating shop maybe $1k-$30k. After paying for demolition labour, hazmat disposal and refiner charges (a few percent of value plus fees), net value is maybe 2-10x what was spent on the right and the swab. A swab hit does not make the right itself worth 10^3x more, because no market trades swab-proven salvage rights. The candidate's own '10-1000x' is measured against a near-zero base, which inflates it.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Unsourced estimate: a swab and fire-assay campaign costs $5-15k per the candidate, but $1-3k per site is more realistic (fire assay is roughly $30-80 per sample). The base hit rate for 'measurable precious metal' at a known former plating, jewelry or dental site is probably high, maybe 50%+, because the use type itself is the signal. With a hit rate that high, the 1/hit-rate cap limits ML to about 2x, nowhere near 10x. The real uncertainty is how much metal is there and what recovery costs, not whether metal is present.
scored.data: The industry history is in illegible sources: Sanborn maps, city directories, the Thomas Register and old plating permits. But the outcome is effectively written into a legible field: the business type, plus TRI and NPDES/pretreatment records for metal discharges. The owners can read it too. Sweeps and plant-decommissioning recovery are standard practice in jewelry and dental manufacturing; refiners like Hoover & Strong, Garfield, Sabin and Metalor have offered plant-cleanout and carpet/floor recovery for decades (from my knowledge; not verified this run). Owners therefore know about the metal, and a plant that closes usually gets cleaned out by its own refiner before the building is sold. The ML edge over a lookup by SIC code (3911 jewelry, 3471 plating, 3843 dental) is small.
scored.right_bought: Salvage rights can be bought by negotiating with building owners or demolition contractors, so the right is bought, not claimed first-come. But the owners are not unable to read the data. And buying the building or taking control of plating sites exposes the buyer to CERCLA and RCRA owner/operator liability for cyanide, chromium and nickel contamination, which can cost far more than the metal is worth. That is the same failure as the earlier powered-brownfields candidate, where cleanup cost 10x the uplift.
scored.buyer: The refiners named in the candidate (Heraeus, Sabin, Metalor, Asahi, plus Hoover & Strong and Garfield) are well capitalised and buy any assayed precious-metal lot. But they buy recovered material, not proven rights. They are also direct competitors, because they already run plant-decommissioning recovery for their own customers.
scored.ladder: Weak. The rungs above are refining, which is consolidated, low-margin and capital-heavy, and general urban mining or e-waste recovery. The supply of decommissioned US jewelry, plating and dental plants is finite and shrinking, so the total addressable market is probably tens of millions of dollars a year (estimate). There is no clear path to a very large company.
scored.fatal_flaw: There is no information asymmetry and discovery is not the bottleneck. Owners and their refiners already know metal sits in the floors, drains and ducts and routinely harvest it at closure. What remains is labour- and hazmat-heavy physical recovery with environmental liability attached, so the 95-5 discovery frame does not exist.
scored.one_line_reason: This fails the core rubric. The work is physical recovery, not discovery. The business type already identifies the sites, and refiners already sweep them. Value steps up maybe 2-10x, not 10^4, and plating-site liability can wipe out the uplift.
sources: No web searches ran: the shared 200-call per-turn search budget was used up before this candidate's first query. Every number is the evaluator's estimate from prior knowledge.
Prior knowledge (not verified this run): Hoover & Strong, Garfield Refining, Sabin, Metalor and similar refiners advertise plant-cleanout and sweeps recovery for jewelry and dental manufacturers.
Prior knowledge: plating wastes (F006 sludge, cyanide) are RCRA-listed hazardous wastes, and CERCLA owner/operator liability can attach to whoever acquires a contaminated site.

scored.name: Orphan Source Capital: disused Am-241, Cf-252 and Pu-Be sources
scored.one_line: Take title at negative cost to disused neutron and gauge sources found via licence records; leak-test, recertify and resell into a constrained Am-241/Cf-252 market.
scored.unproven_right: Sources held as $2-50k disposal liabilities.
scored.proving_step: Leak test, activity verification, re-encapsulation, licensed transfer.
scored.proven_buyer: QSA Global, Eckert & Ziegler, Troxler/InstroTek, ESA/NNL Am-241 RPS, Cf-252 users.
scored.public_data: NRC/agreement-state GL registrations and ADAMS files, NSTS summary stats, OSRP reports, bankruptcy dockets.
scored.frame: The rung would be 'take title to a disused sealed source and recertify it for resale'. Inside that rung, discovery (finding the source) is maybe 10-20% of the work (my estimate). The other 80%+ is physical and regulatory: an NRC/agreement-state specific licence to possess and distribute, Type A/B shipping, leak testing, and re-encapsulation in a licensed hot cell for anything outside spec. Only a few firms worldwide can do the re-encapsulation (QSA Global, Eckert & Ziegler, and DOE/LANL for Pu-Be). This is the geothermal-in-coal-mines pattern again: the hard part is the bespoke licensed handling, not the finding.
scored.step_up: Rough step-up, all my estimates (I could not verify any of them, see the data field): from about -$2k to -$10k (commercial disposal of an Am-Be gauge source, worse for greater-than-Class-C sources) up to about +$0.5k to $5k resale for a recertified 10-50 mCi Am-Be source. A typical Troxler source is about 40 mCi Am-241, roughly 12 mg of Am. That is a swing of a few thousand dollars per source, i.e. 3-30x at best on small dollars, not 10^3-10^4. The Cf-252 sub-thesis is weaker: Cf-252 has a 2.65-year half-life, so a disused source is mostly decayed and is worth nothing. The Pu-Be sub-thesis is worse: the plutonium is DOE/NNSA-controlled material, which goes back through the Off-Site Source Recovery Program (OSRP) and is not freely resaleable.
scored.hit_rate_capex: The leak and activity tests are cheap (my estimate: about $50-300 per wipe test) and pass most of the time. The base 'hit rate' is near 100% because the source's identity and activity are already known from its registration. So there is no low base rate for ML to improve; the lever is capped near 1x. The real costs are re-encapsulation (my estimate: $5k-50k+ per hot-cell campaign), licensing and transport, and ML does not reduce those.
scored.data: The source inventory is already legible. NRC general-licence device registrations record the device, the isotope and the activity. The National Source Tracking System (NSTS) tracks Category 1-2 sources by serial number. OSRP keeps registries of disused sources and actively solicits them. Agreement-state licence databases list the possessors. So the outcome (what the source is, where it is, how active it is) is already summarised in structured fields, which kills the ML edge. The rights are cheap (owners pay to get rid of sources), but the owners know exactly what they hold because the registration tells them. They are not mispricing an illegible asset; the liability is real. Caveat: my web search budget was exhausted before I could run any searches, so no figure here was checked against a source.
scored.right_bought: Yes, title to these sources can be taken at negative cost: owners pay to be rid of them. But OSRP (DOE/LANL) collects many qualifying Am-241, Pu-Be and Cf-252 sources for free or at subsidised cost, which caps the negative price the company can capture. Sealed-source manufacturers (QSA Global, Eckert & Ziegler) and gauge makers (Troxler) already run take-back and recycling for their own sources.
scored.buyer: Sealed-source manufacturers and gauge makers: QSA Global, Eckert & Ziegler, Troxler, InstroTek. They are capitalised, but each buys only small volumes, and some recover Am-241 themselves. The ESA/NNL Am-241 radioisotope power programme gets its americium from UK civil plutonium stockpiles, not from scavenged gauge sources. On-spec Cf-252 comes from ORNL's HFIR reactor; nobody buys decayed sources.
scored.ladder: Climbing would mean moving from source recovery to re-encapsulation to manufacturing sources to producing the isotopes. Production needs reactor or reprocessing access (Mayak, HFIR, NNL), which is state-controlled. The market is small (my estimate: global sealed neutron sources are a market in the low hundreds of millions of dollars). There is no plausible trillion-dollar path.
scored.fatal_flaw: There is no illegible discovery problem. Every disused source is already registered by isotope, activity and holder in NRC GL registrations, NSTS and state licence records, and OSRP already collects many of them for free. The value-adding step is licensed hot-cell and regulatory handling, not finding. That handling caps a step-up of a few thousand dollars per source.
scored.one_line_reason: Discovery is trivial because the sources are registered, while licensed handling dominates the cost. The step-up is about 3-30x on a few thousand dollars, the hit rate is near 100% (so there is no ML lever), and OSRP and the manufacturers already recover these sources.

scored.name: Warbird Registry / Provenance Air: wartime-identity proof for airframe wrecks
scored.one_line: Buy unidentified WWII wrecks, data plates and parts lots cheaply; ML over scanned aircraft record cards, MACRs and loss reports proves combat identity; sell provenanced projects to collectors and museums.
scored.unproven_right: Title to anonymous wrecks or parts lots (~$1-50k) or recovery rights from landowners.
scored.proving_step: OCR matching of constructor numbers to record cards and casualty reports, physical plate inspection; buyer restores.
scored.proven_buyer: Warbird restorers and collectors (Flying Heritage, Collings, CAF), museums; provenanced projects $0.5-5M+.
scored.public_data: AFHRA/NASM Individual Aircraft Record Cards, NARA MACRs (Fold3), RAF Form 78/1180 cards, Navy history cards, Joe Baugher serials.
scored.rough_step_up: ~10-1,000x on parts; restoration is bespoke, small market.
scored.frame: Rung: own an unidentified wreck or parts lot and sell it once its identity is proven. Discovery is maybe 5-15% of the work that sets the value (my estimate). What buyers pay for is a restorable or restored airframe. A P-40 or P-51 restoration costs about $1-3M+ (estimate, consistent with restored P-40s at ~$1.15M and two P-40N projects with restored fuselages listed at $895k). That is bespoke work, so this fails the same way the geothermal-in-coal-mines counter-example does. The physical step is not trivial, and the buyer prices the metal and the work, not the ID.
scored.step_up: An identity premium exists but it is small. Example: two P-40N-5 combat-veteran projects (one with 3 kill flags) at a combined $895k (Courtesy Aircraft, 2022). That fits the market rate for P-40 projects of that completeness, so I see no 10^3 jump from proven combat identity. Loose data plates sell for a few hundred dollars generic versus about $1,000 with a notable history (WIX, 2005 anecdote), about 2-5x. Identity on a whole wreck probably adds 1.2-3x (estimate). Most of the value comes from the type and the amount of airframe surviving, both of which are visible before any research.
scored.hit_rate_capex: The proving step is cheap and mostly succeeds already. Researchers, Pacific Wrecks, WIX members and the Joe Baugher serial lists identify most significant wrecks by hand, at an estimated $1-10k of archive time each. Wrecks that can't be identified usually lack plates or stampings, and ML over record cards can't fix missing physical evidence. Base hit rate is high (estimate >50% for intact types), so the 1/hit-rate lever is under 2x. Capex is dominated by recovery and restoration, which ML does not touch.
scored.data: The records are public: IARCs, MACRs on Fold3, RAF Form 78s. The outcome is already largely summarised in legible form, because the Baugher serial lists and Pacific Wrecks give per-serial fates. An obsessive enthusiast community reads exactly this data. The rights side is also weak. Wrecks in the field often fall under sovereign or foreign-government rights (the US Navy keeps title to its wrecks, and PNG/Russia export controls apply), and plate stripping triggers theft and identity disputes (e.g. the N251L vs N98CF P-51 dispute). Owners of anonymous lots are usually the same enthusiasts who can read the records.
scored.right_bought: Sometimes, from landowners or estates for ~$1-50k. However, the sellers who matter are dealers and restorers who know the data. Military wrecks are often not legally purchasable at all (US Navy sunken military craft rules, foreign heritage laws).
scored.buyer: Capitalised but tiny: a few dozen collectors and museums (Flying Heritage, Collings, CAF, Fagen). Estimated tens of warbird project trades per year globally, worth a total of tens of millions of dollars.
scored.ladder: Recovery, then restoration, then operating or selling flyable warbirds. Every rung above is bespoke craft with a total addressable market of maybe $100-300M/yr (estimate). There is no trillion-dollar or even billion-dollar path.
scored.fatal_flaw: This is the geothermal-in-coal-mines failure. Buyers pay for the bespoke $1-3M restoration and for the physical airframe, not for the proof of identity. Identity adds only about 1.2-3x, and an obsessive enthusiast community has already worked it out and published it in legible serial databases. The market is also tiny.
scored.one_line_reason: Proving identity is a small, already-crowdsourced part of a bespoke restoration business with a small premium and a tiny market, so it fails C1, C2 and C5.

scored.name: Provenance Wine Vault: estate cellars proven via merchant and château records
scored.one_line: Buy undocumented old cellars from estates at discount; OCR over scanned merchant invoices, import records and release ledgers establishes custody; authenticate and resell at auction.
scored.unproven_right: Bulk cellar contents at unknown-provenance discounts.
scored.proving_step: Document matching plus physical bottle authentication.
scored.proven_buyer: Acker, Zachys, Sotheby's Wine, HK collectors.
scored.public_data: Partial Berry Bros/J&B archives, customs/import records, château label references, auction price archives.
scored.frame: The rung would be: buy an estate cellar, prove its custody, resell at auction. Discovery is only about 20-40% of the work in that rung (my estimate). Most of the cost is physical and per bottle: expert inspection, lab tests on questionable bottles, condition grading (fill level, labels, capsules), insured transport, storage and cataloguing. Documents can show custody, but they cannot show storage condition or rule out a refilled bottle, so the physical step is never abstracted away. The buyers (Acker, Zachys, Sotheby's Wine, HK collectors) are well capitalised, but they buy bottles, not proof.
scored.step_up: I found no matched-lot study of ex-cellar versus unknown-provenance prices. My estimate is that unknown-provenance lots of the same wine sell at a 20-50% discount, so proving provenance is worth about 1.25-2x. The upside is not 10^3. Comparison points: auction prices for Lafite ran 102-294% above trade prices (Decanter), which is an auction-versus-trade gap, not a provenance effect. A Christie's 1973 Stag's Leap lot hammered at $22,500, 275% over its high estimate, but that is a single outlier. The buyer's premium of about 20-27.5% eats a large share of the uplift. The asset never starts near zero: an old Bordeaux cellar already has a liquid market value before it is proven.
scored.hit_rate_capex: The base hit rate is high, not low. My estimate is that the large majority of genuine old estate cellars authenticate as authentic. The real variable is condition, which ML on documents cannot change. Cost per proving attempt: Chai Vault priced bottle authentication at $700 per bottle or $1,200 per inspection and report (Decanter, 2015). Bill Koch spends about $800 per bottle on expert inspection plus lab tests (Punch). The cost scales with bottle count, so ML can only remove the archive-research part. That makes the lever about 1.2-2x, nowhere near 10x, and with a high base hit rate the 1/hit-rate cap is also near 1.
scored.data: The data is mostly private, not public. Berry Bros & Rudd and Justerini & Brooks ledgers are private company archives. Château release records belong to the châteaux. Customs and import records are not public at bottle or lot level. Auction price archives (Wine-Searcher, WineAuctionPrices, Liv-ex) are already legible and commercial. An auction house's catalogue already states the outcome in a legible field ('ex-château', 'from the cellar of', 'OWC').
scored.right_bought: Cellars can be bought, but there is little discount to capture. Estates and heirs usually go straight to the auction houses, which do valuation and provenance research free as part of consignment. So the seller already has incumbents who can read the data for them, and you would be bidding against consignment terms (sellers' commissions are often 0-10%), not buying at $1/ha-style prices.
scored.buyer: Acker, Zachys, Sotheby's Wine, Christie's, Hart Davis Hart, Baghera, HK and Asian collectors, and Liv-ex merchants. They are capitalised and liquid, but they pay for bottles, at a modest premium for documented provenance.
scored.ladder: The ladder is thin. The rungs above would be merchant or négociant, then storage and bonded warehousing, then perhaps owning an estate or label. These are niche, low-growth and reputation-bound. The global fine-wine secondary market is only about $5-10B a year (my estimate), so there is no path to a trillion-dollar company.
scored.fatal_flaw: No 10^3 step-up. A cellar of unknown provenance already sells at roughly 50-80% of the proven price (my estimate), and proof costs $700-1,200 per bottle in physical inspection that ML cannot remove. Auction houses already do the provenance research free when they take a cellar on consignment.
scored.one_line_reason: This is a low-multiple wine-arbitrage service. Proving provenance is worth about 1.25-2x, costs hundreds of dollars per bottle in physical work, uses mostly private archives, and runs into auction houses that already do provenance checks for consignors, so it fails C1-C4.

scored.name: Relight: dark but alive TV licences for ATSC 3.0 datacasting
scored.one_line: Buy silent or distressed TV licences still alive under the 312(g) rule in top markets, relight cheaply and lease the channel to ATSC 3.0 datacasters.
scored.unproven_right: Dark stations sold near zero by owners facing licence loss.
scored.proving_step: ML over silent-STA filings and contours; relight via transmitter-as-a-service before deadline.
scored.proven_buyer: Sinclair/Edge Networks, Pearl TV members, datacasters.
scored.public_data: FCC LMS silent STA and licence records, ECFS, DMA/contour data.
scored.frame: The rung would be: buy a silent licence, relight it before the 12-month deadline in 47 USC 312(g), then lease or sell it. Almost none of the work in that rung is discovery. Finding the stations takes about 5% (my estimate), because LMS already marks every station on a silent STA. The other ~95% is physical and regulatory work: transmitter, tower or site lease, power, getting the FCC to approve the transfer before the licence dies, and then finding a datacasting tenant. That is the inverse of Terranox. It looks like the coal-mine geothermal counter-example: getting the licence back on air is harder than finding it.
scored.step_up: No live numbers: the shared web-search budget was used up before this agent ran, so every figure here is my estimate from memory. Small or mid-market full-power stations normally trade for low single-digit $M. LPTV licences trade for about $50k-$1M. A distressed silent station in a top market might sell at a 30-70% discount to a lit one. After relighting, the value rises by about 1.5-5x, and the candidate's own ~3-20x is the optimistic end. ATSC 3.0 datacasting lease income is small and unproven: Edge Networks and Pearl members mostly use spectrum they already own. That is 10^0-10^1, nowhere near 10^3-10^4. The asset never starts near zero, because a top-market licence is priced off spectrum value (2017 incentive auction clearing prices were tens of $M in large markets, from memory).
scored.hit_rate_capex: There is no low-hit-rate proving step for ML to improve. Relighting is a deterministic engineering job that almost always works if funded: estimated $150k-$1.5M for a full-power transmitter, antenna, site and installation, or about $20k-$150k for LPTV (my estimates; not checked because the search budget was gone). The uncertainty is about the market (will a datacaster pay a lease?) and about regulation (FCC reinstatement or transfer timing). Neither is a discovery problem. The lever, capped at 1/base hit rate, is about 1x.
scored.data: The data is public and already legible. FCC LMS records silent STAs, silent and resumed-operations notices, and licence status as explicit structured fields, and it publishes contours and DMA assignments. The outcome (silent, deadline date) is written into a status field, which is exactly the failure mode the rubric warns about. Broadcast brokers such as Kalil and Media Services Group, and spectrum aggregators (for example the LPTV aggregators active before the 2017 auction), already watch these filings. Buying the right is plausible because distressed owners do sell. But those owners can read their own status, and the 312(g) deadline is no secret, so there is little information asymmetry to buy into.
scored.right_bought: Yes. The licence is bought from its current holder through an FCC assignment application (Form 314/345). That takes time (weeks to months for FCC consent) and can run past the 312(g) deadline. It is a real purchased right, but it is not cheap because of an illegibility gap.
scored.buyer: The pool is thin. Sinclair/Edge Networks, Pearl TV members and datacasting startups would be the buyers, but most of them use their own owned spectrum, and ATSC 3.0 rollout depends on an FCC transition order and consumer receivers. The other exit is selling to a station group or a religious or ethnic broadcaster at an ordinary market price.
scored.ladder: Silent licence, then relit station, then a regional ATSC 3.0 datacasting network, then a national broadcast-data utility (single-frequency networks, broadcast positioning as a GPS backup, IoT datacast). The higher rungs exist on paper, but the industry is in secular decline, consolidated, heavily regulated, and the spectrum is capped by FCC ownership rules. It is not a trillion-dollar ladder.
scored.fatal_flaw: There is no discovery problem. Silent status and the 312(g) deadline are legible fields in FCC LMS. The value comes from capex-heavy relighting and from a thin, unproven datacasting lease market, so the step-up is about 2-5x, not 10^4. ML adds nothing over a database query.
scored.one_line_reason: Finding dark licences is a lookup of FCC status fields. The work and the risk are in relighting and in demand, and the uplift is about 2-5x, so this fails C1-C4.

FCC LMS / CDBS public licence and silent STA records (structured status fields, from memory)

scored.name: Buildout Rescue: unbuilt auction licences near forfeiture
scored.one_line: Buy auction-won licences from small winners about to miss build-out deadlines, meet substantial-service with cheap fixed-wireless, sell to carriers.
scored.unproven_right: Licence facing automatic termination at distress pricing.
scored.proving_step: Minimal deployment plus accepted construction notification; ML picks carrier-wanted licences.
scored.proven_buyer: T-Mobile, Verizon, AT&T, cable MVNOs, regionals.
scored.public_data: FCC ULS build-out deadlines, National Broadband Map, auction results.
scored.frame: The rung is "take over a licence with a build-out deadline coming up, meet the construction requirement, then sell it to a carrier". Discovery inside that rung is about 10-20% of the work (my estimate). Finding the licences is a database query: the FCC's ULS licence database lists every call sign, licensee, interim and final construction deadline, and whether construction was filed. Picking the ones carriers want is mostly common sense from carrier spectrum holdings plus the National Broadband Map. The other 80%+ is physical and regulatory. The construction requirements are coverage percentages, not token deployments (from FCC rules as I remember them, not checked this run): 600 MHz and AWS-3 need 40% of population at the interim deadline and 75% at the final one. Auction 108 (2.5 GHz) needs 50% of population in 4 years and 80% in 8. C-band needs 45% (mobile). CBRS priority licences have fixed-use safe harbours based on link counts. On top of that come FCC assignment approval (Form 603), designated-entity unjust-enrichment repayments if the buyer is not a small business, tower leases, backhaul and RF engineering. This is the geothermal-in-a-coal-mine pattern: the build is harder than the find.
scored.step_up: About 2-5x, and that is my estimate; I found no sourced transaction prices because the web search budget ran out before any search returned. Reasoning: a near-forfeiture licence sells at a distress discount, maybe 20-50% of auction-clearing value. Auction 108 raised about $428M for roughly 7,900 licences (memory, unverified), so many rural licences cleared for tens of thousands of dollars. A built-out licence trades near market $/MHz-pop, which is not orders of magnitude more. The upside is capped hard because the carrier can just wait. A licence that misses its deadline terminates automatically (47 CFR 1.946(c)) and goes back to FCC inventory for re-auction, where the carrier can bid without paying for anyone's build. The candidate's own 3-30x guess looks generous. Nowhere near 10^3-10^4.
scored.hit_rate_capex: There is no low base hit rate to improve. Whether a build-out succeeds is a matter of engineering and money, not chance. If you spend enough on sites to cover 40-50% of the licence area's population, it passes. Cost per attempt (estimate): roughly $50k-$300k per macro or fixed-wireless site including lease, radio and backhaul. A rural county or partial economic area needing 50% population coverage could take several to dozens of sites, so about $0.3M-$5M per licence, likely more than the licence is worth. ML might rank which licences carriers want, but that only saves a little diligence cost. It does not buy 10x more attempts at a big jump. The lever is roughly 1x.
scored.data: Everything that matters is already in legible, structured fields. ULS has the construction deadline, the construction-notification status, the licensee name and contact, and any extension or waiver requests in machine-readable form. Auction results are public spreadsheets, and the National Broadband Map is a structured dataset. This is the failure the earlier hunts kept finding: the regulator writes the answer into a status field, so there is no illegible signal for ML to extract. Incumbent spectrum brokers and carrier spectrum teams already watch these deadlines.
scored.right_bought: Yes, the licence can be bought from distressed small winners, but only through an FCC-approved assignment. That takes weeks to months, does not extend the deadline, and may trigger designated-entity unjust-enrichment repayment of the bidding credit if the assignee or eventual buyer is not a small business. Every seller knows exactly when its deadline is, because the FCC sends notices. The information gap between buyer and seller is small. The discount comes from distress, not ignorance.
scored.buyer: T-Mobile, Verizon, AT&T, UScellular's successors, cable MVNOs (Comcast, Charter) and regional and rural carriers. They have the money, but their walk-away option is better than paying a premium: let the licence lapse and pick it up in a re-auction, or lease the spectrum. T-Mobile already bought most of the 2.5 GHz inventory directly.
scored.ladder: Plausible but conventional: a portfolio of built-out licences, then a neutral-host or fixed-wireless operator, then a regional carrier. Spectrum aggregators that took this route (NextWave, Dish's spectrum roll-up, Columbia Capital-type funds) show the ladder exists. They also show it is capital-intensive and gated by regulation, and that the build-out obligation is what crushed them (Dish's own build-out struggles). Each step up is more construction, not more discovery.
scored.fatal_flaw: The proving step is physical construction (40-80% population coverage under FCC rules), not discovery. The opportunity is fully legible in ULS status fields. And carriers can wait for the licence to terminate and buy it at re-auction, which caps any step-up at a low multiple.
scored.one_line_reason: This fails the core test the same way geothermal in coal mines does: building out is harder than finding the licence, the data is already legible, and the step-up is roughly 2-5x, not 10^4.

scored.name: ReAuction Picker: FCC defaulted-licence inventory
scored.one_line: Bid in thin re-auctions for leftover blocks ML flags as must-have fill for a specific carrier, then sell to that carrier.
scored.unproven_right: Licence won near reserve in a thin re-auction.
scored.proving_step: ML over coverage maps and holdings; winning the licence.
scored.proven_buyer: T-Mobile, AT&T, Verizon, regionals.
scored.public_data: FCC auction inventory/results, ULS, coverage maps, ASR.
scored.frame: The rung would be "own a defaulted spectrum licence and resell it to the carrier it completes". There is almost no discovery inside it. Which blocks a carrier needs is plain from ULS holdings and published coverage maps, and every carrier's spectrum team and the outside consultants (e.g. Allnet Insights, Spectrum Financial Partners) already model it. My estimate is that discovery is under 10% of the work. Most of the work is putting up capital, qualifying to bid (short-form, upfront payment), working through FCC anti-collusion and quiet-period rules, then the 6-18 months of transfer approval and holding cost. The licence is a legal right, so there is no physical step. But the 'proving' is just winning an auction against the same carriers you want to sell to. That is a pricing game, not discovery.
scored.step_up: From memory, not freshly sourced: Auction 97 (AWS-3, 2015) cleared about $2.7/MHz-pop on average for $44.9B gross. Later secondary deals for AWS and mid-band spectrum have mostly traded at roughly 0.8-2x the auction-implied $/MHz-pop. A re-auction is thin only if the carriers who need the block stay out. When they do stay out, the block wasn't must-have. When they don't, the price clears at roughly what they'd pay you later. My estimate of the realistic step-up from winning near reserve to selling to a carrier is 1-3x, with a fat left tail when the price clears high or the carrier doesn't buy. That is not 10^3. The candidate's own ~2-10x figure is optimistic.
scored.hit_rate_capex: There is no low base hit rate to improve. Winning is a matter of bidding more, so the 'hit rate' is set by your price, not by skill at finding things. The cost per attempt is the full licence price plus an upfront deposit, typically millions to hundreds of millions per block. Unlike a ~$100k-1M exploratory drill, that capital isn't spent and gone; it is locked in an asset at roughly market price. ML cannot cut the cost of an attempt 10x. At most it sharpens bid shading a little. The 1/base-hit-rate cap is about 1x. These are estimates.
scored.data: Everything is legible and structured. The FCC Public Reporting System publishes round-by-round bids and results, ULS holds licence holdings and buildout status as fields, coverage maps are published (BDC and carrier maps), and ASR tower data is a database. The 'outcome' (who holds what, what is in re-auction inventory and why) is already written into status fields: the defaulted inventory lists and the reasons for default are public notices. The right is bought, but at an open auction whose price is set by the end buyers themselves. You are not buying from an owner who can't read the data. The FCC is the seller and the carriers are your fellow bidders. There is no information asymmetry to exploit.
scored.right_bought: You buy it at the FCC re-auction (e.g. the planned Auction 113 re-offering of about 200 AWS-3 licences defaulted by DISH-affiliated designated entities after Auction 97). It is not first-come. It costs a refundable upfront payment and then the winning bid. The price is set competitively, with carriers in the room. It is not a cheap purchase from an uninformed owner.
scored.buyer: T-Mobile, AT&T, Verizon, UScellular successors and regionals do have the capital. But they bid in the same re-auctions directly, so the middleman captures almost nothing. Speculators who won and resold in past re-auctions (e.g. Auction 58 in 2005, PCS re-auction of NextWave/DE defaults, about $2.04B, mostly won by Cingular and Verizon) were rare and made thin margins.
scored.ladder: There is a weak ladder. A spectrum holdco could aggregate into a spectrum portfolio, then lease it, then build a neutral-host or private network, then become a regional carrier. Each rung up is capital-heavy, and none of them is driven by discovery. It does not lead naturally to a very large company the way the mineral-right-to-mine path does. Holding spectrum to sell to carriers is a known, crowded business (e.g. NextWave, Straight Path, Columbia Capital vehicles), and it is driven by regulatory arbitrage, not information.
scored.fatal_flaw: The end buyer is a bidder in the same auction, and every input (inventory, holdings, coverage, bids) is legible structured FCC data. There is no illegible signal and no uninformed seller, so there is nothing to discover and the step-up is about 1-3x, not 10^4. The FCC's anti-collusion and unjust-enrichment rules and the transfer-approval process add cost and delay on top.
scored.one_line_reason: This is spectrum arbitrage against informed carriers who are also bidding, using fully legible FCC data, for at best about 2x. It fails C1, C2 and C3.

scored.name: Conserved Consumptive Use Credits (Colorado River)
scored.one_line: Lease senior basin irrigation rights and ML-certify conserved consumptive use via OpenET for federal and municipal conservation programs.
scored.unproven_right: Fallowing rights leased cheaply from farmers.
scored.proving_step: ML-certified field ET reduction; fallowing or deficit irrigation.
scored.proven_buyer: Reclamation (SCPP, IRA), SNWA, MWD, Arizona ICS buyers.
scored.public_data: OpenET, CDSS/ADWR diversions, Reclamation CU reports, Cropland Data Layer.
scored.frame: The rung is "lease a fallowing right, deliver certified conserved acre-feet to a program buyer." Discovery is close to 0% of the work in this rung. You already know which fields are senior, irrigated and consumptive from CDSS/ADWR diversion records and the Cropland Data Layer. The "proving" step is the farmer choosing not to irrigate, and OpenET-style measurement of that is commodity work. Most of the effort goes into contracting, relationships with irrigation districts and ditch companies, and state-engineer/Reclamation verification. That is the opposite of 95% discovery. It is not a hard exclusion: this is a leased surface-water right, not groundwater exploration.
scored.step_up: From memory (my web search budget was used up, so I could not check these): the Reclamation Lower Basin IRA/SCPP offers in 2022-23 were about $400/AF for a 1-yr commitment, ~$485/AF for 2-yr and ~$518/AF for 3-yr. The Upper Basin SCPP paid roughly $400-$500/AF in 2023-24. Farmers know these posted prices and want most of the payment to lease. My estimate of the farmer's ask is $250-$400/AF, so the step-up from unproven to proven is about 1.2-2x and the margin is thin. Owning the permanent right would cost about $5k-$40k/AF in Colorado/Arizona (estimate), while the annual conservation payment is ~$400-$500/AF, so owning gives no immediate jump either. Nothing goes from near-zero to 10^3. The candidate's own rough figure (~1.5-3x) is right or even generous.
scored.hit_rate_capex: My estimate: once a field is fallowed, the hit rate for producing conserved consumptive use is close to 100%, because ET drops by construction. Each attempt costs roughly lease plus verification, ~$300-$450/AF (estimate). There is no expensive, mostly failing proving step. The lever is capped at 1/base hit rate, which is about 1x, so ML cannot cut discovery capex 10x. Deficit irrigation adds measurement uncertainty, but that is an accounting problem, not discovery.
scored.data: The data is public but already legible. OpenET is a free public field-level ET product. Reclamation and the states already use it, or its constituent models, to verify SCPP conservation. CDSS (HydroBase) and ADWR publish structured diversion records and priority dates. Water rights seniority is a legible field (appropriation date) in state tabulations. The outcome, conserved CU, is literally what Reclamation's CU&L reports and program verification compute. That is the known failure mode: the regulator writes the answer into the field. There is no illegible signal that only ML can extract.
scored.right_bought: The fallowing or lease right can be bought from farmers or districts. But they can read the data (posted program prices, their own diversion records) and often negotiate as blocs through irrigation districts (IID, PVID, Grand Valley, the Colorado River Indian Tribes). Many enroll directly with Reclamation and need no intermediary. There is no information asymmetry to buy cheaply.
scored.buyer: The buyers are capitalised: Reclamation (SCPP; IRA drought funds of about $4B), SNWA, MWD, and Arizona ICS/municipal buyers such as Phoenix and Scottsdale. But prices are posted or negotiated as public program terms, and buyers often contract directly with districts and tribes.
scored.ladder: There is a ladder: water-rights aggregation, then permanent rights ownership, then water banking/ICS storage, then municipal supply contracts, then a regional water utility or water-market operator. It is constrained by anti-speculation law (Colorado's anti-speculation doctrine, beneficial-use requirements, buy-and-dry political backlash, state-engineer review). Incumbents such as Water Asset Management and Vidler/PICO show the ceiling is a few billion dollars, slow and politically capped. It is not a trillion-dollar path.
scored.fatal_flaw: Nothing is discovered. Which fields can conserve water and how much is already known, legible and measured by public tools (OpenET, CDSS, Reclamation CU reports). Fallowing succeeds about 100% of the time. Program prices are posted, so the step-up from lease to sale is about 1.2-2x. ML has no hit-rate lever and no information asymmetry to exploit.
scored.one_line_reason: Fails the rubric. There is no discovery-dominant rung, the step-up is about 1.5x against posted prices, the hit rate is about 100% so there is no ML lever, the outcome is already summarised by public OpenET and Reclamation accounting, and anti-speculation law caps the ladder.

scored.name: Unregistered LCFS / Clean Fuel Credit Origination Rights
scored.one_line: Buy multi-year clean-fuel credit rights from unregistered fleet depots and workplace chargers under CA LCFS, OR CFP, WA CFS, BC LCFS and Canada CFR; register, meter and sell forward.
scored.unproven_right: Long-term assignment from site owners unaware the right exists.
scored.proving_step: ML matching AFDC/NRCan locators and EV tariff filings against registered lists; metering and registration.
scored.proven_buyer: Refiners and importers (Chevron, Phillips 66, Parkland), aggregators.
scored.public_data: CARB LRT-CBTS reports, OR/WA registered lists, AFDC, NRCan, utility EV tariffs.
scored.rough_step_up: ~10-100x on fee; high hit rate, drifts toward service.
scored.frame: The rung is a credit-origination assignment (site owner gives up the LCFS/CFP/CFS/CFR credit rights from charging it already does). There is almost no discovery. Every EV charger that dispenses metered electricity to vehicles is eligible by rule, and the chargers are already listed with locations in AFDC and NRCan. Finding unregistered sites is maybe 10-20% of the work (my estimate). The other 80%+ is sales, contracting, installing or connecting meters, quarterly reporting, verification, and credit trading, which is an ongoing operations business. Buyers (refiners and importers with deficit obligations, plus traders) are well capitalised, but what they buy is credits, which are fungible commodities. They do not buy a proven asset at a premium.
scored.step_up: From memory, not verified (search budget was used up): CA LCFS credits traded about $50-80/t in 2024-25, down from about $200/t in 2020. A light-duty EV charger yields very roughly 0.5-0.8 credits per MWh (EER about 3.4 versus the CI benchmark). A 10-port workplace L2 site (about 50 MWh/yr) therefore makes about $2-4k/yr, and a fleet depot at 1 GWh/yr makes about $30-60k/yr. Unproven price: an assignment costs nothing up front, but hosts expect a revenue share. Aggregators commonly pass 70-90% of credit value to hosts (my estimate, industry norm). The originator's margin is 10-30% of the stream, and any assignment of that stream is priced near its NPV. Value does not jump 10^3-10^4 on a hit. The upside is roughly 1.1-1.5x on the right's value, or about 10x on a near-zero signing fee at best.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Base hit rate is near 100%. Any operating charger qualifies, and the only real failure is a host who declines or already works with an aggregator. A proving attempt is a sales call plus metering, about $500-5,000 per site (my estimate; a revenue-grade meter or a networked-charger data feed is needed). ML has nothing to raise. The lever is capped at 1/base hit rate, about 1x. ML could at most rank leads, which is ordinary sales targeting.
scored.data: The data is public and legible. AFDC and NRCan locators are structured APIs giving location, network, port count and sometimes ownership. CARB's LRT-CBTS publishes credit totals by fuel and aggregate generation, and there are registered-entity lists, so a registered or unregistered status is close to a legible field. Networked chargers (ChargePoint, Enel X, etc.) often already offer bundled LCFS programs, so many 'unaware' hosts are in fact enrolled through their network provider. Rights are not bought cheaply from owners who cannot read data. The FSE owner is the default credit generator by regulation, and assignment needs only a designation, so competitors can sign the same host at any time. Nothing is locked in first-come or by a purchase.
scored.right_bought: A multi-year credit-generation designation or assignment from the charging site owner, paid as a revenue share, typically 70-90% of credit proceeds to the host (estimate). There is no upfront purchase at a discount. The right is a cash-flow stream the host can see once told about it, and it can be re-designated when the contract ends.
scored.buyer: Obligated parties with deficits (Chevron, Phillips 66, Marathon, Parkland, Valero, Imperial) and credit brokers or traders (Element Markets, 3Degrees, Anew Climate). They buy credits at market price as a commodity, not proven rights at a premium.
scored.ladder: There are possible rungs above: owning or financing the chargers (charging-as-a-service), fleet electrification and depot development, energy management and storage, then renewable power supply and low-CI pathways. Incumbents already occupy each rung (EVgo, Electrify America, Voltera, TeraWatt, Zeem, ChargePoint, BP Pulse). The chain is a capital-intensive infrastructure business with thin margins and policy dependence. It is not a discovery-led monopoly path.
scored.fatal_flaw: There is no discovery problem and no step-up. Every charger qualifies by rule and sits in a public structured locator, so hit rate is near 100% and ML adds nothing. The right is a visible commodity cash flow that hosts keep 70-90% of under competitive aggregator bidding. This is a crowded service and brokerage business (ChargePoint, Enel X, Anew, Element Markets, 3Degrees, Nxu-type aggregators), which falls under the 'sell a service to incumbents' pattern. Its value also rests on volatile, policy-set credit prices.
scored.one_line_reason: The physical and operational work (metering, registration, reporting) is most of the job and finding sites is trivial. The step-up is about 1.1-1.5x on a competitively priced revenue share, not 10^3-10^4, and a near-100% base hit rate leaves ML no lever.

scored.name: Lapsed-Beneficiary Annuity and Demutualization Recovery
scored.one_line: Buy heirs' unknown entitlements to demutualization shares, unclaimed annuities and paid-up policies and claim them.
scored.unproven_right: Heirs' contingent entitlements.
scored.proving_step: Match deceased policyholders to distribution lists; prove heirship.
scored.proven_buyer: MetLife, Prudential, state UP programs.
scored.public_data: NAIC policy locator, UP databases, DMF (limited), probate, demutualization plans.
scored.frame: Rung: acquire (or contract a contingency share of) an heir's claim to unclaimed demutualization shares, annuities or policy proceeds, then prove heirship and file the claim. Discovery (matching the decedent to the holder or list and building the family tree) is about 60-70% of the work. The rest is legal: probate or small-estate affidavits, notarised heirship documents and state claim processing. That work is not trivial, and much of it repeats for every claim. The "buyer" is not a capitalised buyer paying a premium. The insurer or state program just pays out the face value it already owes.
scored.step_up: From my own knowledge, because the web search budget ran out before any search ran, so none of these numbers is sourced: the unproven right costs about $0 upfront, since heir hunters sign contingency agreements. The proven value is the face amount of the claim, which is usually a few hundred dollars to tens of thousands. The company's own capture is set by finder-fee caps: about 10% in CA and TX, about 15% in NY and up to about 20% in FL. Several states also void finder agreements made within 24 months of the property being reported. Where a claim is bought outright, the discount to face is maybe 20-60% (my estimate). That means the real multiple on capital is about 1.5-5x, not 10^3. Even the candidate's own 10-100x figure measures the fee against near-zero cost, not an asset revaluation.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Estimate only, not sourced: an attempt costs about $50-500 in genealogy and records research plus $500-5,000 in legal and probate work on hits. Once the name is already on a state unclaimed-property list, the base hit rate is high, maybe 30-70%, because the listing itself shows the money exists. That caps the ML lever at about 1.5-3x, not 10x. ML would mainly speed up genealogy, which incumbents already do with Ancestry or LexisNexis tooling.
scored.data: The outcome is already in legible public fields. State unclaimed-property databases (MissingMoney.com) list owner name, holder (for example MetLife) and often an amount band. Starting in about 2011, multistate audits forced insurers to cross-match policies against the SSA Death Master File. From memory, unverified because no search ran, regulators reported about $7B+ paid to beneficiaries, and the NAIC Life Insurance Policy Locator reports billions more matched. The DMF settlements removed the illegible-signal edge, which is exactly the failure mode the rubric flags. Buying the rights is also constrained. Many states restrict or void assignment of unclaimed property claims, cap fees and require notarised disclosures. Owners who cannot read the data also get free notices from state programs.
scored.right_bought: Mostly contingency-fee contracts, not owned assets. Outright purchase of heirs' expectancies is possible in some states. It is legally fragile: courts scrutinise unconscionable expectancy assignments, and unclaimed-property statutes restrict assignment and fees. You never own a revalued asset. You collect a capped slice of a fixed sum.
scored.buyer: No capitalised buyer pays a premium for a proven right. MetLife, Prudential and the state programs pay face value they already owe, and only to the rightful claimant. There is no secondary market where a proven claim trades at 10^3x the unproven one.
scored.ladder: Weak or none. The higher rungs would be probate litigation funding, estate administration or a general asset-recovery agency. These are fragmented, regulated and fee-capped service businesses with no path to owning a large physical or financial chain. The pool also shrinks over time: the legacy demutualizations (MetLife 2000, Prudential 2001, John Hancock, Principal) are a one-off stock, and DMF matching now catches new cases automatically.
scored.fatal_flaw: The outcome is already written into legible public fields. State unclaimed-property listings name the owner, holder and amount, and the DMF settlements forced insurers to find beneficiaries themselves. On top of that, statutory finder-fee caps of about 10-20% and assignment restrictions limit the step-up to low single-digit multiples, with no capitalised buyer paying a premium.
scored.one_line_reason: This is classic heir-hunting. The answer already sits in public unclaimed-property listings, fees are capped at about 10-20% of fixed face values, the ML lever is under 3x, and there is no ladder up. Incumbents such as Kemp & Associates and American Research Bureau, plus many unclaimed-property finders, already work it.

scored.name: Clean NOL Shells
scored.one_line: Buy dormant shells with large NOLs; ML reconstructs ownership history to prove no Section 382 change; sell or reverse-merge with profitable operators.
scored.unproven_right: Control of dormant shell, $25-150k.
scored.proving_step: Owner-shift ledger and opinion-ready 382 study.
scored.proven_buyer: Profitable small caps, family offices, NOL-shell sponsors.
scored.public_data: EDGAR history (tax footnotes, 13D/G, Forms 3/4/5), SEC revocation lists, DE/NV registries, PACER.
scored.frame: The rung is "own a dormant shell, prove its NOL is still clean, sell it". Most of the work does look like discovery: rebuilding the ownership ledger from EDGAR 13D/G and Forms 3/4/5. The frame breaks at the sale, though. Buying control of the shell, or reverse-merging an operator into it, is itself a Section 382 ownership change (a more-than-50-point shift among 5% holders). That caps yearly NOL use at the shell's equity value times the long-term tax-exempt rate (my recollection: about 3-4%). Section 382(c) also takes the cap to zero if the old business does not continue for 2 years, and a dormant shell has no business to continue. So proving there was no change in the past does not make the asset sellable, because the buyer's own purchase triggers the change. Discovery may be 80% of the work, but it does not lead to an asset a buyer can use.
scored.step_up: The candidate claims 30-300x on a $25-150k shell. My estimate, not sourced (web search budget was used up): a dormant shell's NOL is worth close to zero to an acquirer. Its equity value is about $0, so the 382 cap times $0 is about $0, and the COBE failure zeroes it anyway. Clean NOL value in the market sits in vehicles that came out of bankruptcy with 382(l)(5) relief and kept an operating business, such as WMIH (the WaMu shell that bought Nationstar) and Signature Group (formerly Fremont). Even those trade at a few cents to the low teens of cents per dollar of NOL, my recollection. For a dormant small shell, the realistic premium over the $25-150k cost of a clean public shell is about 1-3x, not 30-300x.
scored.hit_rate_capex: My estimate, unsourced. A 382 study costs roughly $20-100k from Big-4 or boutique tax firms. Many shells with large NOLs will pass a clean ownership history test, so the base hit rate on "no prior change" is fairly high, maybe 30-60%. A high hit rate leaves ML at most about a 2-3x lever (capped at 1/hit rate), not 10x. The real binding limit is the forward-looking 382 and COBE problem, which ML cannot fix.
scored.data: The data is mostly legible. The NOL amount and the 382 discussion sit in 10-K tax footnotes, often with an explicit statement on whether an ownership change has happened or a 382 rights plan has been adopted. 13D/G filings are structured on EDGAR. Delaware and Nevada registry status and SEC trading-suspension lists are legible fields. Rebuilding beneficial ownership among 5% holders across decades of filings is somewhat illegible, which gives a modest edge. NOLs from before 2018 also expire after 20 years, and that is legible too.
scored.right_bought: Yes. Control of a dormant shell can be bought from custodians, insiders or through Nevada/Delaware custodianship petitions for about $25-150k (the candidate's figure; Nevada custodianship shell flipping is an established, crowded practice). The owners usually know the NOL figure, because it is in the footnote.
scored.buyer: Profitable operators would want the NOLs but cannot use them after acquiring control (382 cap, COBE, and Section 269 anti-abuse rules). Real NOL-shell sponsors, such as Steel Partners-style holding companies and the WMIH/Pendrell-type vehicles, already have tax counsel and buy NOLs that come with an operating business. The reverse-merger shell market prices the public listing, not the NOL.
scored.ladder: The ladder is weak: NOL shell, then a holding company that acquires profitable businesses (the Berkshire/Steel Partners model). That is a capital-allocation business, not vertical integration of a physical chain, and the supply of clean NOL shells is small and shrinking (they expire, and post-2017 NOLs are limited to 80% of taxable income).
scored.fatal_flaw: Under Section 382 the buyer's own acquisition of control is the ownership change. A dormant shell's equity value is about $0 and it fails the 2-year continuity-of-business requirement, so its annual NOL limit falls to about $0 at the moment of sale. Proving a clean history therefore creates almost no value a buyer can use; the asset loses its value when it is sold.
scored.one_line_reason: The step-up disappears at sale: Section 382 and the continuity-of-business rule zero out a dormant shell's NOL for whoever buys it, and the NOL amount is already in legible tax footnotes.
