scored.name: Surplus Capture: micro-caps with overfunded pension plans
scored.one_line: Buy control of small sponsors whose frozen DB surplus is mismeasured; re-price liabilities; realise via termination or PRT.
scored.unproven_right: Equity control of the sponsor.
scored.proving_step: Re-underwrite from Schedule SB, insurer quotes, plan termination.
scored.proven_buyer: PRT insurers (Athene, L&G, Prudential, MetLife), acquirers.
scored.public_data: DOL EFAST2 Form 5500 SB/MB, PBGC, 10-K footnotes.
scored.frame: The rung is buying control of a sponsor and getting the pension surplus out of it. Discovery is maybe 10-20% of the work (my estimate). Most of the effort is the physical and legal part: raising capital for a control stake (proxy fights, tender offers, a premium of roughly 20-40%), ERISA plan termination (PBGC standard-termination filings, IRS determination letter, 6-12+ months), placing an annuity with an insurer, and getting through tax. Discovery is not 80%+ in any frame I can find, because the surplus is not hidden. It is a reported number.
scored.step_up: The step-up is about 1.1-2x on equity, not 10^3-10^4. The step-up is small because the hit is not a new asset. It is cash already shown on the balance sheet that markets discount by some amount (estimate). It shrinks further on the way out. IRC 4980 charges a 50% excise tax on an employer reversion (20% if 25% of the surplus goes to a qualified replacement plan or to benefit increases), plus about 21% corporate tax. So the sponsor keeps roughly 30-60% of the gross surplus (statutory rates; my arithmetic). Annuity buyouts usually price at about 100-105% of the accounting liability (Milliman Pension Buyout Index range, from memory, not re-verified this run). That eats more of the surplus. The candidate's own estimate is 1.5-5x. After excise tax and the control premium I put it at 1.1-2x.
scored.hit_rate_capex: There is no low-hit-rate proving step. Anyone can compute from Schedule SB and 10-K footnotes whether a plan is overfunded. The real uncertainty is execution: whether you win control, the price you pay, and how tax applies. ML does not improve any of that. Each attempt costs the purchase price of a control stake, so for a micro-cap roughly $10M-$100M+ (estimate). On top of that are deal costs: legal, actuarial and termination fees, roughly $0.5-2M (estimate). The capex is the asset price, not a discovery cost, so a 10x capex cut is not possible. The lever is about 1x.
scored.data: The data is public but already legible, and that kills the edge. Form 5500 Schedule SB is machine-readable XML/CSV in DOL EFAST2. It has explicit fields for funding target, actuarial value of assets, AFTAP and funding shortfall/surplus. 10-K ASC 715 footnotes report the funded status as a single line. So the outcome is already in a legible field, the exact failure the rubric describes. The only illegible-ish edge is re-pricing the liability: mortality, lump-sum take-up and insurer pricing compared with the sponsor's assumptions. That is small, a few percent of the liability. Pension consultants (Milliman, Aon, WTW) and insurers' own origination teams already model it.
scored.right_bought: The right can be bought, as equity of the sponsor, but not cheaply or quietly. These are public micro-caps or private companies. A control purchase reveals your thesis and needs a control premium. Overfunded-pension situations are a known strategy among deep-value and activist investors, so the boards that own the surplus are not blind to it. Since 2022, rising rates have pushed many plans to surplus, and this is widely covered in the press (from memory, not re-verified).
scored.buyer: The buyers are annuity insurers: Athene, Legal & General, Prudential, MetLife, Pacific Life, and others. They take on the liabilities, they do not pay a step-up for them. The other buyers are strategic or PE acquirers, who pay ordinary M&A multiples. No buyer pays a 10^3x multiple for the output of this rung.
scored.ladder: A ladder exists: surplus extraction, then a pension consolidator or superfund (there is a UK precedent, Clara-Pensions), then an annuity reinsurer, then a full insurer like Athene/Apollo. That is a large end state. But every rung is capital- and regulation-heavy, and the first rung has no discovery edge, so there is no cheap rung to win first.
scored.fatal_flaw: The surplus is already in legible public fields: Schedule SB funding target versus assets, and the ASC 715 funded status in 10-K footnotes. The realisable value is then capped by the 50% IRC 4980 reversion excise tax. The result is a small-multiple capital-markets arbitrage with no discovery step and no 10^3x step-up.
scored.one_line_reason: This is a known financial arbitrage on a disclosed number. It needs control capital, pays a 20-50% excise tax plus corporate tax, and gives at most about 1.1-2x. Discovery is a small part of the work, so ML has nothing to extract.

scored.name: EU novel-food authorisations with data protection
scored.one_line: Buy rights to underused traditional ingredients, build a novel-food dossier from public safety literature, win EU authorisation with 5-year proprietary data protection, sell exclusivity.
scored.unproven_right: Exclusive supply/ingredient rights plus dossier.
scored.proving_step: ML mining of EFSA opinions, GRAS notices and literature; filing and authorisation ($0.5-2M, 2-3 years).
scored.proven_buyer: DSM-Firmenich, Givaudan, Kerry, ADM, IFF.
scored.public_data: FDA GRAS inventory, EFSA Journal, EU Union list, PubMed.
scored.frame: The rung is "hold an EU Union-list novel-food authorisation with Art. 26 data protection, then sell it." Inside that rung, discovery (picking the ingredient) is maybe 10-20% of the work. The other 80%+ is regulatory: commissioning new studies (compositional, stability, toxicology, often a 90-day study), writing the dossier, and answering EFSA's clock-stop questions over 2-4 years. That is the coal-mine-geothermal pattern again. The bespoke physical and regulatory step is far harder than finding the right ingredient.
scored.step_up: The unproven right (a supply or ingredient right to an obscure traditional plant) is cheap. My estimate is $10k-100k for an exclusive sourcing deal. The proving cost is far larger: commonly cited at EUR 0.3-1M+ per dossier (my estimate, matching the candidate's $0.5-2M). The proven asset is 5 years of exclusivity on a niche ingredient. My estimate is that it sells for $1-10M, or 1-5x what went into it. The candidate's ~100-300x compares against the price of the bare right and ignores that the proving step costs 10-50x the right. Measured against capital in, the step-up is under 3-10x. It is also slow (EFSA assessments typically run 2-4+ years) and expires after 5 years.
scored.hit_rate_capex: My estimate is that the base hit rate is high, not low. Most applications that reach a complete EFSA assessment get a positive opinion. Failures are mostly withdrawals or 'safety cannot be established' opinions caused by missing data, not by a wrong pick. ML cannot do much for a step that already succeeds roughly 50-80% of the time: 1/hit-rate caps the lever at about 1.3-2x, nowhere near 10x. Each attempt costs EUR 0.3-2M, and that cost comes from new studies ML cannot replace. I could not check these figures because the shared web-search budget was used up.
scored.data: The signal sources are EFSA Journal opinions, the FDA GRAS inventory, the EU Union list (Reg. 2017/2470) and PubMed. All of them are public and already legible: structured, searchable, and read routinely by regulatory consultancies. The outcome is written straight into a legible public field: the Union list entry and the EFSA opinion conclusion. That is exactly the kill pattern seen in earlier hunts. Data protection under Reg. (EU) 2015/2283 Art. 26 covers only NEWLY DEVELOPED PROPRIETARY data that the authorisation could not have been granted without. A dossier built from public literature gets no data protection, and the authorisation becomes generic. Also, the faster route for traditional foods from third countries (the Art. 14 notification) carries no data protection at all.
scored.right_bought: Partly. Exclusive supply or sourcing rights can be bought from growers or cooperatives in the countries of origin. But exclusivity over a traditional plant ingredient is weak: anyone can source the same species elsewhere. The authorisation itself is not a right you buy. Anyone can file for it, first-come, and once the 5 years end, competitors can rely on the authorisation.
scored.buyer: Ingredient majors: DSM-Firmenich, Givaudan, Kerry, ADM, IFF, plus mid-size botanical suppliers. They are capitalised, but they mostly file their own novel-food applications through in-house teams or regulatory consultancies (e.g. Intertek, Ramboll, Knoell, SGS). They pay for proven commercial demand, not just for the authorisation.
scored.ladder: Possible rungs: authorisation, then ingredient supply and processing, then a branded ingredient, then consumer products. Each rung is a low-margin, crowded ingredient or CPG business. There is no single concentrated value pool like a uranium mine, so the path to a trillion-dollar company is weak.
scored.fatal_flaw: Art. 26 data protection applies only to newly generated proprietary studies, so a dossier mined from public literature, which is the whole ML edge, wins no exclusivity. Getting exclusivity means paying for new tox and compositional studies. Those studies dominate the cost and are not discovery, and the EFSA outcome is already a legible public field.
scored.one_line_reason: Discovery is a small share of the work, the proving step mostly succeeds already (so ML has little to raise), exclusivity needs costly new studies rather than public data, and the step-up against capital in is at most single-digit.

scored.name: Secrecy-Order Inventions
scored.one_line: Buy rights to secrecy-ordered applications from inventors and estates; predict rescission and commercial relevance; sell issued patents.
scored.unproven_right: Assignment of pending secrecy-ordered applications.
scored.proving_step: Rescission and allowance of claims reading on products.
scored.proven_buyer: Aggregators, funders, strategics.
scored.public_data: USPTO secrecy-order counts (FOIA/FAS), old-filing-date issuances, DTIC, PAIR assignments.
scored.frame: Rung: buy assignment of a pending secrecy-ordered US application, wait for rescission (35 USC 181), get it allowed, sell the issued patent. Discovery is a small share of the work here, maybe 20-30% (my estimate). Most of the work is waiting on DoD/DOE agency review, which nobody can speed up, plus prosecution and then licensing or litigation to turn a patent into money. Neither of those is a trivial physical step. The buyer for the output (aggregators, litigation funders) does exist, but it pays for patents that are proven to read on products, not for ones that have merely issued.
scored.step_up: Unproven: a pending application under a secrecy order cannot be published or licensed abroad, so its market value is close to zero. A token price might be $1k-10k (my estimate; I know of no market for these). Proven: most issued patents sell on the secondary market for about $50k-250k per asset (my estimate from broker-market knowledge from before this task). A rare patent that reads on a current product could be worth $1M+. That is about 10-100x typical, and it only happens if the claims still matter. Many secrecy-ordered inventions are old military technology. Their 20-year term runs from the filing date, although 35 USC 154(b)(1)(C) gives some term adjustment for secrecy-order delay. So what is left after rescission is often obsolete or short-lived.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Base rates from memory of FAS/USPTO FOIA data, not checked in this run: about 5,900-6,000 secrecy orders were in effect around FY2020-2024. New orders run about 70-130 a year, and rescissions about 30-60 a year, so the yearly flow is tiny. Each proving attempt costs roughly $20k-50k in prosecution (my estimate) plus years of waiting. The binding constraint is the agency deciding to rescind, not a hit rate that ML could predict and improve. Rescission timing is set by agency classification review. ML cannot cut the cost of a proving attempt, and with a flow this small there are few shots to take anyway.
scored.data: The core signal is classified, not just hard to read. Secrecy-ordered applications are unpublished by law, so nobody (us, buyers, ML) can read the claims before rescission. Only aggregate counts are public, through FAS FOIA releases. After rescission the application publishes and its status appears in legible fields (Patent Center/PAIR, publication). That is when everyone can see it, so the information edge disappears at exactly the moment it would be useful. DTIC holds related technical reports, but linking them to specific sealed applications is guesswork. On the purchase side, many secrecy orders cover government-funded inventions. In those cases the government or a defense contractor holds the rights or a license, so there are few individual inventors or estates to buy from. Export-control rules also restrict who can receive or see the subject matter.
scored.right_bought: In principle, assignment of a pending application by an individual inventor or an estate. In practice, most owners are defense contractors or government-funded entities, who will not sell cheaply and may not be allowed to. Due diligence is impossible because the content is secret. Buying would be blind, or would require cleared personnel under export-control restrictions.
scored.buyer: Patent aggregators (RPX, Intellectual Ventures-style), litigation funders and strategic acquirers. They pay for evidence of use (claim charts), not just for issuance. That means a second costly rung (assertion or licensing) has to happen before the step-up is paid out.
scored.ladder: The rungs above are licensing, assertion or litigation, and possibly commercialising the technology. That is a patent-assertion business, not a path to a trillion-dollar vertically integrated company. The flow of about 30-60 rescissions a year caps the scale.
scored.fatal_flaw: The asset's content is legally classified and unpublished until rescission, and rescission makes it fully public. No point exists where you can read the signal and others cannot. On top of that, only about 30-60 rescissions happen a year, mostly on government-funded inventions you cannot buy.
scored.one_line_reason: The idea fails because secrecy is the barrier, not illegibility. Without seeing the claims you cannot pick or price which applications to buy, the flow is tiny and mostly government-owned, and the "proven" patent is often obsolete and still has to be licensed or litigated before it is worth anything.

scored.name: Grandfather Clause: 510(k)s bought ahead of device up-classification
scored.one_line: Buy abandoned 510(k)s for device types FDA panels foreshadow up-classifying or predicate-narrowing; sell scarce pathways to device makers.
scored.unproven_right: Clearances for unmarketed products.
scored.proving_step: Predict reclassification from transcripts and proposed orders; final order.
scored.proven_buyer: Mid-cap and large device makers, PE roll-ups.
scored.public_data: 510(k) summaries, AdCom transcripts, Federal Register orders, MAUDE, GUDID.
scored.frame: The rung would be: hold dormant 510(k) clearances and sell them ahead of a regulatory change. Predicting FDA may be 80%+ of the work, and buying a clearance on paper is cheap. But the rung has no real output to sell (see fatal_flaw). Even with the clearance in hand, the buyer still has to make a device that is substantially equivalent and run it under its own quality system. Most of the work of marketing a device is that manufacturing and quality work, not discovery.
scored.step_up: No real step-up. Prices are my estimates, because web search was unavailable (the shared turn budget was used up). Dormant 510(k)s sell through brokers and asset deals for roughly $10k-$250k. That price is capped by the cost of a fresh 510(k): the FDA fee is about $24k for a standard filer (FY2025), and all-in cost is about $50k-$300k plus 3-12 months. The candidate's 10-300x assumes clearances become scarce after up-classification, and they do not. Realistic uplift, my estimate: 1-3x, from saving time.
scored.hit_rate_capex: There is no costly physical proving attempt. The bet is a prediction about FDA, and one dormant clearance costs about $10k-$100k (my estimate). FDA reclassifies only a handful of device types a year, often years after a panel meets. When a type is moved up to Class III, current holders must file a PMA or leave the market, so a 'hit' cuts the asset's value instead of raising it. ML has no 10x discovery cost to cut.
scored.data: The data is public and mostly legible already. FDA's 510(k), product-code and classification databases are structured. Panel transcripts and proposed orders in the Federal Register are public, and law firms and regulatory consultancies already summarize every proposed reclassification. The outcome is written into a legible field: the final order and the device class. Owners of dormant 510(k)s can be found and will sell, but what they are selling is not scarce.
scored.right_bought: A 510(k) clearance can be transferred by an asset sale and updated in FDA's registration and listing system, so the right can be bought. It gives no exclusivity, though: any company can cite any cleared device as its predicate without owning it.
scored.buyer: Device makers and PE roll-ups do buy clearances, but only at a discount to the cost of re-filing, and only bundled with design history files and a working quality system.
scored.ladder: There is a ladder: clearances, then contract manufacturing, then device brands, then roll-ups. But the bottom rung has no edge, so there is nothing to climb from.
scored.fatal_flaw: Both premises are false. (1) A clearance is not a scarce pathway, because any 510(k) is a public predicate that anyone can cite without owning it. (2) Up-classification destroys value instead of grandfathering it. Under 515(i), and in the final orders that moved device types up to Class III (for example metal-on-metal hips in 2016 and surgical mesh for pelvic organ prolapse in 2016, whose remaining 510(k)-cleared products FDA ordered off the market in 2019), existing holders must file a PMA. Owning a 510(k) at the moment its device type is up-classified is a liability.
scored.one_line_reason: This fails: a 510(k) is a predicate anyone can cite without owning it, and under 515(i) up-classification forces existing holders to file a PMA rather than grandfathering them, so the predicted hit lowers the asset's value.

FDA final order of 2016 moving surgical mesh for transvaginal pelvic organ prolapse repair to Class III, and the April 2019 order removing it from the market
FDA final order of 2016 requiring a PMA for metal-on-metal total hip systems

scored.name: EVP Ready: dormant EPA antimicrobial registrations for outbreak claims
scored.one_line: Buy dormant disinfectant registrations whose efficacy data qualifies for Emerging Viral Pathogen claims; add claims; sell in outbreaks.
scored.unproven_right: FIFRA Section 3 antimicrobial registrations.
scored.proving_step: ML over labels and efficacy summaries; EVP claim amendments.
scored.proven_buyer: Clorox, Ecolab, Diversey, private label, janitorial distributors.
scored.public_data: EPA PPLS labels, List N/EVP lists, FOIA efficacy summaries.
scored.frame: The rung would be 'hold an EVP-qualified FIFRA registration'. Inside it, discovery (figuring out which registration qualifies) is maybe 10-20% of the work (my estimate). Qualifying is mechanical: under EPA's EVP guidance (2016, widened in 2024 to all virus types with an enveloped < large non-enveloped < small non-enveloped hierarchy), a product qualifies if its label already carries a kill claim against a hard-to-kill virus such as norovirus or poliovirus surrogates. The rest of the value comes from formulation supply, manufacturing, label compliance, state registrations and distribution in a demand spike. Those are hard physical and commercial steps, not trivial ones. This is the coal-mine geothermal pattern again: the asset is easy to find and running it is the hard part.
scored.step_up: Unproven: a dormant antimicrobial registration costs roughly one PRIA maintenance fee a year (low thousands of USD per registrant, my estimate from memory of the PRIA schedule), and registration transfers are cheap paperwork. Proven: an EVP-qualified registration has little standalone resale value outside outbreaks, because a new registration or an EVP label amendment can be obtained through PRIA in months for an estimated $5k-$50k including testing. During COVID (List N, 600+ products) the shortage was in supply and manufacturing capacity, not registrations. My estimate is about 2-5x on the right itself even in outbreak years, and 1-2x otherwise. The candidate's 10-100x applies to product revenue, not to the right.
scored.hit_rate_capex: Base hit rate: close to 100% predictable from the label. A registration whose accepted efficacy data includes a small non-enveloped virus claim qualifies for EVP tiers by rule, so there is no low base rate for ML to improve, and the lever (capped at 1/base hit rate) is about 1x. Cost per proving attempt: an EVP label amendment PRIA fee in the low thousands of USD, plus about $10k-$30k per virucidal efficacy test (GLP lab, surrogate virus) if new data is needed. Both figures are my estimates, not sourced; the web search budget was exhausted, so none of them were verified this run.
scored.data: EPA PPLS stamped labels are public PDFs, but the outcome is already summarised in a legible public field. EPA publishes List N (COVID), List Q (EVP-claim products, introduced with the 2024 guidance update), List G (norovirus) and others, which name products by EPA reg number and pathogen claim. That is the exact failure mode the rubric warns about: the regulator writes the answer into a public list. Efficacy summaries from FOIA add little beyond the label claims. Dormant registrations can be bought from small registrants, but the owners and the many registration consultancies (for example regulatory firms that handle supplemental distributor registrations) understand their value well. There is no information asymmetry for ML to exploit.
scored.right_bought: Yes, FIFRA registrations can be transferred or licensed, and there are supplemental distributor registrations ('me-too' sub-registrations under a basic registrant). That cuts both ways: anyone, including private-label sellers, can get a sub-registration under an existing EVP-qualified basic registration cheaply, so scarcity is low. My estimate is that buying or licensing a qualifying right costs low thousands to tens of thousands of USD.
scored.buyer: Clorox, Ecolab, Diversey (Solenis), Lonza/Arxada, Spartan, plus private-label and janitorial distributors. In practice these incumbents already hold broad-spectrum registrations with norovirus and other hard-to-kill virus claims. In an outbreak they need manufacturing capacity and raw materials (quats, wipes substrate, bottles), not more registrations.
scored.ladder: Holding the registration leads to toll-manufactured private-label disinfectant, then owned formulation and manufacturing, then branded institutional distribution. It is a real ladder, but it ends in a commodity market of roughly $20-30B globally for surface disinfectants (my estimate), dominated by Clorox, Ecolab and Diversey, with thin margins and cyclical demand. It is not a trillion-dollar path.
scored.fatal_flaw: The outcome is already legible and published: EPA's EVP rules decide qualification from existing label virus claims, and EPA lists the qualifying products by reg number (List Q, N, G). So there is no hidden signal for ML to find. The value in an outbreak sits in manufacturing and supply, not in the registration.
scored.one_line_reason: The answer comes from a published rule plus public EPA lists, there is no low hit rate to improve, the registration has little scarcity value, and an outbreak rewards supply chain rather than rights. This fails the Terranox test.

scored.name: Lapsed-Registration Airframe Recovery
scored.one_line: Buy abandoned GA aircraft with lapsed registration from estates and lien sales; clear title and resell.
scored.unproven_right: Clouded-title aircraft at discount.
scored.proving_step: Registry-probate join, title search, annual inspection.
scored.proven_buyer: GA dealers, flight schools.
scored.public_data: FAA registry expired/deregistered files, probate, airport lien notices.
scored.frame: The rung would be "buy a clouded-title, lapsed-registration GA airframe, clear the title, make it airworthy, resell it." I estimate discovery and proving (registry-probate join plus title search) at about 10-20% of the work. The other 80%+ is physical and bespoke: recovering the plane from a tie-down or hangar, chasing logbooks, an annual inspection on an airframe that has been sitting, and usually corrosion repair or an engine overhaul. This is the geothermal-in-coal-mines pattern, where the build is harder than the find. There is a buyer (dealers and flight schools), but these are small, thin-margin buyers, not capitalised developers. All figures are my estimates; no web searches ran.
scored.step_up: I estimate about 1.5-3x gross, and less than 1.5x net of restoration (the candidate itself says ~2-5x). Example from memory, not sourced: a derelict Cessna 172 with lapsed registration and an unclear lien history might trade at $15-30k as a project. Once it is clean-titled and airworthy with a fresh annual it might sell for $60-90k. But the uplift mostly pays for the physical work: a sitting airframe often needs a $25-45k engine overhaul plus $3-15k of annual and corrosion work. Clearing the title alone (the actual discovery step) adds maybe 1.2-2x. That is nowhere near 10^3-10^4.
scored.hit_rate_capex: These are estimates only; no web search ran. A title search through the specialist aircraft title firms costs roughly $100-300 per tail number. A pre-buy or annual inspection costs about $1.5-5k. The hit rate of "can this title be cleared" is probably already high, maybe 50-80%, because FAA liens and probate are clearable with an attorney and time. The real uncertainty is the airframe's condition, which ML on registry data cannot see. So 1/base hit rate caps the lever at about 1.5-2x, not 10x.
scored.data: The FAA Civil Aviation Registry is a free, downloadable, structured database: the daily ReleasableAircraft file, plus deregistered-aircraft files that carry status codes and expiration dates. Expired, deregistered and lapsed status is already a legible field. That is the exact failure mode from earlier hunts. Only probate records and airport lien notices are scattered and illegible, and joining them to tail numbers is a modest record-linkage task, not deep ML. Context: the FAA's 2023 rule (from memory) extended registration terms to 7 years, which shrinks the lapsed population. Plenty of people already do this: aircraft brokers, salvage yards such as aircraft parts recyclers, title firms, A&P mechanics who buy hangar-queen projects, and airports running abandoned-aircraft lien auctions.
scored.right_bought: Yes, the rights are bought, not claimed first-come. Sources are heirs and estates, airport lien sales, and storage-lien auctions. Owners often cannot read the registry and lien picture, so some discount exists. But the discount mostly reflects the real physical-deterioration risk, not an informational edge.
scored.buyer: GA dealers, flight schools and private pilots. These are fragmented, small-ticket buyers ($30-150k per unit) with thin margins. None is a capitalised developer paying a 10^4 premium.
scored.ladder: The ladder is weak and capped: title clearing, then MRO and restoration, then a brokerage or dealership, then perhaps parts salvage. The US GA used-aircraft market is on the order of single-digit billions a year (my estimate), so there is no trillion-dollar path. Each rung up is more physical labour, not more discovery.
scored.fatal_flaw: The physical step dominates and the outcome is already legible. Making an abandoned airframe airworthy (engine overhaul, corrosion, annual, $10-45k) dwarfs the find, which is the coal-mine-geothermal failure. Lapsed or deregistered status is already a structured field in the free FAA registry download. And the step-up is about 2x net of restoration, three orders of magnitude short of the 10^4 the rubric needs.
scored.one_line_reason: This is a low-margin restoration-and-flip business: the discovery step is a small share of the work, the step-up is about 2x, the hit-rate lever is small, and the status data is already legible in the FAA's free registry download.

scored.name: Grandfathered gaming-entitlement parcels
scored.one_line: Buy parcels at land prices that carry dormant gaming eligibility (Clark County GED etc.); confirm by ruling; sell to casino developers.
scored.unproven_right: Parcels priced as plain land.
scored.proving_step: ML over minutes and use permits; zoning verification.
scored.proven_buyer: Station/Red Rock, Boyd, Golden, VICI, GLPI.
scored.public_data: Clark County minutes, NGCB agendas, GED maps, assessor data.
scored.frame: The rung would be buying land and confirming it can host a gaming licence, then selling it to casino developers. Discovery is near 0% of the work here, not 80%+. Whether a parcel can host gaming in Clark County is set by the statutory Las Vegas Boulevard gaming corridor, the rural Clark County gaming zone and mapped Gaming Enterprise Districts. Any other site needs a public petition and hearing under NRS 463.3086, which is a political and legal fight rather than a discovery problem. Almost all of the value comes from building the casino, which is very hard and costly (Durango Station was about $750M+, my recollection). That is the same failure as the geothermal-in-coal-mines counter-example: finding the site is easy and the physical step is the whole game.
scored.step_up: No verified numbers; the search budget ran out before any price search returned results. My estimate: off-Strip Las Vegas commercial land trades at roughly $0.5-3M per acre, and land eligible for gaming in GED, corridor or Strip-adjacent areas at roughly $3-15M+ per acre (Strip sales in 2022-23 were reportedly around $10M+ per acre, from memory). That is about a 3-10x premium, which matches the candidate's own figure, and it applies only where the eligibility is not already priced in. It is far below 10^3.
scored.hit_rate_capex: There is no costly proving step that usually fails. Confirming gaming eligibility means checking a zoning map, a title report and a land-use attorney's opinion, roughly $5-50k per parcel (my estimate). A petition for a new site costs a hearing and lobbying, and it fails or succeeds on politics and neighbourhood opposition, which ML cannot predict better from the record. Base hit rate is not meaningful. ML gives no cut in discovery capex because discovery is not where the money goes.
scored.data: The outcome is already summarised in legible public fields. GED and gaming-corridor boundaries are statutory and mapped. Clark County zoning and GED layers sit in the public GIS. Grandfathered licensed sites are listed in Nevada Gaming Control Board licensee records. Sellers and brokers in Las Vegas know exactly which parcels carry gaming eligibility and price it in; Station/Red Rock, Boyd and others have held land banks for decades. Rights are bought, but the owners can read the data, so no purchase discount is available. This is the same pattern the earlier 'interconnection queue' kill found: a lookup table matches ML.
scored.right_bought: Yes, parcels are bought on the open market, but there is no information gap. Sellers of gaming-eligible land in Clark County are sophisticated and price the eligibility in. Parcels that are 'dormant' in the sense of being outside the GED cannot be made eligible by discovery; that takes a contested political petition.
scored.buyer: Capitalised buyers exist: Red Rock Resorts (Station Casinos), Boyd Gaming, Golden Entertainment, and REITs such as VICI and GLPI (the REITs mostly buy operating properties rather than land). They hold land banks of their own and do not need to buy outside sites, so the buyer pool for raw entitled land is thin and slow.
scored.ladder: The rungs above are entitle, then build, then operate the casino, then own the real estate through a sale-leaseback (as VICI and GLPI do). That is a real ladder, but the next rung needs hundreds of millions of dollars and a gaming licence. Gaming is also a heavily regulated, mature, local market with a capped number of sites, so it is not a trillion-dollar path.
scored.fatal_flaw: Gaming eligibility is a statutory, mapped zoning designation that sellers already price in, so there is no illegible signal to find. The only way to create new value is a political petition, not discovery, and building the casino rather than finding the site is where all the work lies.
scored.one_line_reason: Fails the frame: the outcome is a public mapped field, sellers are sophisticated, the step-up is about 3-10x, nothing expensive is failing that ML could improve, and the value sits in building the casino.

scored.name: Thorium Legacy to Pb-212 Feed
scored.one_line: Collect aged legacy thorium stocks with Ra-228/Th-228 ingrowth for Pb-212 generators.
scored.unproven_right: Part 40 source material taken as a liability.
scored.proving_step: Gamma-spec ingrowth assay and transfer.
scored.proven_buyer: Orano Med, Perspective, AdvanCell, Eckert & Ziegler, Viewpoint.
scored.public_data: Part 40 licence files, DLA thorium nitrate records, EHS notices, FUSRAP.
scored.frame: The rung would be acquiring and proving aged thorium as a Th-228 feedstock. Discovery is maybe 5% of the work (my estimate). Finding the thorium is easy: Part 40 licensees already declare their quantities. The 'proving' is a deterministic decay calculation from the separation date, which one gamma-spec reading confirms. About 95% of the work is physical and regulatory: collecting a Part 40 liability, then running a hot radiochemistry separation (Ra-228/Th-228 from bulk Th-232), plus the shielding, waste and byproduct licensing that come with it. That is the geothermal-in-coal-mine pattern, where the bespoke physical plant dominates. Radiopharma buyers do have capital, but they buy purified Th-228 or Ra-224/Pb-212 generator product, not 'proven' raw thorium.
scored.step_up: The unproven right is legacy thorium taken as a liability, so its value is about zero or negative. Disposal costs avoided are an estimate, roughly tens of $/kg. The gamma assay itself does not raise the value much. Physics (my calculation): Th-232 specific activity is 4.06 kBq/g, and at secular equilibrium (more than about 25-30 years since separation) Th-228 activity equals that. So one tonne of aged thorium holds only about 4 GBq, or about 0.11 Ci, of Th-228, spread through tonnes of material. Value appears only after chemical separation and purification. The ratio looks large only because the starting value is negative, and that uplift comes from processing, not from proving. On proving alone I estimate under 3x. I could not verify current Th-228 market prices because the search budget was used up.
scored.hit_rate_capex: The base hit rate is effectively about 100% (my estimate, from physics): any thorium more than about 25 years from its last chemical separation is in Th-228 equilibrium, and the separation date is usually known. A gamma-spec assay costs on the order of $100s-$1,000s per sample (my estimate). Nothing is failing, so there is nothing for ML to raise. The 1/base-hit-rate cap gives a lever of about 1x. The real capex is the separation hot cell and licensing, which I estimate at $10M+ (unsourced), and ML does not reduce it.
scored.data: Part 40 licence files, FUSRAP site records and DLA records are public and somewhat scattered. But the key variables, thorium quantity and age or separation date, are either written into licence or inventory fields or follow from simple decay math. There is no hidden signal for ML to extract. The largest US stock, the DLA thorium nitrate stockpile of about 3,200 t, was shipped for disposal at the Nevada site in the mid-2000s. That is from memory: I could not check it against a source this turn, so the largest legible source is likely gone.
scored.right_bought: Holders would likely give the material away or pay to be rid of it, so the right is cheap or even negative-cost. However, the holders know exactly what they have, so there is no information asymmetry to exploit. Taking title also means taking on Part 40 possession, transport and eventual disposal liability.
scored.buyer: The capitalised buyers would be Orano Med, Perspective Therapeutics, AdvanCell, Eckert & Ziegler and Viewpoint. They buy purified Th-228 or Ra-224/Pb-212 generators, not raw aged thorium. The incumbent suppliers are the DOE Isotope Program (ORNL Th-228/Th-229 from U-233 legacy, plus Ra-228 recovery work), Eckert & Ziegler, and Orano. Orano/Orano Med already has captive thorium stocks inherited from Rhodia's monazite processing, so the largest buyer is vertically integrated upstream (from my knowledge, unverified this turn).
scored.ladder: The ladder exists: aged-thorium feed, then Ra-228/Th-228 separation, then generator manufacture, then Pb-212 CDMO, then radioligand therapeutics. The top rungs are large, since Pb-212 alpha therapy is a fast-growing radiopharma segment. But the bottom rung is not a discovery rung, so the Terranox mechanism never starts.
scored.fatal_flaw: There is nothing to discover. Th-228 ingrowth is deterministic decay physics from a known separation date, and holders already declare quantities in licence files, so the hit rate is about 100% and ML has no edge. Value comes only from a bespoke radiochemistry separation plant processing tonnes of material for about 0.1 Ci of Th-228 per tonne. That plant is the dominant cost and risk, which is exactly the geothermal-coal-mine counter-example. On top of that, Orano already holds captive thorium, and the DLA stockpile was disposed of.
scored.one_line_reason: This is a radiochemistry processing business, not a discovery business. The hit rate is about 100% and the outcome is legible from licence files plus decay math. Yield is only about 0.11 Ci Th-228 per tonne of Th-232, and the value is captured by whoever builds the separation plant, which incumbents like Orano and DOE already have.

Physics: Th-232 half-life 1.405e10 y, specific activity about 4.06 kBq/g; Ra-228 half-life 5.75 y; Th-228 half-life 1.91 y; secular equilibrium after about 25-30 y (standard nuclear data, e.g. NNDC/ENSDF)
DLA thorium nitrate stockpile disposal at Nevada site, mid-2000s (from memory, not verified this turn)
Orano/Rhodia legacy thorium stocks feeding Orano Med Pb-212 (from memory, not verified this turn)

scored.name: Ghost SRECs: unregistered behind-the-meter solar
scored.one_line: Detect rooftop systems in imagery and permits missing from PJM-GATS in DC/NJ/MA SREC markets, buy owners' SREC rights for a lump sum, register and sell.
scored.unproven_right: Uncollected SREC right of an existing system.
scored.proving_step: Panel detector diffed against GATS, owner sign-up, meter feed and registration.
scored.proven_buyer: PJM suppliers with solar carve-outs, SREC brokers.
scored.public_data: PJM-GATS lists, DC DOEE/DCRA permits, DC PSC lists, orthophotos, LBNL Tracking the Sun.
scored.frame: The rung is 'aggregate and register an existing system's SREC stream'. Discovery (spotting a rooftop array missing from the PSC/GATS list) is maybe 10-20% of the work (my estimate). Comparing orthophoto panel detections against the public DC PSC certified-facility list is a solved CV problem and can be done in a weekend. The other 80%+ is door-to-door owner acquisition, getting the owner to sign, getting the meter/inverter data feed, filing with the DC PSC and GATS, and 10+ years of servicing and remitting. That is the reverse of the 95/5 split. A capitalised buyer does exist (DC load-serving suppliers with a solar carve-out, plus brokers like SRECTrade, Sol Systems/Sol, Karbone), but they buy the SREC flow, not the 'discovery'.
scored.step_up: Estimates only; the web search budget was used up, so these numbers come from prior knowledge, not fresh sources. DC SRECs trade around $400-450/MWh, below an SACP of about $500/MWh. A typical 6-8 kW DC rooftop makes about 7-9 MWh/yr, so roughly $3k-4k/yr of SRECs. An upfront lump-sum buyout from an aggregator usually pays about 40-70% of the discounted strip. If you buy the right from the owner at 0.5x and sell or monetise at 1.0x, the step-up is about 1.5-2x, not 10^3-10^4. The 'unproven' right is not near zero: the owner can register for free in an afternoon through SRECTrade and similar sites, which sets a floor on what you must pay. NJ legacy SREC closed to new registrations in 2020 (replaced by TREC/SuSI ADI, which need pre-registration). MA SREC I/II are closed and SMART needs pre-qualification. So older ghost systems in NJ and MA mostly cannot be registered retroactively, which leaves only DC open.
scored.hit_rate_capex: There is no expensive, mostly-failing proving step. A detection-vs-list diff costs pennies per parcel and should hit most of the time for systems that really are unregistered. The real cost is customer acquisition, which I estimate at $300-1,500 per signed residential owner, in line with residential solar and SREC-aggregator CAC. The 'failure' is owners refusing, already being registered under an installer/aggregator name that does not match the address, or systems being ineligible (vintage, interconnection, data). ML does not cut that cost by 10x. The lever is about 1x.
scored.data: The data is public but already LEGIBLE. The DC PSC publishes a searchable list of certified renewable facilities, with addresses for many residential systems. PJM-GATS publishes generator listings. LBNL Tracking the Sun aggregates installs. DC DOB/DCRA solar permits are structured records. The outcome field ('certified: yes/no') is exactly the regulator-written status field that kills the ML edge. Rights: you do have to buy the SREC right from the owner, but the owner can read their own situation easily. Installers and aggregators (Sol Systems, SRECTrade, Altus/Sunnova-type financiers) register almost every system at install, so the unregistered pool is small (my estimate: low single-digit percent of DC's roughly 10-15k systems, so a few hundred systems and maybe $1-3M/yr of SRECs in total).
scored.right_bought: A contractual assignment of the owner's future SRECs (with meter data access) for a lump sum. It can be bought, but there is no deep discount, because the owner's free alternative (self-registering via a broker) is one web form away.
scored.buyer: DC competitive electricity suppliers with RPS solar carve-out obligations (they buy SRECs or pay the SACP), plus SREC brokers and aggregators (SRECTrade, Sol Systems, Karbone, Flett Exchange). They are capitalised, but the market is small and has a price ceiling at the SACP, and the DC carve-out schedule tapers off over time.
scored.ladder: In theory: SREC aggregation, then residential solar financing/ownership, then a DER/VPP aggregator, then community solar development. But each rung up is a crowded, low-margin, sales-driven business (Sunrun, Sol Systems), and none has a discovery-dominated frame. A ladder exists but does not compound a discovery edge. Realistic ceiling: a small DC aggregator business.
scored.fatal_flaw: There is no information asymmetry for ML to resolve and no 10^3 step-up. Whether a system is certified is already written into the public DC PSC/GATS list. The owner can self-register for free, so the right cannot be bought near zero. NJ and MA legacy programs are closed to retroactive registration. What remains is a tiny DC pool where the bottleneck is door-knocking (customer acquisition), not discovery.
scored.one_line_reason: Discovery is a trivial list diff against a legible regulator status field, the step-up is about 1.5-2x because owners can self-register for free, and the market is a few hundred DC systems. This is a sales business, not a discovery business.

scored.name: Orphaned ZEV / GHG Credit Banks of Defunct Automakers
scored.one_line: Buy regulatory-credit balances stranded in defunct EV makers' estates (UK ZEV, EU pooling, Canada EVAS, CARB) from trustees and sell to short OEMs.
scored.unproven_right: Credit balances held by bankrupt or dormant makers.
scored.proving_step: Match orphaned balances to controllers; confirm transferability and transfer.
scored.proven_buyer: Stellantis, Toyota, Ford, Mazda, JLR.
scored.public_data: CARB ZEV reports, UK VETS, EU pooling decisions, ECCC EVAS, claims-agent dockets.
scored.frame: The rung is buying a credit balance from a trustee and reselling it to an OEM that is short on credits. Discovery (finding the balance) is maybe 10-20% of the work, and that is my estimate. Most of the work is legal and administrative: getting the estate or trustee to sell, confirming the regulator allows the transfer (UK VETS needs a registered manufacturer, and EU pooling is set year by year, not a bankable asset), and finding one of a handful of short OEMs to buy. There is a capitalised buyer, but very few of them, and they hold the pricing power. Discovery is not 80%+ of the work in any frame I can find.
scored.step_up: From memory, all estimates (no web search ran: the shared search budget was used up). Trustees already know a credit balance is an asset and list it in the estate schedules, so the price paid to the estate is probably 20-60% of market, not near zero. That gives roughly 1.5-5x on resale at best. Price references: the UK ZEV mandate fine is about £12k per missing car after the April 2025 change, and traded credits sit well below that, likely about £3-8k (estimate). US CARB/GHG credit value collapsed after the 2025 federal changes: CAFE penalties set to zero, and California's waiver revoked by a CRA resolution. Canada EVAS was paused in 2025. Nothing about this asset goes from about $1 to $10k.
scored.hit_rate_capex: There is no expensive, mostly-failing proving step. Finding a balance is close to certain because regulators publish balances by manufacturer. Most failures come from legal rules on transferability or credit expiry, which ML cannot change. Cost per attempt is legal fees, about $10k-100k per estate (estimate). Because the base hit rate is high, the 1/base-hit-rate cap on the lever is about 1-2x.
scored.data: The outcome is already written in a legible field. The CARB annual ZEV credit report lists banked credits by manufacturer, the UK VETS/DfT publishes compliance positions, EU pooling decisions are published in the Official Journal, and the ECCC GHG/EVAS reports list balances. Bankruptcy dockets list the credits as an estate asset, so buyers can search for them easily. There is no illegible signal for ML to extract.
scored.right_bought: The right can be bought from the trustee, but sales go through 363 auctions or a trustee process, so the price gets discovered and other bidders can compete (including the short OEMs themselves and credit brokers). The sellers can read their own balance perfectly well, so there is no information gap to buy cheaply against. In the UK and EU it is doubtful a defunct, unregistered maker can still transfer credits at all.
scored.buyer: Short OEMs such as Stellantis, Toyota, Ford, Mazda and JLR. It is a buyer's market with very few buyers, made worse by policy rollbacks in the US and Canada and by the extra flexibility added to the UK mandate in 2025. Credit brokers and existing sellers like Tesla, Polestar and BYD already supply them.
scored.ladder: The rungs above are weak. This could grow into a regulatory-credit trading desk or brokerage, which is small, cyclical and depends on policy. It does not lead naturally into making cars. The total opportunity is a few hundred million dollars of credits that end up stranded each year, at most.
scored.fatal_flaw: The balances are already published by regulators and listed in bankruptcy schedules, so there is nothing to discover and no ML edge. On top of that, the policy rollbacks in the US and Canada and the doubtful transferability in the UK and EU cap the step-up at about 2-5x, with only a few buyers who set the price.
scored.one_line_reason: This is a legal and brokerage arbitrage on assets that are already legible and already priced. No discovery rung exists, the step-up is about 2-5x, and the hit-rate lever is about 1x.

scored.name: Claim Harbor: contractors with unasserted REA/CDA claims
scored.one_line: Acquire small contractors holding unfiled equitable-adjustment claims (Anti-Assignment Act bars buying claims directly); ML reconstructs government-caused changes; file and settle or sell to funders.
scored.unproven_right: Equity in contractor entity.
scored.proving_step: Certified claim and CO decision or board settlement.
scored.proven_buyer: Burford, Parabellum, contingency firms; Judgment Fund pays.
scored.public_data: FPDS mods, ASBCA/CBCA/COFC decisions, USAspending; core data private.
scored.frame: The rung would be: own an unasserted claim, then prove it by getting a certified CDA claim decided or settled. Finding the claim is maybe 20-30% of that work. The other 70-80% is building entitlement and quantum from the contractor's own records (daily logs, correspondence, cost records), certifying the claim, negotiating with the contracting officer and often litigating at the ASBCA, CBCA or Court of Federal Claims for 1-4 years. My estimate: that legal and accounting proof is the bespoke plant here, the same failure as geothermal in coal mines. Funders and the Judgment Fund pay, so a capitalised buyer exists, but the output cannot be sold apart from the contractor entity, because 31 USC 3727 and 41 USC 6305 bar assigning the claim.
scored.step_up: No step-up from near zero. To get the claim you have to buy an operating contractor at a normal SDE/EBITDA multiple (about 2-4x SDE for a small GovCon, my estimate), so most of the price pays for the business, not the claim. If you pay about $0.2-0.5 per expected claim dollar (estimate), the step-up on that slice is 2-5x on a win and 0 on a loss. Litigation funders typically price a CDA claim at 10-40% of face before it is adjudicated (estimate, unsourced). The candidate's own figure of ~10-100x assumes the claim is free, which it is not once you buy the entity.
scored.hit_rate_capex: The base hit rate is not low. Contractors who file a certified claim recover something in most cases: from memory of ASBCA annual reports, most appeals end in settlement or withdrawal, and decided appeals are sustained in whole or part at a rate around 30-50% (estimate, not verified this run). Each proving attempt costs about $50k-$1M+ in legal and claim-consultant fees plus 1-4 years (estimate). The problem is not a low hit rate. It is that the contractor never filed, which is a matter of choice and relationships (fear of losing future work), not missing information. So the ceiling on the ML lever (1/base hit rate) is about 2-3x, not 10x.
scored.data: The signal is mostly private. Entitlement evidence such as directives, delays, differing site conditions and defective specs sits in the contractor's files and the contracting officer's correspondence. FPDS modifications and USAspending show only bilateral mods and changes in obligated value, which hint at scope change but cannot show a compensable government-caused change. Board decisions cover only claims already asserted. The outcome is partly legible already: anything settled appears as a mod in FPDS. Owners can read their own data better than an outsider can, so there is no information asymmetry to buy against. The right can only be bought by acquiring the whole entity, because claims are non-assignable and successor-in-interest rules apply. The CDA's 6-year limitations period (41 USC 7103(a)(4)(A)) also caps the inventory.
scored.right_bought: Only by buying the equity of the whole contractor entity, at going-concern prices, from owners who know about their own unfiled claims. You cannot buy the claim on its own: the Assignment of Claims Act (31 USC 3727) and the Anti-Assignment Act (41 USC 6305) void transfers. Assignment only works for financing to a bank under strict conditions.
scored.buyer: Litigation funders (Burford, Parabellum, LexShares-type) and contingency-fee GovCon firms finance claims; they do not buy them outright. Payment comes from agency funds or the Judgment Fund (31 USC 1304) after a board or court judgment. Incumbents already doing the work: claims consultants (Long International, Ankura, FTI construction claims practice) and GovCon law firms working on contingency.
scored.ladder: Thin. Possible rungs are: claims roll-up, then a GovCon contractor holding company, then a prime contractor. But that turns into a GovCon services roll-up (low margin, priced like PE deals), not a trillion-dollar chain. And the claims business works against the contractor business, because filing claims hurts past-performance relationships with the same agencies.
scored.fatal_flaw: The proving step is bespoke legal litigation that takes years, not a trivial physical step, and the evidence is private to the contractor. On top of that, the claim cannot be assigned, so you have to buy an entire operating company at full price from owners who already know their own claims. That leaves no information asymmetry, no cheap right and no 10^3 step-up.
scored.one_line_reason: This fails on every axis that makes Terranox work. Proving the claim is lawyering, not cheap discovery; the evidence is private, not public and hard to read; the right costs a whole company at going-concern value, not $1/ha; and a win returns about 2-5x, not 10^4.

scored.name: Tritium Sign Harvest
scored.one_line: Take expired tritium exit signs at negative cost and recover tritium and He-3.
scored.unproven_right: Title to expired signs.
scored.proving_step: Collect, count curies, reprocess.
scored.proven_buyer: SRB Technologies, fusion developers, He-3 buyers.
scored.public_data: NRC GL registrations, sign event reports, GSA/DoD surplus.
scored.frame: The rung would be "take title to expired signs, then collect and reprocess them." There is almost no discovery in it, likely under 5% of the work (my estimate). Every sign's tritium content is printed on its label. The NRC general-licence registration and the sign's install date give the starting curies, and decay is fixed (12.32-year half-life). Nearly all the work is physical and regulatory: reverse logistics under licence, breaking the tubes, and recovering gas at a licensed facility. That is the opposite of the 95/5 split.
scored.step_up: About 1x or less, often negative (all of these are my estimates; the search budget was used up and no live searches ran). A new sign holds about 10-25 Ci, and an expired 15-20-year-old sign has about 3-8 Ci left. At roughly 9,600 Ci per gram and roughly $30k per gram of tritium, that is about $3 per Ci, or about $10-25 of tritium per sign. Accumulated He-3 is a few mL STP per sign, at about $2-20 per mL, so roughly $10-70, and some of it has already leaked out. Owners pay about $100-300 per sign for take-back (my estimate, and this is the "negative cost"). The fee covers reprocessing, so the gas recovered is worth about as much as the processing costs. There is no jump from near zero to 10^3.
scored.hit_rate_capex: The base hit rate is about 100%: every registered sign contains tritium in a known, declining amount. There is no failed proving attempt for ML to avoid, so the lever is capped at 1/1.0 = 1x. The cost per attempt is collection plus licensed processing, about $50-150 per sign (my estimate).
scored.data: The outcome is already written in legible fields. NRC 10 CFR 31.5/32.51 general-licence registrations and the sign's own label record isotope, curies and manufacture date, and the Agreement-State registries hold the same data. There is no illegible signal to pull out. The NRC lost/stolen event reports could help locate signs, but that is a logistics benefit, not discovery.
scored.right_bought: Title is acquired at negative cost, because owners pay to be rid of the signs. But the owners know exactly what they hold, so there is no information gap. Incumbents already run take-back programmes: SRB Technologies, Isolite, Shield Source / Best Lighting and the manufacturers' official recycling channels, which are the obvious exit for 10 CFR 31.5 licensees.
scored.buyer: Possible buyers are SRB Technologies, which re-uses tritium in new light sources; fusion developers, though tritium from signs is a negligible gram-scale amount next to their kg-scale needs; and He-3 buyers such as cryogenics firms, DOE isotope programme customers and quantum dilution-fridge makers. The buyers exist, but the volumes are tiny. The world's whole sign inventory is probably only tens of grams of tritium (my estimate).
scored.ladder: The ladder is weak. Above sign reprocessing sit tritium supply for radioluminescent manufacturing, which is a small niche, and He-3 supply. Real He-3 and tritium scale comes from reactors (CANDU heavy-water detritiation at Ontario Power Generation, Savannah River) and future lunar or fusion breeding. Sign harvesting gives no path toward any of those.
scored.fatal_flaw: There is no discovery problem. The tritium content of every sign is printed on its label and in NRC registrations, and it decays on a fixed schedule. The hit rate is about 100% and the step-up is about 1x, while licensed reverse logistics is the whole job. It is a regulated recycling service with tiny volumes, and the manufacturers already run it.
scored.one_line_reason: This is recycling, not discovery. The outcome (curies) sits in legible fields, every attempt "hits", and the gas recovered barely pays for licensed processing, so there is no 10^3 step-up and no ML lever.

verified.name: Orphan Patent Evidence-of-Use (bankrupt estates, FCC/teardown proof; incl. semiconductor, photonics, mature-node)
verified.one_line: Buy patents from Chapter 7/11 estates, ABC sales, dead startups (fabless, LiDAR, photonics, quantum, microLED) and lapse-bound owners for $2-50k; ML maps claims against FCC internal photos, teardowns, die shots, SEM cross-sections, datasheets, driver code and papers to build evidence-of-use charts; sell charted patents to NPEs, aggregators, defensive pools and funders.
verified.unproven_right: Issued patents with remaining term sold in bulk unread by trustees and lapse-bound owners.
verified.proving_step: ML claim-to-product mapping, attorney-verified EoU chart, occasional paid teardown or cross-section ($5-20k), PTAB-survival model.
verified.proven_buyer: RPX, AST, Unified Patents, LOT Network, Dominion Harbor, Acacia, Atlantic IP, IP Edge, Intellectual Ventures-style funds, Burford, Fortress IP, Parabellum, Western IDMs for cross-licence leverage.
verified.public_data: USPTO full text, assignments, maintenance events, PTAB; FCC EAS (fccid.io) internal photos; PACER 363 notices and schedules; die-shot archives; IEDM papers; Linux driver source; ITC 337 dockets; Ocean Tomo/IAM results.
verified.rough_step_up: ~100-1000x per charted hit; base charting hit rate ~1-5%, so ML could cut cost per hit 10-20x.
verified.frame: The rung is "own an unread orphan patent, then hand a buyer a charted, attorney-verified evidence-of-use package." Inside that rung, discovery (finding the infringing product and mapping the claims) is about 80-90% of the work, and the physical step (an occasional teardown or cross-section) is cheap. The catch is that the chart is not the proven asset. It is an opinion. The real value is only realised later through licensing or litigation, which takes years, costs millions per case and carries a ~65-70% PTAB invalidation risk on instituted claims. Buyers know this and discount heavily for it. Zoomed out to the whole monetisation chain, discovery is perhaps 10-20% of the work. So the 80%+ frame exists, but it is a pre-proof frame, not a proving frame like a drill hit.
verified.step_up: Unproven: patents from distressed estates, lapse-bound owners and bulk ABC sales typically clear at roughly $2k-$30k each (my estimate from memory of bankruptcy 363 sales and broker lots; not verified this run). Proven: brokered US patents have averaged about $100k-$250k asking per asset in Richardson Oliver Insights market reports across 2013-2022 (from memory), and only roughly 25-30% of listed packages sell. A strong EoU-charted asset reading on a large product might reach $250k-$1M. Realistic step-up is about 10-30x, with outliers at 100x. The "unproven" asset is not near zero; it already trades at four to five figures. That is far from Terranox's 10^4.
verified.hit_rate_capex: My estimates, not verified this run: perhaps 1-5% of random orphan patents read on a currently shipping product with enough remaining term and damages to be worth charting. A manual attorney chart costs about $3k-$15k, and a teardown or SEM cross-section adds $5k-$20k. Cost per hit today is therefore roughly $100k-$1M. ML triage could plausibly cut that 5-20x, which is a real lever, capped at 1/base rate (about 20-100x). Charting is already being automated by several AI patent-analytics startups, so the lever is not proprietary.
verified.data: The data is public and partly illegible: FCC internal photos, die shots, driver source, datasheets, PACER 363 schedules. The outcome (does it read on a product?) is NOT summarised in any legible field; USPTO only records legal status, assignments and maintenance fees. That part passes the rubric. It is weakened in two ways. Large-company products are already torn down and charted by TechInsights-style firms and aggregators. And the AI claim-charting tools (my recollection, unverified this run, includes Patlytics, IPRally and Amplified) make this extraction increasingly commodity.
verified.right_bought: Yes. The rights are bought, not claimed free first-come, from trustees, ABC assignees and lapse-bound owners who lack the expertise or budget to chart. Prices are low, but brokers (e.g. ICAP Ocean Tomo, Tangible IP) and aggregators already shop bankruptcy estates and surface the best lots. The discount is real only in the long tail. Remaining term and maintenance-fee deadlines also limit the window.
verified.buyer: The buyers are RPX and AST (defensive), Unified Patents, and NPEs and aggregators such as Dominion Harbor and Acacia, plus litigation funders like Burford and Fortress. This is a thin and cyclical market. Volumes are well below the 2011-2014 peak, there are few buyers per asset, and they pay for evidence of use but heavily discount for PTAB risk and time-to-cash. They are capitalised, but unlike a mine developer they cannot readily "develop" the asset at a known cost and payoff.
verified.ladder: The rungs above are: buy and chart, then sell to aggregators, then license directly, then run your own assertion campaigns (NPE), then fund your own and others' litigation, then become a large IP fund or defensive pool. The ceiling is the patent-monetisation market, about low-single-digit $B per year in licensing and settlements. Acacia, Intellectual Ventures and RPX are examples of peak outcomes, in the $1-5B range. There is no realistic trillion-dollar path, and the top rungs carry reputational and legal friction (anti-troll legislation, PTAB).
verified.fatal_flaw: The proving step does not actually prove anything. An evidence-of-use chart is a contestable opinion whose value is only realised after years of licensing or litigation (about $2-5M per case to trial, with roughly 65-70% of instituted PTAB final decisions invalidating all challenged claims). So buyers pay roughly 10-30x, not 10^3-10^4x, and the market is thin. The ladder tops out at a few-$B NPE or fund, not a trillion-dollar chain.
verified.one_line_reason: This is a real ML discovery edge on cheap, illegible orphan patents. But the hit only becomes an opinion, the step-up is about 10-30x into a thin NPE/aggregator market that discounts for PTAB risk, and the ladder caps at a few-billion-dollar patent fund.

The WebSearch budget for this turn was already used up, so I fetched the primary source directly: the 2025 Richardson Oliver Patent Market Report, which covers calendar 2024 and is based on 19,000+ tracked packages and 340,000+ assets.

1) The proving step barely moves the price. Packages that come with evidence-of-use (EoU) material sold at a premium of 32% to 108% over the past five years. That is a step-up of about 1.3-2.1x, not 100-1000x. Only about 21% of listed packages carry an EoU.

2) The proven asset is not worth much. These are 2024 median asking prices:
   - $163k per asset, $286k per US-issued patent, $325k per family (all listed assets).
   - Sold assets only: $95k per asset in 2024, $33k in 2023, $63k in 2022.
   - Closing prices are discounted 0% to 75%+ below asking, and 25-55% time discounts were applied in the market-size model.
   So a realised price per charted asset is roughly $30k-$100k. The finalist's own estimate puts estate and distressed lots at about $2k-$30k each (from memory, not verified). Against that, the full step-up is about 3-30x, and the part attributable to charting is under 2.1x.

3) The market is small. The entire secondary patent market in 2024 was $158M, flat with 2022 and 2023, and the report calls it "advantageous to buyers... rarely competing buyers." In 2024, 1,611 packages were listed, covering 22,795 assets (median 2 assets per package). The sold-package chart tops out at about 300-400 packages a year. NPEs bought only about 2% of assets sold in 2024 (likely understated because of recording lag). Defensive aggregators are moving to licensing models instead of buying assets.

4) The ML edge is becoming a commodity. The report itself says AI tools such as Patlytics produce "a full claim element-by-element analysis against product specifications... at relatively low costs." It also notes that sellers already use ChatGPT and similar tools to build EoUs, so the charting lever will not stay proprietary.

5) Some buyers exist, but none pays a step-up at once. There is no counterpart to a mine developer paying 10^4x the instant a drill hits.

The median sold asset asked only $33k-$95k in 2023-2024, before closing discounts of up to 75%. The whole secondary market is about $158M a year, with roughly 300-400 packages sold and rarely more than one buyer per package. The step-up from charting is far below the ~30x refutation threshold, and AI EoU tools such as Patlytics are already commoditising the proving step.

Search limit: WebSearch was exhausted on the first call because the shared limit of 200 per turn was already used. I used only direct WebFetch of first-party pages. Figures marked "memory" were not verified this run.

(1) Evidence-of-use charting is already productised.
- Patlytics' own site says its infringement module will "Crawl for evidence of use across public sources" and produce "Citation-backed claim charts."

- Listed customers include Quinn Emanuel, Panasonic IP Corp of America, Canon, Nissan and Rivian, plus an Am Law 100 firm.
- So the core ML step (mapping claims to public product evidence) is a funded commodity tool that NPEs, aggregators and law firms can buy. It is not a proprietary discovery edge.

(2) The outcome has legible proxies, and vendors sell scores on them.
- Patent value is routinely triaged from structured USPTO fields: forward and examiner citations from large-company filings, maintenance-fee payment, family size, remaining term and litigation history.
- Commercial patent-value scores built on these fields are sold by PatentSight (LexisNexis), Clarivate/Derwent, Ocean Tomo PatentRatings, and litigation data from RPX, Docket Navigator and Lex Machina (memory).
- Teardowns and die shots are sold by TechInsights, which also offers patent-licensing claim-chart support (memory).
- The illegible-data premise holds only for the long tail: small fabless, photonics and LiDAR products that TechInsights has not covered.

(3) The "unread by owner" premise is weak.
- Distressed-estate IP is usually marketed by specialist liquidators and brokers, not left unread by trustees. These include Hilco Streambank, Tangible IP, ICAP Ocean Tomo, and the Richardson Oliver-tracked brokered market (memory).
- Buyers of exactly this inventory already exist: Dominion Harbor, IP Edge, Atlantic IP, Acacia and Sisvel.
- Richardson Oliver's 2023 report page says "If you were a buyer, 2023 was a good time to be in the market" and predicts 2024 as "a buyer's bonanza and a seller's struggle." That describes cheap assets and thin demand, not a hidden discount.
- The 2025 report page says only that prices are "stabilising" and "better" (richardsonoliver.com). Average asking price is about $100-250k per US asset (memory).

(4) PTAB risk is lower than the finalist claimed, a partial correction in the finalist's favour.
- Source: USPTO PTAB FY26 Q3 Outcome Roundup, petitions filed Oct 2025 to Jun 2026, 1,096 petitions.
- Institution was denied for 545 petitions (50%). Only 197 (18%) ended with all claims unpatentable; 78 (7%) found all claims patentable and 151 (14%) settled.
- 47% of instituted claims were found unpatentable, not the finalist's 65-70%.
- This modestly raises the value of a charted orphan patent, so C2 stays at about 2.5.

(5) The hit rate is low but the lever is limited.
- Base hit rate is about 1-5% (estimate). A manual chart costs roughly $3-15k (memory), so a single attempt is cheap.
- The expensive and uncertain part is monetisation: litigation at $2-5M per case to trial (AIPLA, memory). ML does not shrink that.
- An ML triage lever exists, but competitors can buy the same lever off the shelf.
verifiers.killer: The ML edge is not proprietary and the outcome is not hidden. Patlytics (with a $40M Series B, and Quinn Emanuel and Panasonic IP among its customers) already automatically crawls public sources for evidence of use and outputs citation-backed claim charts. TechInsights sells the teardowns and die shots. Legible USPTO fields (forward and examiner citations, maintenance fees, term, litigation) plus commercial patent-value scores (PatentSight, Ocean Tomo, RPX) already triage which orphan patents matter. Specialist liquidators and brokers (Hilco Streambank, Tangible IP, ICAP Ocean Tomo) market estate portfolios directly to the same NPE and aggregator buyers. What remains is a long-tail arbitrage of about 10-30x into a buyer's market that Richardson Oliver itself calls "a buyer's bonanza and a seller's struggle." LIMITATION: the shared web search budget was already used up when this check started. Both WebSearch calls were refused, a WebFetch of the USPTO PTAB statistics page returned only links to PDFs and no figures, and the ROI reports URL returned a 404. Nothing below was verified this run. It is reasoned from statute and from memory of well-known cases.

The lens checked three things: whether the right can be bought, whether the physical step is trivial, and whether a hard exclusion applies.

(1) CAN THE RIGHT BE BOUGHT: yes, legally and outright.
- Patents are freely assignable (35 USC 261), and a bankruptcy 363 sale passes title free and clear, so there is no first-come-claim problem. It passes the "bought, not free" test.
- The claim that owners "cannot read the data" holds only in the long tail.
- Any estate with visible value is run through brokers and auctioneers with stalking-horse and overbid procedures. Nortel 2011 opened with a $900M stalking horse and closed at $4.5B. Kodak 2012 is another example. Trustees also routinely retain IP brokers or auction firms (Hilco Streambank, Tangible IP, ICAP/Ocean Tomo-type houses).
- So the cheap, unread lots are mostly the ones with the lowest base hit rate. The discount and the hit rate are anti-correlated.
- Lapse-bound owners: the patent must be bought before or within the 6-month maintenance-fee grace period.
  - After a lapse, revival under 37 CFR 1.378 needs a statement that the delay was "unintentional". A deliberate abandonment that is bought and then revived carries the risk of a false statement or inequitable conduct.
  - Revived patents also carry intervening rights (35 USC 41(c)) against anyone who began use during the lapse.
  - This narrows the cheap supply to a timing window, but it does not remove it.

(2) IS THE PHYSICAL STEP INSIDE THE FRAME TRIVIAL: yes.
- Charting is desk work.
- A teardown or SEM cross-section is a bounded $5k-20k cost (my estimate), not a bespoke build.
- So the rung itself does not fail the geothermal test.
- The geothermal-like problem sits one rung up. Realising the value means licensing or litigation, which is bespoke, costs millions per case and is probabilistic (PTAB, §101, claim construction). That is the counterpart of "building the plant is harder than finding the mine". The buyer absorbs it, and that is why the buyer discounts the price.
- Unlike a mine developer at about $40k in and $100k out, an NPE's cost to develop the asset is neither known nor bounded.

(3) NEW DISCOUNTS FOR ORPHAN PATENTS that the finalist did not flag:
- Marking (35 USC 287): dead startups that shipped unmarked products leave damages starting only from actual notice.
- Six-year look-back (35 USC 286).
- Short remaining term.
- Together these compress what a charted orphan patent is worth compared with brokered averages, which pushes C2 down. The finalist's own estimate of roughly 10-30x already sits in the 2-3 band, so C2 goes to 2.

(4) HARD EXCLUSIONS: none.
- The company owns the patent and sells the asset itself, so this is not "selling a service to incumbents".
- It involves no drilling or prospecting.

Verdict on this lens:
- The right can be bought and the in-frame step is trivial, so the finalist is not refuted on right and frame.
- C4 drops slightly because the discount is concentrated where hits are rarest.
- C1 drops slightly because the dominant cost (litigation) is pushed onto a buyer who prices it in.
verifiers.killer: The rung passes the right-and-frame lens: patents can be bought outright, and charting is trivial desk work. But the geothermal problem reappears one rung up. Turning a chart into cash means bespoke, uncertain litigation, and the buyer prices that in. The cheap, unread supply is also exactly the long tail where hits are rarest, because valuable estates are brokered and auctioned competitively (Nortel). Marking (§287), the six-year damages limit (§286), maintenance-lapse revival limits and intervening rights cut the value further. The result is a thin 10-30x step-up rather than 10^4.

RIGHT (buyable?): yes. Farmland options and fee purchases are legal, scalable and cheap relative to the exit, so a real purchase discount exists, unlike brownfields. But owners are not data-blind. Data-center land prices are heavily publicised, and farmers near substations increasingly price that in (pattern from memory, unverified). The illegible-data edge also fails C4:
- Headroom is decided and allocated by the utility through queue position and collateral, not inferred from documents.

FRAME (physical step trivial?): no. Above the study sit:
- ESA/collateral posting
- network and substation upgrades (years and tens of millions of dollars)
- rezoning, water and fiber
This is the bespoke-buildout pattern of the geothermal-in-coal-mines counter-example. Discovery is a minority of the rung.

STEP-UP: a study-only or will-serve site gets roughly 2-5x (estimate). The 30-100x land jump (powered land at $300k-2M+/acre, from memory) needs contracted capacity, which takes capital and not ML.

HIT-RATE LEVER: about $100k+ per attempt against a $10-100M exit, so discovery capex does not bind, and the lever is capped at about 3-6x.

LADDER: genuinely strong: powered shell, then own substation or behind-the-meter generation, then campus developer.

verified.unproven_right: Pending US continuation plus priority chain and specification.
verified.proving_step: ML maps spec paragraphs and figures to teardowns, FCC photos, manuals, competitor filings, code; $3-60k prosecution; notice of allowance plus chart is the hit.
verified.proven_buyer: Burford, Fortress IP, Dominion Harbor, IP Edge, RPX, AST, IV, and OEMs buying defensively (CATL, LG, Panasonic, Tesla, Amazon Robotics, Figure, Agility).
