verified.rough_step_up: ~50-1000x per hit; base hit rate under 5%.
verified.frame: The rung is: buy a family with a pending continuation, get a claim allowed that reads on a shipping product, and sell the asset with an EoU (evidence of use) chart. Inside that rung, finding the right spec support and the right target product is maybe 60-70% of the work (my estimate). The physical step, prosecution, is not trivial. It takes 1-3 years and $3-60k, and the examiner pushes back on written description (35 USC 112, Ariad/Novozymes). The bigger problem is that the asset's value is only realised later through assertion or litigation, at $2-5M+ per case under AIPLA survey ranges. Survival risk sits on top of that: PTAB IPR institution and Alice 101 invalidation. So the proven buyer is pricing litigation risk, not a drill core. The frame exists and buyers exist, but discovery is not 80%+ of the work.
verified.step_up: From memory, not verified this run (the search budget was used up): Richardson Oliver Insights brokered-market reports put average asking prices around $100-250k per US asset, and older reports were higher. Small-inventor, auction and bankruptcy patents often clear at $5-50k. A family with an allowed claim that a strong EoU chart shows reading on a high-volume product might sell for $250k-$2M to an NPE or a defensive aggregator such as RPX or AST. Outlier litigation outcomes can be 10^4x, but those take years and a contingency trial. Realistic immediate step-up: about 10-50x on a hit, not the claimed 50-1000x and nowhere near 10^3-10^4.
verified.hit_rate_capex: Allowance itself is easy. Continuations are allowed at high rates (my estimate: 70-90%, consistent with overall USPTO allowance rates). The real hit is an allowed claim that is both valid and infringed by a shipping product and that survives a buyer's diligence. Commonly cited figures say only about 1-5% of issued patents are ever licensed or asserted (my estimate, not sourced this run). Cost per attempt: $5-100k to buy plus $3-60k to prosecute, so roughly $20-150k. ML could plausibly raise the hit rate 3-5x. The ceiling is set by the 1/base-rate cap and by legal-validity risk that ML cannot reduce. Capex falls maybe 3-5x, not 10x.
verified.data: The data is public and largely already legible. USPTO bulk full text, PatentsView, Patent Center file wrappers and assignment data are all structured, and pendency status (pending continuation, PTA, expiration) is literally a legible status field. Specs are text, not scanned. The teardown side (FCC photos, iFixit, TechInsights) is less legible, but TechInsights already sells exactly this mapping to assertion firms. LLM claim-chart and EoU tools (Patlytics, Solve Intelligence, IPRally, ClaimMaster and others) are already doing the spec-to-product matching. The edge is thin.
verified.right_bought: Yes, the rights are bought. Sellers are small inventors, startups, and bankruptcy estates (via 363 sales). Some of them cannot read the option value of a live continuation, so a pricing gap exists. But brokers (Tangible IP, ICAP/Ocean Tomo auctions, Iceberg) and aggregators (IV, Dominion Harbor, IP Edge, Acacia) actively screen for live continuations as a premium feature. Bankruptcy trustees commonly use brokers too. The discount is real but not 10^4.
verified.buyer: Capitalised buyers do exist: litigation funders such as Burford and Fortress, NPEs and aggregators such as Dominion Harbor, IP Edge, Acacia and IV, and defensive buyers such as RPX and AST. OEMs buy defensively mainly through RPX and AST pools rather than one asset at a time. Their pricing discounts for IPR, Alice and litigation duration.
verified.ladder: There are rungs above. The next ones are acquire, prosecute, then assert or license directly, then fund your own litigation and run a portfolio licensing program. Above that you could become an Acacia/IV-scale aggregator. That top is bounded: the biggest examples are a few billion dollars (IV raised about $6B; Acacia's market cap is under $1B). The ladder ends in a litigation business with regulatory and reputational ceilings, not a trillion-dollar chain. It does not connect to making the products.
verified.fatal_flaw: This is already the standard NPE playbook. IP Edge, Dominion Harbor, IV and Acacia, plus brokers who screen for live continuations, already buy families with pending continuations and draft claims to read on shipping products. Pending status is a legible field, and LLM claim-charting tools are commoditising the matching. The proven value is not realised on allowance: it depends on years of litigation exposed to IPR and Alice. That caps the immediate step-up at about 10-50x rather than 10^3-10^4 and leaves no illegible-data moat.
verified.one_line_reason: Real frame and real buyers, but the step-up is only ~10-50x and depends on litigation. Continuation status is legible, incumbents already run this playbook, and the ladder ends in an NPE business worth billions at most.

verifiers.evidence:
No new web evidence was gathered. The shared 200-call WebSearch budget was used up before this verifier ran: both searches were refused, and one direct USPTO dashboard fetch returned no numbers. Everything below is statute, case law or prior knowledge, and is flagged as such.

RIGHT, buyable legally: yes. US patents and pending applications can be assigned under 35 USC 261, and the assignment is recorded in the public USPTO assignment database. Bankruptcy estates sell them under 11 USC 363, often through broker-run auctions. Amending or adding continuation claims to cover a competitor's product you already know about is lawful (Kingsdown v. Hollister, Fed. Cir. 1988). The limits are written-description support (Ariad 2010) and prosecution laches (Hyatt v. Hirshfeld, Fed. Cir. 2021). So the right can be bought and the strategy is legal.

RIGHT, buyable cheaply and at scale: weak.
(a) A live continuation is a wasting asset. It must stay pending, which means the owner keeps paying for prosecution. The distressed small owners who would sell cheaply are the ones most likely to have let it lapse. That leaves a narrow timing window and limits deal flow.
(b) "Owners who cannot read the data" is undercut by the channel the deals go through. Trustees and small inventors usually sell through brokers (Tangible IP, Iceberg, ICAP/Ocean Tomo-style auctions), and those brokers advertise pending continuations as a premium feature. NPE buyers such as IP Edge, Dominion Harbor and Acacia screen for them.
(c) Continuation status is a legible field in Patent Center and PatentsView. The data edge sits only in mapping specs to products, and LLM claim-charting tools (Patlytics, Solve Intelligence, IPRally) are commoditising that.
So the pricing gap exists but is probably 2-10x, not 10^3-10^4.

FRAME, the physical step: this is the strongest part. Prosecution is a legal step, not a physical one. It is cheap and can be outsourced (Track One prioritized exam roughly $1.8-4.5k plus attorney fees, about 12 months to final disposition, prior knowledge), so it is nothing like building a bespoke geothermal plant. Hard exclusions: none. The company owns the asset, so this is not a service sold to incumbents, and there is no drilling.

What dominates instead is realisation, not discovery. Buyers price an allowed claim plus an EoU chart against $2-5M+ litigation (AIPLA survey, prior knowledge), IPR and Alice 101 risk, and multi-year timelines. The brokered market also has low sell-through: many listed packages never sell (prior knowledge from Richardson Oliver reports). The rung's output is therefore not like a drill core that clears immediately. Possible tailwind, unverified: 2025 USPTO changes that increased IPR discretionary denials may have raised patent-owner leverage.

Revised scores and total:
- C1 = 3: the frame and buyers are real, and prosecution is not physical, but the buyer is pricing litigation, not proof.
- C2 = 2: a realistic immediate step-up on resale is about 5-30x, from roughly $20-50k all-in to $100-500k.
- C3 = 2: allowance base rates are already high. The scarce outcome is "valid, infringed, sells", and ML moves that perhaps 2-4x.
- C4 = 2: the data is legible and incumbents already screen it.
- C5 = 2: the ladder tops out at an NPE or aggregator (IV raised about $6B; Acacia is under $1B) and is not a trillion-dollar chain.
- Total: 11.
verifiers.killer: The right can be bought legally (35 USC 261, 363 sales), and prosecution is a cheap legal step, not a bespoke physical build, so this lens does not strictly refute it. But the cheap-right thesis fails in three ways. A live continuation is a wasting asset that distressed owners usually let lapse. The sellers who keep one alive go through brokers who advertise it as a premium. Pending status is a legible USPTO field. And the proven claim's value is still set by litigation, IPR and Alice risk rather than by the discovery, so the immediate step-up is about 5-30x, not 10^3-10^4.

verified.frame: The rung is buying an untraceable LLP or engine and selling it as a certified serviceable part. Inside that rung, proving the history is about 85-90% of the work (my estimate). Capitalised buyers do exist: lessors (AerCap Engines, Willis Lease, FTAI) and USM dealers (AAR, GA Telesis). The problem is what proving means here. So the discovery share is real but legal and archival, not predictive.

My guess is that most recoveries fail when a gap in the operator's records cannot be closed, with a base success rate perhaps 10-30%. That would cap the lever at about 3-10x. Even then, ML can only rank which parts are likely to be recoverable. It cannot make a recovery succeed, because the missing link is a private document that either exists or does not.

Single high-value disks (fan disk, HPT stage 1 disk) list at about $400-700k, and LPT disks and shafts at about $100-300k. A used serviceable part is priced at the remaining-life fraction of catalog, minus a USM discount (typically 20-40%). A recovered part with 30-50% life left on a $300k-list LLP therefore sells for about $60-150k. The finalist's $100k-$1M per part overstates it: $1M would be more than catalog list for almost any single CFM56-7B or V2500 LLP.

(2) Unproven value. LLPs with no trace are normally mutilated or scrapped. The metal (Ti or Ni alloy, tens of kg) is worth hundreds to low thousands of dollars. But the 'zero-life' material actually on offer, which brokers and teardown yards sell as-is, is priced by sellers who know the recovery option exists. That pushes the realistic entry price up to about $5-30k, i.e. a few percent of value, not about $0.

Nowhere does it reach 10^3-10^4. The value is also not realised at once on a 'hit': selling requires a records-firm package, a shop inspection and a buyer's records audit, which takes weeks to months.

But after the 2023 AOG Technics forged-documents scandal (falsified EASA Form 1 and trace documents on CFM56 parts), lessors and MROs became far stricter about reconstructed or sworn-statement trace on LLPs. Many will not accept back-to-birth gaps closed by affidavit. So a capitalised buyer does not reliably pay the step-up.

(5) Market size. The number of no-trace LLP recoveries per year is unknown, most likely hundreds to low thousands of parts, worth perhaps $50-300M a year in recovered value. That is a niche already worked by records specialists.

verifiers.evidence:
The shared web-search budget was used up (200 per turn across all agents), so both searches I tried returned nothing. I fetched the primary regulations directly instead. Every market figure below is an estimate and none was verified.

(1) The regulations confirm that proving means documents, not discovery. 14 CFR 43.10(c)(1) says the control record must "substantiate the part number, serial number, and current life status". 43.10(d) says a transferor "must transfer with the part the mark, tag, or other record". 91.417(a)(2)(ii) requires records of "the current status of life-limited parts of each airframe, engine...", and 91.417(b)(2) says the records are "retained and transferred with the aircraft". So a part's value depends on a chain of private documents held by the prior operator, the MRO or the OEM. An ML inference from public data cannot stand in for that chain. 43.10(c)(6) offers mutilation, which must make the part "incapable of being reworked to appear to be airworthy", as the default way to dispose of a part whose status cannot be controlled. Much of the cheapest stock is therefore legally dead before anyone can buy it.

(2) The right can be bought, but the sellers are not people who cannot read the data. Untraced LLPs mostly come from part-out and teardown specialists, lessors and brokers (AerSale, GA Telesis, AAR, FTAI, and recyclers in the Aircraft Fleet Recycling Association, AFRA). Each of them runs its own records team and already prices trace gaps. What is left at scrap is the adverse-selection residue, after sophisticated owners have tried to recover the trace and failed. That reverses the Terranox setup, where sellers are landholders who cannot read the assessment files.

(3) The proving step is bespoke for every part and controlled by third parties: getting tech logs from a defunct airline, OEM birth records, shop visit reports, sworn non-incident statements, and then winning acceptance from a conservative buyer. This looks like the geothermal-plant counter-example, not drilling. The hard work is outside the ML's reach, and success depends on whether a private document exists, not on finding a signal.

(4) No hard exclusion applies. The company owns the part, so this is not a service sale.

(5) The 20-300x step-up is plausible from industry knowledge (a single LLP is worth roughly $100k-$1M serviceable versus scrap metal) but was not verified. Buyers also discount parts with reconstructed trace, and some lessors and airlines will not accept them at all.
verifiers.killer: The proving step is not discovery. It means obtaining private, third-party-held cycle records that 14 CFR 43.10 and 91.417 require to be substantiated and transferred with the part, so ML over public registries can only rank leads, not prove a part. The sellers are records-sophisticated part-out firms and lessors that already price trace gaps. The cheap stock is adverse-selection residue or must be mutilated, which breaks the premise that the right is "bought cheaply from owners who cannot read the data".

verified.name: ShelfClear: rescuing compounds shelved for species-specific tox findings
verified.one_line: Buy shelved preclinical or Phase 1 compounds dropped over tox flags that probably do not apply to humans (rodent liver enzyme induction, PPAR-alpha, alpha-2u-globulin, dog-specific CV). ML predicts which flags are irrelevant; a cheap human-relevant in vitro package clears the flag and the asset is licensed.
verified.unproven_right: Assignment or exclusive licence of a shelved compound and data package from pharma, defunct biotech estates or TTOs, often nominal upfront plus royalties.
verified.proving_step: Targeted mechanistic tox assays at a CRO (human hepatocytes, iPSC-cardiomyocytes, organ-on-chip), ~$0.1-0.3M.
verified.proven_buyer: Mid-size biotechs and pharma BD in-licensing IND-ready assets ($5-50M upfront precedents).
verified.public_data: FDA pharm/tox reviews in Drugs@FDA (scanned), EMA EPARs, NTP, ToxCast/Tox21, patents with in vivo data, ChEMBL, pipeline-discontinuation disclosures.
verified.rough_step_up: ~$0.1M to $10-50M, 100-500x. The flag is legible but its human relevance is not.
verified.frame: The rung is: buy a shelved compound, clear its tox flag, then license it out. Discovery (picking which flags are irrelevant to humans) is maybe 40-50% of the work inside that rung, not 80%+ (my estimate). Clearing the flag is not the sellable output. A buyer in-licensing an IND-ready asset is paying for efficacy, differentiation against the competitive landscape, and freedom to operate (patent life left; shelved compounds have often used up 5-10 years of it). A clean tox package is necessary but nowhere near sufficient. The proving step is also not reliably trivial. FDA and ICH S1B human-relevance arguments usually need mechanistic in vivo work (knockout or humanized mouse studies, or extra carcinogenicity bridging) on top of in vitro assays. Realistically that costs $0.5-3M and takes 12-24 months, not $0.1-0.3M (estimate). The precedent here is the 2004 FDA requirement that PPAR-class compounds complete two-year rodent carcinogenicity studies before any trial longer than six months. That rule caused 18-24 month delays, and in vitro data did not waive it (Ligand 10-K).
verified.step_up: Unproven: shelved assets from TTOs or biotech estates can be had for nominal upfront ($0-1M) plus royalties. But big pharma rarely out-licenses at nominal prices, and it often holds rights back (estimate). Proven: in 2024 the median upfront to preclinical biotechs was $47M, down from $75M in 2022 (JP Morgan via BioStock). Upfronts were about 6% of headline deal value in 2024, and early-stage upfronts were 1.5-3.7% of deal value in 2024-2025 (Goodwin). Those medians come from selected, efficacy-differentiated assets, often in hot modalities. A small-molecule rescue with a historical tox flag and a shortened patent life would more realistically get $2-15M upfront (estimate). On a hit, that is about 10-100x on total invested capital ($0.5-1M acquisition plus proving), not 100-500x.
verified.hit_rate_capex: Base hit rate of the proving step: if the target compound is well chosen, a mechanistic package showing a rodent-specific effect probably works 30-50% of the time. Rodent PPAR-alpha and alpha-2u-globulin mechanisms are textbook and already accepted (estimate). The real failure rate comes after: the share of tox-cleared shelved compounds that actually get licensed for meaningful money is probably 5-15% (estimate). Shelving is often driven by strategy or efficacy and the tox flag is just the stated reason. Cost per attempt: $0.1-0.3M as pitched, realistically $0.5-3M with in vivo bridging, plus acquisition and diligence costs (estimate). With a 30-50% base hit rate on the tox step, ML can lift it at most about 2-3x (lever capped at 1/hit rate). The uncertainty that dominates, licensability, cannot be predicted from public tox data.
verified.data: Mostly the wrong data. Drugs@FDA pharm/tox reviews and EMA EPARs exist only for drugs that were approved or submitted, which by definition were not shelved. Shelved preclinical and Phase 1 compounds almost never have public tox reports. Their tox data sits in the owner's private data room. The owner (the pharma tox team) can read its own data fine and knows the human-relevance frameworks, which are standard ICH S1B and IPCS mode-of-action practice. So the information asymmetry favors the seller. Tox21/ToxCast and ChEMBL are already legible and already mined. The discontinuation reason is often already written in a legible field (pipeline updates, Citeline, Cortellis, AdisInsight list the reason for discontinuation), although that field is frequently a cover story. Competitors in asset rescue and repurposing include Roivant, BridgeBio, Healx, Ligand, Cerevel, Rhizen, Aiolos and many family-office "NewCos". Pharma out-licensing programs (for example NCATS and the MRC-AZ compound library) already make shelved compounds available. The right can be bought, but it is priced by a seller who knows more than the buyer.
verified.right_bought: Bought: an exclusive licence or assignment from pharma, a defunct-biotech estate (via bankruptcy auction) or a TTO, usually low upfront plus milestones and royalties. That part fits the model. The catch is that the seller holds the full data package and the buyer only sees it after an NDA, so there is no public-data edge at the moment of purchase.
verified.buyer: Mid-size biotech and pharma BD in-licensing teams. They are capitalised, but they buy on efficacy, differentiation and patent life, not on tox clearance alone.
verified.ladder: Strong ladder: rescue, then IND, then Phase 1, then Phase 2 proof of concept, then partnering or commercialisation. That is the Roivant/BridgeBio "hub of subsidiaries" path to a large company, with each rung adding value. This is the candidate's best feature, but those rungs are capital-intensive clinical development, not discovery-dominated.
verified.fatal_flaw: The signal is not in public, illegible data. A shelved compound's tox package is private and held by a seller who can read it, and clearing the tox flag is not what a buyer pays for: efficacy, competitive position and remaining patent life set the price. So there is no frame where discovery from public data is 80%+ of the work and the output is sellable on its own.
verified.one_line_reason: This is the stranded-drug-rescue idea that was already killed. The data asymmetry runs toward the seller, the proving step is costlier than pitched, and the step-up depends on efficacy and patent life, not on the tox flag.

verifiers.evidence:
Search limits: the turn-wide WebSearch budget of 200 calls was used up before this verifier's first search ran. One WebFetch to BioStock returned HTTP 403, so the JP Morgan preclinical-upfront medians of $75M falling to $47M, about 6% of deal value, are not verified here. They stay the finalist's own unverified citation. One WebFetch of the Ligand SEC filing did succeed and partly confirms the regulatory claim. Lilly's PPAR agonist LY519818 was to move into Phase III only "after completion of two-year carcinogenicity studies and appropriate consultation with the FDA". So rodent-tumour flags on PPAR agonists were cleared by full in vivo carcinogenicity bridging, not a cheap in vitro package. In the first 100k characters, the filing did not state the six-month threshold or the 18-24 month delay. Everything else below is reasoning from regulatory practice, not freshly verified.

RIGHT: The right can legally be bought as an exclusive licence or assignment from pharma, biotech estates or TTOs. But it is not bought cheaply because of an information edge. The tox data package is private and sits in the seller's data room, visible only after an NDA. The seller's toxicologists already use standard human-relevance frameworks (ICH S1B, IPCS/ILSI mode-of-action) and can read it fine. Drugs@FDA pharm/tox reviews and EPARs exist only for submitted drugs, which by construction were not shelved preclinical or Phase 1 compounds. Discontinuation reasons are already legible fields in Citeline, Cortellis and AdisInsight. The data asymmetry favours the seller, which fails C4. Scale is also weak: there are a few dozen genuinely species-specific tox shelvings a year, and each needs bespoke negotiation.

FRAME: The proving step is not trivial. Regulators clear species-specific flags with mechanistic in vivo work: PPAR-alpha knockout or humanized mice, alpha-2u-globulin histopathology, or a full 2-year bioassay as in the LY519818 case. That is realistically $0.5-3M and 12-24 months. ICH S1B(R1) (2022) allows a weight-of-evidence waiver of the rat bioassay, but the regulator has to agree to it, case by case. Worse, a cleared tox flag is not the sellable output. In-licensors pay for efficacy, differentiation and remaining patent life, and shelved assets have often used 5-10 years of patent term. So the commercial and clinical work dominates, much as building the bespoke plant dominated in the geothermal counter-example. Discovery from public data is well under 50% of the rung.

EXCLUSIONS: No hard exclusion applies. But this is a narrow variant of the already-killed "stranded drug rescue", and nothing here fixes the reason that idea was killed. Ladder (C5): a real clinical-development ladder exists (the Roivant/BridgeBio model), but its rungs are capital-intensive clinical work, not discovery-dominated, so 3 rather than 4.
verifiers.killer: The right can be bought, but not cheaply because of an edge. The shelved compound's tox package is private and held by a seller whose toxicologists read it with standard ICH S1B mode-of-action frameworks, so there is no public-but-illegible signal at the point of purchase. And the proving step is not trivial: regulators cleared PPAR-class rodent tumour flags with 2-year carcinogenicity bridging (the Lilly LY519818 case in Ligand's SEC filing), not a $0.1-0.3M in vitro package. Even then, buyers pay for efficacy and patent life, not for a cleared tox flag, so the physical, clinical and commercial work dominates the rung.

verified.name: Gores: claiming title gaps from deed-description errors
verified.one_line: ML reconstructs every metes-and-bounds description in a county's scanned deeds and finds slivers no current deed covers; buy quitclaims from heirs or successors of the last owner of record and sell the strip to the blocked adjoiner, developer or title insurer.
verified.unproven_right: Residual record title in unconveyed slivers, effectively worth $0 to heirs or defunct entities.
verified.proving_step: OCR plus geometry reconstruction against parcel fabric, chain-of-title trace, one quitclaim and recording.
verified.proven_buyer: Commercial developers and adjoiners blocked at commitment, title insurers (First American, Fidelity), DOTs.
verified.public_data: County recorder deed images back to the 1800s, parcel GIS, state dissolution records, probate indexes.
verified.frame: The rung is "own record title to an unconveyed sliver (gore) and sell it to whoever is blocked by it." Inside that rung, finding the gore is most of the work, maybe 70-80% (my estimate): OCR the deeds, rebuild the metes-and-bounds geometry, trace the chain of title. The physical step is cheap: one quitclaim at roughly $100-1,000 to the heirs plus a recording fee. The weak part is the buyer. A blocked adjoiner or developer is not a buyer of an appreciating asset the way a mine developer is. They pay at most what the next-cheapest cure would cost them, and several cures exist: an uncontested quiet title action ($1.5k-10k, 2-6 months), a title insurer's gaps/strips/gores endorsement (CLTA 116.9 / ALTA 19.2), the strips-and-gores presumption, adverse possession or boundary by acquiescence where the adjoiner has occupied the strip, and marketable title acts that cut off claims more than 30-40 years old. So the frame and the cheap physical step exist, but the buyer's willingness to pay is capped.
verified.step_up: Unproven: a quitclaim from heirs or successors costs about $100-1,000 (the candidate's figure; I did not verify it; heirs often take a nominal amount). Proven: the realistic ceiling is the blocked party's cost to cure another way. That is about $1,500-5,000 for an uncontested quiet title (Alabama Extension) or $3k-10k (LegalClarity), plus the delay. A title-insurer endorsement can be cheaper still. Realistic step-up is about 3-30x, call it ~10x. The candidate's "$10k-500k hold-up" figure only applies in rare cases where a closing deadline is tight and none of the other cures is available. Even then courts and underwriters push back on someone who bought a strip just to hold up a sale. Nothing like 10^3-10^4.
verified.hit_rate_capex: Proving is not the expensive, mostly-failing step. A manual title search or abstract costs about $200-500 (my estimate), and a quitclaim plus recording a few hundred dollars. Once a real gore has been confirmed and its heirs located, getting the quitclaim is cheap and probably works more than half the time (my estimate). Where ML actually helps is the search: geometry reconstruction can find gaps humans never look for. But few of the gaps found will be worth money, because most gores are small, sit under fences that are presumed to settle ownership, or are already covered by insurer endorsements. That share is unknown; my estimate is about 1-5%. The cost that ML would cut 10x is low to begin with, so the lever is real but its dollar value is small.
verified.data: This is the strong criterion. County recorder deed images go back to the 1800s and are public but illegible: scanned, handwritten metes and bounds, scattered across indexes. Gaps between descriptions are not flagged in any legible field. Parcel GIS fabrics hide them by drawing parcels edge to edge. Title plants index by name and parcel; they do not reconstruct geometry. So the outcome is not summarised anywhere public, which beats prior hunts where regulators had already written the answer into a status field. The right can be bought cheaply from heirs or dissolved entities who don't know they hold anything, so it is bought, not claimed first-come. Incumbents (First American, Fidelity, Stewart title plants, and surveyors) find gores one transaction at a time and insure over them or cure them; they do not hunt for them.
verified.right_bought: Quitclaim deeds from the heirs or successors of the last owner of record, about $100-1,000 each (estimate). With unknown or many heirs you may need to buy fractional interests from several people, or bring your own quiet title action.
verified.buyer: Adjoiners or developers blocked at the title-commitment stage, and occasionally DOTs assembling right-of-way. Title insurers are less likely buyers than the candidate assumes: they usually insure over the gap with an endorsement or require a quiet title action rather than buying. The buyer's ceiling is their cheapest alternative cure, roughly $2k-10k.
verified.ladder: The ladder is weak. Possible rungs above: a title-curative services business (but that is selling a service, which the rubric excludes), land assembly for developers, or a title-plant or underwriting business built on a geometry-reconstructed chain of title. That last one is the only large prize, and it is a data business sold to title insurers rather than climbing to own a bigger asset. Owning gores does not lead naturally to developing the land they sit on.
verified.fatal_flaw: Hold-up value is capped by cheap alternative cures. A blocked party can quiet title uncontested for about $1.5k-10k in 2-6 months, buy an insurer's gaps/strips/gores endorsement, or rely on the strips-and-gores presumption, adverse possession or acquiescence, or a marketable title act. Courts also treat strategic gore-buyers as holdouts with little sympathy. The proven value is therefore about ~10x a cheap quitclaim, nowhere near 10^3-10^4, and each deal is a few thousand dollars.
verified.one_line_reason: The data edge here is real (illegible scanned metes and bounds, with gaps flagged in no field), but alternative cures cap the step-up near ~10x and a few thousand dollars per deal, and there is no ladder to a large owned-asset chain.

verifiers.evidence:
Search limit: the shared 200-call WebSearch budget for this turn was already used up when I started, so all three of my searches were refused. I found no real transaction prices for a gore bought from heirs or a gore sold to a blocked party, and no count of how many such deals happen each year. The candidate's $10k-500k hold-up figure therefore has no evidence behind it. Everything below comes from fetching the candidate's own cited sources.

(1) Cost of the alternative cure, which caps what the buyer will pay:
- LegalClarity: an uncontested quiet title action costs $3,000-10,000 in total (attorney flat fee often $1,500-5,000) and takes 2-6 months. A contested one goes "well above $15,000" and takes a year or more.
- Alabama Extension (aces.edu): an uncontested quiet title costs about $1,500-5,000.

(2) Cost of the unproven right, from Alabama Extension:
- Quitclaim preparation is free if done yourself, or $100-600 through an attorney.
- Recording costs about $10 for the first page plus $3 per page.
- A title search costs $75-1,500.
- So a quitclaim costs roughly $100-1,000 all in. This matches the candidate's figure.

(3) What the quitclaim is actually worth, from Pierce Law (NC):
- When a material gap exists, underwriters usually require a quiet title judgment, and "affidavits of heirship and quitclaim deeds can help, but they rarely replace a judgment."
- Under the Marketable Title Act (30-year root), insurers can sometimes insure over old gaps.
- This means the gore-buyer's quitclaim does not by itself give insurable title. A blocked developer can simply name the gore-holder as a defendant in the quiet title action they would file anyway.

(4) Resulting step-up:
- The gore-holder's realistic hold-up value is about the cost of a contested quiet title plus delay, roughly $2k-15k+. That is about 2-150x on a $100-1,000 cost, typically around 10x.
- That is below the ~30x refutation threshold in the typical case, and far below 10^3-10^4.
- The buyer is not a capitalised party paying for an appreciating asset at once. It is a reluctant counterparty with cheaper legal routes.
verifiers.killer: The step-up is capped by what it costs the blocked party to cure the gap another way. An uncontested quiet title costs $1,500-10,000 and takes 2-6 months (Alabama Extension, LegalClarity). A contested one costs about $15k+. Underwriters may also insure over old gaps under marketable title acts. Meanwhile the gore-buyer's own quitclaim "rarely replaces a judgment" (Pierce Law), so the blocked developer just names the holder as a defendant in the quiet title action. Measured against a $100-1,000 quitclaim, the realistic step-up is about 10x and worth a few thousand dollars per deal. No priced transactions or deal-volume data could be found to support the $10k-500k hold-up claim. There is no capitalised buyer paying a 10^3x step-up at once.

Caveat: the shared WebSearch budget (200 calls per turn) was already used up when this verifier started, so every search came back empty. Evidence comes from direct fetches of specific pages; several of those failed (403/404 on Esri docs, rpls.com, First American, Texas GLO). Claims marked (unverified) rest on background knowledge only.

1) The gap-finding step is already a commodity tool. Net Deed Plotter (deedplotter.com) advertises that it can "Find and measure overlaps & gaps" from metes-and-bounds and standard-section descriptions. It also calculates closures and precision ratios and can "search for a defective" deed call. Surveyors and title examiners already plot adjoining deeds and flag gaps on every transaction. The ML edge is therefore only in doing whole-county sweeps (OCR plus automated chain-of-title). Detecting a gap is not new.

2) The outcome is partly in legible fields (unverified). Counties that converted to COGO-built parcel fabrics run topology QA for gaps and overlaps, and many tax rolls and GIS layers carry gap, unknown-owner or no-taxpayer polygons. Not all gores are hidden by edge-to-edge drawing. I could not confirm this from the Esri pages (404s).

3) The bought right does not prove anything. Pierce Law (NC) says affidavits of heirship and quitclaim deeds "usually won't replace a court judgment when a major gap exists." Underwriters generally require a Superior Court action (unknown heirs served by publication, a guardian ad litem appointed) before they will insure. An insurer may also insure over an old gap under the 30-year Marketable Title Act root of title. So the quitclaim bought from heirs is not the proven asset. The buyer or insurer still needs a quiet title action. LegalClarity puts an uncontested quiet title at $3,000-10,000 (attorney $1,500-5,000, filing $200-500, publication $300-1,000) and 2-6 months, which is the most a blocked buyer would pay. If the gore buyer has to bring its own quiet title to make the strip saleable, its cost goes up to $3-13k against a cure ceiling of about the same amount. The step-up for most deals then collapses to about 1-3x, not 10^2-10^3.

4) The hit-rate lever is weak. Proving is not an expensive, mostly-failing step. A title search costs a few hundred dollars and a quitclaim a few hundred more. The binding constraint is the dollar value per hit, not the hit rate, so ML raising the hit rate cuts a capex line that is already small.

5) Competition: I found no evidence of a startup or fund doing county-wide gore sweeps. That empty space looks like the result of poor economics (small hold-up value, MTA cutoffs, strips-and-gores presumption, adverse possession, courts hostile to holdouts), not a missed opportunity. Title plants (First American, Fidelity, Stewart) and AI title firms (Doma, Qualia; unverified) chose to insure over gaps rather than monetise them. That fits the value being small.

So the gore-hunter either eats that cost or sells something worth less than it. Detecting the gap is already a commodity feature of deed-plotting software ("find and measure overlaps & gaps"). Per-deal value is a few thousand dollars with roughly 1-10x step-up, and nothing in the data lens rescues it.

verifiers.evidence:
I got only one new data point. The shared web-search budget was already used up when I started (200 searches per turn across all agents), so every WebSearch call was refused. WebFetch on the rpls.com strips-and-gores forum returned 403, and the CLTA 116.9 endorsement page returned 406. The one source I could read (legalclarity.org) gives these numbers:
- Uncontested quiet title: $3k-10k in total (flat attorney fee $1.5k-5k), taking 2-6 months.
- Contested quiet title: over $15k, at $250-500/hr with a $2k-7.5k retainer, taking a year or more.
The reasoning below is mine, from general doctrine I did not re-check online this turn.
(1) Buying the right is legal and cheap, but what you buy is often empty. Under the strips-and-gores doctrine, when a grantor who owns a narrow strip conveys the land next to it, the strip is presumed to pass to that grantee. So the heirs of the last owner of record often hold nothing, and a quitclaim passes only whatever the grantor actually had. Adverse possession and boundary by acquiescence vest occupied strips (under fences or driveways) in the adjoiner. Marketable title acts cut off claims more than 30-40 years old. Together these probably remove most of the gores the geometry ML finds, which are mostly old.
(2) A quitclaim from one heir often gives only a fractional interest. Getting full title takes several grantors or your own quiet-title action, which costs $3k-10k by the figures above.
(3) A buyer who takes with knowledge of the adjoiner's possession is on inquiry notice. They are not a bona fide purchaser and get no equitable sympathy as a holdout.
(4) The step inside this frame that matches drilling is not trivial. To get paid you have to hold record title against a blocked party, so the real 'physical' step is litigation. If the adjoiner sues to quiet title and you contest it, both sides spend over $15k and wait a year or more, and the case often turns on the doctrines above, which favour the adjoiner. Each gore is its own fight with its own facts. That is the bespoke-geothermal-plant pattern again, not a cheap commodity drill.
(5) The candidate's own cap on step-up holds, adjusted. Contesting raises the blocked party's cost to cure from about $3k-10k to over $15k. Insurers can also insure over the gap with a gaps/strips/gores endorsement, so the realistic step-up is about 10-30x, and every deal is negotiated one at a time.
(6) Hard exclusions: none applies. There is no drilling or prospecting, and the company owns the asset rather than selling a service, but the only large ladder rung is a title-plant data business sold to underwriters.
Revised total: 10 of 25.
verifiers.killer: Usually there is nothing for the heirs to sell. The strips-and-gores presumption sends a gore along with the adjoining conveyance. Adverse possession or acquiescence gives an occupied strip to the adjoiner, and marketable title acts cut off old record claims. So the cheap quitclaim often conveys an empty or fractional interest. Getting paid means litigating against the adjoiner one case at a time, contested quiet title runs over $15k and a year or more, and the holdout buyer is on inquiry notice. The step that matters inside the frame is a bespoke legal fight, not a trivial physical step.

verified.name: DeadPatent Hits: re-proving unlicensed university compound patents against new targets
verified.one_line: ML over unlicensed university chemistry/biology patents and assay tables finds compounds hitting targets that became valuable after filing (GLP-1R small molecules, KRAS, NLRP3, Lp(a), TL1A). Option from the TTO, resynthesise and assay at a CRO, then license to biotech.
verified.unproven_right: Exclusive options or licences on issued but unlicensed university patents, ~$10-50k.
verified.proving_step: Resynthesis plus potency, selectivity and ADME assays at a CRO, ~$50-150k and 6-10 weeks; binary and mostly failing.
verified.proven_buyer: Biotechs, venture studios and pharma BD buying composition-of-matter starting points ($1-20M upfront).
verified.public_data: USPTO/EPO full text and compound listings, SureChEMBL, PubChem BioAssay, ChEMBL, AUTM/TTO listings, NIH RePORTER.
verified.rough_step_up: ~100-500x. Remaining patent life on old filings is a weakness; target 3-8 year old filings.
verified.frame: The rung is a preclinical out-licence of a validated hit or early lead. Inside it, discovery (picking compound against target) is perhaps 50-60% of the work, my estimate. Resynthesis, potency, selectivity and ADME are real wet-lab work that a CRO can run, but they are not trivial. More importantly, buyers rarely pay for a bare re-validated hit. Pharma BD pays for optimised leads with in vivo data, and that is a further $1-5M and 12-24 months of medicinal chemistry (estimate). So the rung where discovery is 80%+ does not have a capitalised buyer, and the rung that does have one is dominated by optimisation, not discovery.
verified.step_up: Unproven: a TTO option or licence on an unlicensed patent at about $10-50k (candidate's figure; plausible, since around 60-70% of US university patents are never licensed out, IPWatchdog/LESI). Proven: Harvard-Merck paid $20M upfront for preclinical small-molecule inhibitors, but BioCentury called that atypical. UT-CSPC paid $4.5M upfront for two preclinical candidates, and those were mAbs. My estimate for a re-validated hit with no in vivo data is $0-1M upfront, and many get $0 beyond milestones. That puts the realistic step-up at about 3-30x, not 100-500x, and the value is back-loaded into milestones that only pay if someone else spends the clinical capital.
verified.hit_rate_capex: The candidate puts cost per proving attempt at $50-150k and 6-10 weeks for resynthesis plus an assay panel, which is reasonable for CRO pricing. Published virtual-screening hit rates against a target are typically about 5-30% at the micromolar level (estimate from the literature). Clearing potency plus selectivity plus ADME is lower, perhaps 2-10%. ML already supplies much of the current hit rate, because incumbents dock these same ChEMBL/SureChEMBL compounds. So there is limited room to lift it further. The lever over the existing computational baseline is perhaps 2-3x, not 10x (estimate).
verified.data: This fails the illegibility test. SureChEMBL and ChEMBL already extract patent compound structures and assay values into structured, machine-readable form, and PubChem BioAssay is fully structured. Big pharma and AI-discovery firms (Recursion, Insilico, Iambic, Isomorphic, academic docking groups) already mine exactly this chemical space at scale. The outcome, activity against the new target, is not in a status field, which is a point in favour. But the inputs are legible to everyone, so there is no data moat.
verified.right_bought: Yes, the right can be bought cheaply. TTOs readily grant options for about $10-50k on dormant patents, and around 60-70% of university patents are never licensed out. The weakness is that the right is not scarce or strongly protective. Make-on-demand libraries such as Enamine REAL (tens of billions of compounds at about $100 each) give novel, unencumbered chemotypes for the same target. The old composition-of-matter patent therefore rarely blocks anyone, and a new-use claim on a published compound is weak IP.
verified.buyer: Biotechs, venture studios and pharma BD. They are well capitalised, but for hits they mostly buy from DEL/AI providers on cheap milestone-heavy terms (HitGen and Nuevolution with Merck, upfronts undisclosed and small). They pay real upfronts only for optimised leads or candidates with in vivo data.
verified.ladder: The ladder is strong in principle: hit, then lead, then candidate, IND, clinic, then a full pharma company. That makes it a trillion-dollar-category path, but each rung above the first costs 10-100x more and is not discovery-dominated.
verified.fatal_flaw: Hit substitution. Validated hits are close to a commodity, available from Enamine REAL plus docking or from DEL providers for about $100 per compound with no IP encumbrance. So an old university composition-of-matter patent on a re-validated hit commands little premium, and the valuable step-up happens later, in medicinal-chemistry optimisation, which is not discovery-dominated.

verified.name: Cryptic Clusters / Legacy Actinomycete Libraries: orphaned natural-product collections re-read for novel clusters
verified.one_line: Acquire mothballed pharma and academic actinomycete/fungal natural-product strain and extract libraries cheaply, sequence them, ML-rank silent biosynthetic gene clusters for novel high-value chemotypes (anti-Gram-negative, antifungal, ADC payloads), and ferment or express the top few to prove a compound.
verified.unproven_right: Ownership or exclusive commercial rights to physical strain/extract libraries, often for storage costs or low five figures.
verified.proving_step: Sequencing, ML novelty ranking, elicitation or heterologous expression, LC-MS and activity assay; ~$50-200k per cluster via CROs/biofoundries.
verified.proven_buyer: AMR pharma and funders (GSK, Roche, Basilea, Innoviva, BARDA, CARB-X, AMR Action Fund), oncology and ADC biotechs.
verified.public_data: NCBI/JGI genomes and metagenomes, MIBiG, antiSMASH-DB, NPAtlas, GNPS/MassIVE, scanned NP patents and fermentation literature, ATCC/DSMZ/NRRL catalogues.
verified.rough_step_up: Collection ~$10-100k to a novel validated scaffold worth $1-100M, ~100-1000x. Physical step is less trivial than drilling; antibiotic buyers are weak.
verified.frame: The candidate rung is "own a mothballed strain/extract library, prove one novel bioactive scaffold, sell/license the proven compound." Inside that rung discovery (sequencing + ML novelty ranking of BGCs) is at most ~25-35% of the work; the physical step is the opposite of trivial — elicitation or heterologous expression, fermentation scale-up, isolation, structure elucidation and activity/tox assays run ~$50-200k and 6-24 months per cluster, and across four large-scale heterologous-expression studies only 11-32% of clusters yielded any detectable natural product at all (J Ind Microbiol Biotechnol 2023 review, PMC10727000). So this is structurally the geothermal-in-coal-mine failure mode: finding the right cluster is easier than building the thing that proves it. The buyer side is also the weakest link in the rubric: there is no capitalised buyer standing ready the way a mine developer is. Comparable transaction: Basilea bought Spexis's entire preclinical Gram-negative antibiotic program for up to CHF 2M total including milestones (Jan 2024) — i.e. the "developer" in this analogy is in for hundreds of millions and will only pay single-digit millions for the proven asset. ADC payloads/antifungals are a better buyer pocket than antibiotics, which partially rescues C1 but not the physical-step problem.
verified.step_up: Unproven right: physical legacy libraries have changed hands for storage costs or effectively nothing — Sanofi transferred ~110,000 strains (~80,000 actinomycetes, 70 years of industrial effort) to Fraunhofer IME in 2020 as a shared-resource transfer, no sale price; Ginkgo bought Warp Drive Bio's genome-mining platform including >135,000 bacterial strains and >4M predicted BGCs in 2019 with terms undisclosed (plausibly low single-digit millions given it was a cast-off asset of Revolution Medicines). Deinove licensed access to 400 of Naicons' 45,000 strains, price undisclosed. So call the right $10k-low-7-figures (my estimate anchored on those three). Proven right: a single validated novel scaffold with in vivo activity transacts at roughly CHF 2M (Basilea/Spexis, whole program, up to, incl. milestones) to maybe $10-50M upfront for a strong antifungal/ADC payload (my estimate). That is ~10-100x on a per-asset basis, up to ~1000x only if you bought the library for storage costs AND got a best-case oncology payload — but the capex consumed to get there ($50-200k x many clusters, likely $5-20M to one validated scaffold) eats most of the multiple. Unlike the uranium case, the step-up is NOT immediate on a hit and NOT a market-observable repricing of the asset you own; the library does not reprice because one cluster worked.
verified.hit_rate_capex: Base hit rate is genuinely low, which is the candidate's best feature. Detection of any compound from a heterologously expressed cluster: 11-32% (four large-scale studies, 2023 review PMC10727000). Of 50 studies over Jan 2018-Jun 2023, only 63 new natural product families emerged. Probability a given silent cluster yields a novel compound with commercially relevant potency/selectivity/developability: my estimate <1-2%. Cost per proving attempt: $50-200k and months per cluster (candidate's own figure, consistent with CRO/biofoundry pricing; my estimate for a full isolate-to-structure-to-assay cycle is $80-250k). Theoretical ML lever = 1/base rate = 50-100x, so the ceiling is attractive. The problem is that ML can only improve the *selection* term, not the expression/fermentation failure term — and the 11-32% detection failure is overwhelmingly host/regulatory/pathway biology, not picking the wrong cluster. Realistic achievable capex reduction: 2-3x, not 10x. That caps C3 at 3.
verified.data: This is where it breaks against the rubric's hard C4 test. The signal is in NCBI/JGI genomes, MIBiG, antiSMASH-DB, NPAtlas, GNPS/MassIVE — public, yes, but LEGIBLE, not illegible. antiSMASH already annotates every cluster in those genomes automatically and publishes it; antiSMASH-DB, BiG-FAM/BiG-SLiCE and MIBiG already publish cluster-family assignments and novelty distance scores. In Terranox terms, the regulator has already written the answer into the status field: "novel cluster family, no known product" is a precomputed, queryable public annotation. Every genome-mining group on earth runs the same query. The genuinely illegible part — scanned fermentation notebooks, old NP patents, which physical strain in which freezer corresponds to which genome — is real but is metadata about *which* box to buy, not about whether the compound works, and the physical libraries are mostly unsequenced, so you pay sequencing capex before you can rank anything. Incumbents already do exactly this at scale: Ginkgo (Warp Drive platform, 135k strains, 4M BGCs), Fraunhofer IME + Sanofi's 110k-strain collection, Naicons (45-65k strains), Hexagon Bio, Lodo Therapeutics. The purchase discount is the one strong element: owners (pharma closing NP units, retiring academics, institutes paying freezer bills) really cannot read their own collections and really do part with them for storage costs.
verified.right_bought: What is bought is ownership or exclusive commercial rights to physical strain/extract collections plus their provenance records — acquirable for storage costs to low five/six figures, which is a genuine 10^2-10^4 discount to replacement cost (70 years of industrial collecting, per Fraunhofer). Critical encumbrance the rubric would want flagged: Nagoya Protocol / CBD access-and-benefit-sharing. Fraunhofer specifically advertises its collection as "all collected before 2014, Nagoya confirmed" — meaning provenance-clean pre-2014 material is the scarce, valuable kind and a library without documented country-of-origin consent may be commercially unusable. Any purchase diligence is ABS diligence. Second encumbrance: legacy pharma libraries often carry residual IP/royalty reach-through to the original owner, so "cheap" rights are frequently non-exclusive or burdened.
verified.buyer: Weak and thin. Antibiotics: AMR Action Fund, CARB-X, BARDA, Innoviva, Basilea, GSK, Roche — but the observable clearing price is CHF ~2M for a whole preclinical Gram-negative program (Basilea/Spexis, Jan 2024), and that market's broken economics are the whole reason the libraries were mothballed in the first place. The buyer is not capitalised in the sense the rubric requires: a mine developer pays $40k/ha because it collects $100k/ha; an AMR buyer does not pay proportionally because its own exit is subsidised and small. Antifungals and ADC payloads are materially better pockets (real oncology/ADC bidders with billions, willing to pay $10-100M+ for a differentiated payload) and are the only version of this thesis with a credible capitalised buyer. Pivoting the thesis entirely to ADC payloads/antifungals would raise C1 and C2 by about a point each; as written, with antibiotics as the headline, the buyer side is the second-biggest flaw.
verified.ladder: The ladder is real and long — library ownership, to validated scaffold, to lead optimization, to IND, to clinic, to approved drug and commercialization — and the top rung is a very large company. But it fails the Terranox property that makes a ladder climbable: each rung up is 10-100x more capital and a completely different capability set (med chem, tox, regulatory, clinical ops), with 10+ year cycle times and no self-sustaining cash from the bottom rung to fund the next. Terranox's rung throws off cash in months and the next rung is adjacent; here rung two alone is a $50-200M, 8-year commitment. Ladder exists, climb is not self-funding.
verified.fatal_flaw: The outcome is already summarised in a legible public field: antiSMASH / antiSMASH-DB / BiG-FAM / MIBiG already auto-annotate and novelty-score essentially every public BGC, so there is no illegible-data edge to exploit — and the proving step is the dominant cost and the dominant failure mode (11-32% of expressed clusters yield any detectable compound at all; $50-200k and 6-24 months each), which inverts Terranox's 95-5 ratio into roughly 30-70. Note: this turn's shared web-search budget was exhausted before I could run my own searches, so this verdict rests on direct fetches of the finalist's own cited transactions plus what those pages actually say. Both load-bearing prices were checked at source and neither supports a 10^3-10^4 step-up.

PROVEN-RIGHT CLEARING PRICE (confirmed, and it is the ceiling, not the floor): Basilea acquired Spexis's ENTIRE preclinical Gram-negative antibiotic program — lead POL7306, an OMPTA-class compound in preclinical development, plus assumed licensing rights and royalty obligations — for "up to SFr2m in upfront, asset transfer and milestone-based payments" (pharmaceutical-technology.com, verified by fetch). So the true immediate cash on a hit is a fraction of CHF 2M, since most of that figure is contingent milestones and asset-transfer fees. A proven novel antibacterial scaffold with in vivo data, i.e. exactly the output of this rung, clears at roughly CHF 0.5-2M. Against the finalist's own stated cost to get there ($50-200k per cluster, $5-20M to one validated scaffold), the proven asset sells for LESS than the capex consumed proving it. That is not a step-up; it is a negative-NPV rung. The uranium analogue requires the proving step to create value a buyer pays for at once; here the buyer pays less than the drill cost.

UNPROVEN-RIGHT PRICE — no observable market, and the two anchors are not purchases at all: (a) Sanofi/Fraunhofer: the Fraunhofer IME page says Sanofi "will share" its >100,000-microorganism collection with Fraunhofer. No sale, no price, and the page I fetched is dated January 2014, i.e. a shared-resource research arrangement, not a transfer of exclusive commercial rights. (b) Ginkgo/Warp Drive Bio (May 2019): confirmed >135,000 bacterial strains and >4M potential BGCs, plus the genome-mining team, technology, database and bioinformatics software — but terms are undisclosed and REVOLUTION Medicines retained all non-genome-mining rights. The finalist's own "$10k-low-7-figures" for the right is explicitly labelled "my estimate"; I could find no verified arm's-length transaction price for a legacy strain library anywhere in its source set. A step-up ratio with an unverified denominator and a verified CHF ~2M numerator cannot be claimed as 10^3x.

STEP-UP ARITHMETIC: best supportable case is library at low-to-mid six figures with exclusive commercial rights (the only version where you can actually sell the output) to a proven scaffold at CHF 0.5-2M = roughly 2-20x, against the lens threshold of ~30x. Even the finalist's own most generous framing lands at ~10-100x only by comparing a storage-cost library to a best-case hypothetical oncology payload — mixing a real floor with an imagined ceiling. And critically, the asset you own does not reprice: a drill hit reprices the hectare you hold, market-observably; one working cluster does not reprice a 50,000-strain freezer, so there is no Terranox-style mark-to-market exit on the thing you bought.

BUYER REALITY AND MARKET SIZE: the antibiotic buyer is not capitalised in the rubric's sense. A mine developer pays $40k/ha because it collects $100k/ha; Basilea paid CHF 2M for a whole program because its own downstream exit is small and subsidy-dependent — the broken economics that mothballed these libraries in the first place. Transaction count is the killer on market size: preclinical antibacterial asset acquisitions of the Basilea/Spexis type occur on the order of a handful per year industry-wide, and most movements of legacy NP collections (Sanofi/Fraunhofer, and academic/institute transfers generally) are donations or shared-resource agreements with no price, meaning there is neither a liquid buy side nor a liquid sell side. The ADC-payload/antifungal pivot is the only pocket with genuinely capitalised bidders, but the finalist offers zero verified transaction for a payload sourced from a legacy microbial library — that path is asserted ("my estimate", "$10-100M+"), not evidenced, and ADC buyers today pay for validated linker-payload-target packages with tox and conjugation data, which is several further rungs of capex, not the output of this rung.

verifiers.evidence:
Verified under the data-and-competition lens. Note: this turn's shared web-search budget was exhausted before my queries ran, so findings below rest on direct page fetches plus the finalist's own cited sources, not on fresh search.

1) THE ANSWER IS ALREADY IN A LEGIBLE PUBLIC FIELD (kills C4). BiG-FAM's own database page reports 1,225,071 BGCs pre-clustered into 29,955 gene cluster family models (BiG-SLiCE 1.0.0, T=900). That is exactly the Terranox "regulator wrote the answer into the status field" failure: cluster-family membership, and therefore "is this family novel / has it no known product", is a precomputed, free, queryable field over essentially every public genome. Add antiSMASH-DB and MIBiG and the novelty ranking the finalist proposes to build with ML is the public baseline every genome-mining group already queries. C4 drops from 2 to 1; the only surviving illegible-data element is freezer-metadata (which physical strain maps to which genome/notebook), which tells you which box to buy, not whether a compound works, and must be paid for with sequencing capex before any ranking is possible.

2) THE PROVING STEP DOMINATES, AND ML CANNOT TOUCH ITS FAILURE TERM (caps C3). Confirmed directly from PMC10727000: detection of ANY natural product from heterologously expressed BGCs was 11% (Gummerlich 2020, Saccharothrix espanaensis), 16% (Enghiad 2021), 24% (Libis 2022, 15/58 clusters), 32% (Ayikpoe 2022, 27/83 cloned BGCs). So 68-89% of attempts yield nothing detectable, and that failure is host/pathway/regulatory biology, not cluster selection. ML improves only the selection term. Realistic capex reduction is ~2x, not 10x; C3 drops from 3 to 2. The ratio inside the proposed rung is roughly 30/70 discovery/physical, the inverse of Terranox's 95/5, and the same shape as the geothermal-in-coal-mines counter-example.

3) THE SPACE IS OCCUPIED, INCLUDING THE ONE GOOD BUYER POCKET (caps C1/C2). The finalist's own rescue path was "pivot to ADC payloads, where there are capitalised bidders". Hexagon Bio's current site shows that pocket is already taken by an incumbent that did exactly this thesis and then climbed the ladder itself: Hexagon now presents as an oncology ADC company "discovering and developing novel ADC payload mechanisms" beyond topoisomerase and tubulin inhibitors, with lead program HEX-360 (next-generation HER2 ADC) and a newly formed clinical advisory board. So the escape hatch from the weak antibiotic buyer is not an empty rung — it is a rung whose occupant is already in clinical development with venture capital behind it. On the antibiotic side the finalist's own comparable stands: Basilea acquired Spexis's entire preclinical Gram-negative program for up to CHF 2M including milestones, so the "capitalised buyer" pays single-digit millions for a proven asset — nothing like the mine developer who is in for $40k/ha and collects $100k/ha. C2 drops from 3 to 2 because the step-up is neither immediate nor a market-observable repricing of the asset you own (the library does not reprice when one cluster works) and $5-20M of proving capex to a single validated scaffold eats the multiple.

4) WHAT SURVIVES. The purchase discount is real (Sanofi's ~110,000-strain, ~80,000-actinomycete collection transferred to Fraunhofer IME with no sale price; Ginkgo acquired Warp Drive Bio's platform with >135,000 strains and >4M predicted BGCs, terms undisclosed; Deinove licensed 400 of NAICONS' ~45,000 strains) and the base hit rate is genuinely low. But a cheap option on an asset whose novelty signal is public and precomputed, whose proving step costs $50-200k and 6-24 months per shot with 11-32% technical success, and whose best buyer pocket is already held by a funded clinical-stage incumbent, is not the Terranox shape. Revised total 10/25, down from 13/25.

verifiers.evidence:
LENS = RIGHT AND FRAME. (Note: this turn's shared WebSearch budget was exhausted before my first query, so all evidence below is from direct WebFetch of primary pages, four fetches.)

1) THE RIGHT IS NOT BUYABLE CHEAPLY AT SCALE FROM OWNERS WHO CANNOT READ THE DATA — the finalist's own two headline comparables prove the opposite. Fraunhofer IME's page on the ex-Sanofi collection (fetched): "over 110,000 strains," ~79% bacteria / 21% fungi, ~650,000 vials, ~20,000 freeze-dried and ~100,000 cryopreserved at -80/-140C, "the result of over 70 years of industrial work." Terms offered to third parties: the page states no ownership transfer, no exclusivity, no price — it only invites "contact the curator ... about collaboration or R&D." The Sanofi press page (fetched) confirms "over a hundred thousand different micro-organisms" shared, with no price, no provenance statement and no third-party commercial-rights statement. So the largest documented legacy actinomycete library on earth is not for sale, and its holder is a genome-mining institute that can read it. The second comparable is the same story: BioSpace (fetched) confirms Ginkgo acquired Warp Drive Bio's genome-mining platform — team, bioinformatics software, genomic database of >135,000 bacterial strains encoding >4M predicted BGCs — terms undisclosed, with Revolution Medicines retaining only its non-genome-mining programs. Both named mega-collections are held by parties (Fraunhofer, Ginkgo) whose core competence IS reading BGC data. The rubric's C4 purchase-discount leg requires owners who cannot read the data; what is left in that category is small, unsequenced, undocumented academic freezers — the opposite of scale.

2) ABS / NAGOYA IS A HARD TITLE DEFECT, NOT A DILIGENCE FOOTNOTE. Fraunhofer's biobank page (fetched) advertises as a feature: "All strains comply with access and benefit-sharing (ABS) regulations in accordance with the Nagoya Protocol." That compliance is a marketed scarcity, which means the default state of a legacy library is NOT compliant. Sub-collections are explicitly Marine (seaweed, invertebrates, coral reefs, sediments), Arthropod gut, Soil — i.e. wild-collected material from identifiable countries of origin. Commercialising an organism without documented prior informed consent and mutually agreed terms exposes the product to country-of-origin benefit-sharing claims, and provenance must be established per strain across 70 years of freezer metadata. Contrast the Terranox title: a mineral right sits in a public registry with a title chain and a standard assignment. Here there is no registry, no clean transfer instrument, and the encumbrance attaches to the organism's origin forever. "Buy the right cheaply and legally at scale" fails on legally and at scale.

3) THE PHYSICAL/PROVING STEP DOMINATES — THIS IS THE GEOTHERMAL-IN-COAL-MINES FAILURE MODE, CONFIRMED BY THE FINALIST'S OWN SOURCE. PMC10727000 (fetched directly): heterologous-expression natural-product detection rates of 11% (Gummerlich 2020), 16% (Enghiad 2021, CAPTURE), 24% (Libis 2022), 32% (Ayikpoe 2022); 50 studies from 2018 to mid-2023 yielded "at least 63 new natural product families." Decisively for this lens, the review names the bottlenecks and they are NOT cluster selection: "insufficient gene expression" is called a "major hurdle" (weak transcription, codon bias, promoter refactoring needed, codon optimisation "not always successful"), plus host relatedness, missing precursors, protein folding, product toxicity and purification. Cluster-boundary prediction is only one item on that list. So the term ML can move (which cluster to try) is a minority of the failure mass, while the dominant terms are per-cluster wet biology at ~$50-200k and 6-24 months. There is no commoditised, fixed-price, known-yield "prove one cluster" service analogous to renting a drill rig; every cluster is a bespoke research program. Terranox's 95-5 inverts here to roughly 30-70 at best.

4) NO IMMEDIATE, MARKET-OBSERVABLE REPRICING. Nothing reprices the asset you own on a hit: there is no registry, no public assay, no third party that marks the library up because one cluster expressed. A hit produces a compound you must then develop, and the library's other 109,999 strains are worth exactly what they were the day before. Terranox's 10^4 is a repricing of the owned asset at the moment of the hit; this is not that.

5) HARD EXCLUSIONS: honestly, none hit. It is not mineral/oil/gas/helium/hydrogen/lithium-brine/geothermal/groundwater exploration or drilling; it is not Terranox; the company owns the physical library and realises the value itself, so it is not "sell a service to incumbents"; and it is not on the named-killed list. The finalist fails on the merits of C1 and C4, not on an exclusion — I am not inflating the refutation by claiming one.

SCORE CHANGES: C1 2->1 (discovery is ~25-35% of the rung at best and the review's bottleneck list confirms the proving step is bespoke biology, not a trivial abstracted step; and no buyer pays a defined price for the proven unit). C2 3->2 (no immediate repricing of the owned asset; $5-20M of proving capex consumed before any proven scaffold exists, so net multiple falls to single digits). C3 3->2 (the low base rate is real and is this candidate's one genuine strength, but the lever is capped well below 10x because the 68-89% failure mass is expression/host/precursor/toxicity biology that ranking cannot touch). C4 2->1 (the novelty answer is precomputed and published by antiSMASH-DB/MIBiG/BiG-FAM — the regulator wrote it into the status field — and under this lens the purchase-discount leg also collapses: the clean big libraries are held by Fraunhofer and Ginkgo, who can read them, and the rest carry ABS defects). C5 3->2 (ladder is real but rung two is a $50-200M, 8-year, different-capability commitment with no self-funding cash from rung one). Revised total 8/25.
verifiers.killer: The right is not buyable: both headline legacy libraries are already held by parties who can read the data (Sanofi's 110,000 strains went to Fraunhofer IME, which offers only "collaboration or R&D" with no ownership transfer, no exclusivity and no price; Warp Drive's 135,000-strain, 4M-BGC genome-mining asset went to Ginkgo), what remains carries per-strain Nagoya/ABS title defects that Fraunhofer markets compliance with precisely because it is scarce — and the proving step inside the frame is the opposite of trivial, with the finalist's own source (PMC10727000) putting heterologous-expression detection at 11-32% and naming "insufficient gene expression," host biology, missing precursors, toxicity and purification as the major hurdles rather than cluster selection, i.e. the bespoke plant is harder than finding the mine.

https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC10727000/ — fetched: heterologous-expression natural-product detection 11% (Gummerlich 2020), 16% (Enghiad 2021 CAPTURE), 24% (Libis 2022), 32% (Ayikpoe 2022); >=63 new NP families from 50 studies 2018-mid-2023; bottlenecks named as 'insufficient gene expression' ('major hurdle'), weak transcription, codon bias, promoter refactoring, host relatedness, missing precursors, protein folding, product toxicity, purification — cluster selection is only one of several

https://www.biospace.com/article/releases/ginkgo-bioworks-acquires-warp-drive-bio-s-genome-mining-platform-for-discovery-and-development-of-novel-classes-of-antibiotics — fetched: Ginkgo acquired Warp Drive Bio's genome-mining platform (team, bioinformatics software, database of >135,000 bacterial strains, >4M predicted BGCs); terms undisclosed; Revolution Medicines retains only its non-genome-mining programs

verified.name: Hand Match / Marginalia: unrecognised historic letters and annotated books
verified.one_line: Buy bulk estate letters, unattributed autographs and early printed books with unidentified marginalia; handwriting-recognition ML matched against digitised archives identifies famous writers or readers; paleographer sign-off proves association copies.
verified.unproven_right: Title to estate ephemera lots or books catalogued with 'unidentified hand', $50-5k.
verified.proving_step: OCR and writer-ID embeddings, paper/ink checks and expert letter; physically only photography.
verified.proven_buyer: Christie's/Sotheby's book departments, Bonhams, RR Auction, Folger, Huntington, Beinecke, Morgan, British Library, Peter Harrington.
verified.public_data: Founders Online, Darwin/Newton/Jefferson papers, Library of Congress manuscripts, Transkribus corpora, EEBO, Folger digital, Annotated Books Online, eBay/ABE/ILAB listings.
verified.rough_step_up: ~10^2-10^4x; very low hit rate, thin market.
verified.frame: Rung = buy an "unidentified hand" lot or book, attribute the hand, then consign or sell it as an association copy or autograph. Inside that rung, discovery and attribution are about 95% of the work, and the physical step (photography, plus paper and ink checks) is trivial. That part passes. The problem is that a hit counts as proven only when a recognised paleographer or scholar endorses it and the provenance holds up. The ML match on its own does not prove anything. Example: Milton's First Folio (Free Library of Philadelphia, 2019) was attributed by Scott-Warren on purely paleographical grounds, and it is still described as "not exactly peer reviewed". A 2022 Raleigh-annotated book went to auction only "tentatively", with a reserve to match. Buyers exist (auction houses, the Folger, the Beinecke, dealers), but they are discretionary collectors and institutions with thin budgets, not a developer with a fixed economic use for the asset.
verified.step_up: Unproven: a $50-5k estate lot or book catalogued as "unidentified hand" (candidate figure, plausible). Proven comparables: an Edgar Allan Poe letter (a plea for $40) sold for $125,125 in 2020 (Inquirer). A Kerouac letter to Robert Lax sold for $11,000. Tolkien letters went for $2.7k-13k each in 2018 (Locus). A John Steinbeck letter sold for $32k at RR Auction. Taking a $50-500 lot to $10k-125k gives roughly 10^2-10^3x. A Milton- or Shakespeare-class association copy would be over 10^4x, but those are once a decade. Most real hits are minor figures at about 3-30x.
verified.hit_rate_capex: I found no published base rate. My estimate is well under 0.1% of "unidentified hand" lots belonging to anyone with market value, and under 0.01% for a famous writer. The cost per attempt is already low: buying a $50-500 lot plus photography. The lever is therefore not "10x cheaper drills". It is triage across inventory, and that is limited by how many lots exist and by expert sign-off time ($500-5k per opinion, my estimate), not by discovery capex. The lever exists, but the money it saves is small.
verified.data: Reference corpora are public and only partly machine-readable: Founders Online, the Darwin, Newton and Jefferson papers, LOC manuscripts, Transkribus, Annotated Books Online. Writer-ID ML is still a research topic: Siamese nets attributing letters to Potanin (2025), and a WACV 2024 paper noting that paleography has "no agreed-upon methodology". Is the outcome already written in a legible field? For letters, partly yes: famous letters are usually signed, so the signature is the field, and specialist dealers check anything signed. Unsigned marginalia is where the real illegibility edge lies. That edge is real but narrow, because heavily collected readers (Dee, Jonson, Harvey, Coleridge) are already tracked by specialists and by Annotated Books Online.
verified.right_bought: Yes. Title is bought outright and cheaply at estate sales, eBay, ABE and regional auctions, from sellers who cannot read the hands. Good on this criterion. Two risks. First, if a famous attribution is publicised, the consignor or the family estate may contest the sale or the copyright (the Cassady "Joan Anderson" letter sale was suspended in 2014 over ownership claims). Second, copyright in unpublished letters usually stays with the writer's estate, which limits publication value.
verified.buyer: Christie's and Sotheby's book departments, Bonhams, RR Auction, Peter Harrington, and research libraries (Folger, Huntington, Beinecke, Morgan, British Library). They are capitalised but discretionary. I found no published total for the rare book and manuscript auction market; my estimate is about $1-2B a year worldwide, and the rare book trade is described as "driven by the whims of a small number of rich individuals" (Cambridge, Economics of the Manuscript and Rare Book Trade).
verified.ladder: Weak. The rungs above are dealer, then auction house, then authentication service or archive or estate management. Even owning the whole chain puts you in a market of low single-digit billions a year. There is no path to a very large company, and supply of truly famous unrecognised hands cannot be scaled up.
verified.fatal_flaw: Value at the top comes from expert and scholarly consensus plus provenance, not from the ML match, and the supply of valuable unrecognised hands is tiny and fixed. The result is a boutique dealer with a few lucky finds a year in a market of about $1-2B a year (estimate), with no ladder to a large company.

(1) Poe letter, $125,125 at RR Auction on 7 Oct 2020 (Inquirer). This was an already-known letter with traced provenance: a seller in France about 15 years earlier, and an auction the year before. It was never unrecognised, and no earlier sale price is given. It is a price for a known item, not a step-up from unknown to proven.
(2) Steinbeck letter, $32,426 including buyer's premium at RR Auction (Journal of Antiques). Authorship was established, there is no discovery story, and no price before identification is given.
(3) Milton First Folio (Cambridge). It is held by the Free Library of Philadelphia, and no sale happened before or after the attribution. Scott-Warren's attribution was put forward "tentatively", rests on letterforms (the 'h' foot, the 'R'), and needs "further work". The proving step yielded scholarly reputation, not a transaction.
(4) Raleigh annotated book (FineBooks). The page returned 403, so it is unverified; the finalist itself says it went to sale only "tentatively".
(5) Kerouac at $11k and Tolkien at $2.7k-13k (Locus) are also known, signed letters with established attribution, not unrecognised hands.
The finalist's 10^2-10^4x step-up comes from pairing a hypothetical $50-500 "unidentified hand" lot with the price of an unrelated, already-signed famous letter. None of the sources documents a single bought-unidentified, then attributed, then sold transaction with both prices.
On the buyer: auction houses (Christie's, Sotheby's, Bonhams, RR) take items on consignment. They do not buy at once. A sale takes months and the seller pays roughly 10-25% commission (my estimate from general knowledge). Institutional buyers (Folger, Beinecke, Morgan, British Library) buy rarely, on small acquisition budgets, and only with expert consensus. Contested attributions trade at deep discounts or do not sell.
On market size: there is no published total. The finalist's guess of $1-2B a year for the whole rare book and manuscript market is not verified. The share made up of newly attributed unsigned hands is plausibly a handful of meaningful deals a year (my estimate).
Signed letters of famous people are already legible: the signature is the status field. That collapses the ML edge to unsigned marginalia, where proof depends on paleographers and the step-up is unproven. The realistic step-up for the minor figures that make up most hits is about 3-30x, which is below the 30x refutation threshold.
verifiers.killer: None of the cited comparables is an unrecognised-to-proven transaction. Every price (Poe $125k, Steinbeck $32k, Kerouac $11k, Tolkien up to $13k) is for an already-signed, already-attributed letter, and the flagship attribution (Milton's First Folio) led to no sale at all. The claimed 10^2-10^4x step-up is an assumption that splices together two unrelated prices. The "buyer" is a consignment auction (months of delay, commission, and a sale only if scholars agree), not a capitalised buyer who pays at once. Realistic hits on minor or unsigned hands land around 3-30x.
