deep.name: Orphan Patent Evidence-of-Use (bankrupt estates, FCC/teardown proof; incl. semiconductor, photonics, mature-node)
deep.memo:
## Orphan Patent Evidence-of-Use: feasibility memo

**Search limit:** the shared WebSearch budget for this turn was already used up, so nothing here comes from a fresh search. Figures come from three things: the 2025 Richardson Oliver (RO) Patent Market Report PDF, which I downloaded and read in full; the USPTO PTAB FY26 Q3 PDF, which I parsed; and first-party pages fetched directly. Anything else is marked as an estimate.

### Frame of reference
The rung is: own an orphan US patent that nobody has read, prove it reads on a product that is shipping now, and sell it as an asset with evidence-of-use (EoU) attached. Inside that rung, discovery is about 85% of the work (estimate): picking the right patent out of thousands and mapping its claims onto FCC internal photos, teardowns or driver code. The physical step is desk work, plus the occasional teardown at roughly $5-20k (estimate). This frame does exist. Its weakness is that the output is an opinion, not a proof. The uncertain, costly step of licensing or litigation still sits with the buyer. This is the geothermal problem moved up one rung.

### Step-up ratio
- **Unproven price:** about $0 for lapse-bound patents. The owner simply pays nothing and lets the patent die. The only cost is the maintenance fee: $8,280 large entity or $3,312 small entity at 11.5 years, plus a $540 grace-period surcharge ([USPTO fees](https://www.uspto.gov/learning-and-resources/fees-and-payment/uspto-fee-schedule)). Estate and assignment-for-benefit-of-creditors (ABC) lots go for about $2-30k per asset (estimate, not verified).
- **Proven price:** the median asking price of *sold* assets was $63k in 2022, $33k in 2023 and $95k in 2024. Per US-issued patent it was $83k, $75k and $141k. Closing discounts run from 0% to 75% or more ([RO 2025](https://www.richardsonoliver.com/publications/the-2025-richardson-oliver-patent-market-report), PDF Table 3).
- **Premium from EoU:** +32% to +108% across five years, which is a 1.3-2.1x step-up from the proving step alone (same source).
- **Overall step-up:** about 3-30x from a paid estate lot. It only reaches about 10-100x when you start from a near-free lapse-bound patent, and those are adversely selected (see below). Terranox's step-up is 10^4.
- **Transactions per year:** the whole brokered market was **$158M** in 2024, flat with 2022 and 2023. 1,611 packages were listed, the median package held 2 assets, brokers handled 87% of sales, and about 30% of packages eventually sell (RO 2025).

### Hit rate and proving capex, today and with ML
- **Hit rate today:** about 1-5% of random orphan patents read on a live product with enough term left and damages worth chasing (estimate).
- **Cost per hit today:** a manual chart costs about $3-15k (estimate), so each hit costs roughly $100k-$1M.
- **With ML:** ML triage could cut that cost 5-20x. That would be a real lever, but it is not proprietary:
  - Patlytics advertises "Crawl for evidence of use across public sources" and "Citation-backed claim charts". It reports savings of "$1,000–$5,000 minimum" per detection report, has a $40M Series B, and lists Quinn Emanuel and Panasonic IP among its customers ([patlytics.ai](https://www.patlytics.ai/)).
  - RO says sellers can now produce "high-grade EOUs at relatively low costs" (RO 2025).
- **PTAB risk is lower than the finalist assumed:**
  - Across 1,096 petitions, 50% were denied institution and only 18% ended with all claims unpatentable.
  - 47% of *instituted* claims were found unpatentable ([USPTO FY26Q3](https://www.uspto.gov/sites/default/files/documents/TrialsOutcomeRoundupFY26Q3.pdf)).

### Data source
- **Datasets:** USPTO full text, assignments, maintenance-fee events and PTAB data (public bulk data). FCC Equipment Authorization internal photos ([fcc.gov/oet/ea/fccid](https://www.fcc.gov/oet/ea/fccid)). PACER section 363 sale schedules. Linux driver source, IEDM papers and die-shot archives.
- **Why it is illegible:** the evidence is spread across images, code and scanned schedules.
- **Is the outcome summarised anywhere?** Whether a patent reads on a product is not written in any legible field, so this part passes. The proxies are, though: citations, family size, maintenance payments and litigation history. Commercial patent-value scores (PatentSight, Ocean Tomo, RPX) already rank on them (from memory). TechInsights already covers the products of large companies (from memory).

### How the right is bought
- **Legal mechanics:** patents can be assigned outright (35 USC 261), and a section 363 sale passes clean title. The sources are trustees, ABC assignees and owners about to let a patent lapse.
- **Competition for estates:** any estate with visible value is brokered competitively. Nortel went from a $900M stalking-horse bid to $4.5B (from memory). That leaves only the long tail cheap, and in the long tail the discount and the hit rate move in opposite directions.
- **Limits on lapse-bound patents:** you must buy before the 6-month grace period ends. Revival under 37 CFR 1.378 requires an "unintentional" delay, and intervening rights under 35 USC 41(c) protect anyone who started using the invention during the lapse.
- **Limits on damages:** marking (35 USC 287) and the six-year look-back (35 USC 286) cut what an orphan patent can recover.

### Capitalised buyer
- **Who buys:** operating companies bought 37-90% of sold assets in 2020-24, and NPEs bought 13-50%. NPEs show only 2% so far in 2024, likely understated because of recording lag. Defensive aggregators are "increasingly selective" (RO 2025).
- **How buyers behave:** RO calls the market "advantageous to buyers", with "rarely competing buyers".
- **Why this is not a mine developer:** buyers cannot develop the asset at a known cost and payoff, so they discount the price.

### Integration ladder above
1. Buy and chart patents.
2. Sell them to aggregators.
3. License them directly.
4. Run your own assertion campaigns.
5. Fund litigation, yours and others'.
6. Become an IP fund or defensive pool.

The ceiling is a $1-5B outcome of the Acacia, Intellectual Ventures or RPX kind (from memory). Patent monetisation tops out at a few billion dollars a year, and anti-NPE policy creates friction. There is no trillion-dollar path.

### Who else does this
- **Funded tooling for the proving step:** Patlytics, plus IPRally and Amplified (from memory).
- **People who market estates:** Hilco Streambank, Tangible IP and ICAP Ocean Tomo (from memory).
- **Buyers of exactly this inventory:** Dominion Harbor, IP Edge, Atlantic IP, Acacia, Sisvel, Burford and Fortress.

### Smallest feasibility test (2 weeks)
1. Pull every US patent from the USPTO maintenance-fee events data that has entered the grace period of its 11.5-year fee and belongs to a dissolved or bankrupt assignee. That should be several hundred patents (estimate).
2. Triage them with an off-the-shelf EoU tool and keep the top 10.
3. Have an attorney spot-check those 10.
4. Shop them blind to 5 brokers or buyers for indicative bids.

**Pass:** at least 2 of the 10 draw bids of $75k or more each, and the owners agree to assign for under $5k. **Fail:** bids fall in the 1.3-2.1x EoU band, or nobody bids at all. That would show the asset gets its price from the buyer's litigation budget, not from discovery.

### Verdict
**Does not pass the rubric. Revised total: about 10-11 out of 25.** The 80%+ discovery frame is real and the right can be bought. But the proving step adds only a 1.3-2.1x premium according to RO's measured data, the market totals $158M a year with rarely competing buyers, and the ML lever is already sold off the shelf. The ladder also caps at a few billion dollars. At best this is a cash-flow side business that buys lapse-bound patents for the cost of the maintenance fee; it is not a Terranox analogue. The test above settles that within 2 weeks.

Working files: /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-nuketime/2305f78e-f084-5801-ab25-e340938a9d29/scratchpad/ro/r.txt (the RO 2025 report as text) and /tmp/claude-0/-home-user-nuketime/2305f78e-f084-5801-ab25-e340938a9d29/scratchpad/ptab/p.pdf (the USPTO PTAB FY26 Q3 report).

deep.name: Powered-Land Options: farmland options proven by utility load studies
deep.memo:
## Powered-Land Options: feasibility memo

**Search note:** the shared WebSearch budget (200 calls per turn) was used up before this run, so no searches ran. I fetched the primary pages listed below directly. Any figure without a URL is marked as an estimate or as recalled from memory. A follow-up message can resume searching.

### Frame of reference
The proposed rung: option farmland near a substation, prove headroom with a utility large-load study or will-serve letter, then sell "powered land." Discovery (finding headroom) is about 30-40% of this rung (estimate). The rest is not discovery:
- **Site control.** Texas SB6 requires an ownership interest or lease. [SB6 text, s.37.0561(g)](https://capitol.texas.gov/tlodocs/89R/billtext/html/SB00006F.htm)
- **$/MW financial security or CIAC** for transmission ([SB6 s.37.0561(h)](https://capitol.texas.gov/tlodocs/89R/billtext/html/SB00006F.htm)), plus multi-year minimum bills.
- **Rezoning, water and fiber.**

CBRE reports that utilities are asking developers to "contribute toward capital costs for generation and transmission" ([CBRE H1 2025](https://www.cbre.com/insights/reports/north-america-data-center-trends-h1-2025)). The physical and capital step dominates. This matches the geothermal-in-coal-mines counter-example.

### Step-up ratio
- **Unproven:** US cropland averages $5,830/acre ([USDA NASS 2025](https://www.nass.usda.gov/Publications/Todays_Reports/reports/land0825.pdf)). Options run $50-300/acre/yr (candidate's figure, unverified).
- **Proven:**
  - NoVA data-center land at about $1-3M/acre (recalled, unverified).
  - Secondary-market hyperscaler farmland buys at about $30-300k/acre (recalled, unverified).
  - Prince William Digital Gateway contracts at about $0.5-1M/acre against roughly $20-50k/acre before. That jump came from county rezoning, not a load study (recalled; the Wikipedia page 404'd).
- **What a study alone earns:** about 2-5x (estimate), because buyers price firm, contracted MW. CBRE says buyers want power "within 18 to 36 months" and increasingly need 200 MW or more ([CBRE](https://www.cbre.com/insights/reports/north-america-data-center-trends-h1-2025)).
- **The headline 10^3x is not an asset step-up.** It compares an annual option fee with a fee-simple price.
- **Transactions/yr:** a few hundred large US data-center land deals a year (estimate).

### Hit rate and proving capex today and with ML
- **Cost per attempt:** at least $100k study fee per site for loads of 75 MW and up in Texas ([SB6 s.37.0561(f)](https://capitol.texas.gov/tlodocs/89R/billtext/html/SB00006F.htm)). Candidate's range is $50-250k.
- **Base hit rate:** 15-30% (estimate), so ML's lever is capped at about 3-6x.
- **Speculation is high.** Near Homer City, 181 of 233 interconnection requests (78%) were withdrawn ([LandGate](https://www.landgate.com/news/ferc-rejected-pjm-s-large-load-plan)). AEP Ohio's queue reportedly fell from about 30 GW to about 13 GW after its tariff (recalled, unverified).
- **Capex does not bind.** About $100k per attempt is small against a $10-100M exit. ML would not change the economics by 10x.

### Data source
- **Datasets:** FERC Form 715 (CEII-gated), RTO expansion plans, EIA-860, IRPs, PUC large-load dockets, HIFLD substations, queue withdrawals.
- **The signal is already legible.** LandGate sells offtake capacity for "98%" of US substations (">84K mapped"), with parcel search by distance and capacity, and a PowerLeads landowner marketplace ([LandGate](https://www.landgate.com/energy-markets/data-centers)).
- **The true outcome is not in any dataset.** Firm capacity is created by the utility study plus ESA collateral.
- **Prior hunt:** ML added only about +0.004 AUC over simple screening.
- **C4 fails.**

### How the right is bought
Options or fee purchases come from farmers through standard option-to-purchase agreements, with recording of a memorandum of option. The purchase discount is real, unlike brownfields.

The discount is eroding:
- LandGate's marketplace lists ">100MM acres" ([LandGate](https://www.landgate.com/energy-markets/data-centers)), which narrows the owner's information gap.
- Farmers near substations increasingly ask for data-center-contingent strike prices (estimate).

Capacity does not run with the land. It attaches to whoever signs the service agreement and posts security:
- AEP Ohio: 85% minimum bill for up to 12 years.
- Ameren Missouri: two years of minimum bills posted upfront.
- Evergy Kansas: 80% minimum bill for 12 years.

Source for all three: [LandGate tariff survey](https://www.landgate.com/news/large-load-tariffs-are-redrawing-the-site-selection-map). Texas SB6 also forces disclosure of duplicate requests elsewhere in the state ([s.37.0561(d)](https://capitol.texas.gov/tlodocs/89R/billtext/html/SB00006F.htm)).

### Capitalised buyer
Hyperscalers (Microsoft, Meta, Google, AWS), colos (QTS, Vantage, Stack, Aligned) and powered-land funds. Primary-market vacancy is a record-low 1.6% ([CBRE](https://www.cbre.com/insights/reports/north-america-data-center-trends-h1-2025)). The buyer is real and deep-pocketed, but it buys contracted, energizable MW, not studies.

### Integration ladder above
1. Options
2. Study
3. ESA/collateral
4. Entitlements
5. Powered shell
6. Own substation or behind-the-meter generation
7. Campus developer or operator

Cloverleaf is already at rungs 5-6: Project Red Granite covers up to 1,900 acres next to 345 kV lines, targets 3.5 GW by 2030, and expected zoning by May 2025 ([Cloverleaf](https://www.cloverleafinfra.com/)). The trillion-dollar path exists (site, then power, then compute), but every rung is capital-heavy, not discovery-heavy.

### Who else does this
- **Tract:** powered-land developer (its site returned empty; recalled).
- **Cloverleaf Infrastructure** ([site](https://www.cloverleafinfra.com/)).
- **EdgeCore and Hunt** (recalled).
- **LandGate:** data plus landowner marketplace ([site](https://www.landgate.com/energy-markets/data-centers)).
- **Others:** land brokers and powerflow consultancies.
- **Regulators are tightening:** 29 large-load tariffs approved in 2025, against 14 in the prior seven years combined ([LandGate](https://www.landgate.com/news/large-load-tariffs-are-redrawing-the-site-selection-map)). FERC kept PJM's 50 MW large-load registry on Oct 9, 2026 ([LandGate](https://www.landgate.com/news/ferc-rejected-pjm-s-large-load-plan)).

### Smallest feasibility test (2 weeks)
Pull 20-30 recent hyperscaler or colo farmland purchases in Ohio, Indiana, Georgia and Texas from county deed records. For each, record:
- price per acre against the prior ag sale;
- whether a utility study or will-serve letter existed before the sale, or a rezoning or ESA came first (PUC dockets, county minutes);
- LandGate's capacity score for the parcel before the sale.

Then ask 5 powered-land brokers or funds to quote the same site three ways: study-only, ESA-backed, and energized.

**Decision rule:**
- **Kill** if the price jump tracks rezoning or ESA timing rather than study timing, or if study-only sites quote under 5x ag value, or if LandGate already flagged the winning parcels.
- **Survive** only if study-only sites sell at 30x or more and the winning parcels were not visible in LandGate.

### Verdict
**Kill.** The farmland purchase discount is real and the ladder is large, but the rung fails the 80%-discovery frame:
- Capacity belongs to whoever posts collateral and signs the ESA, not to the parcel or to whoever reads grid data first ([SB6](https://capitol.texas.gov/tlodocs/89R/billtext/html/SB00006F.htm), [tariff survey](https://www.landgate.com/news/large-load-tariffs-are-redrawing-the-site-selection-map)).
- Headroom data is already sold as a legible field ([LandGate](https://www.landgate.com/energy-markets/data-centers)).
- A study-only step-up is about 2-5x (estimate).
- The ML lever is at most 3-6x, on capex that is not the binding constraint.

Revised scores: C1 1, C2 2, C3 2, C4 1, C5 4. Total about 10-11 of 25. This is not worth a YC slot as a Terranox analogue. The 2-week deed-record test above would settle it cheaply if anyone wants a confirmatory kill.

deep.name: Continuation Forge: live patent families with pending continuations
deep.memo:
## Continuation Forge: feasibility memo

*Note: the shared WebSearch budget was used up before this run, so no new searches could be made. Numbers marked [ROI25] come from the primary report, which I downloaded and parsed this run: 2025 Richardson Oliver Patent Market Report, https://static1.squarespace.com/static/62e409548ddf9a45093621ec/t/691788dcafe85415ced5eb9a/1763150044519/The+2025+Richardson+Oliver+Patent+Market+-+The+Brokered+Patent+Market+Report+in+2024+-+A+Smarter%2C+Sharper+Patent+Market+-+IAM+Media+-+20250917.pdf. USPTO fees come from https://www.uspto.gov/learning-and-resources/fees-and-payment/uspto-fee-schedule. Everything else is labelled as prior knowledge or an estimate.*

### Frame of reference
The rung is: buy a family that still has a pending continuation, get a claim allowed that reads on a product shipping today, and sell the asset with an evidence-of-use (EoU) chart. The physical step is legal prosecution, which is cheap and can be outsourced. That passes the geothermal-in-coal-mine test. Discovery is not 80%+ of the rung, though. I estimate that finding spec support and a target product is about 50-65% of the work. The rest is written-description risk at the examiner (Ariad 2010), validity risk the buyer will price in (IPR, Alice 101), and a slow, buyer-controlled sale. The proof does not settle value the way a drill core does. The buyer is still pricing years of litigation.

### Step-up ratio
- **Unproven price:** a small-inventor or distressed family costs about $10-50k (estimate). For comparison, the median asking price of assets that actually sold in 2023 was only $33k, and $95k in 2024 [ROI25].
- **Proven price:** the median ask is $325k per family across all listings and $158k per family that sold [ROI25]. Packages with EoU command a 32-108% premium [ROI25]. Closing discounts from asking run 0-75%+ [ROI25]. A rough proven, EoU-backed close is $325k × 1.54 × 0.65 ≈ $325k (estimate). Deals above $1M per asset happen but are rare [ROI25].
- **Ratio:** about 5-30x on purchase price, and about 3-15x on all-in cost. That is two to three orders of magnitude short of 10^3-10^4.
- **Transactions per year:** the whole brokered market was $158M in 2024, flat against 2022 and 2023. 1,611 packages were listed, with a median of 2 assets each [ROI25]. Only 20-30% of listings sell, and it takes years: 2019 listings have only now reached 30% [ROI25]. My estimate is about 300-500 sales a year. The report says there are "rarely competing buyers" [ROI25].

### Hit rate and proving capex today and with ML
- **Prosecution cost:** small-entity filing, search and exam fees total about $800, plus a $516 issue fee. Track One costs $1,806 for a small entity [USPTO]. Attorney fees add about $5-40k (estimate). Since 2025, continuations filed more than 6 years after the priority date also carry a surcharge (prior knowledge).
- **All-in per shot:** about $20-100k (estimate).
- **Base rate:** allowance itself is high, at roughly 70-90% (estimate). The real hit is an allowed claim that reads on a product and actually sells. Base sell-through is about 30% even for packages that are already marketed [ROI25], and only 21% of packages include an EoU today [ROI25]. My estimate of the true hit rate (allowed, reads on a product, sells for 10x or more) is about 5-15%. That caps the ML lever at roughly 7-20x in theory. In practice, ML improves only the matching step, not validity or buyer demand, so the realistic gain is about 2-4x (estimate).

### Data source
The sources are USPTO Patent Center file wrappers, USPTO bulk full text, PatentsView, the USPTO assignment database, PACER section 363 sale schedules, FCC equipment authorisation photos, iFixit and TechInsights teardowns, product manuals, and GitHub. All are public.

Most of this data is legible. Pending-continuation status is a structured status field, and specs are full text. The teardown side is less legible, but TechInsights sells exactly that mapping, and Patlytics already advertises "crawl for evidence of use across public sources" with citation-backed claim charts (patlytics.ai, fetched by an earlier verifier). The outcome is effectively summarised already: brokers list "open continuations" as a standard quality factor [ROI25].

### How the right is bought
Patents and pending applications are assignable under 35 USC 261, and assignments are recorded with the USPTO. Bankruptcy estates sell them under 11 USC 363. Drafting continuation claims to cover a competitor's product you already know about is lawful (Kingsdown v. Hollister, 1988). The limits are written-description support and prosecution laches (Hyatt v. Hirshfeld, 2021).

The cheap-purchase thesis is weak. Brokers handle 87% of sold packages [ROI25], and they price open continuations in. A live continuation is also a wasting asset: distressed owners often let it lapse before anyone can buy it (prior knowledge).

### Capitalised buyer
From 2020 to 2024, operating companies bought 15-40% of packages, NPEs 11-50%, and defensive aggregators 20-40% [ROI25]. Litigation funders also buy (Burford, Fortress; prior knowledge). These buyers are real, but they set the price; they are not price-takers. Sold packages have a 22% litigation rate [ROI25], which shows that the value is realised through litigation.

### Integration ladder above
1. Prosecute and sell (this rung).
2. License directly.
3. Self-fund assertion.
4. Run a portfolio licensing programme, at Acacia or IV scale.

The ceiling is a few billion dollars at most: IV raised about $6B, and Acacia is worth under $1B (both prior knowledge). The ladder never connects to making products, so there is no trillion-dollar path.

### Who else does this
- **Aggregators and NPEs:** IP Edge, Dominion Harbor, Acacia and IV, all of which run continuation practice on acquired families (prior knowledge).
- **Defensive aggregators:** RPX and AST.
- **Brokers:** brokers who screen for open continuations, such as Tangible IP and Iceberg.
- **Claim-charting tools:** Patlytics, Solve Intelligence and IPRally commoditise the matching step.

### Smallest feasibility test (2 weeks)
1. Pull about 300 small-entity US families with a pending continuation from PatentsView and Patent Center bulk data.
2. Run LLM spec-to-product matching against FCC photos and manuals.
3. Hand-build 5 EoU charts for proposed continuation claims.
4. Get firm purchase quotes from 5 owners or trustees.
5. Show the 5 charts under NDA to 3 buyers (RPX or AST, one NPE such as IP Edge, one funder) and ask for indicative bids conditional on allowance.

**Kill criterion:** median bid divided by (quote + estimated prosecution cost) is below 20x, or owners quote above $50k because a broker is already involved. Based on the ROI25 figures, I expect the test to kill the idea.

### Verdict
**Fails the rubric.** The frame is real and the physical step is trivial, but the step-up is about 3-30x, not 10^3-10^4. The signal is legible and already priced by brokers. Incumbents already run this exact playbook, and the ladder tops out as an NPE.

Scores: C1 2, C2 2, C3 2, C4 1, C5 2, **total 9/25.** Not a lead candidate for the YC memo. Its one useful lesson is that a frame where the physical step is a cheap legal action does pass the geothermal test, so look for a ladder where that kind of legal or proving step sits in front of a buyer that pays at once.
